1, 2006##******************************************************************************* āḍñūṣṭ ṇūṃBEṛīṇṅ FṛOṃ āFṭEṛ 232 [1a] Oṃ! Homage to Mahābhairava, to the deities of the directions and so forth, and to the gurus.
On the delightful peak of Jyotiḥstha, variegated with various minerals,
filled with diverse trees and creepers, and crowded with many sages.
Crowded with perfected Vidyādharas and frequented by the Gaṇas and Pramathas,
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the lords of the gods— all of them assembled there.
Seeing Bhairava joyful, Ambikā went forth to meet him:
"You are indeed the mother of this world; you alone are my refuge. (1.3)
O you of great renown, you are the savior of those terrified by the fear of saṃsāra;
so too are the ṛṣis, the gandharvas, the gaṇas, the vidyādharas, and the rest.
Terrified in this wheel of saṃsāra and fearing old age and death, other living beings as well—being afflicted with suffering—have come to you alone for refuge. (1.5)
Ask Śaṅkara, the Lord of the gods of gods, the benefactor of the world,
who is the very essence of the knowledge of true reality and who bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having heard their words— by which knowledge they are liberated and by which satisfaction they attain success— the Goddess spoke these words.
Having praised the Lord Maheśāna with hymns that embody the true nature of reality—
she who is the Mother, the source of creation, Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Śakti, and likewise Ambikā.
Raudrī is the power who sustains the universe; such is her function and her nature as reality. Thus the Supreme Goddess is to be praised with hymns of praise. (1.9)

I bow to that Lord, the master of all prosperity, who is partless yet possesses all portions, whose power is the celebrated and virtuous activity of Vāmā and Jyeṣṭhā, and from whose station arises the most stable and fully fashioned entire collection of the creation of the principles (*tattva*s) and so forth.
Śrīkaṇṭha is beyond all states of being, considered to be devoid of the three guṇas, free from tamas, and possessed of pure sattva.
I have heard the secret of Rudra, which is hidden from the common view;
the paths of the Left and the Right, as well as the Yāmala traditions in their many forms.
And the Siddhāntas, O Lord of the Gods, consist of ten and eighteen divisions;
through the classification of lakṣas and koṭis, they number many millions.
In the *Siddhayogeśvarītantra*, which extends over a hundred million verses, this [teaching] has emerged from two sūtras within the root-tantra, the great sūtra. (1.13)
Among those, one has been known by me as arising from the ocean of wombs;
I have not heard the supreme *Tantrasadbhāva*, which I now desire to hear.
Tantric conduct, ritual action, knowledge, and yoga are also manifold; yet, O Lord, there is the seeded practice through concentration and the seedless practice which is distinct. (1.15)
Through the union of manifold means, there is sacrifice directed toward the Self;
[the Self] abides in Nāda, is established in Bindu, resides in Cāra, and traverses the six paths.

O God, that which has entered the utterance of power (śakti), that which occurs at the time of abandoning the cause, that which has entered the state of emptiness, and another which resides in the heart established in power. (1.17)
It resides at the end of the twelve, situated on the path yet free from the path;
it abides in the emission, within the space between the eyebrows, and is established in the Brahma-nāḍī.
Furthermore, [he meditated upon] the Supreme God beyond the fourth state (turyātīta), within the interior of the door of Brahman;
likewise, he meditated upon Yoga established in emergence and established in separation for the wielder of the trident.
I wish to understand this state that abides in dissolution and yet transcends dissolution;
for once again, O Lord, they have all returned to a single state of being. (1.20)
O Lord of the Gods, tell me how they exist in their state of fusion, as well as the potency of the mantras which is the cause of accomplishment.
Therefore, O God, best of the gods, for what reason have those mantras which were previously declared by you as bestowers of the fulfillment of desires been concealed once again? (1-22)
There are seven times ten million incalculable [mantras] intended for the benefit of living beings;
why do they not achieve success even when the end of the eon has arrived? (1.23)
O Lord of the World, O Lord of the Gods, people undergo extreme suffering for the sake of liberation;
yet, how can there be liberation or spiritual accomplishment here in the absence of mantra? (1.24)
O Lord of Gods, the syllables, protected by that imperishable power known as Vāmā, who is the mother of all mantras, have attained the state of absolute liberation (kaivalya).
How is that subtle, supreme aspect, whose form is radiant energy, known?
For just as the burning power of fire shines forth, so indeed do its rays. (1.26)
In exactly the same way, it is also figuratively designated as a quality (dharma) of Śiva;
by virtue of its inseparable connection, it is figuratively designated everywhere. (1.27)
Śakti is not devoid of Śiva, nor is Śiva devoid of Śakti;
their separation is never observed, just as that between the wind and the sky. (1.28)
Through his power, which functions as an instrument, Śiva carries out his fivefold task;
there is no other cause here by which he might perform that task. (1.29)
Mantra is declared to be Śiva, and its phonemes are its designators. Through the union of the designated and the designator, one attains Śiva by means of that [mantra]. (1.30)
In this matter, O Lord, from where has your power departed that you have abandoned Maheśvara, whereby your mantras of immeasurable splendor have become fruitless? (1.31)
But how was the Mātṛkā born, she who is the mother of mantras? And how is she the mother of the universe, she whose form is the mantra? (1.32)
"Tell me, what is the source of all the *khecarīs*?
Śrī Bhairava said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one, that you have indeed questioned me."
I shall tell you all of that; listen, O long-eyed one, to those tantras—Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, and Yamala—which have been recounted by me.
Likewise, O Goddess, there are the divisions of Rudra and the divisions of Śiva;
therein, O Leader of the Gods, are conduct (caryā), ritual action (kriyā), yoga, and knowledge (jñāna).
In that regard, all those who were questioned here and there were led astray;
for them, the knowledge was not explained with reference to the fluctuations of the mind. (1.36)
O Goddess, whatever was requested by him has been explained by me accordingly,
through mudrās, maṇḍalas, mantras, and other difficult yogas.
O beloved, though they have been led astray by many methods— such as breath-retentions (recaka), inhalations (pūraka), and meditations (dhyāna)—
along with the expansion of ritual acts, that which was spoken by me has not been understood.
But they, out of pride in their own knowledge, questioned him with contempt:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, Candra, and Prajāpati. (1.39)
All the hosts of Skanda and Nandi, as well as Śukra and the other yogis—
all of them have accomplished their purpose, having fully comprehended that [teaching]. (1.40)
O lady of excellent hips, that very knowledge—which provides every means and is endowed with immediate conviction—is thus grasped by those of dull intellect. (1.41)
O leader of the gods, out of affection for you, I shall briefly relate the joy of the Yoginī-hṛdaya, which has come down through the lineage of succession.
A living being has three principal channels: Suṣumṇā, Piṅgalā, and Iḍā.
Among them, that [Suṣumṇā] extends both downward and upward, carrying the vital breath joined with the individual soul.
Below that, there is a knot with a luster like a hen’s egg;
its stalk extends upward, reaching as far as the *vibhāti*.
Thick like the little finger and situated between the breasts,
there should be an eight-petaled lotus above it, white and reddish.
It is four finger-breadths wide and surrounded by sixteen filaments;
the pericarp has a circumference of one finger-breadth, and is exactly like that.
Situated below, it should be square in its breadth;
it is proclaimed to be shaped like a water-pot and like Mount Meru. (1.47)
Situated in its center, the individual soul (jīva) dwells in happiness like Śiva;
it is as minute as a hundredth part of the tip of a hair, subtle in form, and exceedingly pure.
It shines with brilliance like lightning and revolves like the orb of the sun;
that Supreme Self, residing within the body, is meditated upon by yogis. 1-49.

That very [bindu] is called the "drop" (bindu); it remains pervading all things. When it is non-pervasive and situated in the state of a bound soul (paśu), it wanders through the cycle of transmigration.
Sadāśiva, whose nature is free from the beginningless impurity of Māyā, creates various bonds consisting of the qualities (guṇas) that are of the nature of both existence and non-existence. (1.51)
Those qualities are established as being extracted from their state of bondage;
therefore, in this way, within the non-existents, the *bindu* resides in the womb of its own essential nature. (1.52)
The *bindu* is declared to be the Self; the Self is remembered as the *bindu*.
The *bindu* is all-pervading, supreme, and established beyond dissolution. (1.53)
Having then understood the two drops, one is liberated from saṃsāra;
it is endowed with four parts and has the form of a spark of fire. (1.54)
The Blessed Lord Īśa abides in the heart-lotus, O leader of the gods;
he remains within the womb of Māyā, like a flash of lightning in its brilliance.
Known as the "serpent asleep through illusion" (māyāprasuptanāga), she abides in a coiled form;
therefore she is called Kuṇḍalinī, for she is indeed the nature of consciousness of the Self.
O beautiful lady, led by her, that living soul moves downward and upward;
she is indeed called Māyā, the Kuṇḍalinī who coils to the left. (1.57)
The second, named Jyeṣṭhā, is remembered as a straight line;
its form resembles a lotus fiber, and it sets the path for creation in motion.
Raudrī is proclaimed as the third, having the form of a triangle;
Nirodhī is the fourth, having the form of the full orb of the moon. (1.59)
Desire, knowledge, and action—this universal quartet is recited;
the fifth is Śiva-śakti, who effects coming and going. (1.60)

That which produces desire and performs volition is to be known as intellect (buddhi), which is threefold by way of its divisions: characterized by goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), and darkness (tamas). 1.61
Likewise, the power of knowledge and knowledge itself are then of eight kinds:
the fourfold set consisting of virtue (dharma), knowledge (jñāna), dispassion (vairāgya), and sovereignty (aiśvarya);
as well as non-virtue (adharma), ignorance (ajñāna), passion (avairāgya), and lack of sovereignty (anaiśvarya).
And knowledge, divided into eight kinds, both creates and transforms.
Both volition and conceptualization function for the sake of worldly activity;
it is action alone that performs everything—both merit and demerit—for the bound soul.
The universal awakener is to be known as the power that awakens consciousness;
she who is remembered as the fifth power is established as its support. (1.65)
The one supreme power alone manifests in infinite ways through its various functions; by its power, O Dear One, one enjoys virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation. (1.66)
And this mental creation consists of the qualities of goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), and darkness (tamas);
the creation of virtue (dharma) and so forth belongs to goodness, while that of non-virtue (adharma) and so forth belongs to darkness.
Rajas, which causes agitation in both of them, gives birth to its characteristic marks:
sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth. (1.68)
Intellect, mind, and ego are known as the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka),
along with prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna.
The Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya—these are known as the vital winds (prāṇas) that serve as the support; the channels (nāḍīs), moreover, have those [winds] as their support. (1.70)
Iḍā and Piṅgalā, and Suṣumṇā as the third;
Gāndhārī and Hastijihvā, and likewise Pūṣā. (1.71)
Alambuṣā, Kuhū, and Śaṅkhinī is remembered as the tenth;
O highly fortunate one, the heart-bindu always resides together with these.
The deities beginning with Brahmā are denoted by the syllable *akāra*;
having become twofold, the *akāra* performs its function therein. (1.73)
Desire dissolves into knowledge, and knowledge in turn [dissolves] through action;
action dissolves into the *bindu*, and the *bindu* becomes one with the nature of Śiva.
Each [element] goes to dissolution in its own place, presided over by the portions of Brahmā;
Brahmā also, having withdrawn his own functions, departs. (1.75)
The letter *i* is the supreme state where Viṣṇu resides;
there sound dissolves, withdrawing its own effects. (1.76)
Brahmā, having dissolved into the throat, is established in the anterior foundation;
that is the supreme station of Viṣṇu, wherein the letter *i* resides. (1.77)
One should know that place where the letter *u* resides—where Viṣṇu goes as far as Rudra and which extends to the palate—to be the meeting place of all living beings. (1.78)
Rudra also goes to the state of Īśvara; there the letter *m* resides. That is designated as *Nirodhā*, situated above Lambaka.
Because she obstructs the upward path, she is called Raudrī; above that, one attains the target born of Nāda, and there the letter *M* proceeds.
That place where the emergence of *nāda* occurs is declared to be the abode of Śiva;
and above the *lambaka*, O beloved, are the two *bindus*. (1.81)
O beautiful lady, that [point] is said to be the end of the visarga, the end of the twelve,
the end of the kalās, the end of the vowels, and it is remembered as the end of the sixteen.
And there the sound arises when Raudrī becomes divided;
even the Nāda, O Goddess, goes to where Kuṇḍalikā resides.
One should know that it does not end with the *nāda*, O Dear One, but extends beyond the *visarga*.
Above that is the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), the upward-streaming *manonmanī*. (1.84)
O Goddess, within the pervasive Lord, Manonmanī is dissolved there;
O Beloved, the Sphoṭa arises there from the mouth of the Guru below.
Above that is the mouth of the Guru, which is known as the station of Brahmā;
that is also known as the station of Śakti, and it is called the end of dissolution.
At its end, however, that which transcends dissolution (layātīta) is taught; of this there is no doubt.
O fair-faced one, this is the movement of the *bindu* for those who are awakened.
But those who are unawakened, O Goddess, and are obstructed by Nirodhinī, for them the animal realm is proclaimed—the bond of existence within saṃsāra. (1.88)
This movement has been fully described as it occurs at all times; now, however, I shall explain the seizing by which there will be release. (1.89)
Having abandoned the fivefold causes, one attains the state of moving according to one's own will; this is the yoga consisting of the *bindu*, when one desires to renounce [the world]. (1.90)
Then, O Goddess, the eightfold qualities beginning with *aṇimā* shall belong to him;
when, O beautiful one, his renunciation has reached the station of Brahman. (1.91)
Then it attains oneness with Brahmā and proceeds to sound and touch;
having abandoned those two, it goes upward to the cause of the Lotus-born One.
Brahmā, having withdrawn his own activity, proceeds in the form of the effect;
he goes to dissolution into the essence of Viṣṇu along with the instruments of his own work.
Even Keśava, the Supreme, should be abandoned; that Janārdana too must be relinquished when the states associated with the objects of the senses have been cast off—of this there is no doubt.
Keśava, too, having abandoned his mental activity and merged into Rudra, has ceased his office;
this Keśava is the knower of the secret.
Rudra remains here as the supreme, endowed with the qualities of activity;
yet even Rudra, O Lord of Gods, goes into the Lord who consists of the form of splendor.

That is declared to be the station of the bindu; one should point it out as a mass of splendor, as well as the division consisting of splendor and the very activity of the vital breath (prāṇa). (1.97)
Having abandoned these two, one ascends to the qualities and functions of Rudra;
likewise, even Īśvara [is transcended] in the Sound called Śabda, which belongs to Sadāśiva.
Endowed with the qualities of ego and joined with those intent upon the seat of the intellect,
the Lord likewise proceeds, perfectly withdrawn from his own activities.
Where the god Sadāśiva, the repository of the qualities of auspicious knowledge, resides,
there the Lord Īśvara, the bearer of wisdom, remains as the supreme goal.
Having completed its own function, it goes to its own dissolution;
having gradually abandoned that supreme state which transcends dissolution, it departs. (1.101)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as Rudra, and the fourth, Īśvara—
all of them assume the forms of ritual action and proceed, each taking hold of his own specific quality.
May they all be absorbed into Śivā, their physical forms withdrawn by her own power;
will, knowledge, and action are indeed the instruments of them all.
O fair-faced one, the process of returning is described here as being the same as before;
it occurs separately for emergence, conjunction, and dissolution.
The supreme Śakti, who transcends the state of dissolution (layātītā), is all-pervasive and identical with Śiva;
therein, O Queen of the Gods, the supports move one after another in successive order.
Even the Lord Sadāśiva performs the act of withdrawal by his own will, O lady of excellent hips;
he who is the Bindu of the Mind is the consciousness within the Great Path.
As soon as that [consciousness] is withdrawn, the body remains like a piece of wood;
at that moment, bondage consisting of merit and demerit is destroyed, without a doubt. (1-107)
O lady of beautiful hips, when that [impurity] has perished, one goes to the supreme state,
O fair-faced one, provided one is not released from these great bonds.
As long as even the sixfold object has not been purified, how can there be liberation for him?
Thus, O Goddess, renunciation has been explained by me to you through this knowledge.
O Goddess, when Śiva also departs, endowed with all qualities,
he goes to where that Kuṇḍalinī power resides— beyond the mind, the state of Manonmanī.
Endowed with the three powers, she is the awakener and the restrainer;
she should be known as the downward-moving obstructress and the upward-moving arouser. (1-111)
For one [power] resides in existence in two ways, while its infinity arises from the diversity of its functions;
it creates the entire universe, extending as far as the world of Brahmā. (1.112)
And he should withdraw [the energy], O Pārvatī, without doubt, according to the distinction of the ritual act;
first, she who is Vāmā creates, while Jyeṣṭhā is the support for preservation.
O Dear One, withdrawal (saṃhāra) is indeed one, yet it is threefold in its fierce form;
it is further said to be fivefold, as well as eightfold and ninefold.
Divided into fifty varieties, it has reached a state of infinite infinity;
that very [reality], O Leader of Heroes, is to be known in its supreme form.
O beloved, whatever remains of this entire body of speech is pervaded by her;
therefore she is called Māyā, yet Kuṇḍalī is to be known as having the form of the object of knowledge.
In that state, O Goddess, one becomes attained to the Transmental (unmanā), free from the mind, endowed with the eight qualities, and possessed of omniscience and the rest. || 1.117 ||
O Goddess, those elements which exist through their causes—by being joined with them, he too goes to dissolution in the void, the lotus-like cavity, O Beloved. (1.118)
But that place beyond the mind is the hollow of the Lotus-born;
therein, joined with the Liberated One, he has withdrawn his own activity.
Above that, however, is known the all-pervading one, who is beyond qualities yet the source of qualities;
he is both insentient and perfectly conscious, transcending the qualities—thus say those seeking liberation. (1.120)
That Śiva is supreme liberation, the ultimate beyond conceptual construction;
he is neither merit nor demerit, the supreme bringer of all bliss.
O Dear One, by this sequential method, that which consists of the *Yogabindu* should be understood in brief by the wise; thus it has been proclaimed. (1.122)
Henceforth I shall explain that which resides in *nāda*; listen, O beloved! *Nādakuṇḍalinī* is to be known as being situated in the center of the navel.
Having emerged through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) and abandoned the five causes,
she pierced everything from Brahmā up to Śiva and ascended upwards.
O fair-faced one, knowledge, action, and likewise desire belong to Brahmā and the others;
yet she departed, having abandoned whatever duty was to be performed in each of their respective stations.
Having grasped the bindu of the mind, she emerged into the fivefold space,
resembling the autumn moon and as radiant as ten million flashes of lightning.
It should be known as having the luster of the rays of the rising sun, resembling a sprout of coral, like a fiber of a spider's web, or like a lotus filament. (1.127)
It is like the rays of the cool moon and resembles the steady flame of a lamp;
before that, there is a drop in the form of a spark of fire.
O Goddess, like a drop of dew upon a lotus petal,
having grasped it in this manner, one should sever the remaining bonds.
Then, having drawn [the breath] situated in the heart very slowly by means of exhalation,
one standing in the sky should draw up the water contained within the lotus stalk.
In the same way, O beloved, the yogi residing within the body should draw up the vital air from the heart, so that it moves without interruption like a lamp placed in a windless spot. (1.131)
In the same way, O Goddess, the mind should be made to rest solely upon the support of Śakti;
when one has abandoned all causes, one attains the state of Rudra. (1.132)
Then, O lady of auspicious eyes, the two eyebrows should be contracted; the gaze should be directed upward, and both eye-lids should be slightly closed.
O leader of the gods, a trident situated in the sky should be fashioned;
moreover, a pressing with both hands must be performed upon that which has gone to the side-door.
But when it ascends quickly to where the lotus-born aperture is, the deity resides within the channel; not otherwise, O leader of heroes.

When one has become established in the state of the channels, then one should abandon the causal [states] by means of exhalations, inhalations, yogic practices, and retention breaths accompanied by their proper methods. (1.136)
When, having thus abandoned the causal factors, one becomes equal to Śakti,
then for him the eightfold qualities beginning with aṇiman will come to be.
One perceives the objects of the past and the future, as well as those of the present; there is no doubt in this matter: Maheśvara has the channels as his support. (1.138)
When one becomes equal to Śakti, the past is not located in the navel, the present resides in the heart, and the future is situated in the uvula (lambaka). || 1.139 ||
Endowed with both knowledge (jñāna) and discernment (vijñāna), one should enter the eternal body;
O Goddess, that which abides in the Nāda has already been described, as well as that which abides in the Bindu.
Now listen to how one should be established as a spy;
O Great Goddess, hear that classification so that it may be known according to reality. (1.141)
The movement [of the breath] from the heart-lotus to that state [the crown] is thirty-six finger-breadths;

it should be marked by time through the sequence beginning with the *tuṭi* and consisting of sixteen parts, until the end of the breath—that shall be a day. This form of calculation, O Dear One, is measured by time. (TSA 1.142ab = SVATA 4.234cd; TSA 1.142cd–143 = SVATA 235ab: "O Dear One, it is measured by time according to the measure of sixteen *tuṭis*.")

Just as one should move from one place to another by way of division, listen to me as I explain the movement according to its divisions—the determination of the doubts regarding the pairs of the unawakened and the awakened. (Tasa 1.144ab = Svata 4.235cd: Listen to me as I describe the movement according to its divisions as it truly is. 1.144.
From the heart-lotus until it has arrived [at the end of the nose], he abandons one part;

at the tip of the nose is the second, and the third is joined with the *śakti*. (According to another reading: "At the tip of the nose is the second, but the third is at the end of the *śakti*"). Remaining there, he should turn back as long as he does not find the *tattva*.
But when the supreme peace is known, even while remaining therein, one is no longer afflicted.

When he goes downward by means of his power (*śakti*), he is then called "unawakened" (*abuddha*). When he goes downward by his own power, he is likewise unawakened. But when he remains situated within the heart, becoming awakened, he is so described. (1–147)
Having attained power, one should be known as a Buddha; he awakens in the pervasive aspect. When fully awakened regarding the past, the state beyond mind (unmanatva) then occurs. || 1-148 ||
Neither time, nor the practice of the arts, nor reality, nor causes—[these do not reach] the supreme, pure, and perfectly liberated state, which is the lineage-descended foot of the Guru. (1-149)

Having known that, one is liberated; having gone [to that state], one is not born again. (Tattvasaṃhitā 1.145–150ab = Svatantra 4.236–241ab) I shall explain to you how the sixfold path is established within the vital breath. 1.150.
That which is the consciousness and perception from the feet up to the top of the head— (from the feet to the crown of the head, that which is indeed the perception of consciousness)—
is to be known as the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*), and likewise the path of the principles (*tattvādhvan*).
That vital breath (*prāṇa*) which, always moving, possesses a continuum fashioned by the creative powers (*kalā*), [is the path of the letters].
And cessation (nivṛtti) and foundation (pratiṣṭhā) are proclaimed as being in the lower portion.
Vidyā, Śānti, and likewise Śāntātītā are established above;
beyond that is the supreme state, the imperishable station situated above it. (1.153)

In this way, the *bindu-kalā* should be known as being of the nature of *nāda* and *śakti*, through the distinction between the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of both the *vyāpinī* and the *kalā*. [According to the *Svataḥ*: "Those which are by nature *vyāpinī* and so forth, through the distinction between the pervaded and the pervader...

All of these reside solely within the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and their dissolution is said to occur at the end of the breath. [According to the *Svataḥ*: "All of these reside solely within the vital breath; through the abandonment of the six, there is dissolution in the seventh. (tasa 1/152-155ab = svata 4/243-246ab)
Thus the path of the arts (kalādhvan) has been explained; now learn the path of the phonemes (varṇādhvan).
All phonemes, which constitute sound, exist in this world of the moving and the unmoving, established through fifty divisions within infinite millions of scriptures. (1.156)
Sound is declared to be the vital breath (prāṇa); therefore, the phonemes arise from the vital breath and dissolve back into it, wherein sound itself has gone to dissolution. (1.157)
Beyond sound, O lady of excellent hips, he is united with reality;
liberated and omnipresent, O Goddess, he is devoid of both merit and demerit.
When one has reached the Śiva-principle, one no longer looks downward;
for by unrighteousness one goes downward, while by righteousness one ascends once more.

Having abandoned duality through consciousness, one attains omnipresence here. (TASA 1.155cd–160ab = SVATA 4.246cd–251ab) The path of phonemes has been fully explained; now the path of the feet is described here. 1.160

The eighty-one words that are established in the King of Vidyās—those words consist of phonemes, and those phonemes are known to consist of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). (Intrinsically, they consist of phonemes here; the phonemes abide as consisting of the vital breath.
Therefore, all these words are thus established by way of the sequence of the vital breath.
Thus the path of the locations has been explained; now learn from me the path of the mantras.
That which is the group of eleven mantras is established by Śakti, and it moves eternally within the vital breath at the end of the eleven principles.
The letter A, the letter U, the letter M, and the bindu;
the half-moon, the nirodhī, the nāda, and the end of nāda (nādānta). || 1-164 ||
Śakti, Vyāpinī, and Samanā are known as the eleventh;
Unmanā is beyond that, and what is beyond that is the stainless (nirāmaya).
The mantras are thus situated within the vital breath; now the utterance by means of power (*śakti*) is described.
The letter *ha* is traditionally held to be the vital breath, well-functioning and having the form of a plow (*halākṛti*). (TASA 1.163–166ab = SVATA 4.254–257ab)

When joined with the letter *a*, the pronunciation of the phoneme becomes clear. (From *Svata*: When joined by the letter *a* and the movement of the letter *u*, and joined with the measure of the letter *m*, the pronunciation of the phoneme becomes clear. *Tasa* 1.167ab = *Svata* 4.258).
Through union with the head-bindu (*binduśiras*), it attains the state of its own vowel (*svasvara*). (1.167)
The mouth is said to belong to Nāda; Nāda utters sound.
By this very yoga, the Self is called Puruṣa. (1-168)
Moving through all living beings by way of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa, one attains dissolution in the principle of Śakti; through higher discernment, one proceeds upward.
Having abandoned the all-pervasive *samanā*, the *unmanā* [state] proceeds to Śiva;
the power (*śakti*) that has reached the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*) does not move about, but becomes omnipresent.

The utterance of the *śakti* has been fully explained; now the abandonment of the cause (*kāraṇatyāga*) is being described. (TASA 1.166cd–171ab = SVATA 4.257cd–262) The letter *ha* is the essence of the vital power (*prāṇaśakti*), and the letter *a* denotes Brahman. (1.171)
The abandonment [of the breath] at the heart belongs to him; the syllable *U* is the designator of Viṣṇu.
The abandonment [of the breath] at the throat belongs to him; the syllable *Ma* is the designator of Rudra.
One should abandon that [Viṣṇu] in the middle of the palate; he himself is the very sound Viṣṇu.
One should abandon him between the eyebrows; he is Sadāśiva, who is expressed as Nāda.
The abandonment of that [breath] is prescribed from the forehead up to the crown of the head;
Śakti, Vyāpinī, and Samanā—of these, Śiva is said to be the object of expression.
One should abandon the Śakti at the center of the head; above that, one should abandon the Vyāpinī;
having abandoned the Samanā and the Unmanā, dissolution is said to occur thereafter. (1.175)
O Dear One, in this very way one should abandon [the self] through states that are increasingly subtle;
[likewise], it bestows the fruits of various accomplishments through states that are increasingly gross.
That which is the supreme state, exceedingly subtle, is ordained as non-existence.
The state of Unmanā is the supreme reality; it is considered the ultimate beyond the gross.
Beyond that, moreover, is the supreme void, which is likewise beyond touch;
then sound, light, the mantra, the causal principles, and the worlds. (1.178)
The worlds, whose nature consists of the five elements, are presided over by their causes;
that which pervades these worlds shall be described according to its essential nature.
One attains the status of a lord of the worlds and should maintain that which is identical with Śiva;
furthermore, in the practice of the causes beginning with Brahmā, one should contemplate their embodied forms.

And one shall attain that state of identity with the previously described characteristics. Through mantras, one attains the perfection of mantra, as well as the fruits of recitation, fire-offerings, and worship. (Tattvasaṃhitā 1.177–181ab = Svacchanda-tantra 4.268cd–272) 1.181.
Through the previously described figurative meditation (rūpakadhyāna), one attains perfection; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, through the meditation on light (jyotidhyāna), the lord of yogis shall attain the perfection of yoga.
When he attains identity with that [the sound], he becomes the sovereign of yogins; and through meditation on the sound, being of the nature of sound, he becomes the fulfiller of all speech. (1.183)
From meditation on contact, one whose self is contact would become the cause of the world;
and from meditation on emptiness, one whose self is emptiness would become all-pervasive and omnipresent. (1-184)

Through the yoga of continuous meditative concentration, the yogi shall go everywhere. (Tasa 1/181cd–185ab = Svata 4/273–276) He should always contemplate the supreme, subtle non-existence that culminates in the state beyond mind (unmanī). 1-185.

That which transcends all sense faculties and is indefinable is called "existence" (bhāva), having rendered existence free from affliction through the state of being both non-existence and existence. (1.186)
One attains the state of non-existence, liberated from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
This is the relinquishing of causes for you; now learn the relinquishing of time.
The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is said to consist of sixteen *truṭis*.
Relying upon two *truṭis*, each one is remembered as a Bhairava.
By means of the division of day and night, O fair-faced one, they proceed;
indeed, from his splendor, they utter the ninth supreme deity.

I shall likewise tell you how one should abandon [the breath] at all times when the vital breath [is present]. (TASA 1.188–190ab = SVATA 4.279cd–281) Those sixteen *truṭis* which belong to time are its instruments. (1.190)
By means of which, when well-established, the entire domain of speech proceeds:
the *truṭi*, the *lava*, the *nimeṣa*, the *kāṣṭhā*, and likewise the *kalā*. (1.191)
A muhūrta, a day and night, a fortnight, a month, a season, as well as a solstice, a year, a yuga, and likewise an interval between manvantaras. || 1-192 ||
One should abandon the *kalpa* and the *mahākalpa* at the end of one's power;
however, in the aspect of the Pervasive (*vyāpinī*), one should abandon that supreme time within the aspect of the principles (*tattva*).
That which stands beyond is to be known as the seventeenth *parārdha*;
that is the eighteenth time (*kāla*), at the end of which one should abandon even the level of *Samanā*.
All time, however, is the pervader of time, supreme and imperishable.
The supreme [state] is to be joined within the state beyond mind; there, time does not exist.
Eternal, eternally arisen, and all-pervading, one should abandon [everything] in the form of sound (nāda).
Having attained that which is eternally arisen, one becomes forever equal to it. (1.196)

The abandonment of time indeed occurs, and then the state of emptiness is described: "The upper is empty, the lower is empty, and the middle is empty; this is the third. (Tattvasaṅgraha 1.195–197ab = Svatantrā 4.286cd–288). 1.197.
Furthermore, by means of the support of the three voids—below, above, and in the middle—the pervasive void (vyāpinīśūnya) and the Equal One (samanā) are here the fifth.
Likewise, the sixth [state] belongs to the unmanī; these six are thus established.
All are presided over by reality (tattva), and even that Māyā bestows the fruit.
Having abandoned those [six] in the sixth void, effect their dissolution in the seventh;
for that void is supreme, subtle, and devoid of all states. (1.200)
That which is non-empty is called "empty," and "empty" is said to be non-existence.
That is designated as non-existence wherein all phenomena have come to an end. (1.201)

That supreme, tranquil state of pure existence—how and what is it situated? (Tattvasaṅgraha 1.197–202ab = Svārthānumāna 4.289–293). Wherever there is no entity, not even a gross one, [there it is situated]. 1.202.
In each and every place, the Supreme is empty, abiding by pervading everything;
He alone, having pervaded the gross [elements], becomes that which has gross limiting adjuncts (upādhi). (1.203)
That very [reality] is established through the distinction between the subtle and the gross;
having attained that and its state of equality, one becomes [that reality]—of this there is no doubt. (1.204)

The doctrine of emptiness has been fully explained for your pleasure, O Goddess worshipped by the gods. Now, listen to how it is established within the Śakti. (TASA 1.202cd–205ab = SVata 4.294–296) 11a [kh] Listen now to how it resides within the Śakti. 1-205.
O sinless one, O fair-eyed lady, I shall explain the certainty of how she, though devoid of color, exists through her union with color.
O Goddess, those mantras previously mentioned, numbering seven crores and beyond counting, were formerly hidden; they have now been brought down in the form of letters.
Therefore, those mantras do not succeed even if recited hundreds of millions of times, because they lack that imperishable power which abides as the very life-force of mantras. (1.208)
O lady of beautiful hips, without her, the autumn clouds of the gods, sages, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras are fruitless.
O auspicious lady, this [teaching] is concealed from these Siddhas, the hosts of Nāgas, and these human Yogins; those lowest of men who lack devotion [to it] do not perceive it.
They do not recognize the Guru as a deity, nor do they observe the commitments (samaya) prescribed in the scriptures;
devoted to hypocrisy and crookedness, they are devoid of ritual action for the sake of fleeting pleasures. || 1-211 ||
For this reason, O Lord of Gods, I have concealed my vigor; because it was thus concealed, only the remaining phonemes remain.
O Goddess, that Mātṛkā who is supreme and endowed with splendor—
by her the entire universe is pervaded, as far as the world of Brahmā.

But when, O God worshipped by the gods, that which resides therein exists as all-pervasive, the Lord, though situated in the unmanifested (a-varṇa), abides as the manifest (varṇa) and is omnipresent. (1.214)
Thus, O goddess worshipped by the gods, I shall explain to you for the sake of certain determination that supreme,
subtle power which is celebrated as being beyond all conduct.
O highly fortunate Umā, having encircled the drop at the heart like a slumbering serpent,
she lies there asleep, perceiving nothing at all.
Having cast the fourteen worlds, along with the moon, fire, sun, and stars,
into her belly, that goddess became as if overcome by the stupor of poison.
O woman of excellent complexion, she was awakened by that supreme sound consisting of gnosis, and stirred by the *bindu* residing within her womb.
For as long as there is violent churning within the form of the Śakti, so long do the Bindu and Vaita proceed with great power during the initial emergence of differentiation. (1.219)
By that [process], having churned the drop (bindu), the subtle digit Kuṇḍalinī arises;
the Lord Bindu, consisting of four digits, has entered the womb of Śakti.
Through the yoga of abiding in the center, straightness arises as the Guru;
she is known as the Jyeṣṭhā Śakti, situated precisely between the two points (bindus). (1.221)
The line itself, agitated by the *bindu*, is Amṛtakuṇḍalī;
she should be known as Rekhinī, with both [the *bindu* and the line] situated in her midst. (1.222)
She is declared to be the three-pathed one and is sung of by the name Raudrī;
she is designated as the Obstructress, for she blocks the path to liberation.
Ambikā, who has the form of a crescent moon and is like the light of the half-moon, is indeed the one supreme Śakti; she, however, manifests in three ways. (1.224)
From these [letters], when combined or separated, nine groups are produced;
that [vowels] is traditionally known as ninefold, characterized by those nine groups. (1.225)

O Goddess, leader of the gods, she who resides within the five mantras according to the sequence beginning with Sadyojāta and so forth, is therefore declared to be fivefold; this should be known. (1.226)
O Goddess, you are said to reside in the twelve vowels and to be established in the twelve places;
you abide in fifty divisions, beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with the letter 'kṣa'.

When it is situated in the region of the heart, it is known as having one atom; at the throat, it should be known as having two atoms; and when it is located at the root of the tongue, it should be understood as having three atoms. (1.228)
The manifestation of phonemes occurs at the tip of the tongue; of this there is no doubt.
In this way, sound is produced, and the world of moving and non-moving beings is pervaded by sound. (1.229)
One should first place Raudrī on the head; Vāmā is proclaimed for the face;
Ambikā is said to be the arms; and Jyeṣṭhā is remembered as the weapon.
For Śrīkaṇṭha is proclaimed as the all-pervading Supreme Lord;
just as he is one, so too are all sixteen great winds.
After that, twenty-five [are taught], and above those, nine are recorded.
By this sequential application, the emergence of the fifty [letters] occurs. (1.232)
It was thus taught by the God of gods according to the distinction between cause and effect;
in this way, within the twelve-thousand [verse scripture], the various methods of retention have been proclaimed.
The names of the host of Rudras have been indicated here, O Pārvatī;
these too are all-pervading, eternal, consisting of the form of sound, and endowed with qualities.
This distinction between the signified and the signifier does not exist as something perceived externally;
it has been created by me for the sake of conventional usage, in order to analyze words. (1.235)
There is no sound without the Rudras, nor is there any meaning, nor is there any movement through them.
The body, however, is brilliantly illuminated by the fifty parts of the mass of sounds.
For this Rudrapañcāśikā indeed attains the status of the Mātṛkā;
therefore, O Goddess, one should know that everything originates from that Mātṛkā. (1.237)
There is no designation higher than Mātṛkā, nor is there a mantra higher than Mātṛkā;
through the division of the gross and the subtle, the body arises from Mātṛkā. (1.238)
And wherever sound arises, there it goes to its dissolution;
just as a drop of water, having arisen in the midst of water, perishes there. (1.239)
In that very same way, the essence of sound dissolves into the *manobindu*;
having abandoned Raudrī at the head, one should cast off Jyeṣṭhā as a weapon.
Having abandoned everything, Ambikā remains stationed in the region of the arms;
she alone is to be known as Kuṇḍalinī, and nothing else is perceived. (1.241)
In this way, indeed, there is destruction and likewise origination;
O fair-faced one, he who understands both origination and destruction [is liberated]. (1.242)
He shall become a powerful hero, just as you are my beloved;
he shall become a lord of practitioners, worthy of worship, and most highly revered.
O auspicious lady, Vāmā is remembered as Brahmā; Jyeṣṭhā is proclaimed to be Viṣṇu;
Raudrī is Rudra, O fair-limbed one; and they know Ambikā to be Īśvara.
Union, however, has the form of sound, while Śiva is the supreme, consisting of resonance (nāda);
O Goddess, he who possesses the five causes is established in his all-pervasive nature.
Indeed, powers (śaktis) are likewise seen in each and every caste:
Icchā is proclaimed as Raudrī, and Jñāna is celebrated as Vāmā. (1.246)
O fair-eyed one, Kriyā is declared to be Jyeṣṭhā and should be known as Ambā;
rising is to be known by Vāmā, while Jyeṣṭhā is remembered as midday. (1.247)
The twilight is to be known as Raudrī, and at that very time, sunset occurs;
exhalation (recaka) is said to be by Vāmā, while inhalation (pūraka) is known to be by Jyeṣṭhā.
Kumbhaka is to be known as Raudrī, and Ambikā abides in her own nature;
Kuṇḍalinī is to be known in the state of emergence, and she is proclaimed as Vāmā. (1-249)
Likewise, Jyeṣṭhā is said to reside in separation, while Raudrī is declared to be in dissolution; and Ambā, O leader of the gods, is to be known as that which transcends dissolution. (1.250)
Kuṇḍalinī, located at the navel, should be known as having the form of a sleeping serpent;
above the location of the throat is Raudrī, where Rudra, the Lord of the World, resides. (1.251)
Ambikā, who resides in the flow [of the breath], in the middle between the two points, and situated in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), should be known by the knower of reality. (1.252)
Samanā, together with Kuṇḍalī, is to be known as that which is proclaimed as the waking state;
Jyeṣṭhā is indeed situated in the dreaming state, and Raudrī brings about the state beyond the mind (unmanā). (1.253)
O Goddess, the state known as deep sleep is called *unmanā*; Ambikā, who has transcended the mind, is auspiciously situated in the fourth state (*turya*). (1–254)
Kuṇḍalī is to be known as the first, while Manonmanī is the second;
the third is named Bindu, and the world is permeated by these three powers.
The third [state] pertains to manifestation, separation, and dissolution;
it is the Supreme Lord, who transcends dissolution, is supremely peaceful, and all-pervading. (1.256)
O lady of excellent hips, having realized that which is free from cause and effect and devoid of anything to be abandoned or accepted, one shall not undergo birth again. (1.257)
The wise should understand the grasping of that which resides within the *kuṇḍalinī*;
O beloved, it is like a bird in the sky beholding its prey.
In that same way, he should attract it swiftly with great force;
likewise, the lord of yogis should draw forth the mind-bindu. (1.259)
Just as an arrow situated within a reed rushes forth when struck by a mechanical device, so too, O lady of excellent hips, does the drop (bindu) rush upward through the upward breath (uccāra). 1-260.
Having made the sky-dweller the maker of the sky, one should join the mouth of the sky; the sky is stable.
The tortoise should be joined with Maṅgala, and that which ends in a vowel is joined with two. (1–261)
The impelling occurs by means of udāna until it reaches the aperture of space (khamukha);
purification is achieved through the auspicious [wind] joined with the tortoise (kūrma) by means of the arrow-weapon (śarāstra). || 1-262 ||
It is purified, there is no doubt, on the path of the twice-born, O fair-faced one;
one should observe the grasping [of the breath] by means of that very pure path. (1–263)
The grasping by means of the mind should be performed of that which resides in the support of power; O fair-faced one, there would then arise the cognition of that grasping. (1.264)
Trembling located in the navel, yawning with a disordered face, shedding tears, knitting the eyebrows, and likewise mental agitation—these are to be known [as signs]. (1.265)
These, however, are the signs at the navel; now listen to those occurring when [the breath] resides in the throat.
Residing in the throat, it shakes the body and emits sound in many ways. (1.266)
Shaking of the head, incoherent speech, and the loud sound of the syllable *hūṃ*—
beyond that, O supreme Ambikā, lies the abode of Rudra which has passed above.
But then, listen with a concentrated mind to his signs:
abiding as Rudra, he knows the scripture, the mudrās, and the mantras in their many forms. (1.268)
The practitioner recites the scriptures even though they have not been heard;
above that, O Great Goddess, there shall be the state known as Visarga.
O Goddess, when he is established in the Visarga, then he hears sound and perceives a cool touch, as if upon the peaks of the Himalayas.
Then, O Goddess, the station of Śakti attains oneness with that which is called Sādākhya;
for, O fair-faced one, the state of Unmanā resides within Śakti as the [transcendence of] sense objects. (1.271)
And there is no doubt that the attainment of qualities such as *aṇimā* occurs, provided that, O beautiful one, one becomes firmly established in that very state of absorption (*tallaya*). (1.272)
Then it rises swiftly; this is indeed the truth, there is no doubt.
It should be known as residing in the aperture (*randhra*), all-pervading, and having transcended that, it is omnipresent (*vyāpaka*). (1.273)
Just as space within a jar appears to be limited, so too the all-pervasive [Self] manifests as if delimited by the body. (1.274)
O Goddess, just as when a jar is broken it returns to a state of oneness, so too does the non-existence of the internal and external shine forth as one. (1.275)
For in that very same way, the elemental self (bhūtātman), when released from its bonds, shines forth;
just as a lamp situated within a jar illuminates only a single region. (1.276)

And thus, O Goddess, the Self, residing within the subtle body (liṅga) and skillful in its mental operations, is the illuminator everywhere, just as when a jar is broken [the space within it is revealed] everywhere. (1.277)
Likewise, O Dear One, when the mind is liberated from the fetters, it becomes all-pervasive.
Thus, O Goddess, Sovereign of the Gods, has this pervasion been explained by me to you. (1.278)
For them, there shall be the pervasion by the Self (ātman), and beyond that, the pervasion by Śiva;
being free from all limiting adjuncts (upādhi) through the state of being the Remainder (śeṣa-bhāva) of all bonds. (1.279)
Those who, without knowing the supreme reality, have merely imagined Śivatva, are not true Śaivas who protect themselves; they do not go to the state of Śiva. (1.280)
Those who worship deities by conceptualizing them as having forms reach the state of the reality of the self, being colored by the self-nature of that very reality. (1.281)
These [beings] attain their state, yet they are not liberated in the ultimate sense.
Therefore, having renounced everything, one should worship that which abides in its own nature. (1.282)
Furthermore, I shall explain that which abides in its own nature; listen to how it is:
there is no cessation, nor utterance, nor a characteristic, nor even a conjunction.
Then, having known [the Self] as abiding in its own nature, one is liberated; there is no doubt about this. Volition, however, is a great bondage; its eradication is the cause of liberation.
Having abandoned that, the yogi is liberated; but one who possesses conceptual construction is bound.
Neither the mind, nor the object of thought, nor even the thinker is perceived. (1.285)
O God, as long as one forms a conceptual intention (*saṃkalpa*), so long does bondage proceed;
there is neither the drop (*bindu*), nor the resonance (*nāda*), nor the movement (*cāra*) belonging to the six paths.
There is no path of the utterance of power (śakti) because of the time of abandoning causes;
there is neither the state of meditating on emptiness nor is there power, for it is Śiva alone. (1.287)
For this is the latent impression of ignorance that binds one to the fear of saṃsāra;
since there is no contentment therein, perhaps someone will eventually act [to remedy it]. (1.288)
Having abandoned that [one], everything is abandoned; the noose of hope is relinquished without remainder.
Hope alone is the great bond, by which the entire world is pervaded. (1.289)
As long as that [desire] is not abandoned, indeed, peace is not found.
What hope can there be for those who preach liberation, wherein everything has come to an end? (1.290)
He who has no longing even for liberation attains liberation;
for him there is no abiding place in liberation, nor meditation, nor conceptual construction. (1.291)
The vision extended everywhere—that is liberation for those who proclaim liberation.
Liberation is that which cannot be designated by name; it is free from the conceptual constructions of reasoning and exclusion. (1.292)
One should dispel ignorance and abandon nescience;
the entire world has that as its form, yet it has no form of its own whatsoever. (1.293)
But here, the wise should practice while abiding in the state of being that is formless;
for that is the state of reality called the "elemental," wherein the process of creation proceeds. (1.294)
Bliss is the form of Brahman; it never fears anything.
Having realized that everything has the Self as its essence, there remains nothing whatsoever to be done. (1.295)
If there is the state of existence, then there is bondage without a doubt;
just as the silkworm by itself binds itself with its own self. (1.296)
An elevated state binds [the mind] through such very same mental cultivations; it is released when bound by those two. What liberation can there be for that which is unbound? (1.297)
The innate and adventitious bonds are presided over by the state of duality;
here, the imagined [bond] is the mind itself, characterized by volitional construction.
But having abandoned the mental, O Dear One, whatever consists of speech—all that which is of the nature of existence and non-existence—is characterized by the volitions of the mind. (1.299)
Wherever the mind operates among pure and impure entities, as well as amidst the conceptual distinctions of caste and non-caste, and likewise between what is edible and what is inedible; (1.300)
For one by whom equanimity is known, nothing at all has been produced.
One should first abandon all existents, and then remain firm in non-existence. (1.301)
But having abandoned non-existence, it will abide in its own nature, just as water situated within a stone, when heated by the rays of the sun. (1.302)
It has not been drunk by anyone, nor does it remain in that very place;
thus is the mind of one who knows gnosis, endowed with the absence of logical proof.
Just as the all-pervading wind carries away the sky, the earth, and the child,
making a "dhug-dhug" sound with great force and shattering trees and mountains.
At that very moment, the mind of one who knows that ignorance goes to utter destruction, just as clouds, having reached the twilight, do not remain when they have dispersed. (1.305)
In that very instant, the mind of one who has become thus absorbed goes to utter destruction, just as rain from a cloud falls upon a region of land with both low and high elevations. (1.306)
In that very instant it goes to destruction; likewise, existence is without abode.
Just as one knows [the truth] through the union of the other, it is beyond comparison. (1.307)
At that very moment they attain realization; in the same way, the wise know the mind to be empty.
O Goddess, when the sound of a conch shell is heard with its vast resonance, || 1.308 ||
At that very moment it is destroyed; likewise, the wise know the mind to be empty by relying on detachment from objects and through difficult penances such as the Cāndrāyaṇa.
One should indeed exhaust that [mind] for the sake of liberation within the self that is like rock salt and free from mental constructs (unmanā).
By many who have grasped dispassion (*vairāgya*), the self has been thus exhausted.
Not even one among them exists here that is free from logical justification—the celibacy, the culmination of asceticism, the purity and so forth, as well as those various restraints. (1.311)
Liberation is not accomplished by those [means]; rather, non-existence itself is the cause here.
This applies to the fire, the darbha grass, the mantras, the priest, and the oblation as well. (1.312)
The consecrated waters, the ritual seats, the initiation, and the arrangement of meditative contemplation—this entire collection of ritual intentions is not the cause of awakening. (1.313)

But non-duality is free from conceptual construction, devoid of sense organs, and without defining characteristics. How can there be a definition for that which is indefinable? How can there be a mind for that which is mindless? (1.314)
The wise should always maintain the state of mindlessness within the mind;
non-existence persists eternally, while existence must be abandoned. (1.315)
But when one who exists [in reality] is non-existent, for him that notion "it does not exist" is [an error];
there is no liberation, it is a great bondage. One should contemplate that everything is empty. (1.316)
The consciousness of the moving and unmoving self depends upon the fluctuations of the mind;
no one is able to render the entire body partless.
As long as one cultivates knowledge that is solely based upon consciousness, it becomes agitated by the vital wind (vāyu), and ignorance arises. (1.318)

When the mind has been thoroughly conquered through the hardships of breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and other such means, one should practice at other times; otherwise, that which was previously acquired becomes fruitless.
Therefore, having understood in this way that the objects of the senses are unstable and wavering— fragile in form like a jar, and resembling a flash of lightning— 1.320b–c.
"Having renounced everything for the sake of liberation, fix your mind upon atheism.
The Goddess said:
"O God, O Great Lord, a great curiosity has arisen within me."
What characteristic can there be for that which does not exist? How can there be a state for that which is without characteristics?
Meditation, worship, recitation, and fire-offerings are merely various forms of mental cultivation.
"For what purpose, O God, was she described by you, O Supreme Lord?
Śrī Bhairava said:
"There are various forms, colors, and diverse characteristics numbering in the hundreds of thousands."
All this has been revealed for the purpose of purifying the mind;
for the mind is eternally restless, without support, and beyond the reach of the senses. (1.324)
It is possible to sustain that which has been performed by one whose movement is dominated by wind;
for as long as he cultivates one [thought], another has already arisen. (1.325)
Neither meditation nor the target will ever be accomplished;
for this reason, everything must be abandoned without exception. (1.326)
But as for that mark arising from the mind, or meditation consisting of conceptualization—one should abandon the sense of "mine" everywhere and cultivate the thought, "I am not. (1.327)
"I do not exist, nor does another exist"—one who delights in such non-dual practice, as long as he has not truly realized this, possesses nothing at all. (1.328)
The object of the notion "I" is that which is bound within the three qualities;
O Goddess, as long as one does not abandon it, one will remain obstructed. (1.329)
Desire, hatred, pleasure, pain, detachment, and likewise pride—as long as these are not abandoned, how can there be any spiritual progress for him? (1.330)
For one for whom pleasure and pain are equal, there is no coming or going;
just as when the milk is exhausted, the calf turns away from the mother’s udder. (1.331)
Likewise, for men, the destruction of passion is Nirvana, the supreme state;
yet this entire world is attached to children, wives, and family. (1.332)
Having abandoned that and become free from qualities (nirguṇa), one attains nirvāṇa—
even those who have reached the peak of existence (bhavāgra), being solely intent upon and devoted to that yoga.
Dragged by the hook of egoism, they fall into the ocean of worldly existence;
having abandoned egoism, one should likewise abandon the sense of "mine."
Having abandoned hope entirely, one who is free from desire is highly praised;
even a twice-born man who is a killer of a fetus or a violator of his teacher’s bed [is purified], let alone one who is learned in the four Vedas.
"He who perceives equality"—thus the Śruti has declared. One who is liberated sees; the liberated self sees the Self alone everywhere. (1.336)
"For one who perceives oneness, there is neither 'I' nor another;
oneness exists in manifold states, like a spider's thread branching out in a thousand ways. (1.337)
But he who perceives according to reality, abiding in the state of equal flavor, possesses equanimity toward all beings, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as the same. (1.338)
By that, it attains equality; he is called the changeless one.
Beyond conceptual construction and indescribable, he is the supreme, having transcended all means of valid cognition. (1.339)
Therefore, there is no such instrument for that; the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) abides in its own nature.
The Lord (Īśvara) is immutable, his nature being the movement toward the realization of the true essence. (1.340)
No conceptual construction is taught for him whose name is Great Renown;
he should be known as Hiraṇyagarbha, by whom this world is pervaded. (1.341)
The Goddess said:
"How can that which is liberated from all states of being, devoid of all marks, and in non-duality where no second exists, remain motionless? (1.342)
The illustrious Bhairava said: O beautiful one, he who abides in his own true nature shall always remain established in that very nature;
he becomes immovable, and he is never moved by anything anywhere.
The movement of self-consciousness is relative to the fluctuations of the mind;
that by which all this is filled is worshipped by the yogis. (1.344)
Where one is constantly purified by austerities and joined with sacrifices—that very Self is "not this, not this" (neti neti); for it is not born from fortune.
For they do not perish, nor are they destroyed; therefore this has been proclaimed.
[These are] sound, touch, taste, form, and indeed the subtle element of smell. (1.346)
O Goddess, these attachments are known to be the cause of existence within saṃsāra;
from attachment arises desire, and from desire comes the grasping for wealth. (1.347)
From grasping arises conceptualization; therefore, one should abandon attachment.
Having relinquished attachment to the world, as well as attachment to the scriptures. (1.348)
Completely liberated from all attachments, he goes to the supreme state— non-existence beyond conceptual cultivation, devoid of both the object of awakening and the awakener. (1.349)
But that which is past indeed has as its sphere of experience that which transcends conceptual proliferation (prapañca);
it is free from action and cause, and devoid of logical reasoning regarding causes. (1.350)
O Goddess, he in whom this shall abide goes to the supreme state;
having gone there, O lady of excellent hips, he never again descends.
O Goddess, this is considered the supreme, partless reality consisting of truth;
there exists nothing higher than this within the three worlds. (1.352)
For one whose mind is always deluded regarding the world, which consists of the self of all beings, his state of being "mind" alone is the truth—this is the truth, there is no doubt. (1.353)
The Goddess said:
O Lord of the Gods, on the left and right paths as well as in the Siddhānta, [the path] is proclaimed to be threefold: gross, subtle, and supreme. || 1.354 ||

For those who are endowed with meditative absorption and retention, and possessed of yoga, mantras, and ritual action, there shall be accomplishment and liberation, but never for others. (1.355) Where there is no origination, how could there be stability?
Indeed, there is no such thing as dissolution for this ocean of the world, which consists of speech. (1.356)
"Truth, truth, and again truth—this has been established by you in every tantra.
O Mahādeva, there is no truth that has not been proclaimed by you. (1.357)
Bhairava said:
"O my beloved, among the Siddhas, Gandharvas, Yoginīs, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas,
you have stated that there is no truth for me."
Today my mind has understood that your heart is difficult to win over;
you do not believe what is said, and yet you ask again and again. (1.359)
Nevertheless, I shall speak; listen with certainty, my dear.
Just as you have doubts and suspicions, so shall I explain them to you. (1.360)
That reality which is supreme, peaceful, inconceivable, and free from atoms— I have described that reality according to its gross, subtle, and ultimate aspects.
That reality is the source of all things, which is devoid of causal signs.
If it is argued that this is an overstatement, [we reply that] here, the source consists of its own qualities. (1.362)
That supreme deity is like a piece of wood, and likewise the self is of the nature of dissolution;
since both are identical in this regard, who here is the master of transmigratory existence? (1.363)

How can there be the arising [of the world] from that dissolution, and how could the Self, which is not its own master, be stained by it of its own accord? Such reasoning is considered external, belonging to other philosophical systems. (1.364)

[He is] liberated from the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka), beyond the sphere of causes, and devoid of any trace, being inseparable from the relationship between the signified and the signifier. || 1.365 ||

It is understood that its emergence from the ultimate reality (paratattva)—which is devoid of all conceptual proliferation (prapañca) and beyond the range of the senses—is due to its own inherent nature (svabhāva). (1.366)
Just as rice arises from a rice sprout and kodrava from kodrava, there is no arising of the higher reality from another reality, nor of the Supreme Self from anything else. (1.367)

How can an origination that is seedless yet possesses seeds be both existent and non-existent by nature? How can it be endowed with the four qualities while being the sphere of that which transcends those qualities? (1-368) For the Self is indeed without beginning or end, and karma is likewise held to be without beginning. There is also the power (*śakti*) and the five elements; what, then, is produced here? (1-369)
How could an origination that is mutually dependent attain permanence?
Therefore, because it is established as being posterior [to its cause], it is accepted as impermanent. (1.370)
The connection with manifold wombs proceeds from that conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
How is it that even that which is free from conceptual proliferation is understood by those who see reality? (1-371)
Inconceivable and immeasurable, likewise beyond thought and supreme, with a nature in which all defects are entirely abandoned—how could such a one, having awakened, be an awakener? (1.372)
Sound is the quality of space, and its perception is auditory cognition;
if this were so, how could the supreme reality be the bliss of the object of apprehension? (1.373)
The self is ignorant, eternal, and a bound soul (paśu), while Śiva is another, the object of recollection;
how then can that [Self] know Him who is without means and untainted? (1.374)
If scripture (*āgama*) is the means, then there would be a contradiction regarding the "lack of means.
And how could the Lord, whose domain transcends words and the senses, possess a means? (1.375)
That means is slightly accessible as that which is designated by the mind and the senses;
how, then, O Lord, can there be transcendence of the senses in Him? (1.376)
That which is delimited by the instruments of perception is gross and perishable;
how, O Lord, could that which is imperishable be the Supreme Self? (1.377)
If consciousness regarding the supreme reality were conceptual consciousness, how could there be an entry of conceptualization into that which is non-conceptual? (1.378)
"Buddha," "Jina," "Śiva," "Ātman," "Viṣṇu," and "Brahman" are indeed synonyms;
how could an ignorant person have conflicting views regarding the object of worship when there is only a difference in names? (1.379)
One who is rendered unconscious by poison likewise becomes free from conceptual construction;
so too does one in deep sleep within the womb, or a tree being cut down. (1.380)
Liberation shall come first for them, but for others there is doubt;
who knows whether the destruction of conceptual construction has occurred or not? (1.381)
"Why? How? When? Of what? By whom? Who? Where established?"—these are questions that cannot be answered regarding [the ultimate reality], whereas the horn of a rabbit can indeed be described. (1.382)
The horn exists and the rabbit also exists, yet they are seen separately elsewhere;
there is no connection whatsoever with a horn because of the absence of a rabbit on its head. (1.383)
Furthermore, no connection has ever been observed anywhere between the sense faculties and the mind, which are mutually contradictory, and the Supreme Self. (1.384)
But that [Self] is difficult to discern; even if it were ever known, since the mind is fickle and not stable, how could liberation occur therein? (1.385)
Knowledge, pride, and likewise the immediate—these three are clearly perceived.
By means of this knowledge, the entire world of the Omniscient One is brought forth. (1.386)
Beyond the senses and inconceivable, characterized by the nature of the non-conceptual Self, it is held to be the body consisting of knowledge belonging to the exceedingly subtle Lord Śiva. (1.387)
By which the self, having taken on a body that is powerful and pleasing to behold, and having demonstrated its own dharma, goes by its own will to that state. (1.388)

In one moment that form is seen, and in a moment it dissolves into consciousness; because it proceeds spontaneously toward the desired object, it is therefore proclaimed as "immediate" (sadyas). || 1.389 ||
Even after cutting and splitting the roots, no appearance of fruit is seen there;
yet it is seen suddenly, and that arises from the desire of another. (1.390)
From the seed comes the tree, and from that tree come seeds; thus there is mutual origination.
Furthermore, arising occurs by its very nature as something without beginning or end. (1.391)
The fruit of the mango tree is the manifestation for the bees;
there is no succession of seeds in other trees such as the *āmalaka*. (1.392)

Since the arising of contradiction is observed on the ground, in a net, and likewise in space, even here, the production of things from a void would be established by the fact that their arising is restricted. (1.393)
For it is impossible for anything to arise in a form other than its own;
the Lord of the World has established this very rule regarding their production. (1.394)

Having known [this], he who is free from objects and free from conceptual construction through the power of knowledge—how could that ignorant one, who is as if in a swoon, be liberated? He remains a transmigrating being and wanders in saṃsāra. (1.395)
The conceptualization of dwelling in the worldly life of a householder is "with conceptual construction" (savikalpaka).
Thereafter, the self arises as a householder and subsequently as a head of a family.
That in which the destruction of the intellect, the ego-sense, and the mind occurs—that is the reality, the abode of all accomplishments, and imperishable. (1.397)
He who has cast off attachment to mental cultivation and brings about the cessation of saṃsāra is led to that state by the very nature of existence. (1.398)
When the ego (ahaṃkāra) has awakened, the intellect (buddhi) becomes absorbed in the mind;
as long as it remains dissolved in that manifold and non-manifold state, so long is that the supreme state.
Saṃsāra is the sacrifice of the Sun, and likewise, the other is the sacrifice of the Moon;
because both [arise] from that, its entry is into the ocean of consciousness. (1.400)
One who perceives reality does not conceive of either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa;
how could the mind of such a person, having swiftly moved, go to that state? (1.401)
Just as the wind, having moved, departs after leaving space behind, even so the mind of yogis departs after leaving reality behind. (1.402)
The mind, however, is by nature mobile; its movement arises from that [nature], and through that [movement] it perishes. How then can the Self become unmoving and steady? (1.403)
Deceived by their own minds, men devoted to the practice of karma are liberated through the application of wisdom; of this there is no doubt. (1.404)
That which has proceeded by means of an object of perception should be known as having a fixed basis of meaning;
however, that which abides in all objects of perception is always characterized by their discernment.
For those whose minds are attached to grasping, the thorough knowledge of ultimate reality is described as a cognition directed toward an objective referent for the foolish. (1-406)

Having mastered the exhaustion of objective referents up to the remaining duration of time, one whose senses are fully disciplined shall attain the state of perfect accomplishment in all things. (1.407)
For the yogi whose mind delights in grasping, the thorough knowledge of the ultimate truth is proclaimed as omniscience in the ultimate sense. (1-408)
For that supreme state is traditionally taught as being unmanifested and yet connected;
nevertheless, for these [beings], liberation is likewise connected with the Supreme alone. (1.409)
The connection consisting of pleasure and pain arises from the physical body and the sense organs;
because it consists of pleasure and pain, this cycle of existence (saṃsṛti) is abandoned by one who is liberated through these two. 1.410ab.
Even if stainless, one who is attached to dissolution is considered to possess dissolution and is thus stained;
such a self wanders in transmigratory existence, while one who is established in its own nature is proclaimed to be liberated. (1.411)
Consciousness accompanied by signs is impermanent because it is subject to obstruction;
consciousness without signs is permanent, and that is indeed liberation.
That is knowledge, that is the supreme state, that is liberation, and that is union.
This knowledge is signless; everything proceeds from it. (1.413)
Therefore, the manifestation of this very [reality] is its signlessness;
there is no cessation, because it is always perceived through direct perception. (1-414)
If reality were something delimited by the senses, then everyone would have become knowers of reality; what need then would there be for another teacher? (1.415)
If that which is perceived by the sense faculties were not reality, then what further means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) could there be to assert its existence? (1.416)
That which is gross, delimited by the eyes and other senses, is perishable;
how can one become a knower of reality merely through that? (417)
That which is the ultimate limit of the gross is itself the supreme state beyond limits;
between these two, there exists not even the slightest difference, however subtle. (1.418)
A blind person does not see forms, nor does one whose mind is elsewhere;
because there is deviation from what ought to be remembered, even the aggregate [of causes] does not exist. (1-419)
The eye does not see form, nor is the mind the unifier;
for this is the supreme secret, wherein one who has dissolved no longer enters.
One adds something to that, and nothing more than this;
however, one who perceives it perversely sees what is faultless as perverse. (1.421)
For the one Maheśvara exists through the differentiation of all causal agents;
yet he does not attain a state of diverse forms through that differentiation of causal agents. (1.422)

By whatever form it is grasped, by that very same [form] it attains the state of the grasper from the perspective of ultimate reality; such is the course of one born into a [spiritual] family. (1.423)
Then, through the thorough knowledge of non-duality, with all impurities utterly destroyed, he becomes stainless and immovable, like a lamp in a windless room. (1.424)
By virtue of his previous aspirations, having correctly attained prosperity through enjoyment, he—though possessing a supreme form and being omnipresent—enjoys all supernatural powers. (1.425)
Therefore, an entity does not abide, nor is it dead; it is neither born nor is it discarded.
It exists as the ultimate reality in the form of that which is to be expressed. (1-426)
If that which has arisen does not exist, how can there be existence? If it does not exist, how can there be duration?
How can there be destruction for that which lacks duration? These are mutually contradictory. (1-427)

That which has not perished undergoes arising; for that which has arisen, stability is established. The non-stability of that [which is stable] is what is called "destruction"; there is no contradiction here whatsoever. (1.428)
Consciousness is not the effect of anything, nor is it the cause of anything.
Since both exist as a single entity, there is neither effect nor cause. (1-429)

Furthermore, wherever conventional usage occurs, knowledge and the object of knowledge exist by their very nature; because they are mutually dependent, [the ultimate] is lost therein and remains as the inexpressible. (1-430)
This worldly convention always operates within the domain of the expressible;
how then could speech and mind not function here in that which is free from conceptual proliferation? (1.431)
Furthermore, this conventional discourse regarding the yoginīs is here chanted;
the common world has no authority here, for it proceeds in the midst of the street.
Brahmā is established in Viṣṇu, and likewise Viṣṇu in Rudra; Rudra also is in Īśvara, and Īśvara is established in Śiva, and he too is established in the Supreme Self.
Then that is the supreme secret, then that is the supreme state, wherein, through the reasoning of authoritative words, no contradiction is found. (1.434)

Cognition arising from the sense-faculties and their objects is understood to be perception; and inference is preceded by that [perception]. How, then, can there be the apprehension of those two [the universal and its relation] therein? (1.435)
Just as one might go from village to another and eventually leave the Middle Country behind, so too, by gradually abandoning the deities, one shall attain that state. (1.436)
The word of the Guru is the means characterized by the attainment of that state;
it is the authority for yogis alone, for it does not arise from the eyes or other [senses]. (1.437)
Thus, O Goddess, this most wonderful secret has been told to you;
there is nothing superior to this as a means for liberation itself.
The Goddess said:
[That which] resides in the *bindu*, resides in the *nāda*, resides in the *cāra*, and traverses the six paths (*adhvan*);
that which has entered the upward movement of power (*śakti*), and another [state] occurring at the time of abandoning the causal principles (*kāraṇa*). (1.439)

O Śambhu, that which has entered the state of emptiness, which abides in power (śakti), and which is situated in the heart—standing in its own essential nature—it is all specifically brought down [into manifestation]. (1.440)
"Now, how does it come to be established within the castes?
Bhairava said:
I shall explain its establishment within the castes; listen, O large-eyed one. (1-441)
The wise should know that the Mātṛkā resides within the three wheels.
These vowels have been fully described; these sixteen are the great winds. (1.442)
That wheel has sixteen spokes and is inflamed by fire and wind;
O lady of excellent vows, these [deities] stand upon the pericarp, endowed with power.
O Goddess, having emerged into the fivefold space with the form of an autumnal lamp-flame,
she blazes again at the end of the twelve like the sun.
There, that power (śakti), being absorbed and beyond the mind (amanaskā), is Manonmanī;
