for as long as a moment, O Goddess of Gods, the supreme practitioner remains [in that state]. (1.445)
To that extent, there would quickly be a stobha, as well as manifold binding of mudrās, speech of various forms, and numerous treatises on the Dharma. (1.446)
At that very moment, he causes all the scriptures, beginning with the Vedas, to resound;
and when questioned, he also speaks of both the past and the future. (1.447)
One may leap into the expanse of the sky and become a lord of the Vidyādharas;
having abandoned the group of neuter [mantras], the twelve-spoked [wheel] is proclaimed. (1.448)
Through the combination of thirty-two phonemes, the Great Wheel (mahācakra) is proclaimed;
thus all the Mātṛkās have entered into the three wheels.
In the center of the heart is a twelve-spoked [wheel], where the sun is situated;
in the palate is a sixteen-spoked [wheel], where that [channel] which brings nectar is located.
At the head, [the wheel] consists of all the phonemes and is endowed with thirty-two petals;
its emergence is to be known as occurring in the heart-cakra, while its dissolution resides in the piercing-cakra.
The dissolution, however, located in the head-wheel, is to be known by those who have realized the self;
the grasping is situated in the region of the navel, while for sentient beings it rests in the throat. (1.452)
Furthermore, O Goddess, yoga is there in that stainless dissolution;
having understood this, O lady of excellent hips, one should join [the self] to the eternal state.
The reality of the self (ātmatattva), however, resides in the heart; the knowledge (vidyā) rests upon the pendant (lambaka).
But the reality of Śiva (śivatattva), O beloved, is situated in dissolution and has reached the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
It has been previously explained how [the path] resides within Śakti according to its established state;
now I shall tell you how it resides within the Lord of the Worlds (Bhuvanīśa). || 1.455 ||
O Dear One, when each individual phoneme is established in its power and swiftly enters the circle-garland, there is the attainment of mantra for those who desire victory. (1-456)
O Lords of the World, I shall describe that exactly as it is,
according to their respective authority over their castes, so that their pervasion may be understood in its true sense.
O Mistress of the Gods, hear now from me about its pervasiveness and its movement, according to the division of the three principles: Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva. (1.458)
Likewise, the renunciation of the causal factors as they are established for each respective caste;
and those wheels previously proclaimed, known as Fire, Sun, and Moon. (1.459)
The Yoginīs are their pervaders; listen as I describe their individual positions:
Jvalinī, Jvālinī, Jvālā, Tejasā, and Tejavarcasā. (1.460)
Tejormiṇī, Tejā, Tejavatī, Tamopahā,
and Tejonidhi are proclaimed as the Yoginīs residing in the fire-wheel (agnicakra).
Arising from the form of the fire of time, they withdraw the entire world;
now hear about the Yoginīs born from the solar disc.
Sūryā, Sūryavatī, Kāntā, Svadhā, Svasti, Sudhā, as well as Sumanā, Unmanā, Kāntā, Śāśvatī, and another likewise. (1.463)
Saṃvartā and Saṃharī are the Yoginīs situated on the solar wheel; they are to be known in the second enclosure. Now I shall describe them to you in the third.
Śaśinī, Śāśvatī, Śāntā, Sevanī, and Śaśiprabhā;
Śītā, Śītavahā, Kāntā, Pṛthvī, and Priyakārikā. (1-465)
Pṛthivī, Pārthivī, Prītā, Kṣobhaṇī, Kṣubhitā, and Akṣayā are proclaimed in the lunar wheel (somacakra) as the sustainers of creation. (1–466)
In each and every wheel, those situated in the station of Bhuvaneśa are to be seen;
undecaying, they sport together with the yogins who are lords of the worlds.
O Varārohā, O leader of the gods, there is no known number for those Rudras who, together with the yogis, possess the power of Rudra, when distinguished individually.
Divided by the distinction between moon and sun, and further divided into millions upon millions of parts,
they all sport there as the agents of creation and maintenance.
Just as each one has been described, and just as they are situated within each wheel,
their pervasive presence (vyāpti) has been declared by me in brief according to the Kaulika tradition.
The wheels (cakras) beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with the final letter 'kṣa' are traditionally known;
these fifty wheels alone are said to pervade the entire universe.
O fair-faced one, all of them should be known as residing within the power (śakti);
without them, a mantra cannot exist for the accomplishment of visible or invisible goals. (1.472)
Having uttered each individual phoneme, differentiated by the twelve vowels,
joined with the wind and fire, and adorned with the bindu.
There, one should contemplate Ātman, Śakti, and Śiva as being of the nature of light;
all this, having become liquefied, has gone to dissolution in the station of Śakti.
Resembling shimmering rays, blazing like ten million flashes of lightning,
possessing the luster of the rising sun’s beams, it is devoid of both decay and non-decay.
When that knowledge of time attains a state of absorption (layatā),
then one perceives that which abides in the station of Sadāśiva with the divine eye.
O Great Goddess, O Beloved, the sixfold path beginning with the worlds is seen by one situated below through the power of this wheel. (1.477)
Within six months one shall quickly fly up; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
O Mahāgaurī, this wheel has not been told by me to anyone.
O Goddess, this has been truly declared to you; it is the truth, there is no doubt.
It is a secret more secret than the secret, O fair-faced one, and must be kept hidden.
It must never be given to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who has no son;
nor to those who delight in other scriptures, nor to those who maintain hypocritical vows.
Those who are devotees of other deities, as well as those who are deceitful in their actions, who are intent on hypocrisy and crookedness, and who revile the practice of non-duality; || 1-481 ||
O woman of excellent complexion, one should not cause those who are possessed of these great defects to receive the most excellent Kaula knowledge.

O you who are devoted to your vows, he who out of negligence gives away the tradition of the Tantra is merely a bound soul (paśu) among the assembly of Yoginīs, even if he is a practitioner (sādhaka).
When a disciple has approached who is endowed with devotion and firm in his vows, devoted to the Guru, the gods, and the sacred fire, and dedicated to pure conduct— (1.484)

Having understood this, O lady of excellent limbs, one should examine at the time of initiation even a disciple who possesses auspicious marks, sequentially by means of the paralysis of bonds (*pāśastobha*) and other such rites. (1.485)
And that [attainment] is proclaimed to be of two kinds according to the distinction of falling: I shall describe first the superior, which is the "supremely middling. (1-486)
Then, once the disciple has been examined, in the presence of the Guru, the deity, and the fire,
he should cause him to hear the pledges (samaya) and those [rules] which are enjoined in the scripture.
Then, having bestowed the consecration, one should transmit the oral instruction:
"O lady of excellent vows, as it is with one, so it is with all the fifty wheels."
O sinless one, when they are joined with fire and wind and rendered well-disposed,
all these [elements] are said to perform every action once they have been brought into harmony through their source (yoni).
He by whom the Mātṛkā is worshipped obtains the threefold accomplishment.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Section on the Yoga of Inquiry," in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, a great tantra of the Vidyāpīṭha within the Bhairava-stream, measuring seventy million verses. || 1 ||
The Goddess said:
Today my birth has become fruitful; today my ascetic penance has become successful, since you, the granter of boons, have spoken this supreme knowledge to me. (2.1)
O Lord, even now there remains doubt regarding the worship of the Mātṛkās;
please speak so that there may be no doubt concerning their distinct arrangement within the wheels (cakras). (2.2)
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the worship of Mātṛkā.
The first wheel is Śrīkaṇṭha, which is pierced by the twelve vowels. (2–3)
One should place the seed-syllable of Śakti in both forward and reverse order;
one should color it with the essence of the lotus, resembling the flame of an autumn lamp.
O Goddess Umā, one should contemplate within the heart, situated inside the pericarp,
that which is shaped like a *kadamba* bud, like the very essence of a spray of water.
Upon seeing that supreme splendor, the knowledge of time proceeds;
indeed, the sovereignty of the qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) arises without deliberation. || 2.6 ||
That second [syllable] should be infinite, differentiated by the twelve vowels;
having performed the meditation upon it as illuminated by the seed-syllable of Śakti, as before. (2.7)
The third is known as Sūkṣma, the fourth is Trimūrti,
the fifth is to be known as Careṣa, and the sixth is declared to be Ū.
By the letter *ṛ*, however, the seventh is to be known;
by the letter *ṝ* alone, O Goddess of Gods, one understands the eighth. (2-9)
In the letter *lṛ* the ninth is to be known; they know the tenth to be in the letter *lṝ*.
The eleventh is declared to be in the letter *e*, while the twelfth is indeed by the letter *ai*.
O lady of virtuous vows, that which was declared as the thirteenth by means of the syllable *oka*,
and that which was declared as the fourteenth by means of the syllable *aum*, O Maheśvarī.
O Goddess, that which is the pentad-triad is known through the syllable *aṃ*;
O lady of excellent hips, the sixteenth is proclaimed to be through the syllable *aḥ*.
[10b] 25b kh] O Great Goddess, these sixteen indeed are the great path within the wheel;
they are mutually entwined and differentiated by wind and non-wind. (2-13)
It is taught that they bring about all accomplishments when they are fashioned as liberated powers (śakti), beginning with the letter *ka* and ending with the letter *ma*. (2.14)
O Great Goddess, these twenty-five wheels have been proclaimed;
I shall explain them all to you in their proper sequence, exactly as they exist. (2.15)
By the letter *ka*, the first [is attained]; by the letter *kha*, the second;
and likewise, O Goddess, by the letter *ga*, the third is proclaimed. (2.16)
The fourth is by the syllable *gha*, the fifth by the syllable *ṅa*;
likewise, the sixth is by the syllable *ca*, and the seventh indeed by the syllable *cha*.
O Goddess, by the letter *ja*, the eighth [syllable] is proclaimed;
by the letter *jha*, the ninth; and by the letter *ña*, the tenth (two-fifths).
By the letter *ṭa*, the eleventh [is attained]; likewise, by the letter *ṭha*, the twelfth;
and by the letter *ḍa*, O Great Goddess, the thirteenth is proclaimed. (2-19)
O Maheśvarī, the twelfth [letter] is to be known by means of the letter *ḍha*;
O Śobhanā, the fifteenth [letter] is said to be by means of the letter *ṇa*.
The sixteenth is said to be in the syllable *ta*, the seventeenth in the syllable *tha*,
the eighteenth with the syllable *da*, and the nineteenth in the syllable *dha*.
The twentieth is said to be in the letter *na*, the twenty-first in the letter *pa*, and the twenty-second is briefly proclaimed to be in the letter *pha*. (2.22)
Likewise, O Goddess, the twenty-third is proclaimed by means of the letter *ba*;
and the twenty-fourth, O beautiful one, is declared by means of the letter *bha*.
By the syllable *ma*, however, the twenty-fifth is to be known as proclaimed;
these wheels, O Great Gaurī, are considered to be twenty-five in number. (2.24)
At the end of the Śakti, however, one should attain dissolution; this must be observed by the teacher:
the Self, the mind, the mantra, Śiva, and likewise Śakti. (2.25)
Having known that all this has become liquefied (lolībhūta), success is attained without a doubt;
this is declared to be the seizing (graha) [of the essence], and it is sung as the power of Rudra (rudraśakti).
O Goddess, knowledge equal to the Self does not exist within the three worlds; that state which is the *avadhūta* is called *unmana*. (2.27)
The state of the word beyond conduct is accomplished here; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, it begins with the letter *ya* and extends as far as the letter *kṣa*. (2.28)
Nine wheels have been fully described, which produce immediate conviction:
the first is to be known by the letter *ya*, while the second is by the letter *ra*. (2.29)
The third [syllable] is by means of the letter *la*, and the fourth by the letter *va*;
the fifth is by the letter *śa*, and the sixth by the letter *ṣa*. (2.30)
The seventh is to be known in the syllable *sa*, and the eighth by the syllable *ha* itself;
the ninth is declared in the syllable *kṣa*; thus it has been proclaimed in brief. (2.31)
By means of the section on the nine syllables, these thirty-four [mantras], which produce immediate conviction, have been fully explained together in one place. (2.32)
In brief, the Rudras situated in the center of the thirty-four wheels are indeed the accomplishers of desired goals. (2.33)
O Dear One, when they are differentiated by the vowels, they are declared to be the Bhairavas;
they should be joined with the Śaktis and employed in the center of the wheel. (2.34)
The short vowels are the designators of the Rudras, and the long vowels are the designators among the Yogīs;
I shall state their names together with those of the Bhairavas and the Yogīs. (2–35)
Oṃkāra, Kalohārī, Svabhāsya, Bhasmaka, Prabhu, Kalambā, Revatī, Ghorā, Bharī, Yogī, and Ahetikā. (2–36)
And Dardurā is proclaimed as one of the Yoginīs joined with Rudra;
she who has arisen from the letter Ka should be known by those desiring spiritual accomplishment. (2–37)
Svadīpta, Gopati, Svāmī, Gomukha, and likewise Bharaṇa—these six are proclaimed as the Vīreśas, endowed with all limbs. (2-38)
Kaṅkālī, Koṅkaṇā, Kolā, Caṇḍamātaṅgī, and Jambhikā—these, who have arisen from the letter Kha, must be known by the practitioner. (39)
Aśiva, Darśaka, Viṣṇu, Ṛṣabha, Mūrtija, Anala, Kolā, Bhadanikā, Ceṭikā, and Karmakārikā are the attendants. (2.40)
Kauśalā and likewise Indrī arise from the letter Ga;
they are proclaimed as Sūkṣmanāma, Bhava, Vāyu, Kāla, and Bhīma. (2.41)
Goduhā, Jhaṇṭikā, Kālī, and likewise Bharaṇī,
as well as Nandinī and Nandaghoṣā, are born from the syllable Gha.
When cultivated by the foremost of practitioners, they bestow the highest accomplishment:
Diśeśa, Vigrahīśa, Arbuda, and likewise Bhāskara. (2.43)
Ānanda and Parameśa—these, O beloved, are proclaimed as the six Rudras;
likewise Harilālā, Padminī, and Nandinī.
Saumyā, Rūpā, and Candrā arise from the syllable *ṅa*; Pavana, Ekarudra, Kīcaka, Sāti, and Koḍadhi [arise from the following]. (2.45)
The bindus are thus fully described; indeed, they are proclaimed to be exactly six:
Parikhā, Sumukhā, Kāntā, Mardalī, and likewise Kāṃsalī. (2.46)
And Keśinī is proclaimed; they are established in the syllable Ca. Śivaniṣṭha, Para, Saumya, Narasiṃha, and Anantaka [are likewise established]. (2.47)
Those known as the Devamātṛs are proclaimed to be the six Rudras:
Kekarā, Hārasā, Mudrī, Girikā, and likewise Kodrikā. (2.48)
And those born from the letter *cha* are declared to be Sumukha;
[the others are] Sarvātmā, Vīrabhadra, Nidhaneśa, and Viriñcaka. (2.49)
Asurā, Tejas, and Rudra—these are proclaimed as the Rudras.
Mukhajvālā, Kālakarṇī, Karṇamoṭī, and Sumekhalā. (2.50)
Ākāśī and Bhūtalī are produced from the syllable *ja*; likewise arise Brahmaśaṅkha, Nandīśa, Īśāna, and Maheśvara. (2.51)
Devānanda and Saṃvarta are proclaimed as the six Rudras:
Jvālā, Vanitā, Vilāsī, and likewise Damanī.
Viṣṇumāyā, Mahākālī, and the Yoginīs born from the syllables JHĀRṆA;
their dissolution, as well as Bhairava and the fire named Vyoman. (2.53)
Then, O Goddess of the gods, the sixth is proclaimed as Janya;
likewise Prerikā, Gaganī, Jhiṃjinī, and Durbalī. (2-54)
Gollī is known as Vajriṇī; they arise from the syllable *ña*. Vijaya, Pārvata, Hasya, Gautama, Bhṛgu, and Pulastika [are likewise]. (2.55)
These six are declared to be established within the Kula tradition:
Pretā, Pretamukhī, Ekapādā, and likewise Nakhī. (2.56)
Jambala is the presiding deity and the *ceti* originates from the letter *ṭa*; Parameśa, Prajeśāna, Mātaṅga, and Mahāmuni [are the deities]. (2.57)
And Pulaha—these are proclaimed as the Rudras.
Kālī, Śaktikā, Kapotā, and likewise Dhvaninī; || 2-58 ||
Cakravākī and Haṃsī are born from the eight Yoginīs;
likewise [there are] Ekapāda, Vīra, Vāmadeva, and Para.
Niḥśvāsa, Adhaḥśvāsa, and the six others who possess great power:
Mayūrī, Ṭeṭibhī, Meghinī, and Meghaḍāmarī. (2.60)
Patākī and Ghoṣiṇī are likewise established in the syllable Ḍa;
as well as Pañcāntaka, Bhūta, Ṣaṇmukha, and Nandikeśvara. (2.61)
Prodgītā and Marasā are established in the tantric tradition;
furthermore, there are Dhārā, Dhātrīcarā, Śaṅkhinī, and Koṣavāhikā. (2.62)
And they are declared to be mothers, originating from the letter *ḍha*: Śukra, Dadhīci, Vāṅmati, and Nandikeśvara. (2.63)
Mahākāla and Duryodhya—these are the Rudras who are the protectors;
as well as Sphaṭī, Śrīkarī, Khaḍginī, and Dhvaninī.
Sphoṭinī and Dhūmanī arise from the letter Ṇa;
then there are Mārtaṇḍa, Kaca, Gopati, and Narasiṃhaka. (2.65)
And Bandhīśa, O Great Goddess, and Śālaṅkāyana as the sixth;
likewise Caṇḍālī, Vicitrā, Citrā, and Heruṇikā. (2.66)
Śṛṅkhalā and Ḍākinī are born from the syllable *ta*;
Vyāghrapāda, the best of sages, Narasiṃha, and Kaṭāṅkaṭa [are likewise]. (2.67)
Candrahāseśvara, Soma—these are proclaimed as the six Rudras;
likewise, Vetālī, Ṣaṇmukhī, Śmaśānī, and Bhasmanī.
Rauravī and Ghoṣaṇī are likewise established upon the wheel of the syllable Tha;
as are Dharma, Buddhi, Vīreśa, and Bṛhaspati. (2.69)
The Svayaṃbhū and Mānava [mantras] are proclaimed as the lords of heroes (vīreśas);
and we shall also explain [the mantras] of Ḍāmārī and likewise of Ūrdhvamukhī.
Hotrī, Śavanī, and likewise Vegavatī—these are proclaimed as the daughters of Dakṣa, who are honored by the gods and the Siddhas. || 2.71 ||
They should be worshipped with diligence by practitioners desiring spiritual perfection:
Sanaka, Sananda, Nārada, Aṅgiras, and Bhṛgu. (2.72)
Bhṛṅgīśa is also proclaimed as one of the Rudras of immeasurable splendor;
likewise are Savarī, Vajranākhinī, Rudriṇī, and Calacitrakā.
One should worship them in the wheel of the dharmas—Dīrghanāsā, Mahānāsā, Bhāskara, Vasiṣṭha, Nāga, Trikāla, and Viṣṇu. (2.74)
And Garuḍa is proclaimed as the most powerful among those of great strength;
likewise Hastinī, Daṃṣṭriṇī, Vyālī, Aśvinī, and Nāginī.
Kapardikā is said to be established in the wheel of the spokes;
[the deities there are] Ekarudra, Bindumālin, Amṛta, and the one named Bala. (2.76)
Śikhara, Śekhara, and the Rudras are thus proclaimed;
likewise Śūlinī, Garuḍī, Haṃsī, and Gajānanā.
Gama’s mother, as well as Raudrī, are born from the family of the letter Pa;
[the others are] Hemarekha, Mahāgrīva, Trimūrti, and Tripurāntaka. (2.78)
Ekanetra, Madhuparṇa, and the six who are indeed of great strength;
likewise Śuṣkajaṅghā, Kākajaṅghā, Jaṭilā, and Loṣṭhinī.
Bhṛṅginī and Keśanī were born from the wheel of the Phaka;
likewise, Śāraṅga, Munikāla, Krodha, and the great sage [Krodheśvara]. (2.80)
Bindusāra, when joined with the six Rudras, is proclaimed as follows:
Cakrā, Ṛju, Dīrghā, Śrīmukhī, and Sāyakī.
And Manmathī is proclaimed as arising from the letter *ba*;
likewise, Gandharva, Śaśaka, Pakṣī, Rāja, Na, and Agnika [arise from their respective letters].
And Aka is likewise proclaimed as having Rudra as his portion, O fair-faced one;
as well as Sumukhī, Herukī, Gāndhārī, and Tejinī. (2.81)
Mārtaṇḍī and Śarvarī are born within the wheel of the stars; then Mahātala, Sarveśa, and another, Paṭala Aruṇa. (2.82)
Siṃha and Kapiñjala—these are proclaimed as the Rudras;
[the Yoginīs] are Kāminī, Kāmaśāpī, Kāmadevī, and Madotkaṭā. (2.83)
Lalitā, Sarvatobhadrā, and those born from the syllable *makāra*;
likewise Ruru, Kalāpika, Bhūṣā, Hemaga, Aja, and Mukha. (2.84)
Together with Sugrīva, they are proclaimed as the six Rudras:
Kumuda, Kusumā, and likewise Anaṅgamālinī.
Anaṅgamathanī, Cetī, and likewise Lelihānā—these were the Yoginīs who arose, proud of their power. (2.86)
The lord of practitioners should worship those who bestow all accomplishments:
Triśiras, the sovereign of the Dānavas, and Hūhuka, the lord of the Bhūta-tantra. (2.87)
Karabha, Vidṛka, and another, Rudra—these are proclaimed [as the Rudras]; Gandhinī, Gandhajihvā, Tejanī, and Śubhāvahā [are the others]. (2.88)
Nandana and Kajjalī are situated in the circle of the letter Ra;
[furthermore, there are] Śarkaroṭa, Mahārāva, Pracaṇḍa, and Caṇḍarudraka. (2.89)
Kuṭilā and Maṇḍalā—these are the six Rudras, O fair-faced one;
likewise Nandinī, Kajjalī, Vīrā, and Vīramukhī. (2.90)
Mātaṅgī and Madantā are situated within the circle of the letter *la*;
likewise, Mahāyoga, Mahānāda, and Aṭṭahāsaka are established there. (2.91)
[12a] Fully blossomed are Yāmyā and Rudrā, these six indeed being of great power;
likewise Kulālī, Śoṇḍikā, Madirocchethikā, and [the others].
Kroñcī and Śūkarī are likewise situated at the feet of the wheel;
and Ghaṇṭārudra, Dhvānya, the one called Tantra, and Bahala as well. (2.93)
Hemarekha, Mahāgrīva—these six are proclaimed as the Rudras;
[the goddesses] Vedanī, Vedamūrti, Śruti, and Smṛtimanthanī.
And Dantinī is likewise proclaimed, stationed at the site of the wheel;
this is Madhukha, the destroyer of Māra, wrathful as Time (Kālakrodhana).
These six Rudras of great strength have been fully described:
Danturā, Vikaṭoṣṭhī, Durgā, and Lolupā. (2.96)
Māhula and Kohula are likewise stationed at Ṣaṭcakra;
so too are the extremely terrible Ṭaṅkapāṇi, Cāmuṇḍa, and Ghurghura.
O fair-faced one, Dhīroddhura, Atha, and Dakṣa constitute the group of six Rudras; then there are Piṅgalā, Caturā, Sīmantinī, and Sitāmbarā.
The attainment of success and prosperity has been fully described; one should worship them within the wheel:
Bhairava, Ghoracipiṭa, Yamaghaṇṭa, and Ghaṭotkaca.
Bhīma, Bhīmacakra, and Rudra—these are proclaimed as the group of six (rudraṣaṭka).
Then there are Bhoginī, Bhogamātā, Madanī, and Madāvahā.
Afflicted by desire, the passionate woman likewise took refuge in the heart-cakra;
[there she saw] Nīla, who, out of fear of her gaze, had his crest of red flames extinguished.
These six Rudras alone are proclaimed to be of great strength;
likewise are Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, and Aparājitā.
Locanī and Mānasī, born from the syllable Kṣa—
these are declared to be the Rudras, together with the Acyutas, by the yogins.
For when these are worshipped according to the prescribed rule, they are remembered as bestowers of desired fruits;
they are the twenty-four Rudras who reside within the wheels.
Their names are proclaimed together with the deities;
then, O Dear One, when they are divided by the twelvefold vowels. (2.105)
For each individual wheel, twelve yoginīs are traditionally taught;
I shall state their names correctly and in proper sequence.
Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Kālī, Karālī, Vikṛtānanā,
Kroṣṭakī, Bhīmabhadrā, Vāyuvegā, and Hayānanā.
The twelve Yoginīs are remembered as being profound and resonant;
by them the entire world, including its mountains, forests, and groves, is pervaded. (2.108)
O lady of excellent limbs, these [mudrās], which bestow all accomplishments, should be placed according to the sequence beginning with Indra and ending with Īśāna. (2.109)
If one desires supreme accomplishment in all undertakings, these [mantras] must be deposited; they must even be deposited within one's own body. I shall now explain how this is to be done.
Having placed Nandādevī on the head, one should place Rudrā on the forehead;
and both Jayā and Kālikā should be placed on the two eyes.
One should assign Karālī and Vikṛtā to the two ears;
one should place Kroṣṭakī on the tip of the nose and Bhīmarudrā upon the faces.
One should place Vāyuvegā at the throat, Halānanā at the heart,
Gambhīrā at the region of the navel, and Ghoṣiṇī in the middle of the secret organ.
In this manner, the ritual placement (nyāsa) should be performed down to the feet;
having performed the placement according to the instructions, both in direct and reverse order.
One should worship the God in the heart-lotus through the practice of visualization, endowed with the three principles and united with Śiva, Vidyā, and Ātman. (2.115)
The visualization should be understood as threefold: regarding the seat and the nature of the image.
Upon that, one should place the god Bhairava, whose face is distorted. (2.116)
The god who wears a garland of skulls, whose weapon is the blazing trident,
who has three eyes and ten arms, who is formidable, and whose seat is made upon a great corpse.
One who knows the ritual procedure should always meditate upon this form situated in the heart: mounted upon a corpse, with disheveled hair, and adorned with all ornaments. (2.118)
Having performed the worship as prescribed, one should cause him to receive the mudrās:
the three-pronged [mudrā], the lotus mudrā, and the third is the yoni mudrā. (2-119)
These mudrās of the Yoginīs and of Bhairava have been fully described;
the mantra-practitioner should display them in three ways: during meditation, worship, and dismissal. (2.120)
Having performed worship in this manner, one should begin the recitation at the conclusion of the worship.
O Goddess, for every unit of the number of recitations, a fire oblation (homa) should be performed consisting of one-tenth that amount.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa as before, just as [it was done] for the body and the vessel for the arghya offering,
so too here the King of Mantras, having undergone the purificatory rites, is placed upon the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila).
A fire sacrifice (homa) must also be performed with sesame seeds mixed with the three sweets;
by a single hundred-thousand-fold homa, one becomes the lord of the Vidyādharas. 123.
O lady of excellent hips, by [reciting] two hundred thousand [times], one becomes the lord of the sky-farers;
O Goddess, having offered three hundred thousand oblations, one merges into the eternal state.
By means of bilva fruits or bilva leaves, one attains supreme prosperity;
likewise by means of palāśa flowers mixed with ghee, dūrvā stalks, and śamī leaves. (2.125)
One attains great peace and shall become invincible.
[31a] Alternatively, one may offer bdellium (guggulu) mixed with clarified butter, whether it be of terrestrial origin or from a human source. 2-126.
O Goddess, one should offer a goat with the śrīvatsa mark, or one with the luster of a cloud;
O lady of excellent hips, one should also offer a lotus or even a blue water-lily. (2.127)
Yūthīs, campakas, punnāgas, bakulas, aśokas, bindukas, jātis, mallikas, kādambas, karavīras, and sugandhikas. (2.128)
Barley, wheat, rice, medicinal herbs, and grains;
wild rice, or wheat, lentils, and horse-gram. (2.129)
Mudga, māṣa, priyaṅgu, and likewise other materials produced for sacrifice should be offered by those endowed with meditative cultivation (bhāvanā), if they desire supreme accomplishment.
Camphor, saffron, or indeed śrīvāsa or the product of a bird (egg-powder), or jujube, or likewise the myrobalan, or whatever else is available. (2-131)
O Goddess, one should offer all of that as a *homa* for the sake of achieving all accomplishments (*siddhi*):
edible food in quantities equal to a village, and grain according to its measure of growth. (2.132)
Having grasped a flower with the fist, or a morsel of food the size of an akṣa fruit, as well as fragrant substances such as guggulu and the like. (2.133)
The wise should always perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a quantity of material equal to a piece of bone from a woman suffering from menorrhagia.
Thus, O Goddess, the auspicious procedure for the sacrificial substances has been fully explained. (2.134)
One should offer sesame seeds, lotuses, and unbroken bilva fruits, having slain a doe as the sacrificial victim;
O Goddess, these should be offered constantly, for through this oblation, they bestow success upon men. (2.135)
Having understood the distinction between rites performed for specific desires and those performed without desire, one should undertake ritual action;
thereafter, one should perform the practice, having understood the wheels (cakras) in their proper sequence.
And just as it is with one, so it is with all the fifty phonemes that arise;
indeed, the twelve yoginīs are traditionally held to be the pervaders of the fifty. (2.137)

Therefore, O beloved, he is threefold: situated on the path of the fifty letters (*varṇādhvan*) which is honored by the gods, situated within the garland of letters (*varṇamālā*), and situated within power (*śakti*). (2.138)
I have described to you the yoga with seed; now hear about concentration (dhāraṇā).
The earth-element is to be known as fivefold, and the water-element is to be known as fourfold. (2.139)
The increase of *tejas* is threefold, while that of the nature of *pavana* is twofold; that which is called *suṣira* is single-fold, and their characteristics are each distinct. (2-140)
A drop resembling Indra’s bow, marked with a vajra-mandala—by that, O Goddess, the enemy is overcome through the application of the syllable of Indra. (2-141)
In rites of immobilization, it is praised when one finds the source (yoni);
it resembles pure crystal and resides in the center of a vajra-maṇḍala. (2.142)
It should be praised during the rite of nourishment; it should stabilize the body during the rite of beauty.
It always has the form of a flickering flame of fire and resides within a circle of vajras.
O beloved, he becomes the awakener of the qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest;
or else, being enraged, he may slay his enemy who is situated within the letter *ra*. (2-144)
Through the agitation of the mind, it may burn, or consume, or else wither away, just as a drop of water resting upon the center of a lotus leaf is extremely unstable. (2.145)
O Dear One, when the fisherman [of the mind] is swiftly impelled by the wind and established in the mind,
situated within the circle of the thunderbolt, he brings about the perfection of speech.
Even in the case of eradication (uccāṭana), by means of the remainder, depending on the state of the mind, a single drop of great power, established in the wind, indeed performs [the rite]. (2.147)

The drop (bindu), having entered the state of emptiness, situated within the power (śakti) in the well-perforated [cavity], and established in the station of Purandara, indeed accomplishes omniscience and other qualities. (2.148)
And it makes the body subtle; O Dear One, there is a single *bindu* in the heart.
The earthly element is situated in the heart, while the watery element is proclaimed to be in the throat. (2.149)

The fiery element is situated in the middle of the palate; the airy element, O Dear One, resides in the sound (nāda); the etheric element is located in the space of the mouth, established within the Brahma-nāḍī.
The earth element is situated in the form of a wheel; understand that the water element is auspicious;
the fire element is in the middle of the fire; and the wind element is mixed with a drop.
The *suśirā* is situated in the middle of the *śakti*; these locations have been indicated.
It should be understood that there is a decrease of one for each individual location. (2.152)
The terrestrial mandala is known as the wind of mantra-activity; the fifth is to be known as the navel; this is the wheel of great prosperity. (2-153)
One should meditate upon that which has reached the station of Brahman, situated within the pericarp and the power of the mantra;
for the yogi who is constantly disciplined through the yoga of perpetual practice. (2.154)
When it attains the state of being well-shaken (tallayatva), then yoga proceeds;
through the application of yoga, diseases arise, and he becomes deluded by hunger, thirst, and the like. (2-155)
The wise yogi who possesses stability shall become a knower of the meaning of all scriptures;
like the self-luminous God, he shall likewise become the creator and the destroyer. (2-156)
The grossness of desire becomes like a mountain, and its form becomes that of speech;
it arises as the state of water, bearing rows of blazing flames of fire. (2-157)

The yogi fills everything, including the quarters of space contained within the wind; possessing a form like that of the Void itself, he becomes the collection of bodies at the time of creation. (2.158)
Whether of beautiful form or deformed, afflicted by disease, one-eyed, or crippled, he assumes a form at will, appearing as one or in many numbers. (2.159)
The yogi may, by his own will, manifest cities, towns, and villages teeming with elephants and horses upon the surface of the earth, and then withdraw them again at will. (2.160)
But some declare that this success in yoga, which arises as an unimpeded fruit, occurs when the earth-wheel is the object of concentration, O blessed lady. (2.161)
When properly worshipped with mantras in eight ways, one becomes a possessor of the supernatural powers (siddhis).
The attainment of fruits for each respective door has thus been revealed in its own place. (2.162)
"O Goddess, the dhāraṇās have been clearly explained as numbering fifteen.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Section on the Worship of the Mātṛkās," in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, a great tantra of seventy million verses belonging to the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*) within the sacred stream of Bhairava.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of the gods, I am satiated by the numerous seed-mantras (bījamantra) and by the various forms of cakras that produce immediate conviction."
O Lord, even now there remains doubt regarding the definitive determination of the mantras—
those mantras which were previously spoken in their numberless seven crores.
Furthermore, their means of accomplishment are accompanied by immediate conviction;
yet men, devoted to recitation and fire-offerings, suffer excessively. (3.3)
Why do they not achieve success through various kinds of vows, such as the difficult cāndrāyaṇa and others, even with hundreds of millions of recitations? (3.4)
But you, O Lord, are the omnipresent creator; what you have spoken is said to be the truth.
That should be accepted without hesitation—O Lord, how could that which you have uttered be false?
"O Bhairavī, the world has been requested by you through your illusory form.
Bhairava said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly wise one, who conceptualizes the inquiry into reality! (3.6)
Those mantras which were previously spoken by me as bestowers of the accomplishment of desires, O Goddess, have been concealed; now they are revealed again in their form of syllables. (3–7)
Established even in the fivefold [mantra], they achieve success through each of those;
O beautiful lady, they are protected by the syllable *oṃ* and by the word of salutation.
By that [syllable] being protected, those remaining classes [of mantras] are protected;
they consist of one syllable, two syllables, or four, five, and nine syllables. (3.9)
And whatever *kūṭa-mantras* there may be, as well as *piṇḍa-mantras*, others consisting of eighty-one syllables, and those of two hundred thousand syllables; || 3-10 ||
All those are declared to be fruitless, yet they are devoid of life;
for it is well known in the world that one who is deprived of life is indeed dead. (3-11)
What life can there be for one who is dead through ritual treatment?
In this same way, O lady of excellent limbs, mantras are established in the meaning of their syllables. (3.12)
"They do not achieve success through the practice of vows; this has been stated as the truth.
Yet they do achieve success when they take the form of living beings—what more is there to deliberate on this? (3.13)
And when they are mutually entwined with the twelve vowels in their distinct forms and colored by the seed-syllable of Śakti, O lady of excellent complexion, they are perfected. (3.14)
All of them have been described as bestowers of desires, all possessing the power of the flood of the left (vāmaugha-śakti).
All have emerged from the mouth of Śiva and possess the nature of protecting through contemplation (manana-trāṇa-dharmin).
Protection (trāṇa), however, is said to be preservation, and that is devoid of phonemes;
it resembles pure crystal and is free from the utterance of syllables.
One should contemplate the Self as empty, established within the heart-lotus, blazing with its own splendor, and unified with her. (3.17)
By means of the yoga of pronouncing through the *suṣumṇā*, [the breath] reaches its end like the solar disc;
then, having pierced the station of Brahmā, Viṣṇu abides in the state of Rudra.
At that moment, this yogi, though still a maiden, attains a state of spiritual exaltation;
he comes to know truly, in their very essence, all mudrās, mantras, and languages. (3.19)
Having attained the state of the Lord, the entire universe indeed arises;
yet, established in the state of deep sleep, he perceives it as a mere impulse.
When he has reached the end of Śiva, he remains like a piece of wood;
even amidst the sounds of kettledrums and clay drums, and various kinds of songs and instrumental music.
He neither hears nor sees, nor does he perceive another as a lord;
even when being cut by weapons such as swords and discuses, he is not born [again]. (3.22)
O fair-faced one, they know only a slight portion while remaining in the state of power (śakti);
but when he has reached that very power, he rises up in an instant. (3.23)
In this manner, O Goddess of the Gods, one should practice the movement of the power (śakticāra) in sequence;
through the yoga of constant practice, immortality arises for him. (3-24)
When practiced for one month, one becomes a composer of poetry; of this there is no doubt.
After two months, one possesses a radiant body and is not afflicted by hunger, thirst, and the like. (3.25)
One may enjoy all pleasures until the dissolution of all beings;
thus has this supreme ritual of mantras been declared by me. (3.26)
The Goddess said:

"O Bhairava, tell me again how the Aṣṭapuṣpī [offering] is differentiated by means of the mantras of the phonemes (varṇa), the mantras of the digits (kalā), the mantras of the words (pada), and the mantras of the clusters (piṇḍa)."
If even a single syllable, a word, or a mere fraction of a piṇḍamantra is pleasing to one, how can the worship of that very mantra be established? (3.28)
O Brāhmaṇī, what indeed are its auspicious limbs, and what are the mantras of the seat? I wish to know this according to the truth.
Bhairava said: The letter *a* is liquor; the letter *i* is desired as the Left (Vāmā);
the letter *u* is the multiformed one; and the letter *e* is remembered as Puruṣa.
The syllable *oṃ* is likewise [the seed of] Īśāna; these five Brahmās are located upon the heads.
They are called the limbs of Śiva, as well as those which are the limbs of Vidyā.
The letter Ā is declared to be the heart, while the letter Ī is remembered as the head;
the letter U is the crest-lock (śikhā), and the letter Ai is remembered as the armor (kavaca).
The syllable *A* is taught as the mantra, while the protracted *Ā* is the Eye.
These limbs are the Brahmans, indeed made resonant by the *bindu*.
The syllable *Aṃ* is the Śiva-gāyatrī; the Sāvitrī is struck by the *bindu*. (3.34)
In their own tradition, the limbs of Śiva are proclaimed to end in the suffix -niṣṭha;
the limbs of Vidyā, beginning with Brahmāstra, follow in sequence according to their essential forms.
The syllable *o* is the great lotus, and the syllable *au* is its pericarp; the syllables *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au* are its petals, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise. (3.36)
The lower covering and the upper covering of this [mandala] should be likewise;
they say that the letter *ṛ* is Dharma, and the letter *ṝ* is indeed Jñāna.
The letter *lṛ* is indeed detachment (*vairāgya*), and *lṝ* is proclaimed as sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).
The infinite (*amananta*) has been declared, and likewise the power of mastery (*prabhuśakti*) is remembered.
And he is declared to be the Lord of Knowledge (vidyādhipa) from among the limbs of knowledge (vidyāṅga).
The desired syllable should be joined with Śiva-nature; [likewise] the causal source beginning with Brahmā. (3.39)

The letter *i* is the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), and the letter *ī* is remembered as the power of action (*kriyā*). The letter *u* is indeed the power of will (*icchāśakti*), and Vāgīśvarī is remembered [as the power of speech]. (3–40)
The letter *e* is remembered as Jvālā; *ai* is proclaimed to be Vāmā;
*o* shall be Jyeṣṭhā; and *au* is declared to be Raudrī. (3–41)
One should apply the syllables of the *kalā*, the *piṇḍa*, and the *pada* at the end in sequence;
this is the fourfold division beginning with the *piṇḍa-mantra* that has been proclaimed. (3-42)
The classification of its eight flowers has been briefly illustrated;
and by means of these *piṇḍa* mantras, the ritual of *sakalīkaraṇa* (the infusion of the deity’s limbs) shall take place. (3-43)
One should place the Gāyatrī and the Sāvitrī on the left and right halves of the body, and [place the rest] of the entire collection of mantras in sequence, beginning with the heart-mantra. (3.44)
The vowels should be conceived in their proper sequence, arising from their own respective numbers;
thus Mātṛkāśiva is established through the various divisions of the source of the vowels.
The fifty phonemes, beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with the letter 'kṣa', established through their union with the limbs of one's own Brahman, are to be known as its "eight flowers. (3.46)
Through the conjunction of twelve and sixteen [syllables], both collectively and individually, the ritual procedure for those mantras which consist of syllables is clearly explained. (3.47)
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, grant me your grace so that the instruction on the meaning of the syllables and the Kaulika tradition may be understood by me."
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall clearly explain the definitive determination of the mantras;
the layout upon the image is likewise performed by means of the compartments of the directions and the groups of letters.
O Dear One, those mantras such as the Nārācī and others that have arisen in manifold ways should be understood, according to their literal meaning, as the *khaṇḍamantras* proclaimed by Śiva. (3.50)
O Goddess honored by the gods, the instructions joined with the coloring agent become the tradition (sampradāya), O Goddess; that too consists of six types. (3.51)
Pallava, yogarodha, saṃpuṭa, grathana, and likewise vidarbha—these six are the methods belonging to the path of the Kula. (3.52)
The Mālinī collection of sounds is the supreme Kaulika rite;
it should be known as the mantra, O lady of excellent hips, consisting of fifty divisions, O observer of good vows.
The lineage (kula) should be known as sixfold; I shall describe its characteristics: the Supreme (para), the Seed (bīja), the Root (mūla), the Tradition (āgama), and the Rule (vidhi). (3.54)
The lineage transmission (kulakrama) consists of six types, joined with the collection of phonemes (varṇarāśi):
the manifest (sakala), the unmanifest (niṣkala), and likewise the manifest-unmanifest (sakalaniṣkala). || 3.55 ||
Subtle, differentiated from the parts, and transcending the parts, O fair-faced one—mantra should be known as being of six types by one who desires accomplishment. (3.56)
The instruction, arising from the pure couple and mixed [with other elements], is threefold according to its divisions.
The Goddess said:
"But those mantras that have been indicated in the path of Mantra, which arise from their defining characteristics... (3.57)
O God, how is it that those who have entered the path of the Kula become known through His grace by means of meditation and concentration? (3.58)
But how is the pallava-yoga initially [established] through six modes? What indeed is the sixfold Kaulika, and what is the sixfold course of the mantras? (3.59)
"And the teaching is indeed threefold; this I wish to know.
Bhairava said:
"The sprout is at the beginning, while yoga belongs to the knower in the middle. (3.60)
The *rodha* [seal] occurs at the beginning, middle, and end; the *saṃpuṭa* [seal] has the beginning within the middle.
The *grathana* [seal] is to be known as occurring between them, through the union of the syllable and the non-syllable. (3.61)
The *vidarbha* [method] occurs at the beginning of the mantra and at the end of the mantra, O Vīranāyikā;
this indeed is the stringing of the garland that must be known by those who recite mantras. (3.62)
O Goddess, whose domain is which? Now hear the division:
the sprout pertains to the awakening of the mantra, while yoga is to be known at all times. (3.63)
O Dear One, yoga is indeed described as being for the purpose of purification, connection, and ritual procedure; thus, it is proclaimed as "obstruction" (rodha).
In the case of fierce mantras, the paralyzing of feet, the paralyzing of speech, the paralyzing of armies,
and those [powers] beginning with elephants and mechanical engines up to the end of all states that have been proclaimed— || 3.65 ||
Among those, the "obstruction" (rodha) is praised for the transgressions of cattle;
one should employ the "encasement" (saṃpuṭa), mantra-protection, and likewise the "subjugation" (vaśya) for the purpose of bringing others under control.

In the rite of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) and for all things both stationary and moving, as well as in rites such as pacification (*śāntika*), the *saṃpuṭa* [mantra arrangement] is praised. (3.67)
Stringing [the beads] is prescribed for all mantra-recitation rites, such as those for attraction and so forth;
O lady of excellent hips, stringing is also declared to be for the purpose of joining. (3.68)
In all matters, whether prescribed or unspoken rites, the minister should always act with discernment if he desires supreme success. (3.69)
O Goddess, this auspicious procedure of the tradition has been fully explained; it has not been told by me to anyone—this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Mother of the Gaṇas.
Now listen to how the path of the lineage truly is:
O leader of the gods, the supreme *bindu* is said to reside in the heart-lotus.
The supreme Kaulika [teaching] is to be known as that means for its grasping, by which the power of the seed-kuṇḍalinī performs the coming and going. (3.72)
Having then understood its end, it is called the Kaulika seed;
likewise, it is the Root Power (mūlaśakti), the Universal One (viśvī), whose nature is the cause of the world. (3.73)
O lady of beautiful hips, by means of which [power] everything that has been born, up to the very limits of the world of Brahmā, is created through the union of cause and effect.
It should be known as being in the subject (*dharmī*) and in the state of subject-hood (*dharmitva*), just as it is for our dark subject (*kṛṣṇadharmiṇaḥ*).
This, O fair-faced one, is declared to be the Kaulika [doctrine], known by the name "Root" (*mūla*). (3.75)
The scripture is your authority regarding the meaning of the Sūtras; therein the rule has been enjoined:
the sequence of the collection of phonemes is to be known according to its essential nature, from the beginning (nādi) to the end (phalanta).
O Goddess of gods, from the letter 'A' to 'Kṣa' according to the sequence of the collection of phonemes—
this, O fair-faced one, is declared to be the sixfold Kaulika.
Understand from me that which will be explained according to the sequence beginning with the Sakala:
the mantra residing in Brahmā is endowed with thirty-eight kalās.
Endowed with the city of eight, he resides in the state of emergence for the one who knows;
O Goddess, when situated in the throat, he is partless and devoid of all parts and fractions.
The mantra situated in the station of Rudra is endowed with two states;
it is liberated from the gross net of kalās and from bonds such as the bindu and others.
The subtle support is indeed known as the one called "touch," which perceives the mantra;
O lady of excellent vows, that mantra should be understood as both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala).
When the Lord of the Bindu has dissolved, being by its very nature in the form of light, the mantra should be known as partless (niṣkala), being entirely free from sound and touch. (3.82)
O Goddess, that which is subtler than the subtle is called the Subtle (sūkṣma); it is known as the Bindu in the form of a digit (kalā). When one pierces through that, one proceeds further. (3.83)
And having ascended to the upper state, that supreme [prāṇa] rests upon the support of the suṣumṇā;
it dissolves into the deity of sound (Śabdadeva), awakened by the power of consciousness (cicchakti). || 3.84 ||
For it is taught that when the [inner] time is divided, one is subject to time; but when one has transcended time, liberation is granted.
There is neither meditation nor recitation, neither worship nor likewise fire-offerings.
Free from action and its causes, he is remembered as transcending all parts (kalās).
Six states have been fully described for mantras of immeasurable power. (3.86)
As long as they do not understand in this way, how could there be accomplishment?
[The letters] arise from the heart, throat, palate, tongue, lips, teeth, and nose. (3.87)
O Goddess, they perish in an instant; as they arise, so too do they decay.
They are produced, conscious, empty, impermanent, and speakers of words. (3.88)

When the differentiated [state] has reached these six stages, it is then accepted as being mantra. Having thus understood the nature of mantra, human beings achieve accomplishment effortlessly. (3.89)

Purity is said to occur in emergence; that which arises from duality is remembered as occurring in separation; and that which pertains to dissolution is indeed mixed. Thus, instruction is remembered as being threefold. (3.90)
Touching, looking, conversing, seeing oneself, and manifesting oneself—transference has these five characteristics. (3.91)
Touching resides in the heart, while looking is located in the region of the throat;
conversing is in the station of Rudra, and seeing is situated in Īśvara.
O Goddess, self-manifestation certainly occurs in the abode of Śiva;
it should be known that this occurs through touch, trembling, vision, and shaking. (3.93)
Through conversation, there shall be a thrill of joy, and one truly understands the meaning of the scriptures;
through the mere sight [of the teacher], one attains qualities, namely the eightfold powers beginning with atomization (aṇimā). || 3.94 ||
O Goddess, when one has manifested [the deity] by oneself, one shall indeed fly up; of this there is no doubt.
Having thus understood the course of the mantra, one attains accomplishment; of this there is no doubt. (3.95)
The Goddess said:

"O All-pervading Lord, regarding this refinement of the mantra which has been proclaimed as consisting of the meaning of the syllables and so forth— for what purpose is the *atatkaraṇa* (the removal of that which is not that) performed through such refinement?"

Therefore, explain the mantras that follow the path of those to be disciplined by the Kula, arising from the root-mantra which is the limb of Brahmā, so that this [practice] may become fruitful. (3.97)
Bhairava said:
Hereafter, O fair-faced goddess, I shall explain the extraction of the mantra (mantroddhāra) pertaining to the discipline of the Kula, along with its very extensive ritual procedure.
Having drawn a square city divided into seven parts, and having multiplied it by seven again, one should cause the cells to be made, O Dear One. (3.99)
One should construct the fifty vowels with the [letter] *ru* according to the prescribed rule;
one should practice the mandala of vowels in the sequence beginning from the northeast (īśāna).
At its end, however, there is touch (sparśa) until they have reached the center—
the deity known as Haṃsa belonging to the Great Soul, situated in the station of Brahman.
The king of mantras known as Kaṣā is produced through conjunction;
when the placement has been performed in this way, O Goddess, one should extract the auspicious Mālinī.
Listen to how it exists in the form of the letters from *na* to *pha*;
one should fashion the head of the Goddess in the middle of the *ai* vowel, endowed with auspicious characteristics.
The middle of the foot, the crest, and the head situated below—this group of four initial syllables is called the *śiromālī*. (3.104)
O Dear One, the third eye should be made situated within the letter *da*;
O Fair-faced One, it should be known as being situated within the letter *na*, thus becoming twofold. (3.105)

The two eyes of the Goddess are remembered as being in the right and left [positions] respectively; preceded by *ṭa*, the nose is to be known as joined together, situated in the middle of the nostrils. (3.106)

Having hidden the *ṭa* situated in the middle and uttered it twice according to the rule of repetition, [the resulting] *ṭha* and *ḍa* are known as the ornaments at the ears when joined below. (3.107)
O Vīranāyikā, the wheel of the Goddess, situated here within the center of the *sacama*, abides as it has arisen through the left and right channels. (3-108)
The letter *visarga* (*ḥ*) and the one situated in the middle of *kha* (*ś*), joined again by the middle of *ka* (*ga*);
this is declared to be the western [letter], and that which is to its north is likewise [the northern]. (3.109)
One should extract the auspicious syllable situated within the *gha* syllable;
these five phonemes are traditionally taught for the visualization of the Goddess. (3.110)
With *ña* preceding it, it is called Rasanā; with *ja* preceding it, Sarasvatī.
One should extract [the seed-syllable] situated in the middle of the hundred [letters], located in the midst of the throat. (3.111)
Likewise, two auspicious *dakṣa* syllables situated in the middle of the *rasa* are known as the *śikhara*s;
in the *bhadra*, the two auspicious ones located on the left and right are also [known as] *śikhara*s.
The two [syllables] *ra* and *ṭha* are located on the right arms, while those on the left and right [shoulders] are likewise;
one should visualize the *ra* situated between the breasts as being divided into two. (3.113)
O Goddess, it is taught that when held in the palms, they are known as the left and right;
likewise, the auspicious [mudrās] are those where the two fingers, preceded by the bending [of the joints], are directed toward the left and the right.
Taking that which is situated in the middle of the letter *ña*, one should fashion it in the left hand as a skull-cup with its opening facing upward, filled with what is called nectar.
O auspicious lady, it should be known that in the right hand is the middle part of the staff;
this trident has been declared as extracted by means of extraction. 3-116.
The trident situated between *a* and *cha*, with its tip facing upward, is the heart of the Goddess that fulfills all desires;
O Dear One, the belly is situated between *na* and *sa*, and [the secret place] is situated between *ca* and *ja*. (3.118)
Likewise, two syllables consisting of the breasts (S and V) situated at the junction of the sound (R) should be known as preceded by Jha; this is declared to be nectar. (3.119)

O Goddess, O Leader of Heroes, the vital breath (prāṇa) situated within the letter ya is the Self (ātman), consisting of the nectar of the seed-syllable, O Goddess, situated within the letter ma. (3.120)
One should fashion the supreme mantra known as Kaṣa, together with the visarga, for Rudra; this king of mantras should be assigned to the goddess of the navel. (3-121)
O Goddess, the syllable *bha* situated between *ya* and *ma* is known as the hips, which consist of all things;
it is to be grasped as being between *va* and *śa*, and is endowed with the letter *pa* at the end. (3.122)
O sinless one, the seed-syllable situated between the letters *ṇa* and *ṣa* forms the shape of the thighs;
likewise, the two beautiful seed-syllables located at the right side form the two knees. (3.123)
O one of auspicious gaze, the two [knees] moving to the left and right should be known in their respective order;
the two shanks, however, are the left and right, extending toward the front and the back.
O Goddess, that which is situated in the middle of the six and likewise in the middle of the seven—these two seed-syllables extracted, O Blessed One, should be known as the feet by the wise. (3-125)
The two [lines] on the left and right are declared to be distinguished by their specific characteristics;
thus, O Dear One, Mālinī has been extracted according to the correct procedure. (3.126)
Of the seventy million vidyās and mantras of immeasurable power,
Mālinī is their one supreme source, granting all desires.
Because she remained there having formed a garland (mālayitvā), she is known as Mālinī;
those who have been born and those who will be born, O lady of beautiful countenance, are immeasurable in number. (3.128)
She is said to be like a mother to the Rudras and the Yoginīs;
she should be known, O fair-faced one, as the union of the unmanifest with the manifest. (3.129)
All mantras consist of phonemes (varṇa), and phonemes are traditionally held to consist of power (śakti).
Power is said to be Mātṛkā, and she is to be known as having Śiva as her essence. (3.130)
O beautiful one, this measure of mantras has been told to you;
this is declared to be the foremost and must be guarded with great effort. (3.131)
The Ekavīrapradhāna has already been described in another scripture;
now, O beloved, I shall explain to you the Aṅga-uddhāra.
The syllable *ya* is to be known as the heart; the syllable *tha* is remembered as the head.
The syllable *ta* is to be known as the crest-lock (*śikhā*); the syllable *ha* is remembered as the armor (*kavaca*). (3.133)
The letter *ca* is said to be the eye, and the letter *ja* pertains to the weapon;
thus, by this correct procedure, the limbs of Mālinī have been extracted.
But now, O Great Goddess, [I shall teach] the supreme and the non-supreme great power, the characteristics, the limbs, the extraction, the non-supreme, and likewise the supreme. (3.135)
Having extracted the three Vidyās, as well as the Heart born of the Mother, the Yoginī Heart, and likewise the Bhairava Heart. (3.136)
O Goddess, the Heart of Śākinī, its ritual procedure in great detail, its practice, and its collective and individual [applications] are all [here]. (3.137)
O beloved, listen attentively to their application:
one should assign *vid* to the right calf, and then *vāk*. (3.138)
The practitioner of mantra should draw the fourth tooth together with the right shank;
having raised the staff of the trident, it is then joined with the knee. (3.139)

O lady of excellent hips, in the southern [channel], one should perceive the vital breath (prāṇa) according to its true nature—seated upon the staff-throne of the trident, pervading the nose, and emitting [the breath]. (3.140)
Taking the Heart alone, as well as the Trident-staff, then taking the Hips alone, and again the fourth, the Tooth. (3.141)
One should again place the staff of the trident near the right calf;
O lady of excellent hips, it is then pierced by the knee of the right [leg]. (3.142)
O lady of beautiful hips, the fourth tooth is joined with the *prāṇa* ornament when it is situated in the secret place, and is not adorned by the right [hand]. 3-143.
Then the wise one, having again taken up the trident-staff in its own form, which was joined with the right shank, [proceeded]. (3.144)

O lady of excellent hips, [one should place] the heart-consonant joined with the left ornament (the bindu) together with the knee (the vowel *u*), and likewise the vital breath (*pra*) with the right [knee] and the visarga. (3.145)
Again, having taken up the second twice-born [finger], one should place the fourth, joined with the shank;
then, having again placed the trident-staff, one should place the buttock in its own form.
The second [face] should be adorned with ear-ornaments and the like;
it should be provided with a tongue and have two teeth. || 3.147 ||

The *śikhara* [mudrā] is formed by crossing the fingers at the nose; immediately after that, the *dakṣiṇa* [mudrā] is formed by grasping only the *nitamba* [fingers], and likewise again the *śikhara*.
Having likewise placed the belly alone and the ear, then again, with the right knee raised and the throat in its natural form. (3.149)
One should offer only the buttocks, the heart joined with the tongue, the mouth alone extracted, and again the vital breath joined with the knees. (3.150)
O lady of beautiful hips, the trident-staff is again divided into two parts on the right;
O beloved, these two are pierced by the one preceding the ear-ornament.
Then again, one should imagine that staff split into two parts;
then, having placed the left foot down, the skull falls once more.
Then one should hold the vital breath (prāṇa) joined with the ear-ornament (the letter *r*), again joined with the bindu,
and then the vital breath with the visarga, ending at the left foot.
Having placed the fallen skull at the end of that where the lamp is located,
there is the auspicious [goddess] Parāparā, consisting of thirty-eight syllables.
Endowed with two half-syllables and distinguished by its characteristic marks,
another [mantra] consists of three syllables and is likewise followed by an additional half-syllable.
Having joined the *prāṇa* with the nose, [forming] *daṇḍāsīna* together with the bindu, one should again place the *prāṇa* conjoined with the left ornament (*vāmabhūṣaṇa*). (3.156)
Then, the wise practitioner, having correctly understood and placed the left foot joined with the *bindu* and the fallen skull, should proceed. (3.157)
But another has been fully described; now hear of the supreme one.
The supreme [state] is to be known as consisting of a single syllable, which produces immediate realization. (3.158)
It must not be given to one who is not a devotee, nor to one who practices deceitful actions, nor to one who hates the guru, nor to the dishonest, the impotent, or the untruthful. (3.159)
It should not be given to one devoted to deceit and crookedness, nor to one who reviles with false speech, nor to one who hates the truth, nor to one who maintains a vow of hypocrisy. (3.160)
One should not cause [the mantra] to be given to those who are devoted to other scriptures;
however, that human being who remembers it for even a moment becomes pure. (3.161)
He goes to his desired destination, and having gone there, he does not return; and all movement within the monastery and on foot proceeds from this [state]. (3.162)
In some cases there may be the state of having long, hanging hair, or coming with the head [downward];
in others, there is leaping like a frog and gliding backward.
In some cases, for one whose eyes are closed, an upward gaze arises;
and by means of the "upward-rooted" practice, there is indeed a state of abiding in the sky.
Beholding [the deity] together with the deities and wandering upon the summit of Mount Meru,
one immediately attains the state of having that as one's own face, which is characterized by the penetration of one's own body.
He certainly causes the supreme true nature of the scriptures to be grasped;
and when questioned, he also speaks of both the past and the future. (3.166)
Accompanied by the left calf, she should always be offered along with one's own self;
she is the supreme, perfected goddess, as has been deliberated upon in the scriptures. (3.167)
I shall now explain in detail that other [movement] born of the mother which occurs while moving:
having raised the left foot, it is pressed by the right knee. (3.168)
Having adorned it with the *bindu*, one should employ it for the sake of nectar.
The fourth letter of the *ca*-group is mounted upon that which is designated as *ka-ṣa*. (3.169)
Below that, one should place Prāṇa, joined with ornaments on the left,
accompanied by the left shank, and endowed with a crescent moon as a crest.
The supreme heart of Bhairava is endowed with the power of Nāda;
another is the Heart of the Yoginīs, and the buttocks are illuminated by the Staff (Daṇḍa).
Furthermore, the staff and the hip are joined together;
situated in the middle of the hollow of the staff is the supreme Heart of the Yoginī. (3.172)
Mounted upon the left peak, adorned with ornament,
O lady of beautiful hips, it is endowed with the bindu, nāda, and śikhā at the left ear.
This supreme heart indeed has a crown (uṣṇīṣa) formed like a half-moon;
the penetration of Rudra’s power is eternally established therein. (3.174)
O lady rich in asceticism, I shall now proclaim the Heart of the Sākinī:
it consists of the third letter of the Ṭa-group, situated upon the seat of the buttocks (the anus). (3.175)
He too [beheld her] seated upon a staff-throne (daṇḍāsana), twice as radiant with the power of the staff,
sitting upon the tip of her left arm, adorned by that very left [arm].
O lady of excellent hips, the cave has been rendered desolate by Bhūṣaṇa;
this is declared to be the heart of Śākinī, which the knower of mantras should never utter.
O lady of auspicious gaze, their virtue, their very life, and their energy wither away and fall under his control; therefore, one should protect them as if they were one's own hands. (3.178)
O Goddess, I shall now describe to you in full the five ancillaries of knowledge (vidyāṅga), by which a practitioner protected by them is not overcome by obstacles. (3.179)
Having uttered the *praṇava* five times, the heart falls from the words;
this is declared to be the Heart in the Rudra [Tantra], characterized by the collection of all [mantras]. (3.180)
O Yoginī, this first word is "amṛta," the second is "tejo," another is "mālini," and then the word "śira" follows. (3.181)
The head-mantra, joined with the ending *svāhā*, indeed grants all desires. One should know that "Oṃ" comes first; thereafter, one should always know [the mantra] as it is. (3.182)
The *śikhā* [mantra] is considered to end with *hūṃ phaṭ* and to end with *vauṣaṭ*.
First the word *oṃ vajriṇe*, and likewise *vajradharāya*. (3-183)
The armor-mantra, joined with *hūṃ*, bestows all desires;
*oṃ harī paśu* followed by the word *śabda* and ending with *huṃ phaṭ* is indeed the most excellent.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the worship that brings about prosperity;
by merely recollecting these [verses], one obtains the highest fruit. (3.185)
Listen now to how the goddesses presided over by Bhairava are to be joined:
on a level and pure patch of ground smeared with cow dung. (3.186)
In a place provided with a profusion of flowers and endowed with perfumes and incense,
one should there draw a three-cubit mandala prepared with colored powders.
Measuring twelve finger-breadths, one should fashion that [mandala] as an eight-spoked wheel joined with three lotus petals, provided with a pericarp and filaments, and made symmetrical. (3.188)
The lotuses should not be made [in this manner], nor should the filaments be made identical to them;
the petals should be white, while the interior should be red in color.
The pericarp (karṇikā) should be made yellow, the lotus-petals (puṣkara) are traditionally held to be green,
and the filaments (keśara) are red-yellow and white, respectively.
The outer [circumference] should be made white, while the space between [the spokes] is red in color;
then, one should draw a twelve-spoked [wheel] provided with petals that are reddish-brown.
Outside of that, the thirty-second [circle] should be brilliant white in color;
at its end, a rotating line should be made, and outside of that, a square.
The pathways should be made auspiciously marked with one cubit;
four doors should be constructed, each measuring exactly one cubit on all sides. (3.193)
The beauty should be fashioned with various pigments, using leaves such as those of the conch-tree (*śaṅkhavallī*), lotuses, and the auspicious *svastika* mark. || 3.194 ||
In this manner, one should diligently prepare the written [invocation] with bells, white mirrors,
archways adorned with banners, and a space crowded with canopies and flags.
Having thus prepared according to one's means, the mantra-practitioner, assuming a majestic demeanor, should then begin the sacrifice together with his own disciples.
One should worship Bhairava there for the sake of individual glory;
that void is the Goddess Gaganā, whose nature consists of the phonemes from *na* to *pha*. (3-197)
Endowed with the auxiliary sciences (vidyāṅga) and adorned with all ornaments,
she has two arms with hands holding lotuses and is seated upon a white lotus throne.

The [deities] known as Varṇas are worshipped with eight groups of attendants (patti) in the sequence from *ya* to *ha*; one should worship and offer oblations to the letter *ka*, which is at the end of Aghora. || 3-199 ||
One should apply the arrangement of thirty-two phonemes in the thirty-second [tattva];
one should employ the supreme [energy] through its twelve divisions for the sake of the twelve meanings.
In that fourfold wheel, however, the worship is performed correctly according to the ritual;
those who are to be worshipped are worshipped by means of the rite seen in the injunctions. (3.201)
The powers (śaktis) beginning with the letter Ya should be worshipped in sequence with filaments,
using perfumes, incense, offerings, and so forth, within the heart of Bhairava.
Whatever is enjoined by the ritual rules should be performed through the yoga of the embryo (garbhayoga) according to reality;
the wise one should worship the Mothers with that which is born of the mother alone. (3.203)
One should offer perfumes, incense, and oblations to the yoginīs;
when they are pleased in the heart of the yoginī, those who are exceedingly powerful attain accomplishment. (3.204)
By means of the *cala* [mantra], all the Mothers are undoubtedly perfected;
when the *hṛdaya* of Bhairava is perfected, all this is accomplished, without a doubt. (3.205)
They are accomplished here without doubt, just like one who knows the Bhairava-mantra;
having recited the mantra ten hundred-thousand times, [the city is subdued] by means of a hundred-thousandfold fire-oblation (lakṣahoma).
Having renounced [worldly attachments], one should offer oblations of sesame seeds, and unbroken lotuses and bilva fruits;
one should cause a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to be made in the western direction, for the pit indeed faces all directions.
One obtains peace and prosperity immediately; of this there is no doubt.
For those devoted to recitation, fire-offerings, and worship, success is achieved without hesitation. (3.208)
The netherworld, the power of moving through the sky, the supreme application of foot-ointment,
mercury itself, the sound, and indeed the retention of one's own semen.
One shall swiftly accomplish the knowledge for extracting nectar, or the state of a sky-walker in dreams, as well as the transformation of form and other qualities. (3.210)

The state of being obedient and subservient to the lords who form the circle, as well as the power to restrain and favor all people, which is like a thorn extracted from their speech—[this is the fruit]. (3.211)
There is no other thing whatsoever that would not accomplish [the goal] through recitation and so forth;
one who observes the pledges, being fully endowed with the practice of vows, [attains success] through fire-offerings. (3.212)
There is no doubt that whatever you desire in your mind shall come to pass.
Hereafter, I shall describe those deities who reside within the wheel.
I shall state their names; listen to them according to the truth, O Pārvatī.
They are situated in that wheel of three spokes, all-pervading and auspicious. (3.214)
In the east, however, Mānasī is proclaimed; likewise, Cakravegā is in the other [direction].
In the north, Mohanī should be known, possessing great strength and prowess. (3.215)
O Dear One, I shall now describe, in due order, the deities beginning with Brahmaṇī on the eight-spoked wheel,
ending with Aghorī, as well as the group of Mothers.
The ears [are adorned] by the Arakāntas, and likewise the eight [deities] beginning with Aghorī;
[the goddesses] are Svacchandā, Caṇḍarūpā, Krodhanī, and Unmādanī. (3-217)
Asitāṅgī, Rurūtī, Ṛṅkarī, and Kapālikā—these are sealed by their names; now hear likewise of those in the twelve-spoked [wheel]. (3.218)
Siddhibuddhi, Lakṣmī, Dīptimālā, Śivāśivā, Sumukhī, Vāmanī, Nandā, Harikeśī, and Hayānanā. (3.219)
O Dear One, their application has been explained as before:
Sumukhī, Gomukhī, Nandā, Havīkeśī, and Mahābalā. (3.220)
Cakravegā, Suvegā, Mohanī, Daṃṣṭriṇī, Calā, Piṅgalā, Kālarātrī, Vāmanī, Harṣaṇī, and Dhruvā. (3.221)
Vamanī, Pibanī, Durgā, Viśveśī, and she who is worshipped by the gods; Vāyuvegā, Suvegā, Manovegā, and Manovatī. || 3-222 ||
Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, Aparājitā, Śaṅkarī, Bhadrakālī, Karṇamoṭī, and Mahāravā. (3.223)
So many goddesses are established upon the thirty-two spokes; whether he be a hero or even one who is weak, whoever should worship this wheel— (3.224).
After a year, having become a Yoginī, she shall enter the eternal body;
the timid one attains heroism when presided over by heroic states of being. (3.225)

Thus ends the third chapter, the section on the Determination of Mantras, in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, a great tantra belonging to the Bhairava current, situated within the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), measuring seventy million verses. 3.
Bhairava said:
Hereafter I shall explain the ritual practice for individual accomplishment;
O lady of excellent limbs, that which is established as the practice for the lower [level] (aparā).
Then, upon the triple wheel, complete with hub and rim,
which resembles the javā flower and has the radiance of the pomegranate blossom— || 4.2 ||
There one should worship the god Hara, who assumes all colors,
and the other auspicious goddess Gaganā, who arises from him and possesses three colors.
Laughing, her mind deranged by passion, her eyes wandering with intoxication,
resembling a thousand flashes of lightning, and adorned with every ornament.
In this manner, that goddess is to be worshipped through meditative absorption (samādhi).
One should worship the deity within the heart-cakra and also worship those situated outside.
Mānasī, Cakravegā, and Mohanyā surround her;
one should worship Śakra and the other world-protectors who stand outside.
They should be worshipped with effort according to the sequence beginning with Indra:
that which resides in the flesh, that which resides in the blood, that which resides in the hips, and that which moves through the vital breath.

Those residing in the throat, those residing in the skin, those residing in the semen, those residing in the private parts, those residing in the nose, and those residing in the milk—these are proclaimed as the mantras. (4–8)

Having thus worshipped with effort using perfumes, incense, and sacred threads, [the mantras] should have one's own name inserted [in the middle], end with "namas," and begin with the syllable "Om. (4-9)
O Dear One, one should satisfy the Guhyakas with food offerings and various kinds of drinks and snacks, accompanied by wine and spirits, as well as with diverse types of meat. 4.10ab [43a]
And here, O beloved, one should perform nine hundred thousand recitations;
furthermore, a hundred thousand oblations should be made with human flesh mixed with clarified butter.
The Śākinīs who are established throughout the three worlds—
whether in cremation grounds, forests, gardens, on mountain peaks, or at crossroads— are all under his control.
In these places, one should recite the mantra and likewise another auspicious vidyā;
one shall accomplish either the inferior, the middling, or the supreme siddhi.
It should be made double or triple, as established in the Kalpa and prescribed by the ritual rules,
if one desires the highest accomplishment.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the knowledge that is both supreme and non-supreme,
which, according to the ritual of the Solitary Hero (Ekavīra), resides in half the body of Bhairava.
One should place the auspicious forty-syllable goddess situated upon the pericarp; O Dear One, one should worship Aghorī and the others on the eight petals according to the division of the words.
Rejoicing, intoxicated with pride, formidable with her fangs, inspiring fear,
hideous, most terrifying, and adorned with a garland of corpses.
[She was] adorned with scorpions, vipers, and serpents as ornaments;
her arms bore great corpses, and she wore beautiful ear-ornaments.
Having the roar of the clouds at the time of universal dissolution, eight arms, and most terrifying, she has three eyes and great fangs, as if vomiting forth fire. (4.19)
He who performs this sacrifice to the Goddess, who assumes forms at will and destroys the suffering of those who bow before her, shall become equal to the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
He is repeatedly liberated from misdeeds, calamities, and diseases;
and here, the recitation of the hundred-thousand-syllable mantra should be performed in its proper divisions. (4.21)
Having offered the food oblation according to the rules, accompanied by perfumes and incense,
one should likewise perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with a tenth part [of the offerings], using ghee mixed with *śrīvatsa* [grains].
Whether it be the *bilva* or the *padma*, if one desires one's own welfare, O beloved, the knowledge should be performed in a disordered manner, accompanied by instability. (4.23)
Intermingled with the twelve vowels and endowed with the six musical scales (jāti),
one should worship [the deities] starting from the heart in due order, according to the division of the words.
In the great lotus with nine pericarp-sections, endowed with eighty-one squares,
and beautified by four gates adorned with arches and banners.
There, in the center, one should worship the Goddess with the nine [syllables] in their proper sequence;
according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should accomplish [the mastery of] all that is moving and unmoving.
And having worshipped Ghorikā with *laḍḍuka* sweets and *aśokavartī* lamps,
the three kinds of liquor— *paiṣṭī*, *mādhvī*, and *gauḍikā*— should be offered.
O Dear One, whatever kinds of flesh are desired by other virtuous beings, one should diligently offer them according to this correct procedure. 4-28.
Then, a meal for heroes should be prepared, followed by a meal for the Śaktis;
O Goddess, one should feed maidens, or prostitutes, or even those born of the lowest castes. (4.29)
But one should maintain an equal vision toward them, as toward the group of mothers, O beloved;
when this is done, peace shall arise and one attains the state of moving through the sky.
Hereafter, I shall explain the supreme procedure for the Parā [vidyā].
The second is known as the natural great wheel (mahācakra), which is mobile.
They call the third "Lamp," while the fourth is "Stable. The fifth is "Designation," and the sixth is indeed "Endowed with Space. (4.32)
The seventh is declared to be Amṛta; the eighth is the state of Khecarī; the ninth is pierced by Śakti; and the tenth is conjoined with Brahma. (4.33)
Ten and one are situated on the left foot, illuminated above by the twelfth;
these, O Great Goddess, are proclaimed as the twelve wheels.
