I shall explain their classification to you correctly and in due order: that which is divided by the twelve vowels is declared to be the natural (svābhāvika) one. (4.35)
Joined with the moving wind (ca), it is radiant and pierced by the syllable ra;
joined with the stable (la), it is liquid and pierced by Varuṇa (va). || 4-36 ||
They know that which is joined with the Bindu at its summit as the one named Space (nabhas);
it is like nectar situated in the center, together with Māyā, as Khecarī. (4.37)
O lady of excellent hips, it is endowed with power (śakti) and is therefore non-different from Brahman;
it is joined with the left foot, and the other [foot] is likewise illuminated above and below. 4-38.
That great wheel is indeed named Mahānna, bestowing great wonders;
all wheels are undoubtedly permeated by the twelve vowels. (4.39)
I shall explain their ritual action as it truly is; listen to that.
One should contemplate the natural great wheel as being white in color. (4.40)
This has been declared to bring immediate success; this truth has been proclaimed.
It is mobile, radiant like the sun, and brings about the mastery of speech for men. (4.41)
O Dear One, one should place the target within its center, impelled by the wind;
for seven days, one should indeed [visualize] the God of gods, and thereby cause the enemy to be driven away.
That which is said to be "endowed with radiance" is accompanied by blazing;
it is employed in all rites such as *stobha* for the accomplishment of the task. (4.43)
In the center of this, one should place the victim, blazing with radiant splendor,
seized by his hands and feet, and pierced upon the trident.

O Goddess of gods, within half a watch (prahara), the target goes to the abode of Yama [in death] through paralyzing, piercing, deluding, the paralyzing of speech, or the paralyzing of an army. (4.45)
The mantras beginning with *hastī* and ending with *svabhāva*, which have been proclaimed, are praised as the "stable wheel" (*sthiracakra*) for all rites of immobilization (*stambhana*). (4.46)
It brings nourishment, as well as peace and prosperity;
it likewise [protects against] fever, seizure, spiders, and the bites of such serpents.
When the mantra has been depleted, or when it is cut, broken, pinned down,
terrified, destroyed, or burnt, one should cause it to be restored by means of a liquid substance.
Thus has the nourishment been declared for all classes of mantras.
If one should desire the state of a sky-walker (khecaratva), one should contemplate the wheel of the sky.
O Goddess of gods, in the stabilization of the body and in the rites of immortalization,
whatever elixirs there may be, immortality is praised as the highest goal.
When one desires the gathering of all the Khecarīs, as well as the accomplishment of moving through the air and the eight qualities beginning with atomization (aṇimā), [one should practice]. (4.51)
One should then practice that which moves through space for the sake of past and future objects;
O Gaurī, this is known as the Wheel of Power (śakticakra). Listen now to its wondrous secret.
When he has performed the excretion, a realization arises for him;
indeed, by means of five upward breaths (udghātas), he knows it for himself at that very moment. (4.53)
One should not entertain doubt regarding the assembly of mantras and mudrās;
[for by their power] a throbbing arises in the body, and one flies up instantly in a moment. (4.54)
The practitioner causes even those scriptures not previously heard to be grasped:
the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvaveda. (4.55)
The Purāṇas with their six ancillaries, Mīmāṃsā, the extensive Nyāya,
together with the Dharmaśāstras— these are the fourteen branches of knowledge.
One understands such treatises both in their textual form and in their meaning, just as one perceives the flow of a mass of water by means of a drop of water from its current. (4.57)
No one can be restrained; likewise, speech alone is the practitioner. With unimpeded footing, the meditator is the garland of the causes and effects of action. (4.58)
He becomes the Lord of Speech in person, established within the wheel of power (śakticakra);
possessing great strength and able to assume any form at will, he may enjoy all pleasures as he pleases. || 4.59 ||
Whatever desires the practitioner contemplates, he obtains them all,
just as the wish-fulfilling gem in this world bestows the fruits of whatever is thought of.
Likewise, O Varārohā, when Śakti is meditated upon as the embodiment of knowledge, she bestows the attainment of one's desires; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (4.61)
There are seventy million mantras, and they are remembered as immeasurable;
O lady of excellent limbs, their heroic power has been revealed.
Deprived of her, O lady of excellent hips, they sport like young bulls, appearing to follow commands while actually desiring only liberation. (4.63)

When the best of practitioners practices the wheel that is non-different from Brahman, he becomes one who has reached the further shore of all the scriptures, beginning with the Vedas, even if they have not been heard by him. (4.64)
O Dear One, when the practitioner recites [the mantra] while pressing with his left foot, he quickly causes agitation among those who are divine, non-divine, or otherwise. (4.65)
The daughters of the yakṣas and gandharvas, as well as the nāginīs who are arrogant in their strength—all of them he quickly agitates by the power of his left foot. (4.66)
At that very moment, the entire earth— including its mountains, forests,
and groves, together with its oceans and islands— extended for a hundred crores [of yojanas].
One should wander [there], of this there is no doubt; this is the truth, the truth, there is no uncertainty.
As for the specific signs mentioned in the scriptures, such as agitation and the rest—
The practitioner of mantra, when ignited from below and above, performs all these acts—killing, expulsion, and so forth, as well as the severing of mantras. (4.69)
The outer wheels have been fully described, along with their respective means of accomplishment.
What else do you ask, O Goddess? I shall tell you all of that.

Thus ends the fourth chapter on the Individual Means of Accomplishment (*vyastasādhana*) in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, a great tantra within the Bhairava current belonging to the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), measuring seventy million verses. 4.
Śrī Bhairava said: Hereafter, O Bhairavī, I shall proclaim the supreme Wheel of the Soul of All (Sarvātmacakra),
which consists of seventy-six divisions plus two additional pairs.
Listen, O fair-eyed one, as I shall describe it to you:
having made the city with its central line straight, it should be divided into four parts. (5.2)
It has four gates with four equal parts, but lacks a central pathway. One should divide the first section into four parts. (5.3)
In the first section, one should fashion the pericarp right there;
in the second, the filaments are to be made; and in the third, the junctions of the petals.
The tips of the petals are at the fourth [circle], and at its end, the "rotating line" (bhrāmaṇī) is prescribed.
One should establish the thread from the east, as well as the south and the north.
In the west it is likewise, and thus it is perfectly circular all around,
endowed with four petals and joined with a pericarp and filaments.
Outside of that as well, O Goddess, is an eight-petalled lotus;
beyond that, a twelve-spoked [wheel], and at the end of even that, a sixteen-spoked one.
Furthermore, O Goddess, at the end of the sixteen [petals] there is that which is joined with thirty-two petals;
thus these five wheels are described as being at the end of the wheels.
On the outside, one should arrange a pathway with a single cubit;
there, four doors should be made according to the measurement of a lotus.
She should be depicted as brilliant white in color, auspicious, and endowed with favorable marks;
or else, having entered into the state of meditative absorption, one should visualize her within the lotus of the heart.

Then one should perform the deposition of the mantra (*mantranyāsa*) by means of the twelve-fold seed-syllables (*bīja*), according to the respective authority of each phoneme, following the sequence of the Supreme Goddess (*parā*).
The Yoginīs should be known as long, and one should arrange the Rudras as short;
O fair-faced one, a group of six Rudras should be assigned to each petal.
The six goddesses situated on its branches are joined according to yoga;
these are the six mudrās and the six yoginīs, and thus this is the group of twelve. (5.13)
Seventy-two [syllables], along with the group of six, have been fully enumerated, O Goddess worshipped by the gods.
I shall now declare their ritual placement (*nyāsa*); listen to the definitive rule for it. (5.14)
O Goddess, one should place the auspicious group of neuter vowels upon the four-spoked [wheel];
however, on the eight-spoked [wheel], one should place the letters beginning with *ya* up to *pra*, ending with *ṇa*. (5.15)
Having assigned the sixteen digits (kalās) upon the twelve-spoked [wheel] according to their number as twelve,
or having assigned them by way of the sixteen, O fair-eyed one, one should likewise assign the supports of the channels (nāḍī).
Then, one should place that which is called "Contact" (sparśa) in the center of the thirty-two petals;
in this manner, O Dear One, the ritual placement (nyāsa) should be performed, extending to the outer circle.

One should place upon the pericarp the auspicious god Ruru, who is the soul of all, having three eyes, ten arms, a formidable appearance, holding a lotus in his hand, and possessing three eyes. (5.18)
The goddess was adorned with a mass of matted locks, bore the moon upon her head,
and was graced by a high forehead and a prominent bridge of the nose.
The all-pervading Lord, whose form is thus, should always be meditated upon as situated within the pericarp;
above him is the Goddess, whose nature consists of the letters from *na* to *pha*.
Possessing all their limbs joined together, the one of great splendor plays;
on each petal there is a pair, intent upon the performance of playful gestures.
I shall state the names of those heroes together with the yogins:
Hari, Vāmanaka, Siṃha, Mahākāla, and Bhairava.
O Goddess, one should place Jayā, Vijayā, Gokarṇī, and Mahābalā—the mighty Yogeshvarīs—at the four corners. (5.23)
Bali, Balinanda, Daśagrīva, Hara, Haya, and he who is known as Mādhava—all possessed great strength and prowess. || 5.24 ||
Viśvā, Viśveśvarī, Hāraudrī, Vīranāyikā, and Ambāpūrvā—these are the names of the Yoginīs born from the womb of Ambhara. (5.25)
In the group of six, O Mahāgaurī, these are to be worshipped as the bestowers of the fruits of one's desires:
Nandin, Mahākāla, Vṛṣabha, and Bhṛṅgin. (5.26)
Sameśvara, Śarman, Ajeśa, Caturānana;
Jambhanī, Mohanī, Vāmā, Andhanī, and Kartṛ. || 5-27 ||
One should worship these powerful Yogeshvarīs on the eight-spoked wheel: Kalanī, Damanī, and likewise Pramathanī. (5.28)
Dakṣa, Caṇḍa, Hara, Śauṇḍī, Pramatha, Bhīmamanmatha, Śakuni, Samati, Nanda, Gopāla, and Pitāmaha. || 5.29 ||
Vāmanī, Jaṭilā, Rambhā, Siṃhī, Haṃsā, Gajānanā, Bhīṣaṇī, Piṅgalā, Śūrā, Gajakarṇī, and Pinākinī. || 5-30 ||
And the renowned Śikhidhvajas are established in the twelve-spoked [wheel]:
Nabha, Bhānu, Ananta, and the mighty Helārāja. (5.31)
Bhīma, Arjuna, Droṇa, Mahārāja, Sundara, Bhasmarāja, Kalyāṇa, Madhu, and Sindūraka; || 5-32 ||
One should likewise worship the four heroic forms:
Śivā, Hariprabhā, Durgā, and Bhadrakālī, who are pleasing to the mind. (5.33)
Kauśikī, Kālī, Viśveśī, Jayā, and likewise Vijayā;
Raktā, Raktapriyā, Karālā, and likewise Kekarā. (5.34)
And the Yoginīs Mahocchuṣmā are established in the sixteen-spoked [cakra];
likewise Saṃvarta, Lakulīśa, Bhṛgu, and Ceta. (5.35)
Vaka, Khaḍgī, Pinākī, Bhujaṅga, Vāli, Mahākāla, Durāṇḍa, Chagalaṇḍa, and likewise Śikhi. (5.36)
Lohita, Meṣa, Mīna, Tridaṇḍin, and likewise Ṣaḍhi; Umākānta, Ūrdhvanārīśa, Dāruka, and likewise Lāṅgalin. (5.37)
Then Someśvara, Śarmāṇa, Caturvaktra, Ekanetraka, Kūrma, Ekarudra, and the supreme Śivottama. (5.38)
And Pañcāntaka, who is fierce and wrathful, should be worshipped in the beautiful wheel;
likewise, Bhagayoginī, Citrākṣī, Viśālā, and another. (5.39)
Dāmoṭī, Kalhoṭī, Daṃṣṭriṇī, and Piṅgalā, as well as Mūlā, Mūlatarā, and Yatrā, who is indeed the destroyer of the root (Mūlaghātikā).
The *mūlakārī* and another known as the *prāṇahārikā*, the *chuchundarī*, the *ratnākṣī*, and likewise the *rākṣasī*—these others should be understood [as such]. (5.41)
Ghorā, Śūkarī, and likewise Valotkaṭā; Piśācī, Atyanāpīḍā, Vyāghrī, Haṃsī, and Halāyudhā.
Sahanī, Grasanī, Mohanī, Priyadarśanā, and Trāsanī—these are proclaimed; one should worship them on the thirty-two spokes.
Then, having performed worship for these with fragrant flowers radiant with color, with food offerings, drinks, and snacks, and with perfumes, incense, and sacred threads; || 5.44 ||
Then, by means of meditative absorption (samādhi), one [visualizes] this wheel situated within the lotus of the heart,
[offering it] with meats, auspicious flowers, and the divine garments of the consciousness of yoga.
This sacrifice, which brings about all prosperity, is the means for accomplishing the state of moving through the sky;
the mighty Yoginīs are established within the enclosure of the lotus. (5.46)
O Goddess, Supreme Sovereign, you are present here;
by the mere performance of the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the wheel, you shall become known within six months.
O Goddess, through service [to this] one attains success; there is no need for deliberation here.
But this Kaula wheel, O Beloved, must not be told to anyone.
But him who, out of negligence, makes known the Cakra renowned throughout the world—I do not favor that evil-doer of wicked soul. (5-49)
I always remain indifferent toward that lowest of men who is being devoured by yoginīs, pūtanas, and dark spirits, as well as by thieves, fire, and other calamities. (5.50)
But he who protects the secret tantric conduct, which is very difficult to attain, achieves perfection without a doubt, just as Bhairava declared. (5.51)
This [tantra] called Yāmala is to be worshipped by Rudra during the three ages;
however, in the most terrible Kali age, practitioners possess little strength.
But for them, I shall describe that which is a singular hero, extremely difficult to attain, known as the Cakra whose essence is Rudra; listen to that from my immortal speech. 5-53.
Having drawn an eight-spoked wheel with filaments and a pericarp,
one should thereafter draw a sixteen-spoked wheel, and outside of that, a thirty-two-spoked one.
Having placed two digits each, interspersed with the *jīva*, at the tips of the eight spokes;
those which are known as the eight groups (*aṣṭavarga*) should be assigned to the middle of the petals. (5.55)
O Dear One, all these [energies] situated in the left channel are interwoven like warp and woof;
the Kalās, beginning with Sumanā and ending with Śivā, are to be joined with the filaments.
O Goddess, one should place the thirty-two syllables upon those very petals; O Supreme Sovereign, they are to be deposited starting from the letter *ka* and ending with the letter *ha*.
That which is called the letter *ma* is Maheśvara in the form of the *bindu*; he stands at the head of all phonemes and is established in action. (5.58)
The letter *kṣa* is Bhairava himself, the Lord mounted upon the Puruṣa;
it is illuminated by the staff (*daṇḍa*) and further impelled by the wind (*vāyu*). (5.59)
His uṣṇīṣa is formed by a half-moon, endowed with the bindu and nāda at its crest;
he resembles pure crystal, throbbing with radiant splendor.
One should meditate there upon Bhairava, who has the form of a flame in the sky, blazing like ten million flashes of lightning, shining above the pericarp. (5–61)
One should place the wheel in the heart, for the Self of all is established therein.
O Goddess, one should practice according to this rule for as long as six months.
To that extent, that yogin attains success; there is no need for deliberation here.
Through the practice of white meditation, he shall obtain peace or nourishment. (5-63)
For subjugation and attraction, one should contemplate [the deity] as red in color;
for paralyzing, piercing, and destruction, [one should contemplate him] with a radiance equal to a rainbow. (5–64)
For killing, one should visualize [the deity] with a black appearance; for causing enmity, with a smoke-colored appearance.
Thus, by means of specific meditations, whatever desire one seeks to accomplish— || 5.65 ||
All that arises for him who is endowed with power, O lady of excellent vows;
he should contemplate the revolving wheel situated between the elements of wind, fire, and earth. 5.66ab [kh]
The supreme practitioner utters the Kaulika languages and performs many different mudrā-bindhas taught in other scriptures.
He will certainly grasp the very essence of the scriptures, and when questioned, he will explain matters concerning the past and the future. (5.68)
Indeed, the attainment of qualities such as *aṇimā* arises from non-discursive meditation;
there is no doubt that it will emerge when one has attained absorption (*laya*) therein. (5–69)
I shall now declare, in due order and according to the truth, the names of those digits (kalās) previously mentioned as being established upon the tips of the filaments.
Sumanā, Spṛhaṇā, Durgā, Devakī, Sumanoharī, Gaurī, Gaṅgā, and Atharvaṇā—Suśivā is remembered as the ninth. (5.71)
These nine Śaktis are indeed remembered as being situated within the filaments;
one should install them in order starting from the east and ending with Īśāna. (5.72)
O fair-faced one, Suśivā should be placed in the center;
this wheel has been fully described, and it must not be given to anyone, my dear.
O virtuous lady, that evil-minded person who speaks out of negligence must perform atonement;
he should recite the mantra of Sarvātman one hundred thousand times as his penance.

O Goddess, that person who has previously been impelled by Śakti and remains pure even after hundreds of births—to him [the mantra] must be given; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. (5.75)
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, you have told something wonderful that is not within the range of the gods;
how then do men of small intellect in this mortal world know it? (5.76)
"But how can those who know one birth, which is difficult to discern, know a hundred births?
Bhairava said:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the birth by which one attains [liberation] here."
Mounted upon the fire of the individual soul (jīva) and kindled by the vital breath (pavana),
one should place it within the center of the womb and smear it with sandalwood paste.
One should fumigate it with refined incense and worship it with auspicious flowers;
one should cause it to be gazed upon and perform the piercing with barley according to one's capacity.
One should contemplate oneself there, in the center of the womb, O goddess worshipped by the gods;
one should contemplate for as long as a muhūrta, and during that time, stobha will undoubtedly occur. (5.80)
Then, one should inscribe this stobhaka-piṇḍa, interwoven with the letters of the Mātṛkā, exactly as far as it extends to its completion.

One should worship with perfumes and flowers according to the rule of counter-clockwise circumambulation; thereafter, one should offer excellent incense, perform the libation (tarpaṇa), and likewise present the offerings.
One should cause the disciple to gaze at that [object] and, possessing great speed, meditate upon the center of the eyebrows;
there is no doubt that he is praised, provided he does not become deluded by the meditation. (5.83)
And then one should cause the *piṇḍa* of Kuṇḍalī to enter;
having drawn it situated within the pericarp, one should subsequently draw the lotus. (5.84)
Then, one should place the auspicious sixteen-spoked [cakra] and again the thirty-four-petaled [lotus];
having assigned the vowels to the sixteen spokes, impelled by fire and wind.
And one should worship the touches according to the ritual procedure until the very end of the limit, just as before, so that the *stobha* arises. (5.86)
O blessed lady, that person who speaks thus in a state of paralysis, O beloved, quickly reveals the womb from which he was born in a previous life— that source arising from a hundred births.
Both good deeds and evil deeds—all that is certainly known [to him].
When the disciple has been examined in this manner, one should impart the instruction. (5.88)

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Authority over the Wheel of All Selves," in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, belonging to the *Vidyāpīṭha* of the great *Mahātantra* within the *Bhairava-srotas*, comprising seventy million verses. || 5 ||
Bhairava said:
Hereafter, O King of Mountains, I shall tell you with absolute certainty about the great secret known as Umāmāheśvara-cakra.
He who knows both the word and the division of the word attains success.
*Oṃ namo bhagavato rudrāya*—this is indeed the single word for the Great Lord. (6.2)
O lady of excellent hips, the ten-syllable mantra has certainly been declared;
"namaścāmuṇḍe" is cited as the second, consisting of five syllables.
Darkness (tamas) and space (ākāśa) constitute another third station,
which is declared to consist of eight syllables and is distinguished by its specific characteristics.
And the fourth station belongs to those who accomplish all desires and purposes.
That which has been proclaimed here as the "word" (pada) is indeed the nine-syllable mantra.
And here, O fair-faced one, is the state of those who are free from old age and death, which brings five qualities;
it is briefly said to consist of six syllables.
The sixth is declared to be the station of those whose movement is unimpeded everywhere;
O fair-faced one, it is known as the ten-syllable [mantra] in terms of its numerical count. (6.7)
The seventh step is that which is unchanging in its own nature and other-natures;
it is the supreme triad of ten syllables in brief. (6.8)
The eighth state belongs to those who have subdued all sentient beings, cut off [suffering], uprooted it, and brought to an end all karmic activity;
this is the summary of the syllables, numbering twenty-four. (6.9)
The secret heart of all Mothers is that supreme, perfected state; it is the ninth, endowed with fourteen syllables, as told, O Goddess worshipped by heroes. (6.10)
The word that cuts off the actions of others and brings about true accomplishment consists of ten syllables;
thus is the number of its letters stated together. (6.11)
O Maheśvarī, this auspicious speech of the Mothers, consisting of eight syllables, is clearly established by a measure of twice seven. (6.12)
This eleventh word, which brings forth all virtues, is joined with "tadyathā" and is considered the heart of the Mothers. (6.13)
One hundred and forty-four syllables have been extracted;
it is declared to consist of eleven words, and there is nothing more than this here.
O beloved, the second [mantra] is auspicious even if deficient in words or syllables;
it is joined with "Oṃ Cāmuṇḍe," while "Brahmāṇī" is the first word.
The second belongs to Māheśvarī, the third to Kaumārī, the fourth to Vaiṣṇavī, and then the fifth to Vārāhī. (6.16)
One should know the sixth [digit] belongs to Aindrī; the seventh would belong to Aiśānī;
and the eighth is to be known as belonging to Āgneyī—thus it has been told to you, O beautiful one.
Thus, O beautiful one, these and others have been declared by the Goddess to you;
they begin with "Brahmāṇī" and so forth, end with "namas," and commence with the syllable Om (praṇava). (6.18)
When these eight [sections] are combined together, they consist of sixty-eight syllables;
this is proclaimed as the Mātṛkhaṇḍa, joined with the word "Cāmuṇḍā. (6.19)
The first [mantra] shall consist of six syllables: "Oṃ namaś cāmuṇḍe," which expresses the entire assembly of Mothers and brings about accomplishment. (6.20)
The second [face], Ūrdhvakeśī, is four-colored;
the third is indeed five-colored, Jvalitaśikhā; and the fourth is Vidyujjihvā. (6.21)
The fifth is Tārakākṣī, with two words of four syllables each;
Piṅgalabhruve is the sixth, and Vikṛtadaṃṣṭre is the seventh.
There are two words of five syllables each, followed by the eighth syllable in the state of wrath; then there is a word joined with flesh and blood, O you who are fond of wine and spirits. (6.23)
The ninth is the letter *va* with ten [vowels], while the tenth consists of two *ha*s.
The eleventh is *nṛtya* with two [vowels]; these two words consist of four syllables each. (6.24)
The twelfth and thirteenth [syllables] should be *vi* and *pra*;
*māyā*, which has the form of the three worlds, is declared to consist of seven syllables. (6.25)
The eighteenth [chapter] is joined with the fourth, consisting of one thousand repetitions;
the pair of nudas and the five triplets are clearly the sixteenth pada.
Know that *ciri* is the seventeenth, *hirya* is the eighteenth word, and *nirya* is the nineteenth; these five [words] consist of four syllables each. (6.27)
The two groups of thirty-three and twenty-one, the two *bhrāmaṇī*s, the two steps consisting of six syllables each, and then the pair of *vidrāvaṇī*s. (6.28)
The twenty-second [syllable] consists of six letters, and likewise there is a pair of Kṣobhaṇīs;
this twenty-third word is indeed Māraṇī, and the twenty-fourth is Turya.
These two steps have been declared as the syllable *ra* and the authoritative [syllable];
and the twenty-fifth syllable is the life-restoring one repeated twice.
The pair of *heri* is the twenty-sixth; *geri* is indeed the twenty-seventh;
and *ghuri* is declared to be the twenty-eighth—these three are the fourth group of syllables.
The twenty-ninth and thirtieth syllables are *ghu* and *ri*, followed by the thirty-first word, *namo mātṛgaṇāya*, which is proclaimed to consist of seven syllables. (6.32)
"Namaḥ namaḥ tathā vicce svāhā"—this thirty-first mantra of eight syllables is supreme and brings about the attainment of everything. (6.33)
O Goddess, the clear glorification of qualities consists of thirty-one words, manifested through one hundred and sixty-eight syllables. (6.34)
O fair-faced one, two hundred and ninety-two syllables more than that [number] are said to be present there, excluding the names of the Mothers.
Indeed, this [mantra], consisting of three parts, is the foremost through its mere recollection;
by the conjunction of its words in one place, it possesses a measure of fifty [syllables].
O fair-faced one, three hundred and sixty syllables are said in the Tantra to constitute the [mantra] known as Samaya, which consists of words. (6.37)

O lady of excellent hips, this Vidyā should be understood by the practitioner through the analysis of its constituent parts with great effort, by means of preserving the tradition of the Tantra. (6.38)
Having recited the vidyā once, he becomes a knower of the samaya;
then, having recited it at dawn, being pure and composed in mind, || 6-39 ||
Whatever impure thing one has seen at the end of a dream, or even [the act of] approaching one who should not be approached, one should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma). 6.40ab [g]

One who has arisen from the sixfold [discipline] and performs recitation should destroy whatever was done unintentionally by means of twenty-one repetitions; if done intentionally, he should perform double the recitation.
At midday, having bathed and being pure, facing either the east or the north and standing waist-deep in water, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
The practitioner, being composed, having recited one hundred [times] at the time of evening, shall purify external defilement within just one month. (6.43)
Whatever arises contrary to this during the day shall be destroyed; of this there is no doubt.
Now, one who is filled with devotion and a protector of the rules of conduct [attains success].
Through service, recitation, fire-offerings, or meditation, one becomes equal to the *cakra*;
O Goddess, this which has been declared is the truth; [one] arises after six months. (6.45)
Having performed the removal of defects arising from transgressions through the recitation [of the mantra], it destroys all impurity;
O Dear One, for offenses against the gods or against the guru, one should perform three hundred thousand recitations.
O Goddess, if one who praises [the deity] should cut flowers or leaves, that [merit] would wither away;
but when the twilight prayer (saṃdhyā) has been omitted, one becomes pure by performing three circumambulations.
If there occurs an interruption of the daily ritual, one should recite one hundred [verses];
likewise in the case of transgressing the rules of conduct and the eating of what is forbidden to eat. (6.48)
O Goddess, purification is required for the thousandth [recitation] when the unspeakable has been spoken;
likewise, when the killing of birds such as the cāṣa, crow, or pigeon has been committed.
O Goddess, one who has been cursed is purified; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
[This applies even to those who eat] goats, sheep, and others such as deer, wild boars, and hyenas. (6.50)
The purification for a thousand [repetitions] has been declared, just as Bhairava spoke:
"One who kills snakes, one who kills ants, one who kills fish, and one who kills cows—" 6.51.
"One is quickly purified by [reciting] a hundred [times]," so it is taught in the scripture, in the case of a dog, a cat, a mongoose, a rat, or even a lizard. (6.52)
Purification from these occurs through fifty recitations; by the destruction of sin, there shall be purification.
A killer of cows is purified by a number of one thousand recitations. (6.53)
But when, O Goddess, one who is observing a vow is killed by the wise through negligence, he is purified by one hundred thousand recitations of the Śravaṇaka, and not by any other means. (6.54)
Having killed one who observes the great vows (mahāvratadhara), one obtains three koṭis of recitations;
for a Pāśupata, two koṭis, and for a Buddha, ten thousand (ayuta).
Others may also be observers of the vow; ten thousand recitations are desired for success.
One who has killed women or is evil-minded becomes pure through ten million recitations.
For other castes and classes, purification shall occur through one thousand [repetitions] for the lowest, thirty-four thousand for the middle, and forty thousand for the highest.
The colors (varṇas) should be performed, both singly and collectively, in due order;
however, O lady of excellent vows, when one has killed a Brāhmaṇa, [the rite is performed] with fifty lakhs.
"It is purified, there is no doubt; such is the certainty of the scripture. He who reviles a Yoginī, even if he be a devotee of Śiva, is himself reviled. (6.59)
He who thus defames the scriptures, or likewise reviles a woman, or he who shouts at a young girl, is required to undergo purification by means of a thousand [repetitions]. 6.60cd–61ab.
O Goddess, even when one is filled with anger, if one utters the loud sound "socca" and recites the vidyā, it quickly bestows peace.
When children suffer from clusters of spider-bites,
boils, or glandular swellings, or from planetary afflictions, fevers, poisons, and the like, [the rite is performed] by means of medicinal herbs to reveal their efficacy.

In the Śaiva teaching, purification from a *vaitaṇḍa* is declared to be achieved by [the recitation of] a thousand [mantras], whether it be for the preceptor (*deśika*), the practitioner (*sādhaka*), the spiritual son (*putraka*), or the knower of the observance (*samayajña*). (6.63)
Indeed, these are censured due to negligence; purification is desired after two thousand [repetitions].
O Dear One, he who should loathe a bee as well as a *phalguṣa* [insect], [is purified]. 6-64.
One becomes pure by a single recitation, as does anyone else who is loathsome:
the *kanduka*, the *mallakausalika*, the *śilpaka*, and the leather-worker (*carmakāra*). (6.65)
Dhvaja, Śūnyakara, Matsyaghāta, Lubdhaka,
Gathodhika, Gauḍa, Naṭacchatru, and Chatrīkā.
Chāyākrīḍa, Māhendra, Laṇḍikā, Indrajālika,
Aṅkelaka, Kathaka, and likewise the palace named Indra.
The panegyrist, the vessel, the utensil, and those skilled in singing and instrumental music—such distinguished persons as these may appear at various intervals of time. (6.68)
O Goddess, [one should avoid] those who live by painting, those with matted hair, Khasas, Kirātas, and Varvaras;
O Great Goddess, [likewise] Persians, female children, and those who deal in Bandhūka flowers.
The Mātaṅga, the Yājana, the Ḍomba, the Hantika, and likewise the Śabara;
the Kāpotaka, the Kulattha, the Kuṭṭaka, and likewise the Goṇḍuka. (6.70)
Siṃhala, Draviḍa, Karṇāṭa, Gotuma, Pulindaka, Varṇaṭa, Bhaṇḍakākāra, and Mahārāṣṭra were also bathed. (6.71)
Koṅkaṇa, Cīna, Vāhlīka, Bāṅgala, Kāmarūpaka, Māgadha, Saindhava, or likewise Gaurjuna and that which is known as Lāṭa. || 6.72 ||
Kulūta, Kaśmīra, Jaṭṭa, Tuḥhāsavyāṭaka, Lampāka, Śvānavaktra, Kīraṇṭāka, and Trimālava. || 6.73 ||

Furthermore, since even those dwelling in the middle of the country, or in the forest, or those of the lowest castes, as well as all others such as courtesans and so forth, are subject to censure, purification is required for them in due order. (6.74)

O Goddess of the Gods, whether unintentionally or intentionally, one who desires success should perform the recitation twice as many times if it was done intentionally; this is according to the Trayāvarta [method]. (6.75)
These forms of cessation have been revealed for the sake of practitioners;
the Vidyā has been taught for that purpose, by which human beings are purified. (6.76)
I have declared this for those seeking the highest good who are resolved upon devotion to me; it shall never be for others, O sinless one, who remain intent on the pursuit of worldly desires.
O fair-faced one, this knowledge has been fully explained along with its applications; now, O Bhairavī, it shall be shown how it is to be employed according to the division of its constituent parts.
I shall likewise explain that to you; listen to it in brief.
That knowledge which was previously taught according to the sequence from *na* to *pha*, [is as follows].
O Dear One, the phonemes contained within that body are to be distinguished by the knees;
those which have the form of the womb (yoni) at the tip of the left [hand] are to be counted one by one.
Bhairava is the mass of sounds, consisting of the nature of the letters from *a* to *kṣa*; those phonemes, each individually, are encapsulated by the seed-syllable of Śakti.
The application [of the letters] in the sequence from *ā* to *kṣa* has been declared;
and the binding should be performed with both together, O fair-faced one. (6.82)
First, one should place the word of the Vidyā within the four syllables;
at the end there should likewise be a group of four, and after that, the word once again.
Furthermore, O Goddess, there is a group of four, and immediately after that, a single step;
by this sequential application and through this culmination, O you whose wealth is austerity.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should indeed apply [the ritual] for as long as it takes to recite the *kṣānta* [mantra];
the total number of words is illuminated by both the completion and the two [other] illuminations. (6.85)
O Goddess, the Mālinī [alphabet] consists of twelve [syllables], while the Śabdarāśi consists of sixteen;
by this sequence, all the phonemes are indeed distinct from one another.
When one worships the science of words (padavidyā) by means of the division of the moving wheel, it then swiftly causes agitation even among those who are divine and others besides them. (6.87)
The five types of wombs are all such that they become moistened, and not otherwise;
[the five powers are] liquefying, agitating, deluding, yawning, and likewise drying. (6.88)
O Goddess, he accomplishes all that; he shall always be equal to Śakti.
O fair-faced one, she has the form of a slumbering serpent at the end of the twelve [fingers]. (6.89)
Nevertheless, the Supreme Goddess is to be seen thus as residing in the navel;
she is perceived within the center of the body, at the end of space, both supreme and non-supreme.
Then, in front of that, the mantra, having the form of the pericarp of a fire-flame, should be uttered;
thereafter, O Dear One, the mantra in the form of sound should be recited within the heart. (6.91)

Having uttered the *śakti* at the end of the sound, with the breath slightly directed toward the middle, that [vowel] should be uttered by one with a beautiful nose, having a form resembling a lotus fiber. (6.92)
At the conclusion of the utterance, O Goddess, it should be known to be like a whirling firebrand;
therein, situated in the center, is consciousness conjoined with mantra. (6.93)
Beyond that, O Goddess, at the end of even those [rays] which are established in the directions by the millions and possess many throbbing rays, is the primordial power Manonmanī.
But when she has indeed passed away, then she is declared to be Viśvī;
at the end of Viśvā, the pervasive Lord is beyond Māyā and free from affliction.
He is Śiva, beyond all conceptualization, devoid of qualities yet the source of all qualities;
changeless yet the doer of all, transcending power, the Great Lord.
O Goddess, by this method, the recitation should be performed with firm resolve;
[one must realize] the self, the mind, the mantra, and likewise Śiva and Śakti.
All should be understood as having attained a state of oneness by one who desires accomplishment;
therefore, the recitation should be equal to the vital breath, at the end of the mantra, within the sphere of the *nāda*.
Having then understood that which does not end with sound, this is called "recollection" (smaraṇa).
Recollection is declared to be Power (śakti), which effects coming and going. (6.99)
At its end, however, is that supreme, subtle digit (kalā), which consists of nectar; it transcends dissolution, is formless, and is to be personally realized through inquiry.
O Goddess, it has no characteristic, no mark, and no measurement; it neither decreases nor increases, nor does it possess either the white or the black [fortnights]. (6.101)
O Goddess of the Gods, there is neither night nor day, nor twilight, nor the solstices; indeed, neither the equinox nor the transits of the sun exist.
Having known the movement through all states, consciousness arises;
this, O beloved, is declared as the Kaulika doctrine by Umā and Maheśvara.
And now again, O Goddess, as it occurs in the manner of play for one who is free from disease, young, healthy, and in the prime of life. (6.104)
And for one situated at the solstice of the transits, within the houses of the days and watches,
and for the calculation of the nāḍīs of one situated in the left and right [channels].
Having understood the solar and lunar eclipses as they come within the range of one's power, whether occurring during the northern course or indeed the southern course of the sun; 6.106.
Therefore, I shall explain that; listen, O large-eyed one:
two yugas, one thousand, and likewise six hundred.
O Goddess of the gods, this movement is declared to be completed in a day and night;
likewise, this is said to constitute a month, a year, and a day.
O Goddess, the transition (saṃkrānti) is obtained divided into twelve stages in succession;
O Beloved, a transition occurs for every one hundred and eighteen breaths (prāṇas).
Five ghaṭikās are to be known as the duration for a yogi who has attained self-mastery;
this is the coarse movement that has proceeded through all living beings.
Externally, even a single *ghaṭikā* is considered here to be a year;
the upward-moving breath (*prāṇa*) is declared to be day, and the downward-moving breath (*apāna*) is its course.
Having understood the movement of the prāṇa and apāna, that is called a day and night (ahorātra).
Thirty prāṇas constitute a month; that is prescribed as a saṃkrānti. (6.112)
Earth, water, fire, air, and space—these five are declared to be the spheres through which the vital wind moves. (6.113)
O beautiful one, that which occurs within the interval of the five muhūrtas is designated as the sixth; thus, six mandalas have been proclaimed.

O Goddess, leader of heroes, it is taught that there are six transits (saṃkrānti) in each individual house (puṭa), which should be understood according to the sequence beginning with Aries (meṣa). 6-115.
Six transits (saṃkrāntis) are proclaimed as occurring during the period of the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana);
thereafter, another group of six is recorded as occurring during the northern course (uttarāyaṇa).
One year is thus fully described, and one *puṭa* is likewise proclaimed;
in this manner, five years constitute a *yuga* of Bṛhaspati’s days.
Furthermore, O Goddess, it migrates upward through the union of the left and right [channels];
this transition occurs sequentially for one who understands the right and the left.
Just as it was previously explained for the left, so too it is for the right;
this should be understood by the wise, as it has been succinctly set forth. (6.119)
When the sun is situated in Aries, the first equinox occurs; when it is in Libra, the second.
Solar eclipses are proclaimed to take place at the beginning [of the cycle], while lunar eclipses are proclaimed at the end.
Having known the sun and the moon, one is then released from bondage. Subtle time has been fully described; now hear concerning the internal (ādhyātmika) [time]. 6-121.
In each of those locations, the calculation is said to be tenfold;
having tripled that tenfold set, O fair-faced one, [it pertains] to Brahmā and the others. (6.122)
Indeed, the excellent practice is the gradual sequence that culminates within the mouth of the Guru;
O fair-faced one, there are exactly twelve transitions established therein.

The wise should understand the characteristics of the transition of reality (tattvasaṃkrānti), as well as the other [types]: the transition of the vessels (puṭasaṃkrānti) and the transition of the channels (nāḍīsaṃkrānti). (6.124)
Having understood the moon's transit, one discerns between the auspicious and the inauspicious;
indeed, in the scriptures, it is declared that [the moon] is auspicious during its entry and inauspicious during its exit.
In the state of equal emptiness, there is no face; here, there is no deliberation regarding what is to be done.
That which is between coming and going is declared to be the twilight (sandhyā).
The morning twilight and the final twilight are declared to be the two twilights; likewise, midday is the solar equinox.
Neither time, nor the practice of ritual arts, nor reality, nor the deity—
supreme, perfect nirvāṇa, the ultimate reality— is established within the mouth of the Guru.
One should perform the recitation while remaining below [the breath], free from all doubts;
there is no mind, nor anything to be thought, nor is there utterance, nor even a support.
Having made the mind free from objective characteristics and devoid of both existence and non-existence,
one should perform recitation absorbed in that [reality], being disciplined for the sake of the highest accomplishments.
Even though the mind is directed elsewhere and the gaze is cast elsewhere, nevertheless, for yogis, this yoga of recitation proceeds. (6.132)
One recites for oneself and knows oneself within oneself;
one is oneself the agent and oneself the enjoyer—neither "I," nor "not-I," nor salutation. (6.133)
O Leader of the Suras, there is no fixed number or specific characteristic for that recitation;
however, for the sake of liberation, one should perform the recitation even while abandoning the rosary.
Through the recitation of the *gamāgama*, the destruction of all sins shall occur;
becoming absorbed in that and dissolved into it, the wise one should always manifest its form. (6.135)
The attainment of qualities such as *aṇimā*, the six limbs (*aṅga-ṣaṭka*), great sovereignty (*maheśvarya*),
the underworld, rising [from it], the sword and so forth, and the elixir of internal meditation (*antardhyāna-rasāyana*).
From this, the *rasa*, the *vaikharī*, and the *anāda* all proceed;
from this, one accomplishes all enjoyments pertaining to both this world and the next. (6.137)

O Dear One, whatever wealth there is in the world and whatever means for one's desired goal, all that the practitioner of mantra shall obtain through the recitation of the coming and going [of the breath]. (6.138)
Having understood the course of one's own conduct as established in the transits and so forth—namely Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, and Scorpio. (6.139)
The two bows are fully described, and the right side is said to consist of six [units].
Time is the southern solstice, endowed with three seasons. (6.140)
The crocodile, the pitcher, the fish, the ram, and likewise the bull,
joined with the twins— these, O beloved, constitute that which arises from the northern solstice.
The six seasons, joined with the two solstices, have been fully described;
however, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, the division according to the sequence of the nāḍīs must be known. (6.142)

The division of the transits through the channels, which grants all desires, has been explained; and the movement of the vital breaths within each successive cycle has been described, O sinless one. (6.143)
That is declared to be the transition (saṃkrānti), consisting of the mandala within the vessel;
it is, O Goddess, the mutual transition from one reality (tatva) to another. (6.144)
The third is proclaimed as the "Transference of Reality" (Tattvasaṃkramaṇa);
and the fourth, O Dear One, is the subtle one, which is appropriate for the heart.
Its characteristic has not been declared because it is, moreover, of a subtle form;
one should indeed understand that the recitation residing within the tantra grants all desires. (6.146)
I shall explain to you according to the distinction of the pronunciation of phonemes,
divided into hundreds, thousands, and even lakhs.
O Goddess of the Gods, by means of twenty-three million divisions, one attains perfection; of this there is no doubt.
Through a hundred divisions, purification for seven lifetimes is achieved. (6.148)
By a thousand [recitations], the yogis are proclaimed to attain renown;
by a hundred thousand, the accomplishment of the dyer (Lākṣikā-siddhi) occurs—of this there is no doubt. (6.149)
But he who recites it ten million times—even a slayer of a Brahmin—is purified;
he attains perfection, there is no doubt. This is the truth, the truth; there is no uncertainty. (6.150)
This is that which is called the *graha*; it has been kept secret and not revealed.
I have declared this very truth to you alone, O Mother of the Gaṇas; it is the truth, the absolute truth. (6.151)
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, the characteristics of recitation (japa) were indeed previously described by you:
it should be known as a hundred single utterances, a thousand, or even a hundred thousand."
And likewise, O Śambhu, a crore [of recitations] is characterized by distinct marks;
yet, O leader of the gods, the measure of my recitation cannot be known. (6.153)
Therefore, I wish to hear [this] for those of dull intellect and meager wisdom.
Bhairava said: That which is the Kuṇḍalinī power, whose form is consciousness, and who is the supreme digit (kalā).
The primordial power of Maheśa, existing in the heart as minute as an atom, is called the *aṇu* in the Tantra; two such *aṇus* are known as a *truṭi*.
O Goddess, that Parāparā should be recited as having become fragmented; Parā is said to be devoid of phonemes, having the form of the letter 'A'. (6.155)
Having understood this, O lady of excellent hips, the wise should always perform the recitation (japa).
For the Goddess who is of the nature of the subtle break (truṭi) is established as the support for that [recitation].
The vital breath (prāṇa), moving through the ten locations in succession, vibrates constantly:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva. (6.157)
Kuṇḍalī, Vyāpinī, and likewise Prāṇānta and Viṣuva;
O Goddess of gods, these are remembered as the ten locations of Śakti. (6.158)
O Goddess, O Sovereign of the Gods, wherever Śiva, the supreme cause, moves— whether upwards, or horizontally, or in his own abode— (there he is present).
Endowed with ten great powers, it should throb;
by that, O beautiful one, the tenfold process of differentiation has been explained to you.

O Goddess, when the utterance is performed with effort until it reaches dissolution according to one's capacity, that is declared to be a hundred [recitations] in the pronunciation of the syllables; of this there is no doubt. (6.161)
Established in its own nature, the Lord of the World is not to be uttered; he is the subtle substratum for the yogin who conceptualizes that form of fragmentation in a hundred ways. 6.162ab
A thousandfold is indeed declared to be a hundredfold, O Supreme Goddess;
by the relinquishing of both, Sadāśiva is the support of power.
Freed from vision, action, and knowledge, it indeed manifests in a thousand ways;
it is taught in the scripture that there are one hundred thousand divisions—of this there is no doubt. (6.164)
For yogins who know reality, only recitation (japa) is prescribed;
it transcends the hundred-thousand-fold [count], transcends the mind, and is liberated from salutations to reality. (6.165)

Always absorbed in the Unmanifest, having the nature of the subtle atom (aṇu) and possessing nothing of its own, the embodied soul (dehin) abides in pure existence as the witness of the qualities (guṇas). (6.166)
O Dear One, freed from the support of objects, it manifests in a hundred thousand ways;
indeed, it becomes ten million in this manner—this is what must be understood by those who practice mantra.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, I have previously described in every scripture the mental recitation (japa) which is internal, silent, and devoid of audible sound. (6.168)
It has been clearly stated for the sake of purification through the application of vocal utterance;
that which is prescribed for the sake of accomplishment is established within the heart in one's own conduct.
The mental yoga, for the sake of the cause, is devoid of both [extremes]; it transcends the mind, O Great Goddess, and is the giver of liberation—of this there is no doubt. (6.170)
Thus, O Goddess, the recitation (japa) has been fully explained as being equal to the vital breath (prāṇa).
One who desires both visible and invisible fruits should perform the recitation as being identical to the vital breath. (6.171)
The non-syllable has been proclaimed by me to you through its union with syllables;
furthermore, another supreme essence of mantra has been told.
The supreme characteristic of the Goddess, as well as the *Yoginīhṛdaya*, has come down through the lineage of oral transmission; it is not to be written in a book. (6.173)
But the Kula, O Goddess, is the Kaulika, which has come down here through the Kula tradition;
yet the hidden meaning of the Kula and the Kaulika is not obtained, O Goddess. (6.174)
The Kulaja and Kaulika [teachings] have been attained by the heroes who are its parts;
furthermore, that attainment is divided again into three types according to their distinctions. (6.175)
The oral instruction (upadeśa) is the first, the tradition (saṃpradāya) is the second, and the Kaulika is the third; learn from me whose [lineage] has descended. (6.176)

O fair-faced one, those oral instructions which were obtained in the house of the Yoginīs, and those traditions spoken by Śiva which were received from the deities of the Yoginīs—[these have been taught]. (6.177)
"Those who have been granted [the teachings] by the Khecarīs and Yoginīs are Kaulikas; of this there is no doubt.
Thus has this distinction been described for one who practices with the moving seed-syllable (calabīja).
There is no doubt that [the power] arises from one hundred thousand recitations; it is attained through the recitation of a hundred thousand.
She is declared to be "Moving Power" (calaśakti) as illustrated by her defining characteristics.
Due to the combination of vowels and consonants, Mālinī is proclaimed; and those which occur through the various divisions of words, O fair-faced one, are innumerable. (6.180)
This is declared to be that *graha* which produces immediate conviction;
O beloved, this Umāmāheśvara has not been told by me to anyone.
He who constantly recites this, O Goddess, becomes beloved by the Yoginīs;
even a slayer of a Brahmin is purified within six months—of this there is no doubt. (6.182)
Success is achieved here, there is no doubt, when one gazes upon that which is stainless, peaceful, and of the nature of light with great splendor from the center of the wheel. 6-183a-b.
But at the end of the single utterance, the supreme state (parāvasthā) is proclaimed;
it is declared to have one hundred divisions, and its qualities are tenfold.
That which is called the "thousand-fold division" is remembered as being a hundred times a hundred thousand;
and the characteristic of the "hundred million-fold division," O lady of excellent complexion, is as follows.
This procedure for recitation has been told to you, O beautiful one;
now listen as I describe the various types of recitation counts, such as the *muktaka* and others.
The *muktaka*, the *yuktaka*, and another known as the *calacakra*, as well as that called the *calacakrapada*—recitation (*japa*) is said to be of these four kinds. (6.187)
The *muktaka* is said to have one hundred varieties; the *yuktaka* is remembered as having ten times that number.
By means of the division of the moving wheel (*calacakra*), it is declared to have one hundred thousand varieties.
O fair-faced one, the division into ten million types has been described externally by means of what is called the wheel of moving feet; now hear the internal division.
In the state of manifestation (udbhava), the wise know there are one hundred divisions; in the remainder, a thousand.
In the state of dissolution (laya), there are indeed one hundred thousand divisions; but in that which transcends dissolution (layātīta), there are ten million.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Viśvī are proclaimed;
and Icchā, Jñānā, Kriyā, and Śāntā, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, in due order. (6.191)

Having understood the movement and course of the self, the wise should always perform the recitation (japa) by means of this external thread, which is characterized by the marks of a hundred thousand.
O Varārohā, in that which is called Bhuvana and likewise in that which is called Śakti,
recitation is declared to be supreme when divided according to movement and utterance.
The garland is said to consist of fifty [letters]; the thread is Śakti, whose essence is Śiva.
The stringing is the goddess Kuṇḍalinī; at the end of dissolution, Meru is established.
O Goddess, this rosary, whose essence is Śiva, must be kept most secret;
it should never be made public, nor should one ever cross over the *meru* bead.
O fair-faced one, those rosaries made of gems that are remembered as excellent include conch, crystal, rudrākṣa, putrañjīva, and karkandhu, among others. (6.196)
Therein no deity exists, nor mantra, nor even consciousness;
wherever the garland is placed, O beloved, no fault is found. (6.197)
O Goddess, when the placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa) has been established, one must indeed cause it to be kept secret.
O fair-faced one, where else must the body be caused to be kept secret?

For when the self has its body made complete through the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*), just as it would not be appropriate for that [self] to remain unprotected, so too is the garland of syllables [to be protected]. (6.199)
The scripture states that the senses are the eyes; she is remembered as Kuṇḍalinī.
She is the supreme, subtle power (kalā), who flows with nectar. (6.200)
Because it effects conjunction in space, it is celebrated as the "thread" (sūtra);
and that which is called the "rosary of the senses" (cākṣamālikā) is for the purpose of grasping numbers. (6.201)
In what does she arise, and how many ways is she revealed?
The first is said to be born from a conch shell, and the second is made of crystal. (6.202)
The third is born from lotus seeds; that which is called rudrākṣa is the fourth;
the fifth should be known as born from jīva seeds; and the sixth would be made of coral.
Know that the seventh is the pearl (mauktikā) and the eighth is remembered as the lapis lazuli (vaidūryā);
the ninth is the sapphire (indranīlā), and the tenth is the great sapphire (mahānīlā).
The eleventh is known as Padmarāga; the twelfth is considered to be born from Ariṣṭa;
the thirteenth is born from bone; and the fourteenth is born from Nāga. (6.205)
O Dear One, on the fifteenth day [the image] is made of bell-metal, while on the sixteenth it is made of iron;
on the seventeenth it is made of gold—thus the distinctions of desire are now described.
Whichever garland is recommended for the practice of recitation (japa) for whichever specific desire:
a garland made of conch-shell is for the sake of prosperity, while one of crystal is for the sake of liberation.
O Dear One, the lotus-seed beads are said to be born from the lotus and bestow fortune and nourishment;
through rudrākṣa beads one attains perfection, as well as the state of the sky-farer (khecarī).
O sinless one, it is always to be known as Gopati;
it is celebrated as Jīvaka, and for that reason it is designated as Putrajīvaka. (6.209)
Those made of coral are for rites of subjugation, while those of pearl grant all desires;
likewise those of lapis lazuli, those called sapphire, and those originating from the great blue gem.
A garland made of rubies bestows threefold accomplishment; as for other garlands made of gems that are mentioned, O Supreme Goddess, [they likewise grant success].
These are always prescribed; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
The rosary known as the *riṣṭaka* is recommended for the practice of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*). (6.212)
A garland made of bones is for the purpose of eradication; it is desired for great accomplishment.
A garland made of snakes is for the sake of attaining the siddhi of the nāgas; one made of lead is for cruel rites.
The iron one is for the purpose of a treasure, and the golden one for the accomplishment of fire;
these garlands have been described to you, and another is also recorded as being a mixture of them.
O Goddess, that [mudrā] is praised for killing, as well as for paralyzing and bewildering; it should be employed for shaking, destroying, and for malevolent rites (abhicāra).
In this way, although others have also been mentioned, the one born from a conch is the best among them;
it is praised for all undertakings and is commended for the practice of recitation.
These eighteen beads have been described as being situated externally;
now learn from me how they are also present within the self. (6.217)
Having perceived the internal as external and the external as established within the internal,
he who knows this shall attain accomplishment, being permeated by the state of existence that is that very reality.
I have already previously explained the single internal Sūtra;
it is the channel known as Saṃkhyāvartā, which is situated at the end of the crest-lock (śikhā).
Therefore, O fair-faced one, it is said that the rosary made of conch-shell is the best;
that which splits at the head and spreads out in two ways is likewise excellent. (6.220)
That crystal has been indicated by you as being established in the mouth of the Guru;
it resides eternally in the lotus of the heart, awakening the senses. (6.221)
A rosary made of lotus seeds is proclaimed in every scripture;
Rudra is known as the state of Raudrī, and he is established at the end of the palate.
Endowed with the subtle elements (tanmātra) of sound, touch, taste, form, and smell,
it proceeds toward the state of transformation, characterized by the nature of cessation.
Therefore, the recitation with a rosary of rudrākṣa beads is declared to be the most excellent;
having placed the sleeping amṛtakuṇḍalin within the belly like a son, [one should perform it]. (6.224)
O beautiful lady, by that [power], this living being is led upwards and downwards,
from the state of the sky-farer up to the sphere of its dissolution.
She shines with the splendor of becoming and non-becoming, her form consisting of the bliss of her own state;
her appearance is like a fine thread of wool, radiant with the glow of vermilion-red.

Having entered through the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) and having contemplated that which abides in Brahma— the nature of consciousness— with single-minded devotion, one should then proceed, remaining deeply concealed.
One should enter the foundation-mandala by way of one's own aperture of Brahma;
it should be contemplated as having entered into the self until it reaches a state of dissolution.

Through the yoga of constant practice, the attraction of consciousness (*cidākṛṣṭi*) will certainly occur. Therefore, O Goddess, trees are indeed said to be [the means] for the attraction of the garland (*mālākṛṣṭi*). (6.229)
Abiding in silence, they contemplate everything, having been liberated from the accumulation of the web of speech;
therefore, those garlands born of pearls are supreme, bringing about the attainment of all things. (6.230)
Having cast the fivefold enemy into this wheel, which is established as the nature of Brahman,
one should recite [the mantra] with a rosary of lapis lazuli, having truly conquered that which has gone outside.
The sense faculties are extremely difficult to subdue, fickle, and greedy; being attached to their own respective objects, one should cause them to abide in the abode of the causal [reality].
The self would become a great jewel, colored by black karma;
here in this body, which has existed since beginningless existence, they have attained the state of substantial reality. (6.233)
O Beloved, that very [wind], when colored by ruby (padmarāga), wanders like one intoxicated through the eight petals; one should recognize it by its very nature.

Those who have attained the state of Indra and are intensely eager for enjoyments and sovereignty—such as the wielders of the *haṭha* weapon, charioteers, servants, and those belonging to the earth and other realms—strive for [this]. (6.235)
When the fire-element is disturbed, one suffers from burning sensations, emaciation, fainting, and fever; or else, the faculty of cognition functions with respect to its intended objects. (6.236)
In the southern direction, there shall be a southern roar, harsh with anger and egoism, crying out, "Strike!
Slay! Cut! Pierce! Destroy the one who speaks words dear to unrighteousness! (6.237)
In the southwest (nairṛta) direction, there is the nature of a *rākṣasa*, greedy for raw flesh and meat;
he is a consumer of all things, a destroyer on land, joyful at the outset, and always happy. (6.238)
The protector beholds one who has the arrow of desire for pleasant impressions among all beings;
one who is always agitated by the wind-like leaf, longing to travel to another land; one who, though agitated by fear, gazes again as if at nectar;
and one who, being of a righteous character and firm in vows, constantly attains wealth through the Yakṣa.
One who is fond of meritorious works (pūrta-dharma), an enjoyer of pleasures, and one who converses with women;
in this [state], there is a disposition directed toward the Lord, and a love for stories of sacred pilgrimage sites (puṇya-tīrtha). || 6.241 ||
One should serve the gods, the fire, and the guru, being ever eager for acts of worship; when one has taken refuge in this [discipline], one should be free from longing for desires and greed. (6.242)
Abiding within the pericarp, knowledge proceeds in all directions;
by that, he perceives the measure [of reality], being conquered by the cleansing of the instruments. One should offer the respective entities;
a rosary made of sapphire and ruby bestows the goals of the gods. (6.244)
O Goddess, they constantly experience many portents consisting of both pleasure and pain, which are their own previously earned [karma] from the past. (6.245)
The garland known as *riṣṭaka* is said to exist in immeasurable numbers in other states of existence;
furthermore, three hundred and sixty bones remain situated separately. (6.246)
When this thread of consciousness has been honored by the thread of power (śaktisūtra) and has established its station in the abode of Brahman, it attains the range of those qualities.
By means of the yoga of the serpent’s movement, she has ascended upwards through those whose nature is dissolution;
therefore, the garland consists of serpents and bestows the siddhi of the serpents.
Having severed that action consisting of defects and disease, one attains equality and the state of oneness with the Cause; for by wearing a garland of limbs, one becomes a beast. (6.249)
That power which has become liquefied (lolībhūtā) and, having destroyed the succession of sins, has departed—
therefore, a rosary made of metal (lohātmikā) is praised for the accomplishment of the ritual injunctions.
Having thus meditated upon that self, which is seized by impurity, as being like a foul-smelling corpse, one who has entered the fire-wheel should subsequently vomit it out using the six flavors.
Just as one who has moved elsewhere does not waver from that place, so should one withdraw the mind;
having become absorbed in that and merged with it, one shines like gold. (6.252)
One should always meditate with perfect stillness upon that which resides within the unity of the cause;
through the power of the mixed garland, one attains the state of its qualities.
O Supreme Goddess, all those synonyms such as these, which are traditionally taught by means of the rosary of the senses, are said to belong to the Self alone.
The procedure for the rosary is proclaimed for those who correctly understand the meaning of the tantras;
having established the method as prescribed, one should then begin the sacrifice. (6.255)
Now I shall explain the ritual placement (*nyāsa*); listen to it in its true nature, O beautiful one: it is innate, mobile, radiant, stable, and fluid. (6.256)
The mere nyāsa is declared to be sixfold, according to twelve divisions.
Śakti is declared to be sixfold, while the supreme one is the auspicious single-syllabled [mantra].
Kuṇḍalinī, situated in the region of the navel, is that supreme one whose form is space;
as the supreme, she is singular, subtle, imperishable, and consists of radiant energy.

Furthermore, this supreme digit (kalā), devoid of the six phonemes, should be understood as situated in the station of Brahmā; it is described as being in a state of sleep, which is called the natural state.
In the station of Viṣṇu she is called Calā; in the station of Rudra she is Dīptā;
in Īśvara she is known as Sthira; and in the station called Nāda she is Dravasambhavā.
She who abides as power and whose form is like the sky should be known by those who know the reality;
she is the support of the qualities such as *aṇimā*, possessed of six attributes, and the awakener of the *guṇas*. (6.261)
Pervasive, having the nature of space, infinite, and not dependent on a protector;
she is both the uniter and the disuniter, established within the qualities of the six states of existence.
The one and only supreme power (parā śakti) exists as such according to the differentiation of its functions;
there may be a distinction due to the differentiation of functions, but there is no distinction from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha). || 6-263 ||
Thus, O Goddess, this nyāsa is remembered as proceeding within the inner self;
in the outer self, it consists of the forms of the phonemes, being both one and manifold. (6.264)
The deposition (nyāsa) in the *gamāgama* is said to be sixfold, by way of twelve divisions.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Extraction of the Samaya," in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, a great tantra of the Bhairava-stream, belonging to the Vidyāpīṭha, measuring seventy million verses.
The Goddess said:
O Lord, I desire to hear in truth about the Umā-Māheśvara-cakra and the accomplishment of the Vidyā according to the ritual procedure for Ekavīrā.
O Lord, tell me how she, endowed with her own limbs and surrounded by the Mothers, is to be joined together by me.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim that essence which faces every direction;
I shall explain it fully, so listen, O large-eyed one. (7-3)
Having drawn an eight-spoked wheel provided with a pericarp and filaments,
one should then draw a twelve-spoked wheel, and after that, a twenty-four-petaled one.
O Bhairava, one should place the god Śabdarāśi in the pericarp;
Umā, who occupies half of his body, exists in the form of the letters from Na to Pha.
The Lord who is half-female, three-eyed, holding a lotus in his hand,
endowed with all ornaments, and adorned with a crown of matted hair.
The Goddess, who assumes such a form and destroys the suffering of those who bow before her,
should be meditated upon as delighting in food and drink, adorned with necklaces, bracelets, and earrings.
In such a form, one should install Mārtaṇḍabhairava;
O Goddess, on the eight petals one should install him together with the eight Bhairavas.
Indeed, beginning with the letter *ya* and extending as far as the letter *ha*,
they are endowed with great splendor and joined to the end of the support of *nāda*.
They should be made endowed with power (śakti), adorned with the vowel *au*, joined with the power of resonance (nāda-śakti), and possessed of the digit of the half-moon (ardhendu-kalā). 7.10b–11a.
These Bhairavas, who exist beginning with Soma and ending with Ketu in their sequential order, have been described by me as having the form of the planets for one who understands them.
Dakṣa, Caṇḍa, Hara, Śauṇḍī, Pramatha, Bhīma, Manmatha, Śakuni, Sumati, Nanda, Gopāla, and Pitāmaha. || 7-12 ||
One should assign these twelve great heroes to the twelve spokes;
having excluded the group of neuter vowels, these [consonants] are established by means of the vowels.
It is said that those zodiac signs which are established in the sequence beginning with Aries cause their respective ascensions month by month. (7.14)
One should place [the letters] upon twenty-four petals, following the sequence from *ka* to *bha*,
according to the order starting from the east and ending at the northeast.
Piṅgalā, Gokarṇī, Lolupā, and likewise Haraṇī; Keekarā, O Goddess of Gods, as well as Bhaṭṭā and Yogeśvarī. (7-16)
Suprabhā, Vīramātā, Jambukī, Kroṣṭukī, Bībhatsā, and Vānarī—these seven are worthy of worship by the thirty gods. (7.17)
Devavratā, Kumārī, Nandā, Nandapriyā, as well as Hayagrīvā, Surūpā, Virūpā, and Kalāvatī. || 7-18 ||
Vāmanī, Devamātā, and Viśveśī are proclaimed [as the deities];
these twenty-four are situated at the edge of the petals. (7.19)
O Great Goddess, every month two [energies] arise in succession;
established near me, they bring about [their effects]. (7.20)
They should be installed with effort according to the sequence beginning with Caitra;
one should offer [the oblation] to whichever Rudra corresponds to whichever month, starting from sunrise.
Having first worshipped that [deity] with effort according to the prescribed rule,
one should proceed from the eastern petal, following the ritual for the remaining directions in due order.
O Goddess, I shall now explain to you how one practices according to the correct procedure for a period equal to a *cakra*-year. (7.23)
The sun situated upon the pericarp should look toward three petals:
Jvalinī, Dhūmā, and Aṅgārā as the third.
Wherever she remains active, she is declared to be Jvālinī;
she should be known as Muktāgāriṇī, while Dhūminī is remembered as being in front.

Whichever planet should afflict a person, one should worship that [planet] in the center; those situated in the directions are to be worshipped for prosperity, in sequence with perfumes, incense, and so forth. (7.26)
That graha shall be a bestower of boons upon him and not a cause of affliction;
the propitiation with one's own mantras is prescribed, as well as the performance of recitation, fire-oblation, and ritual offerings.
Thus one who follows the command of Bhairava attains peace.
Now I shall declare their arising according to the sequence of day and night.
The lord of the day is placed before him, for that is indeed his rising;
it is declared to be four ghaṭikās, but is proclaimed as being three-quarters of a unit less.
The rising of the day and night has been fully explained to you, O one rich in asceticism.
Those who are remembered as the Rudras beginning with Dakṣa, as well as the zodiac signs beginning with Aries, [have been described]. 7.30ab.
Their transitory conjunction and their rising according to sequence [should be known]; in whichever zodiac sign the Sun is situated, established from its rising and so forth. (7-31)
Each one should be known to last for five ghaṭikās in due order;
six risings are thus described until the sun has set.

O Goddess of the gods, just as the sun [traverses] the entire night, so indeed has it been taught by those who speak according to the scriptures; here, a year is said to consist of a single day and night.
O Goddess, he who is named Dakṣa and is Rudra protects the zodiac sign of Aries;
one should worship him first, O Goddess, along with the infallible one and the yogis.
These two pairs, beginning with Piṅgalā and the others, are declared in their proper order;
one should worship them together with Rudra and the Yoginīs. (7.35)
O Dear One, Mālinī is differentiated by the division of the twelve vowels;
furthermore, O God, Śabdarāśi is Bhairava, [differentiated] by the sixteen [vowels]. (7.36)
The god is [worshipped] with twelve [syllables], and likewise the goddess with sixteen;
the solar wheel consists of twelve, while the lunar wheel consists of sixteen.
Having understood the division between the sun and the moon, one should undertake ritual action;
the six seasons are enumerated in order, beginning with the cool season (śiśira).
Two pairs among them have been described; listen, O long-eyed one, to what occurs during autumn, spring, summer, and the rainy season.
Two Rudras each are to be known, and four Yoginīs each;
they have been described in brief as they arise in their proper sequence.
Thus the wheel of the seasons has been proclaimed in its sixfold division;
the wheel, which is like unto the year, should be worshipped according to the distinctions of the seasons. (7.41)
One should perform rites such as pacification (śāntika) when [the moon] is situated in the lunar mansion,
but rites such as inciting enmity (vidveṣa) and eradication (uccāṭana) during the fire-bearing [naksatra], such as the fire oblation (homa).
One desiring prosperity should avoid [fires] that are glowing like embers or smoky;
having specifically understood [the requirements for] pacification and other rites, one should commence the ritual action.

O Goddess, having distinguished between the auspicious and inauspicious, one should perform the practice of pacifying, increasing, and mixed actions for the sake of the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind.
O Dear One, from white meditation there arises peace and nourishment;
likewise, red [meditation] is for the rites of subjugation, as well as for attraction and agitation.
And likewise for causing flight, for delusion, for seizing the minds of others, for creating enmity, for expulsion, for stupefaction, for yawning, and for pinning down. (7.46)
For causing displeasure, one should visualize [the deity] as smoke-colored; for killing, one should visualize him as having a black appearance, fierce with bared fangs and inspiring fear. (7.47)
One should contemplate the very fierce form of the Elder at night;
and at dawn, for the sake of pacification, one should contemplate the Child-form holding a lotus in his hand.
At midday, one should perform subjugation and attraction; [the deity] is youthful and holds a noose and a goad. For paralyzing, he is peaceful and yellow in color.
In the afternoon, the mixed form is proclaimed as the middling;
however, that which is called the child-form is proclaimed according to the oral instruction.
O you of excellent vows, he who has ascended to the lap within the tradition,
in the Kula path that has been fully revealed, is indeed the "woman on the head" in the Kaulika lineage.
The practitioner of mantra should not contemplate deities of fierce form within the body;
rather, O Dear One, one should visualize them with lotuses in their hands, devoted to eating and drinking. (7.52)
The goddess who is the embodiment of action is adorned with garlands of bones; blazing with serpents as her ornaments, she seeks the destruction of the Dānavas. (7.53)
Thus, meditation is specifically taught as having the form of a deity;
one should never meditate upon one's own physical body as being subject to burning.
One should not cause it to overflow, O lady of beautiful hips, nor should one cause it to overflow again, my dear;
thus, at all times, one should always contemplate peace within the Self by means of the mind. (7.55)
O you whose wealth is asceticism, the Umāmāheśvara-cakra has been described;
when joined with the *cala*-seed-syllable, it brings about accomplishment—of this there is no doubt. (7.56)
Now I shall describe the sacrifice according to the science of words (padavidyā);
I shall explain it by means of the ritual for the Solitary Hero (ekavīra), O lady rich in asceticism.
One should worship on the eight petals in the center according to the sequence beginning with Rudra;
those ending with "vicce svāhā" should be worshipped by the wise.
Then, having consecrated [the deities] upon the eight petals with mantras, they should be worshipped with great devotion—
[the goddesses] accompanied by their vehicles and weapons, and adorned with all ornaments.
One should worship them in the sequence beginning with Brahmāṇī and ending with Aiśānī; O fair-faced one, [the mantra] should begin with "Oṃ" and end with "Namaḥ," concluding with "Namaḥ."
Furthermore, O lady of excellent hips, one who desires his own welfare should worship another mantra ending with *viśva* and characterized by the conclusion with *svāhā*. (7.61)

Moreover, by means of the division of the limbs, the Supreme Goddess should be installed in due order according to the sequence of the six births, following the sequence beginning with the heart. (7.62)
O fair-faced one, the heart-mantra called Saṃjīvanī is uttered with a double repetition; it is joined with the syllable Oṃ at the beginning and the word "namaḥ" at the end.
That which is called "ūrdhvakeśī" (upward-haired) is characterized by the word *svāhā* at the end of the head-mantra;
that which is renowned as "jvalitaśikhā" (blazing crest) is remembered as the *śikhā* (crest-mantra) ending with *vauṣaṭ*.
Māyā, whose form is the three worlds, revolves a thousand times;
it is taught as the armor when joined with the word *huṃ* and the syllable *jāti*.
The eye [mantra] is "tārakākṣi" followed by "vaṣaṭ";
"māraṇī" repeated twice, ending with "phaṭ," is known as the weapon.
The limbs have indeed been described in this manner; now hear from me concerning the faces:
Oṃ ruḥ, svāhā to the eastern face.
Oṃ Rukmiṇī, svāhā to the right face!
Oṃ ruhā, to the western face, svāhā!
