Oṃ ruñca, svāhā to the northern face!
O fair-faced one, the faces of the Goddess have been fully described; now hear how they are to be applied.
Alternatively, according to the distinction of colors, each individual color indeed constitutes that [form];
it is endowed with limbs and faces through the division of the year.
But the one called Samaya, O Great Goddess, beloved, is to be worshipped as supreme;
thus, according to the correct procedure, one should apply it through the division of the Vidyā. (7.69)
"O Dear One, his every desire will indeed be fulfilled without delay;
the number of syllables for this supreme Vidyā has been declared. (7.70)
O fair-faced one, three hundred and sixty syllables [constitute the measure];
O beloved, the characteristics previously described are accompanied by movement. (7.71)
One who, being constantly purified, should mutter [this mantra] daily, shall obtain all desires.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, O Sovereign of the Lords of the Discus, that which was spoken by you regarding the Discus is fickle."
"By which, O God, the joy of Calavīra is described.
Bhairava said:
"O Dear One, that which is called 'Moving' (cala) is declared to consist of all mantras."
And the life-force of all mantras is the supreme Heart of the Yoginīs;
by means of that which is accomplished, all the leaders of mantras are accomplished without exception. (7.74)
And that hidden meaning, which is secret and all-pervading, cannot be obtained;
it is attained, O leader of heroes, through the instruction of the goddesses.
The form of the moving nectar, however, produces moving bliss;
it is moving, all-pervading, peaceful, and the supreme state of Nirvāṇa. (7.76)
The self is proclaimed to be mobile, the power is mobile, and the vital breath is mobile;
therefore, a practitioner of mantra must first perform the ritual preparation for that which is mobile.

Having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times in nine ways, the practitioner of the mantra— who consumes red food and follows the teachings of Phalguna— should then meditate upon him as having a radiance equal to the juice of lac.
Whomever one has in mind when reciting the mantra, that person one shall quickly summon—whether it be their blood residing in the body, their vital breath, or even their flesh. (7.79)
Or else, O lady of excellent limbs, if one so desires, one may cause even fat to diminish;
or nectar, or anything else whatsoever that is desired by the mind.
If you, having diligently soaked a mantra-reciter’s garment with the blood of a jackal, put it on while staying in a cemetery at night and recite [the mantra], [success will follow]. (7.81)
O lady of excellent limbs, when one hundred thousand [offerings] have been made, the sacrificial animal falls before him;
having sacrificed it and consumed it, he shall attain the siddhi of the Kaulikas.
Having known the movement of the minds of others, O Goddess of the Gods, [one performs] the transformation into form and so forth, invisibility, and the transference into all bodies. (7.83)
The capacity to ordain the future, the awakening to the present object, and the awakening to the past object—he knows all this in accordance with reality. (7.84)
Thus indeed, O Goddess of the gods, it should be performed according to the prescribed rule;
for by whichever blood the cloth has been infused, O beloved— (7–85)
Having wrapped himself in that [garment], the mantra-practitioner, standing in a cremation ground and naked as the directions, should recite the mantra;
O lady of excellent hips, he assumes those various forms, and even the bound souls (paśus) attend upon him.
O Goddess of the gods, the sādhana of the *pretapaṭa* has been proclaimed to you;
together with the *cala*, these vidyās possess supreme and great power. (7-87)
The wise man, being purified, should recite it; he shall obtain all desires.
Or else, there is the Vidyā known as Samaya, which blazes with all virtues.
One should mutter [the mantra] mentally at night; within a month one will become invisible. Standing in water reaching up to the navel, one shall destroy all sins. (7-89)
One should thus quickly accomplish whatever is desired by the mind;
one should recite the Mālinī, the mass of sounds, together with the *cala* mantra. (7.90)
One obtains all desires; there is no need for deliberation here.
O Great Goddess, [the sequence is] Śabdarāśi and then Mālinī again.
Through the application of the three vidyās, the wise and disciplined practitioner should recite the heart-mantra, which is endowed with five [syllables], one hundred and fifty times.
He attains all desires and is worshipped by the yoginīs;
or else, he is the mass of sounds (śabdarāśi) and Mālinī, endowed with the three times.
O Goddess, the five heart-mantras, together with that which is called the *samaya*, constitute the total number of syllables as proclaimed in one place. (7.94)
O Goddess of the gods, this collection of mantras, numbering five hundred and ten more, is endowed with the seed-syllable of Cala and bestows perfect accomplishment.
There is no doubt that this occurs if it is propitiated according to the ritual procedure;
it is declared to be a power that is exceedingly effective for all desires. (7.96)
O Goddess, there is no collective sādhana superior to this;
O Supreme Goddess, it is especially so according to the procedure for the solitary hero (ekavīra).
For the practitioner who recites with self-restraint, purity arises quickly;
O lady of beautiful hips, when he is purified by the Goddess, they grant him the supreme sacrificial victim.

Or else, having consumed caru prepared from [the flesh of one who has been] inhabited by that [deity] for seven lifetimes, O Goddess of the Gods, by eating it, one becomes equal to that [deity]. (7.99)
One may wander together with the deities and become a traveler through the sky in an instant.
The Goddess said:
"If it be so, then that which has been described by you as 'distinct' (vilakṣaṇa) in this most terrible [state]..."
O Lord, by what ripening of karma is one born as an animal?
What are its characteristics said to be, both external and internal? (7-101)
Bhairava said:
"Everything that was previously mentioned by you has been told by me.
Now I shall describe the characteristics of the sacrificial animal (paśu) for one who desires spiritual accomplishment (siddhi)."
One whose body has been consecrated by mantras, who is a devotee of Śiva and firm in his vows, yet whose mind is averse to spiritual practice and the desire for supernatural powers; || 7.103 ||
He should be known as a betrayer of the guru, a wicked-souled man of evil deeds; for him there is no liberation, even though he may be reborn after being obstructed.
In birth after birth, through the practice of the meaning of initiation and mantra, he is born again as one who is diligent; yet he must indeed renounce even that once more. (7.105)
For if the fruit born of mantra-refinement were indeed powerful, it would not be obstructed by sacrificial rites, except in the case of treachery toward one's guru. (7.106)
Whether they have one birth, two births, three births, or four;
or five, six, or seven births—they are indeed animals, without a doubt. (7.107)

O fair-faced one, by reciting that [mantra], one achieves mastery of the sky (khecaratva), invisibility, emerging from a subterranean opening, and the transformation of one's form and other attributes. (7.108)
And from that point onward, there arises a commonality of the cakras for one whose speech is fragrant and who proceeds with the power of *aṇimā*.
O Goddess, he on whose eyes and ears a *tilaka* is seen, and on whose nails of the hands and feet hair is likewise seen; || 7.110 ||
He obtains his own birth as one who is devoted to Śiva, free from envy, devoted to the gods and Brahmins, engaged in silent recitation, and intent on purity. (7.111)
Thus has the characteristic of those whose souls delight in the conduct of heroes been described;
it is not known, O lady of excellent hips, without their grace.
O beloved, goddesses characterized by a mixture [of qualities] and animals of this same kind bestow [their fruits] upon those great-souled ones whose minds are devoted to recitation and vows. (7.113)
To those who are endowed with the conduct of the samaya and are intent on the propitiation of the mantra,
the goddesses, whose selves are purified, grant the supreme state of true being.
O Goddess, men attain various supernatural powers (siddhis) on earth;
thus it is when, O Goddess, that which is characterized by the state of the bound soul (pāśava) has been attained. (7.115)
One should offer oblations with devotion, or perform whatever is desired;
however, the practitioner of mantras should not eat meat that lacks sacrificial animals, nor should he perform a fire sacrifice with that which is devoid of its proper birth.
O auspicious lady, it is dear to the *sākinīs*, but it is certainly not dear to the *yoginīs*.
O beautiful woman, one should neither eat it nor offer it as an oblation (*homa*). (7.117)
That which is commanded by the divine yogis must be carried out without hesitation;
otherwise, the practitioner of mantra would never slay a living being as if in mere play.
He who eats meat for his own sport, for the sake of his wife, for the sake of his tongue, or for his own nourishment—that sinful soul is the lowest of men. (7.119)
The eater, the stealer, the slayer, the preparer, the seller of meat, the one who buys it, the one who cuts it, and the one who serves it—these eight are sinners in this world. (7.120)
The method has been grasped in a contrary manner by those of dull intellect;
the method consists in compassion toward all beings and a disposition of gentleness. (7.121)
Having thus understood the sequence of the scriptures, the heroic conduct, and the beloved vow, they should be observed by the wise exactly as enjoined by the scriptures. (7.122)
Meditation, worship, recitation, and fire-offering, preceded by devotion, are proclaimed as the fivefold means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) in all tantras. (7.123)
Having thus performed worship with perfumes, incense, and sacred threads, as well as with food offerings and drinks, one should address the Supreme Lord.
At the end of the day, he should partake of the sacrificial porridge (caru) together with his sons and practitioners,
who are seated on low seats separately and well-perfumed with fragrant flowers and incense.

In the Bhairava Tantra, one whose soul is devoted to purity and right conduct should not employ those who are ill-behaved, those with divergent views, those who speak in contradiction, or those who are arrogant. (7.126)
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, why is there a single vessel and likewise separate vessels? For those who are pure and possess equal aims, how can such a distinction be made?"
Bhairava said:
O Goddess of gods, one who is engaged in meditation, worship, and recitation, yet violates other conventional rules, should have a separate vessel prepared for that purpose. (7.128)
O Goddess, just as adamantine plaster [is indestructible], so too is the violation of the samaya;
yet initiation shall purify even such sins as the killing of a Brahmin.
O Goddess, it has been declared that one who violates the samaya will not be purified;
having made themselves appear like practitioners of mantra, they remain greedy in all circumstances. (7.130)
Merged in the confusion of female messengers, devoid of action for the sake of greed—those who are rajasic and tamasic, unconscious and crying out "Alas! Alas! (7.131).
Those who are constantly devoted to food and drink, and those who are addicted to the tongue and the genitals—they are not heroes, O Varohe; one should not associate with them.
"For this reason, O Goddess, one should cause a separate vessel to be made.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, I wish to hear in truth about those who are *rājasa* and *tāmasa*."
Bhairava said:
One who observes vows while characterized by tamas is declared to be adorned with matted locks;
yet one whose limbs are smeared with ashes is a destroyer of the efficacy of mantras.
One whose body is adorned with mudrās, yet whose mind lacks the capacity for sexual union and who is unable to take a female consort (dūtī), is declared to be tāmasa.
The one characterized by passion (rājasa) has an upward-pointing mark, is prone to anger, and is adorned with bracelets;
furthermore, he may have another appearance, being devoid of matted hair and ashes.

Those who are unmanifest and characterized by sattva, though devoid of the practice of formal vows, are to be known as heroes; they follow the auspicious path, being endowed with the performance of the purpose of the scriptures. (7.137)

One who is devoted to the conduct of the sacred observances, who worships the gods, the fire, and the guru, whether established in vows or not, is remembered as a sattvic ascetic (śa-yati). || 7.138 ||
Even if he is in any state whatsoever, one who does not abide by the vows is characterized by tamas and rajas.
Furthermore, those who maintain the vows but subsist upon the manifest meaning [of the scriptures]— || 7.139 ||
Those heroes should be avoided; they are to be known as the wicked, devoid of merit.
Those devoted to the scriptures should not maintain any association with them.
But he who, out of delusion or negligence, indulges in sexual intercourse while devoted to the practice of vows, O Goddess, becomes a great Vetāla. (7.141)
He who emits semen into a non-vagina or into a womb that is not a [proper] womb shall become a vetāla, who carries the product of delusion upon his shoulder. (7.142)
That wicked-minded Rākṣasa who has sexual intercourse with a female ascetic who observes the Bhairava vow is born as such. (7.143)
One who has attained the status of a lord of the Kūṣmāṇḍas enjoys the fruits of that enjoyment;
initiation into a single maṇḍala consists of the consumption of the sacrificial porridge (caru) in one place. || 7-144 ||
Those who dwell here and consume [the offerings] are terrible Piśācas;
they may be a Samayinī, a mother, or even a sister.
That foolish king who, without having given [alms], consumes liquor and meat, will be free from affliction there in the Vaitaraṇī river. (7.146)
One who eats for the sake of his own livelihood, nourishing himself by consuming food without first offering it, is reborn as a Rākṣasa with a putrid mouth and a massive body. (7.147)
That preta Sūcīmukha, too, is of massive body and extremely terrible;
yet those who act correctly, O lady of beautiful hips, in the rite of Vīrabhojana—
Enveloped by darkness, they do not perceive through right vision according to reality;
for a very long time, those who conceptualize wander amidst the distinctions of caste and non-caste. (7.149)
O Supreme Goddess, when that lowest of men, having learned [the teachings] from his gurus, does not act upon them, he shall go to a terrible and insurmountable hell.
A seat, a bed, drink, food, and likewise clothing;
sandals, shoes,
and so forth— none of these exist for one being churned in the ocean of existence.
O Goddess, as long as a wise man remains standing near his own guru, he should behave like a cat seeking food, or like a crane. (7.153)
But him who neglects all duties and his own guru—I do not favor that man of sinful conduct, the lowest of men. (7.154)
Therefore, O Goddess, with every effort one must constantly perform the service of the Guru, either by means of oneself or through wealth. (7.155)
O beautiful lady, as long as he lives, a man should remain like a servant;
he should receive [the teaching] from the mouth of the Guru, being pained by the Guru’s suffering. (7.156)
O Goddess of the gods, those enjoyments which the Guru partakes of here, he dwells in those lands and beholds those worlds. (7.157)
O Goddess of the gods, that best of practitioners who abides by this [path] is the lord of all siddhis, endowed with the conduct of Bhairava.
O Goddess, even those who possess non-existent virtues should indeed proclaim them to their guru;
by having such virtues proclaimed, one obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice.
One who praises the virtues of the Guru will always be healthy, endowed with prosperity, peaceful, long-lived, and free from enemies; he shall obtain unthought-of fruits. (7.160)
One should not dispute with the guru regarding the transmission of mantras and tantras;
nor should one utter such words even if confusion should arise. (7.161)

By that which, when one is angry, causes the seven classes of deities who abide there to become enraged; by that same thing, when one is satisfied, they are satisfied. Therefore, one should not give way to anger. (7.162)
"One becomes an object of ridicule and beyond reproach by laughing at one who is dancing;
therefore, O Bhairavī, one should not engage in improper speech with the Guru. (7.163)
One should never appear before a deity, fire, or a guru with empty hands;
he who protects [these] in this manner is Bhairavī, without a doubt. (7.164)
The observance of conduct is common to all scriptures;
it must indeed be practiced, O beautiful lady, by one who desires his own welfare. (7.165)
By this [it is shown] that those who are devoid of right conduct are of the nature of passion (rājasa) and darkness (tāmasa);
however, at the conclusion of their sins, liberation shall indeed come to them in due course.
O Goddess, even those who have become the sons of their mothers and those who belong to the Kula-Kāpālika sect will attain liberation in due course; of this there is no doubt.

Furthermore, those who, though not mentioned in the Bhairava [tantras], abide by the rules for initiation and knowledge—all of them are declared to be *patis*, consecrated by the knowledge of the *pati*. (7.7.168)
All of them are to be honored, O Goddess, just as I am yours;
this [teaching] of mine, O Goddess, has not been tested by anyone else.

O one of evil intellect, it is not for those who dwell in crookedness, nor for those addicted to the wheel; given to one with a wavering mind or to one who is negligent, it does not bestow accomplishment at all. (7.170)

The practice of the mobile seed (calabīja), together with its secret, has been told; O Goddess of Gods, it is proclaimed as the mobile wheel (calacakra) according to the division of the deities. (7.171)

Endowed with the multitude of mudrās and mantras, and knowing the divisions of the wheel of ritual placement (nyāsa), one who knows the portions of the mandala of mudrās attains accomplishment without delay, O Goddess. (7.172)
The mudrā named Khageśvarī possesses the characteristics of the entire collection;
O Goddess, within seven days, the certainty of its realization arises for him. (7.173)
The ring finger, joined to the back [of the thumb], should press upon one's own instrument;
by this pressing, O lady of excellent hips, there is undoubtedly the power of flight through the sky. (7.174)
One should form the group of six *kha*s situated within the *kha*, located in the middle of the *kha*;
one should join the mouth of the *kha* with that which moves in the *kha*, and contemplate the state of the *kha*, O Dear One. (7.175)
O God, by mere remembrance there will be movement through the sky; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, O Goddess, has the secret of the practitioners of mantra been fully explained.
"One should protect that which is not to be disclosed and must be well-guarded, as if it were one's own life.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Authority on the Umāmāheśvara Cakra," in the *Śrī Tantrasadbhāva*, a great tantra within the Bhairava current belonging to the Vidyāpīṭha, measuring seventy million verses. 7.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, O Great Master, the mudrās have indeed been indicated, yet they are not understood by me.
O Treasure of the World, please explain the mudrās according to their respective seats. (8.1)
The three-pronged [mudrā], the lotus mudrā, and the third, the yoni mudrā—explain their characteristics, which have not been stated by me due to my limited intelligence. (8-2)
Bhairava said:
O Goddess, that supreme power known as Vidyā, from whom this great wonder has arisen—O Goddess, I shall describe the characteristics of the mudrās in brief. (8.3)
First, one should form a hollowed cavity (*saṃpuṭa*) with both hands facing upward;
all the fingers on both hands should be interlaced and slightly pressed together.

Having bent the index and ring fingers together so that both meet at their middle joints, one should form the face with those two [fingers] at their base; one should join the little fingers in the middle.
Having formed the hands into the shape of a hollowed bowl with the two thumbs placed in the middle, one should extend the little finger of the left hand. (8.6)
The *yonimudrā*, O auspicious lady, is known as the agitator of all;
this triad of mudrās, O auspicious lady, is declared to be common to all. (8.7)
This common mudrā should be described for the satisfaction of the Yogin and the Lord of Heroes;
it is said that the fingers of the right hand are to be joined together.
O Goddess, one should fashion the thumb resting at the base of the forefinger;
this "Fearless" [mudrā] should be presented before Skanda to the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Alternatively, for the sake of providing comfort to those who are terrified and afraid, one should move the left hand downward with the face turned down, like a woman in labor. (8.10)
"O Goddess, the tips of the fingers are excellent for bestowing the fruits of one's desired aims;
so too are both the little and ring fingers of both hands. (8-11)
The mantra-practitioner should open his mouth, [place] the two middle fingers on the nostrils, the two index fingers on the pair of eyebrows, and move the two thumbs outside the channels. (8.12)
Standing with a fierce gaze, the wise one should utter three cries of "hā hā";
this mudrā, known as Vikarālī, bestows satisfaction upon Bhairava. (8.13)
O Goddess, by binding this [mantra], one becomes beloved by the Yoginīs;
one shall not be overcome by the lords of obstacles (Vighneśas), and one may liberate those afflicted by the planets.
Indeed, it bestows fearlessness when entering great terrors;
one should place the left hand with its palm facing forward and extend the right hand across it. (8.15)
This is the Svastika Mahāmudrā, which brings victory and provides protection.
Having concealed the little fingers and thumbs, place the other two [fingers] in their middle. (8.16)
The remaining fingers being contracted, this is considered the Śṛṅkhalā-vijayā mudrā;
one should form the Vaktrā mudrā with the index finger of the left hand placed between [the thumb and middle finger].
The remaining fingers should be bent, and one should form the thumb into the mouth; in the middle of that, one should place the other finger, the index finger, made straight. (8-19)
This mudrā, known as Kālakarṇī, is called Lāṅgalā for the purpose of plowing;
it is formed by joining the index fingers and thumbs of both hands into circles. (8.20)

O beloved, those two of great strength are positioned one above and one below; they hold a noose, and the hands should be joined in a hollowed gesture (saṃpuṭa), with the little fingers extended sideways.
One should diligently display it; it is known as the *kamaṇḍalu*.
It should be given to one devoted to Brahman, for it is the supreme purifier of all things.
Having formed a fist with the left hand and raised the tip of the index finger, one should place it on the left shoulder and display the edge of a sword. 8.23ab [73a]
O Great Goddess Maheśvarī, who brings about prosperity for all, having saluted with both hands joined in the *veṇibandha* gesture, O lady of beautiful countenance. (8.24)
Having formed a fist with the right hand, one should whirl it in the air; this is for the maiden, and the *pithaka* is for the consumption by the army. || 8-25 ||
O fair-faced one, having formed the index finger of the left hand into a circular shape, the middle finger and thumb should be joined at their tips. (8.26)
This mudrā, called Saṃkhyā, belongs to Vaiṣṇavī and bestows wonderful results;
having raised the index finger, one should enclose the remaining fingers in a fist. (8.27)
The staff mudrā (daṇḍamudrā) is fully described as that which brings satisfaction to Vārāhī:
the two hands, reaching to the level of the navel, should be joined crosswise at the wrists. (8.28)
One should extend the tips of the little finger and the thumb while the remaining fingers are interlaced;
this Vajra-mudrā, when offered to Vāsavi, brings about satisfaction. (8.29)
It should be employed for the purpose of paralyzing and likewise for the destruction of enemies;
O Goddess, one should diligently press the little finger with the thumb. (8.30)
O Goddess, one should extend the three [lines] that are worshipped by the thirty gods as a trident;
O fair-faced one, it should be offered in the northeast and in the Mālinī [direction]. (8.31)
Having turned the two hands upward, the middle fingers should likewise be closely joined;
then, with effort, the two index fingers, the two ring fingers, and the little fingers [should be positioned]. (8.32)
These Śakti-mudrās placed upon the back of the hand are prescribed for you;
O fair-faced one, they should be offered in the southeast for the purpose of invoking the presence [of the deity].
With the right hand, one should form a fist with the thumb raised up;
this is the mudrā called Liṅga, which one should place upon the site of the deity. (8.34)
One should cause small platforms to be made for the two hands and lead them upward as far as the head;
then, slowly lowering them face-downward, one should release them at the feet as well.
This supreme mudrā called *argha* brings satisfaction to all;
having then contracted the index finger and the others, one should move them together with the thumb. (8.36)
This mudrā, called the goad (aṅkuśa), is declared to be the most excellent of all;
it is formed by making the thumb face downward and binding [the fingers] into a fist. (8.37)
This mudrā, known as Nirodha, has been proclaimed by the God of Gods:
having formed a hollow with the hands like a cup, the index fingers are restrained by the thumbs. (8.38)
Having released each one separately, they are joined together at the middle joint;
this is the mudrā called Amṛtā, consisting of three fingers in the form of a deer skin (ajina). 8-39.
Having joined them crosswise, one should place them upon the shoulder;
one should press the fingers with the thumb so that they form a hollow space in the middle.
One should indeed whirl [the hand] along the path of the left and also along the path of the right,
just as the hand-drum (ḍamaruka) is prescribed when held with the hand raised upward.
One should place the little finger and the middle finger at the tip of the thumb;
with the ring finger and forefinger held stiff, this is prescribed as the Govṛṣa mudrā.
One should place the ring finger and the middle finger at the tip of the thumb;
this is the mudrā named Mṛgī, for the successful accomplishment of the rite of homa.
Having extended the index and middle fingers toward the upper direction, one should press the ring and little fingers with the thumb. (8.44)
The sword mudrā is fully described as the destroyer of wicked beings;
having placed the hand face down, with the surface of the fingers then bent downward. (8.45)
The index finger of the right hand, positioned on the back and tip of the palm, should move;
this is called the *ghaṇṭikā*. Now I shall describe the *patākā* to you.
O Dear One, having extended the index finger of the left hand with its face turned upward,
one should place it in front, while the middle finger belonging to the right hand [is held] by the index finger.
O Dear One, having grasped the remaining two fingers of both hands with the fist,
one should extend and move the finger of the left hand.
The banner has indeed been described, O Goddess; now learn from me the bow mudrā:
having grasped the left thumb with the right fist... (8.49)
One should join the tips of the index fingers; one should place the middle finger in a state of reverence.
One should contract the remaining fingers of the left hand; this ritual action is considered to end with the syllable *huṃ*.
Having formed a fist, one should cast it downward and then bind it once again;
the *muśala* [mudrā] is praised for grinding, as has been taught to you, O beautiful one. (8.51)
And now, O lady of excellent limbs, I shall describe to you the *paraśu* for the purpose of cutting:
the finger should be extended and placed with its tip facing downward within the closed fist. (8.52)
Then, having extended the fingers like a chowrie,
one should wave it from left to right in sequence, just as one raises a chowrie.
The skull-bowl with its opening facing upward, held in the hand with the palm extended—these are declared to be the mudrās for meditation, worship, and dismissal. (8.54)
The general characteristics of the gods and goddesses, as well as the Rudras, have been declared;
the color established for Yama and the others is proclaimed as their name-seal (nāmamudrā). 8.55cd–56ab.
The mantra for that mudrā begins with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ends with *namaḥ*.
[The goddesses] possess massive bodies and great splendor, their heads pierced by their own weapons. (8.56)
Having meditated thus and having invoked them, one should offer the water for honor (*argha*), the water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth.
Thus has the external characteristic of the mudrās been fully explained. (8.57)
Now, O you who move through the sky, out of affection for you, I shall describe in brief the mudrās of the sky-farers, just as they are among the lords of birds.
The ring finger should be joined at the pericarp, and one should press upon the sixteen spokes;
through this pressing, O beautiful lady, it attains straightness on the path of the bird (the central channel).
When one hundred thousand [recitations] ending with the letter *pha* have been completed, there is no doubt that the power of flight is attained.
Having formed a six-petaled lotus above, one should apply it to the tip of the index finger.
Having become empty-minded within the void, one should press them together;
then the six-petalled [lotus] shall manifest, impelled by the *udāna* wind.
One should meditate upon the letters from *na* to *pha*; there is no doubt that one will attain movement through the sky.
One should join it to the end of the *lambaka* with a twelve-fold half-measure of *nāla*.
One should not form the *kuñcita* [mudrā] with the fingers joined like a tortoise;
rather, O Vīranāyikā, one should contemplate the sequence from *na* to *pha*, which possesses the movement of the sky-farer.
The lotus-mudrā is said to be threefold; now hear concerning the yoni-mudrā:
having placed the yoni upon the yoni, one performs piercing with the mallet.
Through the union of the two visargas, one will certainly become a sky-farer;
one should meditate upon the supreme source called Amṛtā at the highest point of the head.

Having traversed the path of the fragrance, extending for a *yojana* from the letter *na* to the letter *pha*, one who is skilled in the path of the womb will likewise attain the power of moving through the sky. (8.66)
Having uttered the left Śakti, one should join it in the middle of the knot; having performed the upward projection, the visualization is then placed within the supreme womb.
By this, one undoubtedly attains the power of moving through the sky;
O Supreme Goddess, the Yonimudrā is thus declared to be of three types.
O Goddess, understand from me as I describe the characteristic of the triple-tufted crest:
one should press the two index fingers with both hands with great effort. (8.69)
By practicing twice through the *brahmanāḍī*, one strikes the abdomen;
this is the mudrā named Triśikhā, an offering by way of the path of the sky-farer.
O Dear One, the *golaka* situated on the path of the sun and traversing the three paths is the *kṣepaṇa*;
it rises above the *bindu* and, having stepped upon the earth, reaches the two feet.
O Dear One, having placed the three-pointed sky-farer within the secret place, the knower of mantras attains the power of moving through the sky by means of this, O best of practitioners.
The instrument (karaṇa) should have its root upward; one should bind it within the sphere of the sky.
Having stepped upon the fifth syllable with both hands, she becomes the Trident-bearer (Triśūlinī).
The knees should be joined at the elbows, and the thrust is from the middle of the secret place;
this piercing of the aperture of Brahmā has been described, O you whose wealth is austerity.
Thus, O fair-eyed one, your movement through the path of the sky occurs;
these mudrās have been fully described, established in nine varieties.
By such synonyms as these, power (śakti) should be expressed individually;
it is called the "mudrā-power" because, being sealed, it will cause [the object] to melt.
Therefore, the Seal (mudrā) has been fully explained by Śambhu, the God of gods;
it is said that what is "sealed" (mudrita) is that which is concealed, having the very nature of the power of consciousness (cicchakti). (8.77)
O lady of excellent limbs, she was not recognized by me when she was described;
for as long as one is bound by the form of the darkness of ignorance, one remains a mere heap of aggregates.
Indeed, as long as one does not know the Supreme Self, one proceeds by means of distinctions;
but when a human being perceives unity once the darkness has been dispelled, [then he attains liberation]. || 8.79 ||
Then she is called Parā, O beloved, the one who effects both bondage and liberation;
she is that single supreme Śakti who exists by the will of Śiva. (8.80)

She who liberates from the seizing spirits and the like, and causes them to flee in vain—because of this liberation and this causing to flee, she is known as Mudrā; such is the power (śakti) that has been described.
Because she moves through the path of space with the state of ultimate reality at all times, she is known as Khecarī (the Sky-farer) among all living beings. || 8.82 ||
In its state as the Other (paratva), it is to be known as manifold; furthermore, it is traditionally taught to be twofold.
The third, however, is will and knowledge, which has come to assume the form of phonemes.
The fifty-fold divisions, though diverse, are thus declared to be one;
complete with all parts and limbs, they remain as a garland encompassing the world.
By virtue of its nature as the sequence from *na* to *pha*, it is known as the "Stained" (*malinī*).
As for the seven crores of mantras that are remembered as being immeasurable— || 8.85 ||
O Supreme Goddess, all those who abide in independence are sealed;
therefore, this is called a *mudrā*, which produces immediate conviction. (8.86)
Through their constituent parts, the forms of the Mothers manifest as conceptualizations within their respective portions:
those of Brahmāṇī consist of the portion of Raudrī, and those of Kaumārī consist of the portion of Kaumārī, O fair-faced one.
O sinless one, she is a portion of Vaiṣṇavī, a portion of Yāmī, and likewise a portion of Indrā;
she is the mistress of yoga, a portion of Yogīśvarī, and the leader born of the union of all yogas.
These seven parts are traditionally taught as being further divided into seven groups of seven;
seven are designated as belonging to Brahmā, and again seven to Maheśvarī.
Seven are indeed assigned to Kaumārī, and likewise seven to Vaiṣṇavī;
similarly, there are seven for Vaivasvatī and seven for Indrāṇī.
Thus, the Cāmuṇḍās are remembered as seven in each of the seven [worlds];
these forty-nine goddesses are established within the series of worlds.
Furthermore, the series of skies is established through manifold divisions;
the hairs on its body are proclaimed to be thirty million in number.
Fifty lakhs of body hairs arise from that,
and in each individual pore of hair, millions of yoginīs reside.
The crores of crores of crores of triplets are manifold;
they exist within the earth and other elements as far as the limits of space.
The atoms are immeasurable, existing in manifold ways within each reality;
likewise, the subtle forms and mudrās are such that their number cannot be known.
Indeed, O beloved, the entire universe is pervaded by subtle internal mudrās;
thus have the mudrās been fully described, for their pervasiveness is immeasurable. (8–96)
There is but one supreme mudrā, by whom this world exists;
whichever limb she touches, that very limb is designated as a mudrā.
Dancing, strength, as well as laughter, nakedness, and leaping; the bristling of the hair, as well as other [reactions], weeping, and even bursting [of boils]. (8-98)
Whatever modification they perform, all that is designated as a *mudrā*; and the finger is called an *aṅganā* because it constantly moves upon the body. (8–99)
O fair-faced one, the fingers are designated by him for the binding of mudrās; that which is known as "ka" is the body (kāya), and from it, the [vowels] proceed there. (8.100)
Is that name truly superior by way of the path of effortless arrival? The Nameless, devoid of names, is established in a million ways. (8.101)
A name cannot be assigned; therefore, it is called "nameless. It constantly functions in the midst of the basis of the person (pudgala). (8.102)
In that state, O beloved, the support (ādhāra) moves upward and there is no returning;
therefore, it is called "the middle" (madhyamā) here by those who speak mantras.
He constantly performs the threatening gesture, the joining together and the separating apart;
he should threaten great delusion and the infinite net of snares. (8.104)
The threatening gesture (tarjanī) has been declared by him to be the supreme mudrā among all;
O Dear One, the thumb, having become a continuous flow, should constantly stream forth. (8-105)
It should proceed with the excrement; therefore, it is remembered as the thumb (aṅguṣṭha).
"Aha" is said to be the upward movement, while "adhas" is declared to be the night.
By that, the two hands are designated as the left and the right;
emanation is said to be on the left, while withdrawal is by the right. (8.107)
O Vīranāyikā, by that [means] the movement to the right and left was explained;
having known that the entire world is pervaded by the left, it was then understood, O beloved. (8-108)
O lady of excellent hips, through that union, she is the self, Kuṇḍalinī;
she is the essence, the supreme womb, the highest womb among all wombs.
O lady of excellent hips, he who knows the primordial power Manonmanī,
by him all this world is known as being beyond syllables, devoid of phonemes.
That supreme mudrā is declared to be the one that effects universal pervasion;
it consists of two dots (bindus), two crests (culikās), and the visarga which is the enclosure of power (śakti).
Know that which arises from that, ending with the sound *nāda*, to be designated as the Void (*śūnya*).
This is declared to be the single mudrā in the actions of speech, mind, and body. (8.112)
"What else do you ask, O Goddess? I shall tell you all of that.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Authority on Mudrās," in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, a great tantra within the Bhairava-stream, belonging to the Vidyāpīṭha, measuring seventy million verses. 8.
The Goddess said: Today my birth has become fruitful, since you, the granter of boons, are mine;
for all that was indicated by you has been understood and grasped.
O Śambhu, initiation has indeed been indicated by you, but it has not been performed explicitly;
now, that initiation consisting of me (māyī-dīkṣā) as well as the paralyzing of the bonds (pāśastobha) must be done.
The Tulā is another rite for men, and the Prasannā is the Veśamāṇavī;
O Śambhu, it bestows immediate liberation, and after this follows the Utkrānti. 9.3b–c.
"O Goddess of the Gods, tell me this: the seizing of the animal and likewise the consecration; for I am prostrate before you, O Lord of the World. (9.4)
Bhairava said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall speak that which was previously requested by you;
I will relate all of that out of affection for you, O leader of the gods.
First, one who is an expert in the science of architecture (vāstuvidyā) should examine the ground;
it should be suitable for sacrifice, thick with trees, abounding in śarapuṣpā plants, and rich in kuśa grass.
It should be crowded with people devoted to Maheśvara, or even accompanied by only one such person;
it should be pleasant and beautiful, or else sloping toward the north-eastern direction.

One should examine [the gem] by means of its own species, its boundaries, and its path, up to its functional capacity; for color, taste, and likewise smell are known through the distinctions of species. (9.8)
That which is white, sweet as honey, and fragrant with ghee belongs to the Brāhmaṇa;
that which is red, has a red fragrance, or is astringent, belongs to the Kṣatriya.
Yellow earth, smelling of wheat, is considered suitable for Vaiśyas; it is sweet and alkaline.
Black earth, smelling of fertile soil, is pungent and bitter; it is considered suitable for others.
One should stir it to the depth of one cubit and then fill it once more;
that which contains less sand is inferior, while that with an equal amount of sand is middling.
Where the soil is predominantly dust, that ground grants all desires;
it should be dug until water is reached, or down to the level of the wind, or even to the neck.

One should diligently purify [the channel] from the heart to the navel, the hips, and the knees, provided it is free from the defects of foreign matter (*śalya*); indeed, one should cleanse it with effort once it is cleared of all obstructions.
One should diligently construct it with thorny branches, charcoal, and skull-bowls; first, one should fill it with clay and then with the roots of the *aśvattha* tree from the edge [of the site].
One should smear with cow dung an area that is level,
measuring five, seven, nine, or eleven cubits.
The knower of mantras should prepare a site measuring thirteen cubits or fifteen cubits for half a yoga-hall by means of formal consecration.
Having made it square and level, with its sides uniform on all four,
one should divide it into nine sections using threads extending from east to north.
O Goddess, having set aside two parts in all four directions, one should place the cloth for laying the foundation in the corners. || 9-18 ||
One should erect pillars equipped with base-bowls so that no vital point (*marman*) is pierced;
they should be raised upwards and provided with diamond-clawed capitals.
At the front, lotuses should be carved upon the balance-beam, provided with great weights;
one should then place the upper end of the beam above that by half its length.
One should set up a pillar that rises one and a half parts in height with its top facing upwards;
then, one should provide an *upatulā* (upper beam) which extends across the width at the interval.
One should adorn it all around with the splendor of banners and flags, using sandalwood paste of that same measurement, joined to the upper portion of the cloth.
Having cut away three-quarters and half [of the space], the walls on all sides are adorned with various lattice windows and balconies in every direction.
The western door, which is the most excellent, should be made equal in measure to the middle section;
it should be raised to a height of two sections and provided with a door-panel and a bolt.
Outside the walls, a pedestal (vedikā) should be constructed measuring one part;
it should be made half a part in height for the sake of beauty. || 9-25 ||
Having caused a circular area to be constructed according to the prescribed rite— either with baked bricks, covered with grass, or covered with stone— one should commence the work of the ground.

Likewise, *ataśī*, *khala*, buttermilk (*takra*), the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the bark of the *udumbara* tree, *triphalā*, the heartwood of the *bījavṛkṣa*, and that of the *khadira* tree. (9.27)
Having sprinkled this very water over it again and again, one should then strike it,
O Goddess, until it becomes hollowed out.
The auspicious Plavanī river, resembling the surface of a mirror, should be directed toward the east or else toward the northeast for the fulfillment of all desires. (9.29)
Having smeared it again, one should rub it with leaf-juice and other substances;
then, having constructed the excellent Sarvatobhadra mandala as before.
Or on the eighth, O beloved, or the one called Bhūta (the fourteenth), or the full moon, or the seventh; or the tenth, or the ninth, or the third, or the twelfth.
One should cause an auspicious maṇḍala to be made during the dark fortnight or the bright fortnight,
in summer, or in spring, or in winter, or in autumn.
The great heroes who have approached [the teacher], being endowed with devotion and pure in their vows, must be tested by him in accordance with what is enjoined in the scriptures. (9.33)
A Śūdra [attains it] in twelve years, a Vaiśya in nine, a Kṣatriya in six years, and a Brāhmaṇa in half of that. (9.34)
A person of low status may be engaged in a high task, and one of high status in a low task;
thus, one should examine them with effort through various methods. (9.35)
Those who have crossed the ocean of examination are indeed fit for the sacrifice of Śiva;
you must bestow grace upon them, for they are ready for the fruit.
But those who are contrary must be avoided; by that [means], they become vessels for accomplishment. Born into the family of the Yoginīs, they perceive that subtle state. (9.37)
For one who has obtained [the mantra] through negligence becomes thus deluded;
having understood this, the high-minded one approached the portion of the mantra.
Just as when the Vāstuyāga has been performed, following that with the Astrayāga, then at its conclusion the Gaṇayāga, and after that again the Śriyāyāga; || 9.39 ||

Then, having restrained his senses, on the following day he should first offer oblations into the fire according to the prescribed sequence of ritual stages, and thereafter he should cause the deity to accept [the offerings].
Having commenced the sacrifice at night and having gathered all the necessary materials,
he should worship there the Lord of Gods, the soul of all, who possesses great splendor.
O beloved, she is seated upon his lap— the supreme Goddess, the embodiment of all syllables,
holding a lotus in her hand, of great body, peaceful in form, and bestowing boons.
Drinking divine wine and laughing with great intensity,
one should worship the group of Mother-goddesses outside, just as previously described.
Having offered various kinds of food offerings and well-satiated [the deity] with wine and spirits,
one should then perform worship in this manner and address the Supreme Lord.
O Protector, may I be free from flaw; whatever has been done by me for the sake of the Five, may all that, O Lord, bear fruit through the grace of your feet.
Having gone near the fire, he should perform the rites beginning with the conception ceremony (garbhādhāna) and ending with the rite for Śiva, exactly as was done previously.
The oblations should be performed without deliberation, five by five;
once purified, perform the sacrifice thereafter as before.
O Dear One, one who presides over the maṇḍala should satisfy the scripture, the group of sciences and mantras;
likewise, one should worship the path within the jar as well.
On a sacrificial mound, in a water-pot, in the fire, and especially within one's own self—the wise should perform the ritual procedure in a manner that is consistent [with these locations]. (9.49)
But the undivided [fire], as previously described, should be established and maintained during the sacrifice;
thereafter, the disciple, with flowers in hand and well-restrained, should enter.
To the western part of the deity, the virtuous-souled one should lead the disciples;
then, having prostrated before the deity, he should go near the fire.
Having meditated on the path with the mind, one should cause it to enter the body;
this libation is for the purpose of bringing [the deity] into proximity, O lady of excellent vows, starting from the beginning up to the stage of patience. 9.52
The practitioner of mantras should indeed prepare a sacrificial oblation (caru) with milk from a cow that yields nectar-like milk,
O Goddess, using either śyāmāka grains, wild rice (nīvāra), or priyaṅgu seeds.
Or, O Goddess, with sixty measures of śāli rice, or with barley, wheat, and vrīhi rice;
[the vessel] may be made of copper, gold, silver, or even of clay.
One should wash [the vessel], which is very firm, free of flaws, and smooth, with the root-mantra (mūlavidyā).
Having taken a firebrand from the Śiva-fire, one should kindle it both outside and inside.
Then, having performed the protection (rakṣā), one who is composed should place it upon that fire.
Then, having prepared a vessel smeared with ghee and overflowing with milk, || 9.56 ||
One should place it in the midst of the fire so that it becomes perfectly steady;
one should perform the movement with the root mantra ending in the syllable *Ṣaḍha*.
When it has become warm from sweating, one should perform the sprinkling with the root mantra;
when it has become cold, one should perform the cooling sprinkling and the descent [of the deity].
One should perform the sprinkling and washing with the root mantra;
having brought the *saṃpāta* (the residual drops) to the heart, one should divide it into four parts.
The first [offering] should be given upon the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), the second to the water-pot (kalaśa);
the third to the bali and the fire, and the fourth to oneself.
One should present the food offering (naivedya) at three locations, and outside, one should give the bali-offering to the children, the Mothers, and the guardians of the field and the spirits.
Having thus satisfied [the deities] and subsequently sipped water with care, one should then prostrate to the God and, being well-composed, perform the ritual dismissal.
O beloved, together with the practitioners and their sons who have approached [the rite],
one should then drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) according to the sequence of the ritual application.
Having consumed the sacrificial oblation (caru) according to the prescribed rule and sipped water for purification with a well-composed mind,
he should then take a tooth-stick that contains milk and is free from knots.

O fair-faced one, the palm leaf should be made one span long, straight, smooth, even, and auspicious; its circumference should be equal to that of the little finger, and it should be made of udumbara wood.
Alternatively, one should observe the falling of other [substances] as well— such as milk and so forth, combined with flowers—
to determine whether it is auspicious or inauspicious.
Falling facing forward is best, as are the directions east and north; the others are said to be contrary, which an attentive person should observe.
Through auspicious [dreams] one attains success, but through inauspicious ones, the opposite occurs. O Dear One, the practitioner of mantra should sleep during the night together with his companions.
Having gone at the clear dawn and performed the morning twilight worship,
and having paid homage to the gods and the ancestors, he should come into the presence of the teacher.

O Goddess, one should report the dream, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious; through auspicious dreams, success is to be predicted, while for inauspicious ones, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa).
By doing thus, there will be peace and the pacification of obstacles;
one should observe the auspicious or inauspicious signs in dreams at the beginning of an undertaking and at its conclusion. (9.71)
O lady of beautiful countenance, I shall describe auspicious dreams as well as inauspicious ones:
drinking liquor in a dream, and the eating of fish and meat; (9.72)
Smearing oneself with worms and excrement, being sprinkled with blood, eating curd-rice, and smearing oneself with white garments. (9.73)
A white parasol situated above the head, adorned with white garlands and wreaths;
a lion-throne, a chariot, a vehicle, a banner, and the royal consecration.
A radiant jewel-ornamented limb, a betel leaf and nut, a vision of Śrī-Sarasvatī, and the embrace of an auspicious noble woman. (9.75)
Having engaged in dialogue with kings, ṛṣis, gods, siddhas, vidyādharas, and gaṇas, as well as with the ācāryas, one attains success in a dream. (9.76)
Crossing rivers and the ocean, traveling through the sky, as well as weeping over the dead and beholding the blazing fire. (9.77)
The sighting of planets, lunar mansions, and stars, as well as the sun and the moon;
or likewise, ascending a palace or even the pinnacle of a temple. (9.78)
Riding upon elephants, horses, and bulls; climbing trees and the tops of rocks; traveling by celestial chariot; and beholding perfected beings and humans. (9.79)
The attainment of gain, the movement of the lords [of the quarters], the vision of goddesses, the pill, the wooden staff, the sword, the sandals, and the yellow pigment (rocanā). 9.80.
The sacred thread, collyrium, nectar, mercury, medicinal herbs, the spear, the water-pot, the lotus, the rosary, and realgar. (9.81)

Flaming substances, those ending with red ochre (gairika), and whatever medicinal herbs bring the attainment of land or wealth—all these are accomplished by the sight [of them] at the end of a dream. (9.82)
In the battle that was an ocean of blood, there was crossing over and victory in the fray;
in the delightful cremation ground of the ancestors, which was filled with heroes and lords of heroes.
And the heroes, vetālas, and siddhas, having respectfully received from the goddesses the sale of great flesh and the portion of the great sacrificial animal— 9.84.
O God, while worshipping himself, reciting prayers, meditating, or even offering hymns,
he perceives himself as being worshipped when he offers oblations into the blazing fire.
It was frequented by swans, cranes, ruddy geese, peacocks,
and parrots, and was accompanied by the Mothers, the eight Bhairavas, and the hosts of Rudras with their mantras.
Having seen Bhairavī and Bhairava, one attains success; there is no doubt in this. (81b) Auspicious dreams have been fully described; now learn from me those that are inauspicious. (9-87)
Anointing with oil, as well as drinking [poison], entering the subterranean realm (rasātala), falling into a blind well, and then sinking into the mud. || 9.88 ||
Falling from trees or mountains while traveling on the backs of bears or monkeys, or the cutting off of the nose, the ears, or the hands and feet. (9.89)
The falling out of teeth and hair, the sight of bears and monkeys, and the sight of cruel creatures, as well as of vetālas and black men. (9.90)
If in a dream a man embraces a woman who is dark-complexioned, clad in dirty rags, wearing black garlands and garments, and has red eyes; (9.91)
If one performs the rite of pacification, there is no doubt that he will die; likewise, there is the destruction of houses, palaces, beds, seats, and umbrellas. (9.92)

One may see the dissolution of one's own self, the seizure of one's own property, or rebirth as a donkey, camel, horse, jackal, heron, vulture, or hawk; or again, one may see mounting upon a crow, an owl, or a buffalo.
The eating of bird-flesh, and [the wearing of] red garlands and unguents. || 9-94 ||
One who has mastered the self sees red and black garments;
in a dream, one laughs, leaps about, and wears withered garlands.
Cutting out one's own flesh, being bitten by a black serpent, and likewise seeing oneself married in a dream—by such sights, one certainly does not attain success. (9.96)
Thus, indeed, the inauspicious has been fully explained; it should be understood by the instructor.
However, auspicious acts are to be approved; one should perform a hundred fire-oblations for the inauspicious.
By offering eight superior *govarikās* with the *aghora* mantra, one who has controlled the senses is liberated from the [sin of] expiation after three repetitions. (9.98)
One should diligently rub that madana leaf with *valī* and other substances;
then, taking a *karaṇī* made from cotton (*trivṛtā*), [one should proceed].
A pure person should diligently bring white lime from a mountain;
then, one should extend the thread reaching the Brahma-position toward the eastern direction.
Or, within the *citrā* [constellation], one desires the east and the west;
with the *mīna* conjunction, the north [is desired], and this same rule applies in the south as well.
Then, having divided [the line] into four parts based on the eastern thread,
O Dear One, one should form two fish-marks using that which is the fourth part.
One should establish the east-west line when the cord has been removed;
likewise, the south-north line shall be established, and afterwards one should establish the intermediate corners.
In the northeast, southeast, southwest, and northwest, respectively;
when the field has been prepared in this manner, one should establish a square.
Once the field has been made square, one should subsequently fashion a lotus;
one should draw an excellent lotus measuring twenty-four finger-breadths in length.
An eight-petaled lotus should be made even, prominent with a pericarp and filaments;
the first part is the pericarp, and the second consists of the filaments.
In the third [circle], one should draw the joints of the petals; in the fourth, the tips of the petals;
and outside the lotus, one should draw the line of the protective border (*prativāraṇarekhā*).
The limbs should be made on the outside with a measurement of four finger-breadths;
beyond that as well, there should be a pathway measuring one cubit.
O Dear One, the doors are said to be one *padma* in measure, or else half of that;
having thus laid out the lines with the cord, one should cast down the colored powders.
The three types of *rajas* are declared to be red, yellow, and white;
the lines should be drawn straight, unbroken, and very beautiful.
One should first ensure that the distance between the lines is exactly one barley-corn (yava);
the pericarp (karṇikā) should be made yellow, and the lotus-petals (puṣkara) red in color.
The filaments (keśara) should be made rich in red and yellow, and indeed white as well;
the petals (dala) are declared to be white, surrounding [the flower] on all sides, O Umā.
One should cause all the intermediate petals to be red and yellow;
the *bhrāmaṇī* should be made yellow, and the *gātrakas* red and yellow.
Just as the beauty should be fashioned in the Sarvatobhadra mandala, so too should the leafy creepers, their number, the winding vines, and the svastikas [be arranged]. (9.114)
One should cause it to be adorned everywhere with beautiful colors.
Then, in the afternoon, the practitioner of mantra [should approach] one who has bathed or indeed merely been dusted with ashes.
Wearing white garments, the yogin, adorned with white garlands and unguents,
enters the sacrificial circle with flowers in hand and well-restrained.
Then one should worship the God who pervades the sky, both supreme and non-supreme,
who bears all colors, who is peaceful, and who is characterized by the nine cowherds.

Having thus worshipped with effort, in due order, with water for the guest-offering (argha), water for the feet (pādya), and so forth— the one who holds a lotus in his hand, wears an even crown, and has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament— || 9-118 ||

O Dear One, one should diligently worship those known as the *vargas* in the place of enjoyment (*bhogasthāna*), with perfumes, flowers, food offerings (*naivedya*), and various kinds of auspicious edibles. (9.119)
Having thus worshipped with various kinds of drinks, meats, birds, and liquors, both upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and likewise in the water-pot (kalaśa), || 9.120 ||
One should worship the Supreme Lord both in the sacrificial pit and within one's own body;
then, having prostrated with devotion, one should carefully summon the disciple.
One should conceive of its path, extending from Śiva down to the earth as its limit;
one should worship it with perfumes and flowers, and then cause the binding of the eyes to be performed.
One should cause the binding of the eyes with a cloth such as dukūla, paṭṭa, cotton, or new [linen], provided it is of a similar white color. || 9-123 ||
Then, having placed a flower in his hand, he should enter the sacrificial maṇḍala;
O Dear One, he should cause the flower to be released on the right side of the deity.
If flowers of a mantra are seen fallen, one should assign its name preceded by that [mantra] and ending with the word *śakti*. (9.125)
That mantra should be given to him, and once given, it indeed becomes effective;
then, having performed the opening of the eyes, he should prostrate with great devotion.
Then, O beloved, having performed obeisance to the water-pot in this manner,
he should lead it near the fire and remain stationed facing the south.
Then, having taken darbha grass in his hand and having cut its tip beautifully,
the Guru should touch it with the treasury of mantras and then perform worship.
Having meditated upon the path with the mind, the teacher who has reached the further shore of reality may,
according to his will, [liberate] bound souls by means of the yoga of the process of withdrawal.
Through reasoning, for those desiring liberation, there is withdrawal by way of the path of emanation regarding the object.
Having thus understood the movement of the mind, one should perform the ritual service. (9.130)
The creation consists of the letters from *a* to *kṣa*, while the withdrawal occurs through the arrangement starting from *kṣa*.
Having first placed the letter *kṣa*, one proceeds all the way back to the letter *a*.
The knower of reality should always effect the joining within the sacrificial pit;
first by means of the joining of the channels, one should then perform the joining of the principles within.
Thereafter, the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed according to the ritual procedure seen in the scriptures,
pronouncing each syllable individually, preceded by "namaḥ" and excluding the Praṇava (Oṃ).
One should pierce that which is free from the six classes and devoid of head and crest-lock with the lotus-womb [mantra], and one should ignite that which is called Kuṇḍalī.
No lamp should be applied to this; rather, when that which is called the *kuṇḍalī* is ignited, one should perform the grasping located at the navel by means of the supreme emission (*visarga*).
Having its form resembling a thread from a spider's web, consciousness is held firmly by power (śakti) in front of it, like the sun in the sky.
One should cause [the deity] to descend through its own respective states, abiding in Brahmā, abiding in Viṣṇu, abiding in Rudra, situated in Īśvara, situated in Nāda, and situated in Śakti.
In each respective principle (tattva), one should effect birth, as well as sovereignty, the attainment of enjoyments, union, and separation, in their proper place.
Having pierced the phoneme, whether it be a *tattva*, what is designated as a *pada*, or even that which consists of *kalās* and *mantras*, one is led to the *dvādaśānta* in due order. (9.139)
O Varārohā, O beloved, whether it be the world or the path of the castes, the application of awareness, abandonment, integration, and conjunction must be performed. (9.140)
But the unification of the entire pure path occurs in the supreme Śiva—beyond all characteristics, devoid of qualities, tranquil, pure, and utterly stainless. (9.141)
O all-pervading one, the sustainer of qualities, the omnipresent, who is devoid of mind; O you who are insentient yet possess perfect consciousness, free from sound and touch. || 9.142 ||

In that which is non-awareness yet has awareness as its form, which is devoid of qualities yet the source of all qualities; which is formless yet possesses every form, and which is insatiable yet characterized by complete satisfaction.
In the great yoga that is without support, the support of all, the abode of qualities; in that which is trackless, yet established in the state of being a track; formless, yet possessing all forms.

Having performed yoga in that which is without support— in bliss and the absence of bliss, in the whole and the partless, in the digit and its absence, and in non-existence having attained the state of existence— (9.145).
O lady of excellent hips, by the contraction of the eyebrows, the practitioner situated at the equinox—when joined with that, O Great Goddess—shall not undergo birth again. (9.146)
One wanders in saṃsāra as long as one does not find oneness;
when the mind has attained the state of oneness, there is neither bondage nor a binder. (9.147)
Just as copper, when touched by mercury, attains the state of gold,
so too one who is united with the supreme reality shall never again fall into the condition of a bound soul.
The Great Bond (mahābandha) is proclaimed as the sixteenth [mudrā] by means of the path itself;
its cause is Śakti, known as Mātṛkā, who is both supreme (parā) and non-supreme (aparā).
The supreme [power] is said to consist of light, and when threaded with gold it is considered the supreme;
she alone is the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) and the cause of bondage for living beings.
O my beloved, I shall briefly describe to you the path of the phonemes (varṇādhvan).
The letter *kṣa* possesses great splendor, with a brilliance blazing like the fire of time (kālāgni). (9.151)
One should place the performer of all destruction beneath the soles of the feet;
the letter *ha* is situated above that, at the big toes of the feet. (9.152)
One should place the syllable *śa* on the two ankles, the syllable *ṣa* on the two knees,
the syllable *sa* on the two palms, and the syllable *va* on the two vocal cords.
The letter *la* is said to be the collection of bones; the letter *ra* is called blood;
the letter *ya* they call the skin; and the letter *ma* they know as the person (*puruṣa*).
The letter *bha* is at the joints of the knees, and likewise the letter *ba* is at the bolt;
the letter *pha* is to be known as resting above the knees. (9.155)
The letter *pa* is to be applied to the thighs, the letter *na* to the joints of the hips;
they say the letter *dha* is for the testicles, while the letter *da* is traditionally taught for the others.
The letter *tha* is situated in the middle of the *liṅga*, the letter *ta* is the semen itself;
the letter *ṇa* is in the secret region, while the letter *ḍha* is in the navel circle.
One should place the letter Ḍa in the center of the navel, the letter Ṭha likewise in the stomach,
the letter Ṭa at the heart, and the letter Ña in the middle of the body.
The syllable *jhakāra* is in the second [position], while *jakāra* is known as the peak;
*śakāra*, O lady of excellent complexion, is on the left, the right, and the other [position]. (9.159)
One should place the letter *ca* at the wrist, the letter *ṅa* at the second [joint],
the letter *gha* at the finger-joints, and thereafter the letter *ga*.
O Dear One, one should place the syllable *kha* in the middle of the hands, the syllable *ka* on the left,
the syllable *a* at the throat, and one should place *aṃ* in the middle of the palate.
Having placed *au* on the tip of the tongue, one should place *o* on the rows of teeth; one should place the vowel *ai* on the left [side] and *e* on the right nostril. (9.162)
The syllable *lṝ* is on the left eye, and likewise the syllable *lṛ* on the right;
the syllable *ṝ* is on the left ear, and likewise *ṛ* on the right. (9.163)
One should place the syllable *ū* between the two eyebrows, the syllable *u* in the middle of the eyebrows,
the syllable *ī* on the forehead, and the syllable *i* in the form of a dot (*bindu*).
One should place the syllable Ā on the head and the syllable A in the domain of the skin;
having thus performed the placement (nyāsa) of the path, one should effect the breaking of the knots.
By this sequential yoga, O fair-faced one, the path to be purified—
namely, dissolution, enjoyment, separation, and likewise union— is [accomplished] in each and every reality (tattva).
Having purified everything in due order, one should unite it with the eternal state.
The Goddess said:
O Lord, I have heard the initiation of the phonemes (varṇadīkṣā), which is the supreme essence of essences.
"Now I wish to hear about the initiation into reality (tattvadīkṣā) according to its true nature.
Bhairava said:
"O Great Goddess, the initiation into reality belongs to Śārā, who faces in all directions."
I shall fully declare that to you; listen, O large-eyed one!
Earth, water, fire, air, and space as well—|| 9.169 ||
O fair-faced one, by the purification of these, the sixfold [group] becomes pure.
Five are declared to be the organs of action (karmendriya), and after that, the organs of cognition (buddhīndriya).
The five subtle elements (tanmātras) are to be known; now hear their characteristics from me:
sound, touch, taste, form, and smell constitute the pentad of subtle elements. (9.171)
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose—these five have been declared by me to be the organs of perception; hear now this certainty. 9.172cd–173ab.
Speech, the hands, as well as the feet, the anus, and the generative organ—O fair-faced one, this is indeed declared to be the pentad of organs of action (karmākṣa). (9.173)

Intellect, mind, and ego, as well as primordial nature (prakṛti) and the rest, are to be known respectively as the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, which arise from the primary principle (pradhāna). || 9-174 ||
The unmanifest (avyakta) is thus described as the twenty-fifth;
and the Puruṣa is the twenty-sixth, the one who makes known pleasure and pain. (9.175)

Whether it be pleasure or pain acquired in the past, that which is born of the field (kṣetraja) and known through experience is declared to be that which must be experienced as the remainder of the latent impressions of karma (karmavāsanā). || 9-176 ||
By that purity, the manifold seed of existence is purified;
having cleansed it gradually, O Goddess, according to the rule upon the path.
Beyond this, that which is called destiny (niyati) is declared to be established in the state of necessity;
O beautiful one, it is the determiner of time and number regarding whatever has been done.

Since that reality (tattva) is pervaded by a portion (kalā) and remains as such, it is for this reason called "portion" (kalā), [referring to] one whose mind is shattered by passion (rāga). || 9.179 ||
And because he is colored by passion, O Goddess, the powerful one is deluded by illusion, O Beloved;
Vidyā should be known as that which brings about perception, for Vidyā knows the auspicious and the inauspicious. (9.180)
A person who knows the meaning of the higher knowledge (parāvidyā) and relies upon the path of purity,
being presided over by the Lord, goes either to the world of Īśvara or indeed to the highest state.
Whether it be liberation or anything else, impelled by the Lord, Sadāśiva alone is indeed the knower and the liberator of bound souls, O beloved. (9.182)
For those whose minds are overwhelmed by enjoyments and who have abandoned the seed of illusion, there exists a pervasive and subtle power that follows the nature of Śiva. (9.183)
Śiva, however, is declared to be all-pervading, established at the end of the thirty-six [tattvas].
Thus, O Goddess, one should purify the path according to the sequence of the number of tattvas. (9.184)
O Goddess, in these thirty-six positions, the wise should perform purification according to the sequence of the nine principles, beginning with *prakṛti*. (9.185)
O Varārohā, that which bestows manifold enjoyments for the atoms (aṇus) must be purified;
it is declared to be the triad of principles known as Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva. (9.186)
These are declared to be the primary [impurities] that must be purified with great effort;
when these are purified, O fair-faced one, the sixfold [impurity] becomes pure. (9.187)
O Supreme Goddess, all these should be seen as being manifested by that [power].
Now, O beautiful one, I shall describe to you the path of the Kalās (kalādhvāna).
The reality is pervaded by the *kalās*, and that reality indeed has the form of Time;
Mahādeva, the omniscient Supreme Lord, is himself the form of the *kalās*. (9.189)
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti; Śāntyatītā is to be known as the supreme (parā), and all [the elements] beginning with earth are traditionally taught [as these kalās]. (9.190)
Indikā, Dīpikā, Rocikā, and likewise Mocikā;
the one known as Ūrdhvagāmī is the supreme (parā), remembered as the fulfiller of them all.
Sūkṣmā, Susūkṣmā, and likewise Amṛtā are remembered as the portions of the self of Śakti, specifically of Vyāpinī and Śiva. (9.192)
Pervasive, having the nature of space, infinite, and not dependent on a protector—O beautiful one, the path of the *kalās* has thus been briefly explained to you. (9.193)
One or another of these should be purified by the high-souled teacher;
having purified the path of mantra, however, by means of the supreme and non-supreme Vidyā.

O lady of excellent hips, one who knows the path of the feet should perform initiation for me by means of my vidyā; those most proficient in the scriptures should perform it starting from the level of Bhuvana. (9.195)
Beginning with Kālāgni and extending as far as Śiva,
this sixfold procedure indeed follows the sequence within the path of the phonemes (varṇādhvan).
The wise should perform the seizing, the joining, and the separation in their proper sequence, according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures. (9.197)
O Goddess, one of these must be purified with effort;
having performed the consecration according to the rules by a Guru who knows the paths.
O Goddess, grace should be bestowed upon the bound souls (paśus) in due order,
having understood [the process] through the distinction between emanation and withdrawal, according to their specific desires.
Then, O lady of excellent hips, the paralysis of the fetters occurs;
when the paralysis of the fetters has arisen, it is not otherwise, O leader of heroes.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, I have heard about initiation as it exists within the sixfold path;
now I wish to hear, in accordance with reality, about the loosening of the fetters."
Those subtle nooses which have been described as arising from Māyā yet devoid of Māyā— being insentient and formless, there is no paralysis (stobha) of them.
That which is performed upon the bound soul (paśu) is known as *paśustobha*. Consciousness, bound by fetters, remains situated in a state of mutual non-pervasion. (9.203)

O Lord, from which two [principles] would there be the stimulation (stobha) consisting of the individual soul (paśu) and its bonds (pāśa)—namely, intoxication, delusion, passion, despondency, and even sorrow? (9.204)
Inconceivability, joy, and its designation—these seven are the innate impurities (*sahaja-mala*).
Bondage consists of dharma and adharma; its essence abides in primordial nature (*prakṛti*). (9.205)
Because they are subtle, formless, and devoid of consciousness, a state of paralysis (stobha) occurs for all [beings], with the exception of the field-born one who possesses consciousness. (9-206)
Therefore, there can be no praise for that which is devoid of qualities and insentient.
Bhairava said:
"The Self is eternal, formless, devoid of qualities, and inactive. (9.207)
One who is a vessel for contradiction should be known as one to be purified and awakened by nature;
however, the "bound soul" (paśu) is said to be non-conceptual, yet presided over by merit and demerit. (9.208)
Previously, he was bound by the snares consisting of the nature of illusion;
for from that [state], the single primordial impurity remains established as the seed. (9-209)
O lady of excellent vows, the quality of sprouting depends upon the field;
for that innate [consciousness], the field is Māyā, which is the impurity of the bound soul (paśu).
Just as a tiny seed of the *aśvattha* tree, having fallen and sprouted in a field, grows with its branches and trunk spreading wide through its connection with the soil of that field; (9.211)
Thus, O Goddess, the impurity of the individual soul (māṇavaka) is eternally dependent upon Māyā;
for that Māyā, being characterized by signs, proceeds from the atom (aṇu). 9.212cd–213ab.
O Goddess of gods, for one who is signless (animitta), illusion (māyā) does not function at all; even so, O Bhavānī, the progression along the pure path (śuddhādhvan) occurs. (9.213)
O Goddess, Śiva does not exist; at that time there would be only Māyā.
Since she arises with the nature of bondage, there is no liberation for anyone therein. (9.214)
O Supreme Goddess, even by the gods, this yoga might proceed incorrectly; however, those who are remembered as the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) and so forth are destined for liberation.
Liberation does not occur for them as long as the signless state has not arisen;
it is just as liberation would not be found even when the true path exists [if one does not practice it]. (9.216)

When the meaning of the scriptures has not been investigated, there arises the path of bondage known as "illusion," just as a king proceeds to inflict execution or imprisonment upon his own fault. (9.217)
Just as there is no bondage in that which is faultless, so too māyā cannot prevail;
for men, the innate substratum is indeed the sole impurity that acts as a continuous bond. (9.218)
Relying upon that, illusion proceeds as the awakener of the continuum;
once reality has been awakened by illusion, it attains liberation. (9.219)
Consciousness is intensified by *kalā*, its object is revealed by *vidyā*, and it is colored by *rāga* while being joined with the instruments such as the intellect (*buddhi*). (9.220)
In this way, bondage consisting of illusion would follow in the continuous stream [of existence]. (9.221)

In brief, dharma and adharma are qualities that have that [puruṣa] as their substratum; the fetters are known to consist of those very qualities, and by means of them the bound one (paśu) remains bound. (9.222)
Having thus understood the separation of one's own *māyā* from Śiva, listen now to how the loosening of the bonds subsequently occurs. (9.223)
O Goddess, just as the fang of a snake whose life has departed is insentient,
yet it still moves and throbs, so too do they indeed send forth the sacred ford.
The power of mantra is seen; what is there to be doubted in this?
The shaking, the paralyzing, the splitting, and the coming and going of stones [are achieved by it]. (9.225)
Entering a dead body, transforming one's form and so forth, becoming small and thin, and exiting through the openings of a lattice—these are [the powers]. (9.226)
O you of virtuous vows, such inconceivable accomplishments as these exist through the power of mantra; how then could there be any doubt regarding the Śiva-āgama? (9.227)
O illustrious lady, among all those means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that have been described by Śambhu as being direct perceptions (pratyakṣa), this indeed is the most excellent direct perception.
But how can there be another conceptual construction regarding that which is perceived by the senses?
O fair-faced one, [this is because] bondage consists of dharma and adharma for the self. (9.229)
