And its very destruction must be brought about through initiation, O Supreme Goddess, regarding those actions which have already been performed and those which one performs now. (9.230)
For by initiation their [bonds] are destroyed; through the casting off of the body, one shall go to Śiva. Those who abide in unrighteousness have their tenfold bonds destroyed.
O Goddess of gods, there is no support by which he might remain on the path;
for when the self is liberated from its bonds, it is proclaimed to be without support. (9.232)
O beloved, just as a tree with its roots severed trembles on the ground due to external forces, so too do the potatoes and the like shake when their roots are cut. 9-233.
And just as there is no doubt regarding the potato, so too is the Self proclaimed;
likewise, the wise should effect the severance of the bonds through initiation. (9.234)
But when separation occurs, then there is undoubtedly *stobha*.
*Stobha* is defined as trembling as well as falling. (9.235)
When [the mantra] is placed upon a yellow bell-metal vessel that is free from defects, there occurs the paralysis of the noose (pāśastobha), resulting in liberation from all bonds. (9.236)
Just as a tree bound at some place by roots reaching to the tips of its branches falls when those [roots] are severed, O beloved, like something deprived of its support; (9.237)
In the same way, the embodied soul, bound by the fetters of dharma and the like, falls;
yet, its liberation occurs—thus it is proclaimed in the scripture. (9.238)
The destruction [of obstacles] through the paralysis of the noose is accomplished by those who have attained perfection, and that too by means of the vows;
for the vows are inconceivable, just as there is the destruction of formless poison. (9.239)
Therefore, when the bonds have been severed, liberation is manifest in this very way;
the severing is declared to be the paralyzing (stobhana), and no other conceptualization is recorded.
But those, O Goddess, whose initiation is of the bound (pāśavī), have their seeds burnt;
when his bonds are paralyzed, then there is liberation, without a doubt. (9.241)
Indeed, all teachings proclaim initiation as liberation;
yet that liberation, though unseen, is accomplished through visible means. (9.242)
O Goddess of Gods, those conditions which are said to be unperceived in the proof of the unperceived cannot be established by means of dry logic, nor even by millions of scriptures.
When liberation is accomplished through initiation, it occurs when *stobha* arises; without *stobha*, there can be no liberation. This is the truth, the truth; there is no doubt. (9.244)
The Goddess said:
"The bonds consisting of dharma and adharma are its supporting forms;
when these are indeed severed at the root, then the self departs. (9.245)
But liberation is eternal, perpetual, blissful, and all-pervading; he should remain as one possessing that which is to be enjoyed, for that which has been consumed is subject to decay. (9.246)
And the Self does not remain within that [body] once the karma consisting of action has been experienced, O Lord.
That which is called "the object of experience" is the karma of the bound soul (paśu), and from that arises bondage. (9.247)

When that has been eliminated, whence can there be bondage? Upon its liberation, one tastes the nectar of immortality; for when the five elements have reached their end, even the support itself ceases to exist.
He should remain with his very body, since that [body] has been rendered subject to decay.
Bhairava said:
"The power that binds the bound soul (paśu) is of the nature of the cause of the universe. [9-249]
By her the entire world is bound, and by her alone it is liberated, O beloved;
she is the binder of those whose forms are ignorant, and the liberator of those who have realized the Self. (9.250)
For that capacity of theirs is metaphorically designated as the means for accomplishing both purposes;
its substratum would continue to function even during the exhaustion of merit and demerit. (9.251)
Arising from external conditions, it cuts away the very nature of form;
yet, because it is sustained by a single quality, no falling down occurs. (9.252)
In the same way, the self residing in the body remains as the support of power;
indeed, there is no falling for the person who is the support of power.
Just as one might enter another city while the body remains immortal, so too [the self] enters [a new body] endowed with the five elements and the thirteen instruments. (9.254)
It quickly restores the life-force of a yogin whose life has departed;
he himself moves, runs, speaks, and eats. (9.255)

Even within one's own body, O Goddess, the Self is one and the same in both [the individual and the universal], being the bestower of consciousness; yet the *pudgala* is the support of power (*śakti*). (9.256)
But that pervasive power which is of uninterrupted mind is the supreme *kalā*;
O Goddess, it is just as one who, while asleep, travels from village to village. (9.257)
The embodied soul wanders through the seven continents and the oceans;
yet it perceives within its own body as it moves, hears, and eats. (9.258)

That indeed becomes empty when consciousness has abandoned its movement; O Goddess, no one goes, nor does another thinker exist. The thinker, the lord, and the knower perceives the support of power (*śakti*).
Where there is power, there is mind; and the mind is established in the vital breath (*anila*). (9.260)
And egoity resides in the blue; indeed, it is established within egoity.
It should be understood as threefold: characterized by sattva, rajas, and tamas. (9.261)
O lady of excellent complexion, [the nature] of those in the animal realm is dominated by tamas, that of humans by rajas,
while that of the goddesses becomes intensified by sattva.
By its power, they indeed behold, go to, and hear;
they even grasp whatever they desire with their minds, wherever it may be.
Thus has Śakti, who is of the nature of Śiva and endowed with activity, been described by me. O Goddess, when there is a severance of that [activity], then the state of Nirvāṇa is attained.
There is no doubt in this matter that it occurs exactly as taught in the scriptures:
in the state with support (sāvalamba), there is the attainment of the eightfold qualities beginning with atomization (aṇimā).
O lady of beautiful hips, those who possess the power of action enjoy the supreme state;
this has been declared as being of the nature of knowledge by Śambhu, the God of gods. (9.266)
Now I shall describe the method of grasping so that it may become steady for you;
O lady of excellent vows, the grasping of that which transcends mantra should be performed by means of one's own power.
O Supreme Goddess, by abandoning both action and knowledge, one should cultivate the state of Rudra; therein, the cessation known as *manas* must be performed. (9.268)
Through the union of wind and fire, there is no doubt that it arises;
its grasping occurs at the region of the navel, having the shape of a *kadamba* bud.
Then, at the tip of the spear, one should visualize [the deity] blazing with garlands of flames;
situated in the midst of the wind and fire mandalas, he falls—of this there is no doubt. (9.270)
One should meditate on the whirling [light] situated at the navel, as difficult to perceive as a firebrand-wheel;
there is no doubt that the grasping of the subtle state occurs thereby. (9.271)

But when one meditates on that which moves in the form of the subtle mind (*manas*), wherever it goes, by means of the yoga of the "serpent's surge" (*nāgodvalana*), it falls [into the state of liberation]; of this there is no doubt. (9.272)
O Dear One, having meditated upon whatever form the Leader of Yoga intends to pierce, he quickly becomes a transformation of that [form], once he has recognized the supreme power (parā śakti).
Having performed the piercing according to whatever form the reality has, the paralysis (stobha) becomes identical with that; for the transformations are indeed of that very nature.

Having understood this, O lady of excellent hips, O you of virtuous vows, the grasping of that which transcends mantra should be performed by way of yoga, as it has been revealed in the scripture. (9.275)
Now listen to how it occurs through the application of mantra:
this "Hara" (HA) conjoined with "Śakti-bīja" (SA) is declared [to be the seed-syllable]. (90b) || 9.276 ||
One should remember the seed-syllable of Śakti and place it upon all the limbs;
one should place the mantra adorned with the twelve vowels upon the heart-cakra.
In its center is consciousness, resembling a hibiscus flower;
it is impelled by the wind and illuminated by fire. (9.278)

One should meditate upon that and recite the mantra through the yoga of interspersing it with the Name; O Goddess of Gods, for as long as a moment, there will undoubtedly be a state of paralysis (stobha).
O Goddess, he perceives himself as being joined to each successive reality (tattva),
until, having reached the supreme reality, he perceives that very [supreme] state.
By this sequential yoga, he perceives all paths;
or else, at that very moment, he masters all the scriptures. (9.281)
There are many mudrās to be bound as taught in the scriptures; of this there is no doubt.
By means of this sequential yoga, one should effect the paralysis of the fetters (pāśastobha).
Without knowledge, there is no empowerment; one is devoid of power, O fair-faced one.
He who knows the supreme power, the primordial power Manonmanī, [is empowered]. (9.283)
Pierced by that [breath], one goes upward to that state which is free from affliction.
The seed-syllable of the Self (ātma-bīja) situated on the buttocks and constricted by the staff—this is that posture (āsana).
O lady of beautiful hips, one who has mounted the left peak and is adorned with ornaments can paralyze the entire world of moving and non-moving beings by means of the left ear.
One should cause the self-prāṇa and likewise the navel to be pressed by the staff;
O Goddess, one should then illuminate it with fire and again with the crest.
O Dear One, with the left hand adorned [with a skull], one should paralyze the three worlds;
the left arm rests upon the hip, and that posture is known as Daṇḍākānta.
Adorned with a left-pointing crest as its ornament, it truly, truly paralyzes all sentient beings; of this there is no doubt. (9-288)
Now, O Goddess, hear from me another supreme [method] which is about to be described:
one should cause the individual soul (jīva) to be mounted upon fire and then conjoined with that [fire]. (9.289)
Impelled by the vital breath (vāyu) and likewise endowed with the sixfold [set], it is permeated by the twelve vowels and situated in the source (yoni), O fair-faced one. (9.290)
In that regard, O Goddess, the power situated in the center effects the piercing, the fixing, and the cessation; it must be grasped by means of the supreme union.
When thus accomplished through mantras, the seizing occurs within the range of one's power;
once seized, he whose mind has departed falls quickly upon the earth of Kāśyapa.
There, cessation must be effected through application to the supreme state;
yet again, the joining of the vital breaths within the channels must be performed. (9.293)
But when the reconnection has been made, O Goddess, it shall become as it was before;
one should then relate what was seen there, in each tattva in due order. (9.294)
As long as that supreme reality exists, for so long does he perceive it in this way;
one should diligently install that knowledge according to the division of its steps.

The grasping [of the object] must be performed by Śakti through her form consisting of the letters from *na* to *pha*, by means of the nature of the nine principles (*tattva*), just as a firefly is perceived by its light. (9.296)
One should bring [the breath] to the dvādaśānta and perform the emission;
the grasping is joined with the instruments together with the five elemental selves. (9.297)
Having repeatedly purified everything—whether it resides in the self, resides in the reality, or resides in that [reality]—one should gradually unite it all with the supreme Śiva. (9.298)

In that which is without marks, without qualities, peaceful, and devoid of all means—this indeed is the seizing of the bound soul (paśu); now hear from me concerning the departure of the breath (utkrānti).
One should diligently place [the seed-syllables] at the navel, the breasts, and the shoulders on the left;
likewise at the secret organ, the navel, the mouth, the ears, and the two eyes.

One should contemplate Kuṇḍalī, who resides in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) and has the form of a womb, as being joined with the letters of the groups [of consonants] in these locations according to their sequence. (9.301)
O Goddess, one should contemplate the wind situated within that, known as fire, which is the Supreme Self, located in the middle of the *suṣumnā* and established in the *brahmanāḍī*.
But with a further emission, there is piercing of the two Brahma-apertures;
having placed the mind right there at the front, one should practice meditative concentration on the state of being.

O virtuous one, O beloved, one should sever [the bonds] at the navel, heart, throat, and the end of the palate, as well as at the *bindu* and *nāda*, using either the king of weapons or a knife. 9-304.
One should mentally sever all the bonds that connect the vital points (*marmasandhana*), and one should contemplate the destruction [of the enemy] with thousands of garlands of flames. (9.305)
Having emerged through the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), it severs the remaining bonds;
O Dear One, one should sever the *śakti* above the *lambaka* by means of the emission (*visarga*).
One should meditate upon the *hiṣkaṃ* located in the region of the throat, which destroys worldly existence;
by means of this sequential yoga, one should utter the division of the syllables. 9-307ab.
O you of excellent vows, as long as he moves with the shifting of his steps,
he causes hundreds and thousands of beings to ascend.

O you whose wealth is austerity, O goddess worshipped by the gods, it is the truth, the absolute truth, that the supreme practitioner performs this seizing of the animal and its departure [from the body]. (9.309)
O beloved, this knowledge of the Goddess must not be told to anyone;
by means of it, the bound souls (paśus) of the Goddess depart from the surface of the earth.
It must be kept secret by him; it should not be told, but always concealed.
Now I shall explain the Kṣurikā as it is characterized by its defining marks. 9-311ab.
The breast of the Goddess, situated on the right and joined with the letter *ra*, should be expanded;
it should be applied twice, and then the second tooth again. (9-312)
Then, having again joined that first syllable with the right shank,
one should first place the tooth (da) conjoined with the letter *ra*.
The navel should first be joined with that [line], O twice-born one;
the characteristic has been declared such that it should be performed exactly as before. (9.314)
O auspicious lady, I have taught you the razor-knife that severs the vital points;
it shall cut through the vital point, and then one should unite [the practitioner] with the supreme state.
Now I shall briefly describe the King of Weapons (Astrarāja):
having extracted the seed-syllable of the Navel (nābhibīja), one should cause it to be conjoined with the Staff (daṇḍa).
Below that, one should again fashion the *nitamba* (the hip-base) and the *daṇḍa* (the shaft);
thereafter, the *śikhara* (the pinnacle) should be joined, followed by its ornamentation.
O lady of beautiful hips, one should place that which is called *kalā* on the head from the left ear;
thus has this King of Weapons, so difficult to obtain, been fully described by me.
One should meditate upon the pervasive deity from the soles of the feet up to the crown of the head;
indeed, the utterance of the King of Weapons (astra), conjoined with Śakti, should be performed.
Resembling a blazing fire, one should always recite while meditating;
then, the contraction of the fingers should be performed, followed by the impelling.
One should then contract the knee; immediately after that, the thighs;
then, having contracted the waist and the private parts, one should then grasp the navel.
It is established in Brahman, established in Viṣṇu, established in Rudra, and situated in the center of the Bindu;
it is established in Nāda, established in Śakti, and established everywhere in Vyāpinī.
One should know it to be situated at the equinox and immediately thereafter situated at the emission;
having known that which has entered the mouth of the Guru, one is liberated and liberates others.
O lady of virtuous vows, having thus understood the path of renunciation for one who possesses power,
[one realizes that] power is subtle, supreme, like moonlight, and the awakener of the highest dharma.
O Goddess, that supreme knowledge, which has come down through the lineage of succession, has been explained along with its secret; it is the state that grants immediate liberation. (9.325)
O auspicious lady, the departure of the self or of another has been described;
it should be performed with knowledge and realization, exactly as demonstrated in the scriptures. (9.326)
Now I shall fully explain another auspicious procedure for consecration;
this is indeed traditional, for those who lack merit do not obtain it.
Having placed his hands at the "scent-direction" (the nose) with a well-composed mind,
he should then place the seat of power (śaktyāsana) there, filled with scented water.
One should place either a water-pot or a conch shell containing gold;
therein one should worship Soma, accompanied by the eight classes [of deities].
Having formed the *śakti* into a circle, one should utter it again and again;
then, having offered praise, that hand indeed causes the water-pot to tremble.
The sound of the falling stream descends upon the head of the disciple;
by means of the descent of that stream, one removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
O Goddess, whoever perceives this through direct experience—that very person is worshipped by the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others. (9.332)
The Goddess said: "But what is the nature of that whose color does not exist? O Lord, when one is devoid of color, how can an object be perceived? (9.333)
"How is that vigor known, and who is the vessel for vigor?
Bhairava said: "One should draw that Power upon the ground in the form of a curved shape. [9.334]
O lady of excellent vows, when one who has approached with a purified soul beholds [the deity] even by means of a slight glance,
then indeed Śakti appears in a curved form.
He who falls a hundred times is proclaimed to have a "severe fall" (tīvrapāta); likewise, one who falls a thousand or even ten thousand times [is so designated].
O Goddess, that for which the descent occurs is proclaimed as the middle;
it may be by twenty-four thousand, or thirty thousand, or likewise fifteen thousand, O Beloved.
"He who [lives] by means of turning potatoes is known as the lowest;
here, in the lineage of the Śakas, he shall explain this division of the *pātas*."
O Goddess, one should initiate the fallen, but one should avoid those who are free from falling.
One who is devoid of falling is a wicked soul and does not deserve the fruit of initiation.
O lady of excellent vows, when the mantras are remembered as one's former birth, they manifest their true nature;
yet for those who have merely cultivated them, the differentiation of consciousness wavers, trembles, and is shaken.
When the bond has been severed, he falls upon the yellow surface of the bronze;
he who falls facing forward has undoubtedly had his bonds cut. (9.341)
This [method] is declared to be the best; the supine is considered middling; and that which is face down is said to be the lowest by Śambhu, the God of gods. (9.342)
O lady of excellent hips, this subtle bond is not cut even by the knife;
O Goddess, it perishes only when the pure, the dualistic, and the mixed states have vanished.
Then, O observer of excellent vows, one is swiftly liberated from the snare of bonds;
O Goddess of the gods, he remains like a piece of wood or a stone.
His initiation must not be performed if she is considered inhuman;
O lady of excellent complexion, by such a fall, he goes to the celestial realm through intense [penance].
By the middling [method], one reaches Pātāla; by the inferior, one lives happily.
Thus has the sign been declared for one who effects the paralyzing of the noose (pāśastobha). || 9-346 ||
O Goddess of the Suras, there is no stimulation without knowledge, nor without vigor;
thus the perfected yogi acts, endowed with the oral tradition.
But he who, being devoid of the traditional lineage (saṃpradāya), desires to perform initiation, his labor is fruitless; the initiation does not lead him to heaven, but rather to hell. (9.348)
Moreover, O Goddess, those who observe the vows indeed become guardians of the field (kṣetrapālas),
provided that initiation (dīkṣā) constitutes liberation according to all the Āgamas.

Therefore, O Dear One, initiation should be understood as occurring when there is the paralysis of the bonds; when one is bound by the qualities of existence (*dharma*), the *piṇḍa* falls therein. (9.350)
Then, the teacher is he who performs the initiation that bestows nirvāṇa, by the mere attainment of which the cage of bonds is shaken. (9.351)
He is declared to be the Guru, the one who delivers [beings] from the ocean of saṃsāra;
O Goddess, if one should bear the dust of his feet upon one's head.
At that very moment, he would be liberated like the slough of a snake;
for such a one, together with his teacher, possesses power, being permeated by the true nature of Śiva.
He who knows reality is thus described; he should shatter the cage of bonds.
He is called a Guru, the bestower of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation. (9-354)
Now, however, I shall again describe the supreme procedure for the balance (tulā). The balance is to be made of cloth; its characteristics are now being told.
The length of the two arms should be made to the measure of four cubits;
the width at the middle should be three cubits, and half of two cubits (one cubit) [at the ends]. || 9-356 ||
The two [pillars] should be made square and equal, provided with three arches (toraṇa);
in the middle, however, a chain should be made, joined with three bracelets (kaṭaka).
The two ears, however, should be made very firm, thick, and with their joints well-knit;
having thus first prepared them, the scales should indeed be placed in front of the pavilion.
Then, having performed the ritual acceptance with perfumes, flowers, purifiers,
many food offerings, and incenses, one should perform the placement of the mantra (*mantranyāsa*).
On the second day, one should begin weighing the disciple against an equal measure;
that equal measure should be made level with a cord and placed on one side together with sand.
Then, having recognized that it is equal, one should cause it to be offered from the side of the fire;
the seizing must be done with the *śakti*, and the joining again with the *śakti*.
Having purified everything gradually and in due order within the sacrificial rites,
the mantra-practitioner should then unite [the soul] with the manifest (sakala) or the unmanifest (niṣkala) reality.
For the sake of bringing about all-pervading purity, one should cause [the offering] to be given in many forms;
the *pūrṇā* [offering] shall bring about fullness, and the ritual procedure shall be free from defects.

Then the mantra-master should cause the practitioner, whose body is composed of Śakti, to ascend; having quickly uttered the Śakti-mantra, he should [unite] the vital breath (prāṇa) which is dependent upon the individual soul (jīva).
Joined with the throat-consonant (ka), accompanied by the bindu, and inflamed by the letter ya;
it is adorned with the ornaments of Yāma’s ear according to one's desire.
O Goddess, lightness arises and he ascends upward by himself;
pure and liberated from sin, he goes to the further shore.
Thus has purification been fully declared by Śambhu even for the slayer of a Brahmin;
likewise, the purification by the balance (tulāśuddhi) must be performed by a wise man even for one who has drunk liquor.
Thus, for one purified by the scales, liberation is proclaimed; O fair-faced one, that which is serene is said to be the grasping of immortality.
Having first consecrated the mirror together with a maiden for the disciple,
the initiation must then be performed on the second day in the Śiva-sacrifice.
One should perform the grasping of the sacrificial animal, which is one's own self, as it abides in the heart;
thereafter, for the sake of purification and for the purpose of binding, one should unite that which resides in reality.
Those with divine vision behold the maiden situated in the mirror—that which resides there within the subtle body on the path of the worlds. (9.371)
O Goddess, one should apply the grasping to each and every principle (tattva) without doubt;
as long as one is joined to the supreme principle, for that long one perceives in this manner.
O Goddess of good vows, having first beheld [the disciple] with the Śakti-mantra, one should then consecrate the water with the Netra-bīja for fifty times. (9.373)
One should wash their eyes and show them a mirror;
there, those maidens shall see the auspicious and inauspicious results.
Now I shall proclaim another supreme rite for those who are devoted.

*Oṃ namaścaṇḍikāyai yogavāhini pravarta pravarta mahāmohaya mohaya yogamukhi yogeśvari mahāmāyādhāriṇi hiri 2 bhūtapriye svakāyaṃ paśyāmi bāḍhaṃ śṛṇomi sarvalokāni paśyāmi turu 2 sādhaya 2 svāhā.* Having become pure, one should perform ten thousand recitations in the abode of Rudra. (9.375)
That vidyā becomes perfected; one should cause the ten rites to be performed [by it] upon the moon or the sun, or on a sword, a mirror, or a lamp.
Whether on the thumb, or even in a jar, one may see a girl or a boy; from the doubt regarding the yakṣa, [one sees] sesame seeds or rice grains. (9.377)
For they indeed tell the past, the present, and the future to one who asks.
Then, having completed the Vidyā-observance, the pure practitioner should cause the queen to sleep upon a red-colored bed.

One will see for oneself, at the end of a dream, whatever is auspicious or inauspicious. Oṃ, O red one, O red-toed one, O Ucchuṣmā, descend, descend! O Piśācinī, speak, speak! Make them speak, make them speak! Svāhā!
[One may see it] on a sword, or in a mirror, or on the thumb, O fair-faced one. (9.379)
The maidens perceive all things, both auspicious and inauspicious, as well as their beneficial and harmful results.
Oṃ piṅgali pāśupati mahāvidye svāhā! O Great Goddess, this mantra performs its work in seven ways. 9-380.
Oṃ rakte virakte avatara 2 mātaṅgini svāhā!
Indeed, this vidyā performs the ninefold action.
Having consecrated one's hand seven times with this mantra, one should place it upon one's own chest. (9-381)
Indeed, one knows this by the power of this mantra oneself:
*Oṃ namaścaṇḍikāyai avatara 2 turu 2 svāhā*.
Having fasted and become pure, one should recite it eight hundred times. (9-382)
Descending during the night in a dream, he shall declare whatever is auspicious or inauspicious;
and for all the vidyās, one should resort to the temple of Caṇḍikā.
Having recited [the mantra] ten thousand times, one should then perform the ritual action;
thus it was examined for the sake of the cause and for the sake of inquiry by the Self-Arisen One.
Thus has been told, together with its secret, the very extensive ritual of initiation,
for one who is initiated, tranquil, and consecrated, O beautiful one.
O fair-faced one, this must not be told to a mere initiate, a son of the lineage, or even an adept, nor to one who lacks authority; this is the truth spoken by the Lord.
To the Kisser (Cumbaka), however, the Śrāvaṇīya [initiation] is given through the rite prescribed by rule.
The Goddess said:
"The Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) shall be the one who holds authority over everything for the Kisser. (9.387)
The consecration of that Śambhu was performed by them together from the very water-pot (kalaśa),
as well as the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the girdle (mekhalā), the large ladle (sruca), or indeed the small dipping-spoon (sruva).
One should likewise grasp the face of the deity of the tongue and so forth, together with the measure and the sound,
as well as the fragrance and color of the flames, by means of the full [mudrā] and the *tucyā*.
"O Lord, I have this doubt: please tell me that which has not been spoken.
Bhairava said:
Eight jars should be collected, whether made of gold or even silver."
They should be made of copper or clay, very firm, without cracks, auspicious,
with a neck like a conch shell, a broad belly, not black, and free from protruding flaws.
First, they should be filled with scented water and adorned with mango sprouts;
they should be covered with white cloth and smeared with white sandalwood paste.
Having adorned them with white garlands, one should indeed place the oceans, beginning with the Salt Ocean, within those jars containing the essences of the gems and filled with water.
The eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas), who are the guardians of the world (Lokapālakas), are known as those given at birth;
having assigned the eight groups [of letters], one should then perform the consecration (abhiṣeka).
Alternatively, O beloved, the entire visualization should be performed with a single [deity];
or, O fair-faced one, the consecration should be performed with a single water-pot.
The entire meaning of the Kṛtasūtra, as it has been set forth in the scripture, must be performed exactly in that manner; otherwise, one becomes a vessel for faults.

Then, having been consecrated, the mantra-practitioner—smeared with white sandalwood paste, wearing white garments, and adorned with garlands—should bring [the disciple] into the presence of the deity. (9.397)

Then, having performed a salutation, the wise man should prostrate himself on the ground like a staff; and having brought [the materials] near the fire, he should always perform the fire-oblation (homa).

O Goddess of gods, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be one cubit (ratni) in measure, or else the size of a fist; it may also be one cubit or four cubits in size, provided with three tiers (mekhalā).
Or the mantra-practitioner may have it made circular according to his own wish, with its orientation determined by the directions;
even if the sacrificial pits are deficient in measurement or lack the girdles.
One should begin the reverse fire-oblation (viloma-homa) when the mouths [of the vessels] are broken or cracked.
The first girdle (mekhalā) should have a width equal to two thumb-joints. || 9-401 ||
The second [channel] is to be known as having three [fingers], and the one situated above has four;
the yoni is nine fingers, seven, or otherwise twelve fingers. (9-402)
Her lower lip is like that of an elephant or a camel, one finger-span in length, triangular, and long-faced; this is beneficial for rites of killing and driving away. (9-403)
And in the rite of causing enmity, it should be performed using [an image] devoid of auspicious marks.
One should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to a single ritual procedure, which bestows excellent accomplishment.
O fair-faced one, for the daily obligatory fire-oblation (nityahoma), the occasional (naimittika),
or the occasional (kāmya) rite, a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit (hastamātra) in size shall be the bestower of fruits.
It is two cubits long for a ten-thousand-fold oblation, four cubits for a hundred-thousand-fold oblation, and six cubits for the oblation known as *prayata*, O lady of excellent complexion. (9.406)
In the case of a ten-million-fold oblation (koṭihoma), a very beautiful pit measuring eight cubits should be prepared;
as for the girdles of a pit measuring one cubit, they have been described [elsewhere].
These should be made double that size for the sake of increased prosperity; however, one should have them made eight cubits long.
The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles are considered auspicious when they are merely the length of an arm.
[The two sticks] should be produced from *vaikaṅkata*, *śamī*-heartwood, *palāśa*, or *khadira*;
or from other auspicious [woods], provided they are distinguished by the proper characteristics.
One should employ these in auspicious homas, but not otherwise in those that are contrary;
[namely] those produced from the great Vibhītaka tree, the Tinduka, and the Śālmali.
Or those produced from wood used for cleaning teeth, or from the bones of a donkey or a human; they are devoid of measure, flat-soled, crooked-faced, and both are cracked. (9-411)
In every way and with every effort, the two wise ones should be beautiful in meaning;
they should not be crooked, cracked, or inferior, even if they are made of auspicious wood. (9.412)
If the auspicious *sruk* and *sruva* ladles are to be avoided with effort,
then the *sruva* is the support for the ritualist, while the *sruk* is honored by the fourfold [deities].
The other [part] should be twelve finger-breadths wide,
while the width of the middle finger [section] should be two finger-breadths and twenty-four finger-breadths long.
Six finger-breadths in circumference, pure, and marked with lotuses;
likewise marked with conchs, svastikas, vajras, or wheels. (9.415)

Having performed such a rite in this manner, the practitioner of mantra, being well-composed and knowing the mantras, should offer oblations into the fire of Bhairava with his own hand when no other master is available. (9.416)

One who knows the reality of the characteristics of the tongues of fire, and who understands the rules for success and failure regarding the forms and colors of the sacrificial fire, should perform the fire-rite (agnikārya).
All deities reside in fire, and Maheśvara has the form of fire;
his embodiment consists of mantra, and his sovereignty indeed originates from Soma.
All deities are indeed established within the mouth of Agni;
one who knows the procedure for the seven tongues [of fire] should commence the rite of oblation (homa). || 9-419 ||
If one who is ignorant of the different types of tongues offers oblations into the fire, whatever ritual act he undertakes will all become fruitless. (9.420)
Having offered oblations according to the prescribed rites and having been fully gratified with offerings of clarified butter,
the Bull-bannered Lord, together with his consort, is pleased with the sacrificer.
The crest-lock (śikhā), as wide as the joint of a thumb, remains burning with many flames;
yet, by means of even a small amount of sacrificial fuel, they remain unified.
The mouth of this fire is the size of a sacrificial fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa);
with thousands of garlands of flames, its face reaches down to the netherworld (pātāla).
Having performed the awakening with the [five] foremost [tastes], one should examine the tongue according to the prescribed rule,
as well as its form as a deity and whatever fruit it yields.
The Jihvāgrahas are established there from the east to the west;
at the time of the fire-oblation, one should carefully avoid these two tongues.
The first is the tongue of Dharma, which is remembered as being blue in color;
the second is the tongue of Yakṣa, which consists of copper and has the luster of taste.
The third has Saumya as its presiding deity; it is white in color and like nectar.
The fourth is Yamajihvā, and she is recorded as being black in color.
The fifth has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity and resembles the flax flower;
the sixth has the Sun as its presiding deity and is recorded as being white in color.
The seventh [tongue] has all the deities as its presiding divinity and shines with all forms;
the first tongue is fruitless, while the second bestows wealth.
The third [day] gladdens the entire world, both stationary and moving;
the fourth brings about decline in the lineage, while the fifth increases the family.
O Goddess, an oblation offered on the sixth day bestows good health;
when worshipped according to the prescribed rite, the seventh day grants virtue, desire, and wealth.
And success is indeed attained especially when Rudra-śakti is offered as an oblation;
likewise Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī.
Vārāhī, the goddess Aindrikā, and Cāmuṇḍā is considered the seventh;
she should be known as praised in the form of the tongue, bestowing accomplishment upon practitioners.
Therefore, with every effort, the fire-oblation (homa) in the center is praised.
When it is being offered, if a sound arises like that of a conch shell or a spider's web— || 9-434 ||
At that time, sounds such as those of a donkey, camel, crow, curlew, vulture, owl, or even a mule are heard; yet for one who has attained perfection, they are like a blade of grass.
If, for the sake of accomplishing the movement of sounds, even a great mass of smoke, or flames appearing in the forms of serpents, birds, or wild beasts, should burst forth; (9.436)
Likewise, those shaped like missiles, as well as those shaped like umbrellas, banners, and canopies, quickly accomplish [their purpose] in reverse order.
If forms resembling white and blue lotuses, a vajra, a conch, the śrīvatsa, mountains, or flames are seen in the expanse of the sky; 9-438.
They are endowed with right-spiraling curls, accomplish auspicious deeds,
and possess the fragrances of sandalwood, uśīra, camphor, saffron, and agaru.

Alternatively, even when using other highly fragrant substances such as jasmine and the like, or even when fatigued, it is taught that a favorable and auspicious fragrance quickly brings about accomplishment. (9.440)
When flesh, bones, and the hair of wild animals are being burned,
a foul odor wafts forth, resembling the smell of putrid meat.
Even in auspicious rites, the reverse should be understood by those skilled in mantras;
even when the oblation is ill-formed, if the fragrance is most beautiful, [it is auspicious]. (9-442)
That should be known as the sign of accomplishment, which bestows the desired object;
when the fragrance of clarified butter arises amidst auspicious and inauspicious substances. (9.443)
That [result] as well, whether auspicious, inauspicious, or a mixture of both, is given as the fruit of the *veṣṭa* [ritual].
The knower of mantras who, knowing this, performs recitation (*japa*) and also offers oblations (*homa*), [attains success]. (9.444)
The knower of reality who performs the ritual at the proper time shall possess success and partake of the fruit;
otherwise, for one who lacks the prescribed method, it is in vain and results in the contrary.
Even in the refined (saṃskṛta) language, one who is devoid of action may accomplish worldly desires; ten fires are proclaimed as bringing victory in all undertakings.
It has the radiance of the rising sun, resembles smooth lapis lazuli,
is like the color of clarified butter, and likewise the color of lac.
Having the luster of molten iron and gold, resembling the juice of safflower,
like yellow orpiment, and likewise the color of smoke.
When the fire has been well-kindled with abundant fuel, and likewise when it is smokeless and flickering,
one should offer oblations for the successful accomplishment of the rite.
Radiant, with a compact crest, resembling clarified butter and gold,
smooth, turning to the right, it bestows the fruits of all desires.
Having understood this, the preceptor must duly perform the application of the purificatory rites for the practitioner; listen now as I explain it exactly as it is. (9.451)
Having fashioned nooses made of thread and empowered them with the Navātman mantra, one should recite the nine principles (tattvas), differentiated by the letter Ā.
One should apply [the mantra] everywhere: on the head, the throat, the heart, the navel, the thighs, the hips, as well as the shanks, the ankles, and the feet. (9.453)
One should place [the mantra] everywhere upon the two arms and the two hands;
one should offer a hundred oblations of clarified butter for the Nine-Self (Navātman) with the utterance of "svāhā."
The sacrificial vessel for the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) is indeed joined with the supreme animal;
now I shall describe the procedure for that final oblation. || 9-455 ||
With the upper body erect, the neck straight, and standing with feet even, the base of the *sruva* ladle is placed at the level of the navel, its tip facing upward and held level. (9-456)
O Goddess, having placed the *sruva* ladle upon the *sruc* with its bowl facing downwards,
and having offered a flower at the tip of the *sruc*, one should join both hands together with a *darbha* blade.
And having grasped [the hand] with effort using both hands as if with a fist, O beloved, [place] the right hand in front and the left hand behind, auspiciously. (9.458)
Having grasped [the vessel] with both hands in the manner of palms turned upward, one should then fill it with ghee; one must not cause it to be deficient.
I alone am the supreme reality, according to the division of the higher and the lower;
for reality is indeed one everywhere, and one should not contemplate it as having any other nature. (9.460)
O fair-faced one, that which has been placed in the jar— the path of six kinds—
situated within the fire of the mandala and ending in Śiva, is both common and conceptualized.

Having placed the two *sruva*-ladles upon that path, and having brought [the breath] situated in the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and located within the channels into equilibrium at the seat of the vital breath (*prāṇādhāra*), one should cast down the base of the *sruc*-ladle.
By means of the *vasordhārā* application, one should pour [the oblation] into the fire;
one should heat the base of the *sruva* ladle at the location of the navel within the range of the *āsānta*.
In whatever manner one casts the stream [of breath], in that same manner one should exhale the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
The vital breath attains the state of phonemes; it is indeed that which constitutes the sixfold path (*ṣaḍvidhādhvan*).
Due to the sixfold path, there is no object of knowledge to be found anywhere.
Therefore, all those [entities] residing within mantra are established as either to be abandoned or to be adopted. (9.465)
Regarding the phonemes, there is a sixfold cause; through the abandonment of these six, there is dissolution in the seventh.
These are the letter *a*, the letter *u*, the letter *m*, and the *bindu*.
The Half-Moon, the Obstructer, the Sound, and the Upward-Moving;
then the Power, the Pervasive Goddess, and beyond that, the Equal (Samanā).
O lady of excellent hips, one should cause that which resides there—the endless web of bonds reaching to the very limit of existence and marked by the six causes—to be abandoned. (9.468)
Wherein Paśupati is the Self, situated in the void, pure consciousness and utterly stainless;
there is the fragrance of the qualities of the Śiva-tattva and the vision of the nature of Śiva. (9.469)
Having abandoned that which conforms to the fetters (pāśa) as well as the observation of one's own nature, there is indeed the pervasion of the Self; for this is different from the pervasion of Śiva.
One should always meditate on those for whom qualities such as omniscience are pervasive; for this pervasion by Śiva exists within consciousness in the form of its very cause. (9.471)
For Śiva is recited as being of the nature of non-dual reality (abodharmin-svabhāva), peaceful, and beyond the mind (unmana);
he is graspable by the mind for one whose self is established in the awakening of the Self. (9.472)
Having abandoned mental activity, one should unite with the nature of pure awareness;
then, being liberated from the ocean of existence, the bound soul attains the state of Śiva. (9.473)
Furthermore, once [the disciple] has been consecrated, the preceptor should again cause the sacrificial ladle (*sruc*) to overflow;
that substance is offered into the fire through the opening of the ladle until it is fully employed.
One should contemplate the external kumbhaka within the supreme reality (paratattva), attaining a state of equal flavor (samarasa) with Śiva through the cessation of external [sensations]. (9.475)
Otherwise, O Goddess, it would not exist, like the current of a river in the ocean;
having come to rest with the water of the sea, it becomes of equal flavor with that born of the Sindhu.
In that manner, the Self does not undergo division within the ocean of Śiva;
one should maintain that state for as long as it takes to fill the sacrificial ladle (sruva). || 9-477 ||
But by this very time, through the practice of external breath-retention (kumbhaka), the self becomes all-pervading within Śiva by virtue of its state of essential oneness (samarasatva).
Thereafter, one should bring about the qualities with six-limbed word-offerings;
just as when sovereignty has been attained, one is consecrated with jars [of water]. || 9.479 ||
Just as even those devoid of virtues are proclaimed on the surface of the earth by bards and others,
so too, once the state of Śiva has been attained, the wise man should manifest his own virtues.
"Be omniscient, svāhā! Likewise, be completely satisfied;
likewise, be beginningless awakening, and from that, exercise sovereignty. (9-481)
Likewise, having again brought forth the qualities from the infinite power while his own power remains undiminished, he should then recollect the root mantra.
Oṃ hūṃ! Accompanied by the self, for the Omniscient One, at the very end;
one should present the oblation through the application of the word svāhā. || 9-483 ||
Three, fifteen, or one [offering] of sesame or ghee should then be given;
O lady of excellent vows, one should then bestow the consecration with the root mantra.
Having stirred the supreme nectar of power (*śaktyāmṛta*), one should cause it to be placed upon the head of the disciple;
for one should visualize it entering through the door of the fourth state (*turya*), both externally and internally. (9.485)
By means of the sharp powers of the mantras, such as drying up and burning, his body is thoroughly purified; then follows the consecration for half that duration.
After the completion of the initiation (dīkṣā), one should cause a flower to be placed in the hand;
then, having caused [the disciple] to release the darbha grass, [one should place it] in the fire of Śiva, in the water-pot (kalaśa), or with the Guru.
Having performed three circumambulations, one should prostrate like a staff before him;
having fulfilled one's purpose, joyful in spirit, one becomes liberated and utterly pure.
One should meditate upon [the deity] with wide-open eyes, peaceful, and of a completely satisfied nature.
This initiation is "nirvāṇikī"; it is "nirbījā" (seedless), while the other is "sabījā" (with seed).
For those whose initiation is "with seed" (sabījakā), one should perform the consecration;
one who possesses Vedic learning, virtuous conduct, and proper behavior should be appointed to the office of a preceptor.
Likewise, immediately after the Śiva-yoga, the consecration of the preceptor (ācārya) is performed with five auspicious jars smeared with white sandalwood paste. || 9-491 ||

Having worshipped with excellent auspicious jars, one should worship the "Womb of Jewels" (Ratnagarbhā) with pure substances such as *ṛddhi* and *vṛddhi*, and with medicinal herbs and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
One should assign the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth to the five [sections] by means of the white lotus, the face, charcoal, and mango sprouts. (9.493)
Furthermore, O Great Goddess, one should again assign the *kalās* to the jars;
in each individual jar, one should perform the assignment beginning with Ananta and ending with Śiva.
O God, one should worship Bhairava according to the sequence of universal dissolution, endowed with the six limbs and the surrounding enclosures, and joined with the union of mantras. (9.495)
O Dear One, having consecrated each individual jar with the Bhairava mantra one hundred and eight times, one should meditate upon the Supreme Reality.
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite in the directions of Varuṇa, Soma, Yama, Indra, and Īśāna, one should commence the consecration.
The wise practitioner should conceive of a seat for the sacrificial vessel in the northeast;
having prepared a mandala there, he should adorn it with svastikas and other such designs.
Covered above with a canopy and adorned all around with banners,
O Goddess, one should place there a seat made from *śrīparṇī* wood or sandalwood.
Leaving his seat in each respective place, he should install the child who has become manifest in form;
having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa as before, he stands facing the northeast.
They should be worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as with stainless garments, food offerings, and balls made of earth, ashes, cow dung, dūrvā grass shoots, and palāśa leaves.
With water from the *siddhārtha* plant mixed with curd and collyrium,
one should thus cause the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) to be performed according to this procedure for the purpose of purification.

O Goddess, having meditated upon Śiva, the preceptor, being well-composed, should sprinkle [the site] with earth and other materials using jars, starting from the northeast and proceeding in order. 9-503.
Having been consecrated, he should then be made to put on other garments and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Having led him in, one should arrange the yoga-pīṭha before the [deity] Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Having established [the deity] and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should offer the empowerment;
[this includes] the uṣṇīṣa, the crown and so forth, as well as the parasol, sandals, and chowries.

The elephant, horses, palanquins, and so forth—all the components of the royal retinue without exception—as well as the *karaṇī*, the *kartarī*, chalk, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, and the manuscript of the womb. (9.506)
Having prepared the rosary and other ritual implements, you, remaining on the path of grace and established in the four stages of life, must always perform initiation and exposition.
"From this day forward, by the command of Śiva, you must perform your duty;
having raised [the disciple] and taken him by the hand, you should lead him into the maṇḍala. (9.508)
Then, having gone to the ground on his knees and worshipped Bhairava, he made this request:
"O Blessed One, you have indeed been consecrated by my command."
For those who follow your command and abide by the path of the Teacher, the preceptors must perform the duty that has come down through tradition.
Standing before Śiva, one should recount the meaning of the principles of Śiva (śivatattva);
having emerged from the world, one should then offer the path of the kalās into the fire.
Having performed the satiation of the mantras, one should offer one oblation and five oblations;
having offered them in each of the five groups of five, one should then present the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having performed the worship with the *argha* offering and more, and having prostrated, he should announce to the Lord:
"The Ācārya has been consecrated by me; for that purpose, there shall be the satiation of the mantra. (9.513)
One should mark the right hand with the five fires beginning with the heart;
then, one should mark the little finger and the others in the Śiva-fire with a bundle of *darbha* grass.
One should place a flower in one's hand and let it fall before the mandala;
having prostrated like a staff in homage to Bhairava, the water-pot, and the fire.

With his soul delighted by having obtained authority, and being joyful, endowed with the fruit of contentment—that Guru is indeed equal to Śiva, the bestower of the fruit of the abode of Śiva. || 9-516 ||
At the conclusion of the rite of pacification (śānti), however, there is the initiation for prosperity (bhūti-dīkṣā), which has Sadāśiva as its essential fruit;
that is to be known as the Śivadharma, while others are considered the Lokadharma.
The initiation known as the Śivadharmī is proclaimed for practitioners;
one should perform their consecration and appoint them as practitioners.
This is the initiation of the practitioner, which occurs immediately after the initiation into the Vidyā.
That initiation into the Vidyā, however, exists according to the distinction of latent impressions (vāsanā).
No distinction of karma exists for one who abides on every path;
indeed, all the karmas that have been performed are traversed throughout the paths. (9.520)
Having purified those [elements] according to the rule while they abide in the five digits (kalās),
there occurs at the moment of union the discernment of the practitioner.
One should contemplate that very Prārabdha-karma, which exists as the object of the animal-sacrifice, as being unified within Him;
having uttered "Śiva," one should place the entire [mantra] within the body of Sadāśiva.
Having meditated upon the god Sadāśiva in the form of the various aspects of knowledge (vidyābheda),
one [attains him] through the application of the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), endowed with the qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest.
Having offered a joyful oblation with the root mantra— which has attained qualities such as *aṇimā*— using its own name, one should consecrate [the disciple] for half a month.
One should perform [the rite] with five jars; one should place Nivṛtti and the others in three [jars], Śāntyatītā in the fifth, and Śānti in the fourth.
Having thus encased the five elements, beginning with earth, within the *śānti* [mantra],
one should subsequently place the *mūlamantra* within each individual flask.
Having performed all the rites with the ancillaries of the Vidyā, one should place the Vidyāgāvaraṇa;
then, one hundred and eight mantras for each individual pitcher.
Having placed the seat outside the mandala with the syllable *praṇava*,
the practitioner, having established [the deity] there, should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa.
Having rubbed [the patient], as before, one should perform the service with all the mantras to be accomplished.
With three jars containing *tṛvṛt* and other substances, one should bathe [the patient] facing the east, as previously described. (9.529)
One should take the jar belonging to the Śāntyatīta [kalpa], and afterwards cause the disciple to partake;
one should then take the Śānti [kalaśa] and cause him to partake by means of the *saṃpuṭa* [mudrā]. || 9-530 ||
This is the consecration of the practitioner, both in reverse and in direct order;
having consecrated him and led him inside, he takes refuge in the southern form.
With the *praṇava*, the maiden [should perform] the preparation of the seat (*āsana*) and the ritual of the limbs (*sakalīkaraṇa*);
she should then arrange the qualifications of the practitioner and the ritual procedures for the mantra and so forth.

Having offered a mantra, ritual manual, rosary, chalk, a parasol, sandals, and a crown—provided it is devoid of [the top] tuft—and having entered into the presence of the preceptor (śiṣya), [he should perform the rite]. (9.533)
The practitioner should inform the Supreme Lord: "This [mantra] has been performed by me;
O Knower, may success of three kinds arise through my devotion. (9-534)
Having uttered the mantra of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it should be offered together with flowers and water into the hand of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) for the sake of success. (9.535)
Having grasped both [hands], the mantra-master should place them upon his heart;
with a joyful countenance, the disciple and the preceptor likewise become greatly delighted.
Having emerged from both [the fire-pit], one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) into the fire together with the mantra,
using either a thousand or a hundred [offerings] for the libation of the mantra of the sādhya.
Having thus satisfied [the deity], one should cause a flower to be placed in the hand;
then, having worshipped [the deity] residing in the three [places], one should perform a circumambulation of the ground and prostrate like a staff.
One whose soul is endowed with devotion should prostrate and obtain the fruits beginning with *aṇiman*;
then, having raised the practitioner, one should say: "Therefore, protect the *samaya*. (9-539)
O Goddess of the gods, at the conclusion of the initiation, the wise one should be made to hear [the teachings].
O fair-faced one, best of all goddesses, having thus completed the initiation, [he should proceed]. 9-540.

Having been authorized and consecrated, one should cause the Guru to hear the pledges (*samaya*): "One must not eat without having made an offering, nor should one consume meat in an improper manner. (9.541)
One should avoid fruitless activity and perform recitation and meditation;
one should not utter the words "rere" nor likewise the words "hehe."
One should not look at a naked woman, nor even one whose breasts are exposed;
one should not watch animal play, nor should one perform any menial labor.
O fair-complexioned one, one should not say "Śākinī" when uttering *dhapyaṭi*;
O Great Goddess, one should instead release *chinnalī* and *sehāriśaiva*.
O lady of beautiful hips, even for a householder, when the rite for great accomplishment is established,
one who desires success must not engage in the duties of a village on that day.
One should constantly perform the ritual actions indicated by one's own scripture and turn away from the two extremes;
for the sake of protecting everything in all undertakings, one should not become attached to desire.
One who is constantly engaged in the light [of wisdom] and disciplined in analytical investigations should not,
like a medicinal herb, be seen together with worldly people, for that would be a path leading to the destruction of one's sacred study.
All these purposes and ritual agents are rendered useless by anything that contradicts the study of one's own sacred texts (svādhyāya). All of this is devoid of meaning.
The bull, the cock, the peacock, the swan, and likewise the boar; the buffalo, the human, the iguana, the owl, the vulture, and the hawk. (9.549)
The goat, the doe, the ewe, the female dog, the female jackal, the female rabbit, the female squirrel, and whatever others there may be that have no bones—[these should be known by the wise]. (9.550)
The flesh of those [animals] is unfit for consumption; one should loathe it even with the mind.
Furthermore, during the nine months of the rainy season, one should not step over the shadow of a linga.

O lady of excellent hips, the initiate (*samayī*), the spiritual son (*putraka*), the master (*ācārya*), and likewise the practitioner (*sādhaka*)—one must not revile them; otherwise, the *yoginīs* will not release [the practitioner]. (9.552)
One should avoid a fisherman, a ball-player, a barbarian, one with two castes, one who is empty-handed,
one who is fond of [low] pleasures, one who is deformed, one who is miserable, a rogue, a eunuch, and likewise one who is afflicted by disease.
The Malla is a bard; the Chiryaka performs manual labor;
the Jaṭṭ is a wrestler; and the Kāpotajāla is an eater of [the meat of] pigeons. (9-554)
The Yeyyabhillas, the Caḍaunvas, and likewise others who perform auspicious deeds—these and other Mānaras have been mentioned, O woman of excellent complexion. (9.555)
O lady of beautiful hips, one should rejoice when a son obtains whatever he desires;
a wise man should not speak harshly to his wife nor revile his daughter.
One should not ever pronounce the syllable *ṛ*, the syllable *m*, or the letter *i* combined with the foot of the goddess *Reḍdham* as a single unit.
A Vaibhāṣika should not speak anything at all, nor should he consume flavors;
he must never sleep under a single tree or at a crossroads. (9-558)
In a field, in a cremation ground, in a forest, and in groves of shrubs; in a temple, on a riverbank, or in the midst of ashes and cow dung. (9.559)
One must not discharge semen, nor should one spit or engage in sexual intercourse; likewise, one should avoid a bed, a wet garment, a grinding stone, an empty house, and a bower.
The fat woman, the potter’s wheel, the hearth, the pestle, and the clod of earth—these are the instruments;
yet the sweeping and the offering with water have not been performed. (9.561)
O lady of excellent hips, this courtyard and likewise the threshold, as well as the churning-stick and the householder, are not [present] for the widow nor for the heroine. (9.562)
In this cruel rite for the supreme destruction of others, I likewise employ the sacrificial post,
the umbrella, the fruit, the spear, and the mace.
The conch, the discus, the mace, the trident, the bell, the hand-drum, the peacock feather, the skull-cup, the rosary, the yogic cloth, and the water-pot. (9.564)
The staff, the antelope skin, the purifier, the axe, and likewise the sharp-edged spear; the head-ornament, the hatchet, the wandering mendicant’s bowl, and the knowledge of the Vedas.
The *kodālaka*, the *vakoddālī*, and likewise the *kuṭaka* for the feet; the *dhanu*, the *nārāca*, the *bhalla*, the *ratīrikā*, the *saraka*, and the excellent [weapon]. (9.566)
The *pūṭa*, the *karṇika*, the *kūṭa*, the *ardhacandra*, the *vilumpaka*, the *vāvallaka*, as well as the *asthoḍru*, the *silla*, and likewise the *ghātana*. || 9-567 ||
The *daṃhikā*, *karṇika*, *ṛvaka*, *kunta*, and *vasunandaka* should be made, as well as the *kurtarī*, the *kartikā*, and the *pādacellaka*. (9.568)
O beloved, the practitioner of mantra should touch even a sword or any other weapon with his foot, but he should never step over it. (9.569)
One should never eat from the hollow of a banyan tree;
O sinless one, a practitioner of mantra should not consume food held in the left hand.
It should never be held in the left hand, but rather in the right;
however, O beloved, that which is given by another should always be received in the left hand.
One should not give medicine, nor should one cause it to be given for the sake of protection. One must not engage in idle chatter regarding the Śiva scriptures with others. 9-572.

One who has not attained mastery over the food [of the senses] should certainly not speak, for authority is established in the ritual injunction; one who has not broken through the assembly of heroes should not disregard meditation, lest he fall into mockery.
One should cause the water to be brought by others or even by oneself;
one should address all the Rudra-sthānas as preceded by "Śrī."
The wise one, established in self-majesty, should maintain the perception of the Guru;
having abandoned his bed and seat, he should take up flowers and incense.
Having prostrated like a staff upon the ground, one should utter the syllable *Śrī* and so forth; then, having bowed, one should likewise state the name of the place and the deity.
In that very way, O Ārya Maheśvarī, the form of the Lord is established;
thus, O Goddess, have the *samayas* been fully explained for one who seeks the *samaya*.
The Guru should cause [the disciple] to hear [the teachings] through the ritual prescribed in the scriptures;
he should worship the God three times a day through the ritual perceived in meditation.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, the section on the initiation of the pledges (*samayadīkṣā*), in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, a great tantra of the Bhairava stream belonging to the Vidyāpīṭha, measuring seventy million verses. 9.
The Goddess said:
"O Mahādeva, the path has been indicated but not fully described.
Please explain it out of your grace for the benefit of practitioners. [41a] 10.1
Bhairava said:
O fair-faced one, I shall explain the path in brief.
Below the Rudra of the Fire of Time (Kālāgnirudra), the cauldron (kaṭāha) is situated.
Its height is ten million yojanas;
above it, however, are the worlds, numbering ninety-nine million and five thousand eight hundred.
The measurement of Suśira is exactly seven times seven crores,
as well as hundreds of thousands, tens of thousands, and likewise millions (niyuta).
Arbudas, vṛndas, nikharvas, and likewise asaṃkhyas, padmas, and so forth—these and many others [are the names of large numbers]. (10.5)
Beyond the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), O Rudra, no measurement exists;
the immeasurable path of Śiva has been described by the Supreme Lord. 10.6ab [57a g]
The leader of these here is indeed the infinite Supreme Lord;
by him, being pure, the worlds together with the Hūhukas are purified. (10.7)
The support of Śakti, however, consists of thirty-two worlds; they are surrounded by millions upon millions of attendants and are endowed with incomparable qualities.
It was crowded with celestial women whose eyes were made lovely by the play of their eyebrows,
and it was adorned with gateways and watchtowers that shone like ten thousand suns.
No one there is suffering, for all have been freed from infinite misery;
those heroes rejoice there with women in playful delight. (10.10)
Residing within the various worlds that exist in the form of wombs,
the inhabitants of those intermediate worlds have thus described the worlds.
In this way, O beloved, all those [beings] are purified once the infinite has been purified;
above that, the Kālāgni is established by Śrīkaṇṭha.
He exercises authority over those who follow his command;
accompanied by many tens of millions of Rudras, he remains established there, O beloved.
Now I shall fully explain the measurement established by Śiva;
O lady of excellent hips, listen to how it is constituted in yojanas. (10.14)
Ten parts of the unmanifest (avyakta) are perceived as gross in the Great Principle (mahat);
five parts of the Great Principle are said to be gross in the Origin of the Elements (bhūtādi).
The *bhūtādi* and the atom (*paramāṇu*) are perceivable by the mind alone and not by the eye;
however, the *rajas* of the wombs is seen as being ten times greater than the *bhūtādi*. (10.16)
When there occurs a conjunction of eight atoms within the lattice of a window-screen through which the sun shines, they describe [that as a particle]. (10.17)
A *trasareṇu* is so designated, and that is said to be a lotus-dust particle (*padmarajas*);
likewise, eight *trasareṇus* are prescribed as a single hair-tip (*vālāgra*).
Likewise, eight tips of a hair are proclaimed to be one nit (līkṣā);
eight nits are known as one louse (yūkā), and eight lice make one barley-corn (yava).
O beautiful lady, eight barley grains make one finger-joint, which is called a finger (aṅgula);
twelve fingers in measure is called a span (vitasti) or a palm (tāla). || 10-20 ||
Two tālas shall constitute a hasta, which is twenty-four aṅgulas;
if one should bend the triad of the index, middle, and ring fingers [into a circle], [that is the *tāla*]. (10.21)
Then, O Goddess, it becomes a *ratni*; from that [length], it is called a *muṣṭi*.
Four *hasta*s constitute a bow-staff (*dhanurdaṇḍa*) as well as a pair of *nāḍikā*s. (10.22)
Two thousand *dhanus* are prescribed as one *krośa*;
two *krośas* constitute a *gavyūti*, and two *gavyūtis* make a *yojana*. (10.23)
By this very measure, O illustrious lady,
is the great, brilliantly shining lion-throne established, extending for two thousand yojanas.
O observer of good vows, that seat of Kāla is one thousand [yojanas] in height;
there the Lord of Gods, Kāla, who has twelve eyes, resides. (10.25)
He has four faces and great splendor, adorned with a garland of flames;
possessing great power, his four faces are white, red, yellow, and black.
Then [he saw] Raktāṅga and Karāla, with tawny eyebrows, beards, and eyes;
blazing intensely with the flames from his mouth, the flames of his recitation, and the flames of the moon.
His extremely fierce weapons, held in the palms of his hands, were blazing;
glowing intensely like mountains, they shone with their flickering flames.
The great-souled one with ten arms, bearing a sword and a shield,
holding arrows, a horn, and a noose, and likewise carrying a goad.
Holding a skull-topped staff and a khaṭvāṅga, with hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
his radiant body shines as it wanders for ten thousand yojanas.
It was filled with Rudras endowed with their own attributes, with worlds of blazing splendor,
with the daughters of Rudra, and with Rudras bearing flaming tridents.
Surrounded by various blazing arrangements of worlds,
ten crores of its flames issued forth upwards.
And above these, it is taught that there is a region of darkness extending for sixty million [yojanas];
nothing at all dwells there, being scorched by the heat of the smoke.
There the lord of the gods, the creator, remains in a form that can assume any shape at will, adorned by ten crores of maidens who possess beautiful forms.
The Great Being played with the sounds of songs and musical instruments,
while the young women, with their full and elevated breasts and dark-limbed bodies, gazed at him with eyes wide with wonder.
O beautiful goddess, in all the netherworlds there are excellent women such as these, who are skilled in pleasant conversation and knowers of reality. (10.36)
And those devoted to the gods remain, proclaimed as being subject to the power of the fire of time. || 10-37 ||
O Goddess, fifty crores have indeed been described in succession;
O fair-faced one, I shall now fully declare the principal hundred among them.
I shall now describe [the hells] endowed with forty [subsidiaries]; listen to this:
Avīci, Raurava, and likewise Mahāraurava. (10.39)
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Saṃjīvana, Kālasūtra, Padma, Mahāpadma, and likewise Kālasūtra. (10.40)
Śūcīmukha, Mahākāya, the mountain with sword-blade edges,
Asitāladruma, and Drumamastaka.
And the Drumārāma hell is renowned, as is Kumbhīpāka;
likewise Ambarīṣa, Aṅgārarāśi, and Tīkṣṇatuṇḍa. || 10.42 ||
Vajratuṇḍa, Śakuni, Mīnodara, Kharodara, Saṃdaṃśa, Vajrakāya, Meda, and Vānarānana. (10.43)
Uṣṭragrīva, Mahākāya, Vetāla, Vaḍavāmukha, Asṛkpūyahradas, Bhramara, and likewise Maśaka. (10.44)
Saṃgrāha, Kapāla, and Taptakavaca; Gajapāda, Mahāvaktra, the one named Kūrma, and likewise Nakula. (10.45)
Pīḍana, Kumbhīra, Kavaca, Śūla, Anaṅga, Aṅkurodbhāva, Pradīpta, and likewise Trimukha. (10.46)
Then there is Pañcavaktraśata, Jalūkeviladhūmaka, and Prataptajatupaṅka—of terrible form and exceedingly cruel. (10.47)
A fracture of the bone, putrid flesh, and the ground itself are not pure;
likewise, an owl, an axe, and a staff are also impure.
Adhocchāśva, Nirūcchāśva, and Vṛkāsa know it likewise;
as well as Aśvāsya, Gopalāda, Alāka, and Dantaka. (10.49)
The Dog-faced, the Forest Fire, the Anukūpa, and the Āyaka;
likewise the Ahīnāḍivaya, and the Taptapāṣāṇa Vaikaka. || 10-50 ||
Virūpa and Rūpavat, Citra and Acitraratha, as well as Netra, Piṅgala, Raktāsya, Mahiṣa, and the Rākṣasa. || 10-51 ||
Kubja, Udvaṅkṣa, Taila, Asatīnī, Vṛṣṭimudgara, Muśala, Cātapatra, Yamalādi, and likewise [the others]. (10.52)
Kṛmikūṭa, Bahuśākhā, as well as Śālmalī trees, Nigaḍa, Loharajju, and Lohapañjara. (10.53)
The varieties of bondage are the serpent, the scorpion, the crow, the thunderbolt, the iron cauldron, and the cloth-covered pit. (10.54)
Ghora, Ajaga, and likewise Mahāvaitaraṇī;
Gṛdhra, Kurara, Kukkuṭa, and Pramardaka. || 10-55 ||
Kardama, Murmura, Lamboṣṭha, Vajranāyaka, Tripiṭa, Khañjarīṭa, Śavala, and Nīla. (10.56)
The Kākakasamukha, and beyond that, the Śivārāva;
likewise the Gajanāda, the Mahānāda, and the Siṃhanāda. (10.57)
Trapuṣa, Ayas-kūpa, Ikṣupatra, Giri, and Latā; Kaṭaṅkaṭa is also well-known, as is Tapta-vāluka. (10.59)
And the hells are proclaimed to be exceedingly terrible and triangular,
intended for the casting down of those living beings who are devoted to evil deeds.

For those who perform cruel deeds, for those who recite [cruel] texts, for evildoers, for the merciless, for those devoid of compassion, and for those whose very souls delight in harming others— 10.61.

And those who take pleasure in the wives of others, those who revile the scriptures of Śiva, those who misappropriate the property of the gods, and those who are slayers of Brahmins and fathers; || 10-62 ||

One who kills a cow, one who has committed sins, one who betrays the trust of his master, one who steals gold or land, and one who is devoid of purity and right conduct— [these are not to be honored].

Those who are devoid of compassion and courtesy, whose minds are intent on backbiting and falsehood, and who walk upon the wrong path of their own actions, are declared to be the inhabitants of the hells. (10.64)
I shall now describe, in brief, according to the facts and in proper sequence, that karma by which people indeed fall into hell. (10.65)
Truthfulness, patience, non-violence, purity, ritual bathing, freedom from greed, compassion for living beings, and lack of fickleness—one who possesses these does not go to hell. (10.66)
Peaceful, self-controlled, with a joyful soul, free from the darkness of mind and ego; non-malicious, not empty [of virtue], and without desire for the sovereignty of others. || 10-67 ||
Freedom from envy, freedom from pride, devotion to Śiva, steadiness, delight in recitation and meditation, firmness, and the avoidance of miserliness. || 10-68 ||

Vows, observances, and indeed the study of one's own scriptures, the practice of the three daily junctions, faith in all things, the recitation of the *ajapya*, and modesty with a composed mind. (10.69)
Tranquility of energy, contentment, the utterance of pleasant speech, constant practice of examination, and the restraint of the mind and ego. || 10.70 ||
Freedom from hypocrisy, absence of pride, lack of deceit, and possession of knowledge and virtuous conduct;
devotion to the worship of ancestors and gods, and seeking refuge in cows and Brahmins. (10.71)
Truthfulness, non-stealing, freedom from anger, modesty, purity, intelligence, fortitude, self-restraint, control of the senses, and the practice of knowledge—these are declared to be dharma. (10.72)
By constant study of the Vedas, by purity, by austerity alone, and by non-injury toward all living beings, one does not fall into hell. (10.73)
With the senses fully restrained, having abandoned passion and hatred toward the village, and being a giver of fearlessness to all beings, one does not behold the hells. (10.74)
By saluting elders, by offering one's own seat, and by carrying out their commands, one does not fall into hell. (10.75)

Performing oblations in the fire, giving gifts to the guru, following the seasonal injunctions of the wise, finding delight in solitude, and meditating with contentment as if with the Self alone. (10.76)
Non-involvement in the affairs of others, being indifferent, and being free from laziness; freedom from anger and freedom from pride—these are proclaimed as the virtues. (10.77)
But he who devotes himself to these states of being is fit for immortality;
even those bonds of human nature that possess infinite great power are destroyed.
Those embodied beings who are devoted to the day of Śiva and are virtuous in character—having understood this, one should therefore fix the mind upon dharma. (10.79)
Those whose minds are always correct, undeluded, changeless, and stainless, go to the supreme world and do not behold the hells. (10.80)
He whose intellect is undeluded and who is free from sin toward all beings— being stainless and full of courage— he does not behold the hells.
He by whom the senses are conquered and whose mind remains under control—by him all the three worlds, including the moving and the unmoving, are conquered. (10.82)
For the embodied soul who has conquered the mind, who is self-restrained,
and who has become the self of all beings, heaven is as good as already attained.
Whether it be one's own task or the task of another, he whose intellect remains steadfast—this alone is true wisdom; all others are merely readers of books. 10-84.
Thus, this has been explained in brief as the means for the ultimate [liberation];
however, that of others is not ultimate, nor is their enumeration known to be exhaustive. (10.85)
But for those who delight in the Śiva scriptures, who are devoted to their gurus, and who know the supreme reality, no evil shall come to them. (10.86)
Now learn from me the principal ones among these hells;
O fair-faced one, I shall describe thirty-five of them in brief. (10.87)
The Avīci hell, the mass of worms, the Vaitaraṇī river,
as well as the Iron [Mountain], the Śālmalī tree, and the Pair of Mountains.
They know Ucchvāsa and Nirucchvāsa to be the highest [of the hells], as well as Pūtimāṃsa;
furthermore, there are Taptatrapu, Kṣārakūpa, and likewise Kūrma.
For these are indeed included within Avīci; now hear of Kumbhīpāka, as well as Asthibhaṅga, Kukaccheda, Kaṇṭaka, and Kūpa.
Vasāmiśa, Ayastuṇḍa, and the Napuṃsaka are proclaimed;
likewise, Kumbhīpāka and Tīkṣṇāsika are to be known. || 10.91 ||
Heated iron, the path of razor edges, the thunderbolt, and intense heat—these twelve are proclaimed. (10.92)
O fair-faced one, it should be known that [Kumbhīpāka] is included among these eleven, O highly fortunate lady; now understand from me what follows this. 10.93b–c.
Kālasūtra, Mahāpadma, Kumbha, Saṃjīvana, Ikṣuka, Pāśāṇa, Varṣaka, and likewise Āpa. || 10-94 ||
Let those of ignoble intellect and terrible form be punished;
O wise ones, Mahāraurava is situated above all [the other hells]. || 10-95 ||
The thirty-five hells are proclaimed to be of four types;
in brief, O lady of excellent complexion, they should be known as one hundred and forty.
By these, that entity is purified; [thus] forty-five crores are purified. When the twenty-five are purified, the thirty-two are purified. (10.97)
I shall state their names according to the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader:
Avīci, Kṛminicaya, the river Vaitaraṇī, and Ayaḥ.
The pair of Śālmalī trees, the mountain, the place of gasping, and the place of no-gasping;
the smearing with putrid flesh and blood, and the caustic pit is considered the last. (10.99)
Kumbhīpāka, Usthitāṅga, Kukkuṭa, Kaṇuka,
Vasāmiśra, and Ayastuṇḍa— these were not heated by the fire of men.
Thus, eleven [hells] belonging to the Mahāraurava group have been described; now listen:
Raurava, Kālasūtra, Mahāpadma, and then Kumbhaka. (10.101)
Pāśaga, Varṣaka, Yodha, Daṇḍayantre, and Amedhyata—these ten, together with Mahāraurava, are considered to be the hells. (10.102)
Just as purity was previously specified in that case, so it is here;
when these have been purified, he becomes pure, just as that [becomes pure] by means of a hundred measures (tāla).
Twenty-nine *nakas*, however, are of four types; three are of eight types.
Thus, O Goddess, they are fully explained as being purified by thirty-two. (10.104)
O fair-faced one, there are exactly one hundred and forty pure [verses];
indeed, by means of three pure [units], they become thirty-two pure [units]. (10.105)
I shall declare the names of those three, O woman of excellent complexion:
Avīci, which is indeed renowned, and the terrible Kumbhīpāka.
Learn from me the location of the king Mahāraurava;
they are situated respectively in the lower, middle, and upper portions.
O Great Goddess, I shall explain their pervasiveness and how these thirty-two hells are situated:
namely, Avīci and the terrible Kumbhīpāka.
The two [deities] with Ātman as the eleventh are indeed called "Great" (mahā), surrounded by ten;
or else, O fair-faced one, they should be purified together with their second [companions]. (10.109)
