One should contemplate that within the Avīci hell there is a mass of worms, while in Kumbhīpāka there is boiling; and in Mahāraurava, one should consider the presence of impure filth. (10–110)
Now learn from me the measurement of the thirty-two hells:
the height of each one is recorded as ninety-nine lakhs [yojanas].
The distance between each of the thirty-two [hells] should be known as one hundred thousand [yojanas] in sequence;
all of them together, condensed into one, are considered to be thirty-two crores.
O Great Goddess, the path of the hells is clearly one hundred and one lakṣas;
above these, there is likewise an interval of twenty.
O Lord of the Kūṣmāṇḍas, he stands beyond thousands [of yojanas];
his city is proclaimed to have ninety-nine lakhs [of villages].
Above that, I shall describe the netherworlds (pātālas) in brief:
Ābhāsa, Varatāla, Sarkara, and Gabhastimān.
Mahātala, Sutāla, and beyond that Rasātala;
the eighth is to be known as Sauvarṇa, which is endowed with all objects of desire.
I shall describe to you the measurement starting from Ābhāsa up to Suvarṇa; each of these excellent cities has a height of nine thousand [yojanas].
The distance between each one should be known as being measured by a thousand;
all their worlds are indeed shaped like umbrellas.
Endowed with all desired objects and possessed of every excellence,
they were filled with golden ramparts and pinnacles, and crowded with sacrificial altars and banners.
With exits adorned with archways and turrets, resonant with networks of tinkling bells, provided with windows, and embellished for great pleasure; || 10.120 ||
With the sounds of stringed instruments, drums, and musical ensembles filled with the resonance of songs, and with rows of various celestial worlds resplendent with all kinds of jewels. (10.121)
With the lofty peaks of palaces possessing a radiance like moonlight,
and with chariot-paths, groves, and gardens always endowed with flowers and fruits.
Sweet with the cooing of cuckoos, teeming with peacocks and bees, crowded with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks, and adorned by ruddy geese; || 10.123 ||
With lakes resounding with the cries of cranes, adorned with clusters of lotus ponds, and with auspicious oblong ponds and reservoirs containing clear water and other such features; || 10-124 ||
And by men of massive bodies, possessing great strength and prowess, endowed with all sovereignty, beautiful forms, and so forth, and possessed of all auspicious marks. || 10-125 ||
With divine garments and excellent betel, with divine fragrant ointments,
with divine ornaments and flowers, and with crowns adorned with jewels.
O Great Goddess, those who are devoted to the worship of Śiva and intent on accomplishing my purpose enter Pātāla, which is frequented by the Siddhas.
They obtain divine elixirs, alchemical potions, and perfected substances;
likewise, others sport together with celestial, excellent women. 10.128ab [kh]

Accompanied by those who were full of desire, capable of assuming any form at will, walking with the gait of rutting elephants, adorned with all ornaments, and highly skilled in the arts of the science of love (kāmaśāstra). || 10.129 ||
Clad in divine garments, elevated by the weight of their breasts,
with slender waists, serene faces, and tremulous, long eyes.
Some were adorned with small bells on their hips, necklaces, and armlets;
their limbs were anointed with fragrant perfumes, and they were decorated with girdles.
With playful glances, laughter, and dance, and with gestures colored by agitation, women—skilled in the arts of love—caress their beloveds with arms held respectfully and take their delight. (10.132)
Thus, O Goddess, have those three—the gods, the nāgas, and the rākṣasas—who dwell within the worlds, been described by me who possesses true knowledge. (10.133)
O fair-faced one, these are to be known as residing in each individual netherworld (pātāla);
likewise, other lords of the worlds are to be known as residing throughout the seven netherworlds.
He is proclaimed as Bala, Hyatibala, Balavān, Balavikrama, Valesa, Balavanta, and Balādhyakṣa. (10.135)
By these pure ones, these pure inhabitants of the seven netherworlds (pātālas) are purified. First, two golden netherworlds are proclaimed. (10.136)
There dwells that god Hāṭaka, the Supreme Lord,
surrounded on all sides by thousands of millions of cities.
Accompanied by divine hosts of Siddhas and Rudras, by sisters, mothers,
Yoginīs, Yogakanyās, Rudrakanyās, and Rudrakas.
With the juices of perfected substances, mantras, wish-fulfilling gems, and elixirs,
and with those enriched by perfected sciences, they reached the temple of Hāṭakeśa.
He forcibly causes those whose minds are absorbed in that state to enter;
therefore, this Great Lord, the God of gods, is called Hāṭaka.
Thus, due to the conjunction in one place on the path of the eight Pātālas,
they are declared to be sixty-four in number, according to the calculation beginning with nine.
Above that, O fair-faced one, the extent of the terrestrial shell (bhūkaṭāha) is specified as one thousand yojanas in measure.
Above that, O fair-faced one, lies the earth, filled with various inhabited lands;
in its center stands the great Meru, made of gold.
I shall tell you the extent of that mountain from top to bottom;
it is eighty-four thousand yojanas in height.
Sixteen thousand [yojanas] were planted in the lower part;
that same extent of the roots doubles as the width at the summit. (10.145)
Above that, however, is the assembly hall known by the name Manovatī, measuring fourteen thousand yojanas in extent.
Abounding in the exquisite splendor of all jewels and accompanied by thousands of women,
they were endowed with every quality of enjoyment belonging to the high-souled Brahmā.
Crowded with perfected Vidyādharas and surrounded by Ṛṣis,
the peak known as Jyotiṣka is situated in the northeastern direction of that mountain.
Resembling ten million suns, served by the foremost of the Gaṇas, filled everywhere with flowers, and frequented by gods and Gandharvas. || 10.149 ||
There dwells the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Sovereign Tryambaka, surrounded by thousands of women and endowed with all sovereign powers.
He is indeed the sovereign of the world-protectors, the leader of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra;
one should know him as the Lord of the Samānas, who is saluted by gods and siddhas.
Impelled by the desire of another, he exercises his authority;
that assembly hall of Brahmā is situated fourteen yojanas below.
A thousandfold circular enclosure is designated all around,
where the eight heavens are designated and the world-protectors reside.
To the east is the renowned city of Indra, named Amarāvatī;
likewise, to the southeast is the city of Citrabhānu, celebrated as Tejovatī.
To the south is the city of Saṃyamanī, named after King Yama;
and to the southwest, the city of Kṛṣṇāṅganā is proclaimed to belong to the Rākṣasa.
To the west of the Lord of Waters, the city known as Śuddhavatī is remembered;
and to the northwest, O Dear One, is the city of Vāyu named Gandhavatī.
To the north of Soma’s city is the one named Mahodayā;
in the northeast is the city of Īśarāja, named Yaśovatī.
O Goddess, between these two is another city, the twenty-sixth; listen.
To the south of Amarāvatī is the city of the Apsaras called Kāmavatī. (10.158)
To the right of that [city] is indeed the assembly of the golden Siddhas;
and further to the right of that very place is another [city], adorned with rubies.
The city of the Ādityas is renowned as the auspicious Aṃśumatī;
that of the Siddhas is the divine and famous Kusumāvatī, which shines with silver.
To the west of the Fire [element], O Goddess, is the city of Viśveśā Revatī;
and to the west of that as well is the divine [city] of Viśvakarman. (10.161)
In the west, the city of Dharmarāja is known as Mātṛnandā;
there the Mothers sport, reeling from the drinking of honey-wine.
To its west is the golden city of the Rudras named Rohitā;
there dwell the trident-bearing Rudras, the attendants of Yama.
To its west, one should know the city named Guṇavatī,
which has walls and gateways of vajra belonging to the eleven Rudras.
In the eastern part of the southwest direction, there is indeed a city named Piṅgalā;
O Goddess of gods, the Piśācas reside there, known by the name Sukarman.
Near the northwestern direction, the city named Kṛṣṇavatī is recorded;
there, in that very place, the fleshless Rākṣasas always dwell.
To the north of that city as well is the golden city Sukhāvatī;
there dwells Mitra himself, surrounded by a multitude of servants and attendants.
To the north of that as well, from a golden mountain, is the famous region named Gāndhārī;
there dwell the Gāndharvas, surrounded by celestial maidens.
Their number is proclaimed to be ten thousand crores;
this is the army of the Siddhas belonging to the Bhūtas on the right side of Varuṇa.
To the north of the Vasus and of Varuṇa is the region known as Hema;
and to the north of that is the city named Siddhavatī.
That city is proclaimed as belonging to all the Vidyādharas;
O Goddess, to the south of Vāyu, the city named Siddhā is remembered.
There dwell the Kinnaras in cities possessing the brilliance of gold and the sun; to the east of Vāyu is Gāndhārī, and Hemā belongs to Citraratha.
There, in the presence of the one known as Gandharvarāja, who speaks with divine fragrance, the Blessed Lady herself appeared, adorned with the seven musical notes. (10.173)
Clad in the three villages, adorned with birth as her girdle,
her limbs variegated by the higher scales (mūrcchanās), she arises through the manifestation of various ornaments.
Endowed with the primary and secondary marks, draped in a middle-sized garment,
that goddess Sarasvatī was there being praised by Gandharvas in song.
It is frequented by sages such as Nārada and others, as well as by nāgas and kinnaras;
there, to the east, is indeed Citrā, which belongs to Tumburu and Nārada.
To the southwest of Soma, the city of the Guhyakas is proclaimed as Pramada;
to the east of Soma is the city named Vaitrāvatī.
The entire realm of the great-souled Kuvera is variegated by me,
surrounded by twenty-six thousand koṭis.
The glorious lord of the yakṣas dwells there with unsurpassed enjoyments.
To the east of that city is a beautiful city named Śubhā, made of gold from the Jambū river. (10.179)
There indeed are the Karma-devas, who have attained divinity through their actions;
in the western quarter of Vasurāja is the city of Viṣṇu, Śrīmatī.
There dwells the glorious Janārdana, the Lord of Śrī, who resembles the flax flower,
holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, and clad in yellow garments.
To the south of Īśa is the city named Padmavatī,
belonging to him who is seated upon a great lotus and who wears a garland of lotuses.
O Goddess, to the south of that Brahmā, who has eyes as broad as lotus petals and whose self is born from a lotus, there is a city named Kāmamukhā.
O Goddess of the gods, the two Aśvins and likewise Dhanvantari are stationed there;
and to the north of Amarāvatī is the one renowned as Mahāmeghā.
And there dwells the city of the Vināyakas, well-constructed;
it belongs to those ten thousand koṭis of virtuous and powerful beings.
For the sake of slaying the blazing Vināyakas, whose splendor is like a flaming fire, I have fashioned these from my own thumb. (10.186)
In this manner, Meru is indeed surrounded by these excellent cities, both below and above; and the cities that I have described are situated on all sides of Meru.
O beloved, all those [cities] were filled with thousands of millions of inner citadels;
they were perfectly complete with every sovereignty and resplendent with all kinds of jewels.
O Goddess, in every city of the gods, there is constant bliss, crowded with divine deities and thronged with celestial women. (10.189)
In the celestial palaces, there were cities adorned with pleasure groves, crossroads, gardens,
and pavilions, as well as umbrellas, banners, and flags, and they were crowded with elephants and horses.
In the abode of the gods, it is always filled with the sounds of kettledrums and joyful cries, the resonance of conchs and trumpets, and the clamor of dancing and singing.
O Goddess, those men in the meritorious land of Bhārata who are devoted to sacrifices and charitable works,
and who always worship Tryambaka, go to Mount Meru.
Sprinkled with the waters of the Gaṅgā, the best of gods sport there.
The Goddess said: "How did the Gaṅgā, who is saluted by gods and siddhas, originate?"
"Tell me, O best of gods, out of your grace, in brief.
Bhairava said:
"O fair-eyed one, I shall tell you of the origin of the Gaṅgā."
The Mother of the World, the Great Goddess, is indeed my supreme consort;
for this water from my eyes is pure for those who delight in the Cause. 10.195cd–196a.
O Great Goddess, formerly you stood as Airiṣyā with your hands;
while the gods were gathered together, your eyes were covered by them. (10.196)
O Mother of the World, your eyes were opened again by you in the past;
the tears flowing from my eyes were wiped away by your ten fingers.
The Gaṅgā emerged from me in ten streams within the covering of my skull;
seven remained there, while one stayed in the city of Viṣṇu.
The second is in the world of Brahmā, while the third extends through the seven worlds;
furthermore, she is established in heaven, specifically within the lunar orb.
And the Soma streams, having issued forth, settled again in the sky;
then I was praised by the gods, with Brahmā and Viṣṇu at their head.
O Mahādeva, out of a desire for the welfare of mortals, bring down the highly meritorious river Gaṅgā and release her into the world of men.
Then, O Queen of the Gods, I spoke to Aparājitā for the sake of the welfare of the worlds: "Come, O beautiful goddess. (10.202)
Having come and rested upon my head, they previously went to the summit of Meru;
from there, O Goddess of Gods, they departed and went to heaven in the four directions.
Śvetā is designated in the east, Suvaṃkṣā in the south;
Sunandā is in the western part, and Bhadrasomā is in the north.

O Great Goddess, Mandara is known as Gandhamādana; Vipula and Svapārśva are situated from the east to the north. These are declared to be the supporting pillars (viṣkambhas); now learn from me their colors:
white, the hue of turmeric, blue, and the luster of a pomegranate flower.
To the east of Viṣkambha, nearby, is the grove named Caitraratha;
there is a pond there called Aruṇodaka, adorned with lotuses.
Near Gandhamādana is the great forest Nandana;
in its center is the supreme lake Mānasa, covered with lotuses.
Near Vipula, however, is the great forest of Vaibhāja;
in its center is the lake Śitoda, which possesses abundant water.
Near Supārśva is a forest named Pitṛvana;
at its edge is a most auspicious and very beautiful lake.
And there are four wish-fulfilling trees; listen as I describe them:
on Mount Mandara, at its very summit, stands the Kadamba tree.
Extending for a thousand yojanas and possessing five hundred branches,
it shone brilliantly, beautifully blossomed with flowers the size of jars.
The Jambū tree on the summit of Gandhamādana is said to be of that same size;
the juice produced from its mass of fruits is like nectar. (10.213)
From that, the river Jambūnadī was born, exceedingly swift and beloved;
having circled Meru to the right, it flows specifically at the foot of the Jambū tree.
From contact with that [fire], gold is produced;
O Goddess, by means of that, the pure Jambūnada gold arises from the best of mountains.
There, the trees, creepers, shrubs, birds, and even the insects and so forth—all those who dwell there, including everything made of gold—were all composed of Jambūnada gold. (10.216)
In that vast region, however, there is the one renowned as Mahāśvatthaketumāla;
even Indra, having conquered the gods here, was adorned with garlands of banners.
Therefore, that tree is known as Ketumāla, frequented by the Siddhas; it is celebrated as being like a banyan tree with very white, well-formed branches. || 10-218 ||
In brief, Meru is renowned as being endowed with manifold qualities;
likewise, I shall describe the four regions on its sides in summary. (10.219)
With Mount Meru at its center, Jambūdvīpa is proclaimed, in brief, to extend for half a lakh [five million] yojanas in each of the four directions, reaching as far as the salt ocean.
Indeed, there are nine divisions there separated by mountains;
and in the southern direction, three mountain ranges are to be known.
Niṣadha, Hemakūṭa, and Himavān—these three are to the north of Meru; as well as Nīla, Śveta, and Triśṛṅgavān.
These six mountain ranges alone extend from east to west;
Nīla and Niṣadha are proclaimed to have a length of one hundred thousand [yojanas]. (10.223)
Śveta and Hemakūṭa are recorded as being ninety thousand [yojanas] in extent;
Himavat and Śṛṅgavat are measured at eighty thousand.
Extending for two thousand [yojanas] and bounded by the salt ocean are Kailāsa together with Himavat, Triśṛṅga, and Gāruḍi. (10.225)
The Niṣadha mountain, shining with white peaks as bright as moonlight and a peacock's crest,
is composed of sapphire, while [Mount] Nīla is made of rubies.
Sauvarṇa, Hemakūṭa, Himarāja, and Himavān—these are to be known as being to the east of Meru, starting from the eastern side. (10.227)
O beautiful goddess, it measures thirty-four thousand yojanas;
its northward and southward course shines forth, and its width is one thousand [yojanas].
In the same way, on the opposite side of the direction, there is Mount Gandhamādana, equal to that [in size],
with a height of thirty-four thousand yojanas.
On the four sides of Meru, there are two boundary mountains in each direction;
O wise one, Jaṭhara and Devakūṭa are located in the eastern part.
One who understands correctly knows that Kailāsa and Himavat are on the southern side, while Niṣadha and Pāriyātra are on the western side. (10.231)
Jārudhi and Śṛṅgavān are situated to the north;
beyond them, equal in size to Meru, lies the celebrated region of Ilāvṛta.
Below, the Cakravāḍa ring is nine thousand yojanas in extent; it is square and level on all four sides. (10.233)
Neither the heat of the sun nor the rays of the moon prevail there; for all the worlds are illuminated by the radiance of Meru. (10.234)
The people there have the luster of lotus petals facing the sun, are exceedingly delicate,
subsist on the juice of jambu fruits, and are free from old age and death.
Their lifespan is proclaimed to be thirteen thousand years;
they include the gods, gandharvas, siddhas, rishis, and vināyakas.
The Gaṇas, Mothers, Sisters, Vetālas, Rākṣasas, and so forth—these and others beyond numbering—dwell there; and such indeed is the region of Ilāvṛta.
To the east of Gandhamādana and the ocean of Varuṇa lies the region renowned as Ketumāla, which possesses the highest of all qualities.
The people there are exceedingly beautiful, dark as the petals of a blue lotus;
having drunk the juice of the jackfruit tree, they live for ten thousand years.
Jāyanta, Vardhamāna, Aśoka, Haritaparvata, Viśālakambala, and Kṛṣṇa—these seven are the primary lineages there. || 10-240 ||
To the east of Mālyavat and to the west of the ocean is the region named Bhadrāśva; there too, the lifespan is ten thousand years.
The people there resemble the moon and subsist on *kadamba* fruit;
they are the Kaurañjas, the Śvetaparṇas, the Nīlas, and the Mālāgrakas. (10.242)
And it is declared that this is indeed the Padma [mandala]; therein are the five families and so forth.
Its length from east to west is recorded as thirty-two thousand [yojanas]. (10.243)
The two regions extending thirty-four thousand [yojanas] from south to north are thus described; now those situated to the north shall be told.
The inhabitants of the world called Kuru eat the fruits of the trees that bear their names;
they live for thirty thousand years, remaining in perpetual youth.
Men and women are born in pairs, free from the fear of separation; they are dark-complexioned, resembling flowers, glossy, and handsome. (10.246)
There, the ground is made of jewels and strewn with golden sand;
it is proclaimed to be nine thousand yojanas in extent and shaped like a bow.
There, the two Kulaparvatas are Sūryakānta and Indukānta;
and right there is the Kalpavṛkṣa named Kuru, radiant with flowers.
It should be known as the most beautiful Kuru-varṣa by its name;
and the salt ocean enters it from the northern direction.
The island of Candra is proclaimed to be five thousand yojanas;
its extent, however, is one thousand yojanas. (10.250)
Likewise, O fair-faced one, having entered the salt ocean in the direction of the northwest for four thousand yojanas, [one finds it].
The island there is proclaimed to be ten thousand yojanas in extent;
it is to be known as Bhadrākara, endowed with all objects of desire. (10.252)
There, people have a lifespan of ten thousand years and subsist on divine nectar-like fruits;
in the land called Candra as well, they live for ten thousand years, feeding upon such fruits.
Possessing a white and yellow complexion, free from disease and possessing stable youth, she resides in the western direction for ten thousand [years]. (10.254)
Having entered the island named Kumuda, its extent is proclaimed to be one thousand yojanas. (10.255)
Living beings with the radiance of white water-lilies live for ten thousand years,
having drunk the juice of the coconut, their breaths joyful.
Likewise, having entered four thousand yojanas into the southwestern direction, Kaṅkadvīpa is proclaimed. (10.257)
There, the inhabitants have a lifespan of ten thousand years and subsist on dates;
they are glossy, resembling black collyrium, and endowed with all enjoyments. (10.258)
In the southern direction, however, enter the waters extending for ten thousand [yojanas],
known as Siṃhadvīpa, measuring five thousand yojanas.
Having drunk the nectar of the rambhā fruit, people with the luster of vermilion live for ten thousand years, their youth remaining firm.
Having gone ten thousand yojanas further toward the southeast, at the edge of the water, there is an island named Kambu,
one thousand yojanas in extent, where the inhabitants subsist on the fruit of the Caipāla tree.
The people there resemble blue lotuses and are proclaimed to have a lifespan of ten thousand years;
furthermore, having entered Kāmbūdvīpa to the east for one thousand [yojanas], they dwell there. (10.262)
There too, the people have a lifespan of ten thousand years; they are nine thousand leagues in extent, resemble saffron in color, and are free from the fear of separation.

Having consumed the fruit of the *tamāla* tree together with *jīvanta*, and having entered into the midst of the waters for a measure of one hundred and eight [breaths], one reaches that world known as Haṃsadvīpa, which extends for three thousand [yojanas]. Its inhabitants resemble pearls and subsist on the fruit of the *rudrākṣa*. (10.264–265)
Those endowed with beauty live for a measured ten thousand years. There are eight auspicious sub-islands situated in the midst of the salt ocean.
And there are the Śvetaśṛṅga winds; this middle region is golden.
Having eaten the fruit of the *lakuca* tree, the people there possess a radiance like that of the moon. (10.267)
They live for thirteen and a half thousand years according to that measure;
[this applies] to the northern region of Nīla and likewise to the southern region of Śveta.
The region named Ramyaka has those who subsist on the fruit of the banyan tree;
their lifespan is proclaimed to be twelve thousand years.
Dark as the petals of the blue lotus and free from old age and disease,
Ramyaka is nine thousand [yojanas] in extent and is made of gold.
To the north of Hemakūṭa and to the south of Niṣadha, the region known as Harivarṣa is declared; there the living beings have the luster of silver.
Twelve thousand [yojanas] live there subsisting on sugarcane juice;
its extent is most beautiful, measuring nine thousand [yojanas].
To the south of Hemakūṭa and to the north of Himavat lies the region named Kiṃpuruṣa; there the people have the luster of gold.
Those who subsist on the *plakṣa* fruit live for ten thousand years;
its extent, moreover, is proclaimed to be nine thousand [yojanas]. (10.274)
To the south of the lord of snow-mountains and to the north of the salt ocean lies the region named Bhārata; it is indeed known as Ālamukha.
There, O beloved, they suffer from the fear of old age and disease; their prosperity is meager; some are handsome while others are ill-favored; some are fortunate while others are unfortunate.
There are those who enjoy pleasures and those whose enjoyment is meager, as well as others who are extremely miserable;
they are fair-complexioned, dark, black, brown, white, and tawny. (10.277)
In the land called Bhārata, others are born according to the distinctions of color and caste, in accordance with their various karmas, as the four castes and the outcaste classes. (10.278)
In many local dialects and across various islands and intermediate lands, there were likewise many scholars, fools, and those skilled in arts and sciences. (10.279)
Yogins and the wise, as well as the most virtuous and even those who commit sins, are born as beggars; and other people likewise become givers. || 10.280 ||
Many male, female, and neuter servants are to be served there;
those residing in that place eat the remnants of the harvest. (10.281)
In that [age], only one quality is remembered; there, the worship of the fruits of good and evil exists.
It does not exist among the eight [qualities] of some who abide in the Tretā Yuga.
O fair-faced one, it should be known that the land called Bhārata possesses four ages;
whatever action is performed right there, whether auspicious or inauspicious— (10.283)
By that [power], the worlds from Śiva down to the middle of Avīci abide;
beginning with Karavīra, Mahākāla, and likewise Ekāmra. || 10-284 ||
Ten million sacred fords (tīrtha) are said to arise with the fruit of great merit;
indeed, five hundred [of these] are to be known as belonging to rivers such as the Gaṅgā.
It is proclaimed to be nine thousand yojanas in length and shaped like a bow.
...and likewise, the place known as Pañcajala should be understood. || 10.287 ||
[46a] Which [places] are mutually inaccessible? Hear their names from me:
Indrī, Paṅka, Seru, Tāmravarṇa, and Gabhastimān. || 10-288 ||
Nāgadvīpa, Saumya, Gāndharva, and likewise Varuṇa;
the ninth is called Kumārikā—these are proclaimed as their divisions. (10.289)
From the point of the Vindut-sara onwards, this is called Kumāridvīpa;
it extends for a thousand yojanas and is endowed with various colors.
O lady of excellent complexion, those qualities previously mentioned that exist in the world of Bhārata are found right there on the island known as Kumārī, O beloved. (10.291)
In this very place, the seven beautiful mountain ranges are to be known:
Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimān, and the Ṛkṣa mountain. (10.292)
Vindhya and Pāriyātra—these are proclaimed as the six auspicious subcontinents situated between the southern ocean. (10.293)
Aṅgadīpa, Yamākhya, Malaya, the one named Śaṅkha, Kumuda, and Varāha—these are proclaimed [as the islands]. (10.294)
It has been told that on the island of Malaya there is a mountain named Malaya;
at its foot is Trikūṭa, and upon it is Laṅkā.
The four auspicious cities, made of gold, were adorned with gardens,
featuring variegated walls and embellished with diamonds and lapis lazuli.
There, the Rākṣasas, who are the thorns of the gods and possess infinite power, great strength, and prowess, take their pleasure, being devoted to young maidens. (10.297)
There, on that best of mountains, Malaya, is the Agastiśikhara;
there is the highly meritorious hermitage of Agastya, radiant as crystal.
There, beings who are otherwise mutually antagonistic play together without fear;
neither pestilence arises there, nor does untimely death occur. (10.299)
There is neither old age nor sorrow, nor is there fear of calamities anywhere;
no one speaks of another [self], and neither passion nor hatred exists. (10.300)
Due to the power of Agastya’s ascetic heat, knowledge departs from afar;
there indeed dwell the steadfast sages who have exerted themselves in the yoga of knowledge.
O Great Goddess, they were devoted to recitation, study, fire-offerings, worship, and praise, and were constantly engaged in the propitiation of Tryambaka, the Great God.
Accompanied by Agasti, all those who proclaim liberation and worldly prosperity remain like fire situated within the salt ocean.
It stands threefold in circumference and is indeed circular in shape;
there the mountains have entered, terrified by the fear of Vṛtra’s enemy.
I shall describe in brief these twelve of great prowess:
the sages Dundubhi and Dhūmra entered from the eastern side.
Candra, Kaṅka, and Droṇa entered by the north;
then Aśoka, Varāha, and Nandana as the third.
By another [opening], Bhūdhara entered Lavaṇidhi;
Candramas entered the one named Nāka, and Valāhaka was the third. || 10-308 ||
O lady of excellent hips, mountains have entered from the south;
the mouth of Vāḍava remains situated between Cakra and Maināka.
Jambūdvīpa has been fully described; now hear about its origin.
There was a son of Svāyambhuva Manu named Priyavrata. (10.310)
To him were born ten sons, endowed with heroism and strength:
Āgnīdhra, Agnivāhu, Medhā, Medhātithi, and Vasu. (10.311)
Jyotiṣmān, Dyutimān, Havya, Savana, Patra, Medhāpatra, and Agnivāhu—these were the ones who became renunciants. The remaining others of great power were consecrated as rulers over the seven islands.
In Jambūdvīpa, however, there are recorded to be nine sons of Agnīndhra.
Nābhi, Kiṃpuruṣa, Vaha, Ilāvṛta,
Bhadrāśva, Ketumāla, Ramyaka, and Hiraṇmaya.
The ninth is named Kuru; these nine are the lords of the regions (varṣādhipas).
Born from the great Agnīdhra, they are heroes, exceedingly fierce and powerful.
These nine divisions are indeed proclaimed to be marked by their names:
the son of Nābhi was Mahāvīrya, and Ṛṣabha was devoted to the Dharma.
His sons should also be known; among them was the powerful Bharata.
It is after his name, my dear, that this region should be known as Bhārata-varṣa.
To him also eight sons were born, as well as another daughter;
in the land of Bhārata, on the continent of Aṣṭadvīpa, those eight sons were established.
They say the ninth belongs to Kumārī; it was assigned to Kanyā. Those continents were designated by Bharata according to their names. (10.319)
Jambūdvīpa, Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śālmalī, Gomeda, and Puṣkara—these are proclaimed as the seven continents. (10.320)
Now, O lady of excellent vows, I shall describe the oceans to you: the salt ocean, the milk ocean, the ghee ocean, and likewise the sugarcane juice ocean. (10.321)
The seven oceans are proclaimed as Madiroda and Svādura;
Jambūdvīpa is recorded as being one hundred thousand yojanas in measurement.
From that, it should be known that the [ocean] is circular; indeed, the ocean of Kṣiroda is exactly like that.
In this way, the oceans together with the continents increase twofold.
O fair-faced one, Agnīdhra is proclaimed as the king in Jambūdvīpa;
in Śākadvīpa, the one named Medhātithi is the lord, and the land is known as Vapuṣpa, called Kuśa. (10.324)
The king of Krauñcajyotiṣmat is known as Dyutimat on Śālmali; O fair-faced one, he who is named Havya is to be understood as the ruler of Gomeda. (10.325)
The time for those dwelling in Śāka and Gomedha is equal to the Tretā Yuga; likewise, the conduct of the social classes (varṇa) of the inhabitants there should be understood accordingly.
The seven sons of Medhātithi, who are honored in Śākadvīpa, are Śānta, Bhaya, the one named Śiśira, Sumukha, Nandaka, and Śiva. (10.327)
Rāma and Dhruva, marked by the names of their respective regions—these are declared to be the seven regions, separated by mountains; listen. (10.328)
Gomeda, Candrasaṃjña, Nārada, Dundubhi, Somakoṭibhava, Vaibhrāja, and others such as Kula. (10.329)
Sukṛtā, Anuśūnyā, and likewise Sasakhī;
Tripadī, Tridivā, Kumbhī, and likewise Amṛtavāhinī. || 10-330 ||
These very great rivers have issued forth from these mountains:
Kumudonnata, Varāda, Droṇa, and Kaṅkata. (10.331)
Mahiṣa and Kumuda—these seven are the Śīta mountains. [The rivers are] Yonitoyā, Kṛṣṇā, Candrā, and Śuklavilocanā. || 10-332 ||
Vibhūtā, Ravivṛndā, and these seven excellent rivers—
these streams with waters from the forest— having entered Dadhnoda, they flow into the Nibhnagā.
But the people there are happy, eating curds and fruits that have the taste of nectar;
all possessing divine bodies and enjoyments, they sport together with yogins.
Jyotiṣmān consecrated seven sons over Krauñcadvīpa;
he was also known as Udbhija, and Veṇumaṇḍala likewise.
Rathākāra, Lavaṇa, Dhṛtimān, Āṃśuprabhākara, and Kapila—these were the kings marked by the names of the [respective] years. (10.337)
Vaidruma, Hemanābha, Dyutimat, Puṣpadantaka, Kuśala, and Harimarda—these seven are the progenitors of the lineages. || 10-338 ||
Mahīvātā, Śivā, Pāpā, Pavitrā, Santati, Dyuti,
and Dambhā are declared to be the most excellent rivers arising from the mountains.
O beloved, these rivers flow with ghee-water and remove all sins;
all the people dwelling there possess their own true forms and are intense with splendor.
Subsisting on food consisting of ghee and ambrosial fruits, well-satiated and free from the pangs of desire,
they sport together with women whose eyes are as long as lotus petals.
Dyutimān shall consecrate seven sons upon Śālmali; then there is Manonuga, Viṣṇu, Pāvana, and indeed Andhakahāraka. || 10-342 ||
They are celebrated as Muni, Dundubhi, and Kuśala;
indeed, these seven are [designated] by the names of the seven regions in successive order.
Krauñca, Vāmana, Andhakāra, Divākṛti, Dvibindu, Pauṇḍarīka, Dundubhi, and others were the founders of the lineages. || 10.344 ||
Pauṇḍarī, Kauśikī, Gaurī, as well as Kumudvatī, Sandhyā, and Rātrī—these are the renowned ones, O lady of excellent vows, in brief. (10.345)
Those rivers, having issued forth from the mountains, flow into the ocean of sugarcane juice;
there, the people who dwell therein drink that sugarcane juice.
Possessing divine splendor and bodies, they are peaceful, handsome, and pleasant-spoken;
they are surrounded by various women and experience the arising of all sensual pleasures.
One should consecrate the seven sons of Havyarāja on Gomeda: Jalada, Kumāra, Sukumāra, Maṇicaka, [Maṇivara, Maṇibhadra, and Maṇimanta]. (10.348)
Kumuda, Unnata, and Mahābhadra—these are proclaimed as their names, O lady of excellent complexion; by these names those regions are marked.
Udaya, Keśarin, Jaṭharoda, Suraivata, Śyāma, Aṃśumeya, Meru, Śailākṣī, Mattagā, and you yourself. (10.349)
Gabhastī, Kusumārī, and likewise Nalinī;
Dhenukā, Ikṣvāhvā, and the excellent river Venakā. (10.350)
O fair-faced one, these meritorious rivers carrying holy waters enter the ocean of wine;
there, O lovely-faced one, are fruits as delicious as nectar.
And those people eat and drink the nectar of wine;
they are enriched with all their desires, handsome, and free from disease.

And it was graced by various throngs of women, proud of their beauty and youth, adorned with pearl necklaces on their limbs, languid from great intoxication and reeling from their drinking habits. (10.353)
Struck by the arrows of side-long glances, men constantly suffer from passion along with the throngs of women.
Then, however, in the place called Puṣkara, there is a leader at that sacrificial ground.
O lady of beautiful countenance, two sons are said to reside in the place called Puṣkara; O lady of excellent hips, it extends for twenty-five yojanas and is endowed with all kinds of jewels.
In Dhātakī-madhya, the king is Mahāvṛtta; outside, the king is Rīti.
They are free from the stains of envy, passion, and ignorance. (10.357)
During those two years, O Great Goddess, the people everywhere were happy; there were five islands, seven sons, and mountains. (10.358)
O fair-faced one, the mental [mandala] should be understood as being circular;
I shall now describe to you the abode of the four world-protectors.
The city of Hari is called Vasvokasārā; that of Yama is Saṃyamanī;
that of Varuṇa is Sukhāhvā; and that of Soma is Vibhāvatī.
O Great Goddess, these cities are surrounded by millions of other cities; they are highly prosperous, endowed with great enjoyments, and provide every desired object for men and women. || 10.361 ||
Established at twice that measure, extending to the end of the Svādūdaka ocean,
it is recorded as having five crores [of yojanas] and being superior to the seven worlds.
The measurement from the peak of Mount Meru down to the Svādūdaka ocean is thus proclaimed;
beyond that, O fair-faced one, is the golden ground extending for ten koṭis.
Beyond this is the Lokāloka mountain, ten thousand *yojanas* in extent and ring-shaped, for the purpose of the gods' play. (10.364)
O fair-faced one, it is one hundred thousand yojanas in height,
endowed with all kinds of jewels, and renowned for its golden color.
At its end, O beautiful goddess, he speaks of another sun;
there the world-protectors abide, as do the Rudras of unfailing power.
Viraja, Sudhāmā, Śaṅkhapāda,
Kaṅkama, Hiraṇyaroman, Parjanya, Ketumān, and Añjana.
In a chasm made of Jambūnada gold, frequented by perfected beings and immortals,
[one should proceed] in order starting from the east as far as the domain of Īśāna.
O Goddess, O lady of excellent hips, the world-protectors stand and protect these subjects;
in the midst of this, there are fourteen wombs.
Streaked with various forms and colored by their own karma,
they swirl above the Lokāloka mountain during the sun’s southern course.
Likewise, the northern course (uttarāyaṇa) is proclaimed there as being in the north;
when it is midnight in Amarāvatī, it is sunset in the city of Yama.
Midday occurs in Vāruṇī, and sunrise is recorded in Saumya;
that very same sunrise is seen there in Amarāvatī.
At midday, the path of the sun between the moon and the sun is the Suvīthī;
its northern part is the Ajavīthī, while its southern part is the [Suvīthī].
Indeed, this path of the ancestors and the gods has been described by me to you;
Mount Meru lies to the north of all [the worlds], while Lokāloka is to the south.
Outside of this is a terrible darkness, difficult to behold and devoid of living beings;
it is recorded as being thirty-five crores and nineteen lakhs [in extent]. (10.375)
O fair-faced one, the Garbhoda ocean, which is beyond darkness, measures forty thousand yojanas and extends as far as the seven seas.
Connected with the shell of Brahmā’s egg and situated in the center of Meru,
fifty koṭis [of yojanas] are to be known as extending equally in all ten directions.
One should know that there are a hundred such great millions of earthly [worlds].
O lady of excellent complexion, I shall now fully declare the measurement beyond this.
Alternatively, O Great Goddess, listen to me regarding the sequence of the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) that have come down in succession at the time of initiation. || 10.379 ||
Understand from me the principle of Śakti, as well as its world-sphere and its womb;
and likewise, the principle of Śakti itself, along with its world-sphere, in brief. (10.380)
One should meditate upon the womb and the union; one should offer incense to all of these in their proper sequence. (10.381)
And likewise Ananta, Kālāgni, and the Ratnas in due order;
then one should purify the netherworlds (pātālas) above them in successive sequence.
Then, O lady of excellent vows, one should perform the installation for the world of the earth;
thereafter, one should worship the goddess Vāgeśvarī with flowers and other offerings.
Then the animal, having observed the beating, the discharge of phlegm, as well as the cutting, the dragging, the seizing, and likewise the binding; || 10.384 ||
One should purify the womb, the birth, and likewise the authority, as well as union, enjoyment, and dissolution; thereafter, one should purify the source.
I shall briefly proclaim these fourteen [types of marriage] in their proper order:
the Paiśāca, the Rākṣasa, the Yākṣa, the Gāndharva, and the Aindra.
The Saumya and the Brahma are recorded as the eighth;
they are to be purified in the sacrifice of Śiva through the application of the sequence of withdrawal (saṃhāra).
Domestic animals, birds, wild beasts, as well as reptiles should be known [as the fifth], the immobile [beings] as the fifth, and the sixth is that born from the human womb. (10.388)
The animal realm is known to be fivefold; this is the circle of saṃsāra.
One should purify these fourteen types within the world of the earth (bhūrloka).

For the self transmigrates here within the sphere of the earth and other realms such as Māyā; therefore, it is called "saṃsāra" (transmigration), because from this state it wanders about. || 10-390 ||
While traveling along the path, he experiences pleasure, pain, and likewise delusion;
he is overcome by the three bonds and presided over by the power of Vāmā.
By means of the Lord as the instrumental cause, on the path of creation and dissolution,
the Self then again joins together the auspicious and the inauspicious in the interim.
Likewise, within the path, the bonds (pāśas) should be known to be infinite crores in number,
distinguished by the primary qualities (pradhāna-guṇa), extending as far as the state of Anāśrita.
Therefore, O Goddess, one should understand that which is the cause of bondage to the path—the fourteen-fold sphere of transmigratory existence (saṃsāramaṇḍala) that has been described. || 10-394 ||
Its divisions are indeed infinite, differentiated according to the diversity of karma;
for the powers of karma are infinite, and the agent of karma is beginningless.
The self binds itself and the self liberates itself within itself;
just as the silkworm tightly encloses itself in its cocoon. || 10.396 ||
Just as it is not possible to wrap oneself around oneself, so too all those in cyclic existence are bound by the fetters of saṃsāra. (10.397)
And the bound souls (paśus) are not capable of liberating themselves from their bonds;
thus, Śiva does not look upon himself by means of his own self. (10.398)
And by the descent of Śiva’s power, one is released from the bondage of the fetters;
otherwise, one does not attain that stainless essential nature. (10.399)
That which is one's own noble birth—pure, incomparable, and free from affliction—is obscured by the delusion of impurity, and beings are bound by the various strands of karma and so forth. (10.400)
They remain there unmanifest, just as fire exists within wood;
yet when stirred, they become clearly manifest, like fire brought under the control of a fire-drill.
He recognizes the true nature of existence as eternal and perfectly pure,
even for other beings whose moments are impaired by the cataracts of ignorance.
Just as [the sun] illuminates objects by dispelling darkness with its rays, so too does the Self perceive that which is beautiful and beginningless. 10.403
O Goddess, it shall not be otherwise by any means through the slaying of Manthaka;
for, O Goddess, when Manthaka himself is indeed Sadāśiva.
Having assumed the body of the Teacher, he is always established in bestowing grace;
the eyes are to be known as the churning-sticks, and the paths as the churning-rods.
Vāgīśī, situated within the womb, is to be known as smoke, like impurities and the like;
the Self is indeed said to be like fire, the supreme Śiva awakened. (10.406)

Just as fire, once awakened, becomes exceedingly bright and pure and does not enter back into wood, so too the Self, when raised above the noise [of the senses], does not enter back into them. (10.407)
Freed from impure karma and the powers (kalās) and so forth, and devoid of exhaustion, one situated there is not slain, just as a leaf [protected by] fire remains perfectly pure. (10.408)
Just as the blackness of copper is removed through the application of mercury and fire, so too, when separated by those who know the method, it becomes gold. (10.409)
It does not return to its original state even after hundreds of millions of eons;
the power of the mantra, like mercury, is to be understood as action, like fire. (10.410)
For those who know it, Śiva is to be known as the one whose body is the form of the teacher;
the self is to be known as gold, while impurity is to be known as blackness.
O beloved, O lady of excellent vows, through the application of mantra, substance, and ritual action, and by means of the instruments such as the *vatī*,
the two-fold self has indeed been purified by the Guru.
No longer remaining impure, he attains the state of Śiva, which is stainless.
Knowing this, O lady of excellent hips, initiation should be performed as it was before.
One should purify the primary bonds which were previously described by me;
O lady of excellent vows, even those bonds that are subordinate are purified.
O Goddess, one should purify the mandala of saṃsāra upon the surface of the araṇī, exactly as the fourteenfold [mandala] was previously described by me. (10.415)
I shall explain all of that in due order, according to how it is to be purified in the sacrifice to Śiva;
one should purify everything in sequence, from Brāhmī up to Brāhmaṇa.
O Indra, having purified the Vahya and Saumya [forms], and the Gāndharva and Yakṣarāja [forms],
one should purify the Paiśāca form in due order, and likewise purify the state of being an animal.
Having purified the Saptacchada among trees, Vāsuki among serpents, Garuḍa among birds, and the lion among beasts, [one should worship them]. || 10.418 ||
One should purify cattle by means of the cow-source, and humans by means of the human source;
[one should purify] the outcaste, the Śūdra, the Vaiśya, the Kṣatriya, and finally the Brāhmaṇa. (10.419)
One should purify the offices (adhikāra) with the Lord of the Seed-mantra, but not with the Lord of the Deity;
by means of the application of ten oblations, this applies to everyone from the lowest castes up to the Brahmins. (10.420)
A Brahmin should perform forty-eight oblations for the rites of entitlement:
the *garbha*, the *puṃsavana*, the *sīmantonnayana*, and the *jātakarman*. (10.421)
Naming, the going forth [from the womb], the first feeding of solid food, and the tonsure ceremony—
these, O lady of excellent hips, are proclaimed as the eight [samskāras] that must be purified.
O Goddess, when these have been turned back, one is then born as a twice-born;
the ninth is the binding of the vow, which is proclaimed as the sacrifice for that.
I shall now describe the constituent parts in their proper order:
the girdle, the wooden staff, the antelope skin, and likewise the *tryāyuṣa*.
The twilight devotions, the fire-sacrifice, and alms-gathering as the seventh—these seven vows, including the girdle, the student (brahmacārī) should perform. 10.425.
And those who are departing [from the world] should be understood at the time of initiation, O fair-faced one, as belonging to these [groups]:
the Pāśupatas, the Gaṇas, and the Gaṇeśvaras. (10.426)
The "madman's blade" and the "ghee-eater" are recorded as the seventh;
these seven are indeed declared to be the vows for the religious student (brahmacārin).
The observances of conduct (*caryāvratas*) should be understood as being proclaimed as constituent parts;
together with these, there is indeed one ninth bond of observance (*vratavandhana*).
O lady of excellent vows, those who are to be understood as being included within that have been described to you;
therefore, O secret one, there are only four Vedic observances, without a doubt. (10.429)
The Iṣṭikā, Parvaṇī, Bhautikā, and likewise the Saumikā;
these are the four observances of vows which the religious student (brahmacārin) undertakes.
Having thus performed these four vows with these [offerings], O fair-faced one, one should know that as the thirteenth; thereafter, one indeed becomes a vessel for the Vedas.
Therefore, O beloved, there occurs the gift of the cow, which is the fourteenth;
one who has completed his Vedic studies should marry a maiden accomplished in knowledge as his wife.
Having made a wife out of darbha grass, one should perform a sacrifice together with her;
that should be known as the tenth [sacrifice], and after that come the pākayajñas.
I shall briefly describe those occasional rites which they have taught:
the Aṣṭakā, the Parvan, along with the Śrāvaṇī and the Āgrāyaṇī.
The month of Caitra and the month of Āśvayuja are likewise known as the seven *pākamakhas*.
Together with these, one should understand them to be twenty-two in number.
The Ādhāna, the Agnihotra, and the Dārśa are considered next;
thereafter, the Paurṇamāsī and likewise the Cāturmāsyas are to be known. || 10-436 ||
The animal sacrifice (paśubandha) has been fully described; after that comes the Sautrāmaṇī.
Thus, the seven Haviḥ-yajñas have been enumerated, as well as the seven Pākayajñas.
Together with these, one should understand the nineteen [stages] of saṃsāra:
the Agniṣṭoma, the Atyagniṣṭoma, and the Ukthya, as well as the Ṣoḍaśin.
The Vājapeya, the Atirātra, and the Āptoryāma as the seventh—these are declared to be the thirty-six Soma-saṃsthās. || 10-439 ||
Hiraṇyapāda, Prathama, Araṇya-guhya, Hiraṇyagha, Hiraṇyamedra, Hiraṇyābhi, and Hiraṇyagarbha. || 10.440 ||
Hiraṇyasrotas, Hiraṇyatva, and likewise Hiraṇyākṣa;
the renowned Hiraṇyajihva—these ten are proclaimed as the Yajñas.
Indeed, these are surrounded by a hundred for each individual who understands;
by all of these, even a thousand [times] purifies the twenty-seventh.
Then, one who is renowned for the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) shall become a householder by means of all these;
the mantra, however, consists of thirty-eight [syllables] and would be the primary [mantra] for the forest-dweller.
Having performed the *paribhrājya* and at its conclusion the *iṣṭi*, one shall attain the state of Brahman;
these, together with the others, constitute the forty purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for the wise man.
I shall now briefly declare the eight qualities of the self: compassion toward all beings, patience, and freedom from envy. (10.445)
Purity, lack of exertion, and auspiciousness beyond this; non-action, gentleness, and untouchability—these are remembered as the eight qualities of the self. (10.446)
Forty-eight purificatory rites have been taught in brief;
by these, when purified, even the innumerable [impurities] are cleansed, O lady of excellent vows. (10.447)

Having performed the final sacrifice and calculated [the results], one should bestow the qualities upon the child with five oblations each, following the sequence of the Brahma-mantras and the limbs (aṅgas).
Having offered oblations of sesame seeds with ghee, one should indeed perform the rite of elevation and then apply it;
for by the word "elevation" (ūrdhva), that action which is impure is proclaimed.
The binding should be performed upon that [object], and it is not prescribed elsewhere;
therefore, its extraction should be performed, and never its shaving. (10.450)
Whatever action is prescribed here according to the sequence, one should apply it there;
then, beginning with *aṇimā* and *māyā*, [one proceeds] in order through the letters from *a* to *kṣa*.

Having performed the oblation with sesame seeds for the sake of enjoyment and not for oneself, that which is established in the world of mortals should be known by the word "upward" (ūrdhva). || 10-452 ||
For one who is absorbed in that [state], there is universality, and never in anything else;
for as long as karma is not exhausted, how can there be yoga while one remains unsatiated?

Therefore, O Great Goddess, by the word "union" (yoga) in that context, one should contemplate single-mindedly on that action; once it has been accomplished, one should then perform the withdrawal-homa.
Having offered eight oblations with the *śiva* mantra, [he should worship] the lords of the worlds (*bhuvanādhipāḥ*) and those who dwell within the worlds,
according to the sequence of the worlds.
The fire sacrifice (homa) must indeed be performed, followed by the severing of the connection;
then the full oblation (pūrṇā), then the extraction (uddhāra), and that which resides therein, in due order.

Then, having performed the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) as an oblation for the sake of remedying any deficiencies in knowledge, one should purify [the elements] in this very sequence up to Śiva. (10.457)
The Bhūrloka has thus been fully described; now learn from me about the Bhuvarloka.
From the surface of the earth up to the sun, its measurement is one hundred thousand [yojanas].
Just as there are ten times ten thousand *ayuta*s between each of the ten winds in the center,
I shall now describe how the clouds are situated on the first wind-path.
Fifty yojanas above that is the Vināma wind;
it increases the nourishment as well as the strength of the medicinal herbs.
And that flowing [ocean] nourishes the entire earth;
therefore, it clearly extends for one hundred and fifty yojanas upwards.
Because he carries away the fragrance of men's exhalations, bringing comfort to them, he is indeed known as Gandhāpaha (the Remover of Odor). || 10.462 ||
And there is one hundred yojanas in extent, named Pracetas by its appearance;
it indeed destroys trees, though it only occasionally arises.
The fire named Pracetas remains laughing for that very reason;
when it burns houses and other such things, then it proceeds forth.
One who dwells happily in the ocean is calmed by its water;
beyond a hundred yojanas, it is called the Senavid wind. (10.465)
When this wind blows, clouds with faces like lightning dwell within it;
they remain at a distance of one *kośa* from the earth and pour down rain.
From this [wind], the great wind named Tugha is grasped according to its measure;
here, at a height of one hundred yojanas, are the clouds that carry sentient beings.
Fish, frogs, and tortoises rain down, as do foul storms;
beyond fifty yojanas, it is proclaimed as the region of wind-disease.
In that [region], the rain falls as diseases and poisonous water;
by means of that, calamities arise, including the death of all embodied beings. (10.469)
The Piśācas known as Dīpyas dwell in the hair; they are born from the shoulders and body, and twenty thousand crores are recorded as the followers of Skanda.
And they worship the Son of Bhava with divine flowers—
those terrible, unfailing-sounding [beings] who have originated from Mahādeva.
Thirty thousand koṭis are established there in the wind;
they carry away the performed karma of men who have not disciplined their selves.
The wind named Vajrāṅga is situated at a distance of fifty yojanas;
in that region are clouds named Upalaka which rain down stones. (10.473)
There, the Mātaṅgas—fierce, most terrible, performers of cruel deeds, resembling crushed collyrium, and formidable—are renowned by the name Tāpanas. (10.474)
Those who are ignorant men achieve the lowest rank among the Vidyādharas, possessing a speed of mind like the wind through the practice of corpse-raising (vetāla) rites in cremation grounds.
Having established that [wind], they indeed reside within it;
fifty yojanas from there is the lightning-wind.
And the clouds belonging to lightning dwell there within the lightning;
due to the agitation of the wind, a great torrent of rain is produced from them, free from thunder.
In that city, which is garlanded with fortresses, perfected Apsarases well-disposed by Vāsava always remain, adorning the earth.
Those supreme men who die by fire, in water, or on the battlefield;
or those who die while recovering cattle or liberating prisoners, [attain the highest state]. (10.479)
Then they proceed upwards in celestial chariots adorned with jewels,
filled with banners and lamps, and resounding with the sound of divine bells.
They lead him away in celestial chariots crowded with thousands of women;
then, at intervals of fifty yojanas, the wind carries them along.
In that place, clouds carrying nourishment pour down sustenance for embodied beings;
and there itself, O Great Goddess, the Siddhas are firmly established.
Having mastered the gorocanā, añjana, and other substances up to the magical sandals (pādukā), those great-souled ones became perfected beings (siddhas) capable of assuming any form at will.
Those great-souled ones dwell there, established as divine Siddhas;
during the dissolution, they are clouds that bring disease, raining down the waters of sickness.
Fifty yojanas away, those hosts of Vidyādharas are stationed;
numbering thirty-one crores, they are adorned with divine ornaments.
Anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with divine garlands and wreaths,
they are carried by the wind named Visaṃvarta at a height of fifty yojanas.
In that place, clouds named Krodhodaka are firmly established;
they are driven by the roar of wrath and are frequently engaged in battle.
When those clouds rain, they bring about the destruction of the king and indeed the destruction of the subjects. (10.488)
Those who dwell as great enjoyers, perfected through the sword and the pill,
are known as the fiery clouds born of smoke and those born of cold and overcast days.
The wind Samāvaha carries these [beings] along at a distance of a hundred yojanas; there dwell those skilled in the Gandharva arts, whose nature accords with that of the Gandharvas.
The clouds named Brahmajas, born from the breath of Brahmā, belong to the bird who knows the ritual and can assume any form at will. || 10.491 ||
Situated a hundred yojanas above, atop Durjaya, there indeed dwell the guardians of Indra named the Durjayas. || 10.492 ||
It is proclaimed that ten koṭis [of beings] endowed with great heroic power [reside there];
it is one hundred yojanas higher than Durjaya, O you who are dear to your vows. (10.493)
The winds Parāvaha and Avaha, born from the lotus-mouths of clouds,
had the wings of the great-souled mountains severed by Śakra.
Parāvaha carries those who obey the command of the gods;
or else, in that [region], there are the Gandharvas named Yuga, whose abode is the sky.
And eleven crores of them have indeed been proclaimed;
beyond that, there are thousands of supreme Brahmās, three times over.
Then I brought forth another wind named Jīmūta; those clouds are called Jīmūtakas, and upon them dwell ten hosts of Vidyādharas known as the Jīmūtakas.
The gods indeed, by way of the path of sound, having performed a thousand-fold rite,
then requested Vāyu for their invocation, taking refuge in the Droṇas.
In that [region], Droṇa is well-known as the protector of the clouds;
he was created by me in the past for the welfare of all living beings.
O fair-faced one, along that very path and route for a distance of many yojanas,
above [the clouds] there are indeed dense clouds called Saṃvarta, arisen from the Kalāpa.
The wind named Mahāparivaha is their support;
thus, in the first wind-path, the clouds indeed move together with the winds.
The Siddhas and the Adhipatis are said to move within the clouds;
and on the second path, the Agnikanyās and the Mātṛs are to be known.
Endowed with virtues and presided over by the power of Rudra, they dwell there;
and on the third path, the Siddhas and Cāraṇas reside.
Perfectly accomplished through the enjoyment of their own karma and empowered by all the Siddhas,
they dwell on the fourth path, bearing the weapons of the deities.
These very beings are of various kinds and belong to the five wombs;
O Goddess, in the fifth path dwell Airāvata and the others.
Airāvata, Jana, and the great elephant Vāmana; Apratīka, Karīndra, and likewise Puṣpadanta. || 10-506 ||
Kumuda is the eighth, following Puṇḍarīka;
these world-guarding elephants (diggajas) are renowned and well-established in their respective directions.
O Goddess, on the sixth path of the wind dwells the king of birds, possessed of great strength;
he is renowned as Garuḍa, invincible and exceedingly heroic. (10.508)
In the seventh [ocean], however, is the celestial Gaṅgā, filled with various aquatic creatures;
it is divine, consists of the water of nectar, is meritorious, and is situated in three paths.
Wandering in the midst of the sky, circular on all sides,
it is known as the celestial Gaṅgā, possessing a hundred streams for the gods.
And she shines there with a garland of flowers, her very head being like the sky;
there, by the highly fortunate Siddhas and likewise by the hosts of Vidyādharas.
And by the Gandharvas and Apsarases, by the Sādhyas and the hosts of Maruts, by the Rudras, Vasus, and Ādityas, and by the Pitṛs, gods, and great Ṛṣis. || 10.512 ||
[50a] And by rākṣasas and guhyakas intent on divine praise,
and by high-souled yogins chanting and singing [prayers].
With those dancing and whirling, with the sounds of divine drums,
with the resonance of kettledrums and clay drums, and with the melodies of lutes.
And with lutes and flutes, set in motion by the mind and the wind,
[he offered] fragrant lotuses with stalks of lapis lazuli and petals of gold.
With two whisks made of rubies, each as large as a great discus,
that most excellent river dances, adorned with hundreds of celestial palaces.
The great river Dharmadhārā, adorned with divine forests, has issued forth from my eye; for she is indeed supreme in the power of action (kriyā-śakti).
The goddess Mahāmandākinī is attended by the gods of the thirty-three heavens; she stands surrounded on all sides by tens of millions of great celestial palaces.
The Blessed Lady is adorned there in the vault of the sky as eternal;
likewise, she is at the summit of Meru, upon the peak of Kāma.
Out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, she fell upon the surface of the earth;
yet even now, this Gaṅgā remains unexhausted, sustained by the wind.
Its width is proclaimed to be a full hundred yojanas;
its circumference and length are ten million, and it is auspicious with a great force of water.
She stands as if wandering, perfectly circular on all sides;
surely that goddess has performed a miracle, for she remains just as she was before from that city.
In that manner, I shall describe them to you in regular order and in reverse order:
in the eighth [position] is Vṛṣarāja, together with his consort, O Sunandana.
He dwells there unimpeded, for he is Dharma itself made manifest;
and on the ninth path is the Prajāpati named Dakṣa.
Brahmā himself dwells there directly, presided over by the power of Brahmā;
but in the tenth path, O Goddess, dwell the Rudras, the Vasus, and the Sun.
Listen as I describe those who are fully endowed with all enjoyments and excellence:
Aja, Ekapāda, Buddha, and Abhaya. (10.526)
Pinākin, he named Ḍiṇḍin, Dhūmaketu,
Kapardin, Śūlin, Kapālin, and likewise Mṛgavyādhamastaka.
Eleven Rudras are remembered as the source of the fulfillment of all desires:
Pratyūṣa, Pradoṣa, Ajaghanya, and Jaghanyakas. (10.528)
Dhātṛ, Dhruva, Āvaha, and likewise Vivaha—these are declared to be the Vasus; now learn from me concerning the Ādityas.
Pūṣan, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, and Bhaga, as well as Indra, Parjanya, Aryamā, Mitra, Tvaṣṭṛ, and likewise Jiṣṇu. || 10-530 ||
Sumati was born of Sāvitrī; these are known as the twelve Ādityas.
They are understood to be the sons of Kaśyapa, born from that treasury of splendor. (10.531)
The great divine [mandala] arising from nectar, endowed with all the gods, is like a sacrificial wheel; within it, the burden consisting of all-knowledge is established. (10.532)
Its seven notes are the seven Vedas, and its sound is like that of a sacrificial fire;
the serpents are its yokes, and Aruṇa is its charioteer.
And there was a divine couch for the chariot, possessing the speed of the wind;
upon it stood the one of great splendor, the sun, red in color.
The body of the Sun is nine thousand yojanas in extent, and his orb is three times that; thus the triple world shines with radiant light.
The remaining [powers], supreme through the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), shine forth from the solar form;
by means of the practice of the monthly movement, one may circulate according to the supreme will.
In a single day and night, it revolves completely around the Bhuvarloka;
beyond that, Soma is situated one hundred thousand [yojanas] above the Āditya.
The entire world is nourished by the lunar days and the planets that send down rain;
indeed, it is the power of action (kriyāśakti) of Śiva that shines forth in the form of the moon.
The lunar mansion circle is situated at a distance of one hundred thousand [yojanas] from the moon;
Mercury is known to be at one hundred thousand, and Venus is understood by the wise to be at two hundred thousand.
Aṅgāraka is at two hundred thousand [yojanas], while Guru is at two hundred thousand; Śauri is proclaimed to be above that by another two hundred thousand.
I shall relate briefly, by way of a mere summary, the sages:
Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu. (10.541)
Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and Marīci are proclaimed as the sages (ṛṣis);
they are devoted to self-restraint and observances, and are capable of both cursing and bestowing grace.
Averse to causing harm to others, they were heroes skilled in the scriptures; all were intent upon the sword of knowledge and were removers of the veil of ignorance. (10.543)
Through the practice of mantra, yoga, kriyā, and caryā, they possess firm faith that is difficult to transcend;
endowed with the host of powers of yoga, they are devoted to the propitiation of Śiva. (10.544)
O woman of excellent complexion, the body of that Dhruva was constructed above him by fourteen stars;
O Great Goddess, above that, the celestial realm (Svarloka) is proclaimed.
Brahmā himself, in another form, was appointed to the position of Brahmā.
O Goddess, it revolves constantly, bound by hosts of luminaries;
yet it should be known as motionless when presided over by the power of Śiva. (10.547)
From the terrestrial mandala up to the end of Dhruva, there are fifteen million [yojanas] situated within the mass of wind; I shall describe them here with complete certainty. (10.548)
The sun, the moon, and the circles of the planets and constellations are free from clouds;
and the seven sages, beginning with their enumeration and ending with Dhruva as the seventh. (10.549)
The heavenly world (svarloka) is proclaimed to extend from the Sun (Āditya) up to the Pole Star (Dhruva).
There, indeed, the king Mahendra dwells, honored by the gods.
Surrounded by sages, gods, and gandharvas, he remains there along with the apsarases;
yet, though he has performed the agnihotra or even a sacrifice, he is devoid of knowledge.
Men go to the heavenly world (svarloka), but they return again to the human realm.
O beloved, the heavenly world is situated two crores of yojanas above.
And eighty-five lakhs [of yojanas], O fair-faced one, is Maharloka;
indeed, the ṛṣis and the Siddhas, such as Mārkaṇḍeya and others, dwell there.
O Great Goddess, O fair-faced one, Janaloka is situated above Maharloka at a distance of eighty million yojanas.
Ekapāda, Athajāhnava, and the sage Kapila, as well as Bhautika and Ādvali, are the inhabitants of Janaloka. (10.555)
Likewise, O Dear One, twelve crores above the world of humans (janaloka) is declared to be the world of heat (tapoloka),
which is the abode of the sages and the lords of yoga.
Śanaka, Sananda, Sanatkumāra, Sanātana,
Śaṅku,
and Triśaṅku— these are the inhabitants of the world of Tapas.
O fair-faced one, starting from the world of Bhūr up to Satyaloka, there are fifty-six crores and twenty lakhs of lotuses.
This number of worlds has been declared in brief, O beloved: by a measure of sixteen crores above the world of heat (tapaloka).
It is known as Satyaloka, where Brahmā himself resides;
there the divine Lord sports, surrounded by twice-born ones who are equal to his own self.
Perfectly accomplished through the meditation on action, firmly established in non-duality, they have attained the state of bliss; they have reached the state of bliss. || 10-561 ||
There, the Rigveda was present in embodied form, possessing a luster like that of sapphire, its limbs anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with celestial ornaments. (10.562)
Situated to its east, blazing with splendor,
it stands within the center of a red lotus, possessing a radiance equal to that of a ruby.
In the north, however, is the Yajurveda, resembling pure crystal;
he wears divine earrings, possesses great illusory power, and has mighty arms.
Situated in the western quarter is the eternal Sāmaveda,
glorious, wearing red garments, and possessing a luster like that of a ruby.
We bow to Atharvan, who wears garlands, is variegated, and adorned with hanging ornaments,
as he stands likewise on the right side.
Tawny-eyed, with a red neck, golden hair, and a massive body;
[he is the source of] the Itihāsas, the Vedāṅgas, and all the Purāṇas. (10.567)
The Vedas, the Upaniṣads, the Chandas, the Mīmāṃsā, the Āraṇyakas, as well as the utterances of Svāhā and Vaṣaṭ, and likewise the secret doctrines (Rahasyas). || 10.568 ||
And the Gāyatrī is situated there where the four-faced God resides;
that is the place of enjoyment for Brahmā, from which one should go to the Supreme Brahman.
O beloved, ten million yojanas above the world of truth (satyaloka) is that which is known as the Seat of Brahmā (brahmāsana), possessing a luster like that of indigo and vermilion.
It has four faces, possesses the four Vedas, and follows the conclusion of the four ages;
it is crowded with those who know Brahman and is served by great sages.
Endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers, he is the agent of the sixfold creation and the bestower, age after age, of the fruits of dharma and the other goals of life.
He is the creator of beings in the animal realm and of those who are divine or human,
as well as the creator of all living beings, including gods, asuras, and men.
Two crores and more than that in yojanas, O fair-faced one,
[are the worlds] resembling blue lotuses and possessing a luster like sapphire.
Beyond the world of Brahmā, the city of Viṣṇu is remembered;
it is endowed with the fruits of all desires and resplendent with every kind of jewel. (10.575)
With pillars and staircases made of emerald, crowded with blue banners, wide with canopies of bells, and adorned with beautiful yak-tail whisks. || 10.576 ||
Surrounded by young maidens whose eyes resembled the petals of blue lotuses, they were startled by the sounds of lovers' bows.
With anklets jingling with sweet sounds, possessing soft and delicate splendor, and shattered by hundreds of strikes from the arrows of the god of love; || 10-578 ||
The lotus-eyed Lord Viṣṇu is served by celestial nymphs whose beautiful eyes are tremulous with the intoxication of their shimmering glances. (10.579)
Having a form like sapphire, resembling the petal of a blue lotus,
four-armed, of great body, clad in yellow garments, and bearing a mace.
Wearing a crown, earrings, and a conch, and devoted to the protection of his subjects,
that Blessed One is served by hosts who possess his own prowess.
And those who are constant devotees of Viṣṇu, devoted to meditation, worship, and the chanting of prayers—
they go there to that abode of Viṣṇu of immeasurable prowess.
Seven crores above that, indeed, is situated the world of Rudra;
it resembles pure crystal and is adorned with four gardens.
It was adorned with rows of palatial mansions possessing hundreds of thousands of stories,
and pervaded by Puṣpaka celestial chariots as pure as swans, jasmine, and the moon.
And with the rustling of groves and gardens everywhere ablaze with flowers, a breeze blows, pleasant to the touch and fragrant with camphor. (10.585)
It is filled with rivers, streams, and lakes, adorned with groves of lotus ponds;
it is most delightful, O giver of boons, and most excellent, O woman of excellent complexion. (10.586)
Virahā, O lady of beautiful hips, and Varāhā as the seventh—
these are indeed declared to be the Gaṅgās that always carry one to the world of Rudra.
Adorned with white lotuses having a hundred thousand petals and the like,
with stalks possessing the luster of sapphires and a fragrance that reaches for a hundred yojanas,
those women resemble the autumn moon and are as soft as fresh butter. (10.589)
With beautiful brows, foreheads, and faces; with slender waists and languid with passion; with hair resembling a swarm of bees and fragrant with the scent of musk. (10.590)
With lips resembling pomegranate flowers and fragrant as blue lotuses, with long, pendulous ears like nooses, and with eyes as broad as lotus petals; 10.591.
With shanks like those of an elephant or a deer, arms as delicate as lotus stalks, feet shaped like the tender shoots of the *aśoka* tree, and resembling lotus petals. || 10.592 ||
With claws resembling karketana gems and teeth radiant as pearls,
she was naturally richly fragrant, flowing like nectar itself.
They are always adorned with necklaces, armlets, and bracelets; with clusters of crest-jewels for the parting of the hair; with girdles, bodices, and fine garments; and with flowers.
With forms like water-jars, with full and elevated breasts, with well-rounded and fleshy sides, and with full cheeks that rise high; (10.595)
Adorned with pearl necklaces that hang down, weighed down by the burden of her heavy hips,
she possesses the gait of a royal swan and the movement of an elephant in rut.

With gentle strides faltering as they were made resonant by the tinkling of their anklets, and with the playful charms of laughter, accompanied by graceful movements of the eyebrows and lovely glances; (10.597)
The limbs of the Rudras dwelling there experience great delight;
they are possessed by the seizing-grasp of desire, afflicted by longing, and overwhelmed by intoxication.
By the mere act of worshiping Gaṇeśvara, they are purified;
likewise, other women of this kind, who are distressed by fear of their lovers, [attain the same]. (10.599)
Terrified and fawn-eyed, they came onto their husband's lap;
having covered him with all their limbs, they embraced him with their faces and mouths.
In the world of Citrabhuvana, the daughters of Rudra play, eager with passion;
for Rudras are of such a form, preeminent in the power of knowledge and yoga. (10.601)
With crowns and variegated earrings blazing with great jewels, with armlets, bracelets, and girdles, and with ornaments of flowers and garments. || 10.602 ||
Adorned with necklaces of pearls and upper garments of sacred threads, they possessed massive bodies and broad chests; they had three eyes and held tridents in their hands.
Therein is neither death, nor old age, nor sorrow born of separation;
they sport together with maidens, freed from the fear of saṃsāra.
When their office has expired, all the Rudras, surrounded by the daughters of Rudra,
go to Śiva upon the dissolution of their bodies, reaching the height of Śrīkaṇṭha.
The scent of fear would not arise even in hundreds of millions of eons;
[this is true] by means of such innumerable celestial chariots and vehicles.
It was surrounded by millions of Rudras, mounted upon great bulls and elephants, and riding on lions and horses, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, tens of thousands, and thousands.
In its center was the Sarvatobhadra [palace], with lion-gates and archways,
resembling clear pearls, and surrounded by the summits of its ramparts.
It was surrounded by the hosts of gatekeepers Nandīśvara and Mahākāla,
and adorned with banners and flags resonant with clusters of small bells.
It was adorned with fragments of canopies and umbrellas, with pearl necklaces accompanied by fruits,
enriched with the beauty of bells and chowries, and further embellished with mirrors.
With water-pots placed at the doors, adorned with jewels and sprouts, and with various experts in the diverse sciences, resplendent with well-prepared jewel-dust; || 10.611 ||
The courtyard of the world was adorned with svastikas and lotus petals,
strewn with hundreds of lion thrones, and furnished with altars radiant with jewels.
It was adorned with gate-towers, watchtowers, chariot-paths, and circumambulatory walkways,
featuring most beautiful door-panels variegated with all kinds of jewels.
With exits and windows, with turrets possessing the luster of crystal,
and with pillars and staircases inlaid with diamonds and lapis lazuli.
With forms like the full moon, complete with eggs and peaks, and with spaces radiant as the luster of pearls, the earths were beautifully fashioned.
It was always enriched with the splendor of theaters abounding in the sounds of dance and song,
and adorned with various pavilions and pure assembly halls.
It was filled with throngs of seated Rudras and multitudes of Rudra-maidens,
with lovely, intoxicated elephants, and most beautiful, variegated halls.
It was perfumed with incense sticks, sprinkled with saffron water,
well-covered with variegated cloths, and strewn with heaps of flowers.
With the sounds of trumpets and the cries of "Victory!", and with the filling of kettledrums,
as well as flutes, lutes, mṛdaṅga drums, gomukhas, and mouth-organs.
With the sounds of small drums and cymbals, with the resonance of conchs and kettledrums,
with the booming of dundubhi drums and the joyful shouts of nandighoṣas, and with the sounds of beaten muraja drums.
With the great sounds of slapping their arms and lion-like roars of those who had been defeated, and with the hosts of Gaṇas roaring with a sound like the thundering of clouds. || 10.621 ||
The women were awakened by the sound of bards' hymns, the chanting of the Sāmaveda,
the sounds of *huṃḍukka* drums, laughter, and songs accompanied by the tinkling of ornaments.
With the sound of the bellowing of bulls, the cries of elephants and horses,
and the tinkling of waist-bands and anklets, that great city resounded.
The glorious temple of Śaṅkara himself, which brings about all success, is there;
therein dwells the Blessed Lord Rudra, worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra.
He was constantly bathed in the Gaṅgā, clothed in divine garments,
anointed with rich perfumes upon the earth, and well-honored with flowers by Śrī.
He was praised by Sarasvatī, led by the seven musical notes,
and a parasol like the full moon was established there of its own accord.
Gaṅgā is in Cīrikācchatra, while Dīpāditya is everywhere; his desire is infinite along with the hosts of Puṣpadanta. Kapila, Karkaṭa, Mimarda, and likewise Kaṭaka—
Vikrama, Ṭaka, Niṣkampa, and likewise Niścala. || 10-628 ||
These eight are declared to be the Haras, three-eyed and of immeasurable prowess;
possessing the form of lions and exceeding brilliance, they stand there, fierce and radiant. (10.629)
By means of mantras assuming the form of Śaktis, endowed with yogic sovereignty, accompanied by recent occurrences, and characterized by great enthusiasm and intense strength.
O Rudra, here he is seated upon the auspicious throne, adorned with the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, endowed with all the auspicious marks, and decorated with every ornament. (10.631)
The three-eyed god with ten arms, adorned with a crown of matted locks,
possessing a pair of full breasts and thighs, full shoulders, and mighty arms.
Seated upon a full-blown lotus throne, white as camphor powder, with hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and beautifully adorned with all [divine] weapons. || 10.633 ||
With hands and feet marked by lotuses and possessing great luster,
they were beautifully adorned with divine fingers and moon-like nails.
With well-knit knees and ankles, and feet that are elevated,
he is honored by hosts of Gaṇas and worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra.
