Each one [of them] has a retinue numbering hundreds of thousands of millions;
they sport in divine worlds that are shaped like lotuses.
Beyond that is the principle of Īśvara; hear now of the worlds situated there:
Vītamāya, who is free from impurity (nirañjana) and joined with the eight Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras). 10-1184.
To the one who maintains [the world] and bestows liberation and sovereignty,
his seat is very extensive, measuring a thousand petals.
Three crores and a half crores of mantras abide upon his seat;
he is the Lord, the God established in the Tantra, the bestower of boons, facing in all directions.
Five-faced, of great splendor, ten-armed, and three-eyed;
white as cow’s milk, gentle, and wearing a serpent as a sacred thread.
The god, wearing divine garments, anointed with divine perfumes, complete with all the auspicious marks, and adorned with every ornament. || 10-1188 ||
He is adorned with a crown of matted hair and a moon upon his head, holding a trident in his hand;
his face is serene and lovely, and he bestows the sovereign power of yoga.
He has his hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and he is meditating together with yogins;
upon his lap sits Vidyā, surrounded by all the sciences.
All were complete with every auspicious mark, adorned with all ornaments,
clothed in divine garments, and anointed with divine perfumes.
Adorned with garlands of divine flower-wreaths and strings of pearls, they resemble pearls themselves;
they have five faces and three eyes.
When propitiated according to the prescribed rites, she bestows knowledge upon the wise;
when pleased, she grants supreme sovereignty and liberation.
The gaze upon the face of the Lord appears as if laughing;
therefore, I shall describe the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras), beginning from the east and ending with the Lord [in the north].
Ananta, Sūkṣma, and likewise Śivottama;
Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, and another known as Vidhu. (10–1195)
Śrīkaṇṭha and Śikhaṇḍin are to be known as the Vidyeśvaras in sequence; beyond that is the great station of Rūpa—there, O Rudra, learn from me [the others].

Knowledge of the principles (dharma-jñāna), detachment (vairāgya), and sovereignty (aiśvarya)—these four constitute the subtle veil; above that, they know there are three powers (śakti). || 10-1197 ||
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī are declared to be her powers (śaktis);
indeed, that retinue consists of many millions, beyond all counting.
All the mantras are omnipresent, omniscient, and granters of all desires;
they resemble pure crystal, possess beautiful eyes, and hold tridents in their hands. || 10-1199 ||
Complete with all the primary marks, adorned with every ornament,
fully endowed with all sovereign powers, and crowned with the beautiful crescent moon.
It was filled with various forms resembling hundred-petaled lotuses, possessing the luster of pure pearls and the moon,
shining with diverse jewels, and crowded with ramparts and gateways.
All those authorized by Īśvara sport in the auspicious world;
there they abide with the Lord of Gods, the Sovereign, the Supreme Lord.
Five-faced, possessing great splendor, ten-armed, and three-eyed;
white as cow’s milk, gentle, and wearing a snake as a sacred thread.
The god was wearing divine garments and was anointed with divine perfumes;
his seat was very extensive, measuring ten thousand [yojanas].
Stationed there, impelled by the will of Śiva, he exercises his authority over the Lord, the God who bestows boons and faces all directions.
Having propitiated him, those great-souled ones who, with their senses conquered, practice the divine Pāśupata vow, become fit for all ritual acts.
Through their devotion to ashes, recitation of mantras, and meditation, they go to the state of the Lord;
he exercises his authority as impelled by the will of Śiva.
The ten and five renowned worlds are likewise to be purified;
one should know them to be located in the palate at the time of initiation, O fair-faced one.
Above that is the pure enclosure; therein they know there are two powers, renowned as knowledge and action, and beyond these are the two sciences (vidyās).
The wise know that therein exist two Rudras, namely Bhava-saṃjña and Abhāva;
Tejīśa and Dhruvīśa constitute the supreme state within Pramāṇa.
I shall now describe, in brief, the enclosure of the Praṇava above:
Brahmā, Rudra, Pratoda, and Ananta as the fourth.
Above that is the Suśuddha-āvaraṇa; there they know the triad of Rudras to be Ekākṣa, Piṅgala, and Haṃsa—this has been stated in brief.
Above the Śivāvaraṇa is one [world] known as Dhruva,
situated above the Mokṣāvaraṇa, where Rudrarāja resides.
I shall describe briefly the eleven Rudras who reside there:
Brahmā, Arkka, Diṇḍi, Muṇḍi, and likewise Saurabhaya.
It removes birth and death, and is the bestower of both happiness and suffering;
it is declared to be fully expanded and is situated above the palate.
Furthermore, above that, the auspicious stainless state (nirañjanapada) known as Dhruva should be understood;
it is described in successive order as being above the triad of Īśa and Śakti.
That which is established as being included within what is designated as the power of will (icchā-śakti),
and which has its veil awakened, I shall now describe briefly in the section above.
Prītipramudita, Pramoda, and Pralambana; Viṣṇu, Mandara, Me, Bāhu, Gahana, and Pravita. (10.1218)
The Rudrāṣṭaka has been fully described; it should be understood according to the sequence previously known. Now I shall briefly explain the Samayāvaraṇa above.
Prabhava, Samaya, Kṣudra, Vimala, and Śivapañcaka are proclaimed as the Atodya; beyond that is Nirañjana.
Rudra, Ahaṃkāra, and these five [tattvas] up to Tālu; there are fifty-nine worlds from Jñānaśakti onwards in sequence. (10.1221)
A wise person should purify the syllable *Rudro* at the time of initiation;
each one has a retinue of many thousands, numbering nearly ten million.
All three-eyed, bestowing boons, their forms are of pure power;
resembling pure crystal, they have ten arms and the moon as their crest-ornament.
All of them held tridents in their hands and were adorned with crowns of matted hair;
all were endowed with every virtue, omniscient, and lords over all.
Complete with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament,
they were surrounded by Rudra-maidens of divine and captivating form.
Impelled by the laws of Śiva’s will, they sport with divine worlds;
above that is the realm of Īśvara, and below it is Sadāśiva.
Above that, one should know the enclosure of Suśiva, which is Sadāśiva—the god with fifteen eyes, who has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament. (10–1227)
Endowed with five faces and ten arms, possessing great strength, resembling pure crystal, and radiating blazing splendor. || 10-1228 ||
Seated upon a throne, established atop a white lotus,
accompanied by the five Brahmās as his limbs, and endowed with all the various offerings.
Endowed with the ten Śivas and accompanied by the eighteen Rudras, I shall proclaim the Sakalā and the others to you; first, listen to me.

The whole (sakala), the partless (niṣkala), the void (śūnya), that which is called a digit (kalākhya), the one adorned by space (khamalaṃkṛta), that which abides within destruction and decay (kṣapaṇakṣayamantastha), and the eighth is remembered as the throat-lip (kaṇṭhoṣṭha).
Between the eyebrows, one should know the God of gods, Sadāśiva,
the Lord surrounded by the Sakala and other [forms], in the sequence beginning with Oṃkāreśa.
Oṃkāreśa, Śiva, Dīpta, Kāraṇeśa, Daśeśaka, Suśiva, Kīlīśa, Sūkṣmarūpa, Ambu, and Tejas. (10–1233)
And Śarva is declared as the tenth; they stand established as they were previously situated.
Outside of them is the group of eighteen Rudras; hear their names from me.
Then there was Vijaya, Niśvāsa, Svayaṃbhū, Agnivīryarāj,
Raurava, Makuṭa, and Visaraccandravimbapraśītavān.
Lalitasiddha, Rudra, Santānarudra, Para, Kiraṇa, and Parameśvara. || 10-1236 ||
That which is designated as Sādākhyā is described as possessing all parts (sakala) and being the embodiment of mantra;
it is the presiding cause of all things and the agent of creation and dissolution. || 10-1237 ||
To him, the bestower of enjoyment and liberation upon practitioners who perform the rites,
seventy million mantras are established in his presence.
On the seat [is] the Lord of four crores and ten thousand *lakṣas* of petals,
the All-pervading One, with five faces and three eyes, beginning with the left and so forth.
Surrounded by Tārā and the other Śaktis as previously described, with Jñānaśakti and Kriyāśakti stationed on the left and right sides respectively.
The Supreme Goddess is the power of will (icchāśakti), by whom everything is presided over:
[namely] creation, maintenance, destruction, concealment, and grace.
O Goddess of the gods, she by whom the path-maker always performs all actions is seated upon his lap and is eternally established within his very self.
The desire for power belongs to Śiva, the God of gods, the Supreme Self;
that indeed is the fifth great body of Him who possesses the supreme form.
The glorious Sadāśiva, the God of gods, assumes forms at will;
indeed, those who have been described as his powers (śaktis) are likewise the leaders of the mantras.
O Goddess, each one was surrounded on all sides by hundreds of millions of billions of lotuses,
as well as by peerless and exceedingly powerful beings of corresponding form.
And by means of the Vidyās, such as Surūpā and others, who are endowed with immeasurable qualities, complete with all the auspicious marks, and adorned with every ornament. || 10-1246 ||
With laughter, graceful dances, and the playful movements of their eyebrows,
they shone like ten million moons, as if distilling nectar.
Together with them, the Rudras always sport at will in cities that are auspicious on all sides and possess a radiance equal to ten million moons.
Free from illusory phenomena, stainless and devoid of feverish affliction,
they exercise their authority here with unfailing power as omniscient ones.

Upon the exhaustion of their [karmic] authority, they become peaceful, all-pervading, and auspicious; having attained Śiva, they are no longer impelled by another and do not come into existence again. || 10-1250 ||
O fair-faced one, that is known as the enclosure of Śiva, containing the essence of mantra;
above that is the enclosure of Vidya, [adorned] with [beings] possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
There, a lotus greatly radiant and ten koṭis in extent;
there, seated upon that lotus, is the deity who has transcended peace and possesses great splendor.
Five-faced, large-eyed, ten-armed, and three-eyed,
he possesses the brilliance of a mass of a thousand lightning flashes and is adorned with shimmering rubies.
O lady of excellent vows, cessation, foundation, knowledge, and likewise peace are known as the retinue of that Śāntātīta.
To his left side are situated the Śāntātītās;
they all have five faces, ten arms, and are adorned with the moon. (10.1255)
The principle of the Bindu (bindutatva) is fully described as being surrounded by crores and arbuds [of petals];
above that is the Half-moon (ardhacandra), and above that is the Nirodhikā.
These two, however, are the great stations (mahāsthāna), each endowed with five parts (pañca-kalā): Jyotsnā, Jyotsnavatī, Kānti, Suprabhā, Vimalā, and Śivā. (10.1257)
These indeed reside in the half-moon and are to be restrained; listen, O you of good vows!
They are Rundhanī, Rodhanī, Raudrī, Jñānabodhā, and Tamopahā. (10.1258)
O Goddess, the half-mora is known as the nature of the vowel (kha), which consists of four kalās;
its half is the half-moon, and the eighth is the nirodhikā.
But those gods beginning with Brahmā, O fair-faced one, are subject to cessation;
therefore she is renowned as Nirodhī. Having pierced through her, O fair-faced one—
The fifth, however, is Sādākhya, the Great Body by virtue of its supreme nature;
above that, Nāda is remembered, resembling the pollen of a lotus filament.
It is pervaded by great beings possessing the radiance of ten million times ten thousand suns;
I shall indeed describe their leaders, five worlds in number.
Randhikā, Dīpikā, Rodhikā, and likewise Mociṅkā;
the fifth kalā of Nāda is declared to be Ūrdhvagā.
Upon that [lotus] is a very wide lotus, situated there, extending halfway;
it resembles a mass of moonlight, has five faces, and three eyes.
The god who has the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, ten arms, and a massive body;
who is surrounded by Indikā and others, peaceful, holding a trident in his hand, and wearing matted locks.
His *kalā* moves upward, constantly proceeding along the *suṣumnā*.
Therefore, the realm of *suṣumnā* exists there, and the *suṣumnā* is established therein. (10.1266)
Established there in the Suṣumṇā, he possesses the radiance of ten million moons;
he has ten arms and three eyes, and stands upon a white lotus.
The illustrious one, whose great body consists of the five mantras, has the moon as his crest;
Iḍā and Piṅgalā are situated on the left and the right respectively.
But Suṣumṇā, O lady of excellent hips, is grey like a particle of frost;
the goddess holds a white lotus in her hand and is adorned with a garland of lotuses. (10.1269)
She has five faces, is richly adorned, possesses three eyes, and holds a trident; she should be constantly meditated upon by practitioners and others as seated upon his lap. || 10-1270 ||
All the paths, both downward and upward, are indeed knotted by her;
Nāda, the support of the channels, truly pierces through this entire world.
Having emerged from the lower Śakti and so forth, up to the head by means of the Śakti,
they dissolve into the aperture of Brahmā through the channel as unmanifest sounds and imperishable syllables.
All beings roar [with vitality], being presided over by the power of Śiva;
knowing this, O lady of excellent hips, one should purify them in the sacrifice of Śiva.
Therefore, Brahmavila should be known as being accompanied by ten million and one hundred million Rudras;
there, the supreme Brahmā is to be known, possessing the splendor of a hundred moons.
He has ten arms and three eyes, five faces, and the moon as his crest-jewel;
the Blessed One holds a trident in his hand and is adorned with a crown of matted hair.
Brahmāṇī is indeed the supreme power (parāśakti), who abides on the path of Brahman;
she is the bestower of the path to liberation and is seated upon the lap of Brahmā. || 10-1276 ||
O beloved, having pierced that door which stands obstructing the path to liberation, one must proceed upward, O lady of excellent hips.
Above this, however, resides the Śakti, shaped like a sleeping serpent;
O lady of excellent vows, I shall describe that which is the support of all the worlds.
Sūkṣmā, Susūkṣmā, and likewise Amṛtāmṛtā should be known as being in the center; the remaining [nāḍīs] are to be understood in order from the east onwards.
Having five faces and three eyes, they are possessed of great splendor and immense power;
this has been fully described as the principle of Śakti (Śaktitattva). Now hear from above regarding the principle of Śiva (Śivatattva).
It was surrounded on all sides by many excellent cities,
constructed with golden walls and adorned with jewels and rubies.
I shall describe the worlds endowed with all enjoyments and the arising of all qualities of desire; indeed, they are situated therein.
O Goddess, the fivefold cause— pervasive, of the nature of space, infinite, without master, and uncreated— is established within the principle of Śiva.
Therein is a vast lotus, arising from the infinite and the infinitely infinite;
situated in the center of that lotus is the God of gods, the Unconditioned.
He bears five faces, is peaceful, omniscient, and the supreme lord;
he has ten arms, is greatly radiant, and is the agent of creation and destruction.
To the one who bestows grace upon all, the destroyer of the suffering of those who bow before him,
the giver of worldly enjoyment and liberation, possessing the radiance of ten million billion suns.
The god was adorned all around by the shimmering rubies of his crown;
he wore divine garments and was anointed with divine perfumes.
Seated upon a lotus throne, adorned with a crescent moon as his crest-jewel, encircled by a serpent-couch, and fanned by the waving of chowries. || 10.1288 ||
It is adorned on all sides by many tens of millions, billions, and trillions of Rudras;
it is pervasive, of the nature of space, infinite, and not dependent upon any lord. || 10-1289 ||
They have five faces and great heroism, ten arms, and the moon as their crest;
they possess three eyes, hold tridents in their hands, and are endowed with the [five] causes.
These are established starting from the east and extending to the north;
O Goddess, the imperishable Lord is situated in the center, not [merely] as a residue.
"O Great Goddess, [the powers] are always situated upon his lap, being unattached.
Thus indeed has the Śiva-tattva been described to you, O lady of virtuous vows. (10.1292)
Having purified that, one should then know the supreme power (śakti) above it, which is called Samanā; beyond that, nothing further is recognized.
Having brought all things to completion, they abide as everything from the earth up to Śiva;
they remain established as the agents of all causes.
Many stages of the Lord were presided over by Śiva;
there, the Blessed Śiva, the supreme cause, became firmly established.
O Great Lord, you are the cause and the agent of creation, maintenance, destruction, concealment, and grace; you are the cause of all causes.
That power is indeed called *samanā*; she is known as his instrument (*karaṇa*).
By her, the Lord presides over the fivefold group of causes below.
The instruments of the God who has flowed forth in various ways are themselves not dependent on anything else;
indeed, the Lord of the World impels them further, even though they are without a protector.
The Lord Ananta, who is infinite and whose form is space, awakens the pervasive consciousness; the Great God, whose form is space, is the Sovereign. || 10-1299 ||
The pervasive one is the instrument, and the pervasive lords are the agents;
Māyā, which is of the nature of the agent, stands below, as does Śaśikuṇḍalī.
The effects, such as sound (nāda) and the point (bindu), which constitute the origin of the universe up to the level of Sadāśiva, are all contained within the [elements] ending with earth. (10.1301)
All that should be known as *prākṛta* (evolvent), joined with destruction and origination;
whereas that which is called the supreme power (*parā śakti*) is above the entire path.

Having meditated upon [the deity] who possesses the radiance of a thousand shimmering suns and manifold splendor of rays, the one who knows the ritual procedure should invoke and establish [the deity]. 10-1303.
Then, having performed the ritual service (upacāra), as well as the invocation (āvāhana) of Vāgīśī,
the installation (sthāpana), the worship (pūjana), and likewise the union with the sacrificial victim (paśuyoga).
The holding of the embryo, birth, and likewise the [respective] offices;
yoga, enjoyment, and dissolution, and immediately after that, expiation.

O fair-faced one, having performed the oblation for the lords of the worlds and those who dwell within the worlds, as well as the oblation for the worlds themselves according to the prescribed rule; 10.1306.

Thereafter, one should purify the three principles (tritatva) and the bonds (pāśa) in their proper order; then, having performed the severing of the bonds through dissociation, one should bestow the full oblation (pūrṇā).
Having performed the expiation and consecrated the razor,
the preceptor then cuts the topknot, completes the rite, and bathes the child.
Having sipped water (ācamana) and become purified, one should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa and so forth;
having placed the top-knot (śikhā) at the tip of the sacrificial ladle (sruc), and having offered oblations, one should immediately thereafter perform the bath.
O fair-faced one, having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, the preceptor, having also performed the rite for the disciple, should worship the Śiva-kumbha.
Then one should worship Bhairavāgni, who resides in the central region as Bhairava;
first the *pūrṇā* offering, O Goddess, and thereafter one should contemplate the Śiva-tattva.

Uttering [the mantra] with effort according to the previously described characteristics, O fair-faced one, one should perform the purification of the path of what is to be abandoned by means of exhalation (recaka), as if it were the remainder.
As far as that power of Sumanā extends upward, it is known as Unmanā;
herein there is no movement of time or its divisions, no ontological principle (tattva), and no deities.
Perfect nirvāṇa, the supreme purity—that is called the mouth of the Guru.
Beyond that, O lady of excellent hips, is the supreme reality (paratattva), free from all affliction.
By means of the application of the Guru’s oral instruction, one should unite [the disciple] with the eternal state—
unshakable, beyond causes, stainless, pure, and auspicious.
O sinless one, this path has been declared by me in brief: [it concerns] the omniscient, supreme reality, which is beyond the ether and indeed free from all affliction. (10.1316)
Having thus known this, O Great Goddess, one attains the supreme state—
within the body, within the deity, within the disciple, and indeed within the vessel and the midst of the fire.
Knowing this, one is liberated in the creation of the universe and is able to liberate others.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, concerning the Paths (adhvan), in the *Śrī Tantrasadbhāva*, a great tantra within the Bhairava-stream, belonging to the Seat of Knowledge (vidyāpīṭha) and measuring seventy million verses. 10.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of the Gods, by your grace I have understood the path;
however, O God, the creation of the world was merely indicated by you, not fully described. (11.1)
O Lord, by your grace, let her be known;
for previously, O All-pervading One, the effect, the cause, and the agent were indeed described. (11.2)
Bhairava said: "O lady of noble vows, that which is subtle, the supreme deity, the all-pervading cause, the auspicious Śiva— he indeed has been described to you as the efficient cause."
O lady of excellent limbs, without desire she emits the entire world, both moving and stationary,
by means of her own splendor, effortlessly agitating the sky.
But that is declared to be grasping (upādāna), because it is agitated by the Samaya;
therefore, the Nāda has arisen, as was previously told to you. (11.5)
That [sound] is manifested eightfold in the Lord of Gods through the differentiation of its types:
resonance (ghoṣa), roar (rāva), tone (svana), that which is called the explosion (sphoṭa) of sound, and indeed vibration (dhvani).
The syllable *jhakāra* and *dhvaṃkṛta* are proclaimed as the eight sounds;
the ninth is the Great Sound (*mahāśabda*), which is remembered as pervading them all.
Because he always resounds, being established within all beings, the Lord should indeed be known as Sadāśiva, whose nature consists of vision and action. || 11-8 ||
Arising from *nāda* and *bindu*, it possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns;
it should be known as tenfold, bestowing the fruits of the ten principles (*tattva*).
In ten ways, it exists in the form of phonemes, conjoined with ten deities;
from the *bindu* was born Sadāśiva, conjoined with eight divisions.
He is endowed with the five Brahmakalās and the Śaktis who are the limbs of knowledge;
He is likewise possessed of the five great knowledges and the [five] Mūrtis.
That very same immutable Śiva, the Supreme Self, exists in two forms; he should be known as Śiva, who is devoid of both utterance and non-utterance. || 11-12 ||

That very [deity] is again twofold by way of the nature of mudrā and mantra; furthermore, it is twofold by way of the nature of action and knowledge, and by way of the forms of will and beauty. || 11-13 ||
In the form of the comprehension of sound, yet by its own nature as the essence of reality;
it is gross, subtle, and supreme, and transcending even the supreme, it is without support.
Through the beautiful form of space, as well as through Samana and Unmanā, the Lord of Gods, Śiva—who transcends Unmanā—is to be known in the Śiva Āgama. (11–15)

He should preside over the principle of Śiva, which is the state beyond mind and the seat of the mind; thus, by means of the fivefold causal form, he [the practitioner] becomes that very same reality once again.
O Goddess, one should firmly establish the fivefold cause below;
it is pervasive, situated at the crown of the power (śakti), and unattached at the opening of the aperture.
And Ananta, the Lord of Suṣumṇā, who moves upward beyond the path;
O Great Goddess, he is proclaimed as Bindvīśa, whose form is space. (11.18)
Brahmā himself, remaining established through his own self-abiding power, is called Anāsṛta;
Viṣṇu is called Anātha, and Rudra is indeed Ananta.
Vyomarūpeśvara is proclaimed [as the first], while Sadāśiva is the pervasive one (vyāpin);
furthermore, O Goddess, Hāṭaka is the supreme lord (parameśvara) of the pervasive one.
Endowed with hosts of sciences and mantras, he is the leader of the seven netherworlds;
having the form of space, he resides within the egg of flowers as the leader of the hells.
And he is indeed Ananta, O Goddess of Gods, Rudra whose form is the fire of time; as Ananta in his infinite form, he stands as the sustainer of the paths.
O Great Goddess, the Lord Huhuka stands indeed unsupported;
resting upon his own power, he is unwearied, and by him this Anāsṛta has been sung.
From him, O fair-faced one, the entire world arose as the Unmanifest;
he was established in the waters in the east as Hūhuka, the support of Śakti.
Then, O Lord, immediately after that, the nature of the fire element (āgneya) descends;
likewise, the air element (vāyavya), the subtle elements (tanmātra), and the sense faculties (indriya).
The objects, the mind, and likewise the ego— in this sequence,
O Goddess of Gods— [constitute] the intellectual (bauddha), the secondary (gauṇa), the primordial (prākṛta), and then the personal (pauruṣa).
Niyati, Kāla, Rāga, Vidyā, and likewise Kalā; then the principle of Māyā, followed by Vidyā, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva. (11.27)
In the center of the drop (bindu) is the moon, [and there] is Nairōdhī; [then] the sound (nāda), the Lord of Channels (nādīśvara), and the supreme.
Below that is indeed the aperture of Brahmā (brahmabila), and beyond that is the principle of Power (śaktitatva).
Beyond this, however, is the pervasive [power] conjoined with the five causes;
it consists of Samanā and Unmanā, O Dear One, together with the cosmic eggs of the creative process (prakriyāṇḍa).
O Goddess, such atoms as these are situated everywhere—below, above, and all around—just like the self, in infinite numbers. (11.30)
In this way, indeed, there are countless millions of such cosmic eggs;
by describing just one, all of them are truly described. (11.31)
For just as it is with one, so it is with all;
indeed, O lady of excellent vows, the process of creation resides within all the cosmic eggs (prakriyāṇḍas) in their true form.
Śiva is all-pervasive, subtle, and situated both within and without;
he is endowed with every excellence and is devoid of all causes. || 11-33 ||
Free from creation and destruction, its sphere transcends the phenomenal world;
it is stainless, pure, and peaceful, established neither above nor below.
Just as space has no top, no middle, and no bottom anywhere, so too, O Goddess, is Śiva, the supreme cause, omnipresent. (11.35)
Having pervaded the entire world, it remains like space within spaces;
knowing this, O lady of excellent limbs, one shall not undergo birth again. (11.36)
Furthermore, I shall explain the pervasion of the reasons as it exists;
this very account has indeed been told by me previously. (11.37)
O lady of virtuous vows, Āditya is remembered as Brahmā, and Soma as Viṣṇu;
Rudra is the lord of the planets, and likewise the Lord [Śiva] is the master of the constellations.
O Goddess of the gods, for the sacrificer, Sadāśiva himself is the deity;
Sadyojāta is indeed Brahmā, and Vāmadeva is proclaimed to be Viṣṇu. (11.39)
Aghora is said to be Rudra, as is Tatpuruṣeśvara;
but Aiśāna, O lady of beautiful hips, is the god Sadāśiva himself.
Sadyojāta is the Ṛgveda, Vāmadeva is remembered as the Yajurveda; Aghora is the Sāmaveda, and Puruṣa is said to be the Atharvaveda.
And Īśāna is remembered as the essence of all knowledge belonging to the most excellent one;
O Goddess of gods, worldly knowledge has emerged from Sadyojāta.
The Vādikam [is from] Vāmadeva, while that which has emerged from the inner self of Aghora is the supreme path, O fair-faced one, which has emerged from Puruṣa. (11.43)
The great wisdom known as Samaya has emerged from Īśāna.
Now, O lady of excellent vows, listen again to [the teaching] according to the division of the principles (tattva). 11.44ab.
Brahmā is established pervading the twenty-four principles;
O Goddess of gods, [he extends] from Pradhāna down to Puruṣa, while Janārdana resides in Puruṣa.
Rudra pervades and abides within everything from Niyati up to Māyā;
and the principle of Īśvara is likewise pervaded by that Great-Souled One throughout the sphere of Vidyā.
Above is the god Sadāśiva, who abides pervading everything;
O beautiful one, I shall speak further regarding him through the division of the three principles (tattvas).
Brahmā indeed abides within the principle of the Self (ātmatattva) as far as the limit of Māyā;
likewise, Viṣṇu [abides] within the principle of Knowledge (vidyātattva) as far as the sphere of the Sādākhya.
Likewise, O fair-faced one, Rudra is to be known within the principle of Śiva;
Sādākhya is situated pervading the entire path above.
Indeed, he whose self is presided over by Raudrī becomes Rudra;
by Vāmā he becomes Viṣṇu, and by Jyeṣṭhā he becomes the Grandfather (Brahmā). || 11-50 ||
Brahmā is known as the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), Janārdana as the power of action (kriyā-śakti), and Rudra as the supreme power of will (icchā-śakti); he is celebrated as Śiva.
Viṣṇu, the god Sadāśiva, Brahmā, and Īśvara know him;
and that Lord Sadāśiva, O Goddess, is the manifested sovereign.
From that [Māyā] arises Vidyā, and from that Māyā arises Vidyā;
and then again, by his own will, the Supreme Lord, with the tip of his hand of the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti), [produces] Īśvara. || 11-53 ||
One should emanate seventy million mantras, whose nature consists of knowledge and action;
and these, O observer of good vows, extend from the level of Sādākhya down to the end of the Earth principle.
Abiding in the world, they bestow grace upon embodied beings;
pervaded by the power of Śiva, they possess three eyes and the moon as their crest-jewel. (11.55)
This Śiva, the supreme cause, the wielder of the trident, endowed with *māyā*, stands pervading the universe in manifold ways through the forms of Rudra.

Furthermore, O fair-faced one, having beheld [the world] with his power of knowledge (jñānaśakti), the Lord enters it through his power of will (icchāśakti) and his power of action (kriyāśakti), O lady of excellent vows. (11.57)

The Lord, who is the principle of Māyā, the seed of the universe, eternal and imperishable, simultaneously agitates the group of principles residing within that [Māyā] as well as the group consisting of the self. (11.58)
O Goddess, O eloquent one, like a female elephant struck by a goad, they emerge playfully in every direction—sideways, upwards, and downwards. (11.59)
But those who are vessels for liberation, followed by Śiva,
all go upwards to Śiva, who is supremely pure.
Those who possess knowledge, however, take on the form of mantras;
whereas those who are vessels for saṃsāra are possessed by the impurities of karma and defilement.
They go downwards indeed into that which is terrible and exceedingly cruel;
from that, Kalā was produced, and likewise Vidyā and Rāga.
Time, necessity, the state of being a person, and likewise primordial nature (prakṛti);
as well as goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), and darkness (tamas)—these are the three qualities of primordial nature. || 11-63 ||
Sattva produces illumination; rajas generates activity;
tamas is declared to be obstructive—thus indeed should the three qualities be understood. (11.64)
In the state of *sattva*, Brahmā is proclaimed; in *rajas*, Viṣṇu; and in *tamas*, Rudra.
In the nature of Brahmā, he creates the worlds; in the nature of Viṣṇu, he is the cause of their maintenance.
In his state as Rudra, he should withdraw the entire world, both moving and unmoving;
waking, dreaming, and deep sleep are the three states belonging to the Great Lords.
From the qualities (guṇas), Intellect (dhiṣaṇā) is born, endowed with various states of existence;
Brahmā is established there within the principle of intellect (buddhitattva) as its presiding lord.
They call him omniscient, the supreme state of all awakenings, the foremost among those endowed with qualities and Arhats, and the preeminent among the proponents of the Vedas. (11.68)

O Goddess of gods, the supreme state is the twenty-sixth principle according to the Pauruṣa system of the Sāṃkhyas, as well as for those who know the Pañcarātra, and according to the Yoga scriptures. (11.69)
In the Pāśupata vow, the imperishable state of Īśvara is proclaimed;
and in the Mausala and Kāraka [vows], the principle of Māyā is celebrated.
Kṣemīśa is the lord of Brahmā; that is their supreme state. Tejīśa is indeed the lord of the impurities, and his station is fixed in the authoritative measure.
Those whose selves are purified by the knowledge of initiation remain until the end of the body;
having undertaken the vow of the skull, they go each to their own station.
The supreme state of the Śaivas is entirely liberated from all temporal paths.
O Dear One, from the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva), the ego (ahaṅkāra) is born again in three ways.
It is proclaimed as being sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa;
it exists in three ways as the bhūtādi, the vaikṛta, and the taijasa.
From Bhūtādi, the subtle elements (tanmātra) arise; from those, one who understands the elements [knows they come] forth. But from Vaikārika, the five organs of action are born.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—
these five are declared to be the subtle elements (tanmātras) in their proper order.
From sound, space is produced; likewise, from touch, wind is produced;
from form, fire is produced; and from taste, water arises. (11.77)
From fragrance, however, earth was born; this has been briefly described to you. Indeed, the mind and the sense organs arise from the fiery elements (tejas). || 11.78 ||
The mind is said to consist of fear; it pervades all the sense organs.
Due to the metaphorical designation of "self," I shall describe its tenfold divisions.
O beautiful goddess, the Self (ātman), the inner self (antarātman), the outer self (bāhyātman),
the selfless (nirātman), and the supreme self (paramātman) are proclaimed to be fivefold.
Arbuda, and Arbuda again, as well as Buddhyamāna; Prabuddha and Suprabuddha—I shall describe them to you once more. (11.81)
O Goddess, when one is established in that state which is equal to primordial nature (pradhāna) and entirely devoid of pleasure and pain, then he is called the Self (ātman). (11.82)
Due to its association with the city of eight, the inner self wanders through higher wombs; it should be known as that which is bound by good and evil deeds. (11.83)
Endowed with the organs of intellect and action, and enveloped by the five elements, it then experiences the objects of the senses through the support of the intellect, O Goddess. (11.84)
Freed from the state of being a living entity, abandoned by the portion of the true dharma, his self is joined solely with impurity and karma, obscured by the nature of māyā. || 11-85 ||
Then that soul of hell should be known as the Supreme Self; I declare this to you when it becomes completely liberated from impurities, karma, kalās, and the like. (11.86)
Having transcended all time and likewise abandoned the delusion of illusion,
one then attains stainlessness, the supreme and imperishable state.
Then, O Goddess, the immutable Lord is called Paramātman;
furthermore, O Goddess, I shall describe Arbuda to you in brief. (11.88)
When the dissolution of the self consisting of the principles has occurred, within the scope extending from the limited powers (kalā) down to the earth (kṣiti),
the Supreme Lord, having indeed withdrawn [all things] during the night of equilibrium that is Māyā, [remains].
One should remain free from activity until the dawning of the Lord, [thereby ending] the karma of the group of selves that experiences pleasure, pain, and so forth. (11.90)
O fair-faced one, when the mind has become subtle through sleep, its consciousness, spatial orientation, and activity are obstructed; it perceives neither sound and other objects nor the Self.
O beloved, it does not discern its cause, nor its own place;
for all this it does not know, since the functions of its senses have been lost.
The unawakened remains there as long as the illusions headed by "I" persist;
that is declared to be the unawakened state, so now learn from me what the awakened state truly is.
When the time for ripening has arrived, action, drawn forth by the will of the Lord,
assumes a manifest form, just as the sun assumes its appearance at dawn.
In this manner, the Lord likewise favors his own selves through the instrument [of the senses]:
with consciousness awakened by *kalā* and the field of experience revealed by *vidyā*. (11.95)
Passion (rāga), by virtue of its coloring nature, is characterized as the bliss derived from sense objects;
time (kāla) indeed constantly differentiates [existence], beginning from the moment of birth until the dissolution of the universe. (11.96)
One should understand that destiny is fixed and eternal, joined with good and evil;
it yields not even a thousandth part of an atom more than what is ordained.
Having attained the state of masculinity, one should indeed invoke the two puruṣas within reality;
"pura" is said to be pradhāna, which is accumulated through manifold manifestations.
Because he fills that city, he is indeed known as Puruṣa;
therein the Lord Śrīkaṇṭha [resides], while the bound soul (paśu) exists through destiny and karma.
One should envelop [the soul] with the net of the primary bonds (pradhānapāśa) in ten heaps;
the aged [soul] is bound by the triple bond through the intellect (buddhi), which is indeed an instrument (karaṇa).
Enclosed by the firm bonds of the subtle elements and the sense organs, thus bound, he indeed wanders through the realm of the earth of Māyā and the other principles. (11.101)
Therefore, he is called a transmigrator (saṃsārī) because he wanders through saṃsāra again and again;
when objects such as sound and the rest exist for him, then he is an enjoyer of objects (viṣayī). || 11-102 ||
They say that objects are the primary [cause], spreading out through various distinctions;
one experiences them through the ripening of names and karma, being permeated by their nature. (11.103)
Because he indeed enjoys in this manner, he is called the enjoyer;
O lady of excellent hips, in that field, those who know it are like a farmer. || 11.104 ||
Beholding the desire of the mind, one ploughs with the ploughshares of greed;
through the state of delusion, the mental, vocal, and physical [faculties] are drawn toward the north-western direction.
Having scattered everywhere the seed consisting of merit and demerit,
from that arises the sprout of the gods and the emergence of the fruits of pleasure and pain.
Watered by passion and drenched with the water of desire, it grows in whatever place, toward whatever recipient, and at whatever age. (107)

The wise one understands that the seed of the auspicious and the inauspicious spoken of there will bear fruit at its time; one experiences its various forms according to the power of prior karma. (11.108)
Because he knows in this way, he is called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña);
because he perceives objects, he is celebrated as the Intellect (buddha). || 11-109 ||
When a person meditates upon that very same [reality] in the form of the *ariṣṭa* (the sign of death), being greatly delighted, I shall now explain it to you. (11.110)
Then one should feel disgust for enjoyments, whether auspicious or inauspicious;
he who would despise what is artificial, I consider him to have taken refuge in dispassion.
From the realm of Māyā down to the earth, one perceives as a magical illusion sons, friends, wives, well-wishers, kinsmen, and relatives. (11.112)
Whatever wealth has been acquired by me, whether through auspicious or inauspicious means, all those who are well-disposed toward me enjoy it without hesitation and without anxiety. (11.113)
And I alone shall go to the abode of Yama;
these [relatives] are indeed not auspicious to me, for they are enemies who cause harm.
One should always feel revulsion even for one's own body, which is produced from semen and blood and is defiled by the serpents of the sense objects. (11.115)
How can I find delight in this world, which is crowded with various diseases and agitated by the fear of old age and death? || 11-116 ||
With a mind constantly anxious, he reflects again and again:
"How might liberation come about from this cycle of existence so difficult to transcend? (11.117)
Thus, one who is awakening and intent upon the propitiation of the Guru is declared to be "awakening" (buddhyamāna); now I shall describe to you the "fully awakened" (prabuddha).
O Goddess of the gods, having received initiation in the sacrifice of Śiva through the grace of the Guru,
when one contemplates, O Goddess, the Śaiva knowledge of great exaltation— || 11-119 ||
With the eye of knowledge, one perceives the entire range of existence— from Śiva down to the earth— in its true nature, like a myrobalan fruit held in the palm of the hand.

Having abandoned everything that is to be discarded and having taken up the supreme Śiva— the all-pervading, omnipresent, and imperishable Lord who extends to the end of Unmanī, O lady of excellent hips— 11–121.
Thus awakened, O Goddess of gods, absorbed in that and devoted to that,
and liberated from all undertakings, one is then called awakened.
Now hear from me concerning the "Awakened" (prabuddha) and the "Well-Awakened" (suprabuddha):
[they are attained] through initiation, knowledge, yoga, or indeed through auspicious conduct. (11–123)
When one has attained the supreme state— which transcends time, is free from affliction, unshakable, beyond causes, omniscient, and facing in all directions— || 11-124 ||
He is indeed eternally satisfied in mind, perfectly awakened, independent, and ever-present; his power and majesty are never diminished, and he is the perpetually awakened, eternal one.
When the self is indeed joined to that [state] and endowed with its qualities, it is called "perfectly awakened," according to the word of Bhairava. (11–126)
Now I shall describe the divisions of the states (bhāva), O fair-faced one;
the thirteenth is the instrument (karaṇa), and the object (kārya) is tenfold, O beloved.
The destruction of the eleven faculties constitutes the threefold ego-sense (ahaṃkāra);
the intellect (buddhi) is eightfold, and error (viparyaya) is fivefold. || 11-128 ||
I shall state the names of the others in their respective order by way of classification:
the five elements, the subtle elements (tanmātras), and the tenfold effects are thus considered.
The five organs of perception, the organs of action, and the ten external instruments;
the mind, ego, and intellect are known as the threefold internal instruments. (11.130)
Muteness, lameness of the throat, as well as the state of being unable to discharge [semen], should be known as joylessness, and likewise as externalization. (11.131)
Indeed, there is the decay of the limbs as well as blindness itself;
furthermore, there is the absence of taste, the absence of smell, and instability of the mind. (11.132)
These eleven are declared to be the destructions of the senses in their respective order;
and previously, O lady of excellent complexion, the threefold ego (ahaṃkāra) was described to you.
Tamas, moha, mahāmoha, tāmisra, and likewise andhatāmisra—these are said to be the five types of error (viparyaya). || 11-134 ||
These eight qualities, beginning with Dharma, are proclaimed as the supreme;
these fifty varieties of states (bhāva-bheda) have been fully described in their proper order.
Furthermore, there are eight divisions of bondage known as dharma and the rest;
I shall now describe how their subdivisions are differentiated.
That [bondage], however, binds sevenfold for men on the path of saṃsāra; but the Sāṃkhya liberates those whose selves delight in knowledge by means of the state of knowledge. (11.137)

Knowledge is declared to be of the nature of sattva; the other three are remembered as being of the nature of rajas, while those beginning with unrighteousness (adharma) are of the nature of tamas—thus, O fair-faced one, there are four. (11.138)
Dharma is said to be tenfold, and knowledge is traditionally remembered as eightfold;
dispassion is ninefold, and they know sovereignty to be eightfold.
And these very same qualities, when inverted, are proclaimed to be unrighteousness (adharma):
namely, freedom from anger, service to the teacher, purity, contentment, and straightforwardness. (11.140)
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and freedom from guile—this tenfold dharma has been described, O fair-faced one. (11.141)
Tāra, Sutāra, Taraṇa, Tārayant, Pramodaka, Pramudita, Ramyaka, and likewise Sadāpramudita. || 11-142 ||
This knowledge has been fully explained as eightfold, O Supreme Goddess;
[the others are] Ambhā, Salilā, Oghā, and likewise the one known as Vṛṣṭi, and the others.
Sutārā, Supārā, Sunetrā, Paramāmṛtā, Aṣṭamātrasumārī, and likewise Uttamāmbhasikā. || 11-144 ||
I have indeed described to you ninefold detachment,
as well as the powers of atomization (aṇimā), levitation (laghimā), magnification (mahimā), and attainment (prāpti).
Likewise, there is the power of irresistible will (prākāmya), lordship (īśitva), and supreme mastery (vaśitva);
the eighth is proclaimed as the power of bringing all actions under one's control (sarvakarmavaśāyitva). || 11-146 ||
O beloved, I have described the eightfold sovereignty as divided into eight types:
anger, lack of service toward the guru, and likewise impurity. (11.147)
Lack of contentment, dishonesty, violence, and untruthfulness, as well as theft, unchastity, and likewise cruelty—these are [the vices]. (11.148)
Thus, O Supreme Goddess, non-dharma is proclaimed to be tenfold: Sutāra, Asutāra, and likewise Ataraṇa, O Dear One; || 11-149 ||
O Goddess of Gods, that which carries one across is proclaimed as the fourth;
they likewise know it as Apramoda, Pramudita, and Aramya. (11.150)
Thus, non-existence and constant joy are indeed ignorance in its eightfold form:
Araṃbhā, Salila, Anaugha, and likewise Avṛṣṭi.
Asutāra, Asupāra, Sunetra, and Mataḥpara;
Asumāra is also to be known, as well as Uttamāmbhasika. (11.152)
These nine varieties are proclaimed as belonging to one who lacks dispassion (avairāgya).
They are known as the absence of *aṇimā*, *laghimā*, and *mahimā*. (11.153)
Non-attainment and lack of desire, as well as lack of mastery; likewise lack of control and total lack of autonomy. (11.154)
Thus, lack of sovereignty is proclaimed to be eightfold;
for these states, beginning with lack of sovereignty, are presided over by the Piśācas and other such beings.
I shall describe to you how these eight alone are established in their respective order:
lack of sovereignty in the Piśāca [state], and lack of dispassion in the Rākṣasa [state].
In the Yakṣa [Veda] there is knowledge, and likewise in the Gāndharva there is dharma;
in the Aindra there is dharma, and in the Saumya knowledge is established.
In the realm of Prajāpati, there is detachment and the sovereignty of Brahmā is established;
that is proclaimed as the sixty-four-fold group within the station of Brahmā.
The sovereignty of fifty-six qualities is established in the realm of Prajāpati;
that of forty-eight qualities is proclaimed as belonging to Soma. (11.159)
The sovereignty of Mahendra is said to possess forty qualities, O Goddess of the gods; the sovereignty of the Gandharvas is said to possess thirty-two qualities. || 11-160 ||

The power of the Yakṣas is remembered as twenty-fourfold, and that of the Rākṣasas as sixteenfold; such is the sovereignty established among the divine classes of beings, O observer of excellent vows.
Another exists in the divine wombs in a sevenfold form;
these very same [qualities], when thoroughly intermingled, are established among human beings.

O beloved, I shall describe the pervasion of the three qualities (guṇas) as they exist, established from the primary elements down to the level of immobile beings according to their distinctions. (11.163)
The gods, beginning with Brahmā and ending with Indra, do not preside over the *satva* [element];
nor do the *gandharvas*, *yakṣas*, *anujas*, *daityas*, and *rākṣasas*. (11.164)
Yātudhānas and Piśācas are proclaimed to be ascetics (tāpasa); those sages of firm vows, characterized by a predominance of rajas and sattva, are to be known [as such]. (11.165)
Established upon the earth, they mutually overcome one another;
likewise, stationary beings and those that crawl are pervaded by extreme darkness.
O fair-faced one, those devoid of hands and feet and characterized by darkness (tamas) are to be known as beginning with the reptiles and ending with the beasts; thus they are proclaimed. (11.167)
Indeed, these others are non-mantric, and their wombs are truly infinite;
among human beings as well, there are endless divisions established in infinite variety. || 11.168 ||
Indeed, it is impossible to describe your powers due to the infinite variety of their manifestations;
however, in the world of humans, only qualities such as dharma and the like are established.
O you of virtuous vows, I shall explain to you how the various types of knowledge are bound to dharma and so forth, and how the womb is pervaded by adharma and so forth. (11.170)

And as for the treatises on logic (*hetuśāstra*) in this world, which mock what is eternal and what is non-eternal, they are determined by the transformations of debates, chatter, and fallacies. (11.171)
O observer of good vows, those [teachings] are devoid of the cause, obscure regarding nirvāṇa, empty of reality, lacking the yoga of knowledge, and bereft of the deity. (11.172)
In this regard, no certainty arises concerning dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
these [beings], increased by ignorance, take recourse to what is non-dharma. (11.173)
Those men who take delight therein lead others to hell;
lacking detachment and mastery, those men suffer in hell. (11.174)
O lady of excellent limbs, these four always bestow suffering in hell;
since they cause delusion for all living beings, they are considered to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
O Goddess of the gods, worldly knowledge is bound by Dharma alone;
likewise, the Pāñcarātra and the Vedic systems are bound by both Dharma and Jñāna.
O you of excellent vows, the Buddhist and the Arhat teachings are both characterized by a single detachment;
and the Sāṃkhya knowledge, O you of excellent vows, is bound to both knowledge and detachment. (11.177)
Knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty are established in the knowledge of yoga; it has transcended the states of the intellect and is established in the path of wisdom. || 11-178 ||
Therefore, that knowledge which transcends the world is called "beyond the path" (atimārga).
Furthermore, those in the world are said to be bound souls (paśu) on the path of creation and dissolution. (11.179)
Among them, those who are established on the path of liberation (atimārga) are to be known as having passed away;
these include the Kāpālikas and likewise the Pāśupatas.
For them, no further creation exists once they have reached the eternal Lord;
therefore, they will attain liberation, which is the cause of non-rebirth.
Furthermore, for worldly beings there is only repeated creation and repeated dissolution;
mounted upon the wheel of saṃsāra, they revolve like a waterwheel. (11.182)
O lady of excellent vows, the eight-spoked wheel is endowed with the spokes of Dharma and the rest;
it is presided over by Sovereignty, O Goddess, and struck by the rod of Necessity. (11.183)
Pierced by the power of impure karma, one wanders with the speed of time;
men are attached to these worldly goals and the like. (11.184)
Those who rely on treatises of logic, as well as others who perform evil deeds—all of them, being deluded, do not see the end of this wheel. (11.185)

Whatever goals are to be accomplished among worldly and other matters within the scope of the Atimārga and its limits—all these one should accomplish with ease through the Śaiva knowledge of great prosperity. (11.186)
Indeed, that which is exceedingly pure is not accomplished by all [means],
O Goddess, because it resides in the supreme state, the absence of the Lord of Yoga.
It is non-existence beyond cultivation, a sphere transcending conceptual proliferation, free from mind, intellect, and the like, and devoid of causal discourse. || 11-188 ||
And by means of direct perception and other valid cognitions, [one realizes] the Lord who is beyond time, imperishable,
all-pervading, omnipresent, tranquil, stainless, and free from all afflictions.
For this consists of all powers; it is beyond the paths, infinite, and without beginning;
it is liberated from all excelling qualities and devoid of beginningless existence.
That supreme primordial wisdom is remembered as transcending the state of all-knowingness;
thus, O fair-faced one, have the principles and the forms of knowledge been created. (11.191)
By these principles, the entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, has been emitted—
variegated worlds by the hundreds and thousands.
The various scriptures situated within the reality, as well as specialized knowledge, the *huḍukka* [instrumental music], the arts, and the characteristics of the awakening to supernatural powers.
Through the initiation of Śiva, the entire process should be seen within the principles (tattvas);
for whatever exists, O Dear One, may it be attained through these very principles. (11.194)
There is no liberation equal to initiation; there is no ritual action higher than that of the Mātṛkā;
there is no knowledge superior to the Prakriyā; and there is no yoga that does not characterize [the goal]. (11.195)
All that, O Goddess, has been told in the great ocean of Śaiva knowledge;
through this knowledge, the yogi becomes free from creation and destruction. (11.196)

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "Emanation," in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, a great tantra within the Bhairava-stream belonging to the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), measuring seventy million verses. 11.
Bhairava said:
The creation of the principles has been explained by me in great detail;
now, however, I shall again speak of their dissolution according to the proper sequence.
For one who is free from disease, youthful, healthy, and young in spirit, I perceive the solar [light] indeed flowing effortlessly through the stream of the path of play. (12.2)
From the solar [lineage] the paternal [lineage] is to be known; one should discern the divine through the ancestors.
And from the divine, the supreme is to be known—thus should it be understood by the wise. (12.3)
Listen to how it occurs through the sequential application of *tuṭi* and the other units:
sixty *tuṭis* are declared to constitute one *ḍhaka*. (4)
By means of those [breaths], sixty are to be clearly understood and diligently observed;
this is declared as the well-known "sixty," which is prescribed as the very breath itself.
Sixty *tuṭis* are said to be formed by sixty flows of breath;
having reached the *dvādaśānta* from there, there occurs a return.
Thus, O beautiful one, the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) has been described to you;
sixty tuṭis are declared to be a lava, and a nimeṣa is equal to that.
Sixty nimeṣas are prescribed as one kāṣṭhā;
sixty kāṣṭhās are known as a kalā, and sixty of those are prescribed as a tatpara.
Gālava is said to be twice that [number];
sixty Gālavas are declared to be a *vipruṣ* (a drop). || 12-9 ||
Likewise, sixty *vipruṣas* are declared to be one *pala*;
and sixty *palas* are said to constitute one *kalā*. (12.10)
Two *kalās* indeed constitute a *muhūrta*, and a *yāma* consists of half a *cayā*; four *yāmas* make up a day, and the night is equal to that. (12.11)
O Great Goddess, a day has indeed been described, of this there is no doubt;
fifteen days constitute a fortnight, and two fortnights are said to make up a month.
Two months are to be known as one season (ṛtu), and three seasons constitute a solstice (ayana). Two solstices are proclaimed to be a year (vatsara). || 12-13 ||
The Kṛta age is proclaimed to consist of seventeen million and twenty-eight thousand years.
The Tretā age has likewise been fully described; its measure is declared by the wise to be twelve hundred thousand and ninety-six thousand [years]. (12–15)
Eight hundred thousand and sixty-four thousand [verses] have been declared;
this is specified as the total measure of the Dvāpara age.
Four hundred and thirty-two thousand [verses] are recorded;
this is the measure for the Kali age, which has reached a unification of all the scriptures.
Furthermore, the solar cycle of four yugas is declared by those who know it to consist of three hundred and forty-two thousand [years]. (12.18)
Seventy-one cycles of the four yugas are declared by the wise to constitute a single year;
this is said, O lady rich in austerity, to be the lifespan of the lord of the gods during a manvantara.
A single day of the Lotus-born [Brahmā] consists of fourteen days of the lords of the gods; his night is of equal duration.
Such a period is a Great Kalpa (mahākalpa), which brings about the destruction of the three worlds as they exist.
Thus has the solar [reckoning] been fully explained; now I shall describe the ancestral (paitṛka).
O lady of auspicious gaze, there are two fortnights (pakṣa) which are declared to be white and black.
O Supreme Goddess, that [period] should be known as a day and night of the ancestors (paitṛya);
in this same sequence, there are fortnights, months, and likewise seasons.
From the solstice, one reaches the year according to the division of the four yugas;
by this very sequence, the measurement of those who speak according to the scriptures is established.
O fair-eyed one, by the very measure of the divine path,
it is four thousand times the divine measure.
The twilight period (sandhyā) shall consist of four hundred [years], and the transitional period (sandhyāṃśa) shall be equal to that;
for each of the ages, Tretā and Dvāpara, they shall be three times as long, while in the Kali age they shall be one-fourth.
O Goddess, these have been declared as being less than the full measure;
at the end of those four yugas, they are proclaimed to be a single kalpa.
Furthermore, O sinless one, the origin of human beings has been fully described,
as well as that of the gods, occurring during the day of Brahmā.
The duration of the day has been fully explained, and the night is likewise the period of withdrawal;
thus, O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, have I spoken in brief. (12.28)
By this sequential yoga and by this measurement, the lotus-born shall live for a hundred years, and then he shall indeed withdraw [them] once again.
Reaching as far as the edge of the Kālāgni ocean, he split the cosmic egg into two halves;
the fierce powers of the Kālāgni are capable of withdrawing the three worlds.
Likewise, intense [flames] fall upon Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Dharmarāja;
hundreds of thousands burn as the self-power of Kālarudra.
The Nāṭyas, Ārka, Sāgara, and Śaila worlds constitute the station of Janaloka;
there, the Rudras headed by Kūṣmāṇḍa enter the imperishable state.
It is groundless to say that this wheel revolves day and night when the Great Enjoyer has dissolved into the qualities, which are themselves superior qualities. (12.33)
The egg of the supporter dissolves into water; the water also attains the state of fire;
the fire goes into the wind; and the wind enters the domain of space.
This dissolution is to be understood as occurring at the end of Pradhāna, proceeding in the reverse order of creation;
having entered Śrīkaṇṭha, the manifest [universe] trembled again and again.
O dear one, when Śrīkaṇṭha reaches the supreme state within the covering of your speech,
and Ananta has attained infinity, the wheel of Māyā ceases to revolve.
All things ending in knowledge surely proceed toward the supreme, which is beyond all birth;
yet states that are higher than the supreme do not go beyond the supreme.
Thus has the agent been described by me; Śrīkaṇṭha, whose body is composed of mantras, having performed his own office, dissolves into the eternal state.
When one hundred Brahmās have perished, that shall become a single day of Viṣṇu;
from that day come the fortnight, then the month, the season, the solstice, and the year.
He shall live for a hundred years, and then I create him again;
after a hundred destructions of Viṣṇus, there occurs one day of Rudra.
Śrīkaṇṭha, the supreme Rudra, is established in the position of authority;
the Supreme Lord exercises his authority for more than a hundred years.
O Dear One, all that belongs to the sphere of speech— whatever exists whatsoever— is entirely and without exception dissolved within the lower casket of Māyā.
This is the summary of the path for those who abide within the sphere of Māyā;
they are all dissolved by Māyā, their physical forms withdrawn by their own power.
Thus has the great dissolution been described by the Lord Śambhu;
indeed, that infinite Supreme Lord shall create once again in this same manner.
The omniscient Lord, the creator of all, is the sovereign over both restraint and grace; all the sciences, empowered by the *kalās*, have their consciousness known by him.

Those whose selves are colored by passion and the like, joined with the faculties of the intellect, arrive in succession and experience [their results], being well-perfumed by their prior latent impressions (vāsanā). || 12-46 ||
By the force of residual past impressions, gods, sages, humans, serpents, and likewise rākṣasas, experience the fruit born of their karma. (12.47)
The Asuras, the Pitṛs, the Yakṣas, the worlds, and likewise the Kalās;
the principles (tattvas), the words (padās), the mantras, and whatever else exists—|| 12-48 ||
The infinite Supreme Lord, the God, creates all that;
he is surrounded by Vidyeshas and others, and is the proclaimer of the wheel of knowledge (vidyācakra).
The Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas), beginning with Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin, are of subtle form;
all of them have been consumed by the fire [of the dissolution], while the remaining ones are the activators of the wheel.
At the end, they gradually attain liberation from the impurity of their office;
while performing their own duties, do these [beings] abandon that which arises from Māyā, being impermanent? || 12-51 ||
O Supreme Goddess, those who abide in the wheel have gone to the supreme abode;
likewise, the seventy million vidyās have been surrounded by the Parameṣṭhin.
Among them, O lady of excellent limbs, their authority has been established;
O Goddess, there are millions of them today who act as planetary influences among mortals.
By virtue of their remaining entitlements, they gradually attain liberation;
O beloved, there are another sixty million [beings] who are enveloped by their own bodies.
Having ceased from their respective offices, they possess bodies of pure capacity;
O Goddess, worshipped by the gods, the station of those [energies] within the principle of Vidyā has thus been described. (12.55)
And for those intent on the propitiation of the Rudra-mantras for the sake of enjoyment,
who are incapable of non-dual practice, [this is prescribed] for those whose souls are devoted to the conduct of the Tantras.
For those who have entered the path of enjoyment (bhukti), enjoyment is proclaimed;
they attain the qualities beginning with atomization (aṇimā) and are endowed with the six colors.
That enjoyment is that supreme state; for its sake, there is reverence for the *golaka*.
O one of great fame, what is called enjoyment is the supreme state, the reality (*tattva*) of knowledge.
And in the absence of [dualistic] cognitions, how could enjoyment be prescribed?
[Rather, there is] supreme bliss accompanied by joy, immutable and free from egoism. (12.59)
It is pure speech, a delight to the mind, imperishable, undecaying, eternal, the supreme state, characterized by being the enjoyer of all experiences. (12.60)

O lady of excellent complexion, enjoyment exists through the very nature of knowledge and not otherwise; O fair-faced one, neither worldly enjoyment nor liberation belongs to those devoid of knowledge.
Initiation with seed (sabījikā) is taught for the purpose of attaining enjoyment;
but in the absence of that which is to be enjoyed, how could there be an initiation that is proclaimed as "with seed"? (12.62)
Therefore, for the sake of the enjoyment of that [enjoyment], the principle of Vidyā was proclaimed by the Supreme Lord, the wise God Ananteśa. (12.63)
Knowledge acquired for the sake of enjoyment serves as a cause for the experience of living beings;
yet, when purified by the King of Knowledge, those [powers] become perfected and exceedingly powerful.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Conclusion of the Sacrifice," in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, a great tantra within the Bhairava stream belonging to the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), comprising seventy million verses. 12.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, tell me of initiation in the great sacrifice of nine naves, presided over by the Ninefold Self (Navātman) and divided according to the nine principles (tattvas)."
The division of initiation into the *padas* was indeed explained by you in the past through the *padas* possessing superior qualities; sixty-four Bhairavas were thus enumerated. (13.2)
Tell me of that which is called Padavidyā, and that which is remembered as Rudraśakti; speak of her who is the mother of all, and the auspicious procedure for her meditation.
"Tell me the names according to the division of eight groups of eight.
Bhairava said:
"Listen, O Goddess, for I shall proclaim that which I have been asked by you. (13.4)

The division of the individual syllables as they are situated within the nine-naved [mandala], and the letters of the King of Vidyās which are characterized by the number nine—[these are described here]. (13.5)
I shall now describe to you their arrangement according to their distinct divisions:
having constructed a city with nine central hubs, its ground resembling a nine-petalled lotus.
O beloved, the wise one should divide the thread from south to north into nine sections, seven parts, and nine knots plus one, for the sake of peace and security. 13-7.
O Śaṅkarī, one should draw the groups of Vidyās and Mantras according to the division of their words within forty-nine squares using a single thread.
O Great Goddess, having drawn a lotus measuring thirty-two finger-breadths in the central square, one should divide it into four parts.
In the first part is the pericarp; in the second, the filaments;
in the third, the joints of the petals; and in the fourth, the tips of the petals.
Having drawn eight lines in the cardinal directions and likewise in the intermediate directions,
one should rotate four circles, each measuring four finger-breadths.
Having first prepared one petal with two lines for each direction using saffron, the wise man should prepare the others in exactly the same way.
Having drawn twenty-four filaments,
one should place a very beautiful circular line at the tip of each petal.
At its center, a square should be constructed according to the correct proportions;
having first established the Brahma-line while the sun is at the equinox.
O Dear One, one should establish a cord extending from east to west using a śaṅkulā;
it should measure twelve aṅgulas, and one should fix another śaṅkulā at its center.
One should rotate the cord, measuring sixteen finger-breadths, in the northeast; the shadow cast in the forenoon should be marked well at its position in the afternoon. (13–16)
O Dear One, one should mark the east with the sun situated in the west;
one should mark the northern direction with the pole star (dhruva) or with a fish-figure.
Then one should draw an eight-petalled lotus with a pericarp,
having taken up two squares each, marked by the number eight.
Having placed the remainder, O lady of beautiful hips, by means of the single-interval arrangement,
one should draw eight lotuses in the directions and write the doors on the exterior.
O Goddess, one should fashion the *śobhā* measuring half a *vīśī*; both *śobhās*, extending from that point, should be drawn as far as the edge of the *kapola*. (13–20)
Likewise, one should fashion the throat; this is proclaimed as the gateway.
Through the division of eight gateways, the city is known as having nine naves (navanābha). || 13-21 ||
Having bathed according to the rule, O Goddess, one should then enter the sacred ground;
there, one should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa and the other rites by means of the procedure previously described. (13.22)
Then, O Goddess, one should worship Bhairava, the supreme Śiva;
having offered a seat with the *praṇava* (OM), O lady of excellent complexion, ending with the word "sarva. (13-23)
In the center, one should worship the god Bhairava, the Supreme Lord,
according to the previously mentioned procedure, accompanied by the six limbs.
One should place the syllables on the eight petals in order, starting from the east and ending with the northeast;
Sadāśiva is represented by the letter *ha*, and so forth, O fair-faced one. (13–25)
One should know that this extends to the end of the *prakṛti*; in the middle, there is the conceptualization of the Lord of the Seat (*pīṭheśa*).
One should worship the eight goddesses situated upon the pericarp within the lotuses of the directions. (13–26)
Having worshipped Bhairava in that place, one should purify the remaining phonemes in due order, from Prakṛti up to Śiva, O beautiful goddess. (13.27)
Beginning from the northeastern direction, one should purify the central pedestal;
one should unite it with the supreme reality, Śiva, the ultimate cause. (13.28)
In this manner, one should purify the worlds sequentially according to their colors and mantras;
then, one should complete the ritual of the *kalās* from Kālāgni up to Śiva.
Then, one should place the eight Bhairavas upon the eight petals,
distributed in groups of eight, starting from the east and ending in the northeast.
O Goddess, one should place the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) there upon the middle petal;
thus should the worship be performed by practitioners who desire spiritual accomplishment. || 13-31 ||
When worshipped with flowers, incense, and the like, as well as with drinks and various kinds of food offerings,
they grant success to the practitioner whose self is purified.
I shall proclaim their names in due order and according to the truth;
sixty-four are enumerated as the guardians of the tradition of mantras.
Prathamomardata, Nandata, Vīravāhaka, Śibika, Yamaghaṇṭa, and another, Kālarātra; || 13-34 ||
O Lord of Gods, Yamadūta, Campaka, Hariṇa, Kutuka, Aṭṭahāsa, and Caitra are thus proclaimed. (13.35)
Jayanta, Rudra, and likewise Anta are proclaimed;
then Krodhana, Vidyujjihva, Ulkāpāta, and Garjana. (36)
Varṣaṇa, Sūrya, Candra, Nakṣatra, and likewise Graha;
Unmana, Manana, Unmatta, and Sumanas as well. (37)
Heruka and the Ḍākinīs, Ḍāmara and Gajanāyaka, Aśani and Tālujihva, as well as Harṣaṇa and Bhīṣaṇa. || 13-38 ||
Mārjara, Siṃha, Vānara, Mūṣaka, Raurava, Jhaṃkāra, Kālamathana, and Dohala. (13.39)
Harikeśa, Piṅgala, and likewise another, Vaḍavānala; Jhaṃkāra, Jhaṃkina, Ghora, and Sarvatokṣisukhaṇḍaka. || 13-40 ||
Bhairava, Jharjhara, and another, Picuvaktra;
Bhadraka, Bhadrakāla, and likewise Haridrāmodara. || 13-41 ||
Vāmacakradhara, Daṃṣṭrāla, and Surānana—these are declared to be heroes, possessed of great strength and exceeding power. (13.42)
When worshipped in the wheel of gnosis (jñānacakra), they carry out the instructions of the practitioner.
Now, if someone who is well-cultivated should wish to accomplish a vidyā: || 13-43 ||
Upon his lap, one should place the goddess Parāparā, who possesses great power;
or else, she has been described by me as both Aparā and likewise Parā.
Alternatively, O Goddess, he who desires to accomplish that which is called the Yāmala in the city of Bhairava, known as the sixty-four families (kulāhvaya), [should proceed as follows].
One should install [the letters] in sequence as before, from the eastern direction up to Īśa;
and in the center, the group known as the Varga should be joined with the Vidyeśas.
O Goddess, if one wishes to accomplish the mantra endowed with the Vidyā,
one should place it within the pericarp by means of nine [syllables] in their proper sequence.
Within six months one attains perfection; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
O Goddess of gods, even a slayer of a Brahmin shall attain the state of a sky-walker (*khecarī*) within a year.
One who knows the ritual procedure should perform worship according to the Kaulika method;
the mantra of the Gaṇa is said to consist of the sixteen vowels.
One should worship each group by means of the division of Rudra and Śakti;
the Rudras are to be worshipped with the short vowels, and the Śaktis with the long vowels.
Having thus performed the worship according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures,
one should then perform meditation upon Ardhanārīśvara in that Kaulika [tradition].
One should perform meditation according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures, following both the instruction on the meaning of the syllables and the Kaulika oral tradition. || 13.52 ||
In the sense of the syllables situated on the lotus, there is the *paṅkaja* (lotus) instruction;
in the *Ardhanārīśa-Kaulika*, however, there is the *ucchaṅga-saṃpradāya* (the tradition of the lap).
O Great Goddess, O Beloved, this wheel has not been told to anyone;
it must be kept secret even by you, if you desire your own spiritual accomplishment.
O Goddess, by the constant recollection of this very [mantra], and through meditation, worship, and recitation,
the practitioner of mantra becomes one with it, becoming a yogi of the host of heroes.
Alternatively, one should perform the Mātṛyāga in the nine-naved [mandala] according to the sequence;
Bhairava is to be worshipped in the center, and [the Mothers] from the letter 'A' to the end of 'Kṣa' in due order.
Having placed [the seed-syllables] upon the pericarp, one should assign those known as the groups (varga) to the petals;
that which is remembered as beginning with 'na' and ending with 'pha' is situated upon the lap of Bhairava.
One should worship according to that procedure in the sequence prescribed for the Garbhayāga;
one should offer eight lotuses and worship [the deities] beginning with Brahmāṇī in due order.
Then, having assigned the Yoginīs according to the division of eight times eight, it is taught that through Kaulika meditation this brings about swift accomplishment. (13.59)
All of these, when illuminated by vigor (vīrya), bestow the transmission;
through the union of vigor and mantra, they yield fruits such as meat, liquor, and so forth. (13.60)
He who knows both you and me through our union attains perfection;
this is declared to be the virility that is the supreme splendor of the Lord.
The *mātṛkā* is declared to be the *kula*, as revealed in the path of mantra;
through the union of mantra and *mātṛkā*, the path of *kula* is illustrated. (13.62)
O illustrious lady, "kula" is said to be the assembly of deities;
that which is their path of movement is called the "kulamārga. (13.63)
When one of dull intellect grasps another object as being something else, he does not obtain that fruit which was entirely sought by him. (13.64)
Now, therefore, O lady of excellent hips, I shall fully proclaim in brief the names of the Yoginīs according to their division into eight groups of eight.
Distributed among each mantra according to the division of the eight Mothers,
all the traditions of the sixty-four families are established within the sacred seats (pīṭhas).
Through many varieties of mantras and through many collections of mantras, she is likewise well-known by other names; learn those names from me.
By those by whom [this] alone is understood, one shall attain all accomplishments;
especially so in the case of worship, fire-offerings, and the performance of bali-oblations.
In all other matters, they protect [the practitioner] without a doubt;
they guard a man who has violated his commitments through his observances, of this there is no uncertainty. (13.69)
Whether it be a practitioner, one who has attained accomplishment, or especially a master—
anyone at all, O fair-faced one, who is not disciplined in mantra and tantra.
She protects them here in this manner like her own sons; of this there is no doubt.
She is the one who crushes at the outset, Nandinī, and Vīravāhinī. (13.71)
Ciñciṭī, Yamaghaṇṭā, and likewise Kālarātrī as another, and Yamadūtī, O Goddess of Gods, who crushes the four seats (catuṣpīṭha). || 13-72 ||
According to the scriptures, the Yoginīs residing in Brahmāṇī should be known as those who are proud of their power;
specifically, Campikā, Hariṇī, and Kulutī. (13.73)
Aṭṭahāsī, Caitrī, Jayantī, and likewise Airuḍī;
Oḍrī, the Yoginī Raudrī, who crushes all sacred seats (pīṭhas). || 13-74 ||
Born of the Maheśvarī lineage, they bestow all accomplishments;
they carry out the command of the practitioner by her authority—of this there is no doubt. (13.75)
Krodhanī, Vidyujjihvā, Ulkāpātī, Garjanī, Varṣiṇī, Sūryacandrī, and likewise Nakṣatrī and Īśagrahī. || 13-76 ||
And these very fierce Yoginīs are the leaders of the family of Yoginīs;
born from the Kaumārikula, they bestow all accomplishments and desired objects.
Unmanī, Mananābhī, Unmattā, and likewise Sumanī;
Herukī, Ḍākinī, Ḍāmarī, and Gajanāyikā. (13.78)
For these, born of the Vaiṣṇava lineage, bestow success upon the practitioner:
Aśanī, Tālujihvā, Harṣaṇī, and likewise Bhīṣaṇī.

The female cat, the lion-faced one, the female monkey, the female mouse, as well as the female boar and the female sheep— these are proclaimed to be the bestowers of all accomplishments and desired goals.
They carry out the instructions of the practitioner and bestow the supreme sacrificial pap (caru):
Rauravī, Śaṃkarī, Kālī, Mathanī, and likewise Ḍohalī. (13.81)
Harikeśī, Piṅgalā, and the supreme Vaḍavānalikā—
these yoginīs of great power are born from the lineage of Aindrāṇī.
Jhaṃkārī, Jhaṅkinī, Ghorā, Sarvatokhimukhā, as well as Bhairavī, Jharjharī, Picuvaktrā, and others. (13.83)
She is indeed remembered as Cāmuṇḍā; these [goddesses] carry out the commands of the practitioner:
Bhadrakī, Bhadrakālī, and likewise Haridāmodarī. (13.84)
