Vāmanī, Cakriṇī, Daṃṣṭrālī, and Surānanī—these are the Aghorīs, O Great Goddess; these Yoginīs are arrogant with power.

Enflamed within the wheel of knowledge (*jñānacakra*), they carry out the command of the practitioner; these sixty-four [goddesses] known as the *kulas* also offer the sacrificial pap (*caru*) according to tradition.
O beautiful one, they grant the state of a sky-farer to the supreme practitioner; the pill, the power of moving through the air—all this indeed becomes accomplished.
O Vīranāyikā, one should worship according to the sequence of eight times eight;
or else, O Dear One, one should worship according to the ritual of Rudraśakti.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, the section on Navātman, in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, a great tantra within the Bhairava-stream belonging to the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), measuring seventy million verses. 13.

She binds the three worlds; she draws forth Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra—what need is there to mention mere mortals? When the Goddess stands upon the staff, she can dry up even the oceans. When the Goddess stands upon the trident, O Śāṅkara, she can destroy everything. When the Goddess stands upon the crest... [the world] is blessed.
The portion from verse 4 to verses 31–32 of the fourteenth chapter is missing.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, I have understood everything regarding the nine principles (navatattva) according to their divisions."
The sacrifice, according to its established form, is performed with the division of steps upon the nine-naved altar.
O Lord, the powers of Rudra have been indicated and described by you; yet they have not been fully understood. I wish to hear the auspicious procedure for the powers of Rudra.
But what, O Lord, is the power of Rudra? And after that, [tell me of] the ritual placement (nyāsa), meditation, recitation, initiation, and the ritual acts—speak of these, O Master. (14.3)

And how his own application of the rules for the limbs is established—Bhairava said: "O Goddess of gods, why do you ask me this? (14.4) [71a] Regarding the state of being the object of worship: "But why, O Goddess of gods, have I been questioned about this? (14.4) [71a]
O Pārvatī, do you not know your own worship?
Nevertheless, I shall describe the auspicious ritual empowered by Rudra. (14.5)
And one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) especially with my auspicious syllables,
exactly as previously instructed by me according to the rules for the limbs of the ritual placement.

Now listen to the procedure for meditation and worship, as well as the sacrifice immediately following it, the initiation, and the ritual acts performed through the application of the *svāhā* formula. (14.7)
O Goddess of the Gods, your body is composed of fifty phonemes and forms,
which abide in an inseparable relationship with you and the mantra.
O lady of excellent limbs, he who knows this shall undoubtedly attain success;
having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should thereafter practice meditation (*dhyāna*).
She is beautiful of form, with lovely breasts, two arms, and three eyes;
she is endowed with all ornaments and adorned with a crown of matted hair.
The skull held in her left hand is filled with that which is called nectar;
she should be meditated upon as delighting in food and drink, adorned with necklaces and armlets. (14.11)
Thus, the goddess who assumes this form and destroys the suffering of those who bow before her;
one should place the goddess in the pericarp and install the limbs (aṅgas) upon the petals.
Established in the directions of Agni, Īśāna, Nairṛti, and Vāyu,
one should place the Eye (netra) in the eyes and the Weapon (astra) situated upon the petals of the directions.
Having thus performed the worship, one should thereafter perform the recitation (japa).
For one reciting the Mālinī, the eight supernatural powers (siddhis) are accomplished.
This is accomplished by the lord of practitioners through mere play; no deliberation need be made here.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, one should then perform the fire-oblation (homa) ten thousand times as its tenth part.
Having performed the fire-oblation according to the prescribed rule, one should thereafter carry out the ritual actions,
specifically those such as the rites for pacification and especially for nourishment.
One should indeed perform that entirely at the throat for the sake of accomplishing all rites;
if one meditates upon it joined with the throat of a peacock at the center of the eyebrows.
O Goddess, one should cause the garland of human heads to descend downward;
for even if he were powerful, O fair-faced one, he would be seized by that very instant.
When the Goddess casts her gaze upon the ear, she withers it in an instant;
when the Goddess gazes upon an ornament situated on the body, then that ornament [shines].
When the Goddess, residing in the nose, takes away the breath in an instant, and when the Goddess, residing in speech, then causes one to become mute; || 14-20 ||
When the Goddess, residing in the tongue, destroys taste in an instant;
when the Goddess, residing in the palate, [destroys] even the terrifying [objects] of the thirty gods.
When the Goddess stands on the left side, she certainly causes [the enemy] to be swiftly eradicated;
but when the Goddess is situated at the vital point (marmasthā), she immediately bestows union.
And at its end stands the Goddess, possessing the supreme power of emasculation (śaṇṭīkaraṇa);
when she holds it in her hand, she swallows every enemy in an instant.
Joined with two skull-caps, it causes enmity toward men;
one should write the five twice-born [letters] in the middle, joined with the sixth and third. (14–24)
Having joined [the materials] with the left hand, one should engrave [the image] in the middle of the stone;
[this applies to] a man or a woman, or even a tiger, or one of evil intent.
One should arrest [the breath] while it resides in the dyeing [element]; when joined with the heart, Mālinī, conjoined with that, arrests the fivefold divine [elements]. (14–26)
By means of an ointment smeared with *vajrālepita*, she brings swift accomplishment to men;
she is mounted upon the right breast and seated in the midst of swans. (14.27)
When the Goddess, who causes the bondage of vision for men, is smeared by the being Brahmāsattva and established within oneself, she is endowed with her hips. (14.28)
When joined with the words of the Sādhyasūtra, she who moves like a crow’s beak causes [the object] to fall;
and this, O Blessed One, produces immediate conviction.
The illustrious Śikharasthā, endowed with a crest,
should indeed be drawn on a wooden board together with Karṇabhūṣaṇā in the eastern direction.
With a flower fumigated by poison, the mantra-practitioner should smear it with the wood of *khadira* for half a watch; when that half-watch has passed, he shall utterly uproot the target.
When the Goddess, residing in the secret place, is placed within the center of the mouth;
when the Goddess herself is endowed with the staff of the trident.

The practitioner of mantra should have [the diagram] drawn upon the back of a tortoise, provided with the body of the person to be subdued; when half a watch has passed, he should bury it in the middle of the house.
O lady of beautiful countenance, even Śakra himself would become subject to one's gaze within seven days;
yet, when he placed his left foot [upon it], the skull fell once again.
Having again placed his left foot upon the skull that had fallen, which served as a support made of a trident-staff and was adorned with severed nostrils; (14.35)
On the eighth or the fourteenth [lunar day], the mantra-practitioner should write [the name] within a hollowed-out skull-cup,
accompanied by the thread of the person to be subdued.
One should smear with the hand itself and then pin it down with pins;
with incense fumigated by poison, one may pin down even the gods.
When the Goddess, stationed within the skull, is placed in the center of the trident,
the Goddess residing within the body of the victim can destroy the three worlds.
But when the goddess is established within oneself, placed in the middle of the throat, joined with the left hand, and settled upon the right knee. (14.39)
Endowed with the *tilaka*, she brings the three worlds under her control;
having caused the skull to fall, she should apply her left foot.
And likewise, the third eye, adorned with a sectarian mark (tilaka), he should place once again;
then he should set down his foot, and the skull falls once more.
O Goddess, with his right arm placed upon his right knee, he should again set down his foot as the skull falls once more. (14.42)
And the fourth tooth, adorned with an ornament, he should place once more; the skull has fallen again. (14.43)
One should again place that [foot], adorned with ornaments;
then, placing the left foot once more, the skull falls down again.
O Mahāmati, first the biting with the tongue is joined;
then, having placed the left foot [upon it], the skull falls down once more. (14.45)
The practitioner should draw the heart alone, separate from the words;
then again he should place the foot, and again the fallen skull.
Immediately after that syllable, one should apply the "falling of the tongue" (jihvāpātana);
then once again, one should place the foot, and the skull falls once more.
One should draw the tongue mounted upon the crest and then place it there;
likewise, one should again place the foot and the fallen skull. (14.48)
The wise one should draw the pride-mantra joined with the word "vācā" as the support for the throat;
then he should again place the foot, and the skull falls once more. (14.49)
One should merely write the syllable *prāṇa*, but cause it to be divided by speech;
then one should again place the foot, and the skull falls once more. (14.50)
One should have it written on birch bark with the name of the person to be accomplished joined at the end,
using lac mixed with the blood of a donkey and [the juice of] the *vilohita* plant, [recited] one hundred thousand times.
One should have an image made with the dust from the feet of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) mixed with *madana* [seeds]; one should then smear it with poison and lac.
Taking the pestle and mortar, he should place them together with care in a hollowed-out spot within the cremation ground at midnight, surrounded by his companions.
Then the mantra-practitioner, naked with his hair disheveled and his eyes bloodshot with rage,
should take recourse in the southern direction and whirl a pestle.
Having recited it one hundred and one times, one should strike [the victim] with a mind full of wrath;
he dies without a doubt, and there is no further rebirth for him. (14.55)
Neither the lunar day, nor the asterism, nor fasting is prescribed;
for even one engaged in any ritual act, if enraged, will certainly cause death. (14.56)
Placing only the third eye joined with speech,
it is situated on the right ear and adorned with a sectarian mark (tilaka) on the hip.
One should again place the arm, split apart by the syllable *mā*;
likewise, one should cause the second tooth to become divided in two. (14.58)
Adorned with an ornament placed upon his right ear,
the practitioner of mantra should strike that very tooth with his right knee.
Seated upon the right foot, one should diligently trace with the tongue;
having performed the placement (nyāsa) together with the crest and the tongue, one should then again place the second tooth.
Then, one should again place the foot joined with the right knee and endowed with the tongue;
having positioned the topknot facing downwards, one should draw it joined with the tongue.
One should carefully write the [mantra] called Akṣarāntarita upon a cloth (karpaṭa) using cow's blood, lamp oil, and likewise the pure menses of a woman. (14.62)
And with the leaves of the *nibārka* and the flowers of the *lāṅgalī*,
a person should write [the mantra] together with these in a skull-casket.
Having smeared it everywhere, one should fumigate it with *phalgu* wood for men;
at the time of the crow's cry, the wise man should bury it and go to the sacrificial tree.
Having placed [the image] within a hollow of a vibhītaka tree belonging to great-souled beings,
the practitioner of mantra, facing downwards, should go once more to a specific location.
Having seized the subject with his lotus-like hands for as long as half a watch,
the subject laughs, weeps, dances, and likewise terrifies [the practitioner].
When trees and houses tremble violently, seized by all the spirits,
it is declared to be the "insanity-inducing" [rite], which produces immediate conviction.
This is declared to be a cause of evil and a performer of great misdeeds;
it must be guarded with effort and must not be told to anyone at all.
Now I shall further explain the vidyā exactly as it was extracted:
*Oṃ cāmuṇḍe khukhaḍhiḍhaḍhaṃ niśācāri khakhapiñcchaṃ vāriṇivicce svāhā*. Having written down the root mantra alone, it should be marked with a *tilaka*.
Furthermore, one should place the Mahāvīra peak on the right;
having placed the left peak as well, they are established at the end of the foot.
One should again place the object of attainment (sādhya) and once more write the mantra;
thereafter, the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) should again write the object of attainment immediately following that.
One should draw them intertwined with one another upon a birch bark leaf starting from the seed-syllable;
having encircled them on the birch bark, the wise man should place it upon the heart.
One should cause the person to be subdued (sādhya) to be placed below and the practitioner (sādhaka) to be situated above;
having fashioned a vomiting vessel in the shape of clarified butter, one should draw [the figures] with yellow pigment (rocanā).

Having carefully placed [the substance] in an earthen vessel and enclosed it within a sealed container, one should then once again render it completely free of cracks by means of vomit and clarified butter.
With great effort, the great yogin should cause [the object] to be placed in the midst of water;
if the mantra-practitioner becomes enraged, he shall bring it under control in that very instant. (14.75)
O Goddess, for whom does accomplishment not arise once they have understood this great yantra on earth, which follows the path of the Kula, as being equal to the power of Rudra? (14.76)
For one who engages in all desires, eternal accomplishment is attained; likewise, the rites of killing, summoning, creating enmity, and expulsion are achieved. (14.77)
Whatever action is performed by one who has reached the further shore, that becomes its fruit.
Now I shall explain initiation (dīkṣā) as well, in brief.

The practitioner of mantra should worship the power of Rudra, by the mere knowledge of which one is liberated and by which one may liberate others, either upon a sacrificial mound or within a mandala. (14.79)
Then, having granted permission, he should lead the disciple into the sacrificial maṇḍala;
having performed the rite of releasing the flower, he should cause him to prostrate himself on the ground like a staff.
Then he should cause the disciple to rise and lead him near the fire;
with his left leg joined [to the right], the self remains seated on a staff-throne (daṇḍāsana).
When one recites [the mantra] joined with the left ornament and trampled by the staff,
it should be intermingled with the twelve vowels according to the internal yoga.
The paralysis of the noose occurs swiftly; there is no need for deliberation here.
Those phonemes which are pervaded by the power of Rudra (rudra-śakti) have the staff (daṇḍa) as their seat. || 14.83 ||
Intermingled with the twelve vowels, they cause all that is moving and unmoving to tremble;
O Goddess, they are the power of Rudra, encapsulated within the secret powers.
Initiation is declared to be the giver [of fruits], bestowing good fortune even upon the unfortunate;
it adorns the life-force seated upon the staff-throne with its own ornamentation.
Purified by that very [seed-syllable] situated in the left ear and located in the secret place,
one should place the seed-syllable, possessing a luster like a peacock's neck, between the eyebrows.
"Make it fall!"—with this [utterance], like a tree struck by a thunderbolt, it violently causes trembling, agitation, and the falling of the vessel; of this there is no doubt. (14.87)
When employed by a preeminent practitioner, one should not entertain doubt regarding this.
Now, I shall further proclaim another auspicious rite, the procedure for the Rudrāvali.
One who recites the Rudra-śakti mantra does not obtain its fruit in whatever manner it may be;
however, one should always recite the Rudra-śakti as merged with Śrīkaṇṭha. (14.89)
Accompanied by Bālā, she attains the state of Śrīkaṇṭha;
thus, when Mālinī is divided by each Rudra individually. (14.90)
The supreme practitioner who recites this mantra shall attain that very state;
this is declared to be "Victory" (Vijaya), characterized by the nature of both the enjoyer and the enjoyed. (14.91)

The division of Rudra’s power and the fruit situated within one's own [nature], as well as whatever object of enjoyment is designated for each according to the sequence of the parts, [are all contained therein]. (14.92)
O Goddess of the gods, [one attains] the state of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, or Īśa; likewise the state of Śiva, as well as that of a Yakṣa, a Nāga, or a Kumāra.
Whether it be the Āsura, Gāndharva, Aindra, or even the Gāruḍa [weapon],
the Lord bestows upon each that which corresponds to their own nature.
The Goddess said:
O Supreme Lord, you have described the attainment [of results] as being dependent upon the *aṃśaka* and *anuvaśa*;
indeed, initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the propitiation of mantras are also held to depend upon those. (14.95)
"Methods of accomplishment that lack specific components do not bestow success;
therefore, please graciously explain how those components are to be examined."
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the characteristics of the *aṃśakas*. The first is the *mantrāṃśa*, the second is the *nāmāṃśa*, and the third is the *bhāvāṃśa*. (14.97)
O Supreme Goddess, the limb of the Goddess is to be known as the fourth;
now listen as I explain the assignment of the portions of her activity.
By means of which the hero or the powerless woman will certainly attain excellent accomplishment;
[the fourfold classification is] the accomplished (siddha), the to-be-accomplished (sādhya), the well-accomplished (susiddha), and the enemy (ari). || 14.99 ||
The mantra is to be known as fourfold in all tantras, and not otherwise:
it is already accomplished (siddha), or it is quickly accomplished (siddhyati), or it is to be accomplished (sādhya) through sacrifices, vows, and other such means. (14.100)
By merely reciting it once, one becomes purified at that very moment;
and by the practitioner who has performed the recitation, even an enemy shall be cut down.
If, according to the final doctrine, the mantra is indeed primordially established,
then accomplishment will surely come to pass in no long time.
When joined with the *sādhya* and other [mantric] elements, it is accomplished only with great difficulty;
however, when perfected at the beginning and the end, it bestows fruit throughout the three worlds.
In the first [case], there will be an enemy, and indeed in the second as well;
having observed such a characteristic, one should avoid it from afar. (14.104)
If the mantra is one whose goal is established by the primordial Siddhānta,
then the rite performed according to the Kalpa will yield fourfold results.
But one endowed with devotion accomplishes it without doubt through persistent application;
indeed, it is perfected from beginning to end according to the sequence previously described.
May she grant success and manifold boons to the practitioner, O fair-faced one!
That which is to be accomplished shall be achieved through both means, and it is perfected by means of the six qualities alone. || 14-107 ||

O Goddess of the Gods, if the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) occurs within mantras that are already well-established (*susiddha*) and so forth, it is accomplished by the very procedure, indeed with sixfold power. (14.108)

The *Siddhānta* is well-established as beginning with *Susiddha*, bestowing divine accomplishment (*divyasiddhi*). Likewise, the *Siddhānta* consists of the system beginning with *Susiddha*, and so forth.
But whatever mantra is well-accomplished and its final conclusion is mastered, O Sulocanā, it slays even a hundred enemies in their midst; of this there is no doubt.
An enemy should always be avoided by the wise both at the beginning and at the end;
for if you are corrupted by an enemy through mantras, even your middle state will be lost.
The body composed of water and meaning (or essence) becomes powerless in an instant;
therefore, one should avoid the mantra of the enemy with every effort. (14.112)
Even for those who have attained success, there is further success through that which is already accomplished;
beyond this, I shall proclaim the rule concerning the enumeration of mantras.
By the mere knowledge of which the practitioner shall partake in accomplishment, [he should practice] in a solitary and pure place, strewn with heaps of flowers. (14.114)
In a place endowed with fragrant scents and gladdened by the aroma of excellent incense,
the preceptor, girded with the mantra, should draw the grid.
Having carefully written [the letters] from the beginning to the end, O fair-faced one,
excluding the group of neuter vowels and avoiding the *saṃhāra* (consonant) groups.
Afterwards, having written down the mantra according to the sequence of the number of its syllables, it should be divided, O lady of excellent hips; for the vowels manifest the consonants.
The syllables of the mantra should be treated individually; they are distinguished by being devoid of vowels.
That which is to be accomplished through the mantra is called "gone," being devoid of conjunct consonants.
One should write exactly as it is well-known in the world, as proclaimed by one's father and mother, O lady of excellent hips, until the end of the mantra is reached. (14.119)
Having carefully counted from the seed-syllables of the names up to the seed-syllables of the mantras, one should place that which has been obtained in the earthen vessel.
In this way, one should count all the syllables until the end of the mantra is reached;
the first [syllable] is called "accomplished" (siddha), while the second is said to be "to be accomplished" (sādhya).
The third is Susiddha, and the fourth is Ari;
likewise, [the four types are] Siddha, Sādhya, Susiddha, and the fourth is Ari.
The wise one should count in one place until the mantra is completed;
at the end of the mantra, he should perform the counting, and that very number will be established there.
The knower of the ritual procedure, having combined both the *siddha* and the *susiddha*, and likewise the *sādhya* and the *ari*, [should calculate] again by multiplying by ten. (14.124)
One should divide by four; that which remains after subtraction below is designated as the *tejaṃśā* for the practitioner of great austerity.
Now, if there remains a trace of existence, something will remain;
these are declared to be the watches [of the day], and no further deliberation is required here. (14.126)
Having thus understood the nature of the mantra, one should then offer it;
thereafter, the best of practitioners should perform recitation, fire-oblation, and meditation. (14.127)
"It is accomplished; there is no doubt here—this is the truth, O fair-faced one.
Meditation, worship, recitation, and fire-offerings bestow fruits that consist of the very nature of one's intention. (14.128)
That which is devoid of being cannot be established; therefore, one should characterize being.
Whatever the nature of a person may be—whether divine, rākṣasa, or human—[that is what they are].
For one who knows the portions of existence (bhāvāṃśaka), the attainment of results occurs through that [portion];
however, one who possesses a divine portion (devāṃśya) and is devoted to the gods is eager for results only in the form of enjoyments.
He was eternally hostile toward the Asuras, yet devoted to the welfare of all beings; though born of the Daityas, he was free from pride, steadfast, yet addicted to desire and utterly merciless.

The Asura is characterized by a fondness for battle; the Deva is free from malice; the Nirmaya seeks out hidden recesses; the Bhogin is devoted to enjoyment; and the Gandharva is intent upon song. (14.132)
Constantly eating sweet foods and surrounded by many attendants, he is a portion of the Nāgas, long-sleeping, foul-mouthed, and possessed of great splendor. || 14.133 ||
O lady of beautiful hips, one who is chronically ill, devoted to mountain gardens, incapable of performing sacrifices, yet pure—such a person is designated by the name "Nāman. (14.134)
One who accumulates everything and possesses wealth is considered a miser;
[he should instead dwell] in a forest cave that is captivating, deep, delightful, and rich with flowers. (14.135)
A Yakṣa or Piśāca who is fickle and intent on the remains of food always delights alone in a palace beautiful with mansions; he desires solitude. (14.136)
He was blind, unattached, pure, and intent on his duties at night;
yet he was like a Rakshasa, cruel, base, a meat-eater, and devoted to liquor. (14.137)
He is a hater of the Vedas and a teacher of falsehoods, always delighting in all states of being;
he is Indra-like in his righteousness and valor, and fond of variegated garments. (14.138)

Always fond of elephants and horses, and devoted to mantras, he should employ mantras for the sake of the kingdom; yet, being intent on the pleasures of women, his mind is distracted by them. (14.139)

He possesses a portion of the fire-god; he is one who performs intense deeds, is skilled in action, fond of making oblations, dear [to others], has tawny hair and red eyes, and is endowed with a virtuous character.
Endowed with purity and right conduct, truthful, firm in his vows, constantly upholding the Vedic observances, disciplined, and engaged in proper reflection. || 14.141 ||
Yama’s son is black in color, red-eyed, and merciless, yet highly intelligent;
he is constantly devoted to the treatises on dharma, truthful, and firm in his vows. (14.142)

One who eats the flesh of Yama, is powerful, and worships gods and brahmins is a Nairṛta; however, a man who is devoted to the ancestors, harsh, and has the appearance of a crow or a vulture is a Rākṣasa.
One with red eyes is a slanderer and a hungry ghost (preta), yet intent on ancestral rites;
one who is handsome, fortunate, affectionate, and of peaceful form is dear [to Varuṇa].
O beloved, one with a portion of wind (vāta) is fickle, mean, harsh, full of deceit, talkative, lacking in essence, a speaker of falsehood, and restless. (14.145)
One who possesses a portion of the Moon is endowed with luster, gentle, and has mild eyes;
he is pleasant-spoken, wealthy, auspicious, and pleasing to behold. (14.146)
A portion of Brahmā, devoted to Brahmā, a practitioner of the Vedas, firm in his vows, constantly intent on the Vedic dharma, and endowed with truthfulness and purity. || 14.147 ||
One who possesses a portion of Viṣṇu, devotion to Viṣṇu, an even-minded perspective endowed with auspiciousness,
and hatred toward the Daityas, should be known as having a portion of Rudra and being intent upon the Liṅga.
A devotee of Śiva, a great hero, truthful and firm in his vows, he was not eager for the acquisition of knowledge or for the enjoyment of fruits that are yet unseen. || 14.149 ||
Whether it be mantra, the yoga of knowledge, or initiation for the sake of liberation, he seeks these everywhere; yet he is not attached to anything pertaining to primordial nature (prakṛti).
He regarded even the garlands and enjoyments of the gods as impermanent; though ever fortunate in his desires, he looked upon the lord of desire on earth as if he were a mere fragment of it.
Through enjoyment, one may be born everywhere with a mind solely intent on desire; having understood this according to the respective portions, O Goddess, there is no doubt. (14–152)
The wise should bestow favor through action prescribed by the scriptures;
now I shall explain the portions of the goddesses correctly and in their proper sequence.
Having understood the pure portion as well as the mixed portion according to their respective dispositions,
[one should worship] Brahmāṇī, Rudrāṇī, Kaumārī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī.
Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, and Yogeśī are likewise remembered as supreme;
these pure portions (aṃśas) should be understood with diligent effort. || 14-155 ||
O Goddess, for one who knows, whatever state arises belongs to that part [of the Self]; yet it may also become a distinct part through the heart, like two sisters.
I shall now explain, without omission, the specific divisions of each one:
O Goddess, there is Brahmamāheśvarī and likewise Brahmakaumārikā.
Brahmavaiṣṇavikā, as well as Brahmavārāhikā;
O Goddess, [these forms of] Brahmaindrāṇikā are worshipped by the Yogīśīs of Brahmā. || 14-158 ||
Just as one is, so are all; however, according to the sequence of distinct parts and so forth, there are forty-nine goddesses who are indeed distinct from one another.
Those [aspects] which are distinct from the divided portion will indeed be the givers of fruit;
likewise, in the pure portion, the pure aspects are to be known as the givers of fruit.
The Goddess said:
"It is not possible to distinguish whether one possesses pure portions or mixed portions;
therefore, you must grant me this favor and provide a definitive decision. (14–161)
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the rules for the *aṃśakas* according to the tradition.
Out of affection for you, O beautiful goddess, I shall speak; there is no doubt about this.
O Goddess of the gods, by the paralysis of the noose, the certainty of success is known:
the enemy-success (arisiddha), the one to be accomplished (sādhya), the one already accomplished (sasiddha), and the fourth.
Listen now without omission to how these [states] abide according to their respective certainties:
they remain, tremble, O Lord, move, and even fall. (14–164)
One should understand the enemies and so forth according to the nature of all the vowels; O Goddess, [one should know] the group of eight letters beginning with *ya* up to the end of *ha* in brief.
Pierced by Kālarudra, they are endowed with great splendor;
situated on the peak, moving to the left, all are joined with the sixfold group and possessed of crests.
Adorned with the crescent moon digit (ardhendukalā) and embellished by Śakti, Nāda,
and Bindu, and joined with the vowel Oṃ, one should employ [these mantras] in all ritual actions.
For one who understands [this] in such a way, the first is known as the Brāhmī;
thus, through the conjunction of the letters of the classes, they are endowed with syllables and words of the left. (14–168)
Joined with the end of *uccāra* and the final [syllable], one should paralyze all that is moving and unmoving;
whichever is the group of syllables belonging to a goddess, it is endowed with the peak-syllable (*kūṭākṣara*).

By that [means], O fair-faced one, there would be a stimulation (stobha) for him; that is a portion [of it], wherein each individual syllable and non-syllable is brought to completion through the various types of *kūṭa* combinations.

O fair-faced one, that portion [of the seed] by which the potato [is produced], having thus correctly understood the pure, distinct portion according to the ritual procedure, [one should proceed]. (14–171)
O Goddess, being purified, one should then offer the mantra;
thus, the mantra together with him shall be perfected, bestowing the fruit of his desired object.
Stobha is said to be threefold in the examination of the disciple's suitability for initiation;
furthermore, stobha may also occur for one whose spiritual state has not yet been attained. (14.173)
O beautiful one, he who possesses the *śaya* posture becomes worthy of all accomplishments;
O lady of excellent complexion, by means of the intense flight, they go to the sky-faring state.
With the middling [practice], one reaches Pātāla; with the inferior, one lives in comfort. Whatever actions there may be, they are accomplished only through the superior [practice]. (14.175)
If there is no praise for one who is evil-minded and a doer of wicked deeds,
initiation should not be performed for him, lest the progeny become devoid of humanity.

The Goddess said: Some indeed say this: "The mantra does not praise [the deity] when it is merely sprinkled with the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) and presided over by extraneous states. (14.177)
"Stobha shall not arise for him," they say, and so forth.
Bhairava said: "Remembering his previous birth, upon seeing Cārudra, he utters stobha. (14–178)

O Goddess of Gods, for one whose body is purified and who has received the transmission of the mantra, there occurs a state of *stobha* regarding the nature of reality; it does not happen otherwise. (14–179)
The evil-minded one who has the form of a beast, though endowed with both dharma and adharma,
does not attain liberation, being bound by his birth as a beast.
If a possession of these [spirits] arises in someone's body even in a slight degree,
the mantra should be given to him, and the tooth [rite] shall indeed be successful.
Stimulation, binding, and liberation were indeed explained by me previously;
now, however, the piercing of the channels (nāḍī-bheda) is revealed according to its beginning and middle.
I shall explain in successive order according to the sequence of the *stobha* descents:
from seeing [the deity] and from touching [the deity], the *stobha* is proclaimed as a "forceful descent" (*tīvrapāta*). (14.183)
Fifteen or twenty oblations are proclaimed as the middling;
O Goddess of the Gods, thirty or forty are the lowest; and fifty oblations are proclaimed as the highest. (14–185)
With one hundred [recitations], it should be known as middling; with two hundred, it is remembered as inferior.
With three hundred, O Goddess, it is to be accomplished; this is proclaimed as the highest.
With six hundred [verses] it is indeed middling, while with nine hundred it is inferior;
the best is known to consist of twelve hundred, and sixteen hundred is remembered as middling.
O fair-faced one, the lowest [division] among the twenty is said to be the *abhibheda*;
thus, by means of the twelve divisions, the twelve portions (*aṃśas*) are indeed remembered. (14–188)
O fair-hipped one, he who is without parts is not fit for the sacrifice of Śiva;
no initiation is performed for him, and one should avoid such a doer of evil deeds.
One whose conduct has been lost, who has fallen from his vows, who is like a mere log or stone, or even one initiated through favor, becomes again a traitor to the guru. (14.190)
Indeed, [the results are] a mole on the forehead, baldness, and likewise having three ears;
being dull-witted, impotent, wicked, cruel, deaf, blind, or mute. (14.191)
Likewise, those with impaired faculties, the Dravidas, the Ambupas, the Pulindas, the Karṇāṭas, those of Mleccha birth, and those who live by exploiting others' weaknesses. || 14-192 ||

One who is intoxicated by the pride of knowledge, one who is critical [of the teachings], one who delights in other scriptures, and one who maintains a hypocritical vow—these are to be avoided. (14.193)
"For those who are initiated out of negligence are certainly not vessels for success;
this, O Goddess, has been explained according to the sequence of the syllables of the portions. (14–194)
Thus has been told, along with its secret, the [teaching] for those whose souls are devoted to the observances of the Vidyās.

This concludes the fourteenth chapter, the Determination of Rudra’s Power, in the *Śrī Tantrasadbhāva*, a great tantra within the Bhairava-stream belonging to the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), measuring seventy million verses. 14.
The Goddess said:
"O Hero, please tell me how a mantra-practitioner who desires heroism should observe the vow of knowledge (vidyāvrata) once he has been authorized and consecrated. (15.1)
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme vow of the Vidyā.
One may be one with matted hair, shaven-headed, or with a topknot; likewise, one may be a celibate student (brahmacārī) or a graduate (snātaka). 15-2.
Whether established in a vow or not established in a vow, in whatever state one may be, one attains perfection—even if wearing the five mudrās, or devoted to ashes, or naked. (15.3)
Either wearing bark garments or adorned with all kinds of ornaments, or else soiled and filthy, or dressed and adorned in white clothes. || 15-4 ||
In whatever attire the supreme practitioner conducts himself, O God, that is declared to be his vow; such is the certainty of the scripture. (15.5)
Whatever ornament he wears, or whatever he speaks with his voice—that is declared to be the rite; it is the mantra itself, without a doubt. (15.6)
That which is called Vidyā is the supreme power (parā śakti); it is established as being twofold.
It is the auspicious power of consciousness (cicchakti), residing in the designation [of the Absolute], and it pervades both the unmanifested and the manifested letters.

Because they exist as all-pervading, they are remembered by me as *vidyās*; just as the entire world has been traversed, established in both the colored (*varṇa*) and the colorless (*avarṇa*). 15.8ab [g]
"Vow" (vratam) is said to mean "state of being" (bhāva); therefore, O Dear One, it is called the Vidyā-vrata.
It gathers (cinoti) the knowledge of consciousness (citi), which awakens the power of consciousness (cicchakti). (15.9)
When the body, like a leaf upon the ocean, has dissolved into the form consisting of the Vidyā and Mantra,
and the Śakti has entered the supreme state, he is called one who has mastered the Vidyā.
The name of the Vidyā consists of seven thousand million syllables;
because it awakens the power of consciousness (cicchakti), it has attained the state of being both without letters and yet possessing letters.
Kuṇḍalinī alone is declared to be the supreme, whose form is knowledge (vidyā).
Therefore, O Goddess, this vow is proclaimed as the auspicious practice of that knowledge.
He who proceeds on the path of knowledge through actions prescribed by the scriptures—
performing meditation, worship, recitation, and fire-offerings— is indeed a protector of the commitments (samayas).
This is declared to be the vow of the Vidyā; it is not otherwise, O Leader of Heroes.
By the command of the Vidyā, she who resides in the navel moves as far as the end of the twelve [fingers].
In all places where vows are observed, the Vidyā-vrata is thus remembered;
[these are] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva. (15–15)
These are indeed the abodes of the vow where she moves in her supreme state;
having known that supreme abode, he has indeed fulfilled the observance of the vidyā-vow.
O Goddess, the five mudrās are that which constitute the five causes;
adorned with them, one should abide in the heart, embellished by the five mudrās. (15–17)
Adorned with these mantras, one should wander while taking refuge in sacred sites:
in cremation grounds, forests, wells, gardens, and auspicious temples. (15–18)
In an empty Rājagṛha, on a mountain peak, at a crossroads, at a triple-path, on village streets, or likewise on the shore of the great ocean, the mantra-practitioner [should dwell]. (15–19)

On the bank of a river confluence, at a solitary tree, or in a cave; likewise at a single *liṅga*, in a grove, and in a sacred field—[these are the sites] in sequence for the eight [types of practitioners]. (15–20)
Prayāga, Varuṇā, Kolā, Aṭṭahāsā, Jayantikā, Caritra, Kāmbuka, and Koṭivarṣa as the eighth. (15–21)

The practitioner of mantra, desiring the siddhi of the Yoginīs, should always wander with these [implements], carrying a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), observing silence, and moving with speed. (15.22)
A club, a noose, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a trident, as well as a shield, an iron arrow, a pair of scissors, a discus, a goad, a mace, and a bow. (15–23)
A mace, a small sword, a spear, as well as a staff and a water-pot—
these indeed are the most excellent weapons that one should carry at the time of ritual practice.

The practitioner of mantra should perform this supreme vow, which is divine in nature, involves a specific number of mantras, and lasts for twelve days, a fortnight, a month, or likewise a season. (15–25)
For six months, or a year, or two years, or indeed three;
likewise four, five, six, seven, or even eight [years]. (15–26)
Whether for nine, five, or even eleven years,
or indeed for twelve years, even a slayer of a Brahmin attains success if he practices [this].
O Goddess of the Gods, in one year [one attains success]...
[in the mantra] without a priest. (15.28)
O beautiful leader of the gods, when the king of the excellent city is peaceful and under control, the daughters of Dakṣa, who are two years old, attain accomplishment. (15.29)
In three years, seven herds of cows will arrive here, auspicious, intoxicated with passion in spring, their eyes wandering with lust. (30)
Moving with the gait of intoxicated elephants, possessing inexhaustible youth, they become agitated at the sight of the lord of practitioners and instantly surrender their lives. (15.31)
One should accomplish the worlds beginning with Brahmaloka by means of four, five, and six [years] respectively;
O lady of beautiful hips, they are established up to the end of Rudra in the seventh year.
"They are accomplished for the foremost of practitioners," so it is taught in the scripture;
the one called Īśvara is in the eighth [cakra], while Sadāśiva is in the ninth. (15.33)
Having become tenfold, it sports greatly in the sky;
O Goddess, in the tenth and eleventh [stages] it is endowed with qualities in the twelfth.
Endowed with the qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, he goes together with the sky-farer (khecarī);
for the yogi is indeed imperishable and unconquerable, and being all-pervading, he sports in auspicious things.
O beloved, this fruit of the vow has indeed been described by me;
now listen to how it comes about through the path of yoga.
The cremation ground is said to be the house, and the body is proclaimed to be the home;
wandering without rest is for one whose mind has gone to the cremation ground.
That which is called the body is said to have two eyes at its end;
for situated there, one indeed perceives the entire world of moving and non-moving beings composed of speech.
O beloved, that which is called the forest is situated at the end of the body;
it is designated as the well of the mind, wherein one forms many volitions.
Therein, the field-knower proceeds as the substratum; therefore it is renowned as the Fourth (turyā).
Arisen and situated within the flame of thought, it thinks among all living beings. (15.40)
Those who have attained that state do not grieve over a garden;
for that nectar, which is situated in the sky, is eternally present within the body. (15.41)
O Goddess, beloved of the gods, it is because the body exists at the end of its [karmic] portion, bound by the self through merit and demerit, that it is so designated. || 15.42 ||
The King is designated as the Self, even on the path of thirty-six [tattvas];
abounding in qualities such as sound and the rest, he is my Lord dwelling within the inner chamber.

By that which stands, one should stand; with that very [state], one stands together. Those who are always joined in the state beyond mind (unmanatva) are said to be "empty" (śūnya) in mind. || 15-44 ||
Therefore, O beloved, Rājagṛha is empty in the state of Unmanā;
one should always rely upon the mouth of the Guru as its foremost support. (15.45)
In the Tantra, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, the mountain peak is mentioned as a synonym;
the crossroads, O Goddess, are Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī. (15.46)
Joined with Ambikā, the pair [of Ma and Ta] forms a group of four; by that, it is declared, it is illustrated in the first [chapter]. (15.47)
O Maheśvarī, the three channels beginning with Iḍā have been described;
situated at the triple-path, they constantly perform the coming and going [of the breath].
He who brings the three paths into a single state attains perfection;
the body is said to be the watch (yāma), and the self is not even remembered as a watch.
The *ālaya*, the abode of all principles, which consists of pleasure and pain, high and low, moves upward and downward; it is the support of the path, the Lord of the World. (15.50)
Therefore, the channel (nāḍī) called Brahma is known as the "street" (rathyā) of the Self;
the bank is declared to be the "shore," and the perfected ones (siddhas) are said to be the "movement. (15.51)
But the end of suffering is beyond dissolution; it is the shore known as the ocean.
Therein dwells the pervasive Lord Śiva, the supreme cause, at the limit of movement. (15.52)
The practitioner of mantra remains constantly there, where the practices have been revealed;
that supreme Kuṇḍalinī is the subtle support that resounds. (15.53)
That river, having become a flood, flows eternally within the ocean of the sky;
it is revealed in the state of *munmanā*, joined with the Supreme at the confluence. (15.54)
The confluence has been fully described, and the river has been proclaimed;
the bank belongs to the Samavāpinī, which is that supreme *kalā* known as Vindhī.
Then one becomes transcendent and all-pervasive; the riverbank is cited as an example.
A single tree is fully described [as such], and here a single power is spoken of. (15.56)
The senses themselves are called "wolves," and their power is known as "wolf-power" (vṛkaśakti).
When they have gone to destruction in the supreme, mindless, and stainless ether, [they are stilled]. (15.57)
Therefore, O Goddess, I have explained to you that which is situated upon a single tree:
there is but one supreme reality, the support of the *liṅga*, O beloved. (15.58)
He should wander about mostly during the day, resting again and again; this is known as the practice of the Single Liṅga (ekaliṅgagati). Now I shall describe to you the Ṣaṇḍa.
The heart is said to be the arrow, and there is an eight-petalled lotus;
by means of the udāna breath, O Goddess of Gods, it blossoms, and that is the sun. (15.60)
The lotus that constitutes the heart is served by swarms of bees;
there moves the primordial power called Haṃsā, which is Manonmanī. (15.61)
That has been described in the tantra as the "eunuch" (ṣaṇḍa); now I shall describe to you the field (kṣetra).
The field is said to be supreme; it is the body endowed with the principles (tattva). (15.62)
The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), who eternally abides in the movement of his own nature and is established in the eight stations,
has himself declared this, O Goddess, as the Eight Fields (kṣetrāṣṭaka).
Those which are pīṭhas are the kṣetras, and those which are kṣetras are declared to be the pīṭhas;
they differ only in their names and synonyms, being listed separately in various scriptures.
Prayāga is situated at the navel, while Varuṇā is in the region of the heart;
Kolagiri is located at the throat, and Bhīmanāda is in the palate.
Vindu is located in Jayantī, while that which is called Nāda is in Caritra;
Ekāmra is situated in the center of Śakti—this should be known by those who have realized the Self. (15.66)
That which has come from the mouth of the Guru is declared to be Koṭivarṣa; likewise, the eighth [is] Aṣṭama.
These places have been described by me as pertaining to the inner self (adhyātma), based on the individual (pudgala). || 15-67 ||
By means of which the eternal heart-cakra constantly revolves;
it is the body composed of all deities, esteemed by all yoginīs. (15.68)
Established upon the three-and-a-half-fold seats of yoga is the Siddhikaulika;
this other [system], O Great Goddess, produces immediate conviction.
Kulūtta, Oḍḍiyāna, Eruḍī, and Pulivallabha—these very places are situated all around within one's own body. (15.70)
That which is called the half-mātrā reveals all vital power;
thus, it is worshipped in every way through its form as the *kūṭa*.
But by the power of their illusion, they always move about at will,
acting according to their own desires and capable in all undertakings.
And those goddesses born of noble families—whether born from Brahmins, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, or Śūdras—he beholds; there is no doubt in this, for she stands everywhere, distinct in all respects.
By the power of that peak, the yogi necessarily perceives it;
they declare their own realization when it is augmented by that peak. (15.74)
The practitioner shall suddenly leap into the sky along with the sky-dwellers and enjoy their pleasures; O Goddess, he will attain the state of being their lord, moving according to his own will.
O Goddess of the Gods, by the power of that peak (kūṭa) and through the knowledge of the path of independent movement, one may sport from world to world.
O Dear One, as long as they do not find this seat situated within the self, how can there be success for them, even if they wander through the three worlds? (15.77)

Having understood the state of being internal and external, as well as the distinction between the internal and the external [aspects], one is liberated from the fetters and becomes equal to the Khecarīs. (15.78)
The goddesses who reside within are those same goddesses who move in the external;
for the sake of explaining the worldly course of events, the external seats (pīṭhas) have been revealed. (15.79)
O beloved, when one is pure within through the state of the feet, one does not see [external objects];
then one perceives the subtle forms residing externally as the cavities of the senses. (15.80)
O beloved, they bestow the *melaka* (meeting) which is free from the exhaustion of effort;
having transmitted it, they grant it or even reveal the sacred place (*sthāna*).
If one should wander the earth with impure internal disposition, O Goddess, they will not grant him a vision [of the deity] anywhere, even in his mind. (15.82)
O Goddess of the gods, even while seeing, one does not see even though seeing;
the goddesses possess mixed characteristics, and thus they cannot be known as distinct. (15.83)
This power is proclaimed to exist even without their favor, whether in a village, a forest, a city, a crossroads, or a capital. (15.84)

O Goddess, [one should practice] in a hamlet, or in a place of uncertainty, on a sacred seat (pīṭha), in a field, or in a forest; likewise, in a garden or a grove, and in those places previously mentioned. (15.85)
In various regions they are born with their internal splendors made manifest;
they are said to be enveloped by earth, as well as by water, fire, and air. (15.86)
O lady of beautiful hips, there is no counting them even in the sky;
they arise in manifold ways according to the divisions of their seats and supports. (15.87)
Constantly delighting in food and drink, they even sport among the lowest castes;
therefore, O Goddess, I have described these seats (pīṭhas) according to their external nature. (15.88)
They know the house of the courtesan as Prayāga, Varuṇa as the tavern, Khaṭikī as Kolāra, and Āyāṭṭahāsaka as Rajantī. (15.89)
One should know Jayantī as Kanduka, Caritrā as Chipparka-gṛha, Ekāmbukā as Kaivartī, and Koṭyākhyā as Kausaṭī. (15.90)
This must be understood by the seeker himself who desires the fruits of enjoyment and liberation;
thus, O lady of excellent vows, have the sacred seats (pīṭhas) and fields (kṣetras) been described externally. 15.91.
In whichever places one travels that are always to be honored by the wise, the knower of mantras should always satisfy them with various kinds of food, edibles, grains, and drinks. (15.92)
Such indeed is their arrangement; these yoginīs are immeasurable in number.
They appear here without a doubt as bestowers of boons upon the practitioner.

When they have been gratified and honored by the goddesses through the observance of the rules and vows of the practice for six months or more, they indeed grant [the fruits] to the practitioner. (15.94)
Now I shall further explain the terminology of those who know the scriptures, both internal and external, so that they may understand it according to reality. (15.95)
I shall tell you that; listen, O long-eyed one!
One practices the internal [discipline], while the external observance of vows is the means of accomplishment (sādhana).
When this is done, success will be attained; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
I shall now describe the khaṭvāṅga according to its sequence and proper order.
Listen to how it occurs from the soles of the feet up to the palate and the crown of the head, throughout all the limbs, including the major and minor members of the body. 15.98
O Goddess of the Gods, because he carries [the skull-topped staff], he is remembered as Khaṭvāṅgin;
he always conducts himself in silence, with the supreme-non-supreme [reality] hidden within his heart. (15.99)
Therefore, O beautiful lady, one should be known as a "silent sage" (maunī) according to all the scriptures;
[the vital breath] moves with speed through the body, without rest, again and again.
By that [means], I have explained the movement of the person (pudgala) according to its impulses;
now I shall describe the *caṇḍaka* in due order and exactly as it is. || 15.101 ||
The one called Amā is the supreme, most subtle digit that carries the nectar;
within it the Self moves, and they emit the resonance in the Bindu.
The Great-Souled One situated at the point of emission (visarga) should cause [the sound] to be played, saying "Speak!
Therefore, the hand-drum (ḍamaruka) is said to reside in the stainless state beyond the mind (amanaska). She who is eternal, residing in the center, is Kuṇḍalinī, whose form is illusory (māyārūpa).
This has been specified as the noose; now hear likewise concerning the sword.
Established in the void (kha), she remains; with the weapon of the visarga, she is the deluding one who casts the nooses.
Like a sword, she is the river by which the Great Goddess (Maheśvarī) resides in the midst of the sky-farer (khaga). 15.105.
That imperishable power (śakti) entered into union with Brahman at the tip of the sword;
therefore, O leader of the gods, this weapon is called "Khaḍga" (the Sword).
This single immortal power, consisting of will, knowledge, and action, is threefold within the circle of the face as Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī. (15.107)
The trident is known as the triple path, consisting of the three powers in their proper sequence;
O Dear One, it wanders in the form of Kha, moving through space, peaceful and stainless. (15.108)
By that [means], the shield is indeed established at the "end of the twelve" (dvādaśānta);
the iron arrow and the spear are established as the utterance consisting of the instrument (karaṇa). || 15.109 ||
But when piercing with the Nirodhinī, there are exactly five causes;
therefore, O fair-faced one, it is called the Nārāca by way of synonym.
The scissor is indeed the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti), by which it cuts the fetters;
that is the supreme, most subtle digit (kalā), the highest awakener of mantras. (15.111)
The practitioner should know the knife (kartarī) in its form as the cutter;
it moves at the end of the twelve [fingers] and gradually releases the principles (tattvas).
Like a wheel, she revolves eternally; the supreme and non-supreme [energies] reside in the goad.
The Goddess, dwelling within the limbs and sub-limbs, abides both externally and internally. (15.113)
They constantly exert themselves while sitting or lying down, and when running, suckling their calves, or being restrained, they resort to the position of the goad. (15.114)
O Dear One, the sound situated at the level of the pestle (muśala) moves upward in the form of a line;
having pierced through that, the upward movement reaches Sadāśiva, who is known as the Pestle (Muśala).
But he by whom the supreme, inexpressible target of the bow is pierced, having filled [the breath] with the emission (visarga) by means of the highest mind-eye. (15.116)
O lady of excellent vows, by means of the hand with its fingers closed and inverted, joined with two finger-joints, O beloved, [the penis] is inserted, but not when it has reached the end. (15.117)
By this very means, O Sulocanā, the mace, whether superior or inferior, attains union with reality. || 15.118 ||
For one [tooth] has indeed gone to the supreme opening; the auspicious nectar of the teeth has departed.
But those who have gone along with the mace do not return. (15.119)
The Self always leads [the individual] through the state of being both power and the locus of power;
O Lord of the Gods, the accomplishment of the yoga of that state is indeed by means of power.
O beautiful one, one should proceed by that path which is as straight as a staff and leads to the imperishable state, supported by the staff.
That which is known as the body (ka), established in the shape of a mandala—O lady of excellent hips, the path therein must be purified by the wise. (15.122)
The supreme, pure Kuṇḍalī is situated in the heart, which is entirely purified;
therefore, O auspicious lady, this is declared to be the auspicious weapon, the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu). || 15.123 ||
And these very subtle weapons have been clearly described through their various synonyms;
they are the subtle energies (*kalās*) led by the fire of equanimity, the mistresses of the universe. (15.124)
O Goddess, I have explained to you the division of the supreme and the non-supreme;
without a messenger (dūtī), one does not attain success, therefore one should rely upon a messenger.
That [nature], however, should be known as both external and internal within the Kaulika lineage.
First, I shall describe the auspicious characteristics of the female messengers (dūtīs) from the perspective of the external.
Even so, listen to the certainty regarding them within the inner circle:
[they are] a mother, a daughter, a sister, one born together, and likewise one of the lowest caste.
The washerwoman, the leather-worker, and the outcaste woman who is his elder sister—along with these Śaktis, he should partake of food, drink, and edibles. (15.128)
If the practitioner desires supreme accomplishment, he must perform the eating of the sacrificial pap (caru) together with both those of the lowest castes and the twice-born. || 15.129 ||
The Goddess said:

"O Lord, what has been spoken is contemptible and improper for those who speak according to the scriptures, since that which is the conduct of beasts has been declared by you, O Supreme Lord. (15.130)
O Great Lord, when that secret of the husbands was revealed, it was truly a marvel.
Bhairava said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly wise one! These questions are indeed very difficult to obtain."
I shall speak in brief out of affection for you, O leader of the gods;
she is indeed that very Śakti who exists as the form of the womb of the universe. (15.132)
For all that has arisen—the entirety of speech and the world of moving and non-moving things—is [produced] by you;
therefore, O Supreme Goddess, you are celebrated by me as "Mātā" (the Mother).
The daughter is the source from which the world is drawn forth;
indeed, the daughter is called the second sister. (15.134)
The supreme, subtle form of Bhaga arose together with the Self; it is eternally established in a state of non-duality, like the heat of fire. || 15.135 ||
In that very same way, the goddess who possesses supreme faith and whose form is the Bhaga [is present].
O Supreme Goddess, O Umā, there is indeed one woman of the lowest caste who is established [there], free from passion and darkness—a great washerwoman. (15.139)
One who moves by means of the vital parts and is colored by her own limb is the one to be accomplished known as Carmakārī; and now the Mātaṅgī is described. || 15-140 ||
Always and eternally abiding within the self, established in the final state of the song, Mātaṅgī is declared to be the messenger (dūtī); likewise, she is called Agrajanmī.
Among all scriptures indeed, the state of being unconditioned (*ayojyatva*) is the most excellent; there, nothing else whatsoever exists, for the primordial power is *manonmanī*. (15.142)
She who is celebrated as the First-born (Agrajanmī) is the supreme Amṛtamālinī;
O Goddess, these are declared to be her synonyms—she is Śakti, whose nature conforms to that [of the Absolute]. (15.143)
O Dear One, those fools who practice without knowing the power born of the body that resides in external locations are evil-minded beasts. (15.144)
* * * * * Those who are impossible [to find] and who mock the vows of Śiva—whatever eating and drinking there may be, it must indeed be done together with them. (15.145)
Thus disciplined, one should always remain with a mind delighted by the bliss of wine;
for my supreme power has colored the three worlds.
For that state of equality with bliss is indeed accomplished for one whose mind is intoxicated by the wine of joy; there is no doubt about this, just as Bhairava has declared. 15.147

For the yogi who is satisfied by the nectar of knowledge and has accomplished all that was to be done, there is nothing whatsoever left to be performed; if there were anything remaining, he would not be a knower of reality.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, the Section on Conduct, in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, the Great Tantra of the Bhairava Current, belonging to the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), comprising seventy million verses. 15.
The Goddess said:

"O Lord, you have described the supreme and subordinate goddesses as they are situated in their respective seats; however, those who reside within the five enclosures have not been known by me in their true nature. (16.1)
O beloved, out of grace, please tell me— who am bowed before you— the specific characteristics, locations, and origins of those [energies].
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the auspicious characteristics of the Yoginīs, as well as their specific creation upon the surface of the moving world. (16-3)
Viśvā, Viśveśvarī, Hā, Raudrī, Vīranāyikā, Ambā, and Pūrvā—these are the names of the Yoginīs, you who have arisen from the best of boons. (16.4)
In the sky consisting of Brahman, upon a six-petalled lotus situated on a trident,
vast and the color of yellow pigment, possessing excellent luster and supremely radiant.
In that stainless, supreme lotus called Amṛta, the highest auspiciousness, the goddesses reside upon the trident; they are of supreme form and great splendor.
Abounding in infinite qualities, pervasive, and arisen from that,
they abide in the midst of nectar, perfectly full and undisturbed.
The creators of the Vaishnava creation are endowed with supreme splendor;
no distinction exists among them, for their rays are not of a single form.
The Bindu arises from the tip of the navel; the Lord, situated within the womb of Śakti, revolves like a whirling firebrand, face downwards, for the sake of creation. (16.9)
When Māyā is agitated by the Bindu, she is known in an instant to attain straightness;
she should be understood as that which is called Nāda, while the supreme power (kalā) is that which is called Sāda.
And that [wisdom] should be known as twofold, being based upon the reality of wind;
for its many divisions are clearly revealed here by their names. (16.11)
The supreme Mother is established in sound; she is Suśivā, possessed of great luster.
Residing in the midst of immortal nectar, she is Ghoṣiṇī, the leader of yoga.
Vyāpikī, Vyāptikāntā, and Śivā are to be known by name;
these twelve are declared to be supported by the qualities of the principle of sound (śabdatattva). || 16-13 ||
Now I shall briefly declare the names of those known as "Contact":
Capalā, Cañcalā, Tīvrā, Vāyuvegā, and Manonugā. (16.14)
Mṛgadhvajā, Spṛśanī, Tvagratā, Śubhā, Jīvanī, Sarpiṇī, and Māyā—these Yoginīs reside in the wind element. (16.15)
There they perform manifold activities by the thousands;
twenty-four names are principal, based upon their qualities. (16.16)
Through the differentiation of each single one, there are tens of millions upon tens of millions;
no measure at all can be found, for these deities are as subtle as atoms.
I shall describe, in brief, those who dwell in the enclosure of fire:
Tejovatī, Tejamātā, Tejinī, and Tejarūpiṇī. || 16-18 ||
Tejonidhi, Tejāḍhyā, and the supreme Tejaḥkāntā are remembered; likewise, Tejasvī and Tejoyoninidhi are known by their function as light. (16–19)
The [eleventh] illuminates both fire and fear, while the twelfth indeed sustains fire;
having attained Rūpavatī, one becomes handsome, and Rukmiṇī is the destroyer of the Ruru deer.
The yogin is beautiful in form and possessed of beauty; his virtues are endowed with beauty.
He is born of beauty, is beautiful himself, can assume any form at will, and is dear to Ruru. || 16-21 ||
Rundhanī and Rūpasaṃpannā are the fourteenth, known as Saṃparkā; then there is the one called Sparśā, and Anantā—these arise from the qualities of youth. (16–22)
But by means of that which is called *tejas*, the thirty-six [principles] have reached the state of infinity in Pradhāna;
now hear from me the name of that which is known as the covering of water. (16–23)
Listen to me as I describe that which is endowed with four qualities:
it is Varuṇā, Vāruṇī, Svacchā, Śivā, Anī, and Kṣālanī. (16-24)
Jalāruhā, Jaladhātrī, Ambhā, Ambhavatī, Ambhasthā, Ambhavāhā, Ambhiṣā, and the supreme Salilā. (16–25)
Salilā, Salilormiṇyā, she whose form is the fluid of water; Draviṇī, Drāviṇī, Drohī, Varṣaṇī, and Meghapātanī. || 16-26 ||
Meghadhārā, Vṛṣṭi, Paryantā, Priyavādinī, Śasyamātā, Dhānyā, Prarohī, and Udakā—these are the others. (16–27)
Udakṣṇatā, Udadmohā, Udakeśvaryā, Parāmbhasā, Ambhoruhā, Ambhavatī, Ambhasthā, and Ambhadāyikā. || 16-28 ||
Ambhovidhā, Ambhavatī, Jaladā, Jalavāhinī, Jaloruhā, Pravāhā, Vṛṣṭikārī, and Supātanī. (16.29)
Sveda, Pravāha, and the others—these forty-eight Yoginīs, born from the Unstruck Sound (anāhata), are proclaimed as the primary ones. (16.30)
There would be no end to their number, for they exist in the form of subtle atoms;
O lady rich in asceticism, I shall describe the earthly [elements] according to their fivefold division.
All phenomena should be understood according to their gross and subtle modes of activity;
the gross ones consist of many varieties, while the subtle ones I shall now describe to you. (16.32)
Dharaṇī, Dhāraṇī, Raudrī, Rundhatī, and Nirodhanī;
Dhātrī, Dhārāvatī, Dhārī, Dhararūpā, and Dharodvahā. || 16-33 ||
She is the mother of dharma, the best among those who uphold it;
she is the earth, and beyond that, the source of wealth, the womb of wealth, the earth, and the sustainer of wealth.
She is the sustainer of the world, the mistress of wealth, the sovereign of riches, the upholder of the earth;
she is fond of wealth, the primordial source of prosperity, the beloved of Vasu, and the medicinal herb of Vasu.
She is the earthly one, she is named Earth, the mistress of the earth;
she possesses vast enjoyments, she reaches to the ends of the earth, she is the sovereign Pṛthu, and she has a broad womb.
Rich in earth (*pārthivāḍhyā*), because she is the earth (*pṛthvī*); the protectress of the earth (*kṣoṇīkṣā*), the imperishable (*avyayā*);
the destroyer (*kṣapaṇī*), the one whose belly is the earth (*kṣodarī*), the one who possesses honey (*kṣaudrī*), and the agitated (*kṣubhitā*). || 16-37 ||
The vast one, the dark one, the earth, and Urvaśī—she who transcends both;
she who leads away, she who protects, the protector, the mother of cattle, and she whose rays are cows. || 16-38 ||
Gaurī, Gomatikā, Goptā, Gorasā, Guṇāgraṇī, Godhānā, Gomavatī, Godampā, and Gosamikṣakā. || 16-39 ||
Gopurā, Goruhā, Gaṅgā, Govatsā, Gosahasrikā, Gaurī, Gauravatsā, Kaṭhinā, and Kaṭhinoruhā. (16.40)
Dṛṣṭi, Piṇḍā, Sugandhā, Pāvanī, Parā, Pārvatī, Himajā, Gaurī, Girijā, Śailajā, and Anagā. (16.41)
Kṛśodarī, Śubhāsyā, Sarasvatī, Sumāninī, Maṅgalā, Bālacandrā, Sumanā, and Manovatī. (16.42)
Vegā, Vegavatī, Śāntā, Kāntā, Kāntikarā, Purā, Kāmarāgā, Viramyā, Raktā, and the supreme Raktānugā. (16.43)
Śānti, Svasti, Svadhā, Tṛpti, Śrī, Lakṣmī, and Suvratā; Prabhā, Jyotsnā, and likewise another, Manovatī. (16.44)
Established through these and many other numerous synonyms,
the one supreme source alone has attained an infinity of infinities.
The principles beginning with earth and ending with space, and those [energies] as well, are established according to their pervasion in the form of their respective emanations. (16.46)
O Goddess, those immeasurable yoginīs have been described to them;
O fair-faced one, these yoginīs should be understood as being the very nature of reality (tattva).
Following the will of Śiva, these immensely powerful ones, swift as thought,
wander throughout the entire domains of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra.

Others, O Dear One, are born of noble lineage, born from a womb, born of the *kula*, born of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*), born of the fields (*kṣetra*), and especially those who move through the sky (*khecarāḥ*). || 16-49 ||

The heroic mistress (vīranāyikā) born of noble family (kulajā) is to be known through seven divisions; she who is born from the womb (yonijā) and possesses form (rūpiṇī) is recorded as being in the mixed (saṃkīrṇa) and the pure (sandohe) [categories]. These, moreover, exist in many ways through primary and secondary divisions.
The Yoginīs should be known as having a divine portion and as the promoters of divine knowledge;
the Sandohas, however, have a mixed portion of deities and are essentially composed of that [divine nature]. (16.52)
Furthermore, those which are called *rūpikās* are known as the minor portions;
I shall describe to you how they exist through their various divisions and combinations.
Beginning with Brahmāṇī and ending with Yogeśī,
forty-nine goddesses are situated, one in each of the seven groups of seven.
I shall now declare their divisions; listen to them accordingly:
the Śākinīs, the Śūdra-Śākinīs, the Sāvyas, the Sāvarikās, and the Śivās.
O sinless one, seven types of deities for the yoginīs are recorded;
O leader of heroes, those who are first perfected as yoginīs must be known. (16.56)
The deity who has attained yoga must indeed be known by the practitioner;
she is one alone, the supreme Yoginī, auspicious and consisting of all phonemes. (16.57)

The supreme power (parā kalā), consisting of the letters from *na* to *pha*, abides as the very form of the Great Lord of all phonemes (sarvavarṇamaheśa), constituting half the body of Bhairava. (16.58)
Indeed, those who dwell upon the trident of Bhairaveśa sport within his heart, bringing about both creation and dissolution. (16.59)
Others, however, are established as qualified [deities], all-pervading and auspicious. || 16-60 ||
I shall declare their locations; listen, O large-eyed one:
in Kulūtā, in Araṇyeśa, in the land of Sindh, and in Nageśvara.
In Samudrakukṣi, Asurāṣṭra, Pretapurī, and the Himalayas; in Kaṃcī, Oḍumbaka-viṣaya, Kaliṅga, Kauśala, and Sthala. (16.62)
Likewise at Triśaṅku, in Oḍra, Kāmarūpa, and Mālava;
at Devikoṭa, Sudhārāma, Godāvarī, and Taṭerbuḍa.
In these regions, whatever maidens or women there are with moist wombs, they are all capable of assuming any form at will and move with the speed of thought.
In the remaining places, there are the Śākinīs and the terrible Mothers who have arisen;
the six Yoginīs are in Kulūtā, and the Śecamātṛs are in the forest.
In the land of Sindh, they are sisters; in Naraśa, they are the leaders of the family; in Samudrakukṣi, they are the Kāpilyas; and in Saurāṣṭra, they are the household deities.
The Mahākālīs are in Pretapurī; the Rūpiṇīs are on Mount Himavat; Ambā is proclaimed to be in Kāñcī; and the Mṛtas are in the region of Laṅpāka. (16.67)
In Kaliṅga, she is Vratadhāriṇī; in Kauśala, she is Piśitāśanā; in Ka*vākyāsthala, she is proclaimed as Trisaṃnyāmarā. || 16-68 ||
In both regions, there are Śākinīs, Nāyikās, and Vīranāyikās; others are Yoginīs and Arucaparas, who are divine, fierce, and exceedingly powerful. (16.69)
These Mothers of the World roam upon the earth, enjoying the pleasures of kings;
by them all is pervaded equally, including the mountains, forests, and groves.
Divine beings of great splendor, possessing divine sovereignty and great power—I shall declare their names; listen to how they are. (16.71)
Bhaṭṭā, Yogī, Citrākṣī, Viśālā, and another, Dāmoṭī, Kahlāṭī, Daṃṣṭriṇī, and likewise Piṅgalā. || 16-72 ||
The rootless, the root-destroyer, the leaf, the root-slayer, and likewise the other known as the root-producer—these should be understood as life-taking [plants]. (16.73)
Dhṛti, Chundarī, Raktākṣī, the Rākṣasī, Ghorā, Śūkarī, and another named Balotkaṭā—[these were] likewise [there]. || 16-74 ||
Piśācā, Nṛtyanā, Pīḍā, Vyāghrī, Siṃhī, Halāyudhā, Haśanī, Grasanī, Mohanā, and Priyadarśanā. (16.75)
Trāsanī, Virūpākṣā, Vikaṭā, and Saindhavā; likewise Sulocanā, Mahālakṣmī, Mahātejas, and Suvarcasā. (16.76)
Sumukhā, Campakā, Vimalā, Karaṅkiṇī, Suvarṇā, Bhāvikambā, Viṣalākṣī, and Tiḍiṇḍimā. (16.77)
Kampā, Nayikā, Maṇḍanā, Trilocanā, Sukeśī, Lambakarṇā, Utphullā, and another, Diṇḍikā. (16.78)
Mahāpīṭhā, likewise Ākarṣā, Vidhṛti, and another, Kūṣmāṇḍī, Mohanī, Mahāvaktrā, and Sanātanā. (16.79)
Sunāthā, Siddhikārī, and another, Siṃhavaktrā; Ānandā, Vāmanā is proclaimed, and likewise another, Vilambikā. (16.80)
Svacchā, Śāśvatā, Jñeyā, Santuṣṭā, Ambinī, as well as Māninī, Aparā, Jñeyā, and Citramukhī—these should likewise be known. (16.81)
Samvarā, Tatodaryā, Subodhā, Padminī, and likewise Vībhatsinī are proclaimed; these seventy-seven are thus celebrated.
Proclaimed in the family traditions (kulāmnāya) as distinct descents, by these [energies] the entire world—including its mountains, forests, and groves—is pervaded. (16.83)
Perfectly endowed with the Great Yoga, long-lived, swift as thought, they can indeed assume any form at will and are free from the fear of old age and disease. || 16-84 ||
O beloved, they behold the entire earth as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of their hand;
yet each acts within its own place according to the power of its own specific function.
The Bhaṭṭās and Yogīs are briefly to be known as residing in their respective places:
Citrākṣī resides in Koṭivarṣanibhāsī, and [the other] in Alakāpura. (16.86)
Viśālā and Jayantī are indeed in Kaśmīra, as is Daṃṣṭriṇī;
Vāmaliptā and Dāmoṭī are in Kahlāṭa, and Vāraṇāpurī is in Vāraṇāpura.
The auspicious Yoginī Piṅgalā dwells in Kāmarūpa,
and likewise, O Dear One, Mūlā dwells in the region of Vāṭavya.
And that which is called Mūlatarā dwells in the southern region;
indeed, in the city of China, there are those who strike at the root. || 16-89 ||
O Vīranāyikā, the speech that causes root destruction dwells in Agnā;
O sinless one, the life-taking Dhṛti is established in Mālava.
O Goddess of the gods, Chucchundarī dwells there in Saurāṣṭra, as does another, Karaṅkiṇī; likewise, Trāsanī dwells at Śaphalā.
Ujjainī and Rākṣasī are established there, and Virūpākṣā is likewise situated;
Raktākṣī dwells in Kalaśāpura, without a doubt. (16.92)
Likewise, there is Ghorā at Gaṅgādvāra, Balotkaṭā at Carmaraṅga,
Śūkarī in Campā, and Piśācinī in Magadha.
O fair-faced one, Nṛtyanā resides eternally in Kurukṣetra;
Pīḍanā is in Laṅkā, and Vyāghrī is likewise in Druviḍa.
Halāyudhā and Siṃhī are likewise established in Koṅkaṇa;
Hasanī is on the bank of the Śyāmā, and Grasani is in Pārśva.
Mohanā dwells in Darada, which is honored by heroes;
Priyadarśanā always delights in the region of Lampāka. (16.96)
Vikaṭā dwells in Citrakūṭa, Saindhavā in Kanyakubja,
and the beautiful Sulocanā resides there in Ḍāhalā.
Mahālakṣmī is in Kollagiri, and Mahātejas is in Kauśala; [79a] the one named Sumukhī is in Turuṣka, while Campakā is in the land of Oḍra.
Vimalā dwells in Bhillamāla, while Suvarṇā resides in Aṭṭahāsaka; and the goddess Viyadvikā always dwells in Vṛddhamāna.
Viśālākṣī is in Jālandhara, and Śiṣṭimā is in Oḍiyāna;
Mahākāyā is in Pūrikā, and Vīranāyikā is in Ayodhyā. (16.100)
In Saṃtrāna she is named Maṇḍinī, and in Kaliṅga she is Trilocanā;
in Rāṣṭrā she is Śukeśī, and in Nāsika she is Laṃbakarṇā.
Kha-ulle, Utphullā, Eḍikā, Aṇḍin, and Ḍiṇḍimā are remembered [as residing there];
at Pratiṣṭhāna dwells Mahāpṛṣṭhā, who is possessed of great strength.
In Elāpura, Karṣā is likewise [located]; in Malaya, Vidhṛti is remembered; in Vatsagulma, Kūṣmāṇḍī; and in Bhogavardhana, Mohanā. (16.103)
She is Mahāvaktrā at Mahendra, Sanātanā at Pūrṇagiri, Sunāmā at Mādrīpura, and she is considered Siddhadā at Śrīpīṭha. (16.104)
Siṃhavaktrā is in Siṃhala, and Ānandā is in Karohana;
Vāmanā is in Kośavardhana, and Vilambikā is in Mātṛdharma. || 16.105 ||
Khasthā is in Nāgapura, and Śāśvatī is in Dharāpura; Añjūkyā is in Saṃtoṣā, and likewise Āśvinī is in Mṛgukaccha. (16.106)
On Arbuda she is named Māninī, on Vindhya she is Citramukhī; on Sahya she is named Sahyodarī, and on Samavara she is Morakhaṇḍikā.
Subodhā is considered to be at Vadārī-kaccha, Padminī at Capalā, and Vībhatsī at the edge of the ocean; now hear concerning Sānugatā in relation to Mātṛ. (16.108)
The Mothers who dwell in the seven worlds are situated everywhere:
Bhaṭṭā, Ghorā, Piśācī, Raktākṣī, and likewise Rākṣasī.
Virūpākṣā, Vikaṭā, Saindhavā, Sulocanā, Mahālakṣmī, Mahātejā, Sumukhā, and another likewise; || 16-110 ||
She is indeed remembered as Cāmuṇḍā; these twelve have been proclaimed:
Patrābalotkaṭā, Pīḍanā, and likewise Trāsanī.
Campakā, Vimalā, and likewise Karaṅkiṇī;
Suvarṇākṣā is well-known, and another is Viḍaṅgikā. (16.112)
Viśālākṣī, Ḍiṇḍimā, and Mahācampā as the leader—
these thirteen, O fair-faced one, have been declared by me to be portions of Māhendrī.
Śūkarī, Prāṇahārī, and likewise Chucchundarī;
Daṃṣṭriṇī, Maṇḍanā, and another, Trilocanā. (16-114)
Sukeśī, Lambakarṇā, Utphullā, Ḍiṇḍipṛṣṭhakā, Ākarṣā, and Sāmyaṃśā—these eleven are proclaimed. (16.115)
Mohanā, Nāpinidāmoṭī, Vyāghrī, Siṃhā, Halāyudhā, Dhṛti, Kuṣmāṇḍikā, and another eternal one, Mohanī. (16.116)
These ten, possessing great mouths and great strength, are portions of Viṣṇu: Hasanī, Grasani, Viśālā, and Priyadarśinī. (16.117)
Sunāthā, Siddhikārī, Ānandā, Siṃhavakrā, Vāmanā, Vilambī, Svacchāyā, and likewise Śāśvatā. (16.118)
O fair-faced one, thirteen portions of Kaumāryā have been described:
Kahloṭī, Nṛtyanā, Citrākṣī, and likewise Piṅgalā; || 16-119 ||
Aśvinī, Māninī, Citrā, Saṃvarā, Satodarā, and Rudrāṃśā—these indeed are proclaimed as the nine [Nakṣatras], in brief. (16.120)
She should be known as Mūlā, Mūlatarā, and Mūlaghātikā; likewise as Mūlakārī, Saṃbodhā, Padminī, and Vibhatsinī. (16.121)
O fair-faced one, these seven Brahmāṇḍas have been fully described;
indeed, they are known to possess a threefold nature, consisting of sattva, rajas, and tamas.
Those who possess portions of Brahmā, portions of Indra, and portions of the gods are considered to be of the *sāttvika* nature;
O fair-faced one, those belonging to the lineages of Kaumārī and Vaiṣṇavī are of the *yakṣa-sattva* type.

Vārāhī, Caṇḍikā, and Raudrī are born of the Kula; they belong to the Rākṣasa and Sāttvika [natures], are endowed with the power of divine yoga, and are suitable according to the divisions of the thirty deities.
