For these [deities], when worshipped with their name-mantras, become bestowers of fruits in this world for the practitioner whose self has been cultivated through his own lineage, O fair-faced one. (16.125)
And whatever other fierce goddesses of terrifying appearance have been specified,
Mahāmanthānarudra is the leader of their mandala.
I shall now describe to you their division into ten and eighteen types;
they exist through various modes of livelihood, all of them terrible and greedy for meat.
By these very beings, this world of the moving and the non-moving is pervaded;
I shall describe it briefly according to the division of the four yugas.
Deities endowed with physical perfection are of two kinds: those born of noble lineages and those born of human lineages; hear now of their respective origins.
Heroines born of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes, having married after the twenty-seventh year, know that state. (16.130)
Born from other lineages, the Sākinīs and Rudramātṛs [afflict] one who is distressed by sound, fear, or likewise tormented by diseases. (16.131)
They strike with crushing force and dry up the fat and flesh;
for the sake of transforming one's form, these supreme Mothers roam about.
The deities previously described are established in the world of the Mothers,
[honored] by the gods, the Siddhas, and by sages whose wealth is their asceticism.
By their power, those who desire honor are honored in the world;
when consuming the sacrificial pap (caru), their form shall become motionless on the path.
That is the accomplishment, that is the supreme state; for its sake, there is reverence for the *golaka*.
O lady of excellent hips, when such [beings] exist in these very lineages (*kula*) in this manner, || 16-135 ||
One attains this very state immediately after the heroic state (vīrabhāva):
the serpent-maiden Rudragomikā, the cave, and the cow-faced woman. (16.136)
Kekarā, Kālarātrī, and Bhaṭānāgeśvarī—
these Yoginīs, worshipped by the gods, will appear in the Kṛta Yuga.
Mālā, Durgā, Śivā, Caṇḍā, Vāmanī, Harṣaṇī, Prabhā,
Suparṇā, and Rukmiṇī are the Kula-mothers in the Tretā age.
Harṣatārā, Suvarṇā, Prabhā, Mohā, Śāntā, Haraṇī, and Pālanī—these, O Hara, are born of my yoga in the Dvāpara age. || 16-139 ||
Badhumālī, Bhānumatī, Śrīvalā, Kapilaprabhā, Muktā, Muktāvalī, and indeed the supreme Bhānunī by her [name]. (16.140)
In the Kali age, these will come to be, as well as others in every household:
Haritā, Gomukhī, Godhā, Dhātrī, Vīranakhī, and Valā.
In the Kali age, these women born of the Caṇḍāla caste will become [leaders];
they shall be known by names such as Mudrā, as well as others like Śivā and Aśivā. (16.142)
And there will be those who have been born; their number is not known, whether through the perfect realization of the circle of Mothers, or through the refinement of their ascetic penance. (16.143)
Some men attain this unsurpassed perfection:
Hari, Vāmanaka, Siṃha, Mahākāla, and Bhairava. (16.144)
These five are the Vīrarudras, the protectors of all tantras:
Śakuni, Sumati, Nanda, Gopāla, and Pitāmaha.
At the end of the Kṛta age, there will be other lords of the Yoginīs:
Bali, Balinanda, Darśagrīva, Hara, and Haya.
At the end of the Tretā age, their lords were Suśrī, Gomukha,
Bhīṣma, Pāka, Sikaṇḍin, the sage, and likewise Akhaṇḍala.
In the Kṛta age [there were] Śakra and Śānaka; in the Tretā, Ṣaṇḍa; in the Dvāpara, Mātṛjambhaka;
and [in the Kali age,] Nabha, Bhānu, Ananta, Helārāja, and Mahābala. || 16.148 ||
Likewise Bhīma, Arjuna, Droṇa, Mahārāja, Sundara, Bhasmarāja, Kalpāṇa, and Madhusindūraka. (16–149)
Catura and Vāmana, as well as Mātṛsāyojyagāmin, are proclaimed to be the one hundred [Manus] at the end of that cycle of four yugas. || 16.150 ||
And how is it that all those goddesses, being worshipped by practitioners who contemplate the scriptures, are satisfied with the supreme true essence of the scriptures? 16-151.
But all of them are lords of their respective lineages according to the division of the four ages; there are heroic kings, and others who are lords of the Mothers.
Ucchuṣma, Vāmadeva, and Ghughuśa as the third, and Mahākāla as the fourth—these are the destroyers of the Yoginī-vīreśas. (16.153)

With the flowers of meditation and the like, refined by the months and the ritual drinking and so forth, the self, free from agitation and unwearied in its effort, attains extinction there through the final rite. (16.154)
To him they quickly bestow the supreme true essence of the Tantra;
this great and most wonderful [teaching] is for the sake of the triple accomplishment of recitation and fire-offerings.
I have indeed related to you this supreme, transcendent merit,
which has been proclaimed as the true nature of the deities and the cause of spiritual accomplishment.
I shall now declare the division of others which indicates distinct meanings;
listen, O Pārvatī, to that in its fivefold summary according to the truth. (16.157)
But in brief, their presiding lord is established in five forms:
Hari, Vāmanaka, Siṃha, Mahākāla, and Bhairava.
These five are indeed proclaimed as heroes, the lords of the families:
the Śākinīs, the Rudraśākinīs, the Sādhyas, the Sāmarikās, and the Śivās.
And the Yoginīs are even more supreme than those [others], by whom the entire world is pervaded—in every region, as well as in every village, city, crossroads, and house. (16.160)
As soon as they are born, they arise through reliance upon the family-siddhi;
by means of the adventitious rite, the yoginīs are consecrated by yoga. (16.161)
Those endowed with all the rules (samaya) have their bodies born from complete knowledge;
the others, having acquired the rules, abide in the performance of the mantra-vow.
He performs no recitation, fire-offering, worship, or observance of vows;
having drawn them in by deceit, he who consists of base creatures always drinks [their essence]. (16.63)
One who, out of greed for the sake of transforming physical form, causes an animal to be slaughtered, should be known as a Śākinī; she always delights in fierce places. (16.164)
She who knows the movements of the minds of others, who effects the transformation of form, and who is greedy for life and death, should be known as that Rudraśākinī. (16.165)
Such a woman is to be known as one who is to be won over; she delights in the worship of the Lord and follows his conduct.
Indeed, they do not cause anyone to be killed, yet they taste everything through a pretext.
Others, however, should be known as being with form, their minds fixed upon the mantra;
they consume the five nectars and cause humans to be carried away. (16.167)
They roam the earth in an instant, assuming manifold forms;
others, through the power of yoga, are knowers of the three periods of time.

Likewise, those women who are endowed with the eight qualities, whose inner sanctuaries are contained within others, who are auspicious, devoted to mantra and meditation, are declared to be Śivās. (16.169)
Through yoga, or through austerity, or by the vision of one's own mantra,
they attain the state of the Yogīśvarīs, as well as by the power of the animal-sacrifice (paśu).
A person who knows all the Mothers shall obtain that very fruit.
Furthermore, I shall fully explain the sevenfold division of the Śivas.
Those who are devoted to men of the four castes are the best among the Śākinīs; others, who are flesh-eaters, should be known as those established in low births.
She who is of moderate stature, fair-limbed, and round-faced, having perceived what has passed, would quickly and excessively relish the blood. (16–173)
Having heard the sound, the supreme and fierce goddess tastes the nectar;
she should be known as white and fair, large-bodied, and possessing gentle eyes. (16-174)
A woman who is reddish-white in complexion, with shriveled yet firm breasts,
drinks blood of every caste while striking herself with her garment.
Another woman is dark-complexioned, always laughing loudly;
she drinks blood while laughing, ever delighting in the slaughter of living beings.
Another, with a dark complexion, red eyes, and a fondness for quarreling—
this Rudrāntyā draws out blood and strikes at the vital organs of living beings.
The large-eyed Karkaṭī, dark-limbed and always arrogant, drinking blood while singing, would vomit it up again incessantly. (16-178)
Another, Prasuptā, should cause [the victim] to eat; Sārayantī devours the animal.
Śirālā, Vikṛtā, Ghorā, Dhvāṅkṣakeśī, and Praroṣaṇī [are likewise]. (16.179)
Having gone to the cremation ground at night, one should draw forth much blood;
seized by that [spirit] as a sacrificial animal, you will perish very quickly. (16–180)
I shall further explain the sevenfold classification of the inauspicious ones;
by knowing which, a hero becomes an expert in their families.
Śākinī, Cūṣikā, Cumbikā, Patralehikā, Uccheṣī, Nakracūṣī, and likewise Ūrdhvaniḥśvāsikā. || 16-182 ||
And their function, O beloved, is indeed that of exhaling downward;
among them, the Śākinīs are considered the most excellent, while the rest are remembered as even more terrible.
But she who constantly defiles blood of every caste, whether he is walking or standing still, is known as a *dūṣikā*. (16.184)
She who, while kissing, devours a child—whether it be a son, a grandson, a brother, or even one who is dead—is to be known as a *cumbikā*. (16.185)
Covering her face with a leaf, she always drinks nectar;
she is known as Patralekhā, who is difficult to restrain and possesses great power.
Having become naked at night and having urinated while performing a circumambulation,
she who constantly consumes [the substance] with her hair loose shall effect an attraction.
She should be known as Ucchuṣmikā by practitioners who are devoted to the heroes;
gazing at the tip of her nose, she always drinks that which is nectar.
She should be known as Nakracūṣī (Crocodile-Sucker), while the other has her face turned upward;
she who drinks with a single inhalation is indeed the Ūrdhvaniḥśvāsikā (Upward-Breather).
She should always go to another's house at night naked,
covering her face with a cloth and keeping her head bowed down.
She constantly drinks blood and has downward breath;
O Great Goddess, I shall further explain their classification according to how it is.
I shall explain to you correctly the three types of *cūṣikā* (suction instruments):
that which rotates along the side and that which draws out blood. (16.192)
That [mudrā] situated at the side should be known as *tuṇḍā*, and likewise another as *moṭī*;
one who is unwearied should perform the twisting of the mouth three times. (16–193)
O Goddess, one will always draw forth blood quickly; of this there is no doubt.
O lady of excellent complexion, the *cūṣikā* has been declared to be of three kinds.
The *cumbikā* is to be known as twofold: *karālī* and likewise *daṃturā*.
*Karālī* has formidable teeth and may pull [the object] at will. (16–195)
She who smells while in the form of a bird is Danturā; of this there is no doubt.
I shall now duly describe to you the three varieties of Patralehā.
The *kekarā*, *nalikā*, and *tantrī* are proclaimed as belonging to Raudrī.
One with squinting eyes and half-closed lids, holding blood, shall always attract [beings]. (16.197)
With a single-piped tube, with eyes half-closed, and with eyes always fixed and motionless, she presses upon her left lower lip. (16.198)
One should always attract the blood or else paralyze the victim;
this [practice] is declared to be threefold, and the *nakracūṣī* is of two kinds.
I shall describe to you the modes of livelihood known as Nidrikā and Cūṣikā;
by these means, a woman may at her will adorn sleeping embodied beings during the night.
Having made sleep her bed, she should intensely savor blood;
thereupon, she attains invisibility and a transformation of form. (16.201)
The Uccheṣikā [goddesses] are to be known as threefold by the practitioners:
the Cumbukās, the Uccās, the Riktās, the Trimūrtās, and likewise the Piśitāsanās. (16–202)
She who is constantly naked quickly reaches the end of her defilement;
having performed three circumambulations, she smells the fragrance right there.
Then consciousness arises, O fair-faced one, and not otherwise;
having passed urine three times in the three locations, beginning with the urine, one should circumambulate [the deity] clockwise. (16.204)
In front of the house, at its side, and behind it, he should do this constantly;
thereafter, he attains invisibility and the transformation of his form.
Having performed circumambulation, another [practitioner] applies anointing oil to the limbs;
then one attains success, namely the transformation of form and so forth.
With feet turned upward, hair standing on end, and breathing upward in two ways, she who has her hair disheveled shall constantly attract the bound soul (paśu). (16.207)
She should be known as Ūrdhvakeśī (Upward-Haired) because she is fond of heroes;
with her head downward and her feet upward, she should perform circumambulations around the thread.
In this manner, O Hero, one should lead the sacrificial animal three times without agitation; I have thus declared to you this supreme Heart-mantra.
Regarding the downward-moving *niśvāsikā*, there are indeed three varieties:
*mūlahārī*, *vyāghrī*, and the third, *pecikā*.
The flesh-eater and the root-stealer, having taken a human skull,
should always prepare a thread therein and trace it three times with the tongue.
O Goddess, having become naked, one should always and constantly perform the attraction;
the tigress-like woman should cast the human hand into the lotus-vessel.
Having extracted that [mantra] at night, one draws in the sacrificial animal with it;
in this way, his success shall be achieved, O Goddess worshipped by heroes, and not otherwise. (16.213)
One should not cast a human bone into the water; rather, having marked three points with thread, one should cast it into the lotus pond while circling it clockwise. || 16-214 ||
One should lick it seven times with the tongue; then one shall attain perfection.
Thus, the eighteenfold division of the minor [tantras] has been described by me.
Adhocchāyī is a portion of Brahmā; Naktacūṣī belongs to Maheśvarī;
Cūṣikā is a portion of Viśākhā, while [the next] is a portion of Vaiṣṇavī, O Pārvatī. (16.216)
Patralekhī is declared to be Cāmuṇḍā, while Śā is Cumvikā;
and Ūrdhvaniśvāsikā, O fair-faced one, is Māhendrī. (16.217)
O Goddess praised by heroes, Ucchuṣmā, who is a portion of Vārāhī, has thus been described;
she leads before her the one who is devoid of the conduct of the observance (*samaya*). (16.218)
O Goddess, this supreme secret of the Mātṛkā-kula is most fierce; he shall not be long-lived, nor shall he possess sons. (16-219)
In extremely terrible regions, one is constantly tormented by practitioners of yoga;
therefore, a wise person should protect their entire wealth exceedingly, as they would their own life. (16.220)
O Goddess, listen as I tell you another lower commonality: the conduct of mortals born of worldly nature, which is beyond the reach of ordinary perception.
She who laughs with "hā hā" upon emerging from the courtyard of her own house and goes outside among the crowds should be known as belonging to the family of Śākinīs.
Having placed a flower at the feet of Brahmā, they stood facing him;
he whose eyes, with their pupils dilated, cast a glance upon them but once—[he is the one]. (16.223)
His first [mark] is the paternal instruction; he is indeed Raudrī and Vaiṣṇavī.
He possesses a forehead upon which two images are seen in his vision.
That *śākinī* may also laugh; she is proclaimed by these signs:
she does not direct her own gaze toward light, but casts it elsewhere.
Whether it be a woman or even a man, she who is to be known as belonging to that family is she who stands alone in a secluded, deserted place and laughs in amazement. (16-226)
If she sings, or weeps, or begins to dance, or shakes her limbs, then she is undoubtedly a Śākinī. (16.227)
O beloved, she who constantly goes to the cremation ground at night, during the twilight, at dawn, and at midday, should be known as one belonging to that [Śmaśānī] division.
One who knows the *samaya* and knows the mantras shall obtain the fruit according to his own desire;
and the hero, established in the rite of heroes, performs the action authorized by that [deity]. (16.229)
Whether in a village, a city, a forest, or even in a temple of the gods—I shall explain in truth the method by which they are perceived. (16.230)
Ḍūṃme ḍūṃme Mahākālī, and likewise Saṃhārā; she is to be conjoined with Viśvaśūla, and [she is] the other known as Vīramātā. (16–231)
"Come, come! The state of yawning, likewise for Brahmā by means of truth, for Viṣṇu, and for Rudra—these are remembered as the forty syllables. (16-232)
This supreme King of Mantras, possessing both beginning and end, brings about close proximity;
with this, one should scatter water with flowers in all directions. (16.233)
By this very [mantra], the goddesses established in the three worlds certainly proceed;
on earth, in the world-realm, in the presence of the Guardian and Śiva. (16-234)
Those [goddesses] who move in this sky and those who are praised by the gods—with them that hero, Maheśvara, shall then roam. (16.235)
This secret of the Guhyamātṛs is not known by anyone else in its true essence:
the letter *i* of Śākinī, joined with the hip (*nitamba*). (16-236)
Seated upon a trident-staff, blazing with its crest,
it is named Śākinī-hṛdaya, the very life-force of the vital points.
O lady of excellent limbs, by means of that [mantra] beginning with "Oṃ" and ending with "Namaḥ," all of them yawn and undergo *stobha* (paralysis) from every side.
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ— thus, in the midst of the *pretasāsani*,
this is the *marmavasatkriyā* for all the *yogeśvarīs*.
They stumble, they fall under control, and they become moist, with their wombs becoming sodden;
one should not act rashly, for that would be self-destructive.
And one should not give [this] to those of great intelligence, O Great Goddess, for the sake of testing them;
thus do they all move about in the world with fierce deeds that provide protection. (16-241)
O Goddess, in every world, and likewise in the worlds of the lords of the worlds, in all the intermediate realms, in celestial enjoyments, and in the waters; || 16-242 ||
What is to be done, what is inference, what was chosen, by whom, and what was performed;
what is the remnant, when it is smelled, death, birth, and life? || 16-243 ||
Those whose vision was obscured saw all that—whatever wealth there was in the world, whether new or beautiful and captivating—as if it were right in the palm of their hands. (16.244)
O lady of virtuous vows, by this rite, either a hero or even his sister who follows the dharma shall obtain all of that. (16.245)
Without a doubt, one obtains the fruit that has been described here;
it is categorized as inferior, middling, or superior, according to the influence of one's own respective portion.

There are seven types of mortal Yoginīs associated with the seven Mothers, who bestow knowledge and *caru* upon the *vīra* of their own *aṃśa*, that is, their own *kula*. Each Yoginī has specific lunar days (*tithi*) for meeting her.
Now, O Goddess, I shall tell you another supreme characteristic:
1] That woman who has the luster of a red or fair complexion, or who is of uniform color and has a slender waist; (16-247)
His face was like a lotus; his teeth were smooth and white, and his breasts were firm;
his thighs resembled the trunks of plantain trees and were most beautiful.
She who stands amidst waves of three folds, possessing a beautiful forehead and excellent luster, whose tresses are curled and whose temples are well-formed. (16.249)
She is exceedingly pure, very peaceful, and always fond of the sound of the Veda;
she is constantly devoted to white garments as well as to an upper cloth.
O Great Goddess, she was devoted to the gods and intent on the worship of the Brahmins, especially on the new moon day and on the first days of the lunar fortnights. || 16-251 ||
These are undoubtedly the sacred festivals (parvan) of the goddesses here;
likewise, [the worship of] the water-pot, the staff, the wooden staff, and the excellent deerskin.
One who draws a svastika on the hand and recites Vedic sentences—by these marks, they are to be known as those with a portion of Brahmā, who are sattvic deities. (16.253)
If one displays the end of the mudrā, then, O Goddess, she will become pleased; within six months, she will grant boons to the practitioner and bestow her own power upon him. (16.254)
O beloved, she who is partless (anaṃśā) yet issues a command within a year;
she who is white and fair (śuklagaurī), who is Gaurī herself with limbs well-proportioned, dense, and lush—[16.255].
She is tawny, with long hair, tawny eyes, and a radiant complexion;
on her forehead, three upward-pointing lines are visible, resembling tridents. (16.256)
She should be understood as one devoted to the ritual rules, intent upon the worship of Rudra, and [should serve] either a Samayika, a Putraka, an Ācārya, or even a Sādhaka. (16.257)
The woman who, filled with great curiosity, looks [upon him] and becomes angry—
that day, O Goddess, is like the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī) and like the festival known as Bhūti.
Having thus recognized her characteristics, one should display her mudrā:
either the trident, or the khaṭvāṅga, or the hand-drum (ḍamaruka), or the bull. (16.259)
Holding a sword and a dagger in his hand, he always grants the transmission of his own heroic portion.
O lady of excellent hips, one should predict the auspiciousness for another after three months;
as for the woman who has a yellowish-white complexion and is always fond of yellow garments, [she will attain her goal]. 16-261.
But Sumālinī was ever devoted to gardens and groves, always delighting in the celibate life; she was deep-toned like the cry of peacocks, pleasant in speech, and beautifully adorned.
The sixth lunar day, however, is her festival; it should be known, O lover of heroes.
Having thus understood with diligence, one should display the mudrā to her. (16-263)
One should display a spear, a bell, a banner, or even a body;
for the hero, this [vision] of the breath indeed bestows boons within six months.
O lady of excellent hips, the location of the other shall be indicated after a year;
as for the woman who is dark-complexioned, resembling the *atasī* flower, [she is the one]. (16.265)
She is eternally fond of yellow garments, passionate for wrestling, and addicted to wine, O lady of beautiful hips; she is the beloved of the lord of the Dānavas. (16.266)
Adorned with betel, flowers, and fine dress, exceedingly lustful, and dear to the Gaṇas,
she should always be known as one who has cast off shame and is constantly devoted to wandering.
Having understood this, the knower of mantras should display to her a mudrā,
such as the conch, the mallet, the deer-marked [bow], the discus, or indeed the pestle.
The goddess bestows boons upon one of her own lineage, while she ordains auspiciousness for one of a different lineage.
[5] She resembles crushed collyrium, is protruding-toothed, and has two teeth that are like plows. (16.269)
With pendulous breasts, a large body, thick proportions, and a dense luster, her eyes are slightly reddish; she is always merciless. (16.270)
O Goddess, she who is sword-like, free from desire, yet fond of quarreling, is declared to be a portion of Vārāhī;
one should cause her to receive the mudrā.
A staff, a mallet, a shield, a pestle, or even a mountain peak—
these he bestows as the supreme rite upon the hero of his own body.
And by serving even the other [mantra] for one year, that woman who has the luster of a campaka flower and is fond of variegated garments [attains success]. 16.273.
Constantly devoted to dance and song, she adorns herself with all ornaments;
she delights in stories of weapons and is fond of the vehicles of the world-guardians.
She is to be understood as Indrāṇī, distinguished by her characteristic marks;
she is to be understood on the eleventh day, for that is indeed the sacred festival—of this there is no doubt.
One should display the mudrās to him; then he will become pleased.
[These are] the vajra, the conch, the shield, the fly-whisk, the spear, and the goad. (16.276)
Then that goddess, the bestower of boons, will speak to you, the practitioner, even though you are without a portion [of the mantra], within six months through this worship. (16.277)
A woman who has white neck and lips, a long neck, and a thin belly;
who has sunken eyes, is pendulous, and has very long hands and feet.
She has pendulous breasts, is fleshless, eats much, and has honey-colored eyes;
she is intent on wandering at night, is unshakeable, and speaks the truth. (16.279)

She who is constantly devoted to the cremation ground, who delights in discourse on the state of the hero (vīrabhāva), whose hair stands erect, and whose radiance is like a blazing flame—she is undoubtedly a yoginī. (16.280)
O Dear One, one should display his mudrā as a skull-cup, or a trident,
or a khaṭvāṅga, or a hand-drum, or even a peacock-feather fan.
And he bestows the transmission upon his own heroic portion,
whether it be an oblation of cooked rice (caruka) or even an animal sacrifice, performed according to rule and in abundance, O Dear One.
For others, through swift service, [this] arises in half a year;
now listen to me as I describe its arising over the course of months. (16.283)
Those born of the *pīṭhas* [attain success] in eight years; those born of the *kṣetras* in twelve years;
those at the gate (*dvāra*) in sixteen years, O Goddess; and those born of the womb (*yonija*) in twenty-seven.
O Goddess of the Gods, listen now to their names and likewise their characteristics;
here, the names are recited according to the groups beginning with the northeast.
The eight groups beginning with 'a' are situated in the eight yogas;
O Dear One, there is one [group] of sixteen syllables, and five groups of five syllables each.
O Goddess, two [groups] of four syllables each are to be observed in sequence:
the Āpas, the Grahas, the Nāgas, the Yoginīs, and the Bhairavas. (16.287)
O Goddess of the Gods, the eight groups [of letters] arising from the mantra have been proclaimed;
those which are designated as the initial, medial, and final among the phonemes [are these]. (16-288)
The characteristics previously described for them should be understood by the best of practitioners;
[they are those] whose names proceed from the obstruction of the initial and final syllables. (16.289)
She should recognize her own portion; she should display that mudrā to him, O Goddess, as well as her own day, her own rising, her own direction, and the rising of her own planet.

He who abandons [the regular practice] and offers [only] on the eighth day will be ridiculed by the yogins. On the fourteenth and the seventh days, the others [the Mothers and the Yoginīs who embody them] are proclaimed to be present. (16–291)
The full moon day, the new moon day, the first lunar day (pratipad), the fourth,
the third, and the sixth are remembered as the days of Kaumārī.
The twelfth and the fourth days are proclaimed as the day of Vaiṣṇavī;
the fifth and the thirteenth days are remembered as the days of Indrāṇī. (16.293)
The ninth and the eleventh are indeed the days for Vārāhī;
the eighth and the second are recorded as the days for Cāmuṇḍā. (16.294)
7] O Dear One, the days of the Yoginīs are on the eighth and the tenth [tithis].
8] Dhvaja, Āditya, Ananta, and Īśānī are considered the Yoginīs. (16.295)
The mantra of one's own class, beautiful and named Bhairava, is proclaimed;
having reached this time, one should cause the *cchoṃmaka* to be bestowed.
I have described the characteristics of all the common siddhis;
hereafter, I shall proclaim the characteristics of those born of the sacred seats (pīṭha).
Regarding those born of the field, the gatekeepers, and those born of the womb as they truly are:
their nose is flattened, their conduct is emaciated, and they appear greasy with sinews.
No one should look upon Umā, for she is always engaged in divine service;
yet she is to be known as born from a womb—listen now to her signs.
Long hair is seen situated upon the upper lip;
having recognized this sign, one should display the yoni-mudrā.
She should display the counter-seal (pratimudrā) to the practitioner; she is known as Liṅgā.
Her hair is upright, she is exceedingly fierce, and her teeth are formidable. (16.301)
She always speaks with a musical tone, her limbs are firm, and her hands are like creepers; O fair-faced one, she is seen with unblinking eyes and a slightly hunched posture. (16.302)
A black line should be made on the cheek; there, the female gatekeepers (dvārapālikās) arise. Having clearly understood that [line], one should display the mudrās toward the directions.
He too shall give a counter-seal and display a slight smile;
O illustrious lady, this is the accomplishment of cessation for practitioners.
Long-nosed, emaciated, with parched limbs and tawny eyes, she has the gaze of a cat; most fierce, she stares fixedly at the corpse.
O beloved, she who has the speed of wind, is extremely fierce, always has warts and hairy limbs, and is slightly protruded-toothed, is born of the field (kṣetrajā).
Having understood that correctly from the beginning, one should demonstrate it below;
she who makes the sound of gnashing teeth is known as Kṣetrasambhavā.
The power of Rudra is eternally supreme, fragrant, and honey-pigmented;
she has a large belly, is ever-contented, crooked, and has hair standing upright.
With eyes slightly coppery, she bears the mark of a deer upon her body;
moving with swift speed, she does not look back at the practitioners who stand at the crossroads.
Having seen such a form, one should display an upward gaze, for it perceives the past, the present, and the future, as well as that which is beyond the senses. (16.310)
She should move her tongue and display a frown;
she is indeed to be known as one born of a sacred seat (pīṭhajā), arising from among the yoginīs. || 16-311 ||
One of fair complexion desires a very long battle;
one who is slightly reddish, with tawny eyes and a fragrant scent, is likewise [auspicious]. (16.312)
At dawn, O beautiful one, her complexion is glossy; at midday, it is somewhat lusterless;
and in the afternoon, its color is only faintly visible.
She becomes invisible at night and likewise during the day;
assuming a form through illusion, she shall be a Siddhi-yoginī.
One should give him one's own mudrā, with the little finger placed upon the crest;
she too should give the counter-mudrā, with her face distorted and positioned below.
Having understood this to be of such a nature, those born of the womb should be avoided by those of mental birth;
likewise, the gatekeepers are those born of the field, while the residents of the sacred seats are those born of the seat itself.
O fair-faced one, another [form] of Siddhayogeśvarī has been described by me;
thus have her characteristics been explained through many different modes. (16.317)
It is not known, O lady of excellent hips, without their grace;
for the goddesses, possessing mixed characteristics, are indeed difficult to discern as powers (śaktis).
O fair-faced one, he does not place trust even in his own son; he would rather be deprived of his life than reveal his secret. (16.319)
Success occurs at that very moment simply by the vision of the deity;
by the vision of the Yoginī alone, one obtains the sacrificial pap within a month.
O Goddess, O lady of excellent hips, when a Śākinī is seen, she bestows upon the practitioner here something that indeed effects the play of mantra. (16.321)
Those who are called gatekeepers, as well as those who reside in the assembly hall,
bestow their own respective knowledge upon the practitioner.
O Goddess, O Beloved, upon seeing the Kṣudrās, nothing at all occurs; for they are incapable and are intent upon binding and further binding.
Otherwise, like other mortals who act under the impulse of another, [one fails] in all vows, mantras, libations, and recitations. (16.324)
She who performs [this] and whose limb is restrained is considered a minor Śākinī;
they take on various forms in the mortal world and become vessels for affliction. (16.325)
Furthermore, O Goddess, upon the destruction of evil, they become lords of the mandala;
knowing this thus, O lady of excellent limbs, as it has been revealed in the scriptures. (16.326)
Therefore, one who desires their own welfare must indeed protect it in that manner.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, O All-pervading One, you have indeed described the characteristics of a Yoginī."
"But regarding their union according to reality, O Maheśvara, we shall explain it.
Bhairava said:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall declare how their union occurs. (16.328)
O Goddess, I shall likewise explain in truth that Bhairava Heart, which brings about the dissolution of the world, for the sake of the best of practitioners.
Constantly joined with that [passion], the goddesses' moistened vaginas become drenched;
they burn, they fall quickly, and many of them release their life-breath. (16.330)
They come under control without a doubt, having been scorched by the Bhairava-fire;
upon seeing a group of young women, one should meditate upon them with the heart. (16.331)
One should meditate on the multitude [of deities] situated in the center of the fire-maṇḍala, heated by the fire of Bhairava, thus restrained by the heart. (16.332)
Whatever Śākinīs come there, there is no doubt that they will recognize your prowess, even though this deed was performed by you [in secret]. (16.333)
Then the mantra-practitioner should dismiss [the deities] at that very moment and must not retain them;
otherwise, they will pierce the practitioner with their enraged minds. (16.334)
One should meditate on either a village or even a city situated in the center of the maṇḍala;
and at night, standing in a cremation ground, one should contemplate it as agitated and blazing with funeral cakes (piṇḍa).
O Goddess of the gods, while that place is being consumed by the most terrifying fire for half a moment, one should then perform recitation while meditating.
As many as thousands of Śākinīs come there and stand surrounding the practitioner, why have they been terrified by you? (16.337)
"Make this wicked person of evil conduct into a sacrificial animal and enjoy [him]!

He too must speak thus for the sake of worship: 'I have been offered by you. (16.338) The mantra-practitioner should cause them to give wine, parched grain, and meat, O lady of excellent hips, according to their desire; otherwise, he seeks a different motive. (16.339)
When they are all satisfied, they praise the practitioner who is firm in his vows;
they bestow a certain measure of wrath by which the mantra becomes manifest.
Having seen the mass of corpses as a single lump in the form of a vajra,
that Great-Souled One drew in that multitude with it while they were being consumed by fire.
O leader of heroes, there is no doubt that the Śākinīs, whether they be powerful or otherwise, come there by means of the Bhairava-piṇḍa.
O Goddess, one should fashion a trident either at the front of the assembly or elsewhere;
it should be surrounded on all sides by the heart-mantra and the power-mantra, possessing the radiance of fire.
When one does not transgress [this], she should be known as Rudraśākinī;
and likewise, O Varārohā, by not transgressing their respective mudrās.
O you who are dear to heroes, if a Śākinī should appear before the heroes, she must be recognized by them through the power of the Heart-mantra; it cannot be otherwise.
The knower of mantras should recognize them; they must not be bypassed if they are unfit for one's own portion.
O Goddess, having resorted to a cremation ground, one should recite the Heart of the Śākinīs.
As long as the practitioner recites [the mantra] for one thousand nights,
so long will there quickly arise agitation throughout the entire city.
Then they come, surrounding the lord of practitioners at the edge;
though they are of great strength and difficult to restrain, they flee, terrified by fear.
Having seen this, O beloved, one must not fear out of mental negligence;
rather, one should contemplate the form of the terrible aspect just as I am.
Afterwards, the *argha* offering should be presented so that it becomes pleasing to them;
then the goddesses should be dismissed with the heart-mantra as before.
O Dear One, having taken the skull-lid from the cremation ground, one should not write all the supreme and non-supreme [mantras] there, for they extend to the end of the seven divisions.
The fivefold origins that have been described within the family of the Rūpikā are completed by means of the heart-mantra of the Śākinī, up until the Vidyā is fully accomplished.
In the *anuloma* [order], one should interlace [the mantra] by means of the "name-interspersed" (*nāmāntarita*) conjunction;
one should worship with flowers and perfumes and touch [the object] with the heart-mantra.
Then the mantra-practitioner, having fashioned the banner, should recite the mantra while staying in a cremation ground;
thereupon, whatever goddesses dwell in the city will arrive.
They become agitated, come under control, and are moistened; those whose wombs are moistened act so that no one knows [the practitioner], yet they converse with the adept. (16.354)

Then, having understood [the signs] through various secret gestures (cchommaka), as well as the auspicious and formidable signs born of the limbs, the practitioner should dismiss [them] with his heart.
Otherwise, O Goddess, they become angry and, being difficult to approach, they cause harm.
Thus, O beloved Goddess, have I described to you the union through force (*haṭha*). 16-356.
It must not be done out of negligence by the practitioner, O lady of excellent limbs;
therefore, what is the use of much speaking? One should not even contemplate it in one's mind. (16.357)
He who desires his own welfare should protect [the woman] like a son;
hereafter, I shall explain how one may have union with the Goddess.
Listen to how it occurs through the state of friendship and kinship:
the heart, together with the vidyā, situated within the enclosure of the syllable *kliṃ*. (16.359)
One should recite [the mantra] in the sequence beginning with 'A' until it reaches the state of the letter ending in 'Pha';
through the twelvefold division of vowels, there is the union with the blissful yogi.
O Dear One, one should recite the heart-mantra joined with the *yoni*, with the syllables *kli*, *kle*, and *kli* folded together;
there are twelve repetitions by way of division, and this is the second *melaka*.
"O Dear One, one should recite the *marmā* syllable *kle kle kle* folded within the *yoni*;
O Beautiful One, the third meeting has thus been explained to you. (16.362)
O auspicious lady, having pierced the vital point with *kliṃ ai* and *kli*, one should recite the mantra joined with the *yoni* in twelve stages; this is the fourth meeting.
O Dear One, one should mutter "kro kli kro" situated within the *puṭa* and joined with the *yoni*;
this fifth *melaka*, divided by the twelve gods, is thus remembered. (16.364)
Hrīḥ kli hrīḥ; this vital point, folded and pierced by the twelve vowels, should be recited as situated in the womb, O Blessed One, joined with the sixth conjunction.
O sinless one, through the division of the moving wheel, the seventh [mantra] arises;
one should recite ten thousand steps of the Mālinī, which is the supreme vital point.
But then, O Goddess, when he recites it according to the division of the distinctions of the words within the assembly of the Yoginīs, that is the eighth meeting, O Pārvatī. (16.367)
Then, for one who violates the commitments (samaya), meditation, worship, recitation, and fire-offerings lead only to the agitation of the world; of this there is no doubt. (16.368)
O lady of beautiful hips, there will be a meeting with the one to be propitiated;
having propitiated him through devotion and easy means, one should not provoke his anger. (16.369)
When provoked, the goddesses indeed find a vulnerability and do not grant peace;
therefore, O Goddess, one should know that they must always be propitiated and satisfied. (16.370)
If the one to be propitiated is indeed angry, the service of the mantra will be in vain;
when the service of the mantra is fruitless, then accomplishment does not arise. (16-371)

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, the section on the characteristics of the Yoginīs, in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, a great tantra within the Bhairava stream belonging to the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), measuring seventy million verses. 16.

The Goddess said: "Tell me, O Lord, the collection of the *sisa* [mantras] of the *sehārīs* according to their lineage—an unsurpassed treasury of mantras for the sake of the practitioner's play. (17.1)
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the play of the true essence of the yogis;
understand from me as it is being told how their restraint is achieved. 17.2
Oṃ, homage to Virūpākṣa! Kiriki-ri! Protect, protect this! Svāhā!
With this mantra, one should perform protection with clay; protection will be established against all fears.
Oṃ, homage to Rudra, who assumes the form of victory! Show, show! Culu, culu! Svāhā!
With this [mantra], one should empower a twenty-seven-finger-long stick made of *kāṣṭhikā* wood seven times; she becomes a courtesan and goes wherever she pleases.
*Oṃ cāmuṇḍe culu culu svāhā*.
With this, one should recite [the mantra] seven times over a *pāṭalā* wood stick and place it upon the bed.
She remains in the form of a woman. *Oṃ cāmuṇḍe parivartaya rūpaṃ muñca muñca liri liri svāhā*.
Having consecrated the hand with this mantra, he touches [the object], and it becomes like a piece of wood.
Oṃ cāmuṇḍe culu culu svāhā! By this, one binds the eyes of people with their own forms. Oṃ cāmuṇḍe matha matha dama dama hara hara svāhā!
Having consecrated a bundle of grass nine times with this [mantra], one should set it down;
it brings forth the dead. Oṃ cāmuṇḍe kili kili darśaya satyaṃ hana hana svāhā.
Taking twelve pills and reciting the mantra seven times over them, one knows the duration of one's life through perspiration. When one pill has been sweated, one lives for one month;
with six [pills], one lives for six years; thereafter, one becomes long-lived for all time.
Then, even if she has not yet lived for twelve days, [one should recite]:
*Oṃ cāmuṇḍe culu culu gṛhṇa vandite svāhā*.
By means of this, twenty mustard seeds, having taken the name [of the person], one should sprinkle them with blood.
At dawn, those that sprout live for only three days; furthermore, all those that sprout live for seven days. Oṃ cāmuṇḍe sādani sādani ādani sura sura svāhā.
By merely seeing this, one draws forth passion; it touches the face, and it becomes filled with blood. *Oṃ cāmuṇḍe ajagari darśaya yavāsisvāmi svāhā*.
By means of this, one should take clay from a stūpa, place it in the mouth, and pour water over it; they become threefold beds.
Liberation by means of water:
*oṃ cāmuṇḍe ūrdhvaṃ tiṣṭha 2 kiri 2 tiṣṭha 2 lulu svāhā*.
Having consecrated water seven times with this mantra, one should sprinkle the house; [the pestilence] will fall upward as ashes.
Oṃ cāmuṇḍe, split it! split it! leap over it! leap over it! kill! kill! Oṃ āgami, the mantra of all commitments, svāhā!

By sprinkling this ash on the entire body, the flesh of the body bursts open; it devours and drinks the blood. Upon the sight of the hand, it restores life. Oṃ cāmuṇḍe, rend! rend! if one touches the speech, it binds the splendor. Ṭiṭṭi svāhā!
By means of this, one takes away the speech of whomever one touches.
One should recite it after seeing [the deity] for one day or one night:
*oṃ cāmuṇḍe viṣū viṣu gṛhṇa svāhā*.
Having consecrated these royal mustard seeds (*rājasarṣapa*) with this [mantra], one should cause them to be applied to the limbs; [thereby] it becomes effective.
Oṃ Cāmuṇḍe, pulla pulla, dhura dhura, it becomes effective for those who possess the *kalāpas*.

*anyarūpadhāraṇi dhāraya dhāraya hūṃ hūṃ allalla gṛhṇa svāhā*. By means of this, having taken the hair of an animal and consecrated it seven times, one should bind [the person]; they will become that very form. When it is removed, there is liberation. *oṃ cāmuṇḍe mahābale devyai cuhu cuhu hūṃ svāhā*.
Having consecrated the hand with this [mantra], one should touch the face; thus one becomes sealed.

*Oṃ cāmuṇḍe vikṛtānane gṛhṇa mātare dhūpaṃ mama siddhikari hā hā kiri svāhā*. Having performed the *prakṛti* [rite] with this, one should take a hide from the sole of the left foot and offer it as incense; he whose soul it reaches will suffer from trembling and fever.
If one applies sour gruel (*kañjika*), a burning sensation arises; if human urine is used, a great burning arises.
Liberation occurs through milk.
One should offer incense with the juice of the *pādaraja* plant; from that, a piercing pain (*śūla*) arises.
Wherever [the substance] is applied to a limb, there pain arises.
Liberation occurs through the incense of blue lotuses (*utpala*).
Oṃ cāmuṇḍe ghātani dharaṇi dhāraṇi mathani dhara dhara bandha bandha svāhā.
By this, one paralyzes the supreme mantra; [the opponent] no longer sees the vision.
*Oṃ cāmuṇḍe tiri tiri cchinda cchinda vidhātre hiri hiri sphura sphura tiṣṭha tiṣṭha vividha vividha svāhā*.

By this, having gone to a cremation ground and holding a human skull, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should offer an oblation of animal flesh before it and recite the mantra until it bursts.
He travels through the sky; wherever he stays in a cremation ground, there he sees a house.
There is a ruby throne, various garments, necklaces of pearls, and foods both hard and soft. Whatever one conceives in the mind, all that comes to pass.
At dawn, the Blessed Lord Īśāna spoke thus; furthermore, the Blessed One becomes the supreme protector of the Śākinīs.
For the sake of this brother’s accomplishment, one must guard against slander; the cowherd (gopa) must be protected with effort, and first of all, two protections for oneself must be performed.

*Oṃ namo yogeśvarāya viśvādhipataye nila nila riri riri mama rakṣa rakṣa gaṇeśvara vidyeśvara śmaśānapriya thavi vi hūḥ hūḥ ghātaya ghātaya svāhā.* Having consecrated flowers, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), dūrvā grass, or a coral knot seven times with this mantra, one should wear it on the head as a topknot-binding (*śikhābandha*). This indeed provides self-protection and shall accomplish all rites.
Oṃ, homage to the one with terrifying fangs, the lord of the Rākṣasas with an adverse tongue, who is dear to the Gaṇas! Dhū dhūpa! Remember, remember! Hūḥ hūḥ! Protect, protect me! Svāhā!
With this mantra recited seven times, one should touch the body everywhere; one becomes invincible against all fears.
Oṃ Cāmuṇḍe, O Gaṇakālī of great power! Destroy so-and-so! O you who perceive the form of others! Do not look! Look here! Tra tra! Mu mu! Ru ru! Svāhā!
Having recited this over the *gocana* seven times, one should anoint the face; then one sees the sisters.
Whichever sister one sees with a fly upon her head, that one must be spoken to.
Now, as for how one does not see a fly: having consecrated the face seven times with the mantra and then washing the face, one knows [the truth].
That sister should recognize the convention as one that binds her closely.
Then, upon seeing the sister, if one should perform a salutation, or touch the nose with the thumb of the right hand or with one's own finger, it constitutes a salutation to the brothers.
Or, if the sister touches [the other's] feet with her left foot, it constitutes a counter-salutation from the sister.
Then, having seen it, he performs everything.
Now, when the sister takes hold of herself, [her face becomes] * * * * * * * *? *litāsyatorayet.
The garment becomes spread out.
Then, when he has been brought under control, the Śākinī makes a request: "I am born from your speech; if you give me an order, I shall do it.
In this manner, one should conduct the interaction by means of such secret signs (*cchommaka*).

Oṃ cāmuṇḍe, bring [them] at the time of subduing! Saḥ 2, cook, cook the spirits! O consecrated one, svāhā! Whatever has been seized by anyone, whether it be something that is being taken or something given—whatever they desire, such as "O Mistress of the Command," they fulfill it; they pacify whatever [ailment] there is, and they become free from disease. If they do not act, then the Sister seals everything. One should perform a fire-oblation (homa) for the afflicted person with this mantra.

Oṃ cāmuṇḍe bhagini bhāgaṃ samiṃsi 2 hara svāhā. Having consecrated seven pieces of wood with this mantra seven times, one should offer them into the fire; then, one should sprinkle [the area] with these ashes. Then, taking a water-pot, one should recite [the mantra];
it pacifies all diseases of cattle, and thereafter they become healthy.

Oṃ cāmuṇḍe haraṇi kara kara karṣaṇi ca rudhana rudhana hana hana bhañja bhañja cala cala yogāṃ svāhā. By means of this [mantra], one should take a sprout of *priyaṅgu* and place it upon the body; it will kill all [enemies] up to the head. With that water, one should apply it to the nails, teeth, hair, or the impurities.
Then he becomes healthy.
Alternatively, one hundred oblations of mind should be offered; by touching him with that incense, he himself becomes free from disease.
For a sick person, one should apply a tilaka mark with yellow pigment (rocanā); then he becomes healthy.

Oṃ cāmuṇḍe cala cāraṇī sama sama jaṃpa jaṃpa juho pātani māraṇi pūraya pūraya culu culu svāhā. Having performed the offering of the bali-oblation with this [mantra], for one whose limbs wither, who suffers from burning fever, or who has hemorrhaging, one should offer a thousand oblations of milk with this very same [mantra]; thereupon, he becomes restored to health.
Then, having fashioned an image within the circle of sisters (*bhaginīmaṇḍala*), one should sprinkle it with milk; pain will arise.
Having empowered seven pieces of *devadāru* wood with the mantra and smeared them with ghee, one should offer a thousand oblations; all pains will perish.
Furthermore, if any limb is afflicted by pain, one should empower some oil with the mantra and apply it; thereafter, one becomes healthy.
Now I shall explain the suppression of a sister: it results in killing, beating, splitting, or subjugation.

*Oṃ namaḥ kṛtāntarūpāya vikṛtāya ajihve jihveśvari jihve mathane matha matha bhūtādhivāsinī pilebhi svāhā*. With this [mantra], one should offer oblations of *madanakaṇṭhaka* seeds smeared with pungent oil while visualizing [the victim] in one's mind; within seven days, that sister dies.
One should offer an oblation of extinguished butter and milk; then he becomes restored to health.

Now, if one desires to cause a woman’s sister to have a flow of blood, one should drive a peg into a milky tree, recite the mantra seven times, and bury it in her vulva; a flow of blood occurs. If sprinkled with milk, she is released from it. One should offer a hundred oblations of perfumes; there will be destruction [of the enemy].
Liberation occurs through a hundred oblations of clarified butter.
If one places a wooden splinter over which the mantra has been recited a hundred times in the place of the teeth, a toothache arises;
liberation occurs when it is removed.
Oṃ cāmuṇḍe bhasmakapāle lala lala dara dara hu hu vama vama hahani pavani svāhā.
Having fashioned an image out of clay with this [mantra], one should urinate upon it.
The sisters will cry out, "What do you command? Then, being pleased, they will say, "Command us; we shall do it."
One should sprinkle an effigy with milk; [the victim] becomes healthy.

*Oṃ cāmuṇḍe māṃsa-śoṇita-khādani māraṇi daha daha vidhvaṃsaya vidhvaṃsaya yogini kili kili cili cili mili mili hana hana paca paca māraya māraya svāhā*. With this [mantra], one should offer eight thousand oblations of salt soaked in pungent oil for seven days. Then, from the third day onwards, sisters will come from within a radius of five *yojanas*; even if they have not yet arrived, they will appear and say, "What command do you have?"
Then one should say, "I do not seek anything.

Thereupon they say, "We shall give you whatever you desire. From the third day onward, for seven days, the sisters say, "Whether it be gold, jewels, clothing, or sexual union; whether it be solid food, soft food, that which is licked, that which is sucked, or that which is drunk—we shall perform whatever you desire; we shall bring about the success of your rite."
One should offer an oblation of milk; peace will ensue.
Now, if that is not pleasing, having performed the binding of the entire circle of sisters (*sarvabhaginīmaṇḍala*), one should cause them to remain.
*Oṃ cāmuṇḍe vajraghoṇeśvari tiṣṭha tiṣṭha bandha bandha paca paca mahāśaile svāhā*.
By reciting this mantra, the binding of the maṇḍala is accomplished.
It effects the binding of all goat-demons (*cchagalikā*) and the binding of the *cchagalikā* itself.
Oṃ cāmuṇḍe, show me your form; cook, cook! *culu culu*, svāhā!
This is the liberation of the she-goat:
*Oṃ cāmuṇḍe saṃsāravartani vartani mokṣaṇi mokṣaṇi cala cala ghu ghu vidhvaṃsaya vidhvaṃsaya bāhukapile svāhā*.
Having fashioned a stake one cubit long from nimba wood, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times; for whatever purpose one intends it, that one accomplishes.
One should recite [the mantra] one thousand times on the left side; then liberation occurs.
Otherwise, if she does not release [the victim], he will certainly die.
Oṃ cāmuṇḍe atikramaya krāma yaṃ rūpaṃ vidyataṃ caṃcale gṛhṇa gṛhṇa cira svāhā.
With this [mantra], one should bind a thread upon the head of that [person]; then his sisters will not prevail over him at night, even when they see a headless trunk (kabandha).
*Oṃ cāmuṇḍe bhasmāṅgāravarṇe vetāli stambhaya mocaya cala cala bhave bhave svāhā*.
By means of this, one paralyzes the gaze of a sister; by reciting it mentally, one accomplishes everything.
The sisters become astonished;
they perform circumambulation, and through mental recitation, there is liberation. Oṃ cāmuṇḍe vicce mahābala muñca svāhā.
By reciting this mantra, liberation is attained:
*Oṃ cāmuṇḍe ghātani dara dara mālido si 2 amukasya phaṭ amuka me phaṭ gātre phaṭ hṛdaye phaṭ cakṣurbhyaḥ phaṭ svāhā*.

Having fashioned an effigy out of salt, kindling a fire with sacrificial wood (*samidh*), and having cut [the effigy] with a sharp weapon, one who has recited it seven times paralyzes the arm and the speech [of the enemy].
One should offer seven oblations three times a day, by night and by day; whichever limb one offers as an oblation, that limb becomes paralyzed.

If one offers [the entire body] without remainder, then one dies. If one offers the eyes after plucking them out, one falls into a state of blindness. If one offers the head, one undertakes whatever rite one desires.
In this way, one should perform what is desired by the person; then, one brings about peace (*śānti*).
Having kindled the fire for those who are full of confidence, one should offer a hundred oblations of milk, and peace ensues.
With this mantra—*oṃ cāmuṇḍe kalu kalu dhvani virutāya vidye svāhā*—one should recite it upon seeing a sister; then they will look at one another.
Or, when one desires to see [the goddess], one should mentally recite the mantra; from that, liberation [is attained].
*Oṃ cāmuṇḍe darśaya rūpaṃ ca jāpine svāhā*.
By this, the sisters appear; they circumambulate [the practitioner], and by seeing them, one becomes worthy of worship.
And just as the Blessed Lord Maheśvara is invulnerable:
*Oṃ namaḥ anantaśikhe agne suravāsini gṛhṇa gṛhṇa māraya māraya vindhyavāsini mahāsavidhanulunulu mā ciraṃ svāhā*.
With this [mantra], one should press the left hand with the right hand; then one drinks.

Oṃ, homage to the one of universal form! Tuṃ tu, come, come! O you of divine form and great power, who are meditated upon by the divine! O you whose form causes agitation among the Kurus! Cu cu, ga ga, seize, seize, O fair-eyed one! Svāhā! (86a) Having taken the hair of a donkey, cow, camel, elephant, or other such animals, and having wound each [strand] around a single thread, one should bind it on the hand of a person on the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight with that thread empowered eight hundred times at the right image of Mahādeva. That person becomes possessed of the form as described. Upon its removal, there is release.
We shall now explain the ritual procedure for accomplishing this vidyā.
Having performed the offering of oblations at a solitary linga on the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, there is a recitation of eight hundred [mantras].
This applies to all mantras of the sisters when consuming meat.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, as declared by Maheśvara regarding sisters and brothers:
*Oṃ namo yogeśvarāya sulahi sulahi*, by which there is protection for all beings. *Oṃ namo bhagavate īśānāya tiri ti ri tiṣṭha tiṣṭha svāhā*.
By this, one paralyzes a corpse;
even when being burned, it does not burn.
By this, a corpse moving along with the current, when struck by a clod of earth, breaks through and moves against the current.
Having grasped the name [of the target], one should mutter [the mantra]; a wasting fever will arise.
Whatever time one contemplates, all that comes to pass.
Oṃ cāmuṇḍe bandha bandha daha daha keli keli svāhā.
Having fashioned an image with this [mantra], one gives ashes as an ointment to all the Śrīs; by means of oblations of milk, there will be an end to her [misfortune].
Now I shall further proclaim the supreme doctrine of the Seḍhārīs—the divine play of all the goddesses; hear now the divine mantra. (17–3)

For the sake of the play of the lords of practitioners, this is the arrangement of the substances of mercury. Oṃ, homage to the Asura-kumārikās! Homage to the hosts of gods! By means of this great vidyā, which accomplishes many rites, I have been dispatched by the Lord of Asuras to traverse this earth. With sharp fangs and a terrible form, tawny and deformed, I terrify all beings, both mobile and immobile. It is as follows:

Kaṭṭobhuṭṭe mahānaṭṭe saṃcāli vicāli hili hili hili kiriṭi kiriṭe madyamūle japa karāle candrakamūle! Whatever desire I wish for, may that desire of mine be fulfilled, svāhā! The ritual offerings (upacāra) consist of the excrement of seven animals: the dog, camel, donkey, buffalo, vulture, cat, and human.

One should consecrate with this mantra: *cili mili vigrahakhadirakīlakam*. By touching [the object] with that which has been consecrated, one removes it entirely. *Oṃ namo vidura vidale cili kili kumārike tiṣṭha tiṣṭha svāhā*.
Having tied a thread from a cloth of the deceased around one's own hand, if one touches a jar in a tavern, it will take away the liquor and show it to him as full.
Oṃ, homage to Kumārikā icchili icchili! Oṃ gomiti svāhā!
This transfers the merit of what has been done.
Having consecrated a full water-jar with this mantra, all that has been fashioned from dust is removed.
Having recited this [mantra] one hundred and eight times, whatever one sees, all that he takes away.
*Oṃ namo kṛṣṇadaitye makule kule svāhā*.
Having consecrated a garment with this [mantra], if one touches [anything] with it, all that he takes away.
Oṃ, homage to the Goddess, homage to Vicce, svāhā!

By means of this, one should cast mustard seeds into the fire; it removes all evil spirits. Having consecrated yellow pigment (rocanā) and applied it as a tilaka on the forehead, whatever one touches with it, that he removes entirely.

Oṃ dayine svāhā. Having recited this twenty-one times and having written it down, one should prepare a *modaka* (sweetmeat), make a single lump, and fashion a small image (*puttalikā*). Having offered a bali-oblation of scents and flowers at that spot, one should cause it to be given with supreme devotion. One should then have [the victim] consume the bali; having presented it, while naked, with hair disheveled, it should be eaten upon a mound of earth. Then, one should consecrate jars with this mantra. Among the grains, milk products, and ritual substances, whichever one desires, by touching it while reciting the mantra, one takes all of that away.
Therefore, one should hold onto only the fruit; [otherwise] it takes away everything. || 17-4 ||
Oṃ, homage! O Damī, divine one, against the Daityas, slay, slay! I seize the eyes of all; let no evil person see me, nor may anyone behold me. Svāhā!

Taking a thread spun by a maiden, making seven knots in it, and reciting this mantra twenty-one times, one should fasten it around the neck and depart while reciting it. Whatever he touches, he takes away entirely. Oṃ, homage to the one who has transcended, to the one of victorious mind. Svāhā!
Having placed this on a stone slab and reciting the mantra, one should throw rice grains; it moves. Having consecrated one's eyes with this, one takes away everything.
*Oṃ namo bhagavate vitale kumbhakāriṇi kumbhaṃ me prayaccha svāhā*.
Having gone to a crossroads with this, one should take a pair [of shoes]; one steals a single object.
Oṃ, homage to the goddess Uli Hili Hili Devikali, svāhā!
While reciting this, whatever one contemplates, all that it removes.
Oṃ, homage to Ke Kiṇḍini, svāhā!
With this, one steals cotton:
*Oṃ namo gigini dhrumi liṃkhu khu svāhā*.
Having consecrated the five fingers with this, whatever one touches, all that one steals.
Now, for all [mantras], the recitation consists of twenty-one repetitions. Now follows the ritual procedure for the family mantra (*kulamantra*).
Having performed the recitation twenty-one times and having touched with the hand, whatever one touches, all of that is transferred [to oneself].
With this, one takes away everything that one touches.
Furthermore, having made twenty-one knots with this very [mantra] on a cord (*selaka*) for all objects, if one places it at the door of the house, protection against all theft is accomplished.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Treasury of Mantras," in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, a great tantra of the Bhairava-stream belonging to the Vidyāpīṭha, measuring seventy million verses. 17.
The Goddess said:
O Lord, I have heard specifically regarding the characteristics of the Yoginīs, the sporting of the Śākinīs, and indeed the behavior of the Seharikās. (18.1)
And just as their meeting has been specifically determined, I wish to hear about their secret signs (chommaka) and their language in particular. || 18.2 ||
By merely knowing the secret signs (chommaka), one becomes esteemed by them;
for the practitioner who is devoted to the mudrās and secret signs, they will indeed grant accomplishment. (18.3)
Bhairava said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the Icchommas by means of the touch of limbs and body parts, as well as their speech and gestures. (18.4)
Listen now to that procedure by which practitioners converse with one another through their Mothers; indeed, hear the characteristics of the *aṅga* and *śchomma* signs. (18.5)
If one touches hand with hand, it constitutes a salutation; and likewise, upon not seeing the ring finger, it constitutes a return salutation. || 18-6 ||
She claps her hands against her own hands, desires to eat the sacrificial offering, touches her forehead, and says, "Where shall I go? (18.7)
But she who touches the navel and says, "I am hungry," it is said that she touches her mother's breast. (18.8)
The spirit touches the elbow and says, "I am going," while licking its tongue and saying, "I shall eat human flesh. || 18-9 ||
"When [the object] touches the eye, [one thinks], 'I do not turn away from what is seen.
When it touches the side... [as before]... as when one says, 'I move my foot,' so when the foot touches the foot, it is said that 'I am enjoying [it]'. (18.11)
When he makes his teeth click together, it means "Give me food"; when he touches both rows of teeth with his tongue, it means "I am satisfied. (18.12)
"He touches the tip of the foot; he dies; one must not go"—this is said to mean that there is no action of non-existence (nāstikarma). || 18-13 ||
To her who shows both hands together, one should show an *utpala* flower;
to her who forms a hollowed cup with her hand, one should extend one's own hand. || 18-14 ||
She who scratches her hand then scratches his forehead;
while scratching her breast, she should let drops fall upon her hand. (18.15)
She who scratches the ground with her big toe, lets her big toe fall [to the ground], stamps her feet, or slaps her buttocks; || 18-16 ||
To her who sees [the deity] anointed with oil, one should grant liberation;
to her who shows the tip of the nose, one should show the tongue.
She who shows her forehead should be given the ear;
[she who shows] the nose, the lips, and the tongue is like a most exalted and wonderful Pratyekabuddha.
* * * *? * *? from [the heart], "Welcome" (*svāgataṃ*) with two [fingers], and "Very welcome" (*susvāgatam*). The *kṣema-mudrā* is prescribed by placing the thumb into the hollow of the hand. ||19||
She who shows her tongue should show it to him;
she who shows her head should show her forehead to him. (18–20)
To her who shows her hair, one should show the topknot;
to her who shows her chin, one should show her ear. || 18–21 ||
To her who shows her neck, he should show his arm; to her who shows her arm, he should also show his hands. (18–22)
To her who shows the eye, he should not show his own; and to her who shows her breasts, he should show his own belly. || 18-23 ||
She who shows her hip should also show her secret place;
she who shows her thigh should also show her knee. (18.24)
She who shows her knee should also show her calf; and she who shows her calf should also show her feet. (18–25)
To those Vināyakas who display a frown and threaten, one should show the form of Garuḍa; to them as well, one should show the trident.
O noble one, O beloved, even addressing someone who is not a worthy recipient, or returning a greeting to one who does not deserve it— such things as these are the common secret signs, my dear.

O illustrious lady, that which has been declared by me according to the literal meaning [of the syllables] is [attained] by those devoted to bodily mortification who have recited it hundreds of millions of times. (18.28)
Through extremely fierce asceticism, they do not reveal themselves at the time of the ministers;
rather, they grant them the supreme sacrificial oblation (caru).
They grant assemblies for those who have been consecrated by the family-initiation and are devoted to the family,
providing the meeting with the yogis of bliss.
But I shall explain their secret signs (cchommaka) as established within the families;
whether it be a hero or even a woman, they attain equality within the family.
Having performed the complete ritual deposition (nyāsa) of Bhairavī by means of Bhairava, one should enter the abode of the Ṛṣis; and when she is seen by women... (18-32).
She who shows her topknot should show him her head;
she who shows her head should show him her forehead. || 18-33 ||
She who shows her head-garland should also show her face;
she who shows her eyes should show him her eyes. (18.34)
She who displays the nose should display Arghīśa;
she who displays the third eye should display Bhārabhūti. (18.35)
She who shows the skull should show Mahāsena to him;
she who shows the *kaṭha* should show Trimūrti to him. (18.36)
She who shows her teeth should show him the *bhārabhūti* [mudrā];
she who shows her tongue should show him the *visarta* [mudrā]. || 18-37 ||
He who shows his speech is Lakulīśa;
he who shows his fingers is Ajeśa, O Four-faced One. (18.38)
She who displays the trident, she who displays the single eye, she who displays the arm, and she who displays Chagammahākāla. (18.39)
She who should display her belly, she who should display a single eye, she who should display her heart, and she who should also display a ram; || 18-40 ||
Whichever woman shows him the Self (ātman), to her he should show Śveta;
whichever shows him Prāṇa, to her he should show Bhṛgu. || 18-41 ||
She who shows her breasts should show him a serpent;
she who shows her hip should show him the Lord (Īśvara). || 18.42 ||
She who displays her hip should display *dviraṇḍa* to him;
she who displays her navel should display *krodhīśa* to him. (18.43)
To her who reveals the secret, one should show Khaḍgīśa;
to her who reveals the subtle, one should show Ananta. || 18-44 ||
She who shows her thigh should show the beloved of Umā;
she who shows her right calf should also show Raudrī. (18.45)
She who shows her left calf should show his eldest [son];
she who shows her knee should show him as Sadyojāta.
She who displays her feet is indeed a Diṇḍimā;
O highly fortunate one, there are hundreds of thousands of such varieties.
They declare this to the preeminent practitioner of that portion; of this there is no doubt.
It should be understood by the mantra-practitioner for the purpose of mutual communication. (18.48)

Perhaps, through a divine conjunction or by the vision of a field-guardian (kṣetrapāla) and others, they may grant an instruction; then one should certainly perform what is to be done with a resolute mind. (18.49)
One should not transgress a divine utterance, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious;
this characteristic has been declared through many different modes. (18.50)
It should be known that for the sake of accomplishing all siddhis, he alone is the kisser;
he is the supreme god Śiva, established here upon the surface of the earth. (18.51)
A wise person should constantly bind the dust of his feet upon their heads;
the deities will always protect them and cherish them like their own children. (18.52)
They do not create a flaw for him; rather, they bestow external favor.
Know that by understanding the characteristics of the sacred field (*kṣetra*) and so forth, one will likewise become beloved. (18.53)

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Section on Chommaka," in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, a great tantra within the Bhairava-stream belonging to the Vidyāpīṭha, comprising seventy million verses. 18.
The Goddess said:
"The secret signs (chommaka) have been understood by me, as well as the Kaula meanings of the syllables;
however, I have not heard [the rest], and I wish to hear it, for my intellect is dull and my wisdom is small. (19.1)
How do the deities abide in the fields (kṣetra), the secondary fields (upakṣetra), and the junctions (saṃdoha)?
Also, [explain] the division of the field-protectors (kṣetrapāla), as well as the mantra-worship and the performance of offerings (bali).
"Explain all of this so that it may become free from doubt.
Bhairava said:
"Henceforth I shall proclaim the classification of the sacred fields (*kṣetra*), which is very difficult to obtain. (19.3)
O lady of excellent hips, the secondary field (upakṣetra) is the collection (saṃdoha) as it exists:
Prayāga, Varuṇā, Kollā, Aṭṭahāsā, and Jayantikā. (19.4)
Caritrekāmraka and Koṭivarṣa as the eighth;
starting from the eastern direction up to the region of the northeast. (19.5)
The arrangement of the fields for the practitioners of mantra should be understood according to their sequence.
Now, listen with a one-pointed mind as I shall describe the secondary fields (upakṣetra). 19-6.
Parastīra, Pṛṣṭhapurya, Kodbhuṇḍīśa, and Pāraraiva;
[123a] Kṣīrī, Māyāpura, and likewise Āmrātikeśvara. (19.7)
The eighth, O lady of beautiful hips, is proclaimed as the royal palace (rājaveśma). These indeed are situated as the external secondary fields (upakṣetra). 19-8.
And I shall proclaim the *sandohas*; listen, O lady of excellent complexion: Virambā, Rūḍī, Melāpada, and Pura. (19.9)
Kāśmīra, Amarukeśa, and the city of Pauṇḍravardhana—these constitute the divisions of the directions starting from the east and extending as far as the northeast. (19.10)
O Goddess, the *saṃdohas* beginning with Virañjā are situated in due order;
they should be known by the best of practitioners as being located sequentially in the eight directions. (19.11)

O you of virtuous vows, the fields (*kṣetra*), sub-fields (*upakṣetra*), and assemblies (*saṃdoha*), as they are established, as well as their names and the divisions of the directions, have been explained to you. (19.12)
The Goddess said:
[Tell me] the sacred fields (kṣetra), the secondary fields (upakṣetra), and likewise the gathering places (saṃdoha);
their names, the division of directions, and their respective numbers.
All this has been known by me through your grace, O Maheśvara:
who is which deity, in what location, and what is their name? (19.14)
How could there be a mantra for them, and how could it come to pass?
What is the name of those field-protectors, and what is their appearance like? (19.15)
"O Maheśvara, explain all of this to me according to the proper method.
Bhairava said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one! You have now understood it correctly."
That secret which has not been told to anyone and is exceedingly difficult to obtain—I shall now fully proclaim it; listen with one-pointed mind, O beloved. (19.17)
O Goddess, Vāyuvegā, born from a portion of Bhīmavaktrā, stands at the entrance with a banner in her hand, warding off all the wicked. (19.18)
O Goddess of great renown, stationed in that field and residing in an udumbara tree, there is the famous protector of the field named Pavana.
The goddesses born from the limbs of Mahocchuṣmā should be known as the Śāṅkarīs of the excellent [weapons];
armed with maces, these goddesses bestow strength and sovereignty. (19–20)
Resorting to a *tāḍa* tree, he remained established in that sacred field;
he is renowned as the guardian of the field (*kṣetrapāla*) known as Ūrdhvakeśa, who is fierce in his power.
At Kollagiri, the goddess Mahālakṣmī resides; she is Karālā, born from the womb, possessing the form of Time (Kāla), holding a staff in her hand, and most terrifying.
O Goddess, situated in that field and resting upon a mountain peak, she is renowned as Agnikā; she is the Kṣetrapāla of Mahādhipa.
The goddesses residing in Aṭṭahāsa are born from the goddess Raktā;
they are renowned as Saumyamukhī and the others, adorned with vajra weapons. (19–24)
In that field, the goddess resides, taking shelter beneath a *kadamba* tree;
the guardian of the field (*kṣetrapāla*) there is renowned as Mahābala, possessed of great strength. (19–25)
The goddess Jayantī is tusked and renowned as Jvālāmukhī;
standing with a sword in hand, she is the one who brings all beings under her control.
In that field resides the goddess who has taken refuge under a nimba tree;
the guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla) is renowned as Mahābala, who is exceedingly fierce.
In the Caritra [section], however, the goddesses Kṛṣṇatuṇḍā and Karālā are born from the womb;
holding spears in their hands, these goddesses stand there as bestowers of all supernatural powers (siddhis). || 19-28 ||
In that field, the Goddess, who destroys all sins, stands there resting against a Karañja tree with a noose in her hand.
In that field resides the Goddess, taking refuge in the Aśvattha tree;
there is also a Kṣetrapāla of massive body, known by the name Kailāsa. (19–31)
But Karṇamoṭī, born of the Mahābala lineage, stands at the place called Koṭi;
the goddess holds a trident in her hand and is the sovereign of all the lords of yoga. (19.32)
In that field resides the goddess, who has taken refuge in a banyan tree;
there is also a large-bodied guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla) known by the name Hetuka.
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the secondary sacred fields (*upakṣetra*); listen, O beloved! On the opposite bank are Prasannā and Raktā, born of the Kula lineage. (19–34)
The goddess stands in the secondary field (upakṣetra), equipped with a vajra weapon;
in that place resides the kṣetrapāla Trikaṭa, who is preeminent in strength. (19.35)
In Pṛṣṭhāpura reside Vidyunmukhī, Karālā, and Kulasaṃbhavā;
these goddesses, stationed in the Upakṣetra, are endowed with the power of the staff (daṇḍaśakti). || 19-36 ||
The Kṣetrapāla, Mahādevī, and the one renowned as Vajradaṇḍā—these should be known as Kohuṇḍikā and Śivā, born from the limbs of Karālā. (19.37)
The goddesses stationed in the secondary fields are adorned with a multitude of mudrās;
the field-protector, O one of great renown, is celebrated as Ulkāmukha.
She should be known as Vahnimukhī, born from Dantura on Sopāra;
the goddess resides in an Upakṣetra, adorned with a khaṭvāṅga in her hand. (19.39)
In that place dwells the flesh-eating Kṣetrapāla, fierce in his strength, with thighs like coconut trees, born from the lineage of Caṇḍākṣī. (19.40)
The goddess stands in the secondary field (upakṣetra), sword in hand and possessed of great strength;
the guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla) Mahāmeru is established in that field.
The goddesses named Bhīmavaktrodbhavā, Bhīmā, Māyā, and Kampanī,
who bear the vajra and the goad, are stationed at the upakṣetras.
In that place stands the field-protector named Bhīma, fierce in his power;
born in the Mahocchuṣma family, he is Pūtanā at Āmrātikeśvara. (19.43)
The goddess Bhīmā, armed with a plow and a mace, resides in the secondary field (upakṣetra);
the Kṣetrapāla of great wrath is established in that field.
In Rājagṛha, there is the goddess Cipiṭanāsā, born of the Mahābala family; she resides in an upakṣetra, endowed with the Vajrāṅkuśa. (19.45)
The field-protector Mahākarṇa is established in that field;
O lady of virtuous vows, the form [of the deity] in the secondary field has been described to you.
I shall proclaim the *sandohas*; listen, O three-eyed Goddess!
Virajā’s goddess is Ambikā, who bears the *paṭṭisa* weapon as her *mudrā*. (19.47)
In the first [section], they have emerged; however, they are supported by the *sandoha*.
Anala and Kṣetrapāla are situated within that *sandoha*. (19.48)
Erūmāgnimukhī is to be known as born from Karālākulasaṃbhavā;
the goddess Vajraśaktidharī is born from Sandoha. (19.49)
The field-protector (kṣetrapāla) renowned as Ghaṇṭārava is exceedingly powerful;
in that field resides the goddess with fierce and terrifying eyes. (19.50)
In Hatapura, there are those born from Karālākulasa;
the goddess Muśalahastodarā, and Kṣetrapāla-Agnijihvaka. (19.51)
Born from a deformed womb in Elāpura, they were harsh-faced;
with axes in their hands, they stood gathered in great numbers.
The field-protector (kṣetrapāla) renowned as Gajakarṇa is preeminent in strength;
and Kasmarī, Gokarṇī, and Caṇḍākṣā are born from the womb [of the goddess]. (19.53)
The mudrā is joined with the chain; Nandī and Jaya are the guardians of the field (kṣetrapa).
The goddess resides in the guardian of the field, and Nandī and Jaya are renowned. (19.54)
In Marukeśa is Cakramaṇī, born from the midst of Bhīmavaktrā;
she is joined with the mudrā and the goad, and accompanied by the Karālākṣetrapas. (19.55)
Mahocchuṣmā is known as Cetanā in the city, born from Aṅga;
and those born in Sandoha are associated with Halāyudha. (19.56)
The Kṣetrapāla known as Romajaṅgha is Mahotkaṭā, and the deity known as Carmamuṇḍā is in Puṇḍravardhana. (19.57)
Born of the Mahābala lineage, adorned with a khaṭvāṅga in hand, O Great Goddess Kumbhakarṇī, the Kṣetrapāla is established here. (19.58)
Henceforth I shall speak; listen with a single-minded focus, O beloved, regarding the sacred field (*kṣetra*), the secondary field (*upakṣetra*), and likewise the place of abundance (*sandoha*).
