I shall now declare the mantra of those deities who reside there:
Oṃ Hrīḥ Hūḥ Spho He Haḥ, adorned with the word Svāhā. (19.60)
The mantra of the Goddess is proclaimed as being joined with the word "namaskāra" at its end;
by this very mantra, the worship of the sacred fields (kṣetras) is prescribed. (19.61)
With this very [mantra] one should offer the bali, and with this one should cause the āli to be given;
one should worship the upakṣetras, the saṃdohas, and the svasthānas.
Henceforth, O Great Lord, I shall proclaim the guardians of the field (kṣetrapālas),
beginning with their own names and endowed with the form of Bhairava.
"Destroy the obstacles," thus [he says], joined with "Accept the offering (bali)," [and] the protective syllables...
O Goddess, offerings (bali) and alms (āli) should be given to them individually and separately.
O you of virtuous vows, I have explained to you all the distinctions regarding the sacred fields;
now I shall further describe another [type] that is common and situated everywhere.
One should indeed [recite] the mantra of the Kṣetrapālas, distinguished by its specific characteristics, whether in a village, a city, a town, or even at a crossroads. || 19-67 ||
Whether in a cremation ground, a garden, a house, or even on a rooftop—wherever the practitioner of mantra may be situated, he should begin his meditation and worship. (19.68)
And one should especially cause the bali offering to be given with this mantra:
"To him who resembles a dark blue cloud, with terrible fangs, and inspiring fear... (19.69)
[One should visualize] Kṣetrapāla with upward-pointing hair, red eyes, and a large belly.
[The mantra is: "Come, come! Act, act! Suru, suru! Muru, muru! Break, break! Strike, strike! O you of deformed and terrifying form, accept, accept your own offering!
This Tārā-mantra and others are thus specified, joined with the word of salutation at the end. (19–70)
The propitiation of the Kṣetrapāla is difficult to obtain in the three worlds;
if a practitioner of mantra wanders through the sacred field devoid of this, [he fails]. (19.71)
Thousands of obstacles will arise for him; of this there is no doubt.
An adept who is struck down by obstacles shall not partake in the fruit of accomplishment.
Therefore, with every effort, it must be understood by the practitioner.
The Goddess said:
"Declare the characteristics of the sacred sites for those mantra-reciters who desire accomplishment. (19.73)
"By which means does the practice of the great-souled practitioners become free from obstacles?
Bhairava said:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall indeed explain this for the benefit of the practitioners. (19.74)
First, according to the characteristics of the site, the ritual for the guardian of the field (*kṣetrapāla*) is likewise performed;
where there is water to the east, such as a pond filled with its own natural waters. (19.75)
A practitioner who desires accomplishment should resort to such a place, where water flows to the right, whether it be a lake or a river. (19.76)
O lady of excellent hips, Yamādheya is proclaimed as Kṣetrapāla;
there is water situated to the north, either a large oblong pond or a deep pool. (19.77)
There, the lord of the Yakṣas is designated as the sovereign; to the west is a divine lake, adorned with blossoming lotuses, [attained] through the cause of desire.
Varuṇa is the presiding lord there; success is not far off.
O Goddess, a pure lake is situated there within the sphere of wind.
There, the lord of the wind was appointed to the task of protection;
and in the southwest was a lake, beautifully adorned with lotuses and water-lilies.
There, by my command, the lord of the Rākṣasas has been appointed;
he is at the lake in the southeast, which is adorned with white and blue lotuses.
There, under the sovereignty of Agnirāja, accomplishment is not far off. To the northeast is a lotus-seat, a lake with the waters of a meritorious river.
There, the lord of Īśāna was appointed to the task of protection;
there, the river flowing eastward turns toward the southeast.
He who stands in the field with the discus in hand is remembered as the Guardian of the Field (Kṣetrapāla).
Water that has come from the southeast flows toward the south and the southwest. (19.84)
Brahmā’s lord was appointed there by Śaṅkara;
the water that had come from the southwest went toward the northwest and the west. || 19-85 ||
O Goddess, by my command, the lord of the Rakṣasas stands there;
the water that has come from the northwest flows toward the northeast and the north. (19.86)
The lord of the Piśācas was appointed there by the wielder of the trident;
O Goddess, when the water had gone to the north-east and to the north-west. (19.87)
In that place, the lord of the yakṣas is said to be Kṣetrasiddhi, the protector of the field.
O Goddess, there is water in the northwest, and it extends toward the southwest and the west. (19.88)
The lord of the Gandharvas is known there as the Guardian of the Field (Kṣetrapāla).
Water that has come from the southwest flows toward the southeast and the south. (19.89)
There, Kapālādhipati is proclaimed as the guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla).
Water has arrived from the southeast, and in the east it is filled with flowers. (19.90)
Bhīma was appointed there as the presiding officer over the work of the field;
when the water that had come from the east flowed out through the west, [he oversaw it]. 19.91ab.
But Kabandha remained there, O Goddess; and from that place, the delightful river flowed southward and then turned toward the north. (19.92)
O Supreme Goddess, O beautiful lady, Kumārakṣetrapāla has been appointed [as guardian] to the north of the delightful river and also to the south.
O lady of excellent vows, he who was described to you as being well-established there in beautiful form has arrived from the west, while the water flows charmingly toward the east. (19.94)
O Goddess, O beautiful one among the gods, Karāla stands as the Lord of the Field (Kṣetreśa);
he has emerged in the northeast and has gone toward the southwest. (19.95)
Sugrīva was appointed there as the overlord by the wielder of the trident;
O Goddess, water is situated in the southeast, and the Gama mountain is located in the northwest.
Subhadra, the mighty guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla), was stationed there;
when the water that had come from the southwest flowed toward the northeast, [he stood there]. (19.97)
But Vijaya, O lady of excellent hips, being appointed by Karālin, approached the water from the east when it had gone toward the south. (19.98)
The mighty Kṣetrapāla Ambuka is stationed there;
to the south is a delightful river, flowing toward the west.
The king of the gods (Indra) was stationed there, causing great obstacles for men;
he emerged from the west and returned again by the north.
Ananta is established there as the lord of great splendor;
O lady of excellent hips, he is to the north, while [the other] is situated in the water to the east.
There stands Ketumāla, which brings fear to practitioners;
to the east is Vimalānandā, and further to the north it extends again.
There, at the base of the smoke and fire, dwells my very powerful Rakṣasa lord;
she has emerged from the north of the Nandī river, facing westward.
Where there stands abundant, beautiful, and fragrant water—alas, alas! O Goddess, you who are stationed on the plow are the great delight of practitioners. (19.104)
The water coming from the south flows into the eastern current;
Bhairava has been appointed by Kapālin to guard that formidable place.
O Goddess, at the confluence to the east, adorned on the left and right, Ghaṇṭārava is situated for the benefit of practitioners.
In the south-eastern direction from the deity, at the auspicious confluence of rivers,
O Goddess, Tryakṣarudra resides, bestowing success upon the practitioner.
In the southern quarter, O Goddess, at that beautiful confluence where Bhīmanāda is situated, he bestows boons upon the ministers.
But when, O Goddess, there is a confluence with abundant waters in the southwest,
one who possesses great splendor and strength there cannot be bound even by the thirty gods.

Having paid homage there to the divine confluence situated to the west, with the left [side] on the north and the right on the south, one should abandon it after bowing to the Lord of the Sovereign Planets.
In the northwest is the vast and divine Saṃgama-aparājita;
there dwells the great Susiddhaprakara, the sovereign lord of the Saurākṣasas.
When there is a confluence with auspicious characteristics to the north of that place,
the pubic bone (bhagāsthi) should be situated there for those practitioners of mantra who desire accomplishment.
In the northeast is a divine confluence, crowded with many trees;
through the worship of Bhīma, it bestows swift accomplishment upon the practitioner. (19.113)
Wherever that confluence may be located, whether it stands upon a circular seat or is situated within the constellation Nīlīgraha, the mantra-practitioner should subjugate that place.
O Goddess, O beautiful one, when the divine mountain peak is to the south, it directly bestows happiness, being eight-armed. (19.115)
To the southwest is a divine peak with a stone surface not very far away;
Bhāskara resides there as its sovereign protector.
O Goddess, situated in the west is a divine place crowded with many trees;
having gone there, O Goddess, one may take refuge [in it] and become invulnerable even to the gods.
In the northwest is a divine mountain, circular and crowded with peaks;
there dwells Kṣetrapāla Kamalākṣa, who bestows the fruit of easy accomplishment. (19.118)
To the north is a divine mountain, beautified by its waterfalls;
there resides the field-protector Hayagrīva, who is known as the one who brings about immediate death. (19.119)
In the northeast is a divine mountain, densely covered with medicinal herbs;
there resides Maṇibhadra, the field-protector of great power. (19.120)
It bestows accomplishment and even liberation upon the practitioner; of this there is no doubt.
To the east is a divine mountain, covered with campaka and aśoka trees. (19.121)
The field-protector (kṣetrapāla), with a frowning face and extremely fierce, is stationed there.
To the southeast is a divine mountain, covered with very dense trees.
Abounding with many flowers and graced by waterfalls, there dwells the one celebrated as the field-guardian (kṣetrapāla) named Agnimukha. || 19-123 ||
Now I shall proclaim the general mantra for all sacred fields, O Great Goddess: "Aliṃ phalguṃ," [for] those who do not cause a bali offering to be given.
Oṃ, homage to Bhairava of deformed appearance; homage to Caṇḍa, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Oṃ, to Amṛtabhairava, svāhā!
Oṃ, make all food nectar, svāhā!

With this mantra one should offer the *bali* to all the guardians of the fields (*kṣetrapāla*). This is the supreme heart-mantra (*paramahṛdaya*) and the ritual mantra: OṂ NAMO LOHAKA GṚHṆA 2 VIKṚTARŪPĀṂ HANA 2 DAHA 2 PACA 2 VIDRĀVAYA 2 GRASA 2 NIHA 2 NAHA 2 TRAILOKYASATRĀSANAKARA HARANE HA PRASAHA 2 NṚTYA 2 GRĀHAYA 2 MOHAYA 2 PRAPĪḌAYA 2 HŪṂ 3 PHAṬ SVĀHĀ.
This is the mantra that effects the presence (*sannidhānakara*) of all the guardians of the fields.
Oṃ, O Goddess Ruru, those many millions who are Sugriva and Nokṛṣṇarudra. || 19-125 ||
In Ujjayinī there is Agnika, and Vṛkodara at Aṭṭahāsa; Kṛṣṇa shall be at Jālandhara, and Prabhākara in Kulūtā.
Turuhuru and Karṇa at the gate of the Goddess, and Bhairava—these eight are proclaimed as the Kṣetrapālas of the Yoga-pīṭhas. || 19-127 ||
But he who constantly upholds it and listens to its recitation always—he is liberated from all sins and attains the state of Bhairava. (19.128)
The sacred fields, together with their presiding deities, have been described along with the procedures for mantra-recitation and worship;
now the nomenclature of these fields is being told according to the different types of forests.
There were banyan trees, *janāśoka* trees, as well as *aśvattha* and *udumbara*;
there were *kadamba*, *sinduvāra*, *śrīvṛkṣa*, and groves of jackfruit trees.
Sarja, arjuna, the highly delightful rudrākṣa, madhūka, ambuka, kumbhavṛkṣa, śrīparṇī, and the bilva family. (19-131)
O Goddess, this maṇḍala of the site is surrounded on all sides by these excellent trees;
that site, named Vijaya, swiftly bestows spiritual accomplishment.
If there is a banyan tree to the east and a pipal tree situated to the south, O Goddess, one should designate that as "Victory" (vijaya) and indeed as "Conquest" (jaya). (19.133)
The Plakṣa tree is on the southern side, while the Vaṭa stands to the west;
these quickly grant success to the practitioner of mantra and are beautifully adorned with victory.
O lady of beautiful hips, for a practitioner, the Aśvattha tree on the southern side and the Plakṣa tree situated to the north, as well as the Sugrīva tree, are highly recommended. (19.135)
To the north is the banyan tree, and likewise to the east is the udumbara;
that place, O Goddess, is known by the name Subhadra, and it is remembered as bestowing victory and success.
O fair-faced one, in the east and the south there is a banyan tree;
there, however, there is fear of disease and illness, and it does not bestow accomplishment. (19.137)
To the south, however, there is a banyan tree adorned with many other trees;
that is designated as "māraka" (the killer), and the practitioner should avoid it.
In the south-western quarter, however, there are the Aśvattha and Udumbara trees;
having abandoned that place, the unfortunate one remains far from success.
Having abandoned even these, if there is a golden [image] in the northeast, a woman named Nārī in the southeast, and likewise Gaurī in the southwest; (19.140)
Likewise, in the northwestern direction, the name [of the place] is said to end with "japa";
when there is a dense grove of *jātī* flowers to the east, together with golden [trees]. (19.141)
That place named Bhadraka should be diligently sought by the practitioner;
it is covered with groves of plantain trees and to the west of a grove of *kadamba* trees.
The renowned Sugandha forest exists for the prosperity of the practitioner;
it stands together with groves of Jātī trees and jambūs, and with Uttarakāñcana trees. (19.143)
The "Royal Tooth" (rājadanta) layout should be understood as being crowded with groves of plantain trees, and likewise adorned with *kataka*, *jambu*, mango, and golden *campaka* trees. (19.144)
To the south is the place named Vinata, where success is swiftly attained and not far off;
it is filled with aśoka, panasa, punnāga, and kadamba trees. 145.
To the west, O lady of excellent hips, is that famous place named Bhīma;
it is covered with groves of plantain trees and crowded with mango and punnāga trees.
Siddhārthaka is fully described as bestowing success within six months; it should be combined with Ketakī and Bakula flowers and placed in the northeastern direction. || 19-147 ||
To the southeast, there is a forest abounding in *kadamba*, groves, and date palms;
that place is known as the Maṇḍala Forest, a sacred field adorned by that woodland. (19.148)
In the forest, O Goddess, there is the Kadamba-tāla grove, filled with mayūkhacampakas; it is renowned on all sides by the name Prasanna, belonging to Ravi.
Abounding in *sarala* and *tāla* trees, with groves of *jātī* and gold, it is known as Gaganavana, situated in the south-western quarter. (19.150)
Abounding with *jāti* and campaka trees, provided with lotuses and rose-apples, endowed with the king of trees (the *punnāga*), and crowded with *aśoka* trees. || 19-151 ||
O beautiful one, it is renowned by the name Surūpa, [established] by the God of gods;
O lady of excellent hips, its division is adorned with red eyes. (19.152)
Joined with *punnāga* and *bakula* trees and graced by perfected *sāraṅga* birds, it was renowned as the grove named Suvana, which increases pleasure and delight. (19.153)
To the east and likewise to the south, it is very dense and adorned with flowers;
shaded by creepers and shrubs, it is celebrated by the name Surāma.
To the east is the forest of Sarja and Arjuna, and to the south is Kadamba;
that place is called Nandana, together with the Ketakī and Kula trees. (19.155)
O Goddess, in the western quarter is the divine Niśāntakavana forest, together with the Aśvattha and Kāñcana trees; there is the famous place known as Bhagasti. (19.156)
O Goddess, to the north, situated on all sides, is the forest of honey-trees, dense with clouds, crowded with groves of oranges. (19.157)
The forest known as Viṣkambha, thick with shrubs and creepers, is famous;
and Trigarta is likewise renowned, filled with groves of kahlāra lotuses.
O lady of excellent hips, for the practitioner, success is not far off in that place;
[one should plant] bamboo, kadamba, and mango trees all around the site-maṇḍala.
In the southern direction (āgneyī diś), there is one seen which is known by the name Suramya;
these indeed are the sacred fields (kṣetra) described, along with the confluences of rivers such as the Vanyā. 19-160.
Whether they be auspicious or inauspicious, characterized by the marks of destiny—one should select one of these, or else one that is entirely auspicious. (19.161)
Complete with all auspicious marks and adorned by stationary beings and others—O lady of excellent hips, they indeed attain accomplishment therein without delay. (19.162)
If success does not arise for him, he should then accomplish the yantras and so forth.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, on the worship of the fields and sub-fields, in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, a great tantra within the Bhairava stream, belonging to the Vidyāpīṭha and measuring seventy million verses.
The Goddess said:
[Please explain] the primary fields (kṣetra), the secondary fields (upakṣetra), and the clusters (sandoha); the worship and the offering of oblations;
the characteristics of the sites and the mantras; and likewise the ritual for the guardians of the fields (kṣetrapāla). || 20-1 ||
"O Lord, O Sovereign of the Gods, everything has been understood by me through your grace;
now, please tell me how to string the garland of yantras. (20.2)
O Bhairava, O Lord of the Gods, I wish to hear how those very rites for subjugation and so forth are performed; please explain them to me. (20.3)
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the practice of subjugation and the other rites, as well as the acts of killing, expulsion, and especially [the rite of] eradication. (20.4)
O Goddess, there is the rite of immobilization (stambhana), enchantment (mohana), and the auspicious rite of nourishment (āpyāyana);
as well as making one blind, deaf, mute, and the binding of the Lord (bhagabandhana). (20.5)
O Goddess of gods, O leader of the deities, out of affection for you I shall explain the attraction and especially the protection; of this there is no doubt. (20.6)
O Goddess, one should apply the Bhairava-heart-mantra at the beginning and at the end; then, O fair-faced one, the name situated within the *sampuṭa* should be given. (20.7)
Meditating upon the deity who has the luster of red ochre, greatly radiant, blazing, and possessing the form of a vajra, one should recite the mantra and establish [the deity] below with fire.
One quickly brings [the target] under control, deluded by the king of mantras.
Then again, in this manner, the *piṇḍa* is ignited from below by the wind. (20.9)
Then, having joined [the mantra] from the beginning to the end, the practitioner should visualize [the victim] as smoke-colored,
being led toward the quarter of Vāyu while mounted upon fangs.
By performing a fire sacrifice with crow feathers upon a banner or a deer skin,
mixed with husks and thorns, one effectuates a powerful expulsion.
The syllable *gaṃ*, pervaded by the letter *ra*, together with the *nirvāha* and *māyā*, is situated within the *saṃpuṭa*; then the name is illuminated both below and above. (20.12)
Then, O beloved leader of the gods, one should meditate upon it as being consumed by fire and enveloped in garlands of flames; this quickly produces a burning sensation in the target.
One should likewise mount the syllable *la* upon the *piṇḍa* together with the *mātṛkā*.
Then, O Goddess, one should fashion [the image] upon a cloth of turmeric.
Furthermore, on a stone slab, one should draw a cow-hide [diagram] with a luster equal to Indra’s bow;
situated in the center of the Indramaṇḍala, it will paralyze [the enemy], of this there is no doubt. (20.15)
Mounted upon the *piṇḍa* stalk and joined with the letters of the *mātṛkā*, the name is then placed within a *saṃpuṭa* (enclosure), positioned above the stalks of honey. (20.16)

O God, one should draw the deity on birch bark with stalks of dūrvā grass and leaves of śamī; one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with sesame seeds smeared with the three sweets, employing the word "vauṣaṭ" at the end.
One should meditate on the nectar flowing forth, flooding [the body] from all sides,
situated within the cavity of Indra and within the cavity of the sun and moon.
O fair-faced one, this is the practice for nourishment intended for the sake of immortality:
the syllable-cluster (piṇḍa) mounted upon the letter 'ma' is indeed of the nature of fire. (20.19)
One should write the name of the target (*sādhya*) situated within the letters of the *mātṛkā*, placed in the middle of its enclosure;
then, one should meditate on [the deity] in the form of Time (*kāla*), and indeed destroy the world. (20.20)
Then, performing a fire sacrifice in a cremation ground with pieces of poison, blood, and bone fragments, one shall kill the enemy without a doubt, even if he is as dear as a Brahmin. (20–21)
One should visualize the *piṇḍa* syllable seated upon a ram’s horn together with the *mātṛkā*;
[this cures] muteness, deafness, blindness, and even the constriction of the womb. (20–22)
There is no doubt that he accomplishes this; for one who performs a fire-oblation at midnight in a cremation ground using husks mixed with milk, there is no uncertainty. (20–23)

O Dear One, when the syllable *piṇḍa* is joined with the letter *na* within the Vidyā, it quickly causes the delusion of the army, even of those possessing the brilliance of a blazing thunderbolt. (20–24)
The *piṇḍa* situated in the middle of the *saṃpuṭa*, joined and overlaid with the letter *ra*, will undoubtedly effect attraction through the visualization of its form as a hook. (20–25)
One should draw a blazing mass [of light] extending downwards and upwards, which is the fire-drill (*araṇi*) for the family of syllables.
Therein, O Dear One, one should write the name of the deity, Devadatta, situated in the middle of the enclosure (*saṃpuṭa*).
Then one should meditate on [the victim] being burned and devoured by Śiva and others,
while a multitude of Śākinīs tear at his hands and feet.
One will kill [the enemy] without a doubt by means of a homa sacrifice using poison and fragments of bone.
One should always employ the syllable *thak* joined with a *piṇḍa* for the purpose of paralyzing speech. (20–28)
It swiftly renders one impotent, mute, and even bound by the penis; it acts upon one situated within the Tantras, just as Bhairava has declared. (20.29)
By means of the *śākinī-hṛdaya* alone, such killing is accomplished very quickly.
O Dear One, the *śākinī-hṛdaya* is to be written within the letters of the alphabet (*mātṛkā*).
Then, O beautiful lady, by placing the name within a *saṃpuṭa* (enclosure) and ending it with *hūṃ phaṭ*, one may kill;
through repeated practice, one may even destroy the earth itself.

The rite to be accomplished, which reaches both the higher and the lower and is joined with the vital points of the Śākinīs, brings about the killing of all sentient beings; of this there is no doubt. (20-32)
Enraged, his sword clashing with a *jhaṇṭiti* sound, he held an irreversible wrath;
shaking his own hair, his eyes were bloodshot with the pain of anger. (20.33)
Then, O Goddess, the knower of mantras should always perform the most excellent rite;
otherwise, O Leader of Heroes, there will be a loss of virility for you. (20.34)
The vidyās, which possess great power both supreme and inferior, are arranged in a disordered manner;
they are joined with the vital points of the Śākinīs and employed with the utterances *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*. (20.35)
"Phaṭ hūṃ ca phaṭ," O Varārohā, one should write the name of the target in reverse order upon a cowhide, O Dear One, ending with the syllable *saṃjñā*. (20.36)

The practitioner, having become naked with his hair disheveled and smeared with the ashes and charcoal of the cremation ground, should place [the substance] in the mouth of a *preta* after mounting upon its breast. (20.37)
With garlands of corpses upon the ground, enraged and with blood-red eyes,
he is a reciter using a conch-shell rosary, devoted to the practice of the great liquor.
O Dear One, one should fashion a triangle or a half-moon in front of the corpse;
however, the *tuṇḍa* (the tip) should be devoid of a girdle (*mekhalā*) and possessed of uneven measures.
The wise one should have an image of a crow or a dog mounted upon a donkey made;
he should then prepare an offering vessel (arghapātra) consisting of a skull filled with blood.
O Goddess, O Beloved, having kindled the fire arising from that with the fuel of a cremation ground,
one should then perform the oblation with pieces of bone smeared with poison.

With husks mixed with thorns and facing away [from the victim], one should recite the mantra ending in *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*; having uttered that, one should cause death by means of [the weapon] joined with two [parts]. (20.42)
Then, having uttered the word "swiftly" (śīghram), followed by the two planets and then the name [of the person],
such as "Amuka," one should cause the oblations to be offered.
Then, O Umā, while standing with the sacrificial ladle, one should meditate upon the Goddess surrounded by a host of Śākinīs, who are consuming the oblation.
Then, having finished the offering of clarified butter, one should remain with the deities.
O Goddess of the gods, with his body divided into many fragments, the victim goes to the abode of Yama within half a watch (three hours).
However, one who knows the mantras should never perform this irreversible rite against a king, nor against those who destroy the gods, the sacred fires, or their gurus. (20.46)
The entire ritual procedure must be performed by the practitioner in that very place;
furthermore, this supreme application should be performed at a solitary linga. (20.47)
The poison consists of hīrādhikā, unmattaka, and salāṅgalī; and the blood of man, buffalo, donkey, horse, and wolf. (20.48)
O Goddess of gods, one should also draw [the image] upon the head of the liṅga of Śaśaka;
just as it was done before, so should it be performed here without hesitation.
Taking a corpse at night in a place called Bhūta, the wise one with disheveled hair should,
O Goddess, fashion a rope from the materials arising from that corpse.
One should cause the worship to be performed with plantains and numerous offerings of used garlands (nirmālya);
the incense should be mixed with *phalgu* and combined with fragments of bone. (20.51)
Then one should cause [the substance] to be offered to the God of gods and recite the mantra;
one whose mind has departed [from the world] should wrap the liṅga with a cord three times.
Having placed one foot upon the head and the second upon the corpse,
and then having raised a cry of "Hā hā!", one should recite the mantra, O Dear One.
O Goddess, in the reverse order, one should begin the churning as before;
for half a ghaṭikā, there is the severing of the enemy’s head by the power of the deity.
This happens here; there is no doubt, it is the truth, the truth—of this there is no uncertainty.
Having gone at the clear dawn, one should cause the ritual bathing with milk to be performed.
Having installed an image of another deity, one who is impelled by the scriptures should then cause the consecration of the *unmanī* [state] to be performed, O lady of excellent hips. (20.56)
Having stationed himself well-restrained at the gate of the village,
they fetch water from there and pour it pot after pot.
That very bath [is performed] on the head of the practitioner within the yoga-maṇḍala;
O beautiful one, it continues here until a thousand jars have been used.
One should bathe in this manner exactly as prescribed in the scriptures;
having performed the previously mentioned sacrifice, one should then undergo the consecration. (20.59)
Having offered dūrvā grass smeared with the three sweets and combined with granulated sugar, one then attains peace; it is not otherwise, O Vīranāyikā. (20.60)
One should place a vessel filled with blood derived from a black goat there,
and upon it, one should install the Goddess, the Vidyā, resplendent as both the supreme and the non-supreme.
First, one should worship [the deity] together with the heart-mantra in the prescribed manner;
then, having donned black garments, one should begin the performance of the ritual practice.
O Goddess, having brought four maidens endowed with auspicious marks, they should be dressed in black attire and stationed equally in the four directions all around. (20.63)
And white [beings], O Goddess, facing one another and gazing at each other, together with human fire-sticks encircled by a cord of hair, O Beloved. (20.64)
One should churn the flask with that [mantra] and likewise recollect the vidyā;
as soon as half a watch (prahara) has passed in this manner, the kṛtyā arises.
Devouring the worlds with her fierce power, she says, "What shall I do? The practitioner should then say, "Eat such-and-such a person! || 20.66 ||
Then that *kṛtyā* runs to wherever she has been commanded by the practitioners;
having slain him, she enters there, back into the place where those of great power were born.
Now, O fair-faced one, I shall explain another method for the rout of an army,
by which the Daityas were formerly defeated in battle by the gods.
Therefore, O Pārvatī, I shall explain that to you in accordance with reality; listen as to how one should write the Vidyā, which possesses the great power of both the supreme and the non-supreme.
Therein, O Goddess, one should arrange the army commanders in due order:
the elephant-riders, horsemen, chariot-warriors, feudal lords, attendants, and great warriors. (20.70)
A warrior skilled with the bow [should practice] upon a hide of oxen or a cloth;
having fashioned a square field marked with the insignia of a thunderbolt. (20.71)
There, in the center, one should draw Bala, who has rendered Parā extremely agitated;
she is situated within the outer enclosure and is endowed with the letters of the Mātṛkā.
The supreme and non-supreme great vidyās, endowed with their own power in the direct order—all of them assume supreme forms, established within their own armies. (20.73)
It was surrounded on all sides by many others of great strength, who bore various supreme forms such as wheels, mallets, swords, and so forth.
On the outside, there are the hosts of nāgas and others, terrifying with their clanging bells;
likewise, further outside from that, there are those who are fierce and terrifying as they breathe forth.
One should depict those with swords raised in their hands, with weapons such as scimitars uplifted, and engaged in combat with bows, afflicted by that [enemy] on all sides. (20.76)
With the fourfold army itself, accompanied by the vidyā, one should cast [the enemy] into the mouth of the preta while standing facing the army. (20.77)
Then the wise one should dig [the pit] in the center of the performance ground;
having installed thereupon the Goddess, the leader of the universe. (20.78)
Then, while devouring the army, the Yogayoginī should be fashioned with banners,
cloth-canopies, and awnings, crowded with flags and strips of cloth.
Having done this, one should thereafter commence the rite of offering (balikarma) with many kinds of foods to be chewed and eaten, prepared like those for a great sacrificial animal.

One should satisfy all the deities, as well as the Kṣetrapālas and other spirits; then, having offered the bali-oblation to the directions, one should likewise offer the bali-oblations to the elemental beings.
Having thus satisfied [the deities] in this manner, the king should then perform the consecration;
having performed the previously mentioned sacrifice, he should take the victory-bestowing jar.
Having worshipped according to the rules as prescribed in the scripture, O Goddess, at the clear dawn, the practitioner of mantras should bathe the Heroic Leader.
O Goddess, one should fashion a pedestal-binding with eight plantain leaves;
then, one should bathe the seated kings with that water.
O Goddess, the supreme practitioner becomes equal to the highest and the lowest;
with this vessel, he should sprinkle his own strength on all sides. (20.85)
Having gone out from there to the exterior, he stood to the west of the goddess,
[surrounded by] the sound of kettledrums, clay drums, horses, elephants, and the leaders of warriors.
O Great Goddess, one should install the Vidyā, which is both supreme and inferior and most terrifying;
thereafter, one should produce a roar that is frightening and exceedingly dreadful.
"Seize! Seize! Strike! Strike!"—these words should be uttered by those stationed on all sides as they charge toward the enemy army; then it becomes overwhelmed with confusion.
Trembling and terrified with fear, he stands with his mouth agape;
and though intent on uprooting the enemy, he falls from his hand in every respect. (20.89)
All turn away, bewildered, and perish, having abandoned their manly valor;
the elephants and horses flee, turning their backs, while the steeds lose their prowess. (20.90)
Thus, O beloved, in ancient times the gods brought about the rout of the army in battle;
now I shall further explain the ritual for the hoisting of the banner.
The army will quickly suffer a rout; hear that in brief:
having made a thick and wide cloth from thread spun by a maiden... (20.92)
There, in the center, one should draw Parā, seated upon a corpse,
formidable, massive-bodied, with eight arms, and most terrifying.
Below, however, one should place the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*), pierced by a radish, while Mahāmāyā is simultaneously devouring the enemy army. (20.94)
One should draw the entire enemy army, both high and low, situated within a skull;
having drawn it thus, one should thereafter perform the worship of the Goddess.
One should satisfy [the deities] in every direction with various kinds of food, edibles, grains, and drinks;
one should construct a most beautiful pedestal for the Goddess using eight plantain trees.
One should worship the Goddess residing there with perfumes, incense, and purifying threads, as well as with beautiful flowers, meats, and offerings of liquor and spirits. (20.97)
Having thus performed the worship and offered the bali-oblation, being well-concentrated,
he should bring eight courtesans who are mature in years and well-disciplined.
One should satisfy [the deity] with liquor and meat until satisfaction is attained,
while the naked woman with loosened topknot recites the mantra in this manner.
O fair-faced one, at the two *bhañjā* syllables, say "take, take" twice and "slay";
[place] the *kandala* in the left hand for each one.
The goddesses stood facing the devouring army as it fled;
seeing her, the army perished at the mere sight of her banner.
But when one turns away from itching, shame, and pride, O beloved, the practitioner, having conquered the army, becomes a hundredfold more powerful, O lady of excellent limbs. (20.102)
O Goddess, his own home shall become inexhaustible; of this there is no doubt.
Now I shall further explain the raising of the banner. (20.103)
Having taken up the word as before, the practitioner, endowed with devotion,
should draw a square city and inscribe the mantra in its center.
Rotating like a wheel according to the sequence starting from the east,
one should write there the *Hanumantra*, which possesses great power and holds a staff in its hand.
One should draw a camel below; on its back, the commander of the army;
in the middle of the camel, the mantra; and then again, upon the feet.
O Dear One, one should install another [deity] in the four directions, situated upon the four feet:

*Oṃ vajrakāya vajratuṇḍa kapilapiṅgalordhvakeśa raktamukha taḍijjihva mahāraudra daṃṣṭrākarālina dṛḍhapraharaṇa laṅkeśvara setubandhaka śailapravāha gaganacara ehyehi bhagavan mahābalaparākrama bhairava ājñāpayati! Bind, bind with the cord of the long [syllables]; paralyze, paralyze on all sides; moisten, moisten; yawn, yawn; *khakhare khakhare*; *kha kha hūṃ* to all the wicked ones!*
*hūḥ phaṭ svāhā* | 130a [g] *oṃ himavantaṃ yāhi yāhi*— one should write this on the body of a camel. *oṃ yamadevī svāhā*.
It should be offered at the four corners:
Oṃ vātali vātali virale varāhamukhi, paralyze, paralyze the bodies of all those with wicked faces until they are struck by the vajra, svāhā!
This should be offered in the four directions within the vajra-maṇḍala.
Having thus written it according to the prescribed rite, one should thereafter commence the worship.
The practitioner of mantras should perform the rite of offering (balikarma) with perfumes, incense, food, drink, and other such items;
he should raise a banner positioned facing the army.
Upon being seen, that which has become disintegrated perishes, its human effort abandoned;
or else, it becomes multiformed, endowed with both the supreme and the non-supreme.
One should perform the piercing (vidarbhaṇa) by means of the very heart-mantra of Śākinī and its conclusion;
it effects the killing [of enemies] and the breaking of their army—of this there is no doubt. (20.110)
Or one should draw Mahāmārī or a Śākinī who pierces the vital points;
with the blood of a rabbit, one should cause Mārī to enter the morsel of food.
With the blood of a donkey, one becomes a destroyer of cities; there is no doubt about this.
O Dear One, with whichever blood one may draw Mahāmārī, [with that same blood she is propitiated].
In various forms, however, the great pestilence prevails; one pestilence after another arises, having been brought about by the disordered state of the world.
A Śākinī joined with the vital points can indeed destroy the entire world;
therefore, O Goddess, one should then employ King Yama and the administration of Yama.
This mantra of Yamāntaka is known as Kālāntaka;
likewise, O Goddess, it is Yamarāja and Bahurūpa as well. (20.115)
When, through conjunction, the state of being the heart-self is joined within Bhairava, there occur killing, withering, destruction, as well as inciting enmity and expulsion. (20.116)
If the supreme practitioner, well-restrained in meditation, applies the Mahāpāśupata [mantra] which pierces the vital points of the Śākinī, [he succeeds]. (20.117)
One shall slay the enemy here, of this there is no doubt—even one as dear as Śakra—by drawing the Mahāpāśupata weapon joined with the Yamarāja-weapon. (20.118)
One would kill [the enemy] without a doubt in half a ghaṭikā; of this there is no uncertainty.
Now, O Goddess, another supreme and unsurpassed treasury of mantras [is taught].
By the mere knowledge of which one shall attain the desired accomplishment (siddhi);
I shall now explain in detail that most excellent *piṇḍaka* for the purpose of eradication (*uccāṭana*).
Oṃ hrāḥ hrīḥ hūṃ haḥ phaṭ!

O Goddess, when this [mantra] residing in the letters of the Mātṛkā is illuminated by both [the breaths] during exhalation and [inhalation], and is impelled by the wind, it performs expulsion (uccāṭana) most effectively. (20.121)
The Mare’s Mouth (Vaḍavāmukha) is of great splendor, arisen like the fire of time;
it effects drying up, destruction, as well as killing and expulsion. (20.122)
When employed by the practitioner, this indeed brings about the destruction of one's family, as well as whatever else is improperly situated; of this there is no doubt. (20.123)
I shall now explain the Vaḍavāmukha; listen to it as it is.
Oṃ! Ho! Ho! O Vaḍavāmukha, great fire! Devour, devour all beings! Expel, expel! Destroy, destroy! Dry up, dry up! Expel, expel! Hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ! Homage!
I shall explain the Mahāmārī; listen to it in its true essence, O beautiful one. (20.124)
First, the word "Oṃ," preceded by a salutation to Rudra;
secondly, [the word] "Vaivasvata"; and thirdly, "Yamāya. (20.125)
The fourth [name] is "Dharmarāja," beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*;
likewise, another is "Mārīye," and after that, "Mahāmārī. (20.126)
One should know that which ends in the fourth case is for the subduing of those with wicked minds;
then there is another word, *raktākṣī*, and another, *kṛṣṇavarṇā*. (20.127)
O Mother of Beings, beyond this is the goddess who carries out Yama’s command;
likewise, she is the one here who effects the destruction of all beings through every sound.
Then, having uttered the great sound *mā*, one should next utter *rīye*;
then *hara* twice, *daha* twice, *paca* twice, and again *chinda* twice. (20.129)
"Bhinda," two "bhakṣa" syllables, and the two words "māraya," joined with "hūḥ hūḥ phaṭ phaṭ"—such is the vidyā in brief. (20.130)
Thus she has been described along with her secret [mantra], characterized by her defining marks:
*Oṃ mārīye mahāmahāmārīye, you are the goddess who carries out the command of Yama, commanded by Citragupta and by the Great-Souled Kāla;
you alone are the messenger of death for all living beings.*
Kill [so-and-so], kill! Dry up, dry up! Overwhelm, overwhelm! Expel, expel! O you who rain down blood and flesh! Marrow! Marrow! O Dear One! Great Plague! Hūṃ Phaṭ Phaṭ Thaṃ Lum!
Oṃ! You who have the form of a *preta*, Great Illusion, naked, wearing a skull-garland—smeared with the very blood of the *dānavas*, intent upon their slaughter.
"Seize the life of such-and-such a being;
O Great Yogi, eat, eat! Perform the rite of eradication!
This mantra, joined with *huṃ* and *phaṭ*, performs the killing [of the enemy] most effectively.
When joined with Ra, it is to be employed for drying up; likewise, when joined with Ya, it is used for eradication.
The letter *la* is said to be for paralyzing (*stambhana*), while *va* is considered for nourishing (*āpyāyana*).
With *sa*, it effects the rite of immortality (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), and likewise, when joined with *huṃ*, it is used for deluding (*mohana*).

For the purpose of subjugation (*vaśya*), one should employ the syllable *kliṃ*; for the state of being neuter (*ṣaṇḍhatā*), one should employ the syllable *ḍha*. One should apply the syllable *pa* as a "sealing of the mouth" (*mukhabandha*); regarding this, there is no need for further deliberation. (20.133)
In this way, the great vidyā of Mārī, when endowed with wrath, should be performed by the best of practitioners; she is remembered as the accomplisher of all rites.
When the *vidyā* of Bahurūpa is employed by the practitioner, it performs manifold activities through the offering of husks and thorns. (20.135)
When joined with the Pāśupata [mantra], it intensely effects expulsion, as well as killing, withering, destruction, inciting enmity, and expulsion. (20.136)
When joined with the Pāśupata [mantra], it accomplishes everything;
when joined with the Piñchka [mantra], it is beneficial for the act of whirling.
131a] Now, what is the use of speaking at length or describing it again and again?
O Dear One, whatever action is performed, all that shall be accomplished.
This second great pestilence is known as the performer of all rites;
now [follows] the supreme king of mantras, most exceedingly terrible.
This is renowned as the Aghora weapon, which effects the destruction of the world, as well as killing, expulsion, inciting enmity, and even annihilation. (20.140)
One should indeed perform all of this—namely, trembling and withering—situated within the letters of the Mātṛkā and joined with the seed-syllables of the wicked. (20.141)
"By means of the distinction between the imperishable and the perishable, according to the sequence of the fifty [letters], and likewise others such as these that were previously mentioned. (20.142)
Having formed them through the division of the *kūṭas*, they are the accomplishers in all rites;
O Goddess, there are fifty *rañjakas*, and likewise ten others are recorded.
Through the external practice beginning with the enjoyment of the Daityas, one may attain supreme knowledge;
by means of the nose, one shall accomplish great enjoyments—of this there is no doubt.
Exorcism is performed with the crest alone; drying up with the staff alone;
immobilization with the left breast; and the increase of life-force with the throat alone. (20.145)
Through the seed-syllable of Time (Kālabīja), one brings about dissolution; of this there is no doubt.
Through the seed-syllable of the Belly (Udara) alone, one effects muteness; herein one should not entertain any hesitation. (20.146)
Furthermore, the navel-seed-syllable bestows dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Thus, O Goddess, have the ten color-inducing [syllables] been described to you. (20.147)
I shall now describe the most excellent source of mantras, which is the self-natured colorant:
the sequences beginning with *kṣa*, *kra*, *kla*, *klā*, and *kṣya*, in their proper order.

The groups beginning with *kra*, *kla*, *akka*, and *rakra*, as well as those beginning with *ha* and *aska*, are situated respectively in the stages of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*). (20.149)
Through the differentiation of the twelve vowels, she bestows all accomplishments upon men;
they are mutually entwined by means of the conjunction of syllables and moments.
There is a state of oneness with the letters of one's name within the channels of the vowels of one's own birth. (20.151)
"Living beings, primordial nature, and mantras that accomplish all aims are united in one place.
The Goddess said: "O Mahādeva, I wish to hear about the Aghora weapon according to its true essence. (20.152)
"By the mere knowledge of which one becomes worthy of all rites.
Bhairava said:
"Listen, O Goddess of great asceticism; I shall proclaim the Aghora weapon. (20.153)
By the mere knowledge of which [one becomes the master] of both fear and fearlessness:

Oṃ hrīḥ! Flash forth, flash forth! O you of terrible, most terrible form! Caṭa caṭa! Pracaṭa pracaṭa! Kaha kaha! Vama vama! Slay, slay! Hrīṃ hrīṃ hrauṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ namaḥ! This is the Aghora-weapon mantra.
Oṃ, to the non-terrible Śiva, hūṃ; obeisance to the heart.
Oṃ, O you of non-terrible form, blaze, blaze! Svāhā to the head. Oṃ, O you who possess a body of flame, vauṣaṭ to the crest-lock.

Oṃ caṭa caṭa dhaka dhaka vandha vandha, O you with terrible fangs, hūṃ! Phaṭ! To the armor, hūṃ! O / A / Hūṃ! Blaze, blaze! Flare up, flare up! Destroy, destroy, O you of terrible form! Slay, slay! Hūṃ! Phaṭ! To the weapon, phaṭ!
I shall proclaim its ritual procedure, which has emerged from the section on rituals. (20.154)
And the missile named Amogha, which issued from the mouth of Śiva—by the mere remembrance of it, O Goddess, the three worlds tremble. (20.155)
Rākṣasas, bhūtas, vetālas, and whatever other malevolent beings there may be, do not remain in that place where this written [mantra] resides. (20.156)
Now, therefore, follow the ritual activities of the Blessed One once he has attained accomplishment;
having seen the emergence of enemies in the battle of the commitment (*samaya*). [20.157]
Having formed the mudrā, one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times in a wrathful form;

at that very moment, [the victim] dies. One should perform the recitation while seated upon a bed for three days; if one desires ascetic power (*tapas*), one attracts it. Then, having formed the mudrā, if one recites eight thousand times with the name of a specific person, one shatters their magical diagram (*yantra*).

It causes the asuras to fall; it kills kings; it attracts women; it paralyzes the wicked; it deludes the learned. If one recites [the mantra] out of anger, it splits doors. Having entered the water, if one recites eight thousand times, it destroys that lineage. Then, having formed the mudrā of the "uplifting" or the "wind-stirring," one causes rain to fall.
One can solidify water; wherever one desires, there one causes it to fall.
Having consecrated a clod of earth, a leaf, or a blade of grass one hundred times with mantras, if one throws it into a merchant’s shop, it destroys the business.
Having consecrated a flower one hundred times with mantras, if one throws it into a tavern, it halts the business and destroys all the liquor.
Having consecrated a human bone seven times with mantras, if one draws [the name] of someone on the ground, that person is expelled from that place.
By erasing it, there is liberation after eight thousand recitations. Having entered the water up to the shoulder, one should recite the mantra one thousand times.
A maiden attracts [him] within three days;
she withers and dies, desiring no other.
By this, one attracts all women.
Merely by the sight of Smara, all sins and misdeeds consisting of evil are destroyed.
Now, I shall describe the means of accomplishment: one who subsists on vegetables and the like should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times;
he becomes liberated from great sins, secondary sins, and those equal to them. (20.159)
Therefore, ritual actions are performed: one should offer a hundred thousand oblations of clarified butter, and it bestows sovereignty;
with sesame seeds, one beholds a great treasure.
On the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having fasted for three nights, one should take collyrium from the eyes of a person of the same caste who has died on the tenth day.
One with eyes like those of a horse becomes invisible.
Having combined saffron, *tagara*, and fragrance, one should have a pill made, encased in the three metals.
Having thrown [the herb] consecrated one thousand times into the mouth, one becomes invisible.
If one travels by way of the middle path, one becomes invincible. Having ascended * * * * *, if one recites the mantra one hundred thousand times, one gains mastery over all elixirs (*rasāyana*).
Now, if one desires to drive away enemies, one should fashion a triangular linga, bind it with a noose of one's own arm, and recite [the mantra] eight thousand times;
at that very moment, they die,
but those who have sons live until the end.

Having consecrated an *arka* leaf seven times with mantras, one should bury it in the ground; eye disease will afflict that person. Upon its extraction, there is liberation. Having consecrated human bone seven times with mantras, if one writes someone's name upon it and buries it in the ground, that person is seized by all diseases; upon its extraction, there is liberation. With funeral ashes consecrated seven times with mantras, if one writes someone's name [upon them], [the same result follows].
At that very moment, O Lord, one dies.

If one drinks ghee consecrated seven times with mantras, one becomes a possessor of the power of hearing (śrutidhara). Having combined yellow pigment (rocanā), yellow orpiment (haritāla), and collyrium (añjana), and having wrapped them in the three metals, one should wear it on the face according to the previously mentioned procedure; whoever sees [the wearer] and whoever is seen by him—all become subject to his will.
Then, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *khadira* wood fuel; all *yakṣiṇīs* will come under his control.

On the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having established the vidyā with three leaves of the *aśvattha* tree and covered it with three [leaves], one should recite it until the threefold accomplishment occurs:
namely, it becomes warm, emits smoke, and blazes.
When the movement of the breath is like heat (*uṣmā*), one becomes the lord of the piśācas, gandharvas, yakṣas, kinnaras, and mahoragas.

When it is like smoke (*dhūmāyamāna*), one lives as long as Brahmā; one attains invisibility, the power of traveling through the sky, mastery over all forms of invisibility, and lives for the duration of a kalpa.

When it blazes like the rising young sun, one with curled black hair shall live for one eon. In that region dwell wicked beings; having lit a lamp with sharp oil consecrated eight thousand times, if those wicked beings see the light of the lamp, their eyes will burst.
This should also be recited at the time of accomplishing other mantras.
Furthermore, if one offers oblations of all kinds of rice until midday, one causes rain to fall in this manner.
By reciting it one hundred and eight times constantly, one becomes beloved by all people.
O Pārvatī, I shall now declare the mantra of Yamarāja; listen to it in its true essence.
Its ritual application has been explained previously, and now I shall speak of its extraction (uddhāra).
This horse of Yamāntaka is proclaimed as Kālāntaka;
divided into twelve varieties, it is celebrated as Yameśa. It is to be measured by the assembly hall of King Yama, and its rising is from the redness of Yama’s thighs.
That which is to be protected by the Yakṣas, that which is the Yakṣa itself, and that which is free from affliction—
preceded by the salutation to Oṃ, this is, in brief,
the incomparable thirty-five-syllable King Yama, O fair-faced one.
Now I shall proclaim the Pāśupata [tantra], which brings about the dissolution of the world and is difficult even for the wicked to behold and unbearable even for the gods. Therefore,
I shall now set forth the Mahāpāśupata.
Right here, the great-souled Tryambaka Paśupati himself [bestowed] the supreme Mahāstra,
the Great Being, the ultimate instrument of destruction,
difficult for gods, dānavas, and daityas to behold, and the bringer of fearlessness.

One should draw [the deity] with fierce, sharp fangs, surrounded by a garland of a thousand flames, possessing the radiance of a thousand-flamed jewel-gem; rising up like a thousand peaks of the glorious Mount Meru, like a second sun;

being worshipped by gods, dānavas, siddhas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, kinnaras, and vidyādharas; like Mount Meru filled with caves, grottoes, and caverns; and with his mouth licking with his tongue.

Just as a wicked great serpent hisses repeatedly, uttering loud laughter, shouting with joy, and making "huḍutkāra" sounds; as one who has been reduced to ashes by poison yet remains surrounded by many serpents, and is constantly celebrated with the chanting of the Sāmaveda by the Bālakhilyas and others.

He has a thousand eyes, a thousand arms, and five heads; he is formidable with ten ears and ten fangs, with ten lips and a flattened nose yet possessing the shape of a broad snout. He shatters the thunderbolts that split the cardinal and intermediate directions with sounds of *ṭiṭibhi-ṭibhi* and *ciricirimirimiri-kiri-kiri*. With his fangs, he makes the sound *karakarāya*, like a well-constructed machine. His belly is filled with marrow, blood, and fat; he is Rudra of fierce form, a follower of Rudra, [subduing] three crores and thirty million supreme mantras.

This [rite] effects the withdrawal of one’s own mantras, brings about nourishment, and grants the accomplishments (*siddhi*) of increase and growth; it is based on the Vedas and devoted to the *agnihotra* sacrifice.

By means of ashes, there is the casting down of the *vidyādharas* upon the earth; by means of charcoal powder or iron filings, there is the casting down of the *rākṣasas*; it is the eradication of gods, *daityas*, *dānavas*, *nāgas*, and so forth, the terrifying of the *vidyādharas*, a great weapon, and the shattering of other weapons. Herein, the words of the mantra are as follows: *ṃs*... (unclear).

Oṃ amogha phaṭ! O unconquered by the immortals phaṭ! O honored one phaṭ! O hero phaṭ! O brave one phaṭ! O you who hold the noose of time in your hand phaṭ! O Time phaṭ! O left-hand one phaṭ! O Vāmadeva phaṭ! O Eldest phaṭ! O Most Excellent phaṭ! O Rudra phaṭ! O you whose form is Rudra phaṭ! O Desire phaṭ! O you whose form is desire phaṭ! O Time phaṭ! O Dissolver of Time phaṭ! O Strength phaṭ! O Dissolver of Strength phaṭ! O Destroyer of Strength phaṭ! O Subduer of all beings phaṭ! O Universe phaṭ! O you of diverse forms phaṭ! O severed one phaṭ! O split one phaṭ! O slain one phaṭ!

Pāta phaṭ! Mohaya phaṭ! Sākṣirudra, saṃhara phaṭ! Pātaya phaṭ! Nipātaya phaṭ! Just as you are endowed with Paśupati Tryambaka, so do you strike down, phaṭ hūṃ phaṭ kha! This is the Great Pāśupata Weapon. Oṃ amṛtagarbhāya svāhā! [This is] the Heart. Oṃ amṛtatejase hūṃ phaṭ! [This is] the Head.
Oṃ vidyut svāhā | [This is] the Śikhā. Oṃ mahāpāśupata kara kara bandha bandha hūṃ phaṭ | [This is] the Kavaca. Oṃ pinākine svāhā | [This is] the Astra.
The Pāśupata [tantra] is known to have its ancillaries (sāṅga); therefore, hear now the Bahurūpa [mantra]:
"To those who are not terrible, to those who are terrible, and to those more terrible than the terrible; to all, to all of them, salutation to you, O forms of Rudra!
Om, salutation to the non-terrible ones, to the heart."
Oṃ *thaghorebhyaḥ* namaḥ to the head; Oṃ *ghoraghoratarebhyaśca* namaḥ to the crest-lock (*śikhā*);
Oṃ *sarvataḥ sarvasarvebhyaḥ* namaḥ to the armor (*kavaca*);
Oṃ *namaste rudrarūpebhyaḥ* namaḥ to the weapon (*astra*).
Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should thereafter commence meditation.
O lady of excellent vows, I shall now declare that which has not been told to anyone else in the tantra. (20.160)
O beautiful lady, as the god Mahābhairava was sporting, [the one] who effects creation and destruction emerged from his heart. (20.161)
He has a body like the fire at the end of an aeon and a roar like the clouds at the time of universal dissolution;
he possesses fangs resembling a mass of lightning and matted locks with the brilliance of blazing fire.
With the sun, moon, and fire for his eyes, having hollowed-out sockets and being most terrifying,
he possessed a broad expanse of chest and wore a serpent as a sacred thread.
Wearing a crown of shimmering rubies, adorned with serpent-earrings,
displaying the majesty of a necklace of snakes, and possessing bracelets and anklets made of serpents.
Clad in a lion’s skin, adorned with a girdle of serpents,
covered by an elephant hide, formidable, and crowned with the crescent moon.
Five-faced, mounted upon a corpse, with ten arms and three eyes,
adorned with a garland of skulls, and bearing a sword and a shield.
The god holds a noose and a goad, descended from Śaraśṛṅgī;
he carries a skull-bowl and a khaṭvāṅga staff, with hands granting boons and fearlessness.
Resembling crushed collyrium, with a radiant lower lip quivering,
he was the granter of boons even to Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu, yet remained powerless even among the gods.
This fierce form of yours has been proclaimed as Svachanda;
this meditation has been fully described as the means for accomplishing the threefold fruit. (20.169)

And regarding this very matter of the ritual of the goal and the means, it was previously taught in another tantra as well, O fair-faced one, by which [it is established] in this very one too. (20.170)
These too should be applied with effort according to the prescribed ritual:
that which is to be recited, established, written, meditated upon, and likewise offered in the fire oblation. (20.171)
O Goddess, the fivefold yantra is proclaimed in all tantras;
hereafter, I shall explain the practice for subjugation and other rites. (20.172)
I shall explain this supreme secret in due order: one should join the syllable *kliṃ* as an enclosure and then insert the name of the deity. (20.173)
I have taught this mantra, joined with the Vidyā, for the purpose of subjugation;
the name encased by the syllable *kliṃ* is known as the "melting and causing to melt. (20.174)
*Kle*: By means of the *saṃpuṭa* (enclosure) yoga, it becomes moist and always flows.
*Kleṃ*: O Goddess, when enclosed by *kā*, it becomes like a springtime lotus.
*Kli ai kli*: When these are joined in a garland (*mālā*), they bring everything under control.

*Kliḥ kliḥ kliḥ*: O fair-faced one, when this supreme garland is joined together, there is no doubt that it will attract even those women who pride themselves on their beauty. *Hrīḥ klīḥ hrīḥ*: This equal garland brings about both attraction and subjugation.
KṢĀ HRĪ KRO AI KLĪ—the garland of equal [syllables] is the agitator and the subjugator;
it will attract even Urvaśī, the beautiful intoxicant, without a doubt.
HRAI KSLAU HRĪ KRAU AI KLĪ—this garland of yoga also bestows helplessness.
"O Goddess, this is the consensus of kings and the certain conclusion of the scripture regarding all the rites of subjugation, categorized according to the divisions of Paśupati. (20.175)
But it should always be performed, O lady of excellent limbs, situated in the middle of the womb;
the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) below, with that of the practitioner (sādhaka) positioned above it. (20.176)
Beneath the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), it is conjoined with fire and wind;
above it resides the syllable of the practitioner (sādhaka), and the throat itself faces downwards. (20.177)
Having understood this, O lady of excellent hips, according to the distinction between what is achievable and what is unachievable, one attains success;
of this there is no doubt, provided one knows the divisions of the mantras.
Now I shall further explain another supreme method for agitating a city,
by means of which one may dwell eternally in any location within a village, town, or district.
In that regard, one should perform meditation; when agitation of the city arises, O Goddess, one should contemplate the central place within the maṇḍala of dissolution. (20.180)
Above that, O beloved, is the seed-syllable of Varuṇa, conjoined with a great cloud,
resembling the sound of falling rain and having the appearance of liquid lac.
Having drunk [the nectar] that has flooded the country, the maṇḍala, and the territory, one should perform this every day until consciousness is produced. (20.182)
The fire does not enter it, nor does the mandala diminish;
for all that is protected by it is likewise illuminated by its flames. (20.183)
And the drawing of the city's agitation has been explained to you, O beautiful one;
or else, it may be done with a red thread, provided with those syllables. 20.184ab [g]
The mantra-practitioner should cause that city to tremble on all sides, even to the edge of the forest.
He should perform this every day until agitation arises. (20.185)
By this sequential yoga, one should bring about the supreme arousal;
or else, at the conclusion, one should utter that name.
A disturbance of the city arises for ten thousand or even a hundred thousand [years];
by this sequential yoga, a disturbance of the country arises. (20.187)
Now I shall explain another unsurpassed method for agitating a city, by the mere knowledge of which the practitioner sports upon the earth. (20.188)
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus, and outside of that, a sixteen-petaled one;
thereafter, O beautiful lady, a twenty-four-petaled one in due order.
Having joined the *sa*-group starting from the east and so forth, one should place the *ya*-group in the intermediate directions;
in the sixteen-spoked [wheel], the twenty-four letters beginning with *ka* follow those beginning with *a*.
One should join the radiant pericarp and place the king (the letter *ka*) within its center;
O Vīranāyikā, it is pervaded by the four non-quaternary groups beginning with the classes of consonants.
One should draw the secret power (guhyaśakti) situated within the petals of the directions and within its own petals;
[this should be done] with yellow pigment (rocanā), vermilion (vāmaja), and combined with goat's milk (ajakṣīra).
O beautiful goddess, having deposited it either in a temple of a god, or at a crossroads, or even in one's own house of worship; 20-193.
Having performed worship, the Great Hero [should know that] the previously established wheel becomes quickly agitated; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (20.194)
The supreme agitation of the city has been declared by me, more secret than the secret;
this mystery has been made manifest for the benefit of practitioners. (20.195)
Therefore, I shall describe the extraction of the *kalās*, the supreme means of attracting all;
having established Kāmeśvara in the heart, who wields the bow and five arrows.
Having mentally worshipped him who is completely surrounded by the arts such as music and the like, with perfumes, incense, and purificatory offerings; || 20-197 ||
Having worshipped according to the rules, one should again perform the withdrawal with the mudrā and contemplate [the deity] in the form of a *kadamba* flower bud, filled with rays of light.
Having understood the arising of that, the practitioner of mantra should then perform the rites;
likewise, he should bring about the arising of the powers for whatever action he desires. (20.199)
O Great Goddess, the one skilled in the yoga of light should join together these two— the Amṛtā and Amṛtanāḍī channels— which are powers whose sight is dear.
At the time of ritual action, he should perform that nyāsa upon his own body as the form of the deity;
having performed the nyāsa of Amṛtāmṛtā, [he becomes] Priyadarśanā.

Having meditated upon another and caused him to meditate as well, one should join the heart-lotus with that desire in the form of a drop (bindu), and unite oneself with the syllable *ṣva* together with the drop.
Above the *bindu*, one should contemplate the *kama-śakti* and then the syllable *au*;
as before, one should cause that *śakti* to enter there via the path of the channel (*nāḍī*).
One should pierce that desire, from the head to the end of the *bindu*, with the thread of power (*śakti-tantu*);
having drawn it forth in vain according to the proper rule, one should join it to the *bindu* of the Self.
When passion is to be accomplished for that person, one should then contemplate it as before;
this supreme attraction of desire, which draws forth time, has been proclaimed by me. (20.205)
Thus, O illustrious lady, everything has been told to you in due order;
there exists nothing more potent for subjugation in the three worlds than this.
This peerless and supreme method of subjugation has been proclaimed;
now, O illustrious lady, I shall explain another [method] regarding the times.
And the names of faith and the others are, in their proper order, as follows: Faith is indeed that which produces contentment, and it is lovely and delightful. (20.208)
Śaśinī is also proclaimed, as well as Chāyā with her full orb;
likewise Amṛtā, Mṛtāvahā, Anaṅgā, and Mekhalā. (20.209)
Moha, Mohanā, Śoṣaṇā, Madanāvahā, and Madanā—these are proclaimed as the sixteen Yoginīs. || 20-210 ||
Having understood this, O knower of mantras, one should agitate the world of the moving and the unmoving.
Now I shall further proclaim another vidyā that agitates the three worlds. (20–211)
Upon a four-petaled, uninjured lotus endowed with a pericarp and filaments,
there are the door-guardians born of the womb, and the resident of the sacred seat (pīṭha) born of the field (kṣetra).
Beginning from the petal of Īśa, one should write those [names] on the four petals;
Siddhayogeśvarī is in the center, surrounded by Mahāmāyā.
One should draw the gentle form containing all wombs on the outside as an eight-petalled lotus;
there, the Mothers should be joined according to the sequence of their own mantras.
Having written [the mantra] as it resides in the secret power (guhyaśakti), one should write it again as it resides in Rudra;
having encircled it with Māyā and marked it with the guardians of the directions, O Dear One.
With the very substance produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, along with *rocanā* and sandalwood, and with saffron, red sandalwood, and the leaf of the *vaṭa* tree; || 20-216 ||
Having unified [the syllables], the practitioner of mantra should write [them] on birch bark on the thirteenth day of the waning moon;
having put on red garments and being anointed with red perfumes. (20–217)
Having performed the sacrifice with wine and other substances according to the previous sequence—thus, O Goddess, has this Vidyā that agitates the three worlds been described. (20–218)
O you who are honored by heroes, in former times you were borne by Anaṅga when he desired to disturb the sage Gautamī in the Dāruvana forest. (20–219)
This spell, O Mistress of the Gods, has also been maintained by me;
it is irresistible and is declared to be secret, having arisen from the secret power.
Now I shall further explain another supreme method for the unshakability of meditation:
there should be a pair of fire-mandalas, and furthermore, [the deity] should be situated in the corner in their center. (20–221)
One should cause the syllable *rau* to be bestowed; one should meditate on the radiant, whirling wheel that is ruddy like a lotus.
Having assumed the supreme *yonimudrā*, [one should perform] the coming and going within the womb (*yoni*) of that [wheel].
It will certainly melt away, just as Bhairava’s word declares,
once one has propitiated Rāma with the Paiśācaka [mantra] while afflicted by disease.
Having smeared her with honey and wine, one should take hold of her by the hand as much as possible;
then she, becoming sour with passion and tormented by the fire of desire, will undoubtedly come to him. (20.224)
With the juice of auspicious lac, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus with one's own hand;
in its center, one should write one's own name, [saying]: "O passionate woman, please delight me! (20–225).
In the same manner, one should draw the female organ; once grasped, it should be loosened by force.
It is situated within the *piṇḍa*, in the middle of the *piṇḍa*, resembling a blazing fire. (20–226)
O Goddess, one should visualize the intensely blazing [power] situated at the forehead at the tip of the *śakti*;
from the throat, the heart, and the navel, one should visualize it agitating the thread.
One should heat that [seed] as it revolves within the secret center;
it is distinguished by the fourth vowel and possesses the shimmering radiance of reddened semen. (20–228)
At that very moment, the girl—even if she is only two years old—becomes agitated;
yet, when one again meditates upon that *piṇḍa* situated at the navel, [she becomes calm]. (20–229)
As it revolves, the stream of power is agitated and releases its fluid;
one should meditate upon it as consisting of fire above and water below, having the nature of Agni and Soma.
In whose womb, O lady of excellent hips, that semen is discharged in an instant;
the letter Ai is Śakti, blazing at the tip like a flaming fire.
One should contemplate [the deity] revolving within the womb; in an instant, he emits the semen.
[The powers are] paralyzing, immobilizing, deluding, drying up, and likewise agitating. (20–232)

thereafter, one should perform whatever rite is desired by the practitioner.
Having taken dust from beneath a tree, mixed with black mustard and salt,
one should fashion an image of the person to be acted upon, incorporating their name interwoven with the vidyā-mantra.
Placed within his heart, it shall burn him like a fire of khadira wood;
whoever has such a rite performed against him will certainly come under one's control.
Sesame seeds combined with human flesh bring men under one's control;
likewise, those of the lowest castes are brought under control by flowers combined with the flesh of a cow and [human flesh] provided by a woman. (21–26)
The practitioner of mantra brings [the target] under control by reciting one hundred and eight times;
through the previously mentioned distinctions of caste, he effects subjugation, attraction, and killing. (21–27)
The knower of mantras performs the rite which is called the "Dwarf Head" (vāmanaśiraḥ).
First is the word *cāmuṇḍā*, and after that, the pair *kili*. (21–28)
Combined with the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*, preceded by *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, this mantra consisting of twenty-seven syllables should be known by the practitioners of mantra. (21–29)
I shall now explain, in brief, the extraction of its constituent parts:
first the word *cāmuṇḍā*, and likewise next, *maghorā*.
The pair of Amoghakīlis, along with *vicce*, *hūṃ*, *phaṭ*, and the *satāraka* [mantra], consisting of eighteen and a half syllables, is declared to be the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*). || 21-31 ||
The word *aghora* comes first, followed by *cāmuṇḍe*;
ending with *hūṃ phaṭ*, this nine-syllable mantra beginning with *bhava* is the *śiras*. (21–32)
The supreme word "Cāmuṇḍā" is joined with the syllable Oṃ;
likewise, the form "Aghorā" follows, and after that, the pair of "Kilis. (21–33)
The Śikhā-mantra is thus declared to consist of fifteen syllables;
it begins with the word "Cāmuṇḍā," preceded by the honorific [Oṃ]. (21–34)
And in the hand, the skull [is held] together with "mahāvicce hūṃ phaṭ.
This is declared to be the armor-mantra (varma), endowed with fifteen syllables. || 21-35 ||
One should first utter the syllable *oṃ*, followed by the word *cāmuṇḍā*,
then *raudrarūpā* (O you of fierce form), accompanied by the syllable *hūṃ* and the *phaṭ* syllable.
The weapon-mantra of the Goddess, endowed with great majesty, consists of ten syllables:
"Cāmuṇḍā," followed by the pair "Kili," and joined with "Vicce Hūṃ Phaṭ. || 21-37 ||
The supreme and most auspicious Heart-mantra, beginning with *tāraka*, has been fully explained.
With this, one should offer perfumes, incense, oblations, and flowers. (21–38)
The ritual service should be performed, including the consecration of the menstrual thread;
it should be placed upon the head, for it is traditionally taught that the tuft of hair (*śikhā*) exists for the sake of purity.

One should perform the purification of the *argha* vessel with the heart mantra, the purification of the feet with the armor mantra, and the purification of the mace with the weapon mantra; furthermore, one should commence the protection on all sides with the root mantra. (21.40)
One should worship the Supreme Goddess on the eight-spoked face;
one whose body is the mantra should worship her as conjoined with the five limbs of her own body.
Now, I shall explain his beautiful ritual manual (*kalpa*), which accomplishes all rites, is proven effective, easy to understand, and yields great fruit. (21.42)
Having meditated in a solitary and secluded place, the practitioner, being thoroughly devoted and deeply focused, should recite that one hundred thousand times as his supreme refuge. (21.43)
Thereafter, ten thousand recitations of the limbs are prescribed;
then the Great Vidyā becomes perfected—of this there is no doubt. (21.44)
In her own abode dwells the goddess Śaṅkarī, the destroyer of all seizing spirits; when remembered, she will effect the removal of the onset of fever by means of skull-cups. (21.45)
Does it ward off the divine, unassailable weapons—terrible with winds, thunderbolts, great rains, and lightning, and blazing with jewels? (21.46)
Having entered into the midst of the blazing fire, the knower of mantras should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
within half a ghaṭikā, he quickly causes the deity to bestow rain.
Having had a six-finger-long stake made of human bone and having consecrated it one hundred times with mantras, if one causes it to be placed in someone's house—? || 21.48 ||
It quickly covers that [person] within seven days; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, when buried in the middle of a cow-pen, it causes the destruction of the milk.
If he is stationed in the midst of the cavalry, he brings about the destruction of the horses;
if stationed in the midst of the elephants, he shall cut them down.
If placed in the house of a dyer, it brings about misfortune;
if placed in the house of a potter, it destroys the vessels. (21.51)
Having fasted on the eighth or the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should effect the destruction of liquor deposited in the house of a liquor-seller. (52)
Having performed a great worship of the Goddess and standing to her right,
one should take cemetery ashes and cause them to be consecrated by reciting [the mantra] a hundred times.
Into whosever house one should cast it, that fever shall arise intensely; no one else can cause it to be released once the preeminent practitioner has uttered it. (21.54)
Having offered an oblation to the Goddess accompanied by meat and liquor,
and having performed a very extensive worship, he should again release her in an instant.
Having kindled the cremation fire at midnight with wood from a funeral pyre, one should take ashes, bones, and the secretions from the anus, together with blood and dust. (21.56)
By means of exactly one hundred and eight [recitations], one shall kill an enemy within seven days;
whether it be a king or a queen, he indeed causes them to die.
Having taken earth from that gate, as well as bone from a cremation ground and ashes,
and then adding black mustard seeds mixed with blood for the fire-oblation (homa), || 21.58 ||
One should strike the enemy with seven hundred and eight [strokes] of a weapon;
having stayed during the lunar eclipse, one should kindle a blazing fire born from a cremation ground.
A wise man should certainly offer sesame seeds smeared with the three sweets;
by means of the name of whomever he performs this, that person, even if situated far away, becomes like a servant.
Is he brought here drawn by force, or does he die through separation?
[The ingredients are: ashes from a cremation ground, salt, mustard seeds, and clay from the foot [of a footprint]. (21.61)
The wise one should have an image fashioned from sesame powder;
having kindled a fire in a cremation ground, the wise one should offer oblations of it smeared with the three sweets.
Having cut [the hair] starting from the left big toe with a sharp blade as before, there is no doubt that the name of whoever [performs this] becomes auspicious. (21.63)
If one gives flowers, leaves, fruit, water, betel, a bath,
or an ointment that has been consecrated with this mantra, the recipient will become thoroughly submissive.
Having consecrated antimony from Śrotāñjana in a skull-cup with mantras, the wise one should apply it to his eyes; he will become beloved by all in every respect. (21.65)

Having collected ashes from a cremation ground and consecrated them with the mantra eight hundred times, one should apply the *tripuṇḍra* mark with it; this brings about what is pleasing in all circumstances.
In a field, in a royal court, at a gambling match, in legal proceedings, and likewise in battle—everywhere one obtains the fruit of recitation; it also paralyzes thieves on the road.
With that ash, he instantly paralyzes the armies;
they retreat with shattered courage, like serpents whose fangs have been broken.
Having drawn a mandala in a cremation ground, adorned with all colors,
one should there worship the Goddess of the Gods, who is seated upon a great corpse.
Holding a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, possessing a radiance like flashing lightning, adorned with a garland of skulls, three-eyed, and having a distorted face. || 21-70 ||
Having worshipped according to the previously mentioned procedure with a concentrated mind,
one should recite the mantra eight thousand times and then offer oblations of human flesh.
By uttering whose name one certainly draws [the spirit] forth;
having brought the hanged corpse, it is bathed and adorned. (21.72)
