The wise one should offer oblations of supreme food mixed with ghee into his mouth until the tongue emerges from it,
up to one hundred and eight times.
Having taken it with effort and cut it with a blade, O Pārvatī,
one should wrap it in three metals and empower the pill with mantras;
as soon as it is placed in the mouth, one attains invisibility.
He becomes beloved by the people, a traveler through the sky, and possessed of great strength. || 21.75 ||
His movement cannot be obstructed by gods, dānavas, or rākṣasas.
Having seized the five limbs of the *udvaṃdha* plant, one should reduce them to powder. (21.76)
The wise one should saturate a wick made of *arka* cotton with that [substance], using either the ghee of a tawny cow or great oil. (21.77)
Having taken soot from a skull, the wise one should consecrate it with the mantra one hundred times; by applying it to the eyes while reciting the mantra, he becomes invisible.
One whose eyes have not been washed will become beloved by all;
through either seeing or touching him, one obtains the desired fruit. (21.79)
As long as that [mud] remains on the eyes, one is not struck by weapons.
One should take the clay from the city gate and mix it with salt. (21.80)
The wise one should offer oblations in a cremation ground, anointed with the three sweets, day after day;
within seven days, the king of the locality and the great multitude will come under his control.
One should perform [the rite] with exactly one hundred and eight [seeds]; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
The seeds of the *unmattaka* plant are to be combined with *āsurī* plants. (21.82)
O wise one, by reciting the name of whichever [deity] while performing a hundred oblations in a cremation ground, one who has been seized by the great *grahas* quickly becomes intoxicated. (21.83)
The garment of a menstruating woman, along with urine and earth, and ashes from a cremation ground mixed with black mustard seeds, [should be applied] to the feet. (21.84)
Then, having combined them together in one place, one should bury them in a cremation ground after consecrating them seven times with the name [of the victim] appended. (21.85)
In twenty-one days, its blood will begin to flow;
having then extracted the cloth, one should wash it again with milk.
Having worshipped the Goddess with diligence, the knower of mantras brings her to propitiation;
this is the Blessed One, perfected in that which is known as the *Tantrasadbhāva*. (21.87)
The Great Goddess, free from impurity, self-awakened,
and the bestower of enjoyment and liberation, is to be propitiated according to the prescribed rite.
Now I shall proclaim another vidyā, complete with its means of accomplishment—
the Great Vidyā, endowed with all its limbs, the sovereign of all mistresses of vidyās.
One should first write the auspicious word "Tārādyāṃ raktacāmuṇḍe," followed by "mahābhairavarūpe" accompanied by the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*. (21.90)
The root mantra is declared to be auspicious and consists of fifteen syllables:
"Mahābhairava Cāmuṇḍe Hūṃ Phaṭ," preceded by the Praṇava (Oṃ). || 21.91 ||
Know that the heart-mantra proclaimed for Bhairava Raktacāmuṇḍā consists of eleven syllables; it begins with the Praṇava and ends with Svāhā. (21.92)
The Śikhā-mantra is proclaimed to consist of eleven syllables: Oṃ, Raktacāmuṇḍe, Devī, and Vare. (21.93)
Therefore, protect everything from the fears of spirits through this gift of ten million [repetitions];
the twenty-one-syllable *śikhā-mantra* of the Blessed Lady has thus been proclaimed. (21.94)
"O Raktacāmuṇḍā, who is the beginning of existence! Likewise, 'Pratihata' (the Obstructed)!
And the words 'flesh' and 'blood', and 'eating cruel food'! (21.95)
The armor is proclaimed to consist of twenty-one syllables;
it begins with *bhava* and ends with *hūṃ phaṭ*, and likewise concludes with the word *canti*.
This weapon-mantra has been fully described; it consists of eight syllables and possesses the brilliance of fire.
Endowed with the true cause, O Viśve, it is the supreme and auspicious heart-mantra.
The goddess Ghoranāyikā has been described together with her six limbs;
I shall now proclaim her ritual manual (kalpa) exactly as it was spoken by the Lord.
Having fasted on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, or likewise on the fourteenth,
one should enter the Mother’s temple, fearless and unwearied.
One should recite it eight thousand times and obtain the fruit of initiation;
O Goddess of the Gods, having drawn the skull-bearer of terrifying form upon a skull.
Mounted upon a corpse and bearing the khaṭvāṅga as her weapon,
the practitioner, subsisting on sweat and flesh, should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times before her.
From that time forward, O Goddess of gods, she bestows both inferior and superior siddhis;
[this is achieved] by means of one thousand and eight [offerings] of *raktāśvamāra* flowers.
Today, the wise man should strike the *liṅga* with [the rosary] that has been rotated a thousand times;
he should then swallow whatever flower sticks there, without touching it with his teeth. (21.103)
Then, the wise one should perform the summoning with the *aśvamāra* flower;
whether having seen a woman or not having seen her, one should recall her and whirl the flower. (21.104)
One might even bring them from a distance of a hundred yojanas; of this there is no doubt. Through speech one attains accomplishment, and likewise through the mind.
By offering oblations of fruits, courtesans become submissive;
by using white mustard seeds, all castes; and by using salt, excellent women.
Likewise, by means of those belonging to the Asuras, the king brings his ministers under his control;
[he should employ] one who, through passion, has assumed a female form and is adorned with the beauty of noble lineage and physical limbs. 21.107cd–108ab.
O Goddess, having written a very beautiful [image] on birch bark with cow's bezoar,
one should then place it inside the core of the image using *madana* thorns.
Then, having filled [the crucible] on all sides with one made of *puṣpaloha* iron,
and having inserted the needle into the womb [of the crucible], one should heat it in a fire of *khadira* wood.
By recollecting whose name can one bring [an enemy] from afar?
Then, the wrathful mantra-practitioner desires to conceal someone. (21.110)
One should offer three thousand oblations consisting of *bhallātaka* fruits mixed with blood; this will bring about the destruction of one's lineage. || 21.111 ||

Then, having mixed the blood of a goat with one's own [blood], the wise one should smear human bones with it and perform the fire-oblation (homa) using the name of the person against whom the rite is directed.
Enraged, one should kill him with eight hundred oblations of ghee; Brāhmaṇas must certainly do so, while Kṣatriyas [should kill] with goat's blood. || 21.113 ||
And Vaiśyas [attain their goal] by an oblation of sesame seeds, and Śūdras by an oblation of rice grains;
through eight thousand [oblations], this occurs within seven days—of this there is no doubt. (21.114)
Then, having painted the Goddess upon a cloth, adorned with all colors—
four-armed, mounted upon a corpse, and decorated with all ornaments— || 21.115 ||
Holding a skull and a trident in her hands, and likewise a noose and a chisel in her hands,
one should install her on the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, or at any time.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with perfumes, flowers, incense, and offerings of liquor and meat, one should then commence the fire-oblation (homa).
One should offer guggulu resin together with human flesh and clarified butter;
one hundred, eight thousand, or a hundred thousand times for the highest attainments.
Then the wise one should perform the ritual action with a tenth part of the recitation (*japa*).
[The materials are] *śrīvāsa*, *guggulu*, and *rālā*, combined with the three sweet substances.
By performing eight thousand oblations, one shall obtain a princess;
now, for the benefit of practitioners, I shall indeed describe another method of accomplishment.
O Goddess, when the skull of a woman has been prepared and anointed with the self-protection mantra,
one should install it at the base of the trident, relying upon that which is proclaimed as the trident.
Having worshipped with all offerings and other requisites, one should perform the recitation while seated on a leaf-seat;
at dawn, having taken up the trident and fashioned it into an excellent *khaṭvāṅga*.
Having established that [liṅga] there in the cremation ground, O Goddess of the Gods, the practitioner of mantra should observe the vow;
by reciting ten million [times], the knower of mantra becomes perfected. (21.123)
The mantra-practitioner who has fulfilled the observances of the vidyā is always attended by divine beings;
he lives for an eon, possesses great luster, and has a radiance equal to the rising sun. || 21-124 ||
Wherever the mantra-practitioner desires, there a city arises, born of the *rūkṣa* element,
perfectly filled with various foods and drinks, and endowed with all objects of desire.
Surrounded by divine maidens and provided with beds and seats, the knower of the tantra and mantras, having enjoyed the pleasures of sexual union at night... [21.126]
One should withdraw [the visualization] once again using a peacock feather;
thus the mantra-practitioner plays, surrounded by his companions. (21.127)

Alternatively, if the practitioner (mantrin) desires to bring the Mothers under his control, he should kindle a fire with wood from a funeral pyre and [offer] that which has arisen from a twice-born [tree]. (21.128)
One who knows the ritual procedure should offer ten thousand oblations of meat;
then the Brahmāṇīs come under his control, and she becomes the bestower of all accomplishments.
Raudrī [is pleased] by the flesh of a bull; Kumārikā by that of a peacock; Vaiṣṇavī by the flesh of a buffalo; and Vārāhī by that of a pig. (21.130)
And Aindrī is accomplished by means of elephant flesh; there is no doubt in this matter.
Thus, O best of gods, these goddesses become bestowers of siddhi.

The knower of mantras, through meditative absorption (samādhi), should offer the feathers of a crow into the fire while reciting the name of the person; by means of that great seizure, he causes that person to be swiftly seized.

For the purpose of eradication, one should employ vulture flesh; for subjugation, one should gather *phalgu* wood; and for the performance of pacification rites, one should use milky trees and *śamī* wood, as prescribed for milk-related rituals. (21.133)
One should perform the binding of the mouths of the nāgas and the summoning of the nāgas;
upon being seen, they quickly rise up and shatter even their fetters.
The wise practitioner should cause a boy or even a girl to recite;
the mantra-master may paralyze treatises or cause them to fall swiftly upon a treasure.
In the destruction of living beings, even [substances] made of divine vajra should be dissolved; for the summoning of yakṣas, one should offer dog meat in the fire-oblation for seven days. (21.136)
By means of an oblation of white sandalwood, one will certainly attract the Gaṇas;
through an oblation of guggulu resin, the practitioner of mantra brings all mantras under his control.
A practitioner, being composed in mind, should perform the propitiation of the deities;
thus has been declared the ritual manual for Raktacāmuṇḍā, complete with its methods of accomplishment.
Now, O Goddess, I shall tell you another supreme ritual; listen to it, by the proper recollection of which a practitioner of mantra attains the highest accomplishment. (21.139)
The accomplishment of Tārā and the others is proclaimed with the word *cāmuṇḍā* preceding it;
one should utter "Bhairava" joined with the Great Wrath (*mahākrodha*). (21.140)
This auspicious sixteen-syllable root mantra begins with *hrīḥ* and ends with *phaṭ*. Having thus fully explained it, I shall now tell you the ancillary mantras (*aṅga*). || 21.141 ||
The heart-mantra, beginning with the syllable Om, consists of the name "Mahācāmuṇḍa" followed by the vocative case ending and the suffix "svāhā. (21.142)
O lady of excellent complexion, the mantra known as Daśārṇa, which begins with the syllable Om and ends with Svāhā, is proclaimed as the "Head" (Śira), having the form of Mahābhairava. (21.143)
And the Śikhā-mantra is to be known as beginning with *praṇava*, ending with *vauṣaṭ*, consisting of eleven syllables, and having the form of the great and terrifying sound. (21.144)
"Bind, bind the fanged one!"—this armor, accompanied by the protection "protect," has been fully declared to you; now I shall state the weapon-mantra.
And the sound made by the skull, the pair of ornaments "Ghorī," and the word "Mahāghorī," preceded by Tārā and ending with "Hūṃ Phaṭ. (21.146)
This mantra of nineteen syllables indeed causes terror to all malevolent beings;
this vidyā is most formidable and bestows all accomplishments.
Having placed her upon a human skull, one should visualize her mounted on a corpse, four-armed,
bearing a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff, and likewise holding a great corpse in her hand.
One should cause the previously mentioned offerings, beginning with flowers and incense,
to be presented through the Upacāra mantra alone, joined with the vowel *ai*.
But this heart-mantra of another, when recited while submerged within the syllable KĀRE, swiftly draws forth nectar through the yoga of meditative visualization. (21.150)
Having recited the mantra three hundred thousand times in the midst of the circle of Mothers,
the practitioner of mantra should subsequently offer as oblation beef together with cow's blood in due order.
Then, indeed, mental accomplishment arises from non-discrimination; O Brahmins, one quickly brings others under control by offering oblations with beef. (21.152)
Then the Kṣatriya [should offer] human flesh, the Vaiśya with the meat of a goat, the Śūdra with buffalo meat, and those of the lowest castes with whatever they can obtain. (21.153)
One should accomplish whatever is desired according to the previously mentioned procedure;
this, which grants all desires, has been declared in the Siddhacāmuṇḍakalpa. (21.154)
Beyond this, I shall speak of Aghorī, who possesses terrifying prowess;
beginning with the word "Cāmuṇḍā," followed by "Kapālini" thereafter. (21.155)
This auspicious root mantra begins with the Praṇava and ends with Svāhā; likewise, the supreme Heart mantra begins with the Tāraka (Oṃ) and ends with Nāda (Phaṭ). || 21-156 ||
The five-syllabled [mantra] is Śiva himself, adorned with seven phonemes; and [the mantra] beginning with Bhava for Kapālinī is conjoined with the word "Mahānta. (21.157)
This Caṇḍā Dhāmeśvarī is indeed endowed with the true movement;
she should be known as the Cūlikā ending in Svāhā, clearly composed of the syllable *nau*. (21.158)
Then, the six-syllable mantra beginning with *Oṃ* for the fierce Caṇḍeśvarī is proclaimed as the divine armor, impenetrable and the protector of the body. (21.159)
"O fierce one, O terrible mistress"—thus is the weapon-mantra uttered with its true cause;
it consists of nine syllables ending in *phaṭ*, and it cuts through all obstacles. (21.160)
In the case of Caṇḍā, Krodheśvarī, and so forth, it is established that they begin with the Praṇava (Oṃ).
The eight-syllable mantra of the Goddess, consisting of the Netra-mantra, has been definitively declared among them. (21.161)

At the time of sacrifice, one who is endowed with the marks of a swan and a line on the forehead, and who is honored by the Lord, should perform the rites involving perfumes, incense, and so forth. (21.162)
The Vidyā known as Daśārṇarecitā is characterized by the assembly of Siddhas;
I shall now describe its method of accomplishment exactly as it should be performed.
Having thus fashioned the four-armed [deity] within the skull of Mahāvīra,
[one should visualize him] adorned with a garland of skulls and wearing a sacred thread made of a serpent.
She holds a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, is mounted upon a corpse, and is most terrifying;
she is naked, four-faced, holds a noose and a goad, and is auspicious.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and being adorned with the five mudrās, one should worship while remaining in the rite of the remnants of Madhu, clothed only by the directions and with hair disheveled. (21.166)
One should worship the goddess Bhairavī with flowers that have been discarded after death, or with other cast-off flowers, as well as with various kinds of blossoms.
The best of the twice-born should offer this fragrance, consisting of the roots of the tooth-tree, karṇa, akṣa, and nāsā, produced from bali and mixed with perfume. || 21-168 ||
Garlic, guggulu resin, and likewise human flesh, combined together with the excrement of a black cat—these, when employed as one, [achieve the desired effect]. (21.169)
The mantra-knower, having awakened the woman with passion,
should offer incense using blood from his own left side into a skull-cup.
One should offer him the *argha* oblation and satisfy him with liquor,
as well as fish, meat, *caru*, and likewise the sacrificial portion for the deity.
The wise man should cause an offering to be presented consisting of cakes, stuffed pastries, incense, and raw meat, as well as onions and garlic.
Then the mantra-practitioner should perform the fire-oblation with human flesh;
she should satisfy [the deity] with cow-flesh and blood produced from her own hand.
Then, having performed a circumambulation with whatever other gain he had obtained,
Mahāśaṅkha, free from sloth, recited his prayers while holding a conch-shell rosary.
One who desires his own success should recite the Goddess while eating the remnants of the meal;
by reciting syllable by syllable, he beholds Mahocchuṣmā.
In the end of his dream, the goddess sees a terrible being with twelve eyes, resembling crushed collyrium; having seen him, the knower of mantras attains success.
One should offer twelve thousand oblations of dog meat;
likewise, one obtains the supreme fruit with beef as well. (21.177)
By offering ten thousand oblations of deer meat together with ghee and guggulu,
they swiftly bestow mental accomplishment.
O best of men, when the hair of one slain by a weapon is offered as an oblation while smeared with blood, there is no doubt that they enter into servitude to the practitioner. (21.179)
Having eaten the supreme rice-milk dish (paramānna) prepared with the juice of black cow-dung and saturated with clarified butter,
one should afterwards expel it and offer it as an oblation (homa) accompanied by clarified butter.

Having consumed the flesh of a jackal, together with its blood, and having extracted [the heart] by means of the name of the one whom he wishes to bring under his control, that person shall remain subject to him for the duration of their life. (21.181)
One should perform the fire-oblation with the name of whomever one wishes, and that person shall be drawn forth in an instant.
One should offer tooth-sticks together with cow’s blood. (21.182)
By uttering his name three times a day, a hundred times each,
one quickly draws him forth, and he shall always remain under one's control.
Having prepared collyrium in a human skull with human oil and having consecrated it one hundred times with mantras, the entire world is brought under control by using it as eye-salve. (21.184)
But whoever should eat *caru* prepared with rice and milk,
having recited [the mantra] one hundred times, he shall become a slave for as long as he lives. (21.185)
One should offer as oblation that which has been eaten and then vomited, combined with *dhattūra*;
when offered into a kindled fire, this is the supreme means for causing madness.
Picumanda oil is recommended for the purpose of inciting enmity;
one should offer it into the fire upon the funeral pyre, mixed with hair, bone ashes, and blood.
That very [mantra] is the weapon for killing; by means of liquor, there is delusion.
Having written the *kṛti* (the ritual act) upon a female skull with blood from the ring finger, [one should perform the rite]. (21.188)
One should heat that [image] in the fire of the funeral pyre while reciting the mantra together with the name;
the knower of mantras, facing it, should do so at midnight while recollecting her.
And she comes swiftly to that place where the lord of practitioners is;
[there one should offer] saffron, neem leaves, as well as yellow myrobalan and soapberry.
A warrior should perform the oblation for the purpose of inciting hatred as well as for expulsion;
likewise, [he should offer] the hair from the long necks [of animals] and the feathers of crows.
An oblation of mustard seeds, charcoal, and urine is beneficial for eradication;
one should perform the oblation with the feathers of a crow and an owl using the urine of a ram. (21.192)
Through homa, one may instantly effect hatred, strife, and the eradication of an enemy; likewise, ashes, bones, and earth from a cemetery, when combined with pungent oil, [achieve the same]. (21.193)
At midnight, this causes intense fever and conflict with enemies;
likewise, mustard seeds mixed with blood and pungent oil [achieve the same]. (21.194)
Anointed with the bile of a cow and a human, and consecrated with mantras, it causes a burning sensation by means of five handfuls of earth. (21.195)
A wise knower of mantras, having taken the eye of a jackal together with cow bile, should bind it upon the royal highway; thus he becomes worthy of worship.
Then, having performed the *tilaka* with eight thousand recitations of the mantra,
whatever person the practitioner gazes upon becomes like a servant.
Taking a tube for suspension measuring nine finger-breadths in length,
one should [place] cow-bile, human bile, and likewise the eyes of a jackal.
If one gazes at a person while reciting the mantra with a heated iron rod,
one comes to know that very person's former birth, up until the point where they first understood the mantra.
Having taken the eye of a Bhāsa bird as well as that of a jackal,
mixed with human bezoar, and empowered one thousand times with mantras.
Having anointed the eyes of the mind, one should observe within the tube whether it appears as a single form, two forms, or even three, four, or five.
Or else, one sees [them] with six or seven forms; there is no doubt in this matter.
Or again, [one sees] donkeys, camels, wild beasts, birds, and reptiles. (21.202)
One should observe a painted image or a mantra according to its specific class;
this is known as the examination of the sacrificial animal (paśu) for those who seek the accomplishment of the animal sacrifice.
Having obtained which, they attain perfection and go to union with the Mother;
by grasping these two eyes of the corpse, as well as the eyes of a cat, [one achieves this].
Having ground together the bile of an owl, a crow, a vulture, a potter,
and a sacrificial vessel, along with human bile, one should then perform the saturation.
Having consecrated [the ointment] with the mantra one thousand or one hundred times, one should apply it to the eyes; then, one should look at a mirror.
One certainly perceives one's own kind as well as that of others; there is no doubt.
One beholds one's own form through a sequence of one, two, or three [stages]. (21.207)
Furthermore, by means of analysis, the mantra-practitioner perceives the body of others;
one who consumes meat, being devoted to recitation and fire-offerings, [perceives it] through meat. (21.208)
Bound with the five mudrās at night according to the prescribed time, one shall quickly accomplish even that which is difficult to achieve; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
Cāmuṇḍā and Mahocchuṣmā are saluted by Bhairava,
as well as by the Rudras, Vasus, Ādityas, Piśācas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas.
The Mahāghorā of the Yoginīs, who reveals all castes,
having entered the Mother’s House and worshipped the mandala, (21.211).
One should recite the mantra of the goddess Yogeśvarī while keeping one's gaze fixed upon a fine cloth; as soon as that [cloth] appears to be revolving in the sky, the house resounds.
Then the goddesses and yoginīs with distorted faces arrive;
they grant every desire to the wise practitioner.
But one who desires the supreme fruit should mutter that very same [mantra] three times over;
O Goddess of the Gods, he beholds [the deity] directly, and having seen [him], they attain the state of Śiva.
Even if unaccomplished, once ten million recitations have been performed, one becomes capable of attaining even minor siddhis;
this *kavya* of Raktacāmuṇḍā, which has been kept secret, has now been told to you. (21–215)
Having drawn two *kili*s, one should then [recite] the great vidyā, Vajravidāraṇī, preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *hūṃ phaṭ*. (21.216)
If one recites [the mantra] one hundred thousand times while stationed at the entrance of a cave,
it shatters even mantras composed of divine vajra.
The knower of mantras, firm in his resolve, should sometimes recite the vidyā five times while wandering there with his wife, reaching as far as the innermost cities of Pātāla.
This spell, when employed for the purpose of warding off the wicked, brings about the prevention of rain, falling meteors, and weapons.
Then, having joined "kilivicca," followed by two "cilis," and then "vicca" at the beginning, one should subsequently join the Praṇava (Oṃ). || 21-220 ||
This vidyā, conjoined with the utterance of "svāhā" at its end, bestows all accomplishments.
Having placed a lamp in a skull using fat and lac, [one should perform the rite]. (21–221)
One should worship the Goddess in the maṇḍala and then satisfy her with fat;
this vidyā becomes perfected even for the purpose of attracting divine beings.
By recollecting a celestial being or a celestial maiden, one will certainly attract her;
using the blood of a horse and a goat mixed with human oil. (21–223)
A wise person should perform the fire offering (*homa*) eight thousand times at night;
whatever one has contemplated in the mind, that very thing one shall swiftly attract.
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) with "Bhūtamātā," then [recite] "Gaganacāriṇi hūṃ saḥ vicce svāhā"; this is the vidyā-mantra beginning with the syllable Om and ending with Svāhā.
When worshipped on a mountain peak, she bestows the power of moving through the sky; after one year, the practitioner who maintains a well-guarded conduct shall become a traveler of the heavens.
He becomes the lord of all beings, like the god with matted hair;
praised by gods and asuras, he may wander to the ends of the seven worlds.
"Aghore Hrīḥ," preceded by the word "Pada" and joined with "Huṃ Phaṭ"—this mantra, when conjoined with the word "Sat," is of great majesty. (21–228)
By reciting this mantra, the practitioner becomes beloved by the yoginīs,
whether he is in mountain torrents, gardens, caves, temples, or deep ravines.
Having remained [in this state] for one year, he attains the station of the Yogeshvari;
or else, if he desires enjoyment in the world of mortals, [he shall obtain it].
By offering oblations of *vilva* and *guggulu*, one shall attain the state of sovereignty;
by means of human flesh and fish-flesh, however, one shall bring a lord of the earth under one's control.
Through excrement and crow feathers, one effects hatred;
through chaff and ashes, killing; and through oblation with milk and ghee, there is pacification.
With lotuses one gains sovereignty; with sesame seeds, happiness; and with beautiful garlands, one becomes auspicious.
Through various distinctions of ritual action, one may accomplish even minor and base objectives.
"O fierce one! O most terrible one! O you who were formerly fearsome and terrifying! HŪM!"—these [names] are placed in the vocative case and joined with the word *svāhā*. (21–234)
This Vidyā, impelled by its true cause, bestows success and renown; it is remembered as the one that makes manifest all the most formidable [powers]. (21–235)
Having constructed a maṇḍala in a cremation ground and remaining established in the ritual procedure of mudrās and mantras,
one should perform a thousand sacrifices and offer oblations of beef.
Clad in the directions (naked) and with disheveled hair, one should recite the eight hundred thousand [mantras];
one attains invisibility and the transformation of one's form.
The transference into another body and the extraction of the nectars—this goddess was formerly worshipped by Bhairava. (21–238)
As many vidyās as have been declared by Umā, Vīrabhadra, Rudra, Vasu, and Divākara in the work known as the Tantrasadbhāva—[so many are they]. (21–239)
Of these, she is indeed the Mistress of Knowledge (Vidyeśvarī), the bestower of fierce accomplishments (caṇḍasiddhi);
she is the Mother of Beings (Bhūtamātā) consisting of thirteen syllables, endowed with seventeen vowels.
Kālī should be known by the wise as consisting of thirteen syllables;
Aghorā, however, should be understood by the best of practitioners as having four and a half syllables.
Krodheśvarī is clearly proclaimed to consist of nine and a half syllables;
she is the goddess who dwells in the cremation ground, adorned by the three deities.
She who is endowed with twelve syllables and dwells at the crossroads, and she who is joined with thirteen syllables, is known as Cilibimbā. (21–243)
O Goddess, one situated in the presence of a hero should recite this group of eight vidyās;
one should place the [six] limbs on the petals and the weapon in the intermediate directions.
Beginning from the south-eastern direction up to the range of Indra, the assembly of the Vidyās is superior, whereas that which sets forth minor matters is inferior. (21–245)
For those who are devoid of the practice of yoga and whose minds are attracted by sense objects,
some become utterly deluded, while others likewise seek only inferior goals.
Now, for the sake of accomplishing the middle [state], that which is one's own door is described:
it is endowed with the pair of *hulu* syllables and joined with the *yakṣakumārī* [mantra]. (21–247)

Aṃ sa hrīḥ—this supreme vidyā, joined with the mantra and characterized by the word "svāhā" at its end, consists of fifteen syllables beginning with tāra (oṃ) and becomes perfected through recitation. (21–248)
A maiden born in the house of a lord of treasures, accompanied by a hundred thousand attendants,
is brought there when ten thousand clearly manifest *nyagrodha* trees have been offered as oblations at its base.
One who is unencumbered by the primary qualities and limbs smeared with demon-slaying oil,
being a knower of the virtues, shall sport upon that mountain for as long as the moon and stars endure.

The most excellent one is worshipped with incomparable enjoyments and celestial women; he is honored with reverence at the beginning of his arrival, while [his] nails and teeth are cleansed and [he is] humbled by proper conduct. || 21-251 ||
This vidyā consists of twelve syllables ending with *svāhā*, arranged according to its constituent parts;
it is named Vinatā, which possesses a protector and resides in the abode of the yakṣas, [granting] a hundred thousand [blessings]. 21–252.

One who turns [the wheel] without desire, having conquered the senses and being armored with the limbs of restraint, [sees that] a woman of divine form approaches; what does she do as she comes? || 21-253 ||

Impelled by the desire of the practitioner, she brings forth from the netherworld, the celestial realms, and the guardians— Asuras, Yakṣas, and the noble daughters of the Nāgas— the elixirs of mercury and other such alchemical substances.
If she should desire me incessantly, being herself desirous for your sake, the lord of practitioners should not enjoy her if he wishes for a long life. (21.255)
Then, one who is deluded by desire may go astray, O Yakṣa, just as a man might fall;
having placed Nandinī, Vijayā, Svāhā, Tārakā, Hrīḥ, and Āditya [in their respective positions]. (21–256)
Having drawn the Yakṣiṇī Pretapaṭā, fashioned from ten syllables of the Vidyā, adorned with all ornaments, wearing red garments, and possessing a beautiful form and weapons; || 21-257 ||
One should recite the vidyā one hundred thousand times while seated before her, who resembles a blue lotus and is resting upon an aśoka branch.
One should strike the head with eight thousand *dinakara* flowers;
[one should strike] the mother on the heart, the sister on the chest, the messenger (*dūtī*) on the genitals, and likewise the wife on the genitals. (21.259)
A mother protects one who has sons; a sister brings even the entire three worlds under her control;
a wife bestows everything along with milk, and she grants the highest pleasure.
Because they delight the mantra-body, they therefore ascend upwards at the end;
the word "hulu" and its pair would be the state, while the state "contisthapumbalike"? || 21-261 ||
In the rite of honoring and so forth, this [mantra] consists of fourteen syllables ending with *svāhā*.
At the time of the three periods, having lit a lamp with lac at the abode, [one should perform the ritual]. 21-262.
Having performed the recitation one hundred and eight times, the wise man should extinguish [the lamp];
then, having approached himself, he should rub his feet with that oil over which the mantra has been recited one hundred times.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should then sleep while devoted to celibacy.
After six months, she who is Dhānānikā, possessing a divine form and bestowing boons, will appear.
Accompanied by her, the practitioner rejoices for as long as the time of the moon, sun, and stars lasts;
[the mantra] ending with "yakṣakumārī" is enclosed within the syllables *kroḥ* and *hrīḥ*, and concludes with the word "pradāna. (21–265)
For these [deities], the vidyā consists of eleven syllables together with the *praṇava*.
Having prepared it with *pretālaktaka* and having written it with *gorocanā* at the end.

Then, having recited the mantra eight thousand times over a wooden plank or a garment from a corpse, and having worshipped it with fragrant flowers, one should [invoke] a maiden of the best Yakṣas adorned [therein].
One who is anxious for offspring should have sexual union with her during three menstrual periods;
then his wife will become joyful and remain so for a duration of a yuga.
Seated upon the summit of Mount Meru, the Mantrin delights in incomparable enjoyments.
KROṂ MĀDIRĀKṢASI YE KILI KILI [twice] HŪṂ is joined with the root yoga. (21–268)
Having lit a lamp with human oil and a skull-bowl in an empty house, the wise practitioner should hang a pair of human skin and blood from both sides of the door for the *preta*s. (21.269)

Furthermore, having spread out a pair of garments and standing upon them, one should recite the mantra while remaining in a single form until a thousand [recitations] are completed, appearing beautiful, naked, and pierced. (21–270)
The protector maiden approaches; he should give her that pair of garments.
Remaining silent, having taken her hand, he should desire her until she is satisfied. (21–271)

When the lamp has been extinguished, the wise man should take one wick and place it upon his head; having done so, he should sleep, and at the time of dawn, [he should perform the ritual]. || 21.272 ||
One who is undeluded and skilled in its application will obtain a gold *māṣaka* for every expenditure;
after six months, she becomes a fully accomplished *rakṣī*.
He enjoys pleasures with her after having recited the thirteenfold vidyā: "Arise, O Earth! Though overcome by fainting, take another morsel of food. (21.274)

One who is established in the ritual procedure should recite ten thousand times according to the rules this twenty-syllable vidyā, which begins with the word *piśāci*, ends with a cruel term, and concludes with the word *jātika*. (21–275)
Afterward, having recited [the mantra] twenty-one times, one should prepare the first *piṇḍa* for twenty-one days;
the *piśācī* becomes accomplished and bestows five forms.
And when questioned, she whispers into her ear news from the three times concerning the three worlds; O daughter of Kaśyapa, she is known by the name Nāgakumārī. (21.277)

Having entered the water, one who knows the mantra should recite seventeen times the Vidyā accompanied by the Praṇava; first, the knower of the mantra should perform one hundred thousand recitations for each of the three [sections]. || 21-278 ||
The Naga maiden brings elixir (*rasāyana*) or even inexhaustible wealth.
O Goddess, another procedure for immediate accomplishment is now being proclaimed. (21.279)
By means of which the mantra-practitioner, having reached the world of mortals, wanders among those who are not to be slain;
[this consists of] the sound of *kāli* joined with the pair of *chi*, and my body as *karāli* conjoined with *meṣa*. (21.280)
The eighteen-fold Vidyā, ending with the gift of clothing and accompanied by the Praṇava, consists of these [mantras].
With this, human bile mixed with the bile of a cat, having been recited three hundred thousand times, [is used]. (21–281)
A wise man should cover with a peacock-feather plume a wound inflicted by a vulture’s claw;
he should touch it with his fingernails, and having seen it, he should not reveal it to another. (21.282)
Having vanished, one should wander at the end of the night until the sun has risen.

Having extracted "sa-ra-vi-sa-re-ti" twice with the speed of the wind from one side, that seed-syllable of the wind (ya) together with the visarga is joined with the root-mantra and its birth-class. (21.283)
One should recite this eighteen-syllable vidyā one hundred thousand times:
"O you with eyes like a white cuckoo, O Śambhu who bestows intoxication, O you with the head of a wagtail. (21.284)

One should smear one's feet with these substances together with ghee, oil, and *māṇimantaka*, consecrated by reciting the *vidyā* and other mantras; thus, one travels a thousand *yojanas* in a single day.

One whose soles of the feet have not been washed, who has a long neck and no toenails, and who is free from fatigue—recited even once into the ear, this [mantra] destroys the virulent poison of scorpions and snakes. (21.286)
"Turum, Hara, Yugayojyā, Vṛṣṭinipāta, and Krodhayugmayuta—transform my form; this is the mantra ending with the gift (dāna), impelled by the Praṇava. || 21-287 ||
One who abides by the ritual procedure should recite twenty-one thousand times a mantra composed of twenty-six syllables;
[the rosary] should be made from elephant bone, cow horn, peacock bone, conch shell, sparrow bone, or human bone. (21.288)
If one whose body hairs have been smeared with these consecrated substances contracts [the target],
Śatarūpa shall remain upon his head until he is thoroughly awakened.
One who wears a girdle, has a crest, and carries a staff, endowed with the "Endless Gift" (Dānānantaka), should stand upon a mountain peak and recite this sixteen-syllable spell. 21-290.
Having performed the counting of the syllables of the target [name] according to the prescribed rules, and being established in the ritual procedure,
one should thereafter take a beautiful peacock feather and consecrate it with this [mantra].
One should not touch anything visible with that [liquor], nor should one perform a bath with *śīdhu* until [the ritual is complete];
the knower of the secret procedure should ensure that the machine (*yantra*) is not touched by one another, nor even looked upon.

If the pair *dha-ra* and *dha-ra-kha* occurs, followed by *yā-di-yu-gaṃ-hur-ja-sau*, with *niṣṭhā* at the end, the wise one should apply the word "space" (*vyoma*) together with the word "supporting" (*dhāriṇī*). (21.293)
Beginning with Tārā and ending with Svāhā, this mantra consisting of twenty-three syllables,
when recited previously over a single liṅga by a knower of mantras, becomes a means of attaining accomplishment.
Having prepared pills from the flower of an outcaste girl combined with the seed of Śiva, ending with *rutā*, and mixed with human bezoar, one should encase them in three metals. (21.295)
Having worshipped the Liṅga according to the prescribed rules, one should afterwards recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times;
having done so, he sports with her within his own womb, situated in the depths of the waters.

"O Kālī, O Karālī! Paralyze the adamantine body, joined with two *kili*s, ending with the pair *hara* and *hūṃ phaṭ*, preceded by the *praṇava*, and endowed with three times four and a half syllables. (21.297)
Having entered the middle of the river, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times while turning over the sand;
afterwards, taking a handful of that same sand, one should scatter it. (21.298)
If one emerges from the midst of water, that wise person becomes renowned;
likewise, those who possess various machines for moving through dense clouds and the movement of the wind will attain their desired state.

Having touched it, one paralyzes even the great with sands; likewise, yakṣiṇīs and other beings [are paralyzed] by feathers from a peacock's tail consecrated with the mantra *ustambho hara hūḥ*. The sequence for the delusion [of the enemy] is: *mohaya* (delude), followed by the pair, the two *kali*s, the two *bandha-lisam*s, and the two *samayuga*s, ending with *hūḥ*.
This is the distinctive Vidyā-mantra beginning with *Oṃ* (Praṇava) and ending with *Svāhā*. (21–300)
One should first recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, composed of thirty-one syllables.
By means of this, one should cast a horse-ear creeper (*hayamāra-latā*) upon the corpse bound in the cremation ground.

One who knows the ritual procedure should swiftly extract [the mantra] from a length equal to one's own arm; then, having recited it while thus enraged, whatever the person touches falls to the ground, utterly bewildered.

Having recited twenty-one thousand times the mantra consisting of twenty-one syllables, beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namo yakṣasenāpataye māṇibhadrāya*, followed by *kili kili dāna*, [one attains success]. || 21-303 ||
Having recited this twenty-one times, one should chew a tooth-stick in the morning;
thus, one obtains food and drink unasked for, according to one's heart's contentment. (21.304)

Having recited ten thousand times the mantra beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ), followed by *sutejolvaṇa*, *hūṃ*, and ending with half a syllable of *phaṭ*, one should then draw the form of the enemy upon the ground.
A wise person, by consuming those [leaves] of the *arkalatā* plant three times a day while facing that direction,
quickly brings on a fever born of mental anguish and anger within seven days.
O Ulkāmukhī, Raktākṣī, Vidyujjihvā, and you of great power!
Bring the fever of [Name]! Kill, kill! Cook, pair! HŪM PHAṬ—this is the end.
Having mounted the great *kāma* tree bound with thirty-five [threads] and having recited [the mantra] ten thousand times, one should crush the branch with the left foot at the conclusion of the rite.
Having prepared a wooden plank for that [remains], one should burn the residue in a fire consecrated with the principles (tattva).
Then, having taken the Bhr̥ṅgarāja juice poured according to the "donkey-thread" (kharasūtra) method, together with the Vidyā-mantra...
Whosoever’s name is inscribed therein is swiftly seized by a piśāca,
and no one can liberate him until that [inscription] has been washed away with milk.
“O Cāmuṇḍā, [I drink] the heart of so-and-so; utter this further:
‘O Cāmuṇḍinī, Vicce! preceded by the Tāraka and ending with the word for ‘bestowing’ (pradāna). (21.311)
It is proclaimed as being composed of eighteen syllables, yet devoid of the letters of the name.
By means of this, O Goddess, [one should practice] at the time of dawn until the crow can no longer see.

If one recites [the mantra] over water a hundred times and drinks it from a skull-cup for seven days during the day, it brings about the destruction of the age resulting from women, men, and hermaphrodites. || 21-313 ||
O Cāmuṇḍālī, who possesses the elephantine gait of the stars!
Having embraced me with your form as if after deep reflection, utter the words "Such-and-such a woman am I" and kiss my bhaga.

This vidyā, consisting of thirty syllables, is characterized by sprinkling and non-sprinkling, joined with the cruel [syllable], marked at the end by the word *dāna*, and devoid of the word *māraya*. || 21-315 ||
One should drink water consecrated in this very manner at the three times of day;
by doing so, one brings under control even a woman who is haughty with wealth and honor, and she becomes submissive before long.
"O horse, wander with a moving mind; wander and indeed speak. This sixteen-syllable mantra, ending in *svāhā* and joined with the *praṇava*, is thus fully described.
Having consecrated seven times a red *svamāra* flower with a mantra, if one stands before a woman and causes it to revolve, that excellent woman will instantly discharge her semen.
One should diligently recite this vidyā, which consists of thirty-three syllables, beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with "mātaṅgadārike svāhā" after a pair of consonants. || 21-319 ||
Like a potter’s wheel with its clay still clinging to it before the hand has fallen away,
she was covered all over her vital points by thorns arising from the god of love.
Having passed urine upon her private parts, one who knows the ritual should recite [the mantra] one hundred times at the twilight; within seven days, he shall attract the maiden.
The sounds "siddha" and so forth are joined with the words for the faces and arms of Cāmuṇḍā;
"gṛhṇa," "dve," "vicce," and "tāraka" are likewise included, for this [mantra] is characterized by the conclusion of the gift. || 21-322 ||
The eighteen-syllable Vidyā, having been previously recited ten thousand times while being transformed,
one should burn *rājika* seeds, grass, and *madana* wood, and heat them in the fire until they are consumed.
One who abides by the ritual rule should recite this knowledge one hundred times during the three daily libations;
within seven days, he brings here a king’s concubine pierced by the arrows of love.

The mantra consists of the words *kali-yugma-śarvari-padam*, followed by *hara hṛdayam*, then *sādhanām* with *apādāghaḥ* [added], ending in *svāhā* and beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ); it is devoid of the fifteen-syllable name-mantra. || 21-325 ||
Having constantly eaten for seven days a cooked preparation of molasses and rice-flour mixed with ghee, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred times as desired.

The ritual procedure for service and worship, when properly applied, draws forth the excellent woman from the secret place. Having performed such an incomparable rite, one enjoys immeasurable pleasures.
Thus it has been indicated that one should understand the twelve-thousand-verse [Mahābhārata] as having been composed in the Āryā meter, so that by knowing this, one may fully attain the fruit.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, the *Śrīvidyākośa*, within the *Bhairavasrotas* Mahātantra, belonging to the *Vidyāpīṭha*, measuring seventy million verses. || 21 ||
Śrī Bhairava said: Now I shall further explain another supreme method for the kindling of mantras:
[the syllables] Hrāḥ, Hrīḥ, Hrūḥ, Phaṭ, Ṭa, Phṭṭe, and Hūḥ, joined together as a casing. (22–1)
Therein, O Goddess of Gods, by reciting the mantra or vidyā ten thousand times through the middle channel, one brings about intense eradication within half a watch (prahara).

HRAḤ / STRĪ / STRĪ / A mantra conjoined with these bestows accomplishment immediately. Furthermore, by means of the *saṃpuṭa* (encasement) yoga, there is the kindling (*dīpana*) of mantras. || 22-3 ||
By employing the syllables *hrīḥ* and *kroḥ*, one certainly effects an attraction. Enveloped by the syllable *kliṃ*, the mantra-practitioner should employ it for the agitation of women. (22.4)

*Kli*, *kle*, and *kli*—this is called the "folded" (*puṭita*), the supreme means for agitating women. When joined with *kṣa*, it brings about the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life. (22.5)
In this way, dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa are indeed accomplished; of this there is no doubt.
When joined with the syllable *hrīṃ*, it grants all desires. (22.6)
He becomes beloved and dear to all sentient beings;
through the yoga of the *sampuṭa* [seal], he shall attain the siddhi of Kāmika. || 22-7 ||
By means of the *sampuṭa* (encasement) yoga, it brings about great nourishment;
however, when joined with *mā*, it is taught as the supreme method for making [the offering] nectar-like (*amṛtīkaraṇa*). (22.8)
Combined with three *rakāras* and inflamed by the wind (*vāyu*), the practitioner of mantra should join it with the *mālā*; this is remembered as the supreme method of killing (*māraṇa*).
A garland joined with three *ya*s causes eradication;
a garland joined with three *la*s is known to cause immobilization. (22.10)
Now, through the application of fire and with a divine garland,
one should draw four mandalas marked with the insignia of the vajra.
O Goddess, one should cause her, who possesses auspicious marks, to stand between them;
O Goddess, one should draw her in the center, situated within the interior of the nectar-vessel.
One should place Devadatta surrounded by the gods in the four directions with the syllable *va*; likewise, one should place the syllable *śa* outside in the middle of the maṇḍala.
Outside of that is the Sun, and outside of the Sun is the Wind;
one should draw the letter *kṣa* outside of that, along with the vowels to be recited in succession.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should sequentially assign the Vasu-bhaya-yakṣas one by one upon a birch bark leaf, using either yellow pigment (rocanā) or saffron (kuṅkuma).
Having thus inscribed it with care, one should encircle it according to the prescribed rule;
thereafter, one should have a very beautiful linga made of clay.
Therein, O Dear One, one should place in the center a birch-bark leaf wrapped and bound with thread;
then, one should cast it into the middle of a jar filled with milk.
Having lit a lamp with ghee upon that very jar,
one should worship it with white flowers, perfumes, incense, and sacred threads.
In this way, the divine [state] is indeed uplifted, and auspiciousness arises;
even one who possesses faults [attains it] during a favorable moment—such is the certainty of the scripture. (22-19)
One should likewise write *va*, *sa*, *bha*, *la*, *va*, *kṣa*, *ya*, *va*, *ha*, *svauṃ*, and *kṣmauṃ*.
Having performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) as before, the mandalas are also as before. (22–20)
By this procedure, one should administer the five divine ordeals:
fire, poison, the [divine] vessel, water, and indeed, heated meat.
By means of this ritual application, one shall certainly uplift [the victim]; there is no doubt in this matter.
The name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) should be placed at the end of the seed-syllable (bīja), surrounded by the sixteen vowels.
One should again extract the five divine [syllables] situated in the middle of the abode of Varuṇa, reaching to the end of the seed-syllable of the navel, and situated within the city of Varuṇa.

O Goddess of Gods, one should cause [the substance] to be consecrated with this mantra for the purpose of paralyzing or deluding those who subsist on [only] water: "kṣāṃ jabhakṣāṃ staṃbhe mohe. One should give [the food] that has been consecrated seven times, consisting of śāli rice mixed with curd. (22–24)
O beautiful lady, he to whom one offers even a single morsel of food crosses over [all difficulties],
provided he understands the distinction between friendliness and enmity, even if he is otherwise possessed of faults.
It takes away and indeed carries away; there is no need for deliberation on this point—just as a great blazing fire is extinguished when drenched by Varuṇa (water). || 22-26 ||
Just as coldness comes to what is hot when it has reached the state of fire, and just as the mass of the sun’s brilliant rays is obscured by a thick bank of clouds. (22–27)

Likewise, O lady of excellent hips, when even the divine has been rendered false by the power of mantras, one should accomplish all tasks after ascertaining the nature of enemies and friends as described. (22–28)
One should apply a plaster of fragrant *pāṭalā* root and *jalūkāśaśita*,
combined with the fat of a frog, to both hands.

I shall now describe to you the method for the suppression of fire by means of plants; *sevāla*, *dārdura*, and *steka* are considered effective when applied as a paste for extinguishing fire. (22–30)
Vaṃjālā, alana, sevāla, and phaṭā are names for the kumārikā plant;
smeared with the fat of a red cow, it makes fire as cool as snow.
Now I shall further explain another supreme sport of practitioners, by which one who is faultless may be burned, or paralyzed by another practitioner. (22–32)
One should write the twenty-fourth seed-syllable, ignited by fire and placed above honey; the writing materials should be produced from the essence of fire. (22–33)
The mantra-practitioner should cast that juice onto the written [name] on a cloth from a corpse;
it burns [the enemy], of this there is no doubt, for it was empowered by Vajrapāṇi. (22.34)
Situated in the center of the fire-maṇḍala, joined with fire and wind,
it is conjoined with the name of the person to be accomplished and ignited at the crown by fire.
The practitioner of mantra should write with a pen made of fire using its juice;
having placed it in the juice of fire, he should deposit it beneath the chest.
One should ignite a fire above with wood produced from fire;
it will be burned, there is no doubt, for he has been paralyzed by the wielder of the trident.
Thus, O Goddess, I have explained how practitioners sport with mantras;
by means of the root and the *yonimantra*, the reciter shall obtain all desires. (22-38)

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Illumination of Mantras," in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, a great tantra within the Bhairava current belonging to the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), measuring seventy million verses. || 22 ||
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, I have heard all the secrets that are hidden from the common view; I have especially grasped the classification of the mantras. (23.1)
I have not heard [it]; I wish to hear it. O Lord, tell me the fundamental yoga, as well as subjugation, attraction, inciting enmity, and expulsion. (23–2)
Paralysis, delusion, and especially killing;
as well as the neutralization of poison and the immobilization of weapons. (23-3)
And other elixirs that remove instantaneous death,
as well as other such things that have been mentioned— do not speak of them to you.
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain that which you have asked; for the benefit of practitioners, I shall speak it to you in detail. (23–5)
The wise man should prepare an equal powder of the flowers and fruits produced from sour water (ambilyāmbu) together with the leaves, roots, and stems all in one place.
One should consume rice flour mixed with jaggery, ghee, and milk for a fortnight;
having eaten that, one will become submissive. (23.7)
Subdued by the power of karma born from the seed of action, whether of a woman or a man, one comes under its control and does not serve another again. (23.8)
Black sesame seeds should be infused with the milk of a black cat;
when these are properly prepared and combined with flour, they become fully perfected.
He for whom these are given as food will not survive in separation from her. Taking a male crane, one should grind it with cow's milk. (23.10)
He to whom milk-rice prepared with rice grains is given to eat shall remain under one's control for as long as he lives; upon separation, he shall meet his death. || 23-11 ||
Taking the impurities, the fat, the well-coagulated blood, and the flesh arising from the vulture, one should employ it as food for her, mixed with water, while she makes a sound. (23-12)
She shall not desire another man, remaining under his control for as long as she lives;
[she should carry] either the skull of a hanged man or that of a human being.
Just as sandalwood is rubbed with a stream of nectar,
so too is the fat of a dharmaṇa treated with the milk of a yakṣī.
With the powder of monkey-head [incense], equal to the *adhapuṣpa* flower, even one who is unwilling will become submissive when he becomes free from conceptual construction. (23.15)
Having gathered the *unmattaka* from the son of a woman who has seduced her paramour,
one should grind it together with *devīśikhā* according to the prescribed rite.
Having prepared yakṣī [milk] equal to milk for the purpose of subjugation, it grants success;
having consumed it with sesame seeds, one should prepare oil or even a *śaṣkulikā* (fried cake).
Having consumed that, one comes under control for as long as one lives; of this there is no doubt.
[The herbs] Mohanā, Sahadevā, Bhūdhātrī, and Kulāñchitā [are used]. (23.18)
One should grind *rāmavelā* together with its own seed;
this should be given in food and drink as a supreme means of subjugation.
One should collect the root of the *uttaravāruṇī* plant with the juice of its flowers;
when combined with one's own semen, it is an excellent means of subjugation. (23–20)
The impurities from the ears and eyes, together with saliva, blood, and the sense organs,
combined with *bhūkadamba*, should be offered with milk at night.
It should be given away in secret; otherwise, one will die through separation.
[The cost is] sixty gold seeds and sixteen *maṇi*-crystals. (23.22)
O beautiful woman, one should give this [mixture] joined with human and cow dung;
this Kāpālika yoga follows after him as he goes.
The root of white arka, mañjiṣṭhā, the head of a crow, kuṣṭha grown in a house, and well-red indriya [are to be used]. (23–24)
This supreme means of subjugation should be administered in food and drink;
it is both a deluder and a captivator when used together with peacock crest [grass]. (23–25)
The union of the self with the senses is the supreme means of subjugation;
likewise, the *lajjālukā*, the *gorambhā*, and the bulbous root of the *caṇḍālī*. (23–27)
Mixed with the ichor of the lord of serpents, yet equal to one's own semen;
this divine, supreme yoga is bestowed upon him, O lady of virtuous vows.
Combined with honey, one shall come under control for as long as one lives;
[the ingredients are] the fruit of the *unmattaka*, *kuṣṭha*, *tagara*, and *pakṣaṣaṭpada*. (23–29)
Combined with the offering of a lamp on the fourteenth day (bhūtā), it brings others under one's control.
Gorocanā, govan, tāla, vyādhi, and ghee [are used]. (23–30)

One should cause a person who is destitute of wealth to consume the body [of the victim] mixed with *gīrṇa*; likewise, one should administer the excrement of a pigeon combined with fish bile and its own semen. (23.31)
Eating this and offering it as a gift is the supreme means of subjugation;
one should rise in the morning and chew a tooth-stick made from the *karañja* tree.
One should take it for seven nights, as well as the moisture from the tongue;
this, when prepared with rock salt, is given to whomever it may be.
One should consume [this] for as long as one lives; even after death, it follows [the practitioner]:
the *bhramara*, *kākajihvā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *tagara* combined. (23–34)
This powder, combined with blue lotus, brings about the end of death;
along with *sahā* and *sahadevā*, they are the sons who have joined their palms in reverence. (23.35)
Combined with semen and blood, it brings men and women under control; O fair-faced one, take possession of the Viṣṭi [muhūrta] of Sadyojāta for the purpose of subjugation.
This drink, combined with blood and the sense organs, is a means of subjugation;
likewise are mohanā, sahadevā, bhūdhātrī, and kulāñchanā. (23–37)
One should grind it with one's own blood; this is the supreme drinking of wine.
The Caṇḍālī, having taken the Caṇḍaka, should cause it to be filled with the smooth [substance]. (23-38)

Having taken the *putrāñjārī* plant and its root, which is endowed with the rut of a lordly elephant and which brings one under control when one has drunk *śīdhu* liquor, [one attains] the state of having the sense organs intensely red.
The drink mixed with the ichor of the lord of serpents brings women under control;
the goddess Mohanā, weeping, [is] Mahānīlī, Utpalā, and Ambuṣā. (23.40)
Having prepared it with equal parts, it should be administered with eye-water;
when combined with *prasannā* wine, this drink brings men and women under one's control. (23.41)
Having finely ground together putrañjārī, muśalī, kolla, and markaṭikā, one should cause [the woman] to drink it mixed with semen and blood. (23-42)
This is declared to be a means of securing residence, as well as a subduer of passion;
having taken the root of the *bhūkadamba* and likewise the red *aparājitā*. (23–43)
One should diligently grind sahadevī and mahānīla;
this drink will quickly bring even a powerful man under one's control. Or [one may use] balā as well. (23.44)
Wood from the *cūtavandāka* tree, as well as *kolamarkaṭikā*, mixed with the ichor of a lordly elephant—this drink brings all under one's control. (23.45)
One should prepare the root of the *sūryavarti* plant, the upward-pointing [root], and likewise the flower of the *aśoka*;
it should be made fine and impregnated with blood.
The most excellent practitioner should sprinkle this powder upon the head of a woman;
she will become completely submissive to him for the duration of an entire year.
If ground with the excrement of a crow from an *aśoka* tree, mixed with semen and blood, [the target] comes under one's control; even a daughter will be won for the sake of a living being.
Taking a garland of blue *aśoka* flowers, as well as a blue lotus,
*priyaṅgu*, and *nāgapuṣpa*, one whose sense organs are purified by their own natural redness.
A woman with her head powdered follows one who is departing;
a dog [indicates] the tongue and the heart, arising from the collection of a hundred thousand signs.
A woman whose head is sprinkled with the powder of *bhumareṇuka* combined with the dust of vermilion is pierced, as it were, by the arrows of Love. (23.51)
One should saturate red cloves with human bile; then, having combined vermilion, powdered camphor, and excellent unbroken rice grains into one, [one should proceed]. (23.52)
One should grind it at the region of the head; then they will come under control, overwhelmed.
Having gathered the droṇaka plant, having prepared it... one should uproot and split it open. (23.53)
Having filled that with salt alone, one should place it in a smooth vessel;
one should bury it in the ground for seven nights and then extract it.
Having uprooted it, one who knows the ritual should burn it at night with the wood for the funeral pyre;
alone in the empty abode of Śiva, he should do so until it is accomplished.
Having taken the perfected salt (siddhalavaṇa), one should cause portions to be made;
one portion is to be given to Śiva, and the second to Siddhāyana.
Having propitiated the deity, the lord of practitioners should take one-third as the portion to be accepted;
having offered incense of equal measure, the mantra-master should also take the portion belonging to Rudra. (23.57)
Having discarded the portion for the Siddhas, it then becomes *siddhalavaṇa* (perfected salt).
Indeed, this *siddhalavaṇa* belongs to anyone whose belly has been traversed [by it]. (23.58)
This [practice] makes the practitioner a slave from birth until death;
it is like gold, a black serpent, the five poisons, the king of elephants, or wine. (23.59)
O Bhuvanāṅkuśa, having taken salt accompanied by Putranjīva and Sāmudra, along with silver and pāṭavaka, one should place them into the belly.
One should bury him at a crossroads for twenty-one nights,
beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth.
Then, going there day after day, one should cast a single flower;
having offered the oblation according to the prescribed rite, the wise man should take hold of it.
Having taken one's stand in the eastern direction, one should grind together gold, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the crescent moon with auspicious water.
One should prepare equal portions of Rudracūlika combined with Karavīra and Arka, along with Uragekṣaṇa.
O Pārvatī, one should then make a fine powder by combining them;
having combined sea salt with its own five ancillaries, one should grind them together.
Provided with food and drink, one may bring [the subject] under control for as long as one lives;
likewise, a ripe mātuluṅga fruit and sea salt [are used]. (23.66)
Having placed it in a smooth vessel, one should add these medicinal ingredients:
*sukhāruṇī*, as well as *guñjā* and *garamudga*. (23.67)
O Goddess, one should likewise bury the camel-thorn (*uṣṭreṇṭī*), the white oleander (*śvetakaravīrī*), the datura (*unmattaka*), the *salāṅgalī*, and the *uragākṣī* at the eastern gate. (23.68)

One should urinate [the substance] for seven nights and cook it with the wood of the *unmatta* plant, either at a solitary linga or in a cremation ground; once it is prepared, there is no doubt regarding its efficacy.
One should cause [the powder] to be given to whomever dies from separation;
one who is mad from the bile of a dog should prepare a wick made of lac. (23.70)
Having cast it into the center of the tongue with one's own life-force,
O Pārvatī, one should take its essence with the *kaṅketu* [mantra] and with curd.
Having recited the mantra one hundred and eight times with the [mantra] inverted,
and having anointed both eyes, one may then go to the great battle.
O Goddess, he would become overwhelmed even by that; what need is there to mention base women?
It is like placing goat’s milk in a vessel prepared with flowers, so that it is affected by the flower. (23.73)
One should extract the essence from the flower born of sexual union, but not from the flower born of procreation;
having extracted it, one should prepare clarified butter and, having ignited it, light a lamp with that.
The wise man should take soot from a flower by making a wick out of lac, and let it fall upon the extinguishing of the flame of a *śara* grass flower.
He who, with eyes anointed [with collyrium], sees [the deity] will become a servant;
during the Puṣpa-yoga, he shall obtain various kinds of milk from women.
Having ignited a lamp by pouring the self and the senses [into it], one should collect the soot from the skull using a wick made of flowers and lac, out of affection for that [lamp]. (107b) 23.77.
The ointment for subjugation at night, known as *devī*, consists of *rocanā*, *nāgapuṣpa*, and likewise the flower of *priyaṅgu*. (23.78)
From this collyrium, one becomes beloved by the world of the gods; having prepared the collyrium with boar fat and a wick made of deer blood, one shall attain the most beloved woman. (23.79)
One who desires to see everything as beautiful should apply collyrium to their eyes;
furthermore, one should place collyrium upon the heart of a pigeon and upon a flower.
Having taken that which has stood for three nights, one should place it after consecrating it with mantras;
then, having become naked and loosened one's topknot, one should anoint both eyes.
With eyes anointed by that, whoever one looks upon will fall to the ground, overwhelmed.
The ointment consists of tagara, kuṣṭha, haritāla, and manaḥśilā. (23.82)
A wicked woman, intoxicated with passion, will bring a man under her sway;
[using] bilva flowers, śamī flowers, lotuses, saffron, and sandalwood. (23.83)
Having ground priyaṅgu, rocanā, and an equal amount of añjana together with flowers, one who is established in meditative concentration should apply it to both eyes. (23.84)
With eyes anointed by these, one becomes equal to Kāmadeva.
[The ingredients are: gorocanā, mud from a lotus, filaments of a lotus, leaf, water, wood, and [the practitioner] with palms joined in reverence. (23.85)

Having placed kuṣṭha and tuṭī within a red cloth, a wick [is made] with four trees and water; a tawny cow of the same color as its calf, with ghee, [was offered] at the rising of the flowers in the flower-grove—at that time, I suspected [the truth]. (23.86)
The roots of *sahadevā*, *viṣṇukrāntā*, *gorocanā*, sandalwood, and saffron become collyrium for the lotus-eyes of women and kings, serving as arrows of Kāma. (23.87)
By means of these, a maiden, using the collyrium with *kapilā* ghee, brings one under the power of desire.
A wick made of auspicious lac and the five milky trees becomes effective for those women. (23.88)

Repeatedly sprinkled with milk, containing a powder called *devāhvaya*, dressed in white water-silk garments, and saturated with tawny clarified butter—by means of that [mixture], during the night... || 23-89 ||

On a Tuesday night, having accomplished the rite that accomplishes the beloved desires of Manmatha, [one should take] the bile of a parrot, a blue jay, and a peacock, as well as that of the *rohitaka* tree. (23.90)
Having prepared a wick with these together with *arka* cotton, the wise one should then take soot [produced from it] along with the ghee of a tawny cow.
Having anointed his own eyes with that [substance], whatever wise person sees with it, he quickly brings under his control; there shall be no doubt regarding this. || 23-92 ||
Srotāñjana and mahānīla, thoroughly infused with [the juice of] *rasa*,
should be ground into a powder together with *gorocanā* and lac. (23.93)
Then, having made a wick from that *vaśā* [flesh] at night, one should extract soot using a large conch shell; this brings all the world under one's control.
Prīyaṅgu, śatapuṣpā, rocanā, gośīrṣa,
sauvīra, and śaśapitta— with these, one should prepare lac.
Then, having made a wick with that [substance], one should drop soot onto a skull at night using oil from sexual union; this brings all people under one's control.
With blue lotus, *śamī* flower, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), and *girikarṇikā*, combined with *śrotāñjana*, this collyrium brings about what is dear [to the beloved]. (23.95)
An intelligent person should burn elephant hide, rut-fluid, and human bile combined together, along with the head of a green snake, inside a smokeless fire. (23.96)
Then, having applied an ointment made from powder equal to *śrotāñjana* mixed with clarified butter to the eyes, both the woman and the man shall obtain good fortune.
Having taken the head of a black cobra, a bee, a lotus stalk, costus, a lotus, and then leadwort combined with antimony; || 23-98 ||
When the smoke has vanished and the two eyes have been thoroughly burnt by the fire, then this practitioner of mantra sees everything and shall bring it all under his control. || 23-99 ||
One should cause the flowers of the uttarāraṇi tree, priyaṅgu buds, and the eyes of a buffalo to be ground together with [the aforementioned] powder. (23.100)
In the past, it was ground into powder using a lotus fiber as a pestle;
having prepared it and taken the collyrium, it brings all the worlds under one's control.
One should wrap a wick made of *arka* cotton with lotus fiber;
this, powdered and treated with fish bile, awakens a hidden treasure when applied to a skull. (23.102)
One should rub it with the oil of the musk-shrew and a skull;
there, one should remain established in meditative absorption until the collyrium falls out. (23.103)
This is declared to be the "subduer" (*vaśaṅkara*) for women and the best of men;
one should prepare it by taking the powder of the eye of a peacock that has died in a great battle. (23.104)
One should cultivate [the mantra] with human bile and wrap it with a lotus fiber;
having taken soot from a skull, one should [mix it] with the ghee of a tawny cow.
Having consecrated it with mantras during the night, one should apply it to both eyes;
for this brings about invisibility as long as the sun has not yet risen.
Having taken his brown eyes, one should saturate them with bile;
then, having made a wick from the root of the Mohanī plant, one should grind it into powder. (23.107)
Having taken soot from a skull with the clarified butter of a tawny cow,
one should anoint both eyes at night with that very substance while reciting the mantra.
It renders oneself invisible and likewise makes one's appearance unseen by living beings;
furthermore, yellow orpiment, roots, cinnabar, and the *mohanā* plant [are used for] the crest-lock. (23.109)
O Goddess, having pulverized it, one should repeatedly soak the root of the *arka* plant in human bile; then, at night, one should cause collyrium to fall upon a skull.
At night he sees spirits who announce his desired intention;
with palms joined in speech, [he offers] *kuṣṭha*, yellow orpiment, and mica. (23.111)
One should cook dog’s tongue, the nave of a chariot wheel, and oil from the *vaibhītaka* tree.
This oil brings servants under control and subjugates all the world. (23.112)
It should be applied to the head of women, but to the feet of men;
likewise, *cāṇḍālī*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, and the tongues of a crow and a dog [should be used]. (23.113)
One should cook oil with realgar (manaḥśilā) until it is thickened;
having cooked it gently with these ingredients, its mere touch brings [the target] under one's control.
Haritāla, abhrapaṭala, vacā,
musk, dog’s tongue, and kuṣṭha— one should cook these with castor oil.
This oil should be applied to the heads of women and to the feet of men; whoever employs this oil will always possess virtuous character.
The hide [is placed] on the sole of the elephant's foot, the tongue upon men;
having grasped the eyes and nose, likewise the ear-petals are contracted. (23.117)
Oil cooked with these [substances] is considered to bring others under control, as previously described.
Oil prepared with the eyes, forehead, heart, and nose of a dead man likewise brings others under control. (23.118)
It brings all the queens of the lords of mantras under control; it is the abode of Śaṅkara within the flower;
it is bowed to by Sudarśana; it is the child-son Jārika who removes disease.
One who wears matted hair should cook oil from *vaibhītaka* nuts with these [ingredients] equal to Skanda;
having smeared either the female organ or the male organ, one may then engage in sexual union. (23.120)
A man should not desire another's wife, nor should a woman desire another as her husband;
[she should instead take] from men the fivefold collection consisting of the ears, eyes, tongue, nose, and the lotus of the heart. (23.121)
These [substances], including *mada*, *karavīra*, *sāra*, and cow-dung, should be equalized;
one should prepare oil at a crossroads using these medicinal herbs.
Or else, on the eighth day known as Bhūtāṣṭamī, with disheveled hair and naked,
one should accomplish the rite of the human skull by entering a cremation ground.
One should perform its movement with the [syllable] beginning with *ka* and recite the mantra as desired;
having recognized it as accomplished, one should enter [the state], having consecrated the body through the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa.
The practitioner of mantras, devoted to fasting, should keep [the mantra] well-guarded within his throat;
or else, having deposited it elsewhere, he may apply the yoga according to his desire. (23.125)
By means of garments, incense, flowers, perfumes, or through the application of fragrant substances, wherever it is employed—whether in food or on a bed—[it brings about its effect]. (23.126)
In various ways he will act as a servant;
he constantly gives Sudhana and indeed gives himself as well. (23.127)
It should be administered to wicked horses, and especially to elephants; furthermore, it should be given to other wicked creatures, such as lions, tigers, and the like. (23.128)
All of them come under one's control upon seeing the practice of yoga;
this supreme, divine yoga must be guarded with great effort. (23.129)
It has been repeatedly honored by all sentient beings and by gods and asuras;
there exists no oil superior to this in the three worlds. (23.130)
Always worshipped and honored by gods, asuras, and humans, one should not employ it when lacking self-mastery; otherwise, one will certainly die. (23.131)
With *rocanā*, saffron (*kuṃkuma*), yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), *priyaṅgu*, and the flower called *candana*, one brings the world under control by means of a forehead mark (*tilaka*). (23.132)

A palm tree that has been inhabited by a *piśāca* or a *bhūta*, or one that has resided in the mouth of a *preta*, when smeared with sesame oil while afflicted by disease, brings all the worlds under one's control. (23.133)
Having taken sprouts from a milk-tree, together with *rocanā* and gold,
one should worship this divine [object] consecrated a hundred times in due order.
By whom should the *tilaka* be made so that the world is brought under control? Of this there is no doubt:
it is the *mohanā*, the *sahadevā*, the *bhūlatā*, and the *cakralāñchanā*. (23.135)

Having prepared a mass of yellow pigment and black flowers through excellent application, O lady of beautiful hips, one may bring even enemies under control by means of forehead marks (tilakas). || 23.136 ||
Likewise, snake-antidote (bhujaṅgāri) and harī, along with saffron and gorocanā, together with the fluid from a pigeon’s egg and one's own blood. (23.137)
Having performed the worship according to the prescribed rite, one should grind [the ingredients] together;
by means of the resulting *tilakas*, it is said that one shall bring the three worlds under one's control.

Having carefully taken cow dung mixed with the two types of bile (bile and gallstone) and prepared with human [urine], one should apply a tilaka mark on the forehead; by the mere sight of it, [the person] is brought under control.
Having ground alasāra, samīpuṣpa, kuñjara, and dāna according to the prescribed rite, when a tilaka has been applied with flowers, [the desired result follows].
Whoever one should look upon will come under one's control, even if they possess strength equal to Śakra.
[The ingredients are] the root of white Arka, Bhāṣā-bone, Surasā, and realgar. (23.141)
The wise one should grind the root of the Madana plant together with Śamī flowers and a blossom;
this is the highly meritorious Tilakanda, which brings all sentient beings under one's control.
Tagara, utpala, kuṣṭha, tvak, elā, padmakeśara, śīta, uśīra, śilā, gomṛd, padmaka, dāru, and kuṅkuma. || 23-143 ||
Madhukṛt, surasā, kṛṣṇamāṃsī, and white mustard seeds in equal parts, with water from the moon’s flower when the moon rises; (144)
A beautiful maiden, having smeared herself with this flour paste at the rising of the moon, should go to the king’s palace or to the assembly of his enemies. (23.145)
A courtesan, a wicked creature, another, a king, a horse, and a cat—by the mere sight of these, one comes under control; in battle, one shall obtain victory. (23.146)
Wherever this Candrodaya Yoga remains, cows bring forth calves and buffaloes come under control. (23.147)
Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, Aparājitā, Kanakā, Bhūlatā, and another, Kṣatayoni, who is free from poison and snakes. (23.148)
O Dear One, having rolled it with one's own hand, one should fashion a pill in the auspicious water;
by means of that, making a tilaka on the forehead, one shall bring even Indra under one's control.
O lady of excellent hips, by means of both ambha and ahirakta, as well as pañcāgonmattaka and tilaka, one may bring even enemies under one's control.
