O beautiful lady, having collected the bile of the cow, fish, peacock, and mongoose, and mixing it with the sprouts of four trees and sesame paste, O lovely-faced one. (23.151)
Then, having rubbed one's face with that [substance], one should look about wherever it pleases;
by the mere sight of it, the three worlds come under control, without a doubt. || 23.152 ||
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, one should take the root of *sahadevaja*,
mix it with cow-dung soil, and grind it just as before.
With that, one should apply a tilaka; by this, one shall bring even Indra under one's control. [One should also use] kusuṃbha, nāgapuṣpa, priyaṅgu, and śatapuṣpikā.
Vacā, mustā, jaggery, sarja resin, honey, and madhuka—this is declared to be the best incense, which brings subjugation to men and women. (23.155)
Nail-powder, kuṣṭha, madākāntā, and śatapuṣpā combined, together with kusuma, agaru, lac, and sarjarasa. (23.156)
Incense made from *turuṣka* combined with *kumārī* flowers and saturated with honey brings subjection to both men and women. (23.157)
One should grind sahadevā with the blood of a sparrow;
by anointing the body with this, one shall bring even the Sun under one's control. (23.158)
With equal parts of the dung of a mare, a donkey, and a woman,
one should prepare the pigeon droppings for seven nights.
One should apply a plaster mixed with honey under the constellation presided over by the deity Bhaga;
this plaster undoubtedly brings even an excellent woman under one's control. (23.160)
Long pepper seeds, honey, the fruits of the *kanaka* tree, and the excrement of a pigeon—this ointment brings about death. (23.161)
A man brings his husband under control, and a woman may bring him into her power;
[this is achieved] by a scorpion’s venom mixed with honey and the semen of a monkey combined with clarified butter. (23.162)
These two are the sovereign ointments that bring each other under control:
long pepper, rice, *rondhra*, and white black peppers. (23.163)
One should grind it together with *mātuluṅga* fruits and honey; then, at the time of sexual union, one should smear the penis with that [mixture]. (23.164)
Having abandoned her own family and wealth, she remains under his very control.
[The ingredients are] honey, two types of white mustard, priyaṅgu, and nāgakeśara. (23.165)
One should mix it with cow urine and honey;
this ointment should be applied, for it pierces the heart of women. (23.166)
O Goddess, he is renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Kāmeśvara.
[One should take] śatapuṣpā, honey, haridrā, bṛhatī, and nāgakeśara. (23.167)
One should grind it together with *devadāru* and the bile of a fish.
O beautiful woman, this ointment, when applied with water, is a deluder of the minds of men. (23.168)
A plaster made of hen’s eggs, scorpion venom, honey, sahadevā, and prasannā increases passion. (23.169)
Having combined the juice of betel leaf with honey, moonstone, and *sapi-nākin*, one should churn them together;
this ointment brings about death.
Long pepper, rice, kuṣṭha, rock salt, and realgar, combined with honey—this ointment brings about death. (23.171)
Mañjiṣṭhā, mahānīlī, and likewise harabījaka, combined with honey—this ointment brings about death. (23.172)
A scorpion, a silk-worm, *kuṣṭha*, and the excrement of a pigeon, along with the seeds of *madhuśirīṣa*—this ointment brings about death. (23.173)
Bṛhatī fruit, priyaṅgu, and sephālī, along with the [excrement] of a monkey—this ointment, when combined with ghee, brings about death. (23.174)
The semen of Śiva, the moon, betel, and the juice of the uttamaka plant; likewise, the house-grown suraṇa tuber, cloves, clarified butter, and honey. (23.175)
O wise woman, one should apply this excellent ointment to the superior parts of the body;
it renders the woman overwhelmed and does not grant her satisfaction. (23.176)
One should consume the semen-discharging juice that removes disease, produced from betel leaves, as well as that from jasmine flowers, and the house-grown suraṇa tuber. (23.177)
Indeed, an ointment for the private parts consisting of honey, clarified butter, and camphor is excellent and brings women under one's control. (23.178)
Having gathered fresh flowers from the trees of the sages, which are moon-bright, one should take honey, ghee, kuṣṭha, pippalī, and maṇimattaka. (23.179)
A woman applies a paste that induces intoxication to the penis, consisting of vṛścikālī, piśāca, salt, and combined with camphor. (23.180)
The seed of the *harītakī* and honey—this ointment brings one under control.
Likewise, the juice of *mātuluṅga*, semen, long pepper, and rock salt [form another]. (23.181)
This ointment with honey brings happiness to women;
he who should lick bilva powder mixed with gold and ghee [shall likewise attain this]. (23.182)
If a man or woman becomes excessively passionate even when disliked, [one should use] aśvagandhā, vacā, kuṣṭha, bṛhatī, and white mustard seeds. (23.183)
By this, the penis of the horse itself is enlarged;
likewise, one *bhallātaka* fruit from a house and one *karṣa* of *saindhava* salt [should be used]. (23.184)
When it has been burnt, one should then grind that smoke into a fine powder;
then, one should add the powder of yaṣṭīmadhuka together with harisena. (23.185)
One should prepare this liquid extract from the fruit of the *bṛhatī*;
smeared with this, the penis increases in size when moistened with the water of sexual union. (23.186)
It is pacified likewise by heat; otherwise, there would be no alleviation.
Having prepared the dehusked fruit of *gokṣuraka* with curd, [one should apply it]. (23.187)
Combined with fresh butter, this promotes the growth of the penis:
the roots of *kokilākṣa* and the fruits of *ātmaguptā*. (23.188)
Sugar and milk, when drunk, make a man as vigorous as a horse.
One should lick a pala of powdered black gram combined with ghee and milk. (23.189)
Furthermore, a man who drinks milk after [eating] and consumes the meat of a domestic pigeon fried in ghee, even if he has little semen, [will increase it]. 23.190b-g.
There shall be no flaccidity of his organ, nor shall there be any loss of semen. [One should take] the root of the white Aparājitā and the right [foreleg] of a black cat. (23.191)
O fair-faced one, having taken a bone from a foot, one should bind it with a thread from a virgin’s wick around the waist; this is a means for the immobilization of semen.
The root of the white *sara* arrow-shaft, strung upon a thread and bound according to the prescribed rite, is an exceedingly powerful aphrodisiac for semen. (23.193)
O fair-faced one, having made a wick from the root of the white *sarapuṅkhā*, if it is applied as an ointment to the navel with ghee and honey, it is an excellent means for arresting semen. 194.
Having made a paste with *siddhārthaka* seeds mixed well with black mustard (*rājikā*),
one should place it in a pair of earthen bowls and bury it at the door of the hearth.
One who is joined with the name of [the person] will certainly be drawn forth;
the target is burned, bewildered, and comes, utterly distraught. (23.196)
Taking hold of a noose that has fallen of its own accord from the sole of your left foot,
fashion an image of that potter with it.
Then Madana [should place] that mantra, consecrated with those very thorns, on the forehead, the heart, the private parts, the two breasts, and the two feet. (23.198)
With their limbs smeared with salt mixed with black mustard seeds, they shall remain submerged face-down; the wise man should bury them up to their necks.
One should perform the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) in that [fire] using fuel-sticks of *khadira* wood;
by means of black mustard and salt, [the result is achieved] at the three junctions of the day from the seventh day.
O lady of excellent hips, he comes under one's control without a doubt and becomes a servant; yet, if separated, he certainly dies of his own accord. (23.201)
The fat and flesh of an owl and a bat, well-consecrated with *brahmadaṇḍī*, constitute an incense; he to whom this is given becomes an enemy. (23.202)
One should employ the eye of a snake and a well-goldened tongue, cast with fragrant incenses, for the purpose of preparing the medicinal preparation. (23.203)
The practitioner of mantra, having ground together the eyes of a buffalo, its own hair, and the membranes of its eyes, should offer incense and fumigate [the object]. || 23.204 ||
A woman or a man quickly becomes hated by all and is no longer beloved.
[One should avoid] the hair of an outcaste, a brahmin, and likewise the menstrual blood of an unfortunate woman. (23.205)
With this incense—consisting of *brahmadaṇḍī*, funeral pyre embers, and snake slough—one who is touched becomes utterly loathed by his enemies. (23.206)
One should saturate the hair of a cat and a mouse, as well as the slough of a snake,
with the blood of a buffalo and a donkey, combined with inauspicious substances.
He who would heap up incense becomes unfortunate; likewise, [the smoke of] gumṛkta, locusts, crow-feathers, and husks [brings the same result]. 23-208.
If incense made from nimba, kākagṛhadviṣṭa, and vātapatra, combined with the menstrual blood of a woman, is offered in someone's house, [the following occurs]. (23.209)
One should swiftly uproot that very enemy; of this there is no doubt.
The long hairs of the armpits and the nails located on the head [are to be used]. (23.210)
One should soak powdered, scattered leaves in donkey urine;
when this incense, combined with crow feathers, is offered to someone, [the desired effect occurs]. (23.211)
One should swiftly expel [the target] from their place and never allow them to return;
having taken the hoof of a donkey and the sloughed skin of a snake, [one should perform the rite]. (23.212)
Palala, crow’s bile, and dog’s tongue—these together, infused with crow’s blood, are the incense that should be offered to whomsoever [it is intended]. (23.213)
If the king is hostile, that [sign] quickly departs from its own place;
it arises from the tip of the banner made of bell-metal, brass, or iron.
Having collected these seven types of ash— arising from the Dakṣiṇa fire, the Āhavanīya fire, and the Gārhapatya fire, as well as that situated on the altar— the knower of mantras [should proceed].
One should draw the form [of the target] upon a mirror mixed with black mustard and salt; then, having become naked with disheveled hair, one should stand facing the person to be acted upon. (23.216)
Having placed a sword in the right hand and a mirror in the left,
one should cause that form to depart by means of an extremely violent wind from the void.
If one performs [the rite] at midnight on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, that enraged deity will perform a wondrous act of total destruction for that family in that house. (23.18)
One who is tranquil should draw forth the dust from the feet and from the palms upward toward a man or an excellent woman, mixed with white mustard seeds and salt. (23-219)
With beeswax and red lac, one should draw an image four finger-breadths in height and write the name upon it; one should then place it in the region of the heart.
Having tied a donkey by its throat with a rope made of hair,
one should cast that donkey into the sky after it has been consecrated one hundred times with mantras.
One equal to Śakra quickly eradicates the object to be accomplished; he becomes beloved.
A long cave-heart-lotus, consecrated with the blood of two [beings], [achieves this]. (23.222)
Having mixed clay from the footprint with [the image], the wise one should fashion a form, insert it into the razor of a donkey, and place it at the door of that person. (23.223)
By performing this for seven days, one causes [the enemy] to wither and become subject to a circle of fire;
or one should offer the wings of a crow and an owl mixed with bitter oil into the fire. (23.224)
By performing one hundred and eight oblations, the supreme rite of inciting hatred is accomplished;
having fashioned an effigy from the wood of the Paiśāca tree according to the prescribed sequence, [one should proceed].
Then, O Goddess, one should fumigate with the excrement of a rat and a cat, and with the wings of an owl and a crow, while reciting the desired mantra. (23.226)
One who is hostile toward all living beings should always perform the fire sacrifice (homa) in this manner [using] the excrement of a rat and a cat, or even that of an owl and a crow. 154b] 23-227.
Having offered oblations of the wings mixed with oil and combined with one's own urine,
one should utter the name of the Darbha-grass and perform the fire-sacrifice in a vessel made of gold.
Offered according to the rules at the end of the day for seven days, this is the supreme means of inciting hatred.
[The woman] who is difficult to seize becomes like one burnt by fire when she has been bathed in ashes, vajra, and cow-dung.
Having performed the rite correctly, one should deposit the name in that very place;
having dug into the ground, one should place it at a depth of exactly six finger-breadths.
That person becomes paralyzed for as long as they remain in that very state;
[this occurs when one is] endowed with sulphur, realgar, nirmocā, and arka. (23.231)
Together with clay from the footstep, one should fashion an image of the deceased on the ground for the ancestors, eight finger-breadths in size and inscribed with his name.
In another *Pañcarātra* [text], it is said that if one dies in his absence, or if there is a serpent, an eye, or a gnat, or a corpse's eye in that very place; 23-233.
Having fashioned an image made of those [materials] that is equal to earth from a cremation ground,
one should place it in the region of the heart, together with its name, upon the ground of the spirits (bhūtabhūmi).
Even one who is protected by various [means] goes to the abode of Yama;
likewise, human bone, or human bone, or a human skull, or curd [are causes of downfall]. (23.235)
O fair-faced one, having fashioned an image with clay from the footprints and inscribed with the [victim's] name,
if it is buried beneath a *kañjinī* plant, it kills [the enemy] instantly.
Having fashioned an image in a skull, especially with blood,
and having heated it thus in the fire of a cremation ground, one of timid eyes is consumed.
Having taken the dust from his feet, one should draw a corpse in a cremation ground;
using wood from a funeral pyre, one should recite the mantra while crossing over it.
If one is burned while being equal [to others], yet cut, one shall meet death;
having made a triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with funeral ashes, one may wander about at night.
One should frighten the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and others of evil mind with human flesh and fish meat mixed with ghee and guggulu. (23–240)
Having offered it so that it becomes the ashes of nirvāṇa, one should mix them with human powder and apply it to the heads of excellent women or men.
Taking hold of a serpent’s head together with a *preta*-tongue, the practitioner of mantras, having turned it back toward himself, quickly brings [the enemy] into a state of servitude. (23–242)
The knower of mantras should write the name upon that [substance] smeared with poison and blood;
then, uttering the name, he should strike it with fragments of bone.
Enraged, one should swiftly split open the skull with a potsherd;
as long as it is being cut into pieces, the victim perishes. || 23-244 ||
Having fashioned the form of Sādha’s upper garment, two finger-breadths in length, one should fill its inner side with the name, while its outer side remains nameless. || 23-245 ||
Thrown into a mouth pierced by a trident, it shall kill the enemy instantly;
likewise, fragments of bone smeared with blood and endowed with poison [achieve the same]. (23–246)
At night, one should perform the fire-oblation upon the funeral pyre while recollecting the name of the person to be accomplished;
then, rising with a skull, one should offer a full oblation of blood.
Taking a recently severed human head and fashioning it from clay at a cremation ground, one kills even a long-lived king along with his army instantly.
Having placed it in the mouth, one should smear it with *tthaka* and,
sprinkled with pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*), cook it slowly in the fire of a funeral pyre.
Enraged, he shall cause death within half a ghaṭikā; of this there is no doubt.
[One should take] the menstrual blood of a woman, the excrement of a bat, powdered bone, and earth from a cremation ground. (23–25)½
Having mixed the root of *halinī* with half a *sākhi* in one place,
and having fashioned it into a hollow figure pierced in the secret part, one should cause it to fall.
This practice, praised by yogis, brings about the miscarriage of the wives of enemies:
[the use of] the *citrabheka* (variegated frog), *kauṇḍinya*, *pataga*, and *kuṣṭha*. (23–252)
The Śatapāyu, the Ciṭiṅga, the Kambali, the Indragopaka, the Kṛkalāsa, the Gahe, the Godhā, the Sarpa, the Kañcuka, and the Kaṇṭaka; || 23–253 ||
When putikīṭaka, gomārī, valgulī, and rasaruṣkara are employed according to the prescribed ritual, they instantly take away the life of the enemy. (23–254)
A worm, or any one of these—burnt [substances], black serpent, or priyaṅgu—when combined as a mixture of humors (doṣas), is considered to instantly take away life. || 23-255 ||
The root of *apāmārga* combined with the powder of *bhallātaka* flowers is a formulation effective for half a month or a full month.
The root of *vyādhighātaka* combined with *bhallātaka* flowers is a "insect-formulation" (*kīṭayoga*) effective for one month.
The quantity for men is merely a handful; it is double for donkeys and horses, and fourfold for elephants and camels.

A smoke made from *śatakadrū*, *ciṭiṅga*, *karavīra*, bitter *tumba*, and fish, or from *madanaka*, *kodrava*, *palāli*, and fresh *pravāta* grass, is administered when the wind blows in its favor as long as it continues to move.
Alternatively, there is a powder made from *pūtikīṭa*, fish, bitter *tumbī* seeds, *śatakadrū*, and *indragopaka*.
A fumigation consisting of the powder of *pūtikīṭa*, small *rālā*, and *hemavidārī*, combined with the powder of cloth, horn, and hoof, causes blindness. (23–256)
The leaves of the *patikarañjaka*, yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), realgar (*manaḥśilā*), *guñjā* seeds, the fruits of red cotton (*raktakarpāsika*), and *āsphoṭikā*,
ground with the liquid of cow dung, constitute a smoke that causes blindness. The slough of a snake, cow dung, and the head of a blind snake (*andhahika*) constitute a smoke that causes blindness.

The powder of pigeons, carnivorous birds, elephants, monkeys, boars, elephant claws, and deer—this incense, when prepared with the chaff of *madanaka-odra*, the chaff of *hastikarṇa*, or the chaff of *karṇapālāsa*, kills [the enemy] as soon as it is applied, even down to a single individual.
Alternatively, the incense consisting of the roots of *kālī*, *kuṣṭha*, *nala*, and *śatāvarī*, along with *sarpavalī* and *kaṇṭaka*, or the powder of the five types of *kuṣṭha*, is used as before.
According to the previous ritual procedure, using the chaff of fresh ginger (*ārdraka*), *kuṣṭha*, and *palāśa*, one may cause a battle among monkeys or rams. (23–257)

The dung of the sarika bird, the pigeon, the crane, the alanda, and the marka, ground with milk-pilu and mixed with svahikṣīra, is an ointment that causes blindness and serves for coloring. || 23-258 ||
And for the defilement of water: a mixture of the root of *vajrākadalī*, *madanaphala*, jasmine leaves, and human urine. || 23-259 ||
Is it a fire whose limbs are consumed by lightning, or a flame seized by wood drenched in lightning?
Or does the fire, kindled through fierce rites during the asterisms of Vāsava, Vastra, Kṛttikā, or Bharaṇī, remain here, burning with a blackened glow? || 23–260 ||
Having mounted the fire of the foremost karma, one should offer oblations with honey;
separately, the liquor-seller’s fire [should be offered] with wine and with clarified butter.
One [is purified] by a garland of flowers and by the smoke of the finest jewels and mustard seeds;
by the fire of a *caṇḍāla* after one month, and by the fire of a funeral pyre after a human [year]. || 23-262 ||
One should offer oblations into the fire with a ladle made from the wood of the *rājavṛkṣa* tree, using the mantra while restraining [the senses] on all sides with the *vastuśayā*.
This is the fire that cannot be countered, which bewilders enemies:
*Oṃ, homage to you, Aditi; homage to you, Anumati; homage to you, Sarasvatī; homage to you, Deva Savitṛ; homage to Agni, svāhā!
To Soma, svāhā! To Adya, svāhā!*
Svāhā to the *sruva* ladle! Bhūḥ svāhā! Bhuvaḥ svāhā!
Svaḥ svāhā! Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ svāhā!
Having mixed the powder of *śirīṣa*, *udumbara*, and *śamī* seeds with clarified butter, this is the fortnightly regimen for hunger.
A preparation for a month's hunger consists of *kaseru*, blue lotus root, sugarcane root, poison, *dūrvā* grass, milk, and ghee, boiled with the scum (*maṇḍa*).
Alternatively, a powder of black gram, barley, horse gram, and *darbha* root, prepared with milk and ghee, provides the same nourishment as meat.
Or, having drunk a powder of the roots of *śālaparṇī* and *pṛṣṭhaparṇī* with milk, one who has been purified by the wind-element (fasting) may consume it with honey and ghee and fast for a month.

Oil prepared with white mustard seeds (*siddhārthaka*) soaked in the urine of a white-clad person, and kept for half a month or a full month in pungent water, causes disfigurement in four-footed and two-footed creatures. White mustard oil prepared with the urine and the juice of the *laḍu* of a white donkey that has been eating barley for seven nights—after those seven nights—causes disfigurement. This same oil, prepared with the urine and the juice of the *laḍu* of either of these [two animals], and into which the fibers of a *markaṭī* plant have been added as a post-incense (*prativāpa*), causes whitening.
The whitening [process] consists of the application of the dung of a white cock and a python.

By means of a white thread and a white cloth, one should steep white mustard seeds for seven nights; this formulation—consisting of buttermilk, *arka* milk, *arka* fruit, insects, *kaṭuka*, fish, and *viḍaṅga*—remains effective for a fortnight as a means of whitening.
[156a] The formulation consists of sea salt, *māṇḍūkī*, conch-shell, lime, plantain, alkali, and buttermilk.

A formulation consisting of the juice of the alkaline bark of the *kadala* plant mixed with *plasu-rā*, or one containing buttermilk, *arka* oil, the milk of *sruhī*, and salt, remains effective for a fortnight; this is a means for whitening.
When a man has applied a paste of white mustard seeds for half a month while standing in bitter water or on a creeper, there is whitening of the hair. [Also included are:
*arka*, *tola*, the *janakīṭa* insect, white [mustard], and the house-lizard.
Anointed with this ground powder, the hair shall become as white as a conch shell.
For those whose bones and marrow have not fully developed, there are three hundred and sixty [units];
it should contain an iron nail within, along with black sesame seeds and *praṅkṣa*.
One part of the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*, half of that amount of *bījasāra* oil, and an equal amount of the juice of *akṣataila* and *amlavelī* [should be combined]. (23–266)
Having stirred it and ground it with *madana*, one should cast it into the interior of a jar;
then, one should place it beneath the fragrant substances in a dried-up pond and subsequently fill [the pond] with water.
Then, having extracted it after three seasons, one should open that [vessel] from its base;
having taken the *kūrcikās* from the heads, one should perform an oil massage for the head.
Standing in water that reaches only to the neck and placing rice grains in the mouth, one should crush them one by one; this is the supreme method for blackening.
Three parts of triphalā, equal amounts of nīlī and nīlotpala, as well as añjana, lotus roots, kauraṇḍa, and bhṛṅga. || 23-270 ||
One should take equal parts of the bark of *Arjuna*, the paste (*kalka*), and the fruits of *piṇḍikāra*, each weighing one *karṣa*. (23–271)
One should take ten *palas* of *akṣa* seed oil;
while that oil is being heated, one should indeed stir it with a white-feathered brush.
If it should be black there, one should then cause it to descend;
the nasal medication should be administered with half a month’s worth [of the substance], and the meal should consist of milk-rice (kṛsarā).
Standing in a windless place for half a fortnight, devoted to celibacy,
possessing divine vision and great intelligence, he [beholds] those whose hair is like dark blue clouds.
If there is the fragrance of a blue lotus in the mouth, one shall live for three hundred years.
The well-powdered seeds of the *palāśa* tree, tripled with the juice of *dhātrī*,
and saturated with the essence of *viḍaṅga*, ghee, and honey, destroy leprosy and gray hair within a month.
Iron [vessels], along with triphalā, yaṣṭī, bhṛṅga, and sesame seeds, [should be used] with water.
This nasal medication, prepared with the juice of *bhṛṅga*, *triphalā*, blue lotus (*utpala*), and *sārī*, combined with iron dross and kept in a copper vessel overnight, removes old age. (23–276)
This oil, when cooked, removes even the most terrible [hair loss] and makes the hair white, black, or curled.
Beans soaked in menstrual blood, mixed with the root of *vajrakandālī* and frog fat, should be cooked on a blazing fire in a cauldron;
this is the purification of the cauldron, for which there is no other remedy.
The "electric" ash is equal to fire.
If *pīlu* wood, *payas*, *manu*, or *agnigarbha* is wrapped with the root-knot of *suvarcalā* or even the root-knot of *mūlagranthi* and bound on top, it emits fire from its mouth.
When sprinkled with safflower oil, it blazes even during the rainy season.

Sea-foam and *kauśa* grass, when soaked in oil and floating upon water, burn. Fire produced by churning bamboo with a wooden stick (*kalpāṣa*) among the bones of aquatic creatures is not extinguished by water.
Having ground the *cchucchundarī* and the *khañjarīṭa* birds together, when mixed with urine, it serves as a breaker of fetters.
The foot-ointment for quadrupeds and bipeds consists of the excrement of a crow, a pigeon, and a cuckoo, ground with water.
How does it cause rapid movement?
By anointing sandals made of camel hide with the fat of an owl and a vulture, and covering them with banyan leaves, one travels fifty *yojanas* without fatigue.

Having taken the right or left eyes of a cat, a camel, a crane, a boar, a porcupine, a lizard, a bat, or of any other nocturnal creature—whether one, two, or many—one should have them ground separately into a powder.
Then, by anointing the right eye with the powder from the right eye and the left eye with the powder from the left eye, one sees in the darkness of night.
Furthermore, having anointed one's eyes with the fruit of the *āmalaka*, the eye of a boar, a firefly, or the black *sārikā* bird, one perceives forms at night.

Having fasted for three nights, one should plant barley seeds in the skull of a man killed by a weapon or impaled on a stake. One should then water them with the milk of a sheep. Then, having bound a garland of those sprouted barley grains, one’s shadow disappears.
Having fasted for three nights, one should have a probe and a collyrium-stick made from the bone of a man who has been killed.
Then, by applying it with any one of the eye-powders, one’s shadow disappears and one becomes invisible.
The powder of a snake’s fang, combined with coral dust, the skin of a rhinoceros, and the hair of a deer, causes invisibility.
The powder of an owl’s feet, a *vāgulī*’s tail, its excrement, and its bones, combined with the powder of a *bhastaka* bird, causes invisibility.
By rubbing one’s body with cow dung or the paste of *tendu* and *ariṣṭa*, and drinking the juice of *bhallātaka* for a month, one undergoes the application of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*).
A preparation of *guñjā* and *kuṣṭha* kept for seven nights in the mouth of a black snake or in the mouth of a house-lizard [is used].
Anointing with the bile of a parrot and the juice of its eggs is a preparation of *kuṣṭha*.
The remedy for *kuṣṭha* is a paste of *pipālaka*.
One who consumes food prepared with the roots of *kurkuṭī*, *kośātakī*, and *śatāvarī* becomes fair-complexioned within a month.
By means of a *vaṭaka* (ball) made from iron filings smeared with the paste of *sahacara*, one becomes black.
Or [one becomes black] by [using] *śakuna* and *kaṅguka* mixed with oil at night, or [the paste] of *khadira* and *karṇikāra*.
The oil of *śakunaka* and *aṅgukā*, combined with the powder of *tejini*,
along with *pāribhadraka*, *khaṭvāṅgī*, and the fat of a frog,
causes the body to blaze without fire.
The body smeared with the bark of the *pāribhadraka*, *śakuna*, *kaṅguka*, plantain, and sesame paste burns without fire.
An iron ball made from *pīlu* bark burns when held in the hand.
If smeared with that [mixture] and sprinkled with *asaṃkauśamba* oil, or combined with the fat of a sea-frog and powdered *sarjarasa*, it likewise burns.
With a preparation made from frog fat, or with the fat of *dhūlīpada* insects, one should perform an anointing; smeared with this fat, one burns without fire.
A bamboo pole smeared with moss and anointed with frog fat likewise burns without fire.
With a preparation of *pāribhadraka*, *pratiloṭha*, *julaka*, and the root of *vajrakandalī* processed with frog fat, one whose feet are anointed with the resulting oil can walk upon glowing embers.

One should prepare oil by cooking the root-paste of the *upodaka*, *pratibala*, *vañjula*, and *pāribhadra* together with frog fat. By anointing the feet with this, one can walk upon a heap of glowing coals.
Having left a flower for three nights, one should fill the skull of a man killed by a weapon or impaled on a stake with earth, and then sprinkle it with water from a flowing stream.
Once [mushrooms] have grown, one should take them with that very same flower and bind them with a rope. Then:

One should cut the string of a bow and quiver that have been prepared while they are still in front [of the target]; this is called "breaking the string" (*jyāccheda*). Having filled the nostrils of a corpse—whether female or male—with weapons and poisons, there occurs "nose-inflation" (*nāsikāvardhana*) and "seizing the mouth" (*mukhagrahaṇa*).
Having fasted for four nights and offered an oblation (*bali*) on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should cause stakes of bone from a person impaled on a stake to be fashioned.
If one of those [kila] is driven into a water-trough, it causes the flow of urine to become obstructed;
if it is buried at the feet or on a bed or seat, it kills by means of consumption;
or it brings about the destruction of the livelihood of whoever's field or house it is placed in.
By this very same method, it is declared that human effigies made of burnt lightning-struck wood are effective.
Having ground fresh ginger and the two feet [of the effigy],
one should either bury them in the house of the person against whom one acts or cause them to be administered mixed with honey.
One who cooks for himself alone, along with his sons, wife, and wealth, does not prosper.
One should not take the hair of goats, buffaloes, donkeys, camels, cats, mongooses,
Brahmins, outcastes, crows, or owls.
By grinding these [ingredients], they cause instantaneous madness when applied to the eyes.

Having fasted for three nights, one should take the earth from the head of a man who has been struck by a weapon or impaled on a stake, and mix it with *guñjā* seeds and boiled rice; one should sprinkle this [mixture] under the conjunction of the Puṣya asterism on either the new moon or the full moon night. Having caused a garland of *guñjā* seeds to be made into a circular wreath (*maṇḍalikā*), whatever food, drink, or other items are placed within it will not diminish even as they are being consumed.

When a public spectacle has taken place at night and a fire is blazing, one should cut off the udders of a dead cow and burn them. Having ground the burnt remains with bull’s urine, one should smear the inside of a fresh gourd. After encircling that village and entering it, all the butter therein will come forth. *Oṃ namo bhagavati mānasi mānasi mahāmānasi divyamānasi āgaccha svāhā*.
With this mantra, one should empower green snake-powder mixed with honey and fumigate the painted cloth (*citrapaṭa*). Thereupon, a woman descends; one may sport with her at night.

Whether it be a white mare, a black female cat, a natural-born woman, or whatever is available, once she has given birth, one should take a kitten, grind it into powder, and have a maiden soak it in sesame oil. With that, one should fumigate the painting; she descends.
Liberation occurs again by means of *guggulu* incense.

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Rudra; homage to Umā and Samā! Hili hili! Come, come, O Blessed One! Grant protection! To the Self-Existent One, Oṃ, homage, homage, svāhā! Without having first propitiated him, one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣa*) of this mantra should be performed. When it is completed, one should stand near a wall or similar surface while consecrating it with the mantra. Then, having arrived, Karṇapiśācī will speak what is indicated as auspicious.
[The seed-syllable is: *poṭṭhakha*, *bīje*, *peṭasiphuṃṭṭeśakaddukehuḥ*.
Having bathed with purity, one should recite this *pauṣkaravidyā* one hundred thousand times.
Having performed the rites of purification, whatever one desires, that one attains through austerity. [The mantra:
*ari mustamaṭṭi āye muhakuharaṃ bharidruṇavaṭṭeṇavagulīye*.
One should destroy that in the cremation ground by means of this *peṭṭara* mantra:
Oṃ ucchiṭapacāre pokasanāke peṭṭasi huṭṭeṭakāṭukāphaḥ | iṭṭīmaṭṭīgaṃgeṭṭī tusu bhusupuriyudho dvepeṭṭa mihuṭṭasiphuḥ ||

A Ī Ā Khaḍu! By the name of Him who is the essence of the Viḍuma [coral] jewel, it is said that one should apply [the mud] to the belly of the one whose interior is dense. O Ghe! O Nāmimaṭṭi! O Āśāvujaṇu! I embrace you; I am distressed. O Ullekhi! O Vā Sāvujatu-bhelakṣitayā! O Hela? O Svāhā!
Having taken earth from a crossroads with the index finger and the thumb, and having consecrated it seven times, one should apply a tilaka mark on the forehead.
It renders all the wicked speechless and brings them under control.

*Oṃ bhelakṣiva ā makṣimāsari savacakṣi ā induputtena haḍā vā yā vāsudeveṇa khini ājahaṇa suṇa iṇa peccha iṇa bhasa iṇa vāha i indraputreṇa haḍā vā ā ceḍaputtoṇibhācāro bhelakṣī svāhā.* Having written the name of Devadatta with yellow orpiment on the left hand, having encircled it with this spell, and having clenched his fist, one should enter an assembly; this makes him mute and renders him speechless.

Having inscribed [the mantra] on other objects and set them aside, one should worship them with perfumes and flowers while reciting the mantra; then, wherever one goes, one brings about the confusion of whomever one desires.
*Oṃ bhelakṣī mahābale hanumaparākrame hili hilāvaṇi hiṇḍī vīṇī mohaya mohaya bhañja bhañja parasainyaṃ stambhaya stambhaya svāhā*.
By means of the ritual procedure for hoisting a banner, one shatters all enemy armies.
Oṃ bhelahemantavāli eṣeṇa bhañjanī sakho haṇī nāśanī mohaya svāhā!
Having recited this four times during the night and having performed worship with perfumes, flowers, and incense, one should cause *aliphalguṣa* to be given.
As before, the breaking of the enemy army occurs.
Oṃ prāñjali añjite mahātejo svāhā!

This vidyā, having been written with *gorocanā* on a birch leaf (*bhūrjapatra*) and consecrated one thousand times, should be tied upon the crest-lock (*śikhā*). By doing so, one becomes invincible in disputes involving clarified butter, unrefined butter, the ocean, rivers, and thieves.

Having taken five kinds of clay from an anthill (*vālmīka*), the bark and shoots of five milk-exuding trees (*kṣīravṛkṣa*), wood from seven houses, the seven grains, and substances named after a man—such as black earth, black sesame, and so forth—and having ground these with a young girl, one should fashion an image together with an ointment for the person to be subjugated (*sādhya*). Having written the name on birch-bark (*bhūrja*) with yellow pigment (*rocanā*), one should place it within the belly [of the image]. Then, having placed it in a cow’s horn, one should bury it in a secluded spot of one's own house. On the day the rite is completed, one should strike it three times with the foot;
[the target] becomes submissive.
Having written the name of the person to be bound on the sole of the foot with *rocanā*, one should smear it over that object; thus, the binding of the feet is accomplished.

Having written [the name] on birch bark (*bhūrja*) with *rocanā* and having thrown black mustard seeds (*rājikā*) into it, one should smear it over that object; thus, the binding of the mouth is accomplished.
Then, taking pure rice husks and grinding them together with *nimba*, one should fashion an image of Gaṇapati.
Having written this mantra with *bhūrja*-rocanā, one should place it upon the heart:

*Oṃ gaṇapataye namaḥ*. Afterward, the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) on a piece of cloth (*karpaṭa*) should be performed. One should grind together *nimba*, garlic, *unmatta*, *kalāṅgalī*, and charcoal from a cremation ground, and write [the name] upon that cloth. The name of the person to be incited to hatred—whether he be a king, an enjoyer of pleasures, or some resident of a particular place—should all be given using the word "vidveṣa" (hatred). Afterwards, one should wrap Gaṇapati with that cloth. Having placed him face-down beneath a *nimba* tree stump and smeared him with mud, one should bury him in a heap of bell-metal dross (*kaṃsārakūṭa*). [The result is that] he becomes hated by all people.

Oṃ hrīḥ huṇḍaṇu muṇḍaṇu [amukasya] pāḍi muhi kāli karāli ghughra huṇu muṇḍaṇu rohi! Having written this with seven recitations (*saptajapta*) using *arkapuṭa* (a leaf-cup of the sun-plant), the seeds of the *kākilā* plant, and thorns, and having formed an intention toward the target (*sādhya*), one should enclose it in those thorns. Having smeared the leaf-cup with a paste of turmeric and *kūra*, one should cast it into an anthill and press it down with bricks. While reciting the mantra, one should strike it with the left foot. This results in the paralysis of the mouth (*mukhastambha*) for speakers. The root mantra is: Oṃ kaṭavikaṭa brahmarākṣasa hūṃ khaḥ loṭṭaṇapiṭṭaṇāya namaḥ.

For the purpose of overturning the authority of a single [enemy] army: *hūṃ*, overturn the army, overturn it! For the purpose of crushing it: *hūṃ*, crush the army, crush it! One should visualize him as having a black complexion and a protruding belly (*lambodara*), holding a trident in his hand, with fangs slightly bared and formidable.
Restrained and subsisting on alms-food, one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times. (23–277)
Then, upon the central circle (kaṇikā), the wise practitioner should fashion two images of the Mantrin;
he should offer oblations to Bhairava a hundred times according to the previously prescribed rite.
Thereafter, having bathed with purity and having subdued his senses, he should consume the image; then, seated in the midst of the *mavā* grass, he should perform the recitation (*japa*).
For one night, however, the wise man, free from sleep and laziness, should subsequently perform a homa sacrifice of one thousand *śyāpala* [seeds]. 23–280.
Then, once the mantra has been perfected, one should perform the rite of accomplished action;
by means of raising a banner, one may destroy an army together with its leader.
And by means of the roots, leaves, and fruits of the *unmatta* and *lāṅgalī*,
together with the incense known as *mahiṣākṣa*, one may cause even a thousand [demons] to fall.
One should saturate guggulu with the juices of śirīṣa, sarja, śālmali, and unmattaka, combined with mahāmāṃsa.
One should fumigate the person with this; it causes them to enter [the state] in an instant.
Ten thousand such signs of possession arise, and not otherwise. (23-284)
The white roots of *kokilākṣa* are not found on dark [plants];
when that flower is gathered and placed in the mouth, it is a shield against arrows. (23-285)
By holding the roots of the *kharjūra* and *tāla* trees in one's mouth, one wards off arrows;
likewise, by means of one's own fangs, *kāśmanta*, and fibers (*siphā*), one wards off swords.
The white root of Kaṇṭakārī and that which arises from Vṛhatī, as well as Kaṇṭaka and Vāraṇa, when placed in the mouth, [achieve this]. (23-287)
White-crested [grasses], vacā, and pāṭhā, when placed in the mouth, provide protection against the three arrows; so too does one who acts accordingly in worldly affairs. (23.288)
Pāṭalā, Vijayā, and Mūlā—when placed in the mouth, these three together, even if not practiced through austerity, bring about the warding off of all battle. (23-289)
Tāmraparṇī, Mayūrā, Sūryāvartā, and Aparājitā—these indeed grant success in battle; one should recite them during gambling and when going or returning.
Pāṭhā, sudarśanā, and likewise śikhaśiphāsyagā,
ward off their own respective clusters and are destroyers of poisons.
Dhvajā, Kuñcitapatrā, Mohanā, and Makhāntagā quickly ward off weapons discharged by powerful beings. (23–292)
Likewise, with his own tusk as a mace, he [pierced] even the ocean that was Karikarṇa;
and together with Kadamba, the earth-supporter [struck] Khaṅgavāraṇa.
When properly utilized, they are known to bestow longevity and health;
*gośṛṅgī*, when administered for just one month combined with ghee, [achieves this]. (23-294)
One who possesses a vajra-body, free from old age and disease, performs [this rite].
Oṃ! Homage to Khaḍgastambhanī, to Kaumārī, who dwells in the color of Hara! Descend by the truth of the three persons! Paralyze, paralyze all weapons! Svāhā!
Having bathed in purity at a solitary liṅga, one should then recite this ten thousand times.

It paralyzes all weapons. One should hold all medicinal herbs over which this mantra has been recited seven times; thereby, it paralyzes missiles. Oṃ, I shall proclaim Kalikoṇḍa; I shall proclaim Mahākalikoṇḍa. This was the intended sign revealed by Śaṅkara: "O fire, Koṇḍi, come near! O you whose crest is blazing, burn! Strike! Born from Kalikoṇḍa, i, think! O Ajjuta, together with Sahu!"

*Amge bhamāḍahi vajju vāhi vāhi hatve hatve jaṃghi jaṃghi aṃge aṃge carme carme rome rome haḍe haḍe dhari dhāriya saṃya rakṣa pahara sayaṃ vandha gaṇḍi sayantā varakṣakoṇḍajāvanacchoḍamigaṇḍi hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!* Ghaṇṭulā, torakhallī, śatāvarī, white kokilākṣa, kaṇḍavāriṇī, cavaṃbhī, mayūraśikhā, ṛbhuva, white giri-karṇikā, mogarā, vermilion (sindūra), jasmine (jātī), tāḍa, date palm (kharjūri), white vihat-paṅka, and lakṣmaṇī.

When these [substances] are used in equal proportions, they make one adamantine (*vajrin*); by wearing them as pills, they ward off parasols. Oṃ! I shall proclaim the Great Vidyā, conceived and fashioned by Mahādeva with his formless body. It is the delighter of all armies, the destroyer of all [enemies], the remover of iron, steel, and bronze; it is *aśikālā*, *īhulla*, *īkāla*, and *u-kajjala*. Homage to the Blessed One! O *Phullacaṇḍālī*, the warder-off of the strike of the *kaṇḍa* [weapon], the crusher of birds, the bender of the *kaḍitalla* [weapon], the [warder-off] of the *sella*, *savaṭṭa*, *tomara*, and *karṇi* [weapons]; O you who take away and fill, O *kaṇa-amo*, O you who spread the hood [of a serpent], the warder-off of the *vaḍipaṇa* [weapon].
Oṃ aṇi arthabhaṇi jaha hanu mantra husavu devu vaddhusaddadevehi | taṃ ha ma i bandhu dehu acchejju adhbhejju amaru a ḍa hu parihi aṃ bhairava kavaca hūṃ phaṭ svāhā || 159b g ||

Girikarṇikā, Koli, Lekhana, Sahadevī, Vṛhatī, Kṣudrā, Śarapuṅkhā, Jhiṃjharīṭaka, Sauvarcalī, Nirguṇī, Sarpākṣī, Yaṇḍaraphalā, Prahārabhañjanī, Viṣṇukrāntā, Khalvāṭī, Pāṣāṇabhedikā, Praskarī, Ṛtuvarī, Kaṃjha, Kaṇḍālī, Peṇḍirā, Vīrā, Paṇṇī, Jhaṇuvā, Indravāruṇī, Vacchaṇī, Vāṇamogarā, Jātī, Sendūra, Rakojjā, Jṛdhvī, Kaṇḍārī, Javāvettavaranellī, Kālagirikarṇikā, and Seridanti.

Vandā, dhāmaṇī, nāgolī, moreḍi, śikhā, caṇḍālī, kṛtāñjalī, ajjulahatthī, mohaṇī, varavatī, lekkhaṇī, aṭavya, sahadevī, nīlasindūra, kālasamvarī, mādaṅgī, śaṅkhiṇī, gadhāṇi, uttaravāruṇī, śvetārka, guñjā, kaṭvaḍu, vālluga, ḍavattharanī, kāmarakkhā, bhūtā, mahāyavārāhāṃ, kolluke, kallutagaru, and devadāsī—these are the medicinal herbs. Together with musta, honey, clarified butter, or milk, when administered while restrained and consecrated by the Great Vidyā-mantra, [they grant the desired results].
And thus, after half a year, Atikāya became possessed of great strength.
When a pill is placed in the mouth, one is not slain by weapons or spirits as if they were ghosts;
now I shall further describe another *jāṅgulī* [incantation] in the form of a *śarabha*.
First is the word *ari*, then the word *viparīta*;
the third should be *śavīrī*, and the fourth is *śāvatī*. (23–297)
The word *śavarī*, the syllable *huḥ*, and again [the syllable *kāra*]—these words should be preceded by the letter *mā* individually and in sequence. (23–298)
The syllable *huḥ* should be applied as before; then the illuminator (*dīpaka*) follows as the fifth. Then *aṭī*, *māmaṭī*, and finally *māmāmaṭī*. (23–299)
The syllable *puḥ* should be joined with *mā viśa*, and likewise again;
having joined *sā pannaga*, one should then join the syllable *huḥ*. (23–300)
Likewise, having joined the seventh [syllable] as "Siddhikirātā" and "Śavarī," thereafter follows that of Kumārī. (23–301)
Then, having joined this word together with the word "śavara," and having joined the auspicious word ending in the vowel *e* as "jāṅgulīye. (23-302)
Then one should give the syllable *huḥ*; this is proclaimed as the vidyā.
It is joined with the *praṇava* at the beginning and illuminated by the *svāhākāra* at the end. (23-303)
Formerly proclaimed by the Trident-bearer in the guise of a Śabara, this [mantra] consisting of seventy-four syllables was extracted as the granter of all desires. (23.304)
I shall proclaim its ritual procedure (kalpa) in brief, but not in detail.
For this [mantra], one should recite it ten thousand times for the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) in a temple of Rudra.

He raises up Kālarudra; he also increases each member of the fourfold army. Blows do not shatter his limbs. At the end of the watch, at the time of death, by sprinkling water, or with a peacock feather from the sky, or by means of an ablution, he renders the fangs of Death poisonless.
There exists no science equal to this for the purpose of all toxic operations.
For one who holds in their mouth the roots of *govālī*, *putra*, *jārīpāṭhā*, *vṛścikālī*, and *śarapuṅkhā*,
consecrated a hundred times, all the scriptures [are mastered] within the body.

The powders of these very substances—mixed with white *kokilākṣa*, *kṣaṇabhr̥ṅga*, *śikhā*, *smaṇtaka*, and *agnika*—colored red, yellow, or white, doubled in length by thread, consecrated one hundred times with the vidyā, and having inserted a *madanaphala* fruit [into them], if one wears them on any part of the body, one will not be robbed by thieves on the road;
one becomes undefeated in gambling, in royal courts, and in legal disputes;
and one becomes invulnerable to all *nāgas*.

Having placed inside a single *karañja* fruit the root of white mountain-*karṇikā*, *tama-paṇī*, and *somarājī*, each recited over one hundred times and combined with twice that amount of purified [substance], and having cast it into the mouth, one becomes victorious everywhere.

Having written [the mantra] on birch bark (*bhūrja*) with four, eight, or one parts of lac-dye mixed with red *āmikā* and *gorocanā*, using a stalk of *dūrvā* grass as the pen, and wearing it, one protects against all families of *nāgas*;
the poison of one who has been bitten does not spread, whether artificial or natural.
And in battle, thirty-two companions of his are seen striking at the enemy heroes;
and having seen them, the enemies, their pride destroyed, flee.
There is great protection and great peace.
Having taken eight unharvested *vikarṣa* flowers, one should make eight knots with a twenty-one-fold thread spun by a Brahmin girl.
Having performed seven recitations over it, one should bind it on the wrist; by means of that which is held on the hand, one becomes invulnerable to the eight families of *nāgas*.
And in battle, eight assistants are seen striking for him:
Vindhyā, Vāgeśvarī, Mūla, Cuccuphala, Mayūraśiras, Chucchundarīkarṇa, Gṛhālikā, and Samudraphena.
One should have these made into a powder in equal parts.
One should place [the powder], over which the mantra has been recited one hundred times, in pure water.

By the name of the King of Yakṣas, this powder is used for all poisons and those who have died; when smeared on the body, it causes them to rise up with a hissing sound, provided that their breath has not ceased. Now, if one wishes to make one bitten by the "Time-Biter" (Kāladaṃṣṭra) speak, one should place the letter *A* on the tip of the bitten person's tongue, the letter *U* in the middle of the tongue, and the letter *M* at its base—thus placing these three syllables upon the tongue—and then the *Praṇava* (*Oṃ*) likewise upon the tongue. Then, at the time of twilight, the Time-Biter speaks in a form that is truly ablaze.

The *karavīra* root, *jāla*, *mahāyudhā*, *girikarṇikā*, *karṇikāra*, and *gandhamākulī*: when these roots are taken in equal parts and finely ground into a paste, a woman becomes free from [the effects of] poison by its scent; all serpents perish, and poisons vanish upon her touch. Likewise, bile from a mongoose, a cat, and a *śiśu*—having combined these in equal measure and applied them to the eyes—one quickly conquers even a fanged serpent. (23–306)
If one is bitten by great serpents, one quickly becomes free from poison by using the root of the ancient *tumbinī* as well as the bulb of the *kumārī*.
Or one should administer an enema or a potion of clarified butter to one afflicted by poison;
however, if he has been bitten by great serpents, he should first become free from the poison himself. (23.308)
Having taken the root of *nāginī* and likewise *devadālī*,
one should grind them with milk and administer them as a nasal drop (*nasya*) and a drink.
When administered, it quickly removes the two types of poison; there is no doubt about this.
Drinking white Aparājitā makes one free from poison. (23–310)
Combined with clarified butter, it removes both types of poison;
likewise, *priyaṅgu* and saffron [are used] with the water of the blue lotus. (23.311)
Ground with cold water, these remove the two types of poison:
nagnikā, phaṭā, nagnā, vāgeśī, and likewise sumanā. (23.312)
One should drink this, which cures diseases that burn all the limbs;
likewise, a paste of triphalā, nimba, citraka, and kañcukī [should be used]. (23–313)
He who constantly consumes this is not afflicted by diseases;
it consists of *hayagandhā*, *haṃsapādī*, and powdered *gopadā*. (23.314)
If one should eat [these] for six months combined with ghee and *āragvadha*,
one will be freed from the fear of old age and disease, becoming radiant, strong, and possessed of a firm body.
The *tālaka* (mica) shining with the blood of *bhānuvajra* (copper), when processed for seven days,
will quickly turn white *girikarṇī* and *nāra* into a white color.
Furthermore, white glass (*kāca*) mixed with silver, once ground into powder and drunk with *hika*-milk, [achieves the same].
Gold infused with mercury and cast here into cow’s urine becomes joined with the moon-like whiteness of silver.
Alternatively, with the roots and fruits of the *guñjā*, lac, the two types of turmeric (*rajanī*),
and *mātuluṅga*, it is processed to produce excellent tin (*vaṅga*).
Thus, when pure tin has been purified with alkaline salt (*pheṇita*), heated, and sweated, these ten *palas* of tin shall become eleven *kācī*s. (23.318)
In the region, in the vessel, in the alms-food, and in the anklets and ornaments...
Having meditated upon it one hundred times by means of that, [the essence] becomes eightfold in the *vaṅga*;
it becomes free from the ten defects in the *vaṅga*, and not otherwise.

Having ground the *andhāsthi* into powder, [mix it] with *jyotiṣmatī* oil... two parts of *varṇa*, one part of *śaśāṅka*, and three parts of *manaḥśilā*. Having combined these, they should be infused with the juice of *antavāruṇī*.

One should perform this infusion twenty-one times. By means of that, how is the pouring (*niṣeka*) of the copper performed? Having done so twenty-eight times with the juice of *uttaravāruṇī*, it becomes free from blackness (*kālikā*).
Having combined three parts of this copper (*aśulva*), four parts of iron (*ravibhāṣa*), and one part of gold, one should melt them; from that, it becomes *jātarūpa* (gold).
[The metals] are *rasalāṅgalī*, *kāntā*, *ṛṣikā*, and *antiphalā*;
their collection follows the sequence of one, two, three, four, eight, and five. (23–321)
Two parts of ghee and one part of honey should all be ground together;
having made thirty pills, one should consume them day by day. (23-322)
Moving and eating according to his own will, he becomes young again within one month;
[the measurement] from the tip of the thumb to the wrist is a *varaṇa*, and that of a *guñjā* is half of that. || 23-323 ||
It decreases and increases according to the size of the fangs;
one should crush [the powder] with an amount equal to the iron-fillet and [administer it] with the water of the three myrobalans (triphalā). 23-324.
Through the practice of liquefaction for six months, one may live as long as the moon and stars;
whether external or internal, one should not conceive of [the distinction] by means of time.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, concerning the section on the Yoga of the Pramada, in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, a great tantra within the Bhairava stream belonging to the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), measuring seventy million verses. 23.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, this supreme knowledge has been told [to me];
yet even now, O Master, there remains a doubt regarding the certainty of the knowledge of time."
Bhairava said:

O beloved, the Kalpa is to be understood as being of two kinds: the solar and the supreme spiritual (adhyātmika); [the former] consists of the days of the week, lunar days, constellations, along with their conjunctions and karaṇas.
Ī O YA CA? When it is SYĀYĀ? the supreme yantra is in the south;
[it is used for] the eclipse of the moon and sun, as well as the ascendant and so forth, according to the seasons. (24-3)
By means of the fortnights, months, times, and so forth, as well as the openings of the mouth and other cavities,
it is situated in the center of the navel, below the navel at the penis, and above the navel.
Emerging from that today, O Dear One, they spread downwards, upwards, and across;
there, ten principal channels are situated like a wheel. (24.5)
Seventy-two thousand channels have emerged from the navel;
others have issued forth again and again from those, and from them yet again. (24.6)
As many as there are millions of pores on the skin, so many channels are said to exist;
just as the leaf of a Palāśa tree is pervaded on all sides by its fibers.
The body of all living beings is likewise pervaded by channels; they are always filled with vital air and laden with the power of the Self. (24.8)
O fair-faced one, the distinction of names arises from the differentiation of separate forms, from the differentiation of the winds, and from the differentiation of modes of conduct. 24.9
The divisions of the channels and the vital airs are to be known by the thousands;
yet, O fair-faced one, ten principal channels have been declared. (24.10)
Among those [channels], O Lord of Gods, the winds that are situated therein have their designations and functions previously described. (24.11)
O beloved, the winds and the channels are situated like a wheel; O fair-faced one, through the movement of the wind, there is accomplishment as well as sacrifice.
These ten principal channels are said to carry the vital breath; however, O Goddess, another triad of channels is proclaimed as superior. (24.13)
The two [channels] consisting of bindu and nāda are situated in the middle; they are remembered as being of the nature of Śakti.
These are declared to be in the heart-cakra, bringing benefit to practitioners. (24.14)
The vital breath indeed moves within them according to the division of day and night;
I shall explain that to you clearly, through its detailed classification. (24.15)
Drawn together by the power of the Lord, these three—wind, vital breath, and the self—reside within one another; indeed, they move everywhere inseparably.
Since one should cause [the breath] to reach upward from below and flow through all the channels,
the forms of the phonemes are manifold through the various distinctions of their functional designations.
Seventy-two thousand are born from the ten, O beloved; and in ten million ways, O lady of excellent hips, they are established as that one.

The vital breath (prāṇa) consists of the out-breath and the in-breath; because it constantly fills [the body] in relation to exhalation and inhalation, it is therefore proclaimed as "prāṇa. || 24-19 ||
I shall now describe to you the movement of day and night within the vital breath (prāṇa). Its rising occurs within sixteen breaths, as was previously stated by me. (24.20)
The *telava*s are proclaimed to consist of exactly external time;
by four of those, O Goddess of Gods, one *prāṇa-yāma* is prescribed. (24–21)
O Goddess, four of those watches constitute a day;
a night is to be known as consisting of four [such watches], and thus a full day and night consists of eight.
In the auspicious Dharma, the *haṃsa* is indeed the sun, endowed with the splendor of the *haṃsa*;
the Self (*ātman*) is said to be the *haṃsa*, and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is fully possessed of the *haṃsa*. (24.23)
From the arising of that [time], at what time does the arising of the bodies of the planets occur?
Indeed, the lines, the zodiac signs, the stars, and likewise the degrees—[all arise from it]. (24.24)
O lady of virtuous vows, these two arise within the vital breath (prāṇa) by means of day and night;
I shall now describe to you the division of that very arising of day and night.
O Dear One, that which flows from above the heart down to below the throat, minus one finger-breadth, is known as the first watch (prahara). (24–26)
But the second [junction] is to be known as occurring at midday above the middle of the palate;
indeed, the fire-oblation, recitation, and meditation performed there become bestowers of liberation. (24–27)
O lady of excellent vows, O woman of beautiful complexion, when [the breath] has reached two finger-breadths above the tip of the nose, it indeed becomes the third watch.
At the end of Śakti, the fourth watch is proclaimed as the day;
and at the end of the fourth [watch], O Goddess of Gods, that sun of the vital breath sets.
Then, O Dear One, the twilight of sunset lasts for half a *truṭi*;
having lingered at that time, it proceeds downward once again. (24–30)
And that night, O Goddess, is established at the rising of the moon;
likewise, she moves through the watches of the night according to the previously mentioned sequence. (24–31)
Furthermore, it is ordained that he remains in the palate for half a night;
likewise, when he reaches the heart-lotus, it is the time of dawn.
O lady of excellent hips, the morning twilight does not occur for half of that duration;
from that point, the rising of the sun takes place once again. (24–33)
By means of the sequential yoga as before, they always move within the auspicious [state]:
the sun moves during the day, while the moon moves in the stream.
Thus, these two, the moon and the sun, have been described by me to you;
the planets beginning with Mars likewise move in their respective divisions.
O beloved, these two indeed rise at every watch;
whichever deity has the specific time and day, that one shall move for two watches.
Rāhu moves through the Moon, while Ketu moves through the Sun;
Śani and Kulika are likewise known as the rising of the planets.
Those who are the planets (grahas), their respective portions indeed constitute the eight world-protectors (lokapālas);
and those eight forms are the eight lords of the group of eyes.
And those fifty Rudras, as well as the eight lords of the [five] groups of eight, beginning with Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin—this is the group of eight Vidyeśvaras. (24–39)
Likewise, the principles (tattvas) beginning with Sakula are situated as those that are even higher;
and all those eight Bhairavas previously mentioned are established within them all.
Presiding over the planets and other celestial bodies, they cause the rising of all things;
together with the zodiac signs and constellations, they indeed rise day and night.
If the rising occurs at midday and at the end of the second night, there the practitioners shall obtain their desired fruit in this world. (24.42)
Thus have I explained to you the division of day and night;
now I shall explain to you the fortnights, months, and years.
Within the internal [body], one external *kalā* is established per day and night; by means of a month, there is indeed no internal [portion], and only one external *kalā* remains. (24.44)
O woman of excellent complexion, thirty such days constitute a month;
and with twelve such months, there is one external ghaṭikā.
One hundred and sixty parts of day and night constitute what is known as a year externally, consisting indeed of *ghaṭikās*.
They say that sixty *ghaṭikās* constitute a day and night externally;
by means of that same internal movement, sixty years are traditionally reckoned.
Furthermore, O fair-faced one, I shall now tell you the number of breaths: twenty-one thousand and six hundred. (24.48)
By means of an external day and night, within the internal [body] of the Lord of the Gods, the number of breaths is fully described; that must be known by the practitioner. (24.49)
When the vital breath (prāṇa) is dissolved into the Haṃsa, the practitioner becomes a knower of the supreme reality;
this is declared to be his recitation (japa), which brings about the fruits of both spiritual perfection (siddhi) and liberation (mukti).

O virtuous lady, as long as [the breath] flows downward, there is accomplishment (siddhi) when it has reached the heart-lotus; and liberation occurs when it moves upward into the supreme reality (paratattva).
The eye cast upon this [object] falls away elsewhere;
likewise, O Lord, this vital breath always proceeds without a controller. (24.52)
Therefore, no one can utter it, nor indeed can anyone strike it;
for the *haṃsa* residing in the chest of living beings breathes by itself. (24.53)
This enumeration of months and years has been declared to you;
now listen as I describe the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
O beautiful goddess, that which is called a day and night within this vital breath— by means of two such fortnights, I shall now describe a month to you.
But above that, rest is proclaimed;
in the middle, fifteen lunar days (tithis) are said to be celebrated. (24–56)
When the lotus rises, the heart-lotus [opens]; half of that time constitutes the day.
And when it moves during the second half of the *truṭi*, it becomes night. (24.57)
The zodiacal signs, planets, and lunar mansions rise in their proper sequence during this very day and night, O fair-faced one, just as before. (24.58)
In this manner, fifteen *truṭis* constitute one *pakṣa*.
When there is a decrease in the lunar day (*tithi*), it should be known as a debt; when there is an increase, it becomes wealth. (24–59)
The Kāśa wind becomes a debt, and exhalation is said to be wealth;
through the upward movement during the dark fortnight, there occurs the withdrawal (saṃhāra) of the two fortnights.
Indeed, by performing cruel deeds, one may attain success;
however, O lady of excellent vows, auspicious deeds do not lead to success through Kṛṣṇa.
O fair-faced one, that which is designated as a *truṭi* consisting of twenty breaths is to be known as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) in the dark fortnight. (24.62)
In the upper portion of the middle of Śakti, that which is proclaimed as half a *truṭi* should be known as the junction of the two fortnights (*pakṣasaṃdhi*),
which is the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) at the midpoint of the first day of the lunar phase (*pratipad*).
Indeed, at that time, by the cutting of the lunar day (tithi), there occurs an eclipse of the sun;
O Goddess, the lunar disc then appears within the solar disc.
In that interval, O fair-faced one, Rāhu appears for the sake of the nectar;
the Moon pours forth the nectar, and Rāhu swallows it.
Having drunk that, he abandons the physical body; then he is called "liberated.
This is indeed what is designated as a solar eclipse in the world. (24.66)
When Rāhu, the Sun, and the Moon— these three planets—
are seen together in conjunction, that shall be a great eclipse.
At that time, it shall become the most meritorious of all places for all people;
bathing there, as well as meditation, worship, fire-offerings, recitation, and so forth [yield great fruit]. (24.68)

O Goddess, whatever is performed by practitioners shall yield infinite fruit; and that very [fruit] becomes twice as great, having abandoned the deficiency of the dark fortnight for the bright fortnight. || 24-69 ||
From the womb, Śakti flows downward; from that, creation arises, and from it, growth is produced.
Having commenced the ritual actions (tantra), one performs auspicious deeds leading to prosperity. (24.70)
For one who is devoted solely to meditation, these are accomplished; there is no doubt in this matter.
When the *prāṇahaṃsa* has reached the bottom, that is the first *tuṭi*. (24.71)
The first half of the day is declared to be [the breath], while the other half of a *tuṭi* is at night; so too are the zodiac signs, planets, constellations, yogas, and *karaṇas*. (24.72)
Arising day and night through the sequential yoga as before, that first lunar day (pratipad) should be understood as consisting of a single digit of the moon and the asterism. (24.73)
The second [tuṭi] increases by the second [unit] in due order;
and thus, beginning with the lunar days (tithis), it continues until the fifteenth tuṭi.
That lunar day should indeed be known as the full moon (paurṇamāsī) by the practitioner;
there, worship, recitation, and fire-offerings shall become complete and fruitful. (24–75)
And when that moon becomes full, O moon-eyed one, that which is its half-of-a-half *tuṭi* is known as the junction (*saṃdhyā*) of the fortnight. (24.76)
Its half is the full twilight (pūrṇasaṃdhyā), situated above the first lunar day (pratipad).
In the lotus of the heart, between the two twilights, there occurs the eclipse of the Moon.
In this world, the eclipse of the moon occurs even without the sun;
and therein there is great merit through meditation, fire-offerings, recitation, and other such practices. (24.78)
O Goddess of the gods, during both lunar and solar eclipses,
these two bestow various accomplishments upon the diligent practitioner.
And I shall further explain liberation, which arises from the complete transcendence of the two pairs [of opposites], by abandoning both sides through the previously mentioned method. (24.80)
They arise while remaining eternally supported by the supreme transformation;
having abandoned everything below, one should establish the meditation and apply it. (24.81)
For him there is liberation, of this there is no doubt, but never for others;
however, for all embodied beings, there is a seizing [of the soul] during both lunar phases.
Thus has this been fully explained, O fair-faced one, up to the end of life; now the arising of the year from within this very day and night is being told.
The seats of the Rāśis are situated from the heart-lotus up to the end of the *ūrdhvaśakti*;
each one extends for six finger-breadths, from the heart-lotus as far as the *śakti*.
For in each finger-breadth, five lunar days (tithis) are established; one should designate the first half of that [finger] as the day and the latter half as the night. (24.85)
Sixty-five lunar days constitute thirty full days and nights;
thirty such days and nights are said to form a month consisting of two fortnights.
For this is the rising of the zodiac signs as the vital breath moves upward and downward;
the rising from the heart is known as the transit (saṃkrānti) in Capricorn.
Having abandoned six finger-breadths below, it again enters Aquarius;
having abandoned two finger-breadths above the throat, it again enters Pisces.
Having abandoned [the breath] as far as the palate above the throat, one should cause it to enter the ram;
the transition reaches as far as the end of the nose, which is exactly six finger-breadths.
This equinoctial transit is established as occurring in the north.
Recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and meditation bring about great prosperity;
yet, having abandoned the tip of the nose, the swan of the vital breath moves toward the bull.
Having abandoned six finger-breadths, she should again transition into the *mithuna* (the pair);
remaining in the *mithuna*, she stays on the path until the end of the *śakti*.
O virtuous one, beginning from Capricorn (Makara) up to Gemini (Mithuna),
this is indeed the northern course (uttarāyaṇa), which is devoid of worldly accomplishments (aihikī-siddhi).
Bathing, meditation, as well as giving, worship, fire-offerings, recitation, and so forth—
whatever is performed with the *putrajīva* seeds and other such materials becomes multiplied many thousands of times.
In this world one attains [merit], and in the next world it stands by one;
indeed, the days increase there from Capricorn until Gemini. (24.95)
At that time, he should withdraw the vital energy from this world of moving and non-moving beings;
having drawn it in with his rays, the Haṃsa should cause it to abide within the womb.
And that ancient embryo, which was taken up in manifold forms beginning with the crab and so forth—all of that rains down once again. (24.97)
Therefore, beginning from the sign of Capricorn, one who performs fire-offerings, meditation, recitation, and so forth for the sake of the next world shall obtain its infinite fruit. (24.98)
Furthermore, for the sake of the path of conduct, one should observe the vow of mantra-grasping;
one should begin everything for the purpose of attaining mantra-siddhi starting from the month of Mīna.

Thus, the practices of the vows, impelled by the days according to the [proper] time, are ignited by the awakening to that which is to be known, and they bring about the accomplishment of both siddhi and liberation. (24.100)
Within the self, its nature being sound and form, it delights in tasting the six flavors;
ignited by the awakening of the *haṃsa*, it rests upon the fish in the throat. (24.101)
Since the nature of the perception of sound would not be clear therein, the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) for one who begins the recitation (*japa*) starts from that point. (24.102)
O Goddess of gods, as long as the couple remains so, success (siddhi) arises;
for the Haṃsa, abiding in the power of the Bindu, is indeed downward-facing at the gateway of success.
From Cancer until the end of Libra, it rains within the cavity of the palate;
here [is] the end of the Kaṭha [tradition]. Thereafter, it proceeds from the heart-lotus throughout the entire body.

Therefore, for the sake of attaining one's own goal and for the sake of nourishment, one should practice during the period born of the sun’s southern course (dakṣiṇāyana), because from that [practice] the sixty-fold [result] arises. || 24-105 ||
O Dear One, when the calf rises below the Śakti, it enters Cancer;
then, having passed six finger-breadths, it indeed enters Leo again. (24.106)
When six finger-breadths have been left behind at the transition into the female [channel],
and when [the breath] has indeed reached the tip of the nose and is abandoned at the end of the palate, that is the equinox (viṣuva).
The transition into Libra is indeed said to be the southern equinox;
whatever practice is performed there yields the fulfillment of desires both in this world and the next.
One should likewise undertake the rites for conquering death, as well as those for peace and nourishment;
for food consisting of the six flavors nourishes the body from the throat downwards. (24.109)
Having left six finger-breadths [above], it proceeds again in Scorpio;
having left three finger-breadths above the throat and four finger-breadths below the throat.
Having abandoned Scorpio, the transition into Sagittarius is said to occur;
situated six finger-breadths below, it moves within the heart.
Having moved within the heart-lotus, the *haṃsa* indeed rises with upward force;
during the transits at Capricorn and the other signs, it always enters the twelfth [house].

By this very sequence mentioned above, for embodied beings, there arises—through the upward-moving breaths—the inferior, middling, and superior attainments pertaining to this world and the next. (24.113)
This is declared to be the method for attaining bliss;
moreover, at the end of the two solstitial steps, they always abide in the state beyond mind (unmanī).
Staying there, one shall attain the perfection of liberation as described through recitation and meditation;
having gone to liberation, one shall not return—such is the vow of Bhairava.
In this very rising, hear further about the arising of twelve years;
for it is from this that the arising of mantras occurs within the year beginning with Caitra. (24.116)
Therefore, the practitioner of the primary [mantra] should perform the mantra-sādhana;
it should be understood as lasting twelve years, beginning with the month of Caitra, O fair-faced one. (24.117)

I shall describe its characteristics according to their divisions within this vital breath (prāṇa), as well as that which is stated regarding the year of the breath in the Ambara [Tantra], O fair-faced one. (24.118)
One should divide that which is called a day and night by twelve;
indeed, these twelve days and nights constitute one year.
In twelve days there are five seasons; in twelve years, one season occurs. Having doubled that very [period], time is thus established. (24.120)
By three [transits] there is an ayana; by six, a year.
Twelve transits are proclaimed to constitute a year.
In the arising of twelve years, those years are proclaimed to be within the vital breath (prāṇa).
Now, learn from me their number as days and nights within those twelve years. (24.122)
O Goddess, four thousand and thirty-two [breaths] more than twenty [thousand]—this arising of twelve years has been described by me in this vital breath (prāṇa). (24.123)
The arising of the sixty-year cycle occurs right here; furthermore, O fair-faced one, I shall explain them to you:
those beginning with Ānanda are to be known as the sixty years. (24.124)
O Goddess, one should worship the three mantras beginning with Svānanda;
therefore, O Goddess, bliss is always produced together with the mantra. (24.125)
And those very [channels], O beautiful goddess, move through the single vital breath as it travels upward and downward by way of their respective portions; thus I shall explain them to you.
In twelve years, however, the days and nights are fivefold;
indeed, the days and nights in sixty years are proclaimed to be exactly five.
And those [months], when multiplied by six, are proclaimed as one month;
and when multiplied by twelve, that end is indeed ordained as a year. (24.128)
This measurement is proclaimed to be fifty-one finger-breadths;
and by six finger-breadths, those [planets] rise during the five-year periods within the sixty-year cycle.
Indeed, from the heart-lotus up to the power (śakti), thirty years arise;
likewise, from below the power down to the heart-lotus, there is again an emergence of thirty [years]. (24.130)
I shall state the number of days and nights in a sixty-year period: twenty-one thousand six hundred and one. (24.131)

O fair-faced one, I have explained to you that within a single breath, sixty years are reckoned as the emergence of sixty years, with each year consisting of a countable number of days and nights. (24.132)
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, at the end of a fortnight, a month, a solstice, or a year, and after twelve years or sixty years, O fair-faced one. (24.133)
Whatever has been performed through bathing, giving, sacrifice, worship, fire-offerings, recitation, meditation, yoga, and austerity, by means of external time; || 24-134 ||

O lady of beautiful hips, when this has been spoken, whatever great fruit one obtains, and even the movement of the vital breath as the *haṃsa*, shall come to pass once that is known within this single [reality]. (24.135)
The movement [of the breath] becomes clearly self-evident through the recitation of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the channel;
or else, O Goddess, it is augmented by the recitation of the *prakṛti*. (24.136)
Having understood the yoga of the mantra-born [elements], the practitioner of mantra shall attain omniscience.
Furthermore, I shall explain again the division of the three channels (nāḍīs) in detail. (24.137)

O lady of virtuous vows, just as that *haṃsa* moves through this world of the moving and the unmoving during the southern and northern solstices and at the equinoxes, [so does the soul move]. (24.138)
Abiding within in the form of Time, he fashions the universe through his creative powers (kalās);
supported by the three channels, he is established in the three paths.
Pervaded by the three qualities (guṇas), situated in the three states, overcome by the six causes, and presided over by the three powers (śaktis). || 24.140 ||
Pierced by will, knowledge, and action, situated in the midst of the moon, sun, and fire;
the channel in the right nostril is indeed known as Piṅgalā. (24.141)
The *iḍā* is indeed situated on the left, while the *suṣumṇā* stands in the middle;
the path of the gods (*devamārga*) is on the right, and likewise the path of the ancestors (*pitṛmārga*) is on the left.
Having gone there to the middle path of Śiva, one is not born again;
the sattva-guna resides in the right [eye] while one is awake, and the rajas-guṇa resides in the left while one is dreaming. (24.143)
In the middle, Tamas should be known as that which provides the state of Suṣumṇā;
Brahmā is the Lord situated on the right, while Viṣṇu and Sadāśiva are on the left.
In the center is declared Rudraśiva, the supreme Śiva who transcends all;
Jyeṣṭhā and Jñātṛ are situated in the south, while Kriyā and Vāmā are likewise in the north.
The fierce will is situated in the center as the supreme and yet supreme-non-supreme power (parāparā);
the sun blazes on the right, while the moon shines on the left.
The Purifier (Pāvaka) is indeed the cooker, the illuminator, and the mediator;
he shall burn away all sins arising from qualities since beginningless time.
One should reveal the stainless reality to another through one's own capacity;
for all the zodiacal signs and planets [arise] from the conjunction of the lunar mansions.
All follow the paths of the moon and sun in successive order;
O beloved, even all those [planets], including the moon and the sun, experience them in turn. (24.149)
