These indeed exist as the essence of the moon and the sun, established upon the three paths:
the sun heats, while the moon sheds the nectar of immortality.
From that [source], which consists of the moon and the sun, arises this world of moving and stationary beings;
the solar path is the southern route, known as the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa).
That which is called the left is indeed Soma, wherein lies the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana);
the equinox (viṣuva), consisting of both Soma and Sūrya, issues forth from the two nostrils.
There are five transits in the north and five indeed in the southward course;
the two equinoctial transits are situated between the southern and northern courses.
The southern path belonging to Śauri grants success in the rite of sorcery (abhicāra); the northern path, which nourishes with nectar, brings nourishment and bestows peace. (24.154)
When the sun moves from the south to the north, and from the north to the south, those are respectively the southern and northern transits (saṃkrānti), and they are defined in this manner. ||155||
When there is a transition into the southern channel, it moves to the north;
as long as it remains there, it flows toward the north for half [the duration].
That is declared to be the equinox; and in the northern course, it is the northern [solstice].
O fair-faced one, its sequence in the southern [course] is as follows.
When it flows there for half a *yāma*, it indeed flows for half [a day] in the south;
that much, O beloved, is the southern equinox born of the southern solstice.

In that state, worship, recitation, fire-offerings, and sacrifice become bestowers of liberation. Through the yoga of meditation during initiation, one established therein indeed liberates the guru. (24.159)
O fair-faced one, in the internal sense, there are twenty-four transits during a day and night; thus the *haṃsa* of the vital breath undergoes these transitions. (24.160)
Twelve [muhūrtas] are said to be in the forenoon, and twelve are recorded in the night; indeed, there is one equinox (viṣuva) in the morning and a second at midday.
The third occurs in the afternoon, and the fourth at midnight;
O lady of virtuous vows, these four equinoxes (viṣuva) are said to occur within a single day and night.
The twenty-four transits are by nature of an equal constituent;
the *haṃsa* always carries nine hundred [breaths] in each one. (24.163)
This is declared to be the measure; when it flows otherwise, then it indicates both what is desired and what is undesired.
Therefore, for the sake of oneself or for the sake of others, the yogi should perform this examination when the first rising of the sun has arrived, O lady of beautiful countenance. (24.165)
Firmly restraining the mind and remaining steady in the yogic posture, the wise yogi should investigate life and death with reference to that [breath]. (24.166)
O beloved, remembering the Self-born one who dwells within the *suṣumṇā* of the vital breaths,
one should then remain perfectly serene, with the mind focused solely on the vital breath.
It increases by increments of five, starting from five up to twenty-five;
thereafter, it increases by one for each successive day.
O Goddess, as for the unsurpassed tenfold set multiplied by three, they worship the two feet of the qualities with the number of months [twelve] and one [thirteen]. (24.169)
In the eastern direction, there are three nights and two days for the Moon;
one should understand that the commencement occurs during the time of the Sun according to the aforementioned count. (24.170)
O virtuous lady, when the nāḍī flows for five days during the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana), one's lifespan should then be known to be three years. (24.171)
Two [units] are to be known by ten, and a year is traditionally reckoned by three and five;
likewise, twenty months constitute the number six (rasa), O fair-faced one. (24.172)
For twenty-five days, O Goddess, he lives by means of the measure of the qualities;
beyond this, the number of months and days is considered to be two and one [three]. (24.173)
The lunar day (tithi), the nāḍīs, the arrows (five), as well as the feet of time (four) and the moon (one)—
O Mistress of the Gods, thus is the number of breaths known through this sequence.
O fair-faced one, those sixteen days that have been mentioned in the interval are to be subtracted in their respective order, sequentially, from seventy-two.
Having understood the thirty-sixth, the eighteenth, and the tenth [fingers], O lady of excellent limbs, one should remove them gradually, each by nine [joints] in due order.
But whatever remains as the final remainder should be known as the measure of life in terms of the number of days within the wheel consisting of time, O beloved. (24.177)
O virtuous lady, when the arrays [of days] amount to six by a single utterance,
O beloved, three years multiplied by three hundred and sixty [days] should be calculated.
I shall now state, in brief, the measure of the remaining portion:
two years are prescribed, and the months are equal in number to Rudra (eleven). (24.179)
The measure of fifteen days has been declared to you;
when the wind blows on the seventh day after abandoning [the body], [it is auspicious]. (24.180)
O beloved, two years are declared for the common [period] in the tenth;
that life-span is thus described, and after that comes the eighth.
His lifespan is two years and ten months;
however, O Goddess, he does not live for two years unless he has been married for that many days.
Furthermore, for those who know the measure of time, eight months is the duration;
O Goddess, with ten days [remaining], he lives for two years. (24.183)
When the channel (nāḍī) flows for exactly eleven days, it is declared to be one year, with months numbering according to Rudra (eleven). [118b] 24.184.
Twenty days have been declared, O Supreme Goddess;
by the flow of twelve such days, one year is proclaimed. (24.185)
O beautiful goddess, when ten months— numbered as eleven by Rudra—
and ten days have passed, O goddess, [the breath] flows through the southern path for thirteen days.
O beloved, he shall live for one year and ten months;
O sinless one, twenty days are also said to be proclaimed by you. (24.187)
The conduct of days is likewise defined by the number fourteen (two times seven),
while that of those with a lifespan of years is indicated by the number nine months.
The measure of his life is indeed ten days;
by the movement of three and five days, he lives for one year—of this there is no doubt. (24.189)
O Supreme Goddess, by the movement of two sets of eight days,
life is measured according to the Rudra count by means of months.
I have stated that the measure [of life] is twenty-five days when the wind flows for exactly seventeen days. (24.191)
At that time, O beloved, its duration is eleven days and twenty days in total; this has been declared without doubt.
O beloved, through the movement of ten and eight days, there are eleven months.
The number of days is ten; this is what has been declared by those who know the [proper] time.
O Supreme Goddess, when twenty minus one days remain in the course [of life], the lifespan there is declared to be ten months; of this there is no doubt.
Twenty days are declared for those who worship the Kālacakra;
when twenty [days] have passed, O Goddess, their life is gone after six months. (24.195)
O Goddess, the Sun flows for twenty-one days;
it declares five months and twenty-seven days. (24.196)
Thirty ghaṭikās are declared to be the measure [of a day]; and when twenty-two pādas are displaced, one has reached the end of life within five months. (24.197)
O Goddess, twenty-five days have been declared for you;
when the triad of twenty flows without weariness, O Goddess. (24.198)
O beloved, life shall last for five months and twenty days;
indeed, O beloved, it shall flow for twenty-four days and one [month]. 24.199b–c.
If five months and ten days have passed here, he lives for twenty-five more days;
having spent three months [in this state], he lives on.
Above this, what was previously described in brief regarding the Kālacakra—O fair-faced one, those sixteen days that were mentioned in the interval [should be understood]. (24.201)
Having subtracted those [values] according to the sequence of parts, that result is made manifest;
the Kālacakra is revealed for the awakening of those of dull intellect. (24.202)
Now, O fair-faced one, I shall explain another [method of] knowledge of time; listen to this, which is easy to understand, for the sake of awakening those of dull intellect. (24.203)
O lady of excellent vows, by means of a single day and night, the yogi lives for one year;
and by means of two days and nights, he shall live for two years.
Three years [are attained] by three [days], and four years by four;
five years by five days, and six years indeed by six [days]. (24.205)
By seven [repetitions], for seven years; by eight, for eight years;
by nine, for nine years; and by ten, for ten years.
O Goddess, O beloved, by eleven days [of practice], one lives for eleven years;
by twelve days, the yogin lives for twelve years. (24.207)
By a flow lasting seven watches, one lives for six months;
by a flow lasting six watches, one lives for three months. (24.208)
For one whose lifespan is one and a half months, [the breath] flows for five watches;
O Goddess, with four watches, he lives for one month. (24.209)
If it flows for three watches, one lives for half a month;
he whose [wind] flows for two watches lives for eight days. (24.210)
If one should carry [the breath] for one watch, one may live for four watches;
if one carries it for half a watch, he shall live for two watches. (24.211)

Immediate death shall come to him for whom the *haṃsa* moves along three paths—namely, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), time, and the Lord (*īśvara*)—starting from which it is described as departing. (24.212)

O lady of virtuous vows, having carefully observed the month, fortnight, day, and weekday starting from that very day, the determination [of the auspicious time] shall be made at that moment with great effort. (24.213)
Now learn from me the knowledge of death even for one who is not disciplined regarding the vital breath;
furthermore, O beautiful one, I shall declare to you another supreme secret.
One should [visualize] the Puruṣa at the dvādaśānta, at a distance of twelve finger-breadths,
resembling pure crystal and endowed with all limbs.
With eyes closed and a joyful soul, while recollecting the heart-mantra, when one sees [the mantra] without a head, then death is certain; of this there is no doubt. (24.216)
Within six months, O Goddess of Gods, there is no need for deliberation here;
when one sees [the deity] as lacking eyes, then eye disease shall arise. (24.217)
One should [perform the rite] for an ear-disease on the ear; likewise on the head for one lacking a nose;
similarly on the hand for one lacking a hand, and on the two feet for one lacking a foot. (24.218)
Whatever limb one should see [as affected], one should diagnose that specific disease;
when one sees it as smoke-colored, one should diagnose a major disease. || 24-219 ||
If it dances, one should know there will be fever; if it cries out, it portends a quarrel;
and if it laughs, there will likewise be gain within twenty-one days.
Thus, O lady of excellent hips, the fruit that takes various forms through the excellence of meditation is not recognized by practitioners who are devoid of virya.
Now I shall fully describe the person who is the very form of Time,
by knowing whom the practitioner of mantra discerns the fruit or lack of fruit of both auspicious and inauspicious results.
Having gone to a secluded place, the practitioner, having become pure, should remain with a one-pointed mind, the yogi, contemplating reality according to its true nature. (24.223)
Having fixed the gaze upon the heart and bound the *mudrā* called *Jvālinī*,
the wise man, with eyes closed, should then behold the water.
There a person is seen, with a luster like black collyrium;
above his head stands a drop (bindu) with a luster equal to green vitriol (haritāla). (24.225)
There will be an agitation of the bile (pitta) for him, and fever itself arises; there shall be a burning sensation, the affliction of thirst, and great pain. || 24-226 ||
Then, a drop situated in the mouth, possessing a luster like lac-dye, becomes a terrible flow of *rajas*, or else it appears as a vessel for weapons. (24.227)
Having beheld that very point, resembling a circle of lightning, located in the place of the heart according to the prescribed method, one should not experience any fear of the remainder.
Fire, heat, civil unrest, and loss of wealth arise;
such a color is perceived when [the sun] has both risen and set. (24.229)
Then one should issue the command and apply the ritual procedure;
one should perform a rite of pacification here and pour forth a stream of milk.
When, in the secret place, one sees a drop with the luster of a blue lotus petal, appearing externally as if of a different color, one should recognize that danger is present here. (24.231)
One should recognize this as a battle between kings and predict the ruin of the kingdom;
famine shall be seen here, and living beings will perish from hunger. (24.232)
When a brownish-tawny drop is seen on the foot, one should know there is danger from thieves and loss of wealth occurs. (24.233)
People would go to other lands that are mutually hostile; they would be seized by misfortune, and indeed unrighteousness would arise. (24.234)
And when such a multitude has come before one's eyes,
this very person stands right before the eyes, his body truly armored with reality.
One should diligently provide instruction out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds;
this accomplishes all goals and is proclaimed as the "piercing of the hundred thousand" (lakṣabhedah). || 24.236 ||
Thus, O auspicious one, by means of this sequential analysis, provide a prediction—whether auspicious or inauspicious, yet irreproachable—for yourself or for another. (24.237)
Now I shall fully explain the signs of death; listen to me.
One should recognize the imminent death of oneself or another. (24.238)
Having thus deposited [the mantras] within oneself as before, one should meditate upon this divine reality, which possesses a radiance equal to the rising sun. (24.239)
The wise one should discern the shadow-form of both himself and another; whether in water or on land, he should observe the target. (24.240)
Having seen a black lion-like form, he dies within a year;
however, if it is blazing like fire, he certainly dies within six months.
If a black and yellow deer is seen situated in the middle of the constellation Śatabhiṣaj,
the practitioner who contemplates reality will die within three months.
O lady of excellent vows, it has been declared by you that when another smoke-colored [shadow] is seen within the center of the shadow, one dies after two months.
O Goddess, when a peacock that is red and yellow appears in one's shadow, death will occur within a single month; this is the truth, the truth, endowed with certainty. || 24.244 ||
O Gaurī, when one sees a blue pigeon situated in the midst of a shadow,
having observed this great portent, one should predict death within six months.
When one sees [a shadow] resembling a dark blue cloud in one's own reflection, the person will die within ten days; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
O Goddess, O lady of excellent hips, having seen a crow with a golden luster situated in the midst of one's shadow, death shall occur within five days.
When one sees a crow within one's shadow possessing a luster like yellow orpiment, death is ordained for him within three nights. (24.248)
O auspicious lady, having seen a cat, tawny like a monkey, situated within one's shadow,
his death is ordained within two nights.
O beloved, when one sees a lizard resembling vermilion, death shall occur within a single day; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (24-250)
He who does not see his own shadow at dawn when the sun has risen will meet death within exactly one year; so too for one on a Saturday or the seventh lunar day.
If death occurs after midnight during the auspicious bright fortnight conjoined with the Hasta nakṣatra,
one perishes in the state of *sannipāta*.
O beloved, if one does not see one's own reflection in ghee, in a mirror, in oil, or in the sky during the night on a Wednesday under the constellation Rohiṇī at that specific time,
then in the eleventh month he shall indeed die; of this there is no doubt.
And on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, under the Uttarā constellation.
O beloved, when half a watch has passed,
the king departs for the great tree known as Śleṣmāntaka, which is highly authoritative among the trees of the axle.
He who sees at the end of a dream a thick mass of spirits and ghosts shall live for nine months; in the month of Āṣāḍha, he shall abandon his life.
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight, under the asterism Anurādhā on a Tuesday,
within half a day and two watches, one perishes through blood-related disorders.
If one sees one's own arm as thin, short, or double its size,
and all things appear inverted, such a person lives for eight months.
On the night of the full moon of the month of Jyeṣṭha, during the first half of a Friday at the time of Pradoṣa,
those who remain awake shall die afflicted by cholera.
When Khaṇḍapāda appears either in front or behind,
he lives for seven months amidst dust, mud, and cow-dung.
At midnight on the third lunar day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika,
when the moon is in the Mūla asterism and it is a Sunday, one's eye-sight perishes.
If a dove, a crow, or a vulture alights upon one's head, death occurs within six months; this is declared to be *kālavelā*.
If the second lunar day of the full moon in Caitra falls on a Monday during the Citrā asterism, his life comes to an end through the stroke of a weapon; that is the limit of his existence.
When one of perverted mind sees [the deceased] as hideous and black in form, being devoured by dogs with their feet pointing upward and faces turned downward; || 24-264 ||
Mounted upon a donkey, a camel, or a buffalo, he lives for five months on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
under the asterism Āśleṣā, on a Tuesday.
One bitten by a snake dies when midnight has indeed arrived;
moreover, one sees lightning in the clear, cloudless, and pure southern sky.
He lives for a night, or for as long as a rainbow remains, or for four months;
or on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, he becomes Vārendra, having Rudra as his presiding deity.
One who is afflicted by severe illness and suffering may experience falling into water or fire;
or one may see a shadow without a head, or likewise see oneself without arms. (24–268)
One afflicted by cough and asthma shall give up life after three months,
[if this occurs] on the second lunar day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, under the Hasta asterism, on a Thursday.
When the afternoon has arrived, the yogi should depart by means of the upward transition (utkrānti);
he should exhale the breath through the mouth without restraint during the eight nāḍīs.
Having abandoned [all else] with a joyful and contented mind, one should cast off life after two months;
on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, the earth indeed possesses many streams.
If one suffers from *viṣūcī* on a Saturday falling under the constellation of Indra (*Jyeṣṭhā*), they perish;
likewise, if there is no scent in their own limbs and there is a terrible horripilation. (24–272)
[He saw him] with a chain and a noose in his hands, a staff and a mallet in his grasp;
infinite, terrible, fierce, and wrathful, with fangs that were formidable and terrifying.
If, at the end of a dream, one sees oneself being struck by the Unmanifest while appearing in the form of Kṛtānta (the God of Death), he shall live for exactly one month.
At midday on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, when Dhaniṣṭhā is conjoined with Wednesday,
one situated in a pit in the forest dies by the weapon of a thief.
He whose thighs, hands, and feet wither away as soon as he has bathed,
or who has smoke-like vapors in his head, lives for only half a month.
On the Puṇyasaṃkrānti-Dvādaśī and on the days of the bright fortnight and the planet Venus, one should perform the act of leaping into the fire; this is declared to be the Kālacakra.
He whose tongue is exceedingly black, yet whose face has the luster of yellow orpiment (gorocana),
and whose cheeks have red circular spots, lives for ten days.
On a Monday in the month of Āṣāḍha, one who is afflicted by disease and illness perishes;
yet, through the Tārā-mantra, he becomes clearly manifest as another self.
Death may occur within five nights during the days of Svāti and Soma; furthermore, excessive sweating arises from the presence of Sarpa, Ākāra, Pulika, and Ambra. (24–280)
If Venus is in Punarvasu on a Tuesday, it foretells death after three nights;
[the signs are] one eye, one's own, and two ear-tubes, all equal.
But for whom there is a movement [of the sun] lasting two full days while the sun is in the constellation Uttarāṣāḍhā, [that person lives for that long]. (24–282)
If a woman wearing black garments and having a dark complexion sees two [birds] with their necks entwined moving toward the southern direction, [it is an ill omen].
If, at the end of a dream, one sees [the deceased] under one's control, he lives for a day and a night;
[if seen] mounted upon the shoulder of a ghost (preta), writhing, yet with a joyful heart.
He would perish from the fall of a weapon,
yet he lives until midday if the dark-souled one sees [his reflection] situated within the interior of a mirror.
Within the *bimba* is the reflection encircled by a black line;
the vital breath (*prāṇa*) residing in its throat awakens through deep, blissful sleep. (24–286)
Suddenly, before the deity, one who has just been born sees a man with a staff and noose in his hands, possessing black hair and great strength.
At that very moment, death does not awaken him even from his dream,
when he sees at the end of the dream a man who is dark-brown in hue.
If one strikes her on the middle of the back with an iron staff,
one should predict her death at that very moment.
And when one dreams of oneself smeared with oil and suffering intense pain during the eighth part of the day, death will certainly occur.
Then, he sees one mounted upon a camel, proceeding toward the southern direction,
surrounded by cruel beings of black complexion who carry iron staffs.
Being beaten, he perishes toward the southern direction before midday;
his body smeared with oil, he sinks into the mud.
If one awakens from a dream while being devoured after six ghaṭikās of the day, one should predict their death within a fortnight or a month. (24.293)
A woman wearing black garments or concealing an oil massage shall go quickly to the abode of Yama as soon as the sun sets.
A woman wearing red garments, anointed with red perfumes and unguents, who embraces one in a dream—that night is his last. (24.295)
Thus should that which occurs in dreams be understood by those who know the times; now hear from me concerning portents, the arising of the one-eyed planet, and the conjunctions of death.
When the fivefold transition flows through the mouth, that becomes the yoga of extraction; one moves from one station to another station. (24-297)
The destruction of the mind, mental agitation, and the increase of diseases arise; the ruin of friends and home, as well as the loss of vital energy, come to pass. (24-298)
In the southern channel alone, during the period excluding the southern solstice,
that arising of the yoga occurs through the flow of the eight transits.
From fistula-in-ano, however, there arise tumors, eye diseases, jaundice, pain, boils, suffering, and disorders of the chest. (24–300)
Indeed, at the end of the left nostril passage, there are thirteen transits:
fever, headache, pain in the head, and likewise the *aryā* and *astaṃmana*. (24-301)
Dysuria, urinary disorders, and anemia increase; O lady of excellent vows, the disease arising from phlegm located in the *iḍā* becomes aggravated. (24–302)
If one examines the movement [of the breath] during that day or on another day,
he will be afflicted by diseases, whether on the left side or on the other side.
Now, another tactile cognition does not arise from below, nor likewise from above;
one touches what is above by means of that which is above, while the afflictions of disease previously impelled [arise]. (24.304)
When it touches the right [nostril], there is verbal abuse and being overcome;
when touching the middle [nostril], one goes to the state of overcoming others. (24.305)
When she, having been transferred in many ways here and there, arrives at a single place with her foot, then there shall be for him worship, great honor, and gain. (24.306)
When the swan of the vital breath moves slowly within the Suṣumṇā, there occurs the acquisition of land, the attainment of dharma, sovereignty, and the arrival of beloved ones. (24.307)
If Viṣṇu alone carries [the breath] during all twelve transits,
then one should predict death within one year.
Then, there is a decrease and a single transition; in each month, it should decrease by one.
O beautiful lady, when thirty breaths are diminished in a single transition, [the next occurs]. (24-309)
Day by day, indeed, for thirty days, it moves outward;
and at the end of the month, O fair-faced one, death occurs instantly.
In this way, the lord of yogis recognizes the signs of death, as well as other portents of death (ariṣṭas), and those [signs] that arise within the internal resonance of nāda.
Having conquered these through yoga according to the sequence thus described,
O lady of excellent vows, even one who is not disciplined and lacks yoga is known as a yogin.
Listen to me regarding those signs of fire and ill omens:
one whose palate, lips, and throat suddenly become dry, and whose complexion turns ashy-grey; || 24-313 ||
If the two shoulders move toward the private parts, one should predict death within six months;
furthermore, he sees a deep blue mandala in the sky day after day. (24.314)
If he sees [the sun] white, green, or black for half a year, he shall die;
he indeed sees the sun devoid of its rays and the moon bereft of its splendor.
One whose lifespan is six months will indeed see the stars as moonlight and the moonlight as darkness;
when one places the thumbs into the openings of the ears and no longer hears the internal sound, [one's life has reached its end].
O Goddess, one should predict his death within six months if he hears a supreme sound amidst a great noise, or the rustling of rags, or the chirping of crickets. (24-317)
He may live for one month if he does not hear what is dear to him;
he lives as long as he sees his own head in the mirror.
Now, regarding the vital points (*marmas*) between the ankles:
he whose [vitality] does not waver within these certainly comes under control. (24.319)
...every human being inevitably dies. || 24-320 ||
The smoke that has entered the cavity of the *tāla* is proclaimed as the Mahāyāna;
the tongue is to be known as Arundhatī, and the tip of the nose is called Dhruva.
When the corners of the eyes are pressed by the fingertips, one who does not see that light of the sun and moon lives for only one season; he becomes deluded. || 24-322 ||
He would be seen as if gasping for breath; such a man also dies in this manner.
Why would he suddenly become stout, and why would he suddenly become emaciated? (24-323)
Excessively angry and excessively terrified, he lives for only one year;
he sees lightning flashes in the absence of fire, and comets and Indra’s bow in the night. (24-324)
And in that region, he lives for one month through divine oblations;
yet, in that very place, his heart withers away as soon as he is born.
If his body becomes excessively hot, he lives for only one season; and if his navel trembles and constantly dries up, [he likewise has but one season left]. || 24-326 ||
O fair-hipped one, he whose neck is crooked has but six months left of his life;
and he whose tongue becomes thick and whose teeth decay, O beautiful woman, [shall likewise die].
O Goddess, that man dies at the end of a year; of this there is no doubt.
His eyes constantly discharge [fluid], and he does not hear distinct sounds. (24.328)
Within one month, one whose life has reached its end perceives a foul odor through the sense of smell;
the face becomes like a red lotus, and the tongue becomes exceedingly hot. (24.329)
He whose body has various colors and whose heart weeps constantly,
and who experiences trembling of the palate and the navel, lives for only half a month.

If one does not smell the odor of a crow's destruction (*kākanāśīra*) in direct perception, nor that produced by smoke or a lamp, and does not recognize what was seen before, he lives for four months. (24.331)
He whose breath constantly follows the mouth and does not perceive the *bindu*, yet always carries the *hiṣkā* [vital energy], lives for one fortnight. (24.332)
O Leader of the Gods, those who see the moonlight as indistinguishable from the stars will indeed die within six months; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
O Goddess, when one does not perceive that person situated in the midst of the sun, who consists of radiant energy, established in his own nature and possessing his own characteristic; || 24-334 ||
Then, O beloved, I shall explain to you what kind of result occurs:
there will be disease for one of black complexion, and strife for one of brownish (babhru) complexion. (24-335)
The destruction of the body should be known from [the loss of] the trunk, and the ruin of one's lineage from various [other signs].
If the head is missing, death will occur; if the hand is missing, there will be imprisonment. (24-336)
But when a foot is missing, O beloved, it should be known as a binding with chains;
thus, the signs of death are to be recognized through various such forms.
I shall speak concerning the *hastaparvan*; listen to how it comes to be.
Whether in the bright fortnight or the dark, I shall explain it in brief.
The left is declared to be white, while the right is said to be black;
having understood the movement of the left and the right, one should then observe it.
Taking up red lac with both hands, perform a cleansing;
then, having offered flowers and incense, one should examine the auspicious and inauspicious signs.
Relying on both sides of both hands,
the wise one should observe that there are three finger-joints.
One should observe both hands; therein, one should look for the mark. When there is a black line following the sequence of the joints, [that is the sign]. (24-342)
One should indicate [the sequence] starting from the first lunar day (pratipad), either on the left or in the middle;
one should observe the joints (parvan) below for those of lesser capacity, joint by joint.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should observe it up to the thumb;
on that day, his death will occur, whether during the bright, the dark, or the auspicious fortnight.
O beloved, if there is a black line on the lower joint and it is a dark new-moon day (asuklaparvan), his death should be known to occur in a lonely place through a killer.
When that very [line] moves upward like a serpent, his death is situated in water;
but if the line moves downward at the middle joint, [he dies on land]. (24-346)
O beautiful lady, death for him is declared by the discharge from the chest;
likewise, when it flows upwards, death occurs from being struck by a weapon.
If it slithers horizontally, death will occur in battle;
if, having reached the third joint, it slithers downward, [death will occur]. 24-348.
His death occurs at a sacred ford (tīrtha); of this there is no doubt.
On the third day, a spreading inflammation arises, extending upwards. (24–349)
His death occurs according to his own wish, yet by the will of Śiva;
however, when both feet [of the footprint] appear on the festival days (parvan), Kṛṣṇa [attains this].
In that case as well, death is said to occur from a single [sign];
one should observe death during the day from the feet and at night from the feet. (24.351)
These signs of death, as well as those portents of bodily dissolution that are preceded by their respective internal [symptoms], have been described by me to you.

O Dear One, through worship, recitation, fire-offerings, meditation, and dhāraṇī, as well as by means of the ritual for peace and protection, [the goal] is attained; indeed, it is not otherwise. (24.353)
"Digestion (jāraṇa) is said to be speech [that is difficult] for those of restless mind.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Authority on Time," in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, a great tantra of the Bhairava-stream belonging to the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), measuring seventy million verses. 24.
The Goddess said: "O Blessed One, O Supreme Lord, O Omniscient One, Lord of Causes!
You have indeed related everything consisting of speech—the entire world of the moving and the unmoving. (25.1)

But you have not explained, O Lord, the characteristics of deceiving death through time, nor the ritual procedure for conquering death (*mṛtyuñjaya*), nor likewise the pacification of Rudra (*rudraśānti*). (25.2)
O Lord, please tell me about worship, oblation, and especially the specific rites of protection, as well as meditation, concentration, and yoga. (25.3)
The Lord of Men dwells in proximity to the death within the egg;
O Lord, [tell me] how there may be an evasion of both birth and death. (25.4)
"In this manner, I wish to hear it through your grace; O Worthy One, please speak.
Bhairava said:
"Listen, O Goddess, for I shall explain that which I have been asked by you. (25.5)
O leader of the gods, out of affection for you, I shall describe in brief the characteristics of the bondage of time through various methods. (25.6)
The wise one should draw a mandala with eight petals, four corners, and adorned with four gates in the center of a lotus for the propitiation of Rudra. (25.7)
First, her lower limb is described as being endowed with the characteristics of a lotus;
and the upper part, the speaker, is likewise proclaimed to possess the characteristics of a lotus. (25.8)
The two [sections] beginning with *Kathyaṅga* belong to the previous Kalpa; after that, forty [verses] composed in the *anuṣṭubh* meter are told on a single day. (25.9)
The faces, limbs, mantras, yantras, petals, and positions beginning with Rudra have been declared; this [goddess] is worshipped by thirty-eight deities.
The Goddess who pacifies all sins, wards off all diseases, bestows all success, is auspicious, and brings about victory. (25.11)
For the Paṅktiyāga, as taught by Śiva, is performed with all the words together,
situated in each of the directions beginning from the northeast.
I shall describe the arrangement of words for the sacrifice, characterized by the gathering of all [mantras];
one should place two supreme words there within the pericarp.
Furthermore, Trijaṭā should place Rudra, Vṛṣabha, Aviśuddha, and Asambhava in the south-eastern direction;
then she should place Aṅkāra, Vaṣaṭkāra, and Svadhākāra. (25.15)
One should place four thousand [deities] on the southern petal;
and one should place Karālavikṛta on the southwestern (nairṛta) petal.
The wise one should place Ananta, Ārdra, Śuṣka, and likewise Āvogata—these four following words—in the Vāruṇa [pavilion]. (25.17)
The four Piṅgalās should be assigned to the northern petal of the wise one [Budha];
one should then place five forms and words in the north. (25.18)
One should worship according to the prescribed ritual with fragrant incense and flowers;
furthermore, an oblation (homa) should be performed in the fire with ghee mixed with honey.
The oblation, consisting of both milk-rice and sacrificial cakes, should be offered for the sake of gratification;
likewise, *śamī* leaves, *dūrvā* grass, and the sprouts of milky trees [should be used]. (25–20)
One should always offer oblations with the sacred leaves of the mango tree, as well as fuel-sticks of *apāmārga*, *palāśa*, and *udumbara*. 25.21ab.
Black sesame seeds, barley, and unbroken grains of rice; white mustard seeds, parched grain, and curd, milk, honey, and milk-rice (pāyasa).
The wise person should constantly offer all of this according to their ability:
various kinds of food, including staple grains, condiments, and diverse edibles. (25.23)
There may be seven, five, or three oblations, or even a single one; this is the rule for the daily fire-sacrifice (nityahoma), or it is prescribed as being accompanied by six hundred [oblations].
A thousandfold [is the merit] compared to worldly desires, because it arises from the divine;
and among all portents, the oblation of battle is the greatest portent.
For those seized by all kinds of diseases, whose bodies are afflicted by planetary spirits, who are overwhelmed by calamities, and whose souls are beset by obstacles; || 25-26 ||
One should employ this rite of pacification for those who have been afflicted by malevolent magic (abhicāra);
furthermore, an empowerment (abhiṣeka) should be performed with water consecrated by the remnants of oblations (saṃpātāhuti).
To one who has been consecrated with the eight jars using the "all-surpassing" formula, the prepared *caru* offering should be given. (25–28)
By merely consuming that, a person becomes accessible to all.
I shall now proclaim the auspicious Rudra-śānti, which accomplishes all aims.
Spoken by the God of gods for the benefit of practitioners, all obstacles perish upon merely hearing this destroyer of sins. (25–30)
Evil dreams and diseases, as well as malevolent planets, flee in the ten directions before Śarva, who possesses many forms and who destroys all forms. (25–31)
To the God who acts for the welfare of the world and who removes all sins;
to Him who is accompanied by Pārvatī and by Nandin and his attendants. || 25-32 ||
I shall proclaim the Rudra-śānti, which destroys the Vetālas that afflict men within the temples and dwellings of the gods. (25–33)
Those women for whom there is no conception of a fetus and no loss of family lineage; those in whom, once born, [the children] perish and do not become males. (25-34)
Wherever Mārī arises, there will be constant strife;
the fetus will miscarry prematurely, or a child will be born with missing limbs. (25.35)
They are oppressed by famine, and there will be terrible portents within the kingdom; wherever a community is divided, so too will be brothers, fathers-in-law, and friends.
The father, the mother, and even one's own sister, afflicted by filth within the house, see a monkey in a dream; [thus] one grows through the field of life.
If cows, buffaloes, dogs, elephants, or other laborers residing in the house are afflicted by adverse omens, one should perform a rite of pacification there. (25–38)
Where a well roars and the backbone breaks, and trees, though unstruck, drip copious amounts of blood. (25-39)
The deities and the trees themselves danced and laughed;
even though it was not the season, the trees blossomed and bore fruit in great abundance. (25.40)
Meteors fall and the earth quakes with terrible violence;
by these and other such extremely dreadful omens, [the world is foretold]. (25.41)
Becoming one-pointed and self-restrained, Janaka, named Giriśa, should apply himself to peace there upon the summit of the king of mountains.
Filled with various inhabited lands and endowed with medicinal herbs,
there stands in the center Rudra, the supreme one, devoted to the welfare of all beings.
It was surrounded by yakṣas, rākṣasas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and numerous bhūtas;
then all the hosts of gods and the sages preeminent in asceticism [approached]. (25–44)
Placing a Brāhmaṇa at their head, they cause [the Lord] to hear from Maheśvara hymns of praise consisting of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas—purifying chants that grant boons. (25.45)
Having praised Nīlakaṇṭha, who bears the bull as his emblem, together with Umā,
all the hosts of gods and the sages whose wealth is asceticism [did so].
Together with Brahmā, they petitioned Hara, the Lord of Gods:
"O Mahādeva, God of gods, the human subjects are suffering. (25.47)
"Grant him peace, you who liberate from all seizing spirits.
Having heard the words of the gods, Hara, the lord of the three worlds, [acted].
Having been thus commanded by the Grandfather, all the hosts quickly obeyed;
so too did all those world-protectors and the invincible guardians of the realm. (25.49)
Piśācas, Pūtanās, Yakṣas, Kaumāras, Grahas, Rākṣasas, Kūṣmāṇḍas along with Vetālas, Pakṣapātas, and Dhanurgrahas. || 25-50 ||

The gods, those who fall from heaven, and those who dwell in the netherworld; the foremost of spirits and night-stalkers; likewise Kālī and whatever other harmful planetary spirits there may be. || 25-51 ||
Epilepsy as well as [diseases of] the limbs, eye diseases and seizures, heart diseases and mouth diseases, abdominal diseases, fevers, and consumptions. (25-52)
Head diseases, jaundice, and most dreadful eye diseases—these and many other ailments have been proclaimed. (25-53)
Those grahas, led by all their hosts into the presence of Hara, prostrated themselves again and again and addressed the Lord of Gods: || 25.54 ||
O Tree of Splendor, how much less can I even look upon him by my own power?
Command me, O Mahādeva; what may be done at your command?
Mahādeva, his eyes bloodshot with anger, said to him:
"By what means, or by whose fault, are human beings suffering? (25.56)
Among them, one excellent one, the lord of the lords of the earth, said:
"This is our way of life here; this too is a boon granted by Brahmā. (25.57)
Those humans in the world who are seized by darkness, who perform evil deeds, who desire to cause harm, and who crave offerings—they are the *grahas*. (25.58)
Men who are elated or distressed, those whose wealth has been lost, and those overcome by various states of mind—seizing upon a vulnerability, they enter [the enemy]. (25.60)
This has been told to you, O God; be gracious to me, O Blessed One.
Command me, O Mahādeva: what should be done after this?
Thus addressed, the Blessed One, the three-eyed Supreme Lord,
the granter of boons and creator of beings, spoke this Rudra-śānti.
But that Guhyaka who, having heard this knowledge, does not desist,
shall clearly be struck seven times on the head with the staff of Rudra.
O Grahas, for seven thousand births one is cooked in the Raurava hell,
and furthermore, it is most terrible for those whose spell one might transgress.
Thus addressed, the Blessed One stood before the planets;
having established them in the pledge (samaya), the Lord spoke this vidyā.
Oṃ, homage to the immeasurable and invincible one; may there be well-being in the supreme refuge.
Oṃkāra, Vaṣaṭkāra, Brahman, Svāhā, and likewise Svadhā. (25.66)
Sāvitrī, Bhūtasāvitrī, and Rudrasāvitrī;
likewise Rudrāṇī, Brahmasāvitrī, and the goddess Sarasvatī. || 25-67 ||
Umā, Kṛṣṇā, and Amitā— whoever is eternally established in the heart among gods, asuras, and humans, and among both the stationary and the moving— 25-68.
Oṃ hiri hiri, obeisance to Rudra, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the one whose vehicle is the bull, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the white-and-tawny one, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Kṛṣṇapiṅgala, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to Madhupiṅgala, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Viśvarūpa, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to the Great Virūpa, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Karālāhata, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Vikṛta, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to the one of deformed appearance, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Ananta, svāhā! Oṃ, homage to the one of beautiful form, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Ekapiṅgala, svāhā! Oṃ, homage to Ekajaṭa, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Dvijaṭa, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Trijaṭa, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to the Lord of the Pramathas, svāhā! Oṃ [fill in the remaining syllables]... svāhā!
Oṃ [123a] Oṃ,
homage to Tatpuruṣa, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Sahasraśīrṣa, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to the one with a thousand faces and bellies, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the one with a thousand hands and feet, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to the one with a thousand lingas, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to the Lord of Beings, svāhā! Oṃ, homage to the Great Lord of Beings, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Paśupati, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to the Lord of Umā, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to the Sovereign of all beings, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to the syllable Oṃ, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Vaṣaṭkāra; svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to Svadhākāra; svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to the bearer of the hand-drum (ḍamaru); svāhā!
Oṃ turu tururuṇḍi śi rudeśi devānāṃ deva viśākhaṃ hana hana daha daha paca paca matha matha curu curu muru muru suru suru rudraśāntimanusmara kṛṣṇe piṅgale kālapiśācādhipativiśveśvarāya namaḥ svāhā.
By constant recitation [of this mantra], one is liberated from all sins.
One should offer oblations of *śānti*-fuel sticks, clarified butter, milk, curd, honey, sesame seeds, barley, *dūrvā* grass, *śamī* leaves, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and all kinds of food.
One should also perform an offering for other aforementioned deities, and peace will prevail.
O lady of excellent vows, the propitiation of Rudra has been declared by me; now hear of another.
I shall fully explain the characteristics, as well as the ritual procedure for Amṛtīśa,
and the rules for the rite of action (kriyāyāga), O daughter of the Wind-god, as they are being told.
First, one should place the pervasive nectar born of Rudra,
the seed-syllable that is the eighth letter after *ka*, joined with the sixfold *kalā*.
The third [vowel] is proclaimed as being joined above the half-measure (kalārdha);
its radiance, curved like a serpent, rises upward toward the moon. (25.72)
If they die three days or more after that, it is likewise; [the initiation] is performed on the head both before and after that.
This indeed is known as Amṛtā, possessing the splendor of the Lord of Immortality (Amṛteśa). || 25-73 ||
That which is indeed established correctly by one who is completely enveloped by this is proclaimed as the Lord of Immortality, the slayer of death. (25.74)
All elixirs, when adorned by the Vināyakas, bestow immortality through the power of Amṛtīśa. (25.75)
Therefore, having set this aside, one should worship and constantly recite this;
having first placed the nectar-water and having likewise prepared the vital breath (prāṇa). || 25.76 ||
Combined with the Rudrāvaraṇa and adorned with half of Yama, they are proclaimed in due order as Raccha, Śiras, Śikhā, and Varma. (25.77)
Having placed [the seed-syllable] *mātṛrodani* (MṚ), surrounded by the crescent moon (*bālendu*),
this is indeed the Amṛtīśāstra, which destroys all obstacles.
Jīvana is mounted upon Śikhi and pierced by Nīlagrīva; Prāṇa is joined with the upper part of the nose, and its first syllable is Indra. (25.79)
Having mounted the bearer of oblations (the sacrificial fire), one should pierce it at the end of life according to the rule with the Rudra-arrow; thereafter, one should adorn [it].

Above the *hantṛ* [the letter *ha*], one should again place another six-spoked wheel; one should place the seed-syllable ending with *dharitrī* (the letter *la*) situated directly upon that very [wheel]. (25.81)
Having placed [the seed-syllable] pierced by the arrow of Rudra and joined with the upper part of *ya*,
one should subsequently place [the syllables] beginning with the weeping of the Mothers.
O Pārvatī, one should place the Self as the sacrificial oblation upon the head of the tawny-haired one;
having placed the armor-mantra in front, the lord of weapons then becomes [manifest] for you. (25.83)
I have described to you this great lord of weapons beginning with the *praṇava*;
one should employ it for the sake of protection between the eyes as well as on the hand. (25.84)
Indeed, those who are wicked, harmful, as well as most terrible obstacles—this lord of weapons, which destroys them all, has been proclaimed on earth as Truth (Satya). || 25-85 ||
The principles (tattvas) are known as those beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*; the deities are the long vowels, and they have been described by me as ending with the anusvāra and visarga.
The short vowels are said to be joined with the anusvāra;
it is taught that the letter *ha* is not [the end], and one should imagine the end of the *kanda*. (25.87)
The [syllables] beginning with *dha* should be assigned according to their sequence by means of the pervasive [syllable].
These mantras are always proclaimed in the ritual procedure of Amṛteśa. (25.88)
Having purified the water with the Astra-mantra, one should prepare the Śakti-vessel;
having rendered it nectar-like with the Amṛta-mantra, one should bathe using the remaining nectar.
Someone should first draw a square city, beginning with the eastern side;
in its center, an eight-petaled white lotus adorned with four colors. (25.90)
When the ritual vessel (kalaśa) has been prepared, one should worship the Lord of Gods therein;
however, O wise one, one should place the Vardhanī vessel on the right with the Astra-mantra.
Having first deposited the seat (āsana) as before, one should place the principle of the person (puṃstattva) upon the pericarp;
then the power of the Lord (prabhuśakti) above that, and the Lord of Nectar (amṛtīśa) above that.
Resembling pure crystal, with ambrosia flowing from all sides, four-armed, holding a trident in his hand, and wearing a serpent as a sacred thread. || 25.93 ||
One should always worship him who sits in the mahāhibaddha paryaṅka posture, grey with powdered camphor, with matted locks bound upward in a crown, and possessing three eyes.
Thereafter, the wise practitioner should perform the ritual of the limbs and sub-limbs according to the prescribed rule:
the principles (tattvas) are at the tips of the filaments, while the powers (śaktis) are at the bases of the petals.

The short vowels are to be placed upon the petals first, according to the sequence beginning with the east; likewise, *ā* and *ī* are the successive limbs, while the weapon (*astra*) is situated in the cardinal and intermediate directions of the petals. (25.96)
The wise one should always worship Astra-Indra at the tip of the southern petal;
he should worship all [the weapons] in due order with their respective mantras. || 25-97 ||
One should cause the offering of the water for the feet, the guest-water, and so forth, with one's own mantra alone.
Having thus worshipped according to the ritual procedure, one should then touch the medicinal herb.
One should sprinkle that medicinal substance according to the prescribed rite and employ it;
and the *caru* should be prepared with the Amṛtīśa mantra according to the rules, as the wise have declared. (25.99)
Having divided [the food] into three parts, one should set aside the first portion for the deity;
thereafter, one should consume the remainder of the oblation offered into the fire together with the auspicious ones (the Śivagaṇas). || 25.100 ||

O fair-faced one, one should worship with medicinal herbs and sacrificial porridge (caru) that have been sprinkled with water by the Lord of Amṛta and touched [by him]; it must not be otherwise. 25-101.

One should perform the rite of offering the medicinal herb with oblations made until the end of the word "svāhā," by means of the deity Amṛteśa, according to the ritual procedure as seen in the scriptures.
By means of a thousand oblations of clarified butter or even milk, an offering of the three sweets (*madhuratrika*) must indeed be performed by the best of physicians. (25.103)
One should cause [the offering] to be given by Amṛtīśa, who is joined with the peaceful state of the Creator;
thus one should perform the rite of oblation, having made one's own body fully empowered (sakalīkṛta).
The wise one should contemplate himself as completely filled by Amṛtīśa;
thereafter, he should perform the ritual of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) with Amṛtīśa.

Then, one should meditate upon a lotus situated on the crown of the head, with its stalk pointing upward and its face downward; above that, one should meditate on the Lord of Nectar, who is filled by the moon.

One should contemplate [the deity] as having been installed with the previously mentioned placement of the limbs, possessing the luster of pure crystal, pouring forth divine nectar, and appearing like the dissolution of the universe.
In this very way, the mantra-sacrifice here consists of drops of flowing nectar;
pure and with an uninterrupted stream, it enters the aperture of Brahmā.
He should nourish himself as being situated within the heart-lotus;
there, that lotus is white as snow, with its face turned upward and consisting of nectar.
Emitting nectar upwards and flooding its own sphere,
both indeed attain that pervasive city of nectar which has reached the ultimate reality.
Should one not contemplate that very nectar which destroys fierce diseases?
Likewise, at the base of the feet, there is a lotus whose nature is upward-facing. (25.111)
With petals joined to one another and two lotuses interlocked with each other, one should contemplate oneself situated in their center as being pierced by the *sampuṭa* [mudrā]. (25.112)
Whether walking, standing, sleeping, waking, speaking, or thinking, the man who [remembers this] is not bound by time; it becomes a medicine that is like nectar.
One should perform the ritual of deposition (nyāsa) in this manner and apply the medicinal herb;
in a very short time, he will conquer death.
The *sampuṭa* known as Amṛta should not be given to just anyone;
having first formed another *sampuṭa* externally, one should then perform worship in the heart-lotus.

Afterwards, having joined the upper and lower [vessels] together, one should take up the fire according to the rule from all sides with Amṛteśa; it should have been previously sprinkled with water by means of the Astra and Indra [mantras]. (25.116)

Having sprinkled it with the Heart-mantra, one should cast it into the womb of the mandala with the Armor-mantra; then, having ignited it with the Amṛta-weapon mantra, one should spread the covering with the Heart-mantra.
Brahmā, Hari, Hara, and Siddhi are to be meditated upon in sequence as they stand upon their seats; likewise, having fashioned the enclosing sticks (paridhi), they are to be visualized.
Thereafter, one should perform the installation of the deities with the *praṇava* (OM),
as well as the consecrations of the clarified butter and other materials, whatever is enjoined by the ritual rules.
All that may be performed with the *praṇava* alone or with the heart-mantra;
thereafter, one should worship the Lord of Gods exactly as was done previously.
Clarified butter, milk, curd, or sesame seeds, or else honey, or rice, or wild grains (nīvāra), cooked on a sacrificial fire. (25.181)
The oblation should be prepared from milk-rice (pāyasa) and other such substances;
the physician should offer it profusely, combined with the three sweet ingredients.

By performing a hundred oblations with unbroken sprouts of *dūrvā* grass, one shall become long-lived for an eon; however, O Supreme Goddess, if the rite is performed with the individual components separately, [the result is as follows].
In the reverse order, it is with seed; otherwise, it would be seedless.
One who knows the ritual procedure should recite the syllables one hundred thousand times according to the rules.
The body of the man who has been consecrated becomes the limbs of the God of gods;
from that, incomparable power arises for the practitioner.
One should cause the teacher to receive the impartation of the partless (niṣkala) Śiva;
then, relying upon the meditation on the part-filled (sakala), one should consecrate the practitioner.

The preceptor, who contemplates the ultimate reality, [should perform the rite] with either water-pots or leaves—either those of the *pālāśa* tree or those born from the lotus—or even with water and flowers. (25.187)
Then, having performed the oblation with the *kala* mantras, one should worship Amṛtīśa;
indeed, for the sake of purifying oneself, one should offer a hundred oblations with the Astra-mantra.
One should purify that [arrow] with either the Amṛta weapon or the Great Weapon (Mahāstra);
likewise, the purification of others is accomplished by these two alone—of this there is no doubt. (25.189)
The invocation should be performed with one’s own vowels and consonants, and the dismissal likewise;
one should worship the deity with one [syllable] and dismiss him with this very same [one]. (25.190)
One should establish the deity with the *hṛdinī* mantra and offer perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
having performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for all [the deities], one should finally offer the *pūrṇāhuti*.
At the conclusion of the initiation, by the God of gods, it is exactly thus, without a doubt;
having meditated upon Śiva as partless (niṣkala), [the rite is performed] for the practitioner by means of the manifest (sakala) form.

Having recited the Amṛta-mantra according to the prescribed rite, the wise man, having offered oblations with a two-fingered sacrificial ladle filled with the substance called Amṛta from the Śakti-vessel, shall become a conqueror of death. || 25.193 ||
In the rite for nourishment, one should offer oblations of whole or broken stalks of *dūrvā* grass;
thus nourished and consecrated, he shall thereafter take away death. (174b) [g] (25.194)
Having fashioned a mortar of udumbara wood and having placed [the deity] therein as before,
one should then duly worship the God of gods with white flowers.
Therefore, the wise man should first employ that which was joined by Amṛtīśa; it is beneficial for the rite of consecration when accompanied by Sṛṣṭikṛt.
It is remembered as bestowing all accomplishments when it is nourished and consecrated;
indeed, it grants a kingdom, as well as sovereignty and the status of a universal monarch.
He is the leader of those who move through the air and likewise of those whose speech is unmanifest;
indeed, he brings about the recitation of mantras and liberation through the investigation of mantras. (25.198)
Whoever remembers daily [the Lord] residing in the city named Amṛta,
should worship Amṛtīśa and perform the fire-sacrifice (agnikārya).
Then that physician should taste it with clearly visible dūrvā and amṛtā;
he indeed destroys wrinkles, graying hair, baldness, and death. (25.200)
The self is encapsulated within the *sapuṭa* (double-casket), and the medicine is encapsulated within the *sampuṭa*;
when applied in this manner as a *puṭa* for the sick, it becomes like nectar. || 25-201 ||
Or he who recites the mantra consisting of the nectar of five syllables—O lady of excellent hips, one should meditate upon and recite the supreme Śiva, the Lord of Nectar (Amṛtīśa). (25.202)
Freed from all diseases, he shall live for an eon;
the practitioner of mantras should worship the Great-Souled Lord of Nectar within the vase.
Then, O Goddess, one who is afflicted by diseases is indeed purified;
the sonless obtains a son, and the maiden finds a virtuous husband. (25.204)
O Goddess, the king shall be liberated from misfortune and attain victory;
even in battle, those who seek victory will undoubtedly obtain it. (25.205)
O fair-faced one, a woman who has performed the worship of the deceased and has been consecrated shall quickly have living sons; and a man without wealth shall obtain wealth. (25.206)
Having consecrated the medicine with mantras, one should drink it; it will destroy that disease.
Or the yogi should drink water consecrated seven times with mantras. (25.207)
O Goddess, he who constantly burns [his impurities] through recitation, even while enjoying worldly pleasures, quickly attains immortality by the power of the Lord of Immortals.
O lady of beautiful hips, if they consume it, there is no doubt that they attain immortality;
O most auspicious one, for the sake of peace, one should offer oblations of dūrvā grass smeared with the three sweets.
O lady of good vows, peace shall quickly be attained through Amṛteśa;
O beloved, having placed the *gaḍūka* upon the top of the *liṅga*, one should cause it to be offered.
O Goddess of the gods, a man afflicted by disease becomes healthy;
O Goddess, one should bathe a child seized by Pūtanā and other such spirits. (25.211)
O Goddess, when one who is afflicted by poison is bathed with that water, he becomes healthy and free from doubt, having abandoned his attachment to the household. 25-212ab [175a]
O auspicious lady, it becomes poisonless or poisonous; of this there is no doubt.
O beautiful woman, the protection must be written on a smooth and auspicious birch-bark leaf.
Then, having encased it with lac, one should place it within yellow pigment (rocanā), white sandalwood (śrīkhaṇḍa), and auspicious saffron (kuṅkuma), and then immerse it in honey.
He will be liberated from all diseases and shall have a lifespan of an eon.
Now, I shall describe another worldly method characterized by the deception of time.
In the sky consisting of Brahman, upon a six-petalled lotus situated on a trident,
located in the midst of the ocean of nectar and adorned with white drops.
In that partless, supreme, subtle state, which is beyond the sphere of activity,
there is within it a subtle digit (kalā), the seventeenth, which is immortal.
Neither decrease nor increase is found; it is not found in the dark fortnight, O fair-faced one, nor is there exhalation, inhalation, or retention of breath. (25.218)
Nothing exists there; indeed, it is remembered as the one supreme *kalā*. There, O Goddess, one should place the Self together with the *kalā* and the *śaṅkhinī*. (25.219)
O Dear One, the yogi should practice until he becomes one with that reality—dissolved, all-pervading, and omnipresent. || 25.220 ||
O Goddess of gods, even when the time has arrived, death does not occur for him;
O Goddess, one should observe that day on which the death of the wise man occurs.
At that time, O fair-faced one, one should unite the self in that place;
when one remains united there, death does not advance upon the earth.
Just as a man who has entered an empty house, O Goddess, departs without obtaining any fruit therein for the sake of receiving honor, so it is here. (25.223)
In the very same way, O beloved, time indeed passes away in vain;
yet time also exists, O Goddess, established as if within the heart-lotus. (25.224)

Endowed with the city of eight (puryaṣṭaka), together with Brahmā and the other causal deities, when he has transcended the great principles along with the supreme ones established in their own natures, O Dear One. (25–225)
Then there is no time, nor the decay of old age and disease;
there is no sorrow, nor indeed suffering, nor fear, nor bondage. (25.226)
Neither death, nor hatred, nor illusion, nor bonds exist;
Śiva, the supreme cause, is indeed ever endowed with bliss. (25.227)
Where speech turns back along with the mind, having failed to reach it—
that bliss which is the form of Brahman, that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
O Supreme Goddess, this true nature of your power and the very reality of the principles, as well as the deception of the supreme time, has been told to you.
O Goddess of excellent vows, even after thousands of births, [this is not attained] by Brahmā, O Lord of the Gods, nor by Viṣṇu, nor by Rudra, nor even by Īśvara.
In age after age, there is dissolution by the hundreds and even by the thousands.
[125a] These are remembered as being self-manifested;
he becomes the enjoyer of those very mantras and vidyās. || 25-233 ||
One should not engage in deliberation regarding this, for it is indeed a single, undivided mass;
O Goddess, the mantra-mass (mantrapiṇḍa) arises through the application of the sequence taught in the scriptures. (25.234)
For the self has indeed gone toward its true being; one should practice day by day, and it becomes that very form for him—whether auspicious or inauspicious. (25.235)
Whether it be a nāga, a bhūta, or a piśāca; a rākṣasa, a yakṣa, or a kinnara; a gandharva, a dānava, or even a preta—divine yet most terrifying. || 25-236 ||
Whether he has a terrifying body with fierce, protruding fangs, or is gentle with a peaceful mind, or even a Garuḍa or a Vidyādhara; || 25.237 ||
Or, O lady of beautiful hips, he may have three eyes, or two arms, or eight arms;
he may be Keśava bearing the conch, discus, and mace, or Trivikrama. (25.238)
Whether it be Brahmā or Indra, or beasts, birds, and reptiles—whatever form the self contemplates, that very form arises for it. (25.239)
Whether it be gross or subtle, or even the supreme [state] born from the body of mantra—it becomes exactly like that without a doubt when one becomes equal to Śakti. (25.240)
The supreme Śāstrā, O Goddess, emanates in manifold ways from the left thigh, just as the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) accomplishes whatever object is thought of. || 25-241 ||
Likewise, O Varārohā, that Śakti who bestows the fruits of one's contemplated desires must be known by the practitioner himself, if he is a seeker of the fruits of the scriptures. (25.242)
O Goddess, this knowledge has come down through the lineage of succession;
it is difficult to attain even for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra, and it has not been told to anyone, O Beloved. (25.243)
O Goddess, I have declared this secret to you and made it manifest;
otherwise, O Goddess, there will be a loss of time.
The Goddess said:
The tip of the palate is proclaimed to be the source of all desires for living beings;
O Goddess, you should explain the yoga by which that is known. (25.245)
Bhairava said:
With a very steady intellect, one who is being pierced by the tip of the nectar at the tip of the rasa, becoming motionless and absorbed in that, should remain for a long time with effort. (25.246)
But with the three-pointed vital breath, impelled by the upward-moving breath (udāna), having placed the tip against the tip, the knower of yoga should quickly pierce it. (25.247)
All those born from the tip of the spear-staff are indeed mixed with the *pudgala*;
situated within the *brahmanāḍī*, one should pierce the supreme state, the lotus of immortality. (25.248)
Endowed with sixteen digits and situated with its face turned downward, the yogi should contemplate the nectar located there, facing in all directions. (25.249)
They covered him with great speed, like the tide of the great ocean;
and having drunk that divine nectar, which was distinguished by the fire of time, [they were overcome].
Within one month, death occurs; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Within two months, the interior of the body is not afflicted by hunger, thirst, and the like. (25–251)
Freed from old age and disease, indeed ageless and likewise immortal,
the preeminent practitioner becomes the abode of both fear and fearlessness.
Having become immortal after six months, bearing eternal youth, he sports unimpeded with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Dharmarāja. || 25-253 ||
The best of practitioners may enjoy all pleasures according to his own will;
first he becomes a yogi, and immediately thereafter [he attains] the second state. (25.254)
Having bypassed that [second] there, the knower of yoga should drink the third;
indeed, he should continue through the fourth, fifth, sixth, and up to the sixteenth.
By this sequential yoga, one should drink the supreme nectar;
at its end is that subtle power called Kuṇḍalī, which is coiled.
She is to be known as the measurer of the immeasurable, established at the end of the vowels;
that digit (kalā) resides in the supreme ether, the abode of perfection.
At its end is divine nectar; having drawn that forth, O beloved, one should drink it by means of the movement through the Suṣumṇā, once it has reached the region of the navel.
Furthermore, one should meditate upon the supreme nectar situated right there;
omniscience will be attained swiftly—there is no need for deliberation on this point. (25.259)
But when that state has indeed been known, there is no doubt regarding liberation;
now I shall explain another unsurpassed rite of protection.
Protected by this, the practitioner of mantra shall recite [the mantra] and overcome death; there is no doubt.
This Cintāmaṇi vidyā performs wondrous deeds. (25–261)
O Goddess, this purifying [mantra], renowned in the world, has been retained by me:
*amṛtaṃ vārimārūḍhaṃ oṃ taṃ bindusamanvitam*. (25–262)
At the end of the word *amṛta*, one should write the name, provided with a dot (*bindu*) above it;
this should be encircled on all sides by a circle formed with the three [syllables] beginning with *srū*.
One should install the god Vīṇādharabhairava as the Kūṭamūrti;
by means of Rodha ending with Kalā, he is situated in the pericarp during the great heat (mahātapa).
Thereafter, O lady of excellent vows, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus, followed by a sixteen-spoked one,
and then a thirty-four-petaled one, proceeding from beginning to end.
Having drawn a goad at the end, and likewise in the cardinal and intermediate directions, one should then draw the auspicious deities established in the peak-syllables upon the eight petals. (25–266)
The wise one [should perform] four for those situated in the cardinal directions and five for those moving in the intermediate directions;
these streams, produced from the eight forms, are fashioned from the primary seed-syllables.
O Goddess, one should assign the sixteen digits born of nectar upon the sixteen-spoked [cakra]. Then, one should assign the auspicious syllables of the third digit, ending with Śāntā. (25–268)
The number thirty-four syllables is stated; they have flowed from the station of Viṣṇu, are conjoined with fire and wind, and are situated upon the seat of Prakṛti.
She who bears the power of Rudra is gentle, yet she is the supreme bearer of Rudra’s power;
having encircled [the object] three times with the noose, one should do so again three times with the goad.
One should block [the movement] in all directions, and then the circle of arrows;
likewise, one should strive for the circle of the earth within the three circles.
One should wrap it with a threefold thread spun by a maiden;
however, it should not be wrapped with the three metals—this the wise one should indeed wrap with care.
Having placed it upon all kinds of grain, one should bathe it with all the ritual ablutions,
using perfumes, flowers, food offerings, and delightful incenses.
Then, having prostrated before the deity, one should hold the vidyā upon the head,
or on the neck, or on the region of the arms, or even at the place of the topknot.
And at its end, O Goddess of gods, one should diligently maintain that;
the man on earth who maintains the deity as the Vidyā is Rudra himself.
And Bhairava, who bestows grace upon the world, is indeed seen as the very embodiment of the mantra, blazing with eyes, by both the divine and the non-divine; of this there is no doubt. (25–276)
That very place would become purified; how much more so the assembly of disciples?
Longevity, health, sovereignty, and prosperity shall always abide in his home. (25–277)
O Goddess of gods, one who performs this ritual dispute shall indeed become equal to Kubera;
he will be beloved by all people and by women, without a doubt. (25–278)
By the power of the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), they experience agitation upon seeing it;
this is true, O Great Goddess, for she is the destroyer of all calamities. (25–279)
This knowledge removes all diseases and dispels all suffering;
it [protects] from the terrifying hands of Death, which consist of the nature of the defects and qualities of karma.
Protected by this king of mantras, one is not seized by these defects;
the mantra-practitioner who wears the five jewels shall live for five hundred years.
Freed from all diseases and invincible everywhere,
one should then bind [the mantra] in the ten directions at the time of battle.
Even when weapons fall upon his body, he is not harmed;
O sinless one, the contact with his limbs should be known as being like that of flowers. (25.283)
The enemy army, numbering ten million and endowed with the four divisions, is shattered and rendered empty;
terrified, they flee with their backs turned through the power of the *cintāmaṇi*. (25–284)
And having abandoned the conceit of lightness, those who have attained the great state are like a lion;
whether in water, on land, or in the forest, they are [unassailable] by fire, serpents, fangs, or the ends of planets, spirits, and piśācas.
This great vidyā destroys the afflictions caused by kings and other enemies, as well as diseases such as malignant consumption, and poisons, both stationary and mobile. (25–286)
One should destroy [them], without doubt, from the calamities in the mortal world;
for those who are known as wicked beings, one should destroy them, there is no uncertainty. (25-287)
And by the power of knowledge, as darkness [is dispelled] by the sun;
what more need be said? For serpents are [overcome] by Garuḍa alone. (25–288)
O sinless one, she is the Vidyā consisting of all mantras, extending to the limit of seventy million;
she is firmly established in the state of being the Guru of both mantras and vidyās.
Therefore, O Goddess of the Gods, one who desires prosperity should maintain this very Vidyā here with every effort; it is proclaimed to be like a wish-fulfilling gem.
The netherworld (pātāla), the world of mortals (bhūrloka), and those who go to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the rest—all these are supported by him by whom the vidyā has been upheld. (25–291)
I am indeed supported by him by whom the Vidyās are supported;
I am indeed supported by him, and he has worshipped me—of this there is no doubt.
I am indeed a bearer of the great vows, by whom this vidyā has been maintained;
while this vidyā is being maintained, whatever woman one approaches— || 25-293 ||
One shall attain liberation; how much more so, then, the one who preserves [this teaching]?
Even a barren woman obtains a son, and a maiden finds a virtuous husband. (25-294)
In this world, one becomes both unfortunate and fortunate; of this there is no doubt.
Even a fool becomes a knower of the scriptures, and the formless becomes possessed of form. (25.295)
By the power of this knowledge, one may indeed summon the five divine beings; and even a person whose disposition is corrupt will undoubtedly be paralyzed. (25–296)
The purification of both oneself and others will swiftly come to pass;
when the three sweets have been properly prepared, one should deposit the vidyā therein.
Then the wise one should dig [the ground] and, with great care and well-restrained, should place it in an auspicious location, such as a temple or a shrine.
O Supreme Goddess, as long as that knowledge remains right there,
one is not afflicted by disease until the ultimate end of time.
Having extracted [this mantra] at the time of death, she who remains established in the temple shall go to the supreme abode, the auspicious state free from all affliction.
O Goddess, these [teachings] common to all tantras—whether Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, Yāmala, or Vidyāpīṭha—are indicated in the Bṛhadgrantha. (25–301)
Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, and Aparājitā—these, beginning with Kṣamā, [arise] from the mutual piercing of the peaks in Jambha and Moha. (25–302)
"Hrāḥ, kūṃ, kāraṃ, and kloṃ—O fair-faced one, this mantra, which grants all desires, has been taught in the first sūtra. (25–303)
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the protection born from the feet of Mṛtyuñjaya:
having first drawn an eight-petaled lotus, and then one of sixteen forms.
On its beautiful exterior, joined with thirty-two petals, one should place the syllable *devadatta* situated in the middle of the interior of the letter *sa*. 25-305.
Having placed the syllable *kṣma* on its exterior and the syllable *ṭha* immediately thereafter,
one should assign the auspiciously characterized *mātṛkā* to each and every petal.
O Dear One, the name is encapsulated, with syllables interspersed;
just as it is for one, so it is for all, up to the thirty-second in sequence. (25–307)
After that, one should cause the principle of Māyā, which consists of the three qualities (triguṇa), to be bestowed;
[one should do so] with the hook and the restraint in the four cardinal directions and the intermediate directions. (25–308)
Thereafter, one should encircle the person with a thread dyed with safflower and bathe them with ghee and milk;
with that very [thread], one should prepare a cord.
On the forehead, the head, the region of the waist, or indeed on the wrist—O Goddess, this Mṛtyuñjaya [mantra] must not be written for just anyone. (25–310)
In battle, or in the midst of thieves, in legal disputes, or even in the forest;
[against] bhūtas, grahas, piśācas, and the like, or by means of poisons, whether stationary or mobile. (25-311)
It is especially for the protection of the fetus, and in cases of danger from water or fire; likewise during various fevers, or when afflicted by other diseases. (25–312)
This Rakṣas, O Goddess, was personally assumed by Bhairava for all undertakings;
by the mere touch of it, one is never again afflicted by diseases. (25-313)
This lore was maintained by Brahmā and the others for the sake of instilling fear in the Dānavas;
it has also been maintained by me, delighted by the abduction of Ūṣā.
O Goddess, this merit-bestowing, purifying, and binding worship is always present within you;
when knowledge is held, it bestows all happiness even in a forest, a cow-pen, on a road, or in the midst of thieves. (25-315)
Henceforth I shall proclaim that which is celebrated as the Jewel of Knowledge (Vidyāratna).
O Goddess, my beloved, understand from me that supreme Garland of Jewels (Ratnamālā). 25-316.
Having drawn an eight-spoked wheel, and again one with sixteen forms,
the wise man should draw five wheels endowed with thirty-two petals.
One should draw four *akāras* in the center and write one's own name therein; O Dear One, it is joined with the letter *ha*, which creates emanation and ends with the letter *m*. (25–318)
O Dear One, having encircled it with the hand up to the end of the withdrawal [mudrā],
one should then write, O Goddess, "Oṃ juḥ saṃ" enclosed within the eight spokes.
One should assign the sixteen digits (kalās) to the sixteen-spoked [cakra],
and having placed Bahurūpa in the center of the thirty-two-petaled [lotus].
With the goad and the conflict, in the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions,
it is joined with the abode of Varuṇa and enveloped by the three qualities of Māyā.
One should wear this supreme gem encased in three metals;
it is purifying, serves for protection, and brings about good fortune.
O Dear One, [this provides] protection against fire, thieves, piśācas, and the like, as well as against the three kinds of poison;
it especially protects children and likewise protects the fetus.
He is not defiled by the faults or sins committed through malevolent magic; he attains victory in battle and is not harmed by the multitude of weapons. (25.324)
"Whatever desires the practitioner contemplates, he obtains them all by entering the Ratnamālā," thus Bhairava spoke. (25-325)
Having written the name of the Haṃsa, white as the rays of the moon, within a peaceful lotus in the center of the womb, situated at the end of the wind-circle, one should meditate upon it. (25-326)
O beloved, if you have been seized by hosts of passions and have even entered the realm of Death, always perform this ritual for total protection in the assembly using this yantra.
Now, I shall further describe another [yantra], the Kuṇḍalā, born from nectar. || 25-327 ||
