Oṃ amṛtakuṇḍale khaṭlihi lihi tiṣṭha tiṣṭha sulu 2 gajaṃ gajaṃ hana hana sarvavidyāṃ vināśaya sphoṭaya sphoṭaya mahāvīrāntakarāya svāhā.
Having fasted for a day and night on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, one should recite this eight thousand times; it becomes effective.
Having consecrated water seven times, if one drinks it upon rising in the morning, all diseases are destroyed.
By constant application, it makes the body emaciated. One afflicted by disease should drink water continuously for fifty days while performing the ritual service;
he lives for a thousand years, rejuvenated.
During a lunar eclipse, one should drink ghee consecrated eight thousand times with the mantra.
One who is wrinkled, aged, and grey-haired shall become a thousand-year-old.

If one, being self-restrained, eats the fruits of the *amṛtā* plant mixed with ghee and honey for one year, he shall become a thousand-year-old. By reciting [the mantra] twenty-one times, one brings under control whatever one desires.
Having consecrated a floral offering (*nirmālya*) seven times with mantras, whoever it is given to becomes submissive.
By means of water, a woman becomes submissive.
Having consecrated a fresh skull at a cremation ground eight thousand times with mantras, if one buries it at someone’s door, that person withers away; by its removal, there is liberation.
Desiring to eat, one should consecrate the first morsel of food seven times with mantras and consume it; by doing so for a year, one becomes rejuvenated.

Whatever food one may eat, having consecrated it with mantras and consuming it after rising in the morning, one thereby becomes immortal. Furthermore, I shall proclaim another auspicious method for conquering death. || 25-328 ||
By which one goes to the further shore, having gone to which one does not return—such is the movement born of the body toward death or indeed toward the inauspicious. (25.329)
Having known this, the yogi shall conquer death and all that is inauspicious;
by meditating upon Kāleśa, Svacchanda, and Haṃsa, he becomes the lord of all.
Situated within the path of the nostril's opening, he emits and withdraws the world;
abiding therein and dwelling within all beings, he is Time (Kāla) who fashions [all things]. (25-331)
Abiding in that state, one should meditate and recite; Death, the Lord, shall not devour [the practitioner].
For one who is liberated from meditation, omniscience arises within six months. (25–332)
O Maheśvarī, for one who recites or meditates upon the Kālahaṃsa-ātman, the three times become moments and the yogis are joined with time.
For he becomes the very form of Time, acting with autonomy like Time itself;
having cast off death and old age, O Goddess, he is abandoned by all that is inauspicious. (25.334)
Through the conquest of time, there shall always be the attainment of the qualities of all sovereignty: consciousness, hearing from afar, reflection, and vision. (25.335)
Having meditated on [the deity] in the right nostril and drawn it forth, one shall obtain sovereign power;
the virility of that man is always known by those who have passed away.
Is the future known to me? Or shall I become equal in strength to Viṣṇu?
Then all such sovereignty and the lifespan of that yogin shall be his. (25.337)
Through the yoga of constant meditation, one comes to know from the very midst of it all that which has been, that which is, and that which will be, for as long as Rudra’s lifespan endures.
Equal to him in lifespan, strength, vigor, form, and sovereignty—by meditating upon that supreme state which is the perfection of Rudra, one becomes Śiva. (25.339)
Through the state beyond Brahmā, one shall attain the station of sovereignty;
thus, while meditating on the immortal one known as Mṛtyuñjaya, one should recite [the mantra]. (25–340)
Having meditated upon that sixteen-petaled heart-lotus situated within the hollows of the channels,
one should contemplate it as fully blossomed and endowed with the sixteen digits.
One should contemplate oneself in the center of that as being like the full moon or a blossoming *karṇikāra* flower, pure and stainless like clear crystal. (25–342)
Indeed, at the proper time, one should visualize the great ocean of nectar situated above the ocean of milk and nectar,
filled with nectar, and supported from above by the second Śakti.
And that downward-facing lotus is complete with the moon as its pericarp;
in its center, one should contemplate the *haṃsa*, endowed with a lower drop and a crest.
One should contemplate [the deities] raining down streams of nectar from all sides, and one should contemplate them entering through the aperture of one's own body. (25-345)
One should contemplate the nectar, cool, very abundant, moist, and the destroyer of death, filling one's own self as it flows forth from that [source]. (25-346)
One should fill the entire body with nectars through the openings of the channels connected like lotus stalks; one should contemplate in this manner. (25-347)
Thus, one whose self is ever-disciplined becomes equal to the Lord of Immortality;
having abandoned disease, death, and old age, he sports with the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest.
Thus, by means of the meditation on the nectar of immortality, one becomes a conqueror of time and death; or else, established in the supreme reality, one is not bound by any times whatsoever.
Up to this point it has been unclear;
one who is free from the movement of time should contemplate the supreme reality.
179a [g] The Goddess said:
"O Lord, I have understood everything regarding the characteristics of being bound by time. (25.350)
"I have not heard it; I wish to hear it. Tell me, Bhairava, about the *utkrānti* (the departure of the soul). Bhairava said:
"Having bowed with the head, the eyes, and the ears, she [should focus] upon the hair of the mouth. (25–351)
The living soul never departs through the anus or the excrement; it is established beforehand by the union of semen and blood. (25.352)
O Great Goddess, that attainment is indeed a convergence within the space of the heart;
just as fire does not depart from its place, so too does it become extinguished right there. (25-353)
Likewise, when the individual soul is equalized within the space of the heart, it does not depart anywhere; like a bubble situated within water, it subsides and does not depart anywhere. (25-354)
Likewise, at the time of death, the individual soul may depart from the heart at any moment, just as a handful of water cast into a full vessel overflows. (25.355)
The wise know that the individual soul does not depart from there, just as the resonance of a bell and its inherent quality subside within it. (25.356)
At the time of the heart [center], how does the individual soul (jīva) thus extinguish and depart?
When it is at the time of a single location, then indeed it departs. || 25-357 ||
Since the entire space—above, in the middle, and below—is uniform and entirely without gaps, and everything is filled by the *jīva*, how could the all-pervading one depart? (25.358)
Nevertheless, O Leader of the Gods, I shall explain the departure [of the consciousness];
listen now for the sake of attaining the power of mantra and other goals. (25-359)
One should strike the two feet with the syllable *phaṭ*; likewise, the waist with *phaṭ i haḥ*;
the navel with the two syllables *haḥ phaṭ phaṭ*; and the heart, accompanied by *he phaṭ hūṃ*. || 25-360 ||
HŪḤ PHAṬ PHAṬ! Vāgeśī, at the tip of the throat-bell: HRĪḤ PHAṬ PHAṬ! One should strike the bracelet upon the *praṇava*. HŪḤ PHAṬ PHAṬ!
Having performed the deposition (*nyāsa*) upon the bound soul (*paśu*) in this manner according to what was previously stated, one should then depart.
But as for the feathers (*piñchaka*), one should place them according to the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) that has been taught.

Oṃ karṇamoṭe! To those with fierce forms and fangs: *bhaḥ*, *rasaḥ*, *grasaḥ*, *kṛḥ*, *kṛḥ*, *cchṛ*, *cchṛk*. Oṃ hrīḥ hūḥ he haḥ phaṭ phaṭ! With the emanation and reabsorption of Kālarātri, one performs the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
By this, both for oneself and for another, one may ascend [to liberation] without effort.
Thus has been briefly declared the method for the twelve [syllables]; it is considered extensive in its full form. (25–362)

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, the section on the Deception of Time, in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, a great tantra of the Bhairava stream belonging to the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), measuring seventy million verses. 25.
The Goddess said: "O Supreme Lord, the yoga of knowledge and initiation have been explained;
O Protector, tell me now of the final rite (anteṣṭi), so that my delusion may be destroyed. (26.1)

"O Lord of the Gods, for what purpose is this creation performed—this world that has passed away due to deeds done, whether auspicious or inauspicious, yet which possesses great splendor? Is it not a delusion? (26.2)
If initiation were liberation, then according to all the Āgamas as well, one who is initiated would have attained the stainless and indefinable state of liberation. (26.3)
"For whom is this sacrifice being performed? Tell me, O Lord of the World!
There is no burning of what is already burnt, nor can there be sprouting from what is withered. (26.4)
For gold that has entered copper does not return to its former state;
so it is with the practitioner, the master, the lord of gods, and the sons who know the observances.
And their great certainty regarding the banner of views has been declared by me.
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain how delusion is destroyed. (26.6)
Initiation (dīkṣā), O beloved, is said to be of two kinds: with seed (sabījā) and likewise the other;
the latter is seedless (nirbījā), supremely peaceful, leading to liberation (nirvāṇa), and imperishable.
Endowed with the conduct of their observances, joined with meditation and concentration,
they remain steadfast in worship, fire-offerings, and the performance of recitation and vows.
O beloved, there are three kinds—inferior, middling, and superior—and through them, accomplishment (siddhi) is especially attained; of this there is no doubt.
Beginning with the Fire of Time (Kālāgni), the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) is proclaimed;
it may consist of principles (tattva), or be designated as levels (pada), or as portions (kalā), or even as the nature of mantras.

Having purified one of these [tattvas], one should not purify the *vidyātattva*, for the sake of the enjoyment of individual souls (*aṇu*) and for the sake of the accomplishment of practitioners (*mantrin*). (26.11)
In the discourse on mantras, enjoyment (bhukti) is primary for one who worships the gods;
liberation (mukti) is said to be incidental. There is no doubt that both enjoyment and liberation are attained. (26.12)
Indeed, the vision of the lower [reality] is said to belong to one who is joined with the supreme reality;
therefore, O lady of beautiful hips, the principle of Vidyā is thus proclaimed. (26.13)
And for one month, it is proclaimed for the practitioners of mantra in the discourse on mantras:
they are seedless, entirely pure, devoid of pledges and the like, liberated from meditation and concentration, and free from recitation and vows. || 26-14 ||
It is absolute liberation in form, blissful and facing all directions; it is established as the primary state, indicated by its connection to enjoyment. (26.15)
For one who has fallen into the state of duality, non-duality is also shown;
and even within duality, non-duality is said to exist, for human beings are subject to the power of their own desires.
It yields fruit according to the differentiation of minds, bestowing the mental enjoyment of atoms; the inclinations of gods, asuras, and humans are each distinct and separate. (26.17)
Therefore, O Goddess, the trident-bearing Lord has declared many varieties of distinctions;
in the Śaiva great sacrifice, O Goddess, they yield fruit according to one's state of mind.
Therefore, having understood this, one should always remain attached to ritual actions;
for actions indeed yield fruit for men, whereas mere knowledge does not bestow fruit. (26.19)
Just as one who knows about women, food, and enjoyments is not happy without action, so too action should be known to be twofold: it is recorded as being external and internal. (26.20)

Through the yoga of internal meditation, external worship, vows, and so forth, the ritual of initiation (*dīkṣākarma*)—extending from the *avaśyakā* rites to the final *niṣṭhyā*—is explained in great detail. (26.21)
This which has been stated by me in brief should be understood by the wise;
therefore, the final rite (antyeṣṭi) must be performed by the Guru who is a knower of meditation. 26-22.
If independence has been attained for the sake of one's own self-interest, it must also be maintained by the disciple through action prescribed by the scriptures. (26.23)
A "son" (putraka) may be made by anyone among those who observe the rules (samayika);
however, O Pārameśvarī, it is traditionally taught that the role of the officiant at the funeral rites (dākṣa) belongs specifically to the Antyeṣṭikas.
Whether they be initiated ascetics, or carriers, or those who maintain the sacred fires. || 26-25 ||
The four guides who possess auspicious marks lead [the body] as far as the cremation ground;
there, at the outset, one should purify the ground, removing husks, charcoal, and bones. (26–26)
There, one should prepare a bright funeral pyre sloping toward the northeast;
at the front of the arrow, one should arrange it so that it extends toward the south.
O Goddess, having taken recourse to the northern direction, one should fashion the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) at the end of all the feet, to the south of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
One should worship the god Virūpākṣa with flowers and perfumes;
O Goddess, one should satisfy the fire in due order, beginning from the rite of conception (garbhādhāna).
Then, O Goddess, one should generate the Śiva-fire according to the entire prescribed ritual;
thereafter, initiation must be performed through the rite as seen in the scriptures.
O fair-faced one, by means of the yoga of the process of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama), that [reality] is investigated as follows: grasping, joining, and reintegration. (26–31)
One should effect birth, sovereignty, the attainment of enjoyments, as well as dissolution and manifestation, in each respective principle (tattva). || 26–32 ||
Thus, beginning from Kālāgni up to Śiva in due order, one should [purify] the office, that which is to be purified, and the observance (samaya) in its entirety. (26–33)
O Goddess, those [faults] established as verbal, mental, and physical,
as well as all conducts whatsoever that obstruct the attainment of siddhi— || 26-34 ||
The paths to liberation and the obstructions are to be purified in the sacrifice of Śiva;
having performed purification completely, he remains established in the form of the Corpse (Śavamūrti).
O Dear One, having fashioned the five [limbs] with the topknot, one should then bathe [the deity];
then, having performed the smearing with ashes, one should offer the sacred thread.
Having made it pure and filled with clarified butter, one should join it to the eternal state; by means of that emission-practice, one should join it—that which does not flow? || 26-37 ||
O lady of excellent hips, one who is absorbed in that which is without marks, stainless, peaceful, pure, and all-pervading, shall not undergo birth again.
Thereafter, he should set fire to that very [fuel] in the fire, beginning from his feet;
having performed three circumambulations to the right, he should cause a stream of water to be poured.
Then, having gone to the edge of water, one should perform the water-rites such as bathing;
after that, having performed the expiation, one should then recite the *bahurūpa* mantra.
By consuming thirty, five, or even one mouthful of clarified butter, one becomes purified;
O Goddess, all those who carry the corpse and those who provide the fire are likewise purified.
When the eleventh day has arrived, one should feed those who practice austerity;
the teacher should be honored, and one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth.
Then, having honored the ascetics as well as the poor and the helpless,
he acted according to the ways of the world and by deeds prescribed in the scriptures.
In this way, one attains peace and is liberated from the three debts.
The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, O Supreme Lord, O Protector of the World, O Lord of the Universe! (26–44)
O Supreme Lord, where situated is that [self] which must be grasped when the self, having the nature of wind, has entered the path of good and evil? (26.45)
O Bhairava, there can be no grasping of that which is formless;
O Great Lord, how could it even be possible [to grasp] that which is devoid of a support? (26.46)
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain for the sake of dispelling your doubt.
The mantras, O lady of excellent hips, are subtle, all-pervading, and eternally manifest. (26–47)
Their movement is unimpeded, inconceivable, and takes on other forms;
they effect their grasping just as one neutralizes the potency of poison.
In the practice of mantra, however, the destruction of planetary fevers is seen;
for whomsoever it is especially perfected, O lady of good vows, it takes on various forms. (26.49)
Whatever state the practitioner of mantras has attained, he who has assumed the form of Garuḍa swiftly performs that very action. (26.50)

O Goddess of gods, by its mere existence it is indeed true; there is no doubt of this, O lady of auspicious gaze—namely, the path of mantra, the path of words, and the path of the principles (tattvas).
O Goddess, the art of the resonance of the ear is established in six modes;
O fair-faced one, one should perform it by means of any one of these.
One situated on the path should first perform meditation and cause the grasping of that [reality] to occur;
O Mistress of the Gods, O Beloved, there is no abiding for it outside of the sacrificial path.
Therefore, having understood this, O lady of excellent vows, regard the *graha* as equal to your own life-force;
by means of the yoga of its movement, it becomes the support of power (*śaktyādhāra*).
All substances are established in the vital breath (prāṇa) by means of the practitioner;
therefore, at the end of the vital breath, one who has reached the further shore of the supreme reality should be joined [to it].
The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, O Supreme Lord, O Protector of the World, O Master of the Universe!
As for that food offering (naivedya) which was given to Bhairava by the Supreme Lord..."

But regarding that, O Lord, whether the master has dismissed [the officiant] or not dismissed him, what should be done with the sacrificial oblation (caru) given by him immediately thereafter? || 26-57 ||
"O Lord, from where does this *bali* [offering] come? This I wish to know.
Bhairava said:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain that which you have asked. (26.58)
Just as I am, O Goddess of the gods, omniscient and facing in all directions, so indeed is Caṇḍanātha proclaimed among those who hold to duality and non-duality. (26.59)
O Goddess, whatever food offering has been presented to the Supreme Lord regarding dualistic or non-dualistic matters, one should present that very remnant to Caṇḍanātha.
O Goddess of gods, one should not release it;
rather, O Supreme Goddess, one should cast it into fire or, O Goddess of gods, cause it to be given into water.
That which belongs to the deity once he has been dismissed is called *nirmālya*.
One should not give it to water, fire, or light; nor indeed should one destroy it. (62)
O beloved, the substance named Caṇḍeśvara was previously given by me;
by consuming it, the god Caṇḍeśa, the Supreme Lord, will be yours.
The remnant of what has been offered is called *caru*, and it is indeed designated as the food offering (*naivedya*).
With that, the heroes (*vīra*), or their sisters, or women, should be fully satisfied.
Or else, O Goddess of gods, having requested that [the vessel] be enjoyed by the Self, one should consume it;
first, however, one should prepare an offering for the protector of the field and the protector of the spirits.
Otherwise, one should not cause harm while standing before the Goddess;
and especially so before the God, as Bhairava has declared. (26.66)
Furthermore, whatever is prescribed for the purpose of external adornment or as an outer covering, the wise man may consume it or cause it to be given; in that case, no fault is found.
Otherwise, it would be contrary to the proper order and the loss of accomplishment (siddhi) would arise;
when the loss of accomplishment has occurred, there is no liberation, and one goes to hell.
Therefore, with every effort, one should avoid [it] as if it were a fierce beast;
by eating it, one enters the mouth of Mahākāla, the great devourer of raw flesh. (26.69)
There is no doubt in this matter; it is the truth, the truth, there is no uncertainty.
By means of the ritual procedure for attracting those who are attached, one shall obtain all desires. (26.70)

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Section on Funerary Rites," in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, within the *Vidyāpīṭha* of the great mantra-system of the *Bhairava-srotas*, comprising seventy million verses. 26.
Bhairava said:
O Pārvatī, listen to the procedure for the extraction of blood as it truly is.
[The elements are] earth, water, fire, air, and space itself. (27.1)
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth;
intellect, mind, ego, and the five subtle elements. (27.3)
O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, when the thirteenfold instrument has been rendered motionless, consciousness should abide in the heart by means of these. 27-4.
One should meditate upon it at the tip of the power (śakti), conjoined with the seed-syllable of the animal (paśu),
having the appearance of a blazing drop and filled with tens of millions of rays of light.
Having filled [the body] with the upward-moving breath (ūrdhvaprāṇa) so that it is not perceived as superior,
one should enter the external secret door by means of the application of the upward-moving vital energy (udāna).
Then, having attained the station of Brahmā, one should withdraw the five elements and so forth;
O Goddess, one should contemplate the thirteenfold [set] within the instruments of action.
When the mind has become devoid of objects and has reached a state of equanimity,
one should contemplate that which resides at the "end of the twelve" (dvādaśānta), thereby piercing the vital points of the bound soul (paśu).
The yogi should contemplate the flowing stream of blood together with Raktā;
by means of the practice of moving through the *suṣumṇā*, he should draw it upward by way of the *ayāna*.
O lady of excellent hips, one should practice very gradually through various sequential methods for the duration of one month, until the face becomes full.
He will be liberated from old age and disease and shall have a lifespan of an eon;
the mantra will take effect for him and will certainly be accomplished—of this there is no doubt. (27.48)
O Goddess, by this method, one who is devoid of animal-seeds (paśubīja) enters the city when he becomes firm in his aim.
Having first purified the channels, one should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) at the end;
a duration of twenty-six mātrās is known and proclaimed as one "upheaval" (uddhāta).

The middling [practice], O Goddess, is with two hundred and fifty strokes, while the superior is with four hundred; and the one that conquers the vital breath is proclaimed by you, O Goddess, as being with one hundred strokes. (27–51)
One should conquer food for a fortnight; after that, one should conquer sleep.
Having then conquered [the desire for] clothing, one should practice whatever pleases [the mind]. (27.52)
O Goddess of gods, one should then conquer any one of these: the Svastika posture, the Paryaṅka posture, the Daṇḍāsana, or the Padmāsana.
Thereafter, the piercing (vedha) should be performed very gradually with sunflower seeds;
likewise, having performed the piercing on jaggery and neem, the knower of mantras [should proceed]. (27.54)
One should draw out the flavor as much as possible; in this manner, the wise practitioner should perform the practice using camphor, agallochum, sugar-candy, and other such ingredients. (27.55)
O Goddess, she should be depicted with great care, having a similar form and the same number of breasts, adorned with all ornaments, and painted with various colors.
In a solitary, secluded, and delightful place, such as a mountain cave with a waterfall, or in a well-concealed underground chamber, or wherever the mind finds delight. (27.57)
In a place well-perfumed with incense, strewn with heaps of flowers,
and free from wicked beings, the knower of yoga should always practice.
The wise one, established in a single-pointed mind, stands before the images;
remaining on that seat which was previously practiced, he stays there with perfect concentration.
Or, O Goddess, one should have it made circular, four finger-breadths in height;
it is a soft, divine, comfortable seat—the most excellent of all seats.
Abiding here, the Great Hero, with a single mind well-restrained, should fix his gaze upon the tip of the nose, having directed his vision to the very point of the nose. (27.61)
There too, having become the mind and mounted upon power, the person (pudgala) should effect cessation, with the consciousness focused upon the image. (27.62)
And the cessation of the piercing of the Vedas must be performed, O Leader of the Suras;
the practitioner of mantra should again bring it back as far as that heart-mantra once more. (27.63)
One should indeed meditate upon the five elements in succession;
O Goddess, one should meditate there upon the thirteenfold instrument.

O Goddess, one should meditate there upon those qualities such as *sattva* and the rest, which are permeated by that [reality]; for they exist in a subtle form for one whose mind has entered into that state of being. (27.65)
For one who practices in this way, whatever image moves about will trouble him with six faces, and as he proceeds, it turns its back upon him. (27.66)
In this manner, O Goddess of Gods, one attains perfection gradually; there is no doubt in this.
Freed from [worldly] yoga after six months, one should be moderate in diet and firm in one's vows. (27–67)
The yogi may wander at will wherever his mind desires;
he is never afflicted by fire, disease, old age, or deaths.
In an instant, whether long or short, the yogi emerges through the beasts, birds, and reptiles,
by means of firm and flawless houses and pavilions.
Whether bound by palatial buildings, underground chambers, or various other such means,
or even by chains or ropes, one is released from that very instant.
With the divine eye, he beholds all the gods beginning with Brahmā;
indeed, the attainment of qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) arises from non-discursive meditation. || 27-71 ||
The yogi sports constantly wherever he pleases according to his own will; having become one whose movement is unimpeded, O Dear One, he may wander at will.
It dissolves into that subtle, auspicious, and supreme cause;
one attains the perfection of yoga and thus succeeds—of this there is no doubt.
Thus has been told the supreme essence of the scripture together with its secret; by knowing the course of one's own conduct, one shall partake in the fruit of accomplishment.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, on the Attraction of Blood, in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, a great tantra within the Bhairava-current belonging to the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), comprising seventy million verses. 27.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O Goddess, [I shall explain] the course of one's own conduct, the channels (nāḍīs), the determination of the lotuses,
the twenty-five principles, and that which is associated with the Puruṣa.
O Bhairavī, I shall explain how all these [letters] abide exactly as they are:
the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma* are situated in groups of five. (28–2)
Their openings should be known as being situated so as to mutually pervade one another;
the self moves constantly from place to place in regular succession. (28.3)
Those which are known as the nine lotuses—ha, ja, da, the two ṭhas, as well as ta, tha, da, and ma—are proclaimed as the nine lotuses, O Great Goddess. (28.4)
One should offer those which have been declared as *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va* in their respective order: in the northwest, in the southeast, in the northeast, and in the southwest. (28.5)

The two syllables *ha* and *sa*, located in both the bellies; and *śa* and *ṣa*, located in the genitals and the anus—thus, O Goddess of the Gods, the nine lotuses have been proclaimed in their proper order.
One should describe the lotus situated in the middle as having eight spokes;
O auspicious lady, the channels are located there, and the winds have them as their support.
The channels beginning with Iḍā and ending with Śaṅkhinī are situated therein,
from the east to the northeast (Īśa), as well as below and above, O beautiful lady.
The channel (nāḍī) is situated within the interior of the lotus; in the case of pain, it is established in the wind (vāyu).
The winds beginning with prāṇa have been declared and described by me, O sinless one. (28–9)
As for that which is called the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka), situated within the petals,
the Lord himself resides in the pericarp, accompanied by the three mandalas.
Agni, Sūrya, Candra, and likewise Catuḥśakti—
among them, by its own radiance, is Hutāśa in the form of a tiny spark.
O Dear One, it remains within the belly of Kuṇḍalinī by virtue of that [essence];
the immortal Kuṇḍalinī lies asleep, having the form of a slumbering serpent. (28.12)
Bound tightly by these pairs, the breathless one of all the gods remains within the heart, joined with exhalation and inhalation. (28.13)
O beautiful one, as far as the upward movement of that God of gods extends, so far is he remembered as pervasive above; for the Visarga of the Emitter [Śiva] pervades even the lower region. (28.14)
The God of gods, the Lord of the universe, situated in the lower part, should pervade [the body];
the syllable *A* is the heart, and Brahmā is the presiding deity there. (28.15)
O Goddess, the letter *ī* is at the throat; there Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Universe, resides.
The letter *ū* is to be known as being in the palate; there Rudra is established. (28.16)
The dot (bindu) between the eyebrows is Maheśa, and the resonance (nāda) in the mouth is Sadāśiva;
he who abides in authority is to be known thus, as I shall describe to you.
One should practice the inner sacrifice as before, intent on its utterance, according to the tenfold path of yoga, so that the self may attain its own freedom (svacchanda). 28-18.

One should meditate upon that which transcends the measure (mātrā) and the bindu, whose nature is sound (nāda), whose form is light, and which is the conceptualization of the characteristic of the kalpa; by this, one becomes all-pervading.
One should fill [the breath] by means of the right [nostril] and exhale by means of the left;
this is the purification of the channels for the path of the way to liberation.
Exhalation, inhalation, and retention are known as the three types of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
These are common and external; furthermore, there are also internal ones. (28.21)
One should fill [the abdomen] with internal [air], and indeed with internal [air];
having performed the kumbhaka breath without trembling, there are three internal [kumbhakas].
From those two, through the movement within the heart and from the domain of the mind and the senses, the fourth [type of] breath control arises; it is renowned as being perfectly tranquil. (28.23)
When the retention of the breath is complete, one should draw [the air] up to the navel and exhale;
then, one should slowly release the wind through the left nostril.
One should hold the Yāmyā at the thumb, the Āgneyī in the middle of the navel, the Māhendrī in the region of the throat, and the Vāruṇī resting upon the uvula. (28–25)
The concentration on space at the crown of the head is remembered as the bringer of all accomplishments;
it is perfected through one, two, three, four, or five upward thrusts (udghātas). 28–26.
When the breath is restrained, it goes to the crown of the head and returns;
that is declared to be the *udghāta*, which should always be known by yogis. (28–27)
Attachment and aversion are abandoned by means of practiced breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma);
all sins are removed by meditative fixations (dhāraṇās), while withdrawal (pratyāhāra) alone brings about self-mastery.
In the heart, the rectum, the navel, the throat, and likewise in all the joints, these [winds] beginning with prāṇa are situated; now hear from me their forms and sounds. (28–29)
The characteristic form of the five [breaths] is like that of a swift star, like a cochineal insect, like milk, and like crystal. (28–30)
The sweet sound of the bell and the great roar of the elephant—this is declared to be the sound of the five [vital breaths], beginning with prāṇa. (28–31)
Now listen to the external and internal movement of these:
situated in the *prāṇa*, it indeed goes upward; situated in the *apāna*, it goes downward. (28–32)
Then, O Goddess, abiding in equilibrium and pervading everywhere, it produces agitation, fear, and terror while stationed in the wind. (28–33)
By that [breath], O woman of excellent complexion, Udāna is proclaimed;
Vyāna, O leader of the gods, performs the activity of exertion. (28–34)
One should release the *nāgodbhārā* [breath], maintain the state of the opening of the *kūrma* [tortoise], and likewise the *kṛkara* when agitated, and the yawning of *devadatta*. (28–35)
O Dhanañjaya, it remains in the body even after death and does not leave it;
this is called the internal course, just as there are ten external ones. (28–36)
Speech, laughter, song, dance, as well as movement in battle,
trembling, and artistic crafts— all such actions are indeed the activity of the vital breath alone.
If one causes food and drink to enter [the wrong path], it will cause blindness and diseases of the ear; furthermore, the downward wind (apāna) will cause [these afflictions]. (28-38)
The *samāna* [vāyu] brings to equilibrium that which has been eaten and that which has been licked, as well as bile;
it is also responsible for the functions of hunger, hiccup, sneezing, coughing, and the upward-moving breath (*udāna*). (28–39)
Horripilation, perspiration, and the sensation of pain, burning, and itching—these are the functions of vyāna, and it also provides the faculty of touch. (28–40)
Established in the thumb, the knees, the heart, the eyes, and the head are the Nāgas and others, who possess many forms; learn from me their respective functions.
It produces delight and agitation, as well as desiccation and terror;
another [quality] causes excessive sleep, for it is indeed the uniter, O Dhanañjaya. (28.42)
The contraction and cessation of the breath, as well as the sinking of the buttocks and the mouth, are the movements of the five vital winds, beginning with Nāga, at the time of death. (28–43)
Nor indeed does Dhanañjaya depart by means of an upward leap, nor does he abandon [the body];
rather, he draws in his limbs like a tortoise and dries up his physical frame. (28.44)
First, one should conquer the vital breath; when the vital breath is conquered, the mind is conquered. When the mind is conquered, the peaceful-souled one shall manifest the supreme reality. (28.45)
One should meditate on the prāṇa and apāna at the anus; the prāṇa together with the manas is located in the navel; the prāṇa and udāna are in the throat; and the prāṇa and udāna are omnipresent.
One should block the [vital winds] beginning with the nāgas, conjoined with the vital breath, within their own respective locations.
Listen to me as I explain the duration for which they are thus restrained. (28-47)
It should be held starting from the palate up until the end of the fifteenth [digit];
thus the breath is indeed conquered during the practice at the conclusion of a transition (saṃkrānti). 28-48.
Divine luster, auspicious fragrance, and wisdom increase for him;
divine vision and hearing arise, and divine speech proceeds.
Moving through the worlds like the wind, one beholds the Siddhas and the gods;
with the attainment of whatever is conceived by the mind's desire, the eightfold group of qualities proceeds.
With all desires perfectly fulfilled and free from all dualities, he becomes liberated from the bonds of saṃsāra and is equal to Śiva. || 28-51 ||

Having joined the prāṇa and apāna breaths together and endowed them with the short [vowel] limit (the *koṭi*), the lord of yogins should hold them at the navel; then perspiration and trembling arise. (52)
Furthermore, one who is thus situated in the heart should restrain the prāṇa and apāna;
through the union with the long-pointed [breath], he falls to the earth at that very moment. (28.53)
In this very way, one should restrain the vital breath (prāṇa) situated in the throat;
through the union with ten million pluta [vowels], one's own activity becomes "well-sleeping" (suta).
One should effect the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa) by means of the [syllable] joined with the drop (bindu) at the center of the eyebrows;
there, deep sleep arises, and in an instant one likewise awakens. (55)
Having fixed the aperture at the crown of the head, one should begin the meditation on the partless (*niṣkala*).
As he practices in this manner, a sign (*pratyaya*) will then arise for him. (28.56)
From the piercing of the ant's neck, the opening at the crown of the head is split;
having pierced all [the centers] in succession, it reaches as far as that which has arisen. (28.57)
O Goddess, having abandoned the previously described characteristics, one should proceed with spontaneous freedom;
for by this means, the practitioner does not attain equality with that [state] within the body. (58)
He may transfer [consciousness] into the bodies of others, yet he is not afflicted by hunger or thirst; indeed, he perceives whatever occurs in the three worlds, both past and future. (28.59)
That becomes manifest to him, and omniscience arises;
thus, having known the movement of the course [of the winds] within the bodies of all embodied beings. (28.60)
Moving by means of eight petals, one should again proceed to another color; O Goddess of the Gods, they produce a modification among those ending with the letter *ha* in the *ka*-group. (28–61)
Abiding in sattva, abiding in rajas, and abiding in tamas, experiencing the qualities (guṇas),
it thus wanders, O Goddess, going from one place to another place.
The channels resemble lotus fibers; the vital air (anila) moves within them. At the thumb and the fingers, the channels are situated there. (28.63)
The index, middle, and ring fingers are there designated as *nāḍī*;
on the thumb is the designation *kha*, and by the letter *ca* is the little finger. (28-64)
O lady of beautiful hips, three channels of the right hand are indicated:
the letter *ka* is situated in the left thumb, and the middle finger is said to be in the letter *ha*. (28–65)
But in the letter *ña*, O lady of excellent vows, is the youngest [channel] of the left hand;
I shall now explain the channels of the feet in their proper order and according to the truth.

By the letter *ṇa*, the little finger is [designated]; by the letter *na*, the middle finger; and by the letter *pa*, the thumb is to be known—thus the triad of channels (*nāḍī*) is proclaimed. (28.67)
O lady of beautiful hips, O fair-faced one, I shall now describe briefly, according to its full power, how the right foot has become as if it were on the left.
The Suṣumṇā, that supreme channel situated in the secret region and extending as far as the aperture of Brahmā, must be known by the teacher. (28.69)
Mounted there, yet free from conceptualization, one moves both downward and upward.
At the palate, however, there is a sixteen-spoked [wheel] situated with its face turned downward. (28.70)
Having reached that point, he should turn back and run through the nostril;
having then reached the *dvādaśānta*, he should enter the city once again. || 28-71 ||
Likewise, O beloved, an eight-spoked [cakra] should always be known to be in the station of the Bindu;
however, a six-spoked one is situated in the station of Śakti within the subtle path. (28–72)
Having worshipped the supreme circle of deities in the station of Brahmā—namely Viṣṇu, Yoginī, and Dūtī who is situated in the station of Rudra. (28–73)

O Goddess, what is to be done regarding the Lord? O Mother Śivā, one should always place the Mothers in the Śaktis, O Queen of the Gods, beginning with Viśvā and so forth, in their proper sequence. (28.74)
The first is the circle of deities (devatācakra), the second is known as the circle of yoginīs; the third, O Goddess, is the circle of messengers (dūtikā)—what then is the fourth? (28.75)
O Goddess, the Mātṛcakra is remembered as the fifth, so it is proclaimed;
O Goddess, the sixth belongs to Viśveśvarī, as has been told by me to you. (28.76)
O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, one should meditate upon the six wheels within the inner self:
the element of air is in the syllable *ya*, and those whose nature is slaying are in the syllable *a*.
With the letter *la*, there is the creation of paralysis; with the letter *va*, it is of the nature of Varuṇa;
with the letter *ha*, there is the creation of vital breath, conjoined with the letter *sa*.
For the sake of the nectar, the best of practitioners should perform that which has been prescribed;
those beginning with the letter *ka* and ending with the letter *ma* are declared to be twenty-five. (28–79)

By means of these, there is the piercing of creation; having understood this according to the divisions of desire, the creation of mantra is taught, and likewise the creation of the principles (tattva).
The creation of the individual soul has been fully described, as well as the subsequent creation of the castes;
likewise, O Goddess, the creation of the elements and the creation of yoga.
O Supreme Goddess, by meditating upon whatever form one may pierce [the target],
the practitioner's consciousness becomes identical with that very nature.
Everything that has the nature of emanation must be understood by the practitioner;
O Goddess of Gods, I shall now describe the five doors in brief. (28.83)
The hands, the feet, and likewise the secret place—these are proclaimed as the five piercings (*vedha*).
Having attained the perfection of the pin (*kīlikī-siddhi*), the perfection of yoga (*yoga-siddhi*) proceeds. (28.84)
Having thus understood the movement of the breath, one should perform the piercing of the emanation (sṛṣṭivedha).
O Supreme Goddess, wherever the piercing is indeed applied within the wheel—
O Goddess of the gods, he perceives that wheel directly;
then the consciousness of the practitioner becomes identical with it. (28.86)
Or else, O Supreme Goddess, the piercing of emanation (sṛṣṭivedha) is performed;
for he who desires to perform the piercing while being devoid of this path [is unsuccessful].
One strikes the sky with one's fist and drinks the mirage;
there is no piercing of the nose, the ears, or the eyes. (28.88)
Those [lines] situated at the fire [corner] are said to be side-doors;
therefore, they are fruitless for piercing, causing enmity, expulsion, or killing. (89)

Thus, having extracted the essence from this Tantra consisting of twelve thousand [verses], which includes its secret teachings, I have composed this work for easy understanding and without confusion. (28.90)

This [teaching], which is full of elaboration and crowded with various forms of consciousness, has been told [to him] by whom I have indeed been propitiated with devotion throughout thousands of births. (185a) (28.91)
One attains this there, while another, upon seeing it, becomes bewildered;
this is the superior thing therein, O Goddess, which has not been told by me to anyone.
O Goddess, this secret has been fully declared and revealed to you;
it is worthy of being saluted by hosts of sages and gods, and is worshipped by the Yoginīs. (28.93)
There is nothing superior to this tantra, which is presided over by the power of Rudra;
for those born into the family of the Yoginīs, whose minds are absorbed in that state, [this is the supreme goal]. (28.94)
O Goddess of great renown, those who know this scripture—which contains hidden meanings and is an ocean of knowledge—know that where this Tantra remains written down, [there it abides]. (28.95)
They too, O fair-faced one, shall attain liberation through alms-food;
for the yoginīs indeed protect them and cherish them like their own sons.
For him, no misfortune occurs, nor is there any lack of auspiciousness anywhere, O beloved, who worships this scripture which is like nectar and full of essence. (28.97)
For he has heard this well-proclaimed teaching and has maintained the observance of the pledge;
yet by his own intellect, he regards as evil-minded those who conceptualize the various paths of the sacred seats. (28.98)
There is no returning for them; they have gone to the vicinity of Raurava.
Therefore, this Kaulika [tradition] of the accomplishment of the meaning of mantra has been handed down through successive lineage. (28.99)
One should listen in the presence of the guru until it becomes pure;
it must be guarded with effort and should not be disclosed to one who is unprepared. (28.100)
But he who, out of negligence, causes it to be heard without understanding the proper sequence, goes to a terrible hell—he who is a wicked-souled traitor to his guru. (28.101)
I am not his protector when he is sinking in the ocean of existence;
standing in the midst of the host of Yoginīs, the practitioner here is nothing but a beast. (28.102)
O fair-faced goddess, whatever destination one who harms his companions, harms his guru, or harms the gods goes to, that same destination he shall go to. (28.103)
Therefore, one who desires one's own welfare should not act openly;
rather, having conducted an examination with great effort through many different methods, [one should proceed]. (28.104)
What is that consecration? It is the Lord of the Ten Beneficent Ones at the crest of the Rakṣas.
[The number of verses from 105b to 132b is missing; 131b does not exist.
But in the primordial reality, the Rudras are proclaimed to be of great heroism. (28.105)
That which is the ultimate limit of the qualities (guṇas) is here called Pradhāna.
Beyond that, however, understand from me the worlds within the principle of Puruṣa: Ambhas, Salilā, Nuprātā, Dhṛti, Tuṣṭi, as well as Supārā, Sunetrā, and Sumārī; beyond these— 28.106–107.
Uttamā and Bhasikā are proclaimed as the nine forms of Tuṣṭi; likewise Tārā, Sutārā, Tārayantī, and Pramodikā. (28.108)
Pramuditā, Modamātṛkā, and likewise Recakī as the next; Tatvadā and Pramuditā—these are declared to be the eight Siddhis.
Aṇimā, laghimā, mahimā, and prāpti are proclaimed;
likewise prākāmya, īṣitva, and that which is called vasitva. (28.110)
Where mastery over desire is attained, the eightfold powers beginning with *aṇimā* are said to exist.
Above this, listen now to the three rows of gurus and disciples. (28.111)
Yaskari, Pūraṇa, Kṛtsna, Kapila, and likewise Kāśa; Sanatkumāra, Gautama, Vasiṣṭha, and Śaṃśaka. || 28-112 ||
Kāśyapa, Nāciketa, Gālava, and Maulika;
likewise Śākalya is mentioned, as well as Durvāsas, the supreme ṛṣi. (28-113)
And Vālmīki, O best of the Kurus, Parāśara with Gālava, Pippalāda, Saṃvarta, Vāyupuṣṭa, and Atidantika. || 28-114 ||
Māṣkarṣi and the others, ending with Madana, were proponents of both the seen and the unseen;
so too were Juhnu, Tṛṇabindu, the sage Carikṣa, and [the rest]. || 28.115 ||
Vanātha, Yotha, Dīrgha, Hona, Jāgara, Agasti, Vasu, and Nātha are proclaimed as the Upādhyāyas. (28.116)
Śukra, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Roma, Jamadagni-suta Urdhvabāhu, Sthūlaśiras, Vālakhilya, and Manuja are thus proclaimed. || 28-117 ||
Vadhvātreyo, Viśuddha, Śiva, Sucāru, Antaka, and those beginning with Jahnu and ending with Cāru are said to be the second row. (28.118)
Harajaṇṭī, Pradāru, Amareśa, as well as Manaḥ, Kṛṣṇa, Rudra, Indrajit, Dṛśabha, and Śiva. (28.119)
Yama, Krūra, and the renowned Gaṅgādhara; Umāpati, Bhūteśvara, Kapālī, and likewise Śaṅkara. (28–120)
And they know him as Arddhanārīśvara, as well as Piṅgala;
likewise Mahākāla, Saṃvarta, Maṇḍalī, and Ekavīraka. (28.121)
Likewise, there is another famous and excellent lord, Bhārabhūteśvara;
and there are twenty-five sages beginning with Jahnu and ending with Cārurūpa. (28–122)
The twenty gurus, beginning with Hara and ending with Dhruva, are recorded as belonging to the three lineages of the sages, comprising both teachers and disciples. (28.123)
O Goddess, I shall now briefly describe the eightfold ignorance of the channels:
Iḍā, Indriṇī, Gaurī, Śānti, and likewise Śāntikarī. (28.124)
Mālā, Maulinī, Svāhā, and likewise Svadhā—these should be known with effort; therefore, O lady of excellent vows, I shall speak of them.
O lady of beautiful hips, I shall explain the eightfold division in brief, but not in detail:
the effect and the instrument, as well as pleasure, pain, and that which is beyond them. (28.126)
Knowledge and faith should be understood as the means and the cause;
having attained this body, O beloved, I shall describe the tenfold Dharma. (28.127)
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, lack of anger, service to the guru, purity, contentment, and straightforwardness. (28.128)
This tenfold dharma has been described as that which cuts through [false] dharma;
now I shall explain to you how the sixteen transformations are to be purified.
Smell, taste, form, touch, and likewise sound—these are known as the five subtle elements (tanmātras); understand from me that they are not the sense organs.
Speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ are designated as the organs of action;
the ear, skin, eyes, tongue, and the nose is considered the fifth [organ of perception]. (28.131)
Having given these [objects] to the sense organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*), one should then cause them to be heard or caused to be given;
otherwise, a fault arises—such is the certainty of the scripture. (28.132)
O Goddess, this supreme scripture must not be given to just anyone.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Section on Self-Conduct," in the *Śrītantrasadbhāva*, a great tantra within the Bhairava-stream belonging to the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*), measuring seventy million verses. 28.28.
The *Śrītantrasadbhāva* manuscript is completed; may it be auspicious!
Two hundred years having passed, plus seventeen more, on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, the most excellent [day].

On the day of the *tārakā* constellation under the asterism of Pūrvaphalgunī, beautifully graced by the planet Venus (*śukragraha*), during the reign of the illustrious King Harṣadeva in the victorious kingdom of glorious Nepāla— a time of excellent form, worthy of honor and respect for one seeking the supreme boon that is the cause of spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*).
The author is marked with the name Śrī Paśupatisthāna-Śaivavardhana. This great and wondrous Tantra, endowed with this conjunction,
is a supreme essence, rich in virtues, a great Tantra not widely disseminated.
This secret, which must be concealed, has emerged from the right face;
it is this most hidden tantra, the supreme *Śrī-mān-tantra-sadbhāva*,
the excellent subject matter of the *Cūḍāmaṇi* known by the name *Phaṇāṅka*.
The Lord of that [tantra], which is adorned with a multitude of glorious qualities,
is a tantra embellished by many virtues;
it is the cause for turning back those who are fearful of rebirth.

Adorned with the qualities of the Master’s very form, obtained under the name Śrī Jayākara, he is the cause for the deliverance of all beings of his own lineage; those who read, hear, or touch him attain everything. 186a [g] All.
All that is auspicious, as well as wealth, grain, and happiness, has been obtained; many [others] have also attained it. [The rest of the passage describes further blessings and attainments.]
As long as one has not reached the further shore,
what is the purpose of the meaning of existence once the further shore has been crossed?
